episodes.title: AMBOSS Resident Training
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This talk introduces AMBOSS Knowledge Plus, a clinical decision support tool for family medicine residents. The platform combines a digital medical library with NEJM question banks, pocket guides, flow charts, and calculators. The presenter demonstrates how to use the tool to quickly find diagnostic criteria, labs, imaging, and treatment recommendations, using acute pancreatitis as an example. The goal is to help residents find answers within 90 seconds to improve patient care.
key_points: AMBOSS Knowledge Plus is a digital medical library covering family medicine, internal medicine, pediatrics, and emergency medicine.
The library is updated within a week of new guidelines, society recommendations, or impactful studies.
The platform is designed to provide answers to clinical questions within 90 seconds.
Pocket guides collapse key information for commonly encountered conditions, including red flags, diagnostic approach, and initial management.
Flow charts are independently searchable and provide step-by-step management algorithms.
Over 2,000 radiographs with overlay features are available for image interpretation.
Treatment sections provide a linear roadmap with critical thinking steps and granular details like fluid choice and rate.
Integrated calculators (e.g., Ranson, APACHE) and drug monographs are available.
The platform is accessible on phone, tablet, or laptop, with most features available offline.
Questions from NEJM Knowledge Plus are linked to library articles for integrated learning.
Amboss provides critical thinking steps in heavy font that guide clinical decision-making for each disease.
The treatment outline tab offers a linear roadmap: stabilize, start goal-directed IV fluids, supportive therapy, and decide on consultation.

episodes.title: Antenatal Testing - Dr. Bea Abraham
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bea Abraham
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the purpose, methods, indications, and management of antenatal testing to reduce stillbirth and long-term neurologic deficits. Dr. Bea Abraham reviews the physiology of fetal hypoxia, describes testing modalities including kick counts, contraction stress tests, nonstress tests, amniotic fluid volume assessment, biophysical profiles, and umbilical artery Doppler. She discusses ACOG guidelines for starting testing in conditions like diabetes, hypertension, IUGR, and post-term pregnancy, and outlines how to manage abnormal results.
key_points: Antenatal testing aims to identify fetuses at risk for injury or death to reduce stillbirths and long-term neurologic deficits.
Fetal hypoxia leads to blood redistribution to brain, heart, and adrenals, decreasing renal perfusion and amniotic fluid.
Kick counts have not been shown to improve perinatal outcomes; there is no magic number, but maternal perception of decreased movement warrants evaluation.
Contraction stress test (CST) has a 0.04% antepartum stillbirth rate within one week of a negative result; it is rarely used due to contraindications.
Nonstress test (NST) has a 0.3% false negative rate and 55% false positive rate; reactive requires ≥2 accelerations in 20 minutes, extended to 40 minutes if nonreactive.
Amniotic fluid volume is assessed by maximum vertical pocket (MVP, normal 2-8 cm) or amniotic fluid index (AFI, normal 5-20 cm); ACOG defines oligohydramnios as MVP <2 cm.
Biophysical profile (BPP) includes fetal breathing, movement, tone, amniotic fluid, and NST; modified BPP is NST plus MVP.
Umbilical artery Doppler is used by MFM for IUGR; absent or reversed end-diastolic flow indicates placental insufficiency.
ACOG recommends starting antenatal testing at 32 weeks for diabetes on medication and chronic hypertension; for gestational hypertension, start at diagnosis.
For post-term pregnancy, testing starts at 40 weeks; practice is to induce at 41 weeks.
Abnormal tests should be repeated due to false positives/negatives; for abnormal NST/modified BPP, get full BPP; if BPP ≤4/10, proceed to delivery.
Oligohydramnios: assess for PPROM, consider delivery at 36-37 weeks; if <36 weeks, expectant management.

episodes.title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls
episodes.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
episodes.abstract: Dr. Brad Beasley, a podiatrist (DPM), delivers an interactive lecture on diabetic foot care for family medicine residents. He explains the role of podiatry, emphasizing the high morbidity of diabetic foot ulcers and the critical importance of neuropathy as a contributor. Key clinical pearls include recognizing Charcot arthropathy in a painless, swollen, red foot, strict non-weight-bearing management, and the fact that over 90% of adults wear the wrong shoe size. He stresses collaboration between primary care and podiatry to prevent amputations and improve patient outcomes.
key_points: Diabetic foot ulcers have morbidity and mortality comparable to some cancers but receive less attention.
Neuropathy is the primary contributor to diabetic foot wounds, as it masks pain and allows microtrauma to progress.
Charcot arthropathy presents as a swollen, red, painless foot with bone fragmentation on X-ray; it is often missed.
In Charcot, strict non-weight-bearing for at least 3 months (sometimes 6) is essential to prevent foot collapse.
Diabetics may not mount an elevated white count or left shift with infection, so clinical exam is key.
Over 90% of adults wear the wrong shoe size; poor shoe fit is a modifiable risk factor for foot ulcers.
If a wound probes to bone, consider osteomyelitis; MRI can help differentiate Charcot from infection.
D-dimer is not helpful for ruling out DVT in Charcot because inflammation elevates it.
Podiatrists can obtain board certification in wound care; collaboration with primary care is vital for limb salvage.
The business of medicine (insurance, prior authorizations) is often harder than the medicine itself.
Over 90% of adults wear the wrong size shoe; check for adequate toe room (half an inch).
Have diabetic patients remove shoes and socks at every visit to inspect feet.

episodes.title: Behavioral Med
episodes.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Satterlee explains how to navigate mental health referrals in a family medicine setting, emphasizing that finding a therapist is more like finding a dentist than a specialist referral. She describes the St. John referral system, noting that referrals go to a social worker who manages a list of providers, and that most St. John mental health appointments are limited to 30 minutes for 6-8 sessions. She advises starting with the patient's insurance list to find in-network providers, and offers practical tips like walking the referral back to the counseling office to expedite scheduling.
key_points: Mental health referrals map more like finding a dentist than a specialist referral; it is not a simple 'send to urologist' process.
The IHI SharePoint site has a list of referral options organized by license, with columns showing areas treated.
Yellow-highlighted entries on the list indicate providers whose status is unconfirmed and may have moved or changed practice.
For patients with insurance, the best first step is to start with their insurance list and cross-reference with other sources.
SoonerCare (Medicaid) offers excellent mental health benefits for children and those under 21, but finding adult providers who accept it is difficult.
St. John mental health providers are typically mid-level (LCSW or LPC) and work in a model of 30-minute appointments for 6-8 sessions, with some flexibility for longer or extended sessions.
Referral notes placed in the St. John system are not passed along to the counseling office; they only receive a list of names and ID numbers.
Walking a printed referral (demographic sheet and referral sheet) back to the counseling office can expedite scheduling by 2-3 weeks compared to the standard email list.
The IHI counseling office does not accept SoonerCare for patients over 21, which is a significant barrier for adult referrals.
The presenter works 40% time as the only psychologist employed by St. John in Tulsa.
To expedite a behavioral health referral, walk the demographic sheet, face sheet, and completed referral sheet to the behavioral health team; they will put it at the top of the pile.
The behavioral health service does not accept adult SoonerCare (patients over 21) and does not have translation services.

episodes.title: Cardiovascular Risk& Reduction
episodes.speaker: Dr. Herrmann
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers cardiovascular risk reduction in primary care, focusing on screening, lifestyle interventions, and pharmacotherapy. The presenter reviews the top causes of death in the US, the five modifiable risk factors for heart attacks, and guidelines for lipid panel screening. A case-based discussion illustrates ASCVD risk calculation, statin initiation and monitoring, and considerations for familial hypercholesterolemia. The talk emphasizes actionable steps like smoking cessation, diet, exercise, and appropriate use of statins, including expected LDL reductions and side effect management.
key_points: Heart disease is the number one cause of death in the US, and stroke is number five.
Half of all heart attacks are caused by five modifiable factors: smoking, cholesterol, obesity, hypertension, and diabetes.
USPSTF recommends lipid screening starting at age 11 for familial hypercholesterolemia, then every five years from age 40 to 75.
Non-fasting lipid panels are acceptable unless triglycerides exceed 400, which requires a fasting sample.
An LDL over 190 mg/dL should prompt evaluation for familial hypercholesterolemia using Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria.
ASCVD risk score guides statin therapy: <10% risk → lifestyle; 10-20% → moderate-dose statin; >20% → high-dose statin.
Statins reduce LDL by 30-35% at low doses (e.g., atorvastatin 10 mg) and up to 45% at higher doses.
Recheck lipids 6-12 weeks after starting a statin, then annually; routine monitoring of LFTs and CK is not indicated.
Common statin side effects include myalgias (7-20%), elevated ALT, and a small increase in diabetes risk.
Short-acting statins (e.g., simvastatin) should be taken at night; long-acting atorvastatin can be taken any time.

episodes.title: Care for the un-homed with Dr. Carroll
episodes.speaker: Dr. Carroll
episodes.abstract: Dr. Carroll discusses the diverse subpopulations within the homeless community, emphasizing that most are temporarily displaced due to bad luck and are easy to help, while others struggle with addiction, severe mental illness, personality disorders, or low health literacy. He stresses that traditional 'ivory tower' medicine often fails in this setting and that clinicians must meet patients where they are, building trust over time. Medicaid alone does not solve access issues because many patients cannot navigate the system, keep appointments, or manage medications without intensive hand-holding.
key_points: Homelessness includes a spectrum: transiently homeless (couch surfing), chronically mentally ill, substance users, personality-disordered individuals, and those with low IQ/health literacy.
Transiently homeless patients are often intelligent and motivated; they need short-term help with medications, transportation, and care coordination to get back on their feet.
Patients with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder may refuse most treatment but can still engage if you offer multiple options and respect their autonomy.
Substance users frequently miss appointments due to intoxication and may be fired from clinics for no-shows.
Patients with personality disorders want to control their own care; building trust may allow you to negotiate a middle ground.
Low-IQ or low-literacy patients need maximal hand-holding at every step, making appointments, getting to the lab, filling prescriptions, even if they have Medicaid.
Medicaid has not solved access problems for the homeless because many cannot use phones reliably, navigate the system, or understand billing.
In homeless care, 'ivory tower medicine' rarely works; you must meet patients where they are and accept incremental progress.
Building trust over repeated visits is key; even a paranoid schizophrenic who refuses most suggestions may eventually accept one.
Clinicians should respect patient autonomy unless the patient is being dangerously non-adherent, and even then should allow a wide margin before terminating care.
Patients in transitional housing often have the same access to resources as those who are unhoused.
Tulsa Housing Authority and Mental Health Association can help house disabled patients, but substance abuse as the sole disability or a sexual offense history can be barriers.

episodes.title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney
episodes.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
episodes.abstract: Dr. Matt Haney presents a practical approach to COPD pharmacotherapy, emphasizing the distinction between chronic symptoms and acute exacerbations to guide treatment escalation. He recommends starting with a LAMA and advancing to LABA/LAMA or triple therapy based on symptom control and exacerbation history, with inhaled corticosteroids reserved for exacerbation-predominant disease. The talk also covers inhaler device education, including dry powder versus soft mist inhalers, and mentions adjunctive therapies like roflumilast and azithromycin for severe cases.
key_points: Short-acting bronchodilators are acceptable for patients with controlled symptoms and no exacerbations; they provide symptomatic relief but do not reduce exacerbations or improve FEV1.
For uncontrolled symptoms without exacerbations, start a LAMA (long-acting muscarinic antagonist) as first-line therapy.
For controlled symptoms with exacerbations, use a LAMA; if already on a LAMA, proceed to LABA/LAMA combination.
For uncontrolled symptoms with frequent exacerbations, consider LABA/LAMA or LABA/LAMA/ICS (triple therapy).
Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are indicated primarily for exacerbation reduction, not for symptom control alone; they may be harmful if used without exacerbation indication.
Elevated blood eosinophils suggest a reactive phenotype and favor adding ICS, especially in patients with exacerbations.
Avoid LAMA/ICS combination; there are no available combination products, and it is not recommended.
If a patient on triple therapy (e.g., Trelegy) continues to have exacerbations, consider roflumilast (Daliresp) for those with FEV1 <50% and chronic bronchitis, or azithromycin in non-smokers.
Inhaler device technique is critical; many patients misuse dry powder inhalers, which require forceful, rapid inhalation.
For patients unable to generate sufficient inspiratory flow with dry powder inhalers, consider switching to a soft mist inhaler like Respimat.
Leukotriene inhibitors have no role in pure COPD but may be considered in asthma-COPD overlap.
Exacerbations are defined as acute worsening requiring systemic steroids, not just chronic dyspnea; two or more exacerbations or one hospitalization are significant.

episodes.title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD
episodes.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller
episodes.abstract: Dr. Gerald Miller presents a COVID-19 update covering the SARS-CoV-2 virus structure, immune response, and vaccine mechanisms. He explains the roles of spike protein subunits (S1 and S2), antibody-mediated neutralization versus T-cell-mediated clearance, and how mRNA and adenovirus-vectored vaccines generate both humoral and cellular immunity. The talk addresses infectious periods, variants of concern, breakthrough infections, and the importance of memory B and T cells for rapid recall responses.
key_points: The spike protein S1 subunit contains the receptor-binding domain (RBD) that attaches to ACE2 receptors; S2 mediates membrane fusion and viral entry.
Antibodies block infection by neutralizing the virus and promoting opsonization/phagocytosis; T cells (especially cytotoxic CD8+ cells) terminate infection by destroying infected cells.
Infectiousness begins 2, 3 weeks before symptom onset and lasts 8, 10 days (based on viral culture data).
Variants of concern (Alpha, Beta, Delta) show increased transmissibility, virulence, or immune escape; no variant of high consequences has emerged yet.
mRNA vaccines (Pfizer, Moderna) use lipid nanoparticles to deliver mRNA encoding the spike protein; J&J uses a non-replicating adenovirus vector with DNA that produces mRNA for the spike protein.

Antigen produced inside the cell (as with mRNA and adenovirus vaccines) triggers both antibody-mediated and cell-mediated (T cell) immunity; injected spike protein alone (like Novavax) primarily generates antibody responses.
Memory B and T cells are stored in lymphatic tissues and provide a rapid protective response within 3, 4 days upon re-exposure, compared to 9, 14 days for primary immunization.
Breakthrough infections occur as antibody levels wane, but memory cells often limit symptoms to mild or short-lived illness.
The immune response to both infection and vaccination includes generation of memory cells (T helper, CD8, B cells) that persist in lymphatic tissues.
Vaccine-induced antibodies remain reactive to spike protein variants; no mutation has yet rendered the spike unrecognizable to vaccine-generated antibodies.
Vaccination mimics infection to educate the immune system through both antibody-mediated immunity and cell-mediated immunity.
IgG is used to determine whether a patient has had infection, for management purposes, not diagnosis.

episodes.title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Cyr
episodes.abstract: Dr. Cyr presents a practical, evidence-based approach to diagnosing and managing migraine headaches. She reviews the International Headache Society diagnostic criteria using the POUND mnemonic (pulsatile, one-day duration, unilateral, nausea/vomiting, disabling intensity) and emphasizes the importance of asking about triggers, relief measures, and red flags (SNOOP mnemonic). She introduces the Migraine Buddy app as a tool for headache diaries and medication tracking, and shares her personal experience with the injectable preventive Ajovy (fremanezumab). Key takeaways include distinguishing migraine from other headaches, avoiding medication overuse (rebound headaches), and knowing at least one rescue and one preventive option.
key_points: Migraine is a recurring headache lasting 4-72 hours, typically unilateral, pulsatile, moderate-severe, aggravated by routine activity, with nausea/vomiting or photophobia/phonophobia.
The POUND mnemonic (Pulsatile, One-day duration, Unilateral, Nausea/vomiting, Disabling intensity) helps identify migraine with high probability.

Ask patients about triggers: stress, sleep changes, caffeine (too little or too much), skipped meals, weather, neck pain, alcohol, bright sun, dehydration, processed foods, aged cheese, chocolate, menstruation.
Red flags for secondary headache should be assessed using the SNOOP mnemonic (Systemic symptoms, Neurologic symptoms, Onset after age 50, Pattern change, Other associated features).
Headache diaries are essential for identifying triggers and tracking medication use; the Migraine Buddy app can automate this process.
Medication overuse (e.g., >10 triptan days per month) can cause rebound headaches and worsen migraine frequency.
Rescue medications include triptans (e.g., sumatriptan) and NSAIDs (e.g., naproxen); timing of rescue medication is critical for efficacy.
Preventive therapy (e.g., Ajovy/fremanezumab, a monthly injectable CGRP antagonist) can significantly reduce migraine frequency and severity.
Non-pharmacologic relief methods include dark room rest, ice/heat packs, hydration, caffeine, and avoiding triggers.
Patients with migraine may have allodynia (sensitivity to touch, clothing, glasses) and prodromal symptoms like yawning or mood changes.
Migraine can be bilateral, though it is typically unilateral; ask about associated symptoms like nasal congestion, tinnitus, diarrhea, and confusion.
In children, asking if they can eat their favorite food or run around helps distinguish migraine from tension headache or appendicitis.

episodes.title: Dianne Hughes on WIR
episodes.speaker: Dianne Hughes
episodes.abstract: Dianne Hughes and her team from the Women's Justice Programs present an overview of their services for women involved in or at risk of involvement with the legal system. They describe three programs: the Women's Justice Team (outpatient services for those in specialty courts or at risk), Women in Recovery (WIR, a structured residential day-treatment program for women facing prison), and Women in Recovery Continuing Care (aftercare). The team highlights the holistic, trauma-informed approach, the challenges of caring for women in early recovery who have heightened somatic symptoms and developmental delays due to long-term substance use and trauma, and the importance of collaboration with medical providers.
key_points: The Women's Justice Programs include three tiers: Women's Justice Team (outpatient), Women in Recovery (residential day treatment), and Women in Recovery Continuing Care (aftercare).
Women in Recovery is a highly structured, three-phase program lasting about 18 months (sometimes 24 months for those with medical issues), with daily programming from 8:30 AM to at least 3:30 PM.
The program is abstinence-based; most women complete a 30-day inpatient detox before entering, though some may be on suboxone if started in jail.
The average age of women in the program is 34, with an average length of addiction of about 16 years.
Early-phase clients often present with heightened pain sensation and somatic symptoms (headaches, stomach issues) due to psychological withdrawal and lack of coping skills.
Many women have developmental delays from trauma and substance use, functioning at about a 10-year-old level, and need to be taught basic life skills like making a bed or managing a headache.
The program provides holistic services including therapy, case management, employment support, parenting skills, culinary/nutrition education, and court advocacy.

Referrals to the Women's Justice Team are open for women with mental health or substance use issues who are at risk of or involved in the legal system; most clients use Medicaid or private insurance (Aetna, Humana, Blue Shield).
The team uses a daily one-hour triage to assess medical complaints, distinguishing between genuine issues and behavioral concerns (e.g., wanting to go home or avoid programming).
Women in Recovery includes a professional chef who teaches nutrition and cooking on a tight budget, and the program helps mothers reunify with their children.

Early-phase clients often present with somatic symptoms (headache, stomach pain) that are manifestations of anxiety, emotional discomfort, or psychological withdrawal rather than acute medical illness.
Many women in recovery have only experienced episodic care and lack a preventive mindset; they need explicit, repeated instructions about completing antibiotics and using protection.

episodes.title: Discernment & Perspective
episodes.speaker: Dr. Simpson
episodes.abstract: This first part of a lecture on discernment and perspective for family-medicine residents focuses on the Christian physician's identity and worldview. Dr. Simpson emphasizes that residency training should foster both personal and professional growth, and introduces the concept of divine appointments, recognizing that God is present in every patient encounter. He challenges the assumption that alleviation of suffering is the ultimate goal, arguing instead for healing that includes spiritual and emotional dimensions. Drawing on biblical narratives and the Velveteen Rabbit, he sets up a discussion on reality and whole-person care, asserting that the Christian worldview sees humans as inseparable biopsychosocial spiritual beings and that ancient biblical thought did not separate the physical from the spiritual.
key_points: Residency training should aim at both personal and professional growth, not just clinical skills.
Every patient encounter is a divine appointment with at least three present: the physician, the patient, and the triune God.
Alleviation of suffering is not the sole purpose; healing includes spiritual and emotional dimensions beyond the physical.
The Christian frame of reference acknowledges biology as part of reality but not the only reality.
Biblical thinking sees no separation between supernatural and natural, or between physical and spiritual.
Patients are to be viewed as children of God, not just biological cases.
Humans are whole, inseparable biopsychosocial spiritual beings.
The ancient world did not distinguish sharply between physical, spiritual, and emotional illness; this integrated view is reflected in Scripture.
Modern dualism (e.g., Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am') artificially splits reality into separate realms, which does not match lived experience.
Science captures an important slice of reality but cannot address spiritual, relational, or existential dimensions.
Biblical shalom means completeness, wholeness, peace, and harmony with self, God, and the created world.
Peacemakers in the Beatitudes are those so embodied with shalom that they share it by their very presence.

episodes.title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes
episodes.speaker: Dr. Christopher Abdo
episodes.abstract: Dr. Christopher Abdo presents an approach to acute vestibular syndrome, defined as sudden continuous vertigo lasting 24 hours with nausea, head motion intolerance, and unstable balance. He emphasizes that only 10% of dizziness complaints qualify, with vestibular neuritis and posterior circulation stroke as the main causes. The talk covers nystagmus patterns (physiologic end-gaze, pathologic primary gaze, direction-changing central nystagmus), key history elements (timing, triggers, medications), and a simple diagnostic algorithm. A case of phenytoin toxicity illustrates the danger of zero-order kinetics and the importance of checking AED levels before imaging.
key_points: Acute vestibular syndrome requires sudden onset continuous vertigo lasting 24 hours with nausea, head motion intolerance, and unstable balance.
Only 10% of patients with chief complaint of dizziness meet criteria for acute vestibular syndrome.
Vestibular neuritis and posterior circulation stroke account for 95% of acute vestibular syndrome cases.
Nystagmus is named for the direction of the fast phase; physiologic end-gaze nystagmus (2-3 beats) is normal and resolves with refocusing.
Primary gaze nystagmus (present when looking straight ahead) indicates vestibular system pathology.
Direction-changing nystagmus is a central finding but can also be caused by intoxication, medications (especially AEDs), or seizures.
Patient symptom descriptions have almost no correlation with final diagnosis; timing and triggers are more reliable.
Episodic vertigo differential includes BPPV, Meniere's disease, and vestibular migraine; constant vertigo suggests stroke or vestibular neuritis.
Phenytoin follows zero-order kinetics; doubling the dose can cause levels to jump from 6 to 30, so increases must be small and gradual.

Medication history is critical: ototoxic drugs (gentamicin) cause bilateral imbalance without nystagmus; sodium channel blockers (phenytoin, carbamazepine, lacosamide) can cause vestibular side effects.
A positive Dix-Hallpike test requires a slight delay followed by upward torsional nystagmus that abates after 15-30 seconds; reproducing dizziness alone is not a positive test.
Failure to extend the patient's head back at least 20 degrees during the Dix-Hallpike test can lead to a false negative result.

episodes.title: Dr. Acker on Shoulder Disorders & Examination
episodes.speaker: Dr. Acker
episodes.abstract: Dr. Acker presents a lecture on shoulder disorders, covering acute and chronic conditions, diagnostic approaches, and examination techniques. He emphasizes differentiating traumatic from non-traumatic shoulder pain and using X-rays for trauma. The lecture details AC joint injuries (grades I-VI), shoulder dislocation reduction, and key extrinsic causes of shoulder pain such as cervical spine disease and MI. Practical pearls include palpation of the coracoclavicular ligament to grade AC injuries and a simple reduction maneuver for anterior shoulder dislocations.
key_points: Distinguish traumatic vs non-traumatic shoulder pain; obtain X-ray for traumatic cases to rule out fracture, dislocation, or AC sprain.
Consider extrinsic causes (MI, cervical spondylitis, herpes zoster, upper lobe pneumonia, PE, lung tumor) when shoulder pain is vague or radiates to neck or arm.

AC joint injuries are graded I-VI: types I-II treated conservatively with ice, sling, rest; type III may need orthopedic referral based on patient activity level; types IV-VI require urgent orthopedics.
Palpation of the coracoid and coracoclavicular ligament helps differentiate AC injury grades: non-tender coracoid suggests type I; tenderness there suggests type II or higher.
Anterior shoulder dislocation is most common and can be reduced by placing thumbs on the scapular spine with medial pressure while an assistant applies inferior traction on the forearm.
Brachial plexus stinger presents as 1-3 minutes of stinging pain from acromion to fingers after compression injury to head or shoulder, common in sports.
A triad of rotator cuff tests (not named in this session) has 98% sensitivity for detecting rotator cuff pathology when all are positive.
Intrinsic shoulder disorders include glenohumeral osteoarthritis, adhesive capsulitis, and rotator cuff tears; extrinsic causes include cervical radiculopathy, MI, and herpes zoster.
Type I and II AC injuries heal well with conservative management given sufficient time.
For type III AC separation, surgical referral is indicated for athletes or those with physically demanding jobs; conservative management is appropriate for older, less active patients.
Anterior shoulder dislocation can be reduced with the patient sitting, applying medial pressure on the scapular spine and inferior traction on the forearm.
Biceps tendon tears present with a visible bulge, ecchymosis, weakness, and a history of a pop with pain; MRI determines need for surgery.

episodes.title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation
episodes.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
episodes.abstract: Dr. Amanda Nichols leads a discussion on sleep deprivation in residency, covering its impact on patient safety and resident well-being. She reviews the history of work-hour restrictions following the Libby Zion case and presents evidence of performance decline in sleep-deprived physicians. The talk emphasizes recognizing signs of sleep deprivation, breaking the cultural stigma around seeking help, and practical strategies for alertness management including sleep hygiene and strategic caffeine use.
key_points: Sleep deprivation in physicians causes a 1.5 standard deviation decline in clinical performance.
Post-call residents make more errors reading EKGs and performing procedures like arthroscopy.
50% of residents experience burnout during training, with sleep deprivation as a contributing factor.
Most program directors are aware of at least one safety incident at their institution related to sleep deprivation.
Sleep deprivation is defined as 24+ hours without sleep or less than 5 hours per night for consecutive nights.
Signs of sleep deprivation appear in order: decreased vigilance, memory, cognitive function, mood, then gross motor performance.
Low-grade systemic inflammation and HPA axis impairment from sleep deprivation lead to impulsivity and disinhibition.
Good sleep hygiene includes consistent bedtime, minimizing screen time, using the bedroom only for sleep, and avoiding food, alcohol, and caffeine before bed.
Caffeine should be viewed as a medicine, not a food, and used only when most fatigued, avoiding it before sleep and after naps.
Moonlighting and charting time must be included in total work-hour restrictions, and moonlighting shifts should be the first to be cut if needed.
Caffeine should be viewed as a medicine, not a food or routine beverage; use it when most fatigued and avoid it before sleep and after naps.
Strategic naps of 10-45 minutes increase alertness and decrease errors; 1-2 hour naps may cause sleep inertia, and 4-5 hour naps are ineffective.

episodes.title: Dr. Amell on Opioid Stewardship 5/14/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Amell
episodes.abstract: Dr. Amell reviews the history of harmful opioid use, from the Civil War morphinism pandemic to the modern prescription opioid crisis and the rise of fentanyl. He discusses inpatient opioid stewardship standards, emphasizing the safety advantages of oral over IV opioids and the role of buprenorphine for both pain and addiction. He introduces the concept of complex prescription opioid dependence (CPOD) as distinct from opioid use disorder (OUD) and argues that buprenorphine is the treatment for both. The talk also covers a successful quality improvement initiative that reduced IV opioid use by 81% without worsening pain scores.
key_points: The first iatrogenic opioid pandemic was morphinism during the US Civil War, caused by widespread use of morphine and the hypodermic syringe.
The 'pain as the fifth vital sign' movement in the late 1990s led to overprescribing and the prescription opioid pandemic, which killed close to 200,000 people.
Complex prescription opioid dependence (CPOD) is more common than opioid use disorder (OUD) when the pathway starts with prescribed opioids; in CPOD, doctors are the drug dealers.
Inpatient opioid exposure is associated with about 10% of patients becoming stuck on opioids afterwards, regardless of the cause of pain.

Full agonist opioids (oxycodone, dilaudid, morphine) are supported for acute nociceptive pain and chronic progressive nociceptive pain (e.g., cancer pain), but not for chronic nonprogressive pain, nociplastic pain, or neuropathic pain.
IV Dilaudid is twice as strong as IV heroin and carries higher risks of nausea/vomiting (4.2 times more likely), hypotension, hypoxemia, delirium, and pruritus compared to oral administration.
Oral opioids provide smoother pharmacokinetics and safer analgesia than IV; sub q is safer than IV, and oral is the safest.
A quality improvement initiative at the health system achieved an 81% reduction in IV opioid usage by MME over 8,000 patient days with no change in pain scores.
Buprenorphine is a safer opioid and is the treatment for both CPOD and OUD, even when true addiction is uncertain.
Physicians must guide decisions about controlled substances when risks outweigh benefits, rather than offering false choices in shared decision-making.
Physicians should guide decisions about controlled substances when risks outweigh benefits, rather than offering false choices.
Buprenorphine is safer than full agonists due to its partial agonist properties, ceiling effect, and lower risk of respiratory depression.

episodes.title: Dr. Anne Hogan on Hearing Loss 3/12/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Anne Hogan
episodes.abstract: Dr. Anne Hogan, an ENT audiologist, presents a lecture on hearing loss for family medicine residents. She covers the types of hearing loss (conductive, sensorineural, mixed, and auditory processing disorder), risk factors including genetics, noise exposure, diabetes, and ototoxic medications, and how to interpret an audiogram. She emphasizes the importance of interprofessional collaboration and provides practical tips for recognizing hearing loss patterns and referring patients appropriately.
key_points: Hearing loss types: conductive (outer/middle ear), sensorineural (cochlea/nerve), mixed, and auditory processing disorder (brain level).
The speech banana on an audiogram shows the frequency and loudness range of speech sounds; moderate to severe loss means missing most speech without visual cues or amplification.
Genetic factors influence both congenital and age-related hearing loss; if a parent had hearing loss starting in their 60s, screen the patient 10 years earlier.
Noise exposure, including single loud events (e.g., hunting), can cause hearing loss; pediatric ear canals are smaller, amplifying sound at the eardrum, making loud noises more damaging.
Diabetes impacts hearing via small nerve damage, arterial damage affecting cochlear blood flow, and peripheral neuropathy affecting auditory/vestibular systems.
Ototoxic medications like cisplatin/carboplatin combinations cause hearing loss in about 80% of pediatric osteoblastoma patients; monitor hearing during treatment and consider dose adjustments.
Cardiovascular disease (CHD, hypertension) is linked to low-frequency hearing loss due to the cochlea's high vascularity; refer to cardiology if low frequencies drop.
Conductive hearing loss risk factors include recurrent ear infections, eustachian tube dysfunction, allergies, snoring (large tonsils/adenoids), smoking, and chronic sinusitis.
Scarred eardrums (tympanosclerosis) do not cause hearing loss; tubes help prevent conductive loss from middle ear congestion.
Auditory processing disorder can result from inconsistent auditory signals during neurodevelopment (ages 2-14), TBI, anoxia at birth, or hormonal changes in perimenopause/menopause.
Audiogram symbols: O = right ear, X = left ear; bone conduction symbols differ and help distinguish conductive from sensorineural loss.
Normal hearing thresholds are at the top of the audiogram (smaller numbers = softer sounds); hearing loss is present when thresholds fall below the normal line.

episodes.title: Dr. Anne Hogan on Vertigo 3/12/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Anne Hogan
episodes.abstract: Dr. Anne Hogan defines dizziness as a broad umbrella term and vertigo specifically as a sense of motion when none exists. She reviews vestibular anatomy, including otolith organs (saccule and utricle) for linear acceleration and semicircular canals for angular acceleration, and explains the vestibulo-ocular and vestibulospinal reflexes. Key risk factors for falls include hearing loss of 20 dB or greater (threefold risk), dizziness (12-fold risk), age over 85 (one in two have fallen), and female gender (twice the rate of men). She describes vestibular testing such as VNG, calorics, and VEMPs, emphasizing patient communication to reduce anxiety. She also introduces BPPV as caused by otoconia from the utricle entering a semicircular canal.
key_points: Dizziness is a broad term; vertigo specifically means sense of motion when there is none.
The vestibular system includes otolith organs (saccule, utricle) for linear acceleration and semicircular canals for angular acceleration.
The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) stabilizes vision during head movement; the vestibulospinal reflex maintains posture.
Hearing loss of 20 dB or greater increases fall risk threefold; dizziness increases risk 12-fold.
Falls are the leading cause of accidental death in those 65+, and women have twice the fall rate of men.
For dizziness evaluation, a hearing test is the first step.
Vestibular testing includes VNG (with calorics) and VEMPs; explaining the procedure reduces patient anxiety.
BPPV is caused by otoconia from the utricle entering a semicircular canal, causing positional vertigo.
cVEMPs assess saccular function via sternocleidomastoid muscle inhibition to loud clicks; oVEMPs assess utricular function.
BPPV occurs when otoconia from the utricle dislodge into a semicircular canal, altering fluid dynamics.
Head impulse testing evaluates the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR); a corrective saccade indicates acute semicircular canal dysfunction.
The HINTS exam (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) differentiates central from peripheral vertigo.

episodes.title: Dr. B Howard on RA & Lupus 10/23/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. B. Howard
episodes.abstract: Dr. B. Howard presents a lecture on rheumatoid arthritis and lupus, with a strong focus on fibromyalgia as a common chronic pain condition seen in rheumatology. He distinguishes peripheral nociceptive, neuropathic, and centralized pain mechanisms, emphasizing that most chronic pain is centralized. The lecture reviews the history and evolution of fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria from 1990 to 2016, including the widespread pain index and symptom severity scale. Dr. Howard also discusses differing expert opinions on fibromyalgia etiology, from central sensitization to somatization, and provides practical guidance on using the criteria in clinical practice.
key_points: Chronic pain is defined as pain persisting beyond three months; most chronic pain is centralized (central pain augmentation).
NSAIDs and opioids are effective for peripheral nociceptive pain but not central pain; tricyclics and SNRIs work for both; gabapentinoids and cannabinoids work for central pain only.
Fibromyalgia disproportionately affects women (9:1 female-to-male ratio), with an overall prevalence of 3.4% in US women.
The 1990 ACR criteria required chronic widespread pain and >11 tender points; the 2011/2016 criteria use the widespread pain index (WPI) and symptom severity scale (SSS).
Fibromyalgia criteria can be met with WPI ≥7 and SSS ≥5 (pain-predominant) or WPI 4-6 and SSS ≥9 (symptom-predominant).
Symptoms must generally be present for at least three months to diagnose fibromyalgia.
Central sensitization involves altered pain processing throughout the body, leading to hyperalgesia and allodynia.
Fibromyalgia often coexists with other conditions and can amplify symptoms of any underlying disease.
Experts disagree on etiology: Clauw emphasizes genetic predisposition and environmental triggers; Wolfe views it as a somatic symptom disorder; Yunus focuses on central sensitization.
When using the fibromyalgia questionnaire, ask about 'pain' (not discomfort) over the last week, and rate fatigue, waking unrefreshed, and cognitive symptoms on a severity scale.
Fibromyalgia is not a distinct entity but a continuum of polysymptomatic distress; all humans score somewhere on a 0, 31 scale.
The 2010 ACR fibromyalgia criteria require a widespread pain index of 4, 6 and symptom severity scale ≥9, or WPI ≥7 and SS ≥5, with symptoms present for at least 3 months.

episodes.title: Dr. Bancroft on Foot & Ankle Basics 9/4/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bancroft
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bancroft presents a practical, primary-care-focused overview of common foot and ankle conditions, including Morton neuroma, plantar fasciitis, hammertoes, and bunions. He emphasizes clinical diagnosis without routine imaging, highlights key physical exam maneuvers, and reviews conservative management strategies such as footwear modification, stretching, and judicious use of injections. The talk also covers when to refer for surgical intervention and important pitfalls like fat pad atrophy with steroid injections.
key_points: Morton neuroma is a swelling of sensory nerves, most commonly between the third and fourth toes due to anatomical movement of metatarsal heads.
Diagnosis of Morton neuroma is clinical: splaying of toes, decreased sensation in the affected webspace, and a palpable, tender nerve that reproduces shooting pain when squeezed.
No imaging is needed for Morton neuroma; X-rays show only splaying, and MRI is not routinely indicated.
First-line treatment for Morton neuroma includes wide-toed shoes (e.g., Crocs), metatarsal supports, rest, and cortisone injection; surgical excision is reserved for refractory cases.
Plantar fasciitis presents with heel pain worst on the first step in the morning; Achilles tendinitis can mimic this symptom.
Heel spurs on X-ray are a result of chronic inflammation and calcium deposition, not the cause of pain.

First-line therapy for plantar fasciitis is NSAIDs, stretching (heel drops: 30 seconds, 10 times per day), and night splints; steroid injections are painful and risk fat pad atrophy if injected incorrectly.
Hammertoes and bunions only require treatment when symptomatic, especially if causing skin breakdown or infection risk.
Conservative management for hammertoes and bunions includes pads, spacers, and orthopedic shoes with a wide toe box to prevent rubbing.

Surgical correction for bunions involves an oblique osteotomy and wiring; it is reserved for cases where conservative measures fail, particularly in older or diabetic patients due to wound healing risks.
PTTD is an acquired flatfoot occurring after age 50, typically without trauma, and is a common cause of medial foot pain.
Physical exam for PTTD includes the too many toes sign (seeing more toes than the pinky when standing behind the patient) and inability to rise onto the ball of one foot.

episodes.title: Dr. Bancroft on Head & Neck in Urgent Care Setting
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bancroft
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bancroft presents a case-based lecture on head and neck emergencies in the urgent care setting, focusing on a 76-year-old female with falls, altered mental status, and a subdural/subarachnoid hemorrhage with splenomegaly. Key teaching points include the importance of a thorough history and exam, appropriate lab and imaging workup, and management of intracranial hemorrhage in a resource-limited setting. The lecture also covers anaphylaxis diagnostic criteria and the pitfalls of treating based on lab values alone, such as elevated BNP in the setting of hemorrhage.
key_points: In elderly patients with falls and altered mental status, consider subdural hemorrhage even if symptoms are stable for a week.
Elevated BNP can be a marker of intracranial hemorrhage, not just heart failure; avoid treating with diuretics if the patient is not fluid overloaded.
For intracranial hemorrhage, manage blood pressure, maintain isotonic fluids, keep sodium above 135, and consider hyperventilation or mannitol only if acutely deteriorating.
Before transfer for neurosurgery, call the receiving facility for acceptance and reverse any anticoagulation.
In anaphylaxis, diagnostic criteria require involvement of two or more organ systems: skin/mucosal, respiratory, cardiovascular, or gastrointestinal.
When triaging a call about shortness of breath, ask about oxygen saturation, stridor, wheezing, and the patient's general appearance to gauge urgency.
A normal creatinine and lack of fluid overload argue against starting diuretics even with a high BNP.
CT head and CT abdomen/pelvis can reveal unexpected findings like subdural hemorrhage and splenomegaly in a fall patient.
In a remote setting, weigh the cost and time of helicopter vs. ambulance transfer based on patient stability.
A patient with a chronic subdural may have minimal symptoms and recover fully with conservative management.
Diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis require two of three categories: skin/mucosal involvement, respiratory compromise (dyspnea/wheeze/stridor), or hypotension/GI symptoms (abdominal pain, vomiting).
Epinephrine for anaphylaxis must be given intramuscularly (IM), not subcutaneously; the presenter describes a case where a nurse argued for sub-Q and the clinician insisted on IM.

episodes.title: Dr. Bancroft on Hematuria Evaluation
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bancroft
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bancroft presents a family-medicine oriented approach to hematuria, emphasizing the American Urologic Association (AUA) guidelines and risk stratification for malignancy. The talk covers the two types of hematuria (gross and microscopic), the importance of confirming dipstick results with microscopy, and the initial evaluation including history, physical exam, labs, and imaging. Key risk factors for malignancy (age, smoking, male sex, prior radiation/chemo, occupational exposures) and reassuring features (flank pain, recent exercise, UTI symptoms) are discussed. The lecture also addresses management decisions in rural versus urban settings, including when to refer to urology and the importance of treating and rechecking hematuria.
key_points: Hematuria is divided into gross (visible blood) and microscopic (≥3 RBCs per high-power field on microscopy of spun urine).
Dipstick hematuria must be confirmed with microscopy because false positives occur with myoglobin, hemoglobin, semen, alkaline urine (pH >9), and contaminants like cleaning agents.

Initial evaluation of microscopic hematuria includes a detailed history for malignancy risk factors, physical exam (including DRE, abdominal, CV tenderness, testicular exam), blood pressure, creatinine, UA with culture, and imaging (CT or ultrasound).

Risk factors for malignancy include age >35 (men >40, women >60), smoking (more pack-years = higher risk), male sex, history of gross hematuria, persistent microscopic hematuria, irritative voiding symptoms, prior pelvic radiation, certain chemotherapies, occupational exposure to rubber/petrochemicals/dyes, and chronic indwelling foreign bodies (e.g., Foley).

Reassuring features that suggest benign causes include transient flank pain, recent increase in exercise, recent procedure, dysuria, vaginal discharge, BPH symptoms, urethral stricture, recent trauma/catheterization, urinary diverticula, and signs/symptoms of UTI.
Patients on anticoagulants with unexplained hematuria should undergo the same workup as those not on anticoagulants.
If a patient has known medical renal disease causing hematuria, refer to both nephrology and urology to avoid anchoring and missing a second cause.
Imaging for suspected stones: low-dose CT for BMI <30, standard-dose CT for obese patients; ultrasound is an alternative.
After treating a cause of hematuria, recheck the urine to confirm resolution; persistent hematuria warrants urology referral, especially in rural settings where access is limited.
Studies show ~50% of women with bladder cancer are treated for a UTI first, and 16% are treated with antibiotics before diagnosis.
For incidental microscopic hematuria with no risk factors, retest at 6 months; if 5-25 RBCs/HPF, consider urology consultation.
Benign causes like BPH, kidney stones, vaginal atrophy, and pelvic organ prolapse can cause persistent microhematuria, but if it continues, referral to urology is prudent.

episodes.title: Dr. Bancroft on Rural ER Medicine
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bancroft
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bancroft gives a practical talk on rural ER medicine, covering financial aspects of 1099 moonlighting work, tax strategies, and deductions. He also reviews BiPAP settings for acute respiratory failure, distinguishing management for COPD versus pulmonary edema. The talk emphasizes the importance of having reliable clinical resources and maintaining a strong work ethic.
key_points: 1099 independent contractors must set aside ~20% of income for taxes (5% state, 15% federal) and pay quarterly via IRS 1040-ES.
Self-employment tax adds ~15% for Medicare and Social Security, totaling roughly 35% marginal tax rate for 1099 workers.
Mileage deduction is $0.65/mile; log all work-related driving with dates and miles.
Per diem meal deductions: $50 for first and last travel days, $60 for full days; no receipts needed if using standard rate.
Educational supplies, scrubs, stethoscopes, and CME expenses (including travel and hotel) are tax-deductible.
A Professional Limited Liability Company (PLLC) offers tax benefits but does not protect personal assets from malpractice lawsuits.
Initial BiPAP settings: IPAP 12 cm H2O, EPAP 5 cm H2O, FiO2 100%, inspiratory time 1 second.
For tachypneic patients, reduce inspiratory time to 0.5 seconds to avoid delivering IPAP during exhalation.
In pulmonary edema, increase EPAP to 8 cm H2O and IPAP to 16 cm H2O; in COPD, use lower EPAP (5) and IPAP (12).
Recheck ABG or VBG at 60 minutes to assess BiPAP response; discontinue or intubate if worsening.
BiPAP settings differ for pulmonary edema (EPAP 8, IPAP 16) vs COPD (EPAP 4-5, IPAP 12).
For tachypneic patients on BiPAP, consider adjusting inspiratory time rather than just pressures.

episodes.title: Dr. Bancroft on Sore Throat, Rhinitis, & Sinusitis
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bancroft
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bancroft presents a practical overview of sore throat, rhinitis, and sinusitis management in the urgent care setting. The talk emphasizes evidence-based diagnosis and treatment of allergic rhinitis, including physical exam findings (nasal crease, bluish turbinates, postnasal drip) and stepwise therapy with intranasal corticosteroids as first-line. For sinusitis, Dr. Bancroft stresses that bacterial infection is rare (0.5-2% of cases) and that antibiotic decisions should be based on symptom duration (≥10 days without improvement) rather than exam or severity. First-line antibiotics are amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate; macrolides such as azithromycin should be avoided. High-dose Augmentin (2 g twice daily) is indicated for patients with risk factors or prior treatment failure. The talk also clarifies common misconceptions (e.g., goldenrod allergy vs. ragweed) and provides practical pearls on nasal spray technique, montelukast precautions, and definitions of recurrent sinusitis.
key_points: Allergic rhinitis is IgE-mediated; exam findings include a nasal crease, bluish turbinates, and visible postnasal drip.
First-line treatment for allergic rhinitis is intranasal corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone) 2 sprays each nostril BID for 2 weeks then taper to once daily; it takes about 6 days to become effective.
No need to inhale when using nasal spray, mucociliary clearance moves the medication to the back of the throat naturally.

Montelukast is less effective for IgE-mediated allergic rhinitis and carries a black box warning for insomnia and suicidality; reserve for patients with asthma or those who cannot tolerate nasal sprays.
Bacterial sinusitis is diagnosed by symptom duration ≥10 days without improvement; early severe symptoms alone do not warrant antibiotics.
Physical exam (percussion, transillumination) is not specific for bacterial sinusitis; treatment decisions are based on timing, not exam findings.

First-line antibiotics for bacterial sinusitis are amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate. For penicillin allergy, use cefpodoxime/clavulanate or doxycycline. Avoid macrolides (including azithromycin/Z-Pak).

For patients with risk factors (age >65, recent hospitalization, antibiotics in past month, immunocompromised, diabetes, CAD) or treatment failure, use high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate (2 g BID) for 5, 7 days.
Recurrent sinusitis defined as ≥4 episodes per year with at least 10 symptom-free days between episodes; recurrence within 5 days is considered the same infection.
Common seasonal allergens: tree pollen in spring, ragweed in summer/fall; goldenrod is frequently blamed but is not a significant allergen.
Nonallergic rhinitis (strong smells, cold, Afrin overuse) is not IgE-mediated and does not respond to antihistamines.
Sinusitis is always preceded by and concurrent with rhinitis; obstruction of sinus drainage leads to secondary bacterial infection.

episodes.title: Dr. Beasley on Diabetic Foot Disease
episodes.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
episodes.abstract: Dr. Brad Beasley, a podiatric surgeon, presents a family medicine lecture on diabetic foot disease. He emphasizes the high morbidity of diabetic foot complications and the importance of recognizing that diabetic patients often do not mount a septic response to severe infections. Key topics include the three high-risk foot types (PAD, neuropathy, diabetes), the urgent need for surgical drainage of septic joints regardless of systemic signs, and preventive pearls such as daily foot checks and proper footwear. He also introduces Charcot neuroarthropathy as a commonly missed diagnosis in diabetics with unilateral swelling.
key_points: Diabetic patients with abscess or septic joint may not display classic signs of sepsis; do not delay surgical intervention based on their absence.
Charcot neuroarthropathy presents with unilateral swelling and redness in a diabetic patient and requires X-ray, not just antibiotic treatment for presumed cellulitis.
Below 8% A1c (even if not ideal) markedly reduces risk of lower extremity complications and is the threshold for elective foot surgery.
Cotton socks absorb moisture and bacteria; recommend synthetic wicking socks (e.g., SmartWool, Thorlo, Darn Tough) for diabetic patients.
Neuropathy is the 'real evil' in diabetic foot disease; patients lose protective sensation and may not detect ulcers or foreign bodies.
Daily self-foot inspection by the patient is essential to catch ulcers early.
A multidisciplinary approach (primary care, podiatry, vascular, endocrinology, wound care) improves limb salvage outcomes.
Partial foot or toe amputations often serve as a wake-up call and can prevent major amputations; major amputation carries high morbidity and mortality.
Lumbar spine MRI is a key workup for idiopathic neuropathy in non-diabetic patients to rule out disc disease.
PAD is often under-evaluated; delayed capillary refill or absent pedal pulses should prompt ABI testing regardless of diabetes status.
Daily foot inspection is the single most important thing to communicate to diabetic patients; use a mirror or phone camera if they cannot bend down.
Most adults wear shoes that are too small; feet grow about half a size every 10, 15 years due to gravity.

episodes.title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bhakta reviews acute GI concerns for family medicine residents, emphasizing triage decisions, initial workup, and communication. Key topics include upper GI bleeding, pancreatitis, cholangitis, obstructive uropathy, and mesenteric ischemia. She stresses the importance of obtaining PT/INR before procedures, asking about red Gatorade to avoid false hematemesis, and using BISAP scores to guide ICU admission for pancreatitis. The talk also covers treatment pearls such as early enteral feeding for pancreatitis and advocating for patients with infected stones to receive urgent urology consultation.
key_points: For upper GI bleeding, always check PT/INR and type and screen before any procedure.
Always ask if the patient drank red Gatorade or other red liquids to avoid misdiagnosing hematemesis.
Unstable patients, high-risk aspiration, perforation, and ascending cholangitis should go to the ICU.
Upper GI bleeds in patients with cirrhosis or varices should go to ICU or step-down.
Use CT to identify pancreatitis by peripancreatic stranding; check lipid panel on first episode to rule out hypertriglyceridemia.
Early enteral feeding in pancreatitis protects mucosal barrier and reduces bacterial translocation.
If pancreatitis patients worsen after 48-72 hours, consult surgery for possible abdominal compartment syndrome.
Obstructing ureteral stone with hydronephrosis and sepsis requires ICU and urgent urology consultation.
Pneumatosis intestinalis (gas in bowel wall) indicates mesenteric ischemia; start heparin and consult surgery.
Be honest with patients about bad findings like pneumatosis or tumors; don't make surgeons the bearers of all bad news.
Residents should prepare patients for bad news by starting conversations early, e.g., 'I don't think the CT is looking good,' rather than waiting for a surgeon to deliver the news.
In small bowel obstruction with distension, positive bowel sounds, and non-tender abdomen, the patient needs a surgeon and possibly an NG tube, not ICU admission.

episodes.title: Dr. Bhakta on Distress in Adults
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bhakta reviews the management of respiratory distress in adults, covering interpretation of blood gases, use of noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP), ventilator settings, and the importance of advance care planning. He emphasizes practical adjustments for oxygenation and ventilation, contraindications to BiPAP, and the critical need to ensure DNR/DNI orders are correctly entered in the electronic medical record.
key_points: A defibrillator can be identified on chest X-ray by the presence of a coil on one or both leads; all defibrillators can pace.
Indications for a defibrillator include CHF with EF under 35% after three months of goal-directed therapy or history of VFib/VTach.
Absolute contraindications to BiPAP include GCS less than 7, vomiting, facial trauma, cardiac arrest, and airway obstruction.
On BiPAP, oxygenation is improved by increasing FiO2 or EPAP (which acts like PEEP); CO2 clearance is improved by increasing tidal volume via IPAP/EPAP adjustments.
If a patient on BiPAP does not improve after two adjustments and repeat blood gas, escalate care (call ICU).
For a nonresponsive patient with suspected opioid overdose, give naloxone 0.4 mg IV; if no improvement after first dose, consider other causes.
Ventilator orders are written in the sequence: rate, tidal volume, PEEP, FiO2.
On a ventilator, FiO2 and PEEP primarily affect oxygenation; rate and tidal volume primarily affect CO2 clearance.
ET tube position should be confirmed on chest X-ray; if in the right mainstem bronchus, retract 1-2 cm.
DNR and DNI are separate orders in the hospital; it is the resident's responsibility to ensure both are entered and that the patient wears a DNR bracelet.
Advance care planning conversations should start in clinic, ideally early in adulthood, to avoid difficult decisions at 2 AM.
If a patient has DNR/DNI orders in the chart but no bracelet, the patient may be coded against their wishes, leading to harm and family distress.

episodes.title: Dr. Bhakta on Rapids, ICU Criteria 8/27/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bahta, an ICU physician, presents a practical guide for residents on how to approach rapid responses and decide between floor, step-down, and ICU care. He emphasizes seeing the patient first, assessing ABCs, and understanding what the ICU can provide that the floor cannot. The talk covers common night calls including hypoxia, hypotension in ESRD, wide-complex tachycardia, and atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, offering specific management pearls and pitfalls.
key_points: The three main differences between floor and ICU are ventilator support, vasopressor support, and nurse-to-patient ratio (1:1 or 1:2 in ICU vs. 1:6 on floor).
When calling the ICU about a patient, you should have seen the patient, know a brief history, and have started the workup if time allows.
For a rapid response, first look at the patient (are they on their phone or slumped over?), then ask the nurse why the rapid was called, then get vitals and data.
Non-rebreather masks can deliver up to 95% oxygen; heated high-flow, BiPAP, and ventilator support typically require step-down or ICU.
Albumin is not more effective than crystalloid if the patient's albumin is above 3; it is only indicated when albumin is under 3.
Midodrine is an alpha agonist used for orthostatic hypotension or dialysis-related hypotension, but it is not FDA-indicated for floor hypotension management.
Telemetry technicians are trained to call any wide-complex tachycardia 'VTach'; it is the physician's job to determine if it truly is VTach using criteria like Brugada or Life in the Fast Lane.
For unstable patients with any tachyarrhythmia (e.g., SVT, VTach, AFib RVR) who are passed out or slumped over, immediate synchronized cardioversion is indicated, do not wait for medications.

Stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response is often difficult to treat; beta blockers or amiodarone can be tried, but rates in the 120s-140s may persist and are acceptable if the patient is stable.
Code status discussions should begin in the clinic, not when the patient is decompensating at night.

Chronic atrial fibrillation in patients with COPD and heart disease is often difficult to rate-control; if the patient is stable with heart rates in the 120s, 140s, calling EP may not change management.
DNR and DNI are separate orders at St. John's; some patients may want DNR but still desire a trial of mechanical ventilation.

episodes.title: Dr. Bothwell on Anemia of Pregnancy
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bothwell
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bothwell presents a 30-minute lecture on anemia of pregnancy, distinguishing physiologic (dilutional) anemia from pathologic causes. The most common pathologic anemia is iron deficiency, diagnosed by ferritin <30 ng/mL. She reviews screening recommendations (USPSTF vs. ACOG/CDC), management with oral iron (every-other-day dosing to avoid hepcidin blockade) and IV iron (safe after first trimester), and touches on folate and B12 deficiency. Key pearls include checking ferritin early, using every-other-day oral iron, and avoiding iron sucrose with benzyl alcohol in pregnancy.
key_points: Physiologic anemia of pregnancy is dilutional: plasma volume increases 40-50% while RBC mass increases only 15-30%, causing hemoglobin to drop normally.
Pathologic anemia is most commonly iron deficiency; ferritin <30 ng/mL confirms the diagnosis.
ACOG defines anemia in pregnancy as hemoglobin <11 g/dL (first/third trimester) or <10.5 g/dL (second trimester), or hematocrit <33%.
Risk factors for iron deficiency include short interpregnancy interval, vegetarian diet, GI diseases, and medications/foods that impair absorption.
USPSTF finds insufficient evidence to screen all pregnant women, but ACOG/CDC recommend CBC at first visit and again at 24-28 weeks.
Oral iron should be dosed every other day (not BID) because hepcidin blocks absorption for 24 hours after a dose.
IV iron is safe after the first trimester (no data in first trimester) and leads to higher hemoglobin at delivery with fewer GI side effects.
Iron sucrose (Venofer) is preferred in pregnancy; iron dextran contains benzyl alcohol and should be avoided.
Folate deficiency is the most common cause of macrocytic anemia in pregnancy; treat with 1 mg folic acid daily.
Preconception counseling should include CBC and ferritin for women with menorrhagia or short interpregnancy intervals.
Macrocytic anemia in pregnancy is most commonly due to folate deficiency.
Folate supplementation: 50 mcg/day before pregnancy, 400 mcg/day during pregnancy (or 1 mg if deficient).

episodes.title: Dr. Bothwell on Breastfeeding
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bothwell
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bothwell presents a comprehensive lecture on breastfeeding for family medicine residents, covering benefits for both infant and mother, latch technique, common complications like mastitis, and practical counseling strategies. She emphasizes the dose-dependent nature of breastfeeding benefits, the importance of supporting mothers through early challenges, and provides specific guidance on recognizing good attachment and managing breast engorgement. The talk also addresses barriers to breastfeeding, legal protections for pumping at work, and when antibiotics are needed for mastitis.
key_points: Breastfeeding reduces infant risk of asthma, obesity, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, ear/respiratory infections, SIDS, and necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants.
Breastfeeding during painful procedures (vaccines, heel sticks) provides an analgesic effect greater than placebo.
Human milk contains immunoglobulins, digestive enzymes (lactase, lysozymes), and amino acids that support gut health and reduce allergies.
Maternal benefits include decreased risk of ovarian, breast, and endometrial cancers, type 2 diabetes, and heart disease.
Breastfeeding burns approximately 500 calories per day and helps revert to prepregnancy weight.
Lactational amenorrhea occurs in the first six months due to high prolactin suppressing estrogen and ovulation.
Only 25.4% of newborns are exclusively breastfed at six months, despite 83% starting; early undesired weaning occurs in 45% of women.
Negative early breastfeeding experiences may increase postpartum depression risk, so screening is important.
Good latch is indicated by lips flanged out, more areola visible above the top lip, chin touching breast, nose clear, and no pain after initial attachment.
Mastitis presents with flu-like symptoms (fever, chills, malaise) and is usually caused by milk stasis; treatment includes continued feeding, warm compresses, and cabbage leaves.
Most mastitis does not require antibiotics; if needed, cover for Staphylococcus aureus.
Oklahoma law (2021) requires employers to provide a clean, private space (not a bathroom) with a chair and paid break for pumping.

episodes.title: Dr. Bothwell on Effects of Vitamin D Supplementation and Pregnancy Outcomes: Pre-Eclampsia
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bothwell
episodes.abstract: This journal club session reviews a 2017 double-blind RCT from Iran examining whether vitamin D supplementation (50,000 IU every two weeks) prevents recurrent preeclampsia in women with a history of preeclampsia and normal baseline vitamin D levels. The presenter and residents discuss the study's methodology, results showing a significantly lower risk of preeclampsia in the intervention group (p=0.036), and limitations including lack of data on concurrent prenatal vitamins or aspirin use. The session concludes that current ACOG guidelines do not recommend universal screening or supplementation for vitamin D in pregnancy, and that while meta-analyses suggest a possible benefit, the evidence is insufficient to change practice.
key_points: Preeclampsia complicates 8% of pregnancies and accounts for 25% of maternal morbidity and mortality.
Vitamin D deficiency prevalence ranges from 18% to 84% depending on the country; the US rate is estimated in the 80% range.
Risk factors for preeclampsia include diabetes, CKD, hypertension, nulliparity, multiple gestation, family history, obesity, and immunologic disorders.
The study was a double-blind RCT with 70 women in the intervention group (50,000 IU vitamin D every 2 weeks) and 72 in the placebo group, all with normal baseline vitamin D levels.
The intervention group had a significantly lower incidence of recurrent preeclampsia (p=0.036).
No side effects from vitamin D supplementation were reported, and adherence was good.

Limitations include the study being limited to Iranian women, lack of control for concurrent prenatal vitamins or aspirin use, and potential bias from participants being counseled by nonmedical family members.
Current ACOG and USPSTF guidelines do not recommend universal vitamin D screening or supplementation in pregnancy due to insufficient data.
Meta-analyses of RCTs and observational studies suggest vitamin D supplementation may be associated with decreased risk of preeclampsia, but results vary across studies.
The proposed pathophysiology involves vitamin D's immunomodulatory effects on Th1/Th2 cytokines and its role in healthy placental implantation.

episodes.title: Dr. Brad Hardy on Contracts, Coding, and Resident Financial Basics
episodes.speaker: Dr. Brad Hardy
episodes.abstract: Dr. Brad Hardy delivers a practical lecture on financial literacy for family medicine residents, covering student loan management, disability insurance, term life insurance, retirement accounts, contract evaluation, and physician compensation. He emphasizes that clinical expertise does not guarantee financial success and urges residents to become the CFO of their family. Key advice includes avoiding unnecessary debt, understanding loan repayment options before refinancing, securing disability insurance early, and committing to ongoing financial education.
key_points: Physicians must treat financial literacy as a second job; clinical expertise alone does not ensure financial success.
Student loans compound during residency; a $45,000 car purchased in residency could cost $100,000 in lost compounding over a career.
Before refinancing student loans, determine if you qualify for Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF), refinancing eliminates that option.
Disability insurance should be purchased during residency, before any medical diagnosis makes you uninsurable.
Individual disability policies are portable and preferable to group policies, which are tied to an employer.
Long-term disability insurance typically pays 60, 70% of income, tax-free if premiums are paid post-tax.
Physicians have a higher rate of musculoskeletal and mental health disabilities; 90% of disabilities are caused by illness.
Read one good personal finance book per year; recommended titles include 'Personal Finance for Dummies', 'The Bogleheads' Guide to Investing', and William Bernstein's free online book.
Primary care physicians in some geographic areas (e.g., Tulsa) can earn more than specialists in high-cost areas (e.g., San Francisco) due to supply and demand.
A written financial plan is essential; consider paying a fee-only advisor $200, $300 for personalized loan repayment advice.
Buy individual disability insurance while healthy and before any diagnosis, as it is portable between jobs.
Group disability insurance through an employer is cheaper but not transportable; losing the job means losing coverage.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Abnormal Uterine Bleeding, Chronic Anovulation, and PCOS
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert reviews the pathophysiology and management of abnormal uterine bleeding due to chronic anovulation, focusing on polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and insulin resistance. He explains the diagnostic criteria for PCOS (two of three: irregular menses, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, elevated free testosterone) and the hormonal feedback loops that lead to anovulation. The lecture covers how to assess insulin resistance using fasting glucose-to-insulin ratios, and outlines treatment strategies including progestin withdrawal, oral contraceptives, spironolactone, and metformin. Dr. Calvert emphasizes that family physicians can manage these conditions without referral to specialists.
key_points: Abnormal uterine bleeding is categorized as organic (pathologic) or functional (menarche, menopause, chronic anovulation).
PCOS diagnosis requires two of three: irregular menstrual periods, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, and elevated free testosterone.
The ultrasound for PCOS must be specifically ordered as a 'polycystic ovary evaluation' to measure follicle diameter and count follicles <1 cm.
In a normal menstrual cycle, low estrogen triggers LH production, which stimulates ovarian androgen production; androgen is then converted to estrogen in granulosa cells.
Progesterone stops endometrial cell division, allowing the endometrium to become secretory; without ovulation, unopposed estrogen increases endometrial cancer risk.
Women with PCOS who do not menstruate should have endometrial evacuation (progestin withdrawal or OCPs) at least 2-3 times per year to prevent cancer.
Insulin resistance is common in PCOS (20-80% of patients) and should be tested even when PCOS is suspected.
Fasting glucose-to-insulin ratio: normal is ~5 (glucose 100/insulin 20); a ratio below 5 indicates insulin resistance.
Metformin can normalize insulin and restore ovulation within 2-3 months; dosing depends on severity (500 mg daily for mild, 500 mg BID for severe).
Oral contraceptives provide estrogen at 3-5 times physiologic levels, increasing sex hormone binding globulin and reducing free testosterone.
Spironolactone prevents conversion of vellus hairs to terminal hairs but cannot reverse existing terminal hair; laser or electrolysis is needed for removal.
Continuous OCPs for 4 months can lower testosterone enough to allow ovulation and pregnancy in the next 2-3 months after stopping.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Abnormal Uterine Bleeding
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert distinguishes physiologic from organic abnormal uterine bleeding, focusing on dysfunctional uterine bleeding including chronic anovulation, PCOS, and insulin resistance. He emphasizes obtaining a detailed menstrual history, interval, duration, and amount, and comparing abnormal bleeding to the patient's own physiologic normal. The lecture reviews the menstrual cycle phases, hormonal feedback loops, and the role of sex hormone binding globulin in PCOS. Clinical pearls include management of post-menarchal irregularity, perimenopause counseling, and use of combination birth control pills for dysmenorrhea and cycle regulation.
key_points: Abnormal uterine bleeding is categorized as physiologic (dysfunctional) or organic (pathologic); this lecture covers physiologic causes.
Menstrual history must include interval, duration, and amount of both the current abnormal bleeding and the patient's normal period off birth control.
Normal menstrual interval is 21, 35 days (or 24, 38 days, pick one and be consistent); duration is 5, 7 days.
Quantify bleeding by asking number of pads/tampons used on the heaviest day or per cycle.
Oligomenorrhea is vaginal bleeding at regular intervals greater than 35 days but less than 6 months.
Progesterone withdrawal causes menstruation; exogenous progestin withdrawal can also induce bleeding.
Low estrogen in first 3 days of cycle triggers LH, which stimulates androgen production in theca cells, converted to estrogen.
Liver increases sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) in response to high estrogen; high testosterone decreases SHBG, as in PCOS.
Birth control pills (high estrogen) increase SHBG, bind free testosterone, and reduce hirsutism in PCOS.
After menarche, up to 2 years of irregular periods is normal; if still irregular at 2 years, evaluate for chronic anovulation.
Perimenopause onset is marked by irregular periods (interval, duration, or amount), not hot flashes; mean onset age 45, duration 2, 8 years (average 4, 5).
Menopause average age is 51, 52; 95% reach menopause by age 54; bleeding at age 60 warrants evaluation for endometrial cancer.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Adnexal Masses
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the evaluation of adnexal masses, emphasizing the importance of clinical diagnosis and pelvic exam. Dr. Calvert presents cases of hydrosalpinx from PID, complex ovarian cysts suspicious for malignancy, and uterine fibroids. Key teaching points include performing bimanual exam during Pap smears, recognizing red flags like fullness, and using ultrasound to confirm clinical suspicion. The presenter stresses that many women with chlamydia are asymptomatic and that PID can cause silent adhesions.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis should precede ultrasound; ultrasound confirms the suspected finding.
Order hemoglobin and hematocrit to assess blood loss in suspected ruptured ovarian cyst.
Risk factors such as early age at first intercourse, multiple partners, and previous STDs warrant a pelvic exam rather than simply refilling birth control.
Sixty percent of women with chlamydia are asymptomatic, so a low threshold for testing is needed.
PID can be silent and lead to hydrosalpinx; the dilated tube cannot empty and the epithelium is damaged.
Fullness on pelvic exam is a red flag that requires further investigation with ultrasound.
A complex ovarian cyst with septations and solid components should be considered ovarian cancer until proven otherwise.
Most women with ovarian cancer are symptomatic at diagnosis, but pelvic exam can detect early-stage disease in asymptomatic women.
Bimanual exam should be performed during Pap smear if the clinician is competent to do so.
Differential for an adnexal mass includes ovary, fallopian tube, or pedunculated uterine fibroid, which can be larger than the uterus.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Cervical Vaginal Infection
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert discusses candida glabrata, which is resistant to fluconazole (Diflucan) and occurs in about 12% of vaginal candidiasis cases. He emphasizes that NAAT testing is the only way to confirm the species. For glabrata, treatment should be with the new nonazole drug ibrexafungerp (Brexafemme), dosed as 150 mg twice a day for one day.
