For chronic recurrent candida (non-glabrata), he recommends initial treatment every three days followed by weekly dosing for six months.
key_points: Candida glabrata is resistant to fluconazole and all azoles.
Glabrata accounts for about 12% of vaginal candida infections.
NAAT testing is necessary to differentiate candida species.
Ibrexafungerp (Brexafemme) is a new nonazole antifungal for glabrata.
Ibrexafungerp dosing: 150 mg twice a day for one day (total 300 mg).
For chronic recurrent candida (non-glabrata), initial treatment every 3 days then weekly for 6 months.
Azoles should not be used for glabrata, even topically.
Ibrexafungerp has a different mechanism of action than azoles.
Many clinicians are unaware of ibrexafungerp.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Chronic Anovulation & PCOS
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Calvert covers the physiology of chronic anovulation, including its four categories: post-menarche, perimenopause, PCOS, and insulin resistance. He explains the normal menstrual cycle, hormonal regulation, and the importance of estrogen and progesterone in endometrial changes. Clinical pearls include how to evaluate abnormal uterine bleeding, the definition of perimenopause and menopause, and the use of birth control pills to manage irregular bleeding and dysmenorrhea. Contraindications such as DVT history are also discussed.
key_points: Chronic anovulation has four physiologic categories: post-menarche (up to 2 years), perimenopause, PCOS, and insulin resistance.
After menarche, irregular periods are normal for up to 2 years; if still irregular after 2 years, it is abnormal.
Perimenopause lasts 4, 7 years; menopause is defined as 12 months without a period.
The menstrual cycle has a proliferative phase (estrogen-driven) and a secretory phase (progesterone-driven); without ovulation, there is no secretory phase.
Ovulation requires an LH surge triggered by a rapid rise in estrogen; without an estrogen rise, there is no LH surge and no ovulation.
Menstruation results from a drop in progesterone level; the progesterone withdrawal test can assess ovulation.
Birth control pills work by maintaining constant estrogen levels, preventing the LH surge and ovulation.
When evaluating abnormal uterine bleeding, first determine the patient's normal interval, duration, and amount of flow.
Perimenopause begins with a change in menstrual periods, not hot flushes; average age of menopause is 52, with 95% by age 54.
Insulin resistance can cause anovulation; normalizing insulin levels can restore ovulation.
Estrogen-progestin birth control pills can treat both irregular bleeding and dysmenorrhea in perimenopause by regulating cycles and reducing prostaglandins.
Estrogen-containing contraceptives are contraindicated in women with a history of DVT; cyclic progestin alone does not control bleeding in perimenopause.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Female Vulva Exam Pathology 5/7/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert presents a lecture on female vulvar examination and pathology, emphasizing normal anatomic variations and common benign findings. He reviews vulvar anatomy, descriptive terminology for lesions, and uses case-based image review to teach recognition of normal variants versus pathologic conditions. Key pathologies covered include ectopic sebaceous glands, epidermoid inclusion cysts, lentigo, angiokeratomas, HPV warts, and lichen sclerosus, with emphasis on clinical features, diagnostic approach, and management.
key_points: Labia majora have hair follicles; labia minora do not. This distinction helps identify anatomic location.
Use clock-face orientation and descriptive terms (color, texture, border, elevation) to document vulvar lesions precisely.
Normal labia minora vary widely in size, symmetry, and pigmentation; asymmetry and hyperpigmentation alone are not pathologic.
Hymenal cobblestoning (papillae) is a normal variant of the hymenal ring, not a lesion.
Ectopic sebaceous glands appear as small, white/yellow raised spots on labia minora; they are benign and require no treatment.
Epidermoid inclusion cysts are firm, filled with exfoliated skin, cannot be drained; excision of the entire cyst is needed for removal.
Lentigo presents as hyperpigmented macules; biopsy is indicated if features are atypical (dark color, irregular borders).
Angiokeratomas are common, benign, red-to-black pinpoint papules often clustered; reassurance is sufficient.
HPV warts (condyloma) are firm, hard, cauliflower-like lesions; palpation distinguishes them from soft normal papillae.

Lichen sclerosus presents with pale, atrophic, thin skin with a silver sheen, often with itching, dysuria, and labial fusion; it carries an increased risk of vulvar cancer, requiring surveillance every six months.
Lichen sclerosus often presents with a silver sheen on the vulva, which may be faint and localized.
Eroded areas in lichen sclerosus are generally not tender.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Female Vulva Exam & Pathology 6/4/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert leads a family-medicine residency session on female vulvar examination and pathology, using a series of clinical images to teach recognition of normal anatomy and common abnormalities. He covers urethral caruncles, Skene's gland cysts, Bartholin cysts, urethral diverticula, vaginal dysplasia, VIN III, and Crohn's disease of the vulva. The emphasis is on careful inspection, palpation, and low-threshold biopsy for any suspicious or unexplained lesion. Dr. Calvert stresses that emergency departments often miss vulvar pathology and that residents must perform their own thorough exams.
key_points: Urethral caruncles are common in older women, present with spotting on the tissue, and are usually left alone unless symptomatic.
Skene's gland cysts can obstruct the urethra and may require catheter placement.
Bartholin cysts: infected (painful abscess) need incision and drainage with a Word catheter; non-infected cysts with clear fluid may be associated with cancer and require further evaluation.
Urethral diverticula present as cystic structures near the urethra; diagnosis is confirmed by MRI.
Vaginal dysplasia (VAIN) and VIN III can appear as subtle changes in skin color (pale or red) with palpable thickness; biopsy is essential.
Lichen sclerosus lacks sharp margination, unlike dysplastic lesions which often have well-defined borders.
VIN III can present in multiple ways: white discoloration, nodularity, or erythematous 'raw' areas; it is often asymptomatic.
Any unexplained vulvar lesion, especially if firm, raised, or with depth, should be biopsied (punch or shave) rather than observed.
Crohn's disease of the vulva can mimic warts or other lesions and is frequently missed on exam.
Always perform a complete pelvic exam including inspection of the perineum; do not rely on emergency department assessments for vulvar pathology.
Any vulvar lesion of uncertain etiology should be biopsied.
Warts are hard on palpation, while other soft tissue lesions are soft and raised.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Female Vulva Examination Pathology 9/4/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert reviews normal vulvar anatomy, common normal variants (such as Fordyce spots, sebaceous cysts, and angiokeratomas), and pathologic findings such as lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, Paget disease, yeast infection, folliculitis, herpes simplex, and melanoma. He emphasizes the importance of recognizing benign findings to avoid unnecessary procedures, the value of palpation to differentiate vesicles from solid lesions, and clinical judgment when microscopy and presentation conflict. He also discusses primary versus secondary herpes infection and their different treatment strategies.
key_points: The vestibular area is between the labia minora; Bartholin glands open there, not on the mons pubis.
Labia minora asymmetry and variation are normal and not a disease.
Fordyce spots (ectopic sebaceous glands) are raised, yellow, hard papules; palpation differentiates them from vesicles.
Cobblestoning of the labia minora is a normal appearance.
Epidermal inclusion cysts are very common (eight to nine out of ten women), filled with epithelial cells; offer reassurance.
A pigmented lesion with asymmetry, irregular border, multiple colors, or change in size/shape/color should be biopsied to rule out melanoma.
Lichen sclerosus typically presents with itching, agglutination of the labia, loss of clitoral hood, and a shiny white appearance.
Lichen planus resembles lichen sclerosus but is painful rather than itchy and often has oral involvement.
Herpes simplex classically has grouped vesicles at different stages (clear vesicles, pustules, erosions) and a prodrome.
Primary herpes is often symptomatic/systemic and requires aggressive treatment; secondary (recurrent) herpes is milder and treated less aggressively.
When clinical presentation strongly suggests yeast, treat even if microscopy is negative, trust clinical judgment.
Angiokeratomas are common benign vascular lesions, also common on the male scrotum; provide reassurance.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Female Vulva Examination & Pathology
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert leads an interactive teaching session on female vulvar examination and pathology using clinical images. He reviews normal anatomy including the clitoral hood, labia minora, urethral opening, and fourchette, then walks through cases of herpes simplex virus, urethral caruncles, Skene's gland cysts, Gartner duct cysts, Bartholin gland cysts/abscesses, urethral diverticulum, vulvar neoplasia (VIN), and syphilitic chancres. He emphasizes the importance of careful inspection for discoloration (red, white, black), palpation for underlying induration, and low-threshold for punch biopsy of suspicious lesions. The session highlights common pitfalls such as misidentifying the location of Bartholin glands and the danger of surgically exploring Gartner duct cysts.
key_points: Herpes simplex virus classically presents with pain before visible lesions, then clear vesicles that become purulent over days, often in different stages simultaneously.
Urethral caruncles are common in older women and are benign; leave alone unless symptomatic.
Skene's gland cysts are blocked normal glands, not pathologic; only incise and drain if problematic.
Gartner duct cysts are embryologic remnants along the vaginal wall; do not remove or drain because they may extend to the kidney.
Bartholin glands are located near the inferior part of the labia minora at the fourchette, not in the upper labia.
First-time Bartholin abscess is managed with a Word catheter; recurrent abscess may require marsupialization.
Urethral diverticulum can be detected by palpating a bulge along the anterior vaginal wall while stripping the urethra.
Vulvar cancer may present as subtle discoloration (red, white, or black) with underlying induration on palpation.
When you don't know what a vulvar lesion is, perform a punch biopsy; a small sample of the discolored or misshapen tissue is sufficient.
Syphilitic chancres are painless; touching the center with a Q-tip wooden end does not cause pain.
Condyloma lata is a secondary syphilis lesion.
Rhabdomyosarcoma is a rare but deadly vulvar tumor seen primarily in children.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Female Vulva Examination Pathology 11/6/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert presents a lecture on female vulvar examination pathology, using a series of clinical images to teach residents how to distinguish normal variants from abnormal findings. He covers common benign conditions such as ectopic sebaceous glands, epidermal cysts, angiokeratomas, and urethral caruncles, as well as infectious and inflammatory conditions like genital warts, herpes simplex virus, folliculitis, and candidiasis. The lecture emphasizes the importance of recognizing key features like sheen in lichen sclerosus, painful purple plaques in lichen planus, and the value of oral examination and biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain.
key_points: Ectopic sebaceous glands are normal, common findings on the vulva, appearing as small yellowish papules in non-hairy areas.
Epidermal cysts on the vulva are benign, filled with epithelial cells (not fluid), and should not be popped; removal requires excising the entire cyst wall.
Angiokeratomas are benign, keratinized capillaries that appear as raised, shiny papules, often multiple, and can be confused with melanoma.
Genital warts (HPV) are contagious, can appear as hard or soft papules, and may require acetowhite staining or palpation to detect in the vagina.
Lichen sclerosus presents with pale, atrophic, wrinkled skin with a characteristic sheen, often with agglutination and erosion; it is pruritic and requires long-term treatment.
Lichen planus appears as painful, purple, polygonal plaques with a sheen; oral examination for white, web-like lesions helps distinguish it from lichen sclerosus.
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) lesions progress through clear vesicles, pustules, ulcers, and scabs, often with lesions at different stages simultaneously.
Folliculitis is typically associated with recent shaving, presents with inflamed hair follicles, and is not painful like HSV.
Urethral caruncles are benign polyps protruding from the urethra, common in older women, and may cause bleeding; removal is only needed if they obstruct urination.
Skene's gland cysts are benign, cystic structures located inferior to the urethra at the 5 and 7 o'clock positions; large cysts may cause obstruction.
Urethral caruncles are benign and usually do not require removal unless they obstruct urination.
Skene's gland cysts are located at 5 and 7 o'clock positions relative to the urethra and are typically managed expectantly unless they obstruct urine flow.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on GYN Adnexal Mass
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert discusses the evaluation of adnexal masses, emphasizing the importance of correlating ultrasound findings with the menstrual cycle to distinguish normal follicles from pathologic cysts. He reviews normal ovarian physiology, including follicle development and cyst formation, and provides practical guidance on bimanual examination technique. Key points include normal ovarian volume thresholds (≤20 cc in reproductive age, ≤10 cc postmenopausal), the red flag of a palpable ovary in a postmenopausal woman, and the significance of uterine mobility on exam. The lecture aims to equip residents with skills to confidently assess adnexal masses and avoid unnecessary alarm.
key_points: Functional cysts (follicular and corpus luteum) are cyclic and related to the menstrual cycle; they are benign and resolve spontaneously.
Ultrasound reports of 'multiple cysts' in premenopausal women often represent normal follicles; ask when the ultrasound was done relative to the menstrual cycle.
In postmenopausal women, the ovary should not be palpable; any palpable adnexal mass is concerning and requires further evaluation.
Normal ovarian volume is ≤20 cc in reproductive age and ≤10 cc in postmenopausal women; a volume of 25 cc in a postmenopausal woman is abnormal.
The uterus normally moves freely on bimanual exam; if it does not move, there may be pathology such as adhesions or endometriosis.
On bimanual exam, push the cervix upward to bring the uterus toward your fingers, then press on the abdomen to feel the fundus.
If you cannot feel the uterine fundus, the uterus is likely retroverted or retroflexed.
To feel the ovaries, slide your fingertip along the lateral cervix toward the fundus; the ovary may feel like a marble slipping between your fingers.
Feeling adnexal fullness on bimanual exam is abnormal and warrants imaging.
It is acceptable to not feel the ovary on exam, especially in obese patients; document that you could not feel it.
Simple cysts on ultrasound are likely benign; complex cysts raise concern for malignancy.
PCOS diagnosis requires 10, 15 follicles less than 1 cm per ovary on specialized ultrasound, not just a cyst.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on GYN Inservice Review 10/2/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert leads a rapid-fire review of GYN in-service exam questions for family medicine residents. He emphasizes picking out key words in question stems, such as androgen levels and menstrual timing, to narrow the differential. Key topics include IUD mechanisms, chronic anovulation and PCOS evaluation, management of severe dysmenorrhea, and the clinical significance of fibroid location. The session also covers breast pain evaluation, hematuria workup, and practical tips for common GYN presentations.
key_points: IUDs work primarily by causing endometrial inflammation; copper adds spermicidal effect and progestin adds hormonal effect, but the main mechanism is inflammation.
Chronic anovulation should be evaluated for both PCOS and insulin resistance; treat the primary driver first.
PCOS diagnosis requires two of three: irregular periods, polycystic ovaries, elevated testosterone.
In chronic anovulation, ensure the patient menstruates at least twice a year to prevent endometrial hyperplasia; use progesterone withdrawal if needed.
Submucosal fibroids cause heavy menstrual bleeding; subserosal and intramural fibroids typically do not.
For severe dysmenorrhea, naproxen may be insufficient; consider combined oral contraceptives to thin the endometrium and reduce prostaglandin production.
Cyclic breast pain is usually physiologic and benign; ask if pain is cyclic or random to narrow the differential.
New guideline for starting mammography screening is age 50 (as of 2022), changed from age 45.
Kegel exercises are a frequent board exam topic and should be routinely counseled for pelvic floor support.
Two influenza vaccines are egg-free; for severe egg allergy, use clinical judgment but risk is minimal.
Hematuria workup must consider bladder or kidney cancer.
Progesterone is the dominant hormone in pregnancy; birth control pills mimic this to thin the endometrium.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Hormonal Contraception 3/5/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert presents a lecture on hormonal contraception, covering non-pill methods and birth control pills. He discusses the mechanisms of action for progestin-only and combination contraceptives, including IUDs, implants, patches, and rings. Key topics include the importance of starting low-dose pills on the first day of the cycle, the role of FSH suppression, and the differences between monophasic and multiphasic pills. Practical advice is given on managing missed pills, weight considerations for patches, and troubleshooting breakthrough bleeding.
key_points: IUDs are the most effective contraceptives, with typical use rates near 99% for copper and hormonal IUDs.
Low-dose estrogen pills (15 mcg) must be started on the first day of the cycle to be effective; starting later may fail.
Progestin-only pills require strict adherence, same time every day, because missing even one pill can lead to pregnancy.
Patches are weight-dependent; BMI >30 reduces effectiveness, and patients >2 days late should use backup for 7 days.
NuvaRing avoids first-pass liver metabolism, allowing lower estrogen doses and fewer side effects like nausea.
Monophasic pills have uniform hormone levels; multiphasic pills vary hormones and are harder to adjust for side effects.
Breakthrough bleeding in the first half of the cycle is managed by increasing estrogen; in the second half, by increasing progestin.
IUDs work primarily via local inflammation; hormonal IUDs add thinning of the endometrium and cervical mucus changes.
Copper IUDs create a spermicidal environment via copper oxide, reducing sperm motility.
Combination pills suppress FSH to prevent ovulation; progestin-only pills primarily thicken cervical mucus and thin the endometrium.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Hormonal Contraception 4/9/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert reviews hormonal contraception, focusing on the physiology of FSH suppression and the importance of starting low-dose pills on day 1 of menses. He presents a classification system for combination oral contraceptives based on estrogen dose (high, low, very low) and progestin type (strong/androgenic, strong/weak androgen, weak/moderate androgen). He provides an algorithm for managing breakthrough bleeding according to cycle timing and emphasizes using monophasic pills, following up at 3 months, and tailoring pill choice to patient characteristics such as acne, menorrhagia, dysmenorrhea, and age over 40.
key_points: Low-dose OCPs (15, 25 mcg ethinyl estradiol) must be started on the first day of menses; even a 3-day delay can trigger FSH and risk ovulation.
Estrogen doses are grouped: high (50 mcg), low (35 mcg), very low (25/15 mcg).

Progestins are grouped: group 1 (strong progestin, strong androgen, norgestrel/levonorgestrel), group 2 (strong progestin, weak androgen, desogestrel/norgestimate), group 3 (weak progestin, moderate androgen).
All combination OCPs are equally effective for contraception; choose based on side-effect profile and patient needs.
Monophasic pills are preferred because they simplify troubleshooting when side effects occur.
For heavy menstrual bleeding or dysmenorrhea, choose a pill with strong progestin (group 1 or 2) to thin the endometrium.
In patients with acne, avoid strong androgen progestins (group 1); use group 2 (desogestrel or norgestimate).
Breakthrough bleeding in the first half of the cycle indicates low estrogen or high progesterone, increase estrogen or decrease progestin; in the second half, do the opposite.
Follow up new OCP users at 3 months for blood pressure check; do not schedule earlier because early spotting often resolves.
In women over 40, use low-estrogen pills (group C) to reduce the risk of hypertension.
Breakthrough bleeding on OCPs is common; most patients just need reassurance if cancer is ruled out.
Do not change the pill regimen until at least three months have passed to allow the body to adjust.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Menopause
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert discusses the pathophysiology and treatment of vaginal atrophy in menopause, emphasizing that estrogen is required to regenerate blood vessels and restore vaginal health. He presents a stepwise protocol using estradiol cream, starting with nightly dosing for two months, then tapering based on clinical response. The goal is to normalize the vaginal epithelium while using the lowest effective dose. He also addresses the use of transdermal estrogen in patients at risk for blood clots and the need for progesterone in women with a uterus.
key_points: Vaginal atrophy results from loss of blood vessels, moisture, and lactobacillus, leading to increased pH and risk of bacterial vaginosis.
Estrogen is necessary to treat atrophy; it must be given long enough for blood vessel regeneration, which takes months.
Estradiol cream is preferred over conjugated equine estrogen because estradiol is molecularly identical to human estrogen.
Initial treatment for vaginal atrophy: 1 gram of estradiol cream nightly for 2 months.
After 2 months, reassess; if improved but not healed, reduce to 1 gram every other night for 2 months.
Once healed, maintain with the lowest effective dose, typically 1-2 grams per week.
If atrophy recurs, increase frequency (e.g., 3 times per week) for a few months, then taper again.
Patients often feel better quickly due to steroid effect, but true healing takes months; do not stop early.
Transdermal estrogen bypasses the liver and may be safer for women at risk of blood clots.
In women with a uterus, progesterone must be given periodically to empty the endometrium and prevent hyperplasia.
Various progesterone regimens exist: continuous estrogen with progesterone 1 week/month, or both given continuously.
Vaginal estrogen has low systemic absorption (about 1%), but still carries some risk.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Pap Smears Colposcopy 8/6/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert teaches residents how to properly collect Pap smears by targeting the squamocolumnar junction and transformation zone, where cervical cancer risk is highest. He explains the anatomy of the cervix, the difference between squamous and columnar cells, and how the junction changes with age, pregnancy, and hormonal status. He also introduces the vocabulary of abnormal uterine bleeding, defines normal menstrual parameters, and outlines the endocrine cycle. The lecture emphasizes clinical judgment in sampling technique and the importance of establishing each patient's unique menstrual normal.
key_points: The squamocolumnar junction is the line between squamous cells of the ectocervix and columnar cells of the endocervical canal; it is the key landmark for Pap smear sampling.
The transformation zone, between the old and new squamocolumnar junctions, is the highest risk area for cervical cancer because cells are actively dividing during metaplasia.
In prepubertal and menopausal women, the squamocolumnar junction is often inside the os and may not be visible.
In pregnancy or with birth control pills, a large ectropion may push the junction outward, making it more visible.
For liquid-based cytology, the sample is placed in fluid; red cells and debris are removed, so a Pap smear can be taken even during light menstruation.
The broom should be inserted into the os and turned; with a large ectropion, use the broom like a paintbrush to sample the edge of the transformation zone.
For women after hysterectomy with no cervix, use the rounded end of the spatula to scrape the vaginal cuff scar.
Normal menstrual interval is 21 to 35 days; duration is 5 to 7 days; amount is variable and must be assessed by asking about pad/tampon use.
Dysfunctional uterine bleeding is physiologic (e.g., perimenopause, chronic anovulation); organic bleeding is pathologic (e.g., polyps, fibroids, cancer).
A rapid rise in estrogen triggers the LH surge and ovulation; a fall in progesterone triggers menstruation.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Pelvic Pain Cases 2/9/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert presents several cases of pelvic pain, emphasizing the importance of classifying pain as cyclic or non-cyclic, physiologic or pathologic. He discusses endometriosis, adenomyosis, interstitial cystitis, Bartholin gland cysts, and mittelschmerz. Key teaching points include the dual pain mechanism in endometriosis (cyclic from implants, chronic from adhesions), the unique cyclic dyspareunia of adenomyosis, and practical management strategies such as OCPs for early endometriosis and marsupialization for recurrent Bartholin cysts.
key_points: Endometriosis causes two types of pain: cyclic pain from endometrial implants and chronic pain from scar tissue/adhesions.
Adenomyosis is characterized by endometrial tissue within the myometrium, causing a boggy, enlarged, tender uterus.
Cyclic dyspareunia is pathognomonic for adenomyosis.
In adenomyosis, bladder compression of the tender uterus causes urinary frequency, and a retroverted uterus causes dyschezia.
OCPs can minimize or resolve pain in early endometriosis by suppressing the endometrial cycle.
Interstitial cystitis presents with bladder pain on filling, relieved by emptying, and is difficult to manage; referral to a urologist with interest is recommended.
Bartholin gland cysts require drainage and creation of a new opening; a Word catheter should be kept in place for at least 1-2 weeks to allow epithelialization.
For recurrent Bartholin cysts after Word catheter failure, marsupialization with absorbable sutures placed very close together is the next step.
Mittelschmerz is mid-cycle, ovulatory pain that alternates sides, lasts minutes to hours, and requires no workup if exam is normal; OCPs can be used for management.
When evaluating abdominal pain, first determine if it is abdominal wall or intra-abdominal; the leg raise test helps isolate abdominal wall muscles.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Pelvic Pain
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert presents a case-based approach to evaluating pelvic pain, emphasizing a structured history using eight questions (location, quality, frequency, duration, aggravating/relieving factors, change over time, radiation). He distinguishes primary vs. secondary dysmenorrhea, reviews common causes including endometriosis, adenomyosis, interstitial cystitis, and ovarian torsion, and highlights physical exam findings such as uterine mobility and nodularity. Treatment pearls include the use of combined oral contraceptives for endometriosis, word catheter for first Bartholin abscess, and marsupialization for recurrent cases.
key_points: Use eight questions to characterize pain: location, quality, frequency, duration, aggravating factors, relieving factors, change over time, radiation.
Secondary dysmenorrhea develops after years of pain-free cycles; primary dysmenorrhea begins with menarche.
Endometriosis is the most common cause of secondary dysmenorrhea and dyspareunia; gold standard diagnosis is laparoscopy.
Posterior cul-de-sac is the most common site for endometriosis; nodularity may be felt on bimanual exam.
Adenomyosis (endometriosis within the uterine wall) presents with a tender, boggy uterus and can be diagnosed clinically 95% of the time; MRI confirms.
Interstitial cystitis is often linked with endometriosis and irritable bowel syndrome; treatment includes a bladder-coating medication taken three times daily.
For suspected abdominal wall pain, use the one-finger test and palpate with the patient raising head/legs to tense the muscles.
First Bartholin abscess is treated with a Word catheter; recurrent abscess requires marsupialization.
Ovulation pain (mittelschmerz) is cyclic, mid-cycle, and can alternate sides; if severe and not desiring pregnancy, OCPs to suppress ovulation are first-line.
In acute pelvic pain with delayed menses, always rule out ectopic pregnancy with a beta-hCG.
Pain radiating to the shoulder suggests diaphragmatic irritation (e.g., from ruptured ectopic).
Acute pelvic pain in reproductive-age women requires consideration of ectopic pregnancy and hemorrhagic ovarian cyst.

episodes.title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup
episodes.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
episodes.abstract: Dr. Catherine Hodge describes her experience opening a neonatal unit at a rural mission hospital in Malawi, starting from a storage room where babies died of hypothermia. She emphasizes the need for a dedicated space and nursing staff separate from the maternity ward, as nurses were focused on maternal mortality prevention. She details building low-cost 'hot cots' from plywood and heating bulbs, using oxygen concentrators, and adapting protocols to limited resources. A key innovation was the use of simple CPAP made from a water bottle, and burettes for safe IV fluid administration in the absence of syringe pumps.
key_points: The biggest initial challenge was lack of designated nursing staff; nurses focused on maternal mortality prevention and were not trained to care for neonates.
Separating the neonatal unit physically from the maternity ward was essential to allow nurses to focus on the baby as the second patient.
Getting hospital administration buy-in is critical because a neonatal unit requires at least 4-5 additional nurses, which is a major ongoing cost.
Low-cost 'hot cots' can be built from plywood and regular heating bulbs to provide warmth for premature infants.
Oxygen concentrators are preferred over cylinders because cylinders are heavy, hard to move, and dangerous when they run out without warning.
Simple CPAP can be made using a bottle of water; pressure is set by the depth of the tube underwater, typically starting at 5 cm H2O for preterm babies.
Burettes (plastic cylinders) allow safe administration of small volumes of IV fluids (50-80 mL) to prevent fluid overload when syringe pumps are unavailable.
Protocols must be adapted to locally available medications and equipment, not simply copied from textbooks.
Once the unit opened and offered treatment, referrals from health centers increased dramatically, exceeding initial needs assessments.
Mothers ideally room in with their babies, but space constraints may force a change in design as patient volume grows.
Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC), skin-to-skin contact with a cap only, achieves near-perfect thermoregulation for almost all preterm infants, regardless of gestational age.
Without blood cultures, neonatal sepsis is diagnosed presumptively; WHO guidelines recommend presumptive treatment for babies born before 34 weeks.

episodes.title: Dr. Christine Liu on Gender Affirming Care
episodes.speaker: Dr. Christine Liu
episodes.abstract: Dr. Christine Liu discusses gender affirming care, focusing on the medical and mental health risks and benefits. She reviews the change in DSM diagnosis from gender identity disorder to gender dysphoria, emphasizing that gender dysphoria has not been linked to a genetic cause and is influenced by psychological experiences. She highlights that early counseling for children expressing gender dysphoria is critical to treat underlying psychological disorders. She references a plastic surgeon who states there is no data showing benefit and data showing harm from gender affirming surgery, and encourages physicians to weigh risks and benefits while considering the traditional paradigm of sex and gender.
key_points: Gender dysphoria replaced gender identity disorder in the DSM, shifting from a disorder of identity to a feeling of dysphoria.
Gender dysphoria has not been linked to a genetic cause and is considered a psychological disorder of unclear origin.
Evidence suggests gender dysphoria can be exacerbated by promoters of transgender ideology.
Early counseling for children expressing gender dysphoria is critical to treat underlying psychological disorders.
There is limited prospective data on transgender medicine; most data is observational.
From a surgical perspective, there is no data showing benefit and data showing harm from gender affirming surgery.
A healthy personal identity aligns with biological reality.
Physicians must weigh risks and benefits of gender affirming care, as with any medical treatment.
Traditional paradigm: sex is biologically determined (XX/XY), culture affirms that, and gender follows.
New paradigm: personal identity defines gender, and the body is aligned to the mind via medications or surgery.
Five principles of medical ethics: autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice.
Harm includes death, morbidity, worsening of the original problem, pain, anxiety, and cost.

episodes.title: Dr. Christopher Abdo on Approach to Lower Extremity Weakness 2.19.26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Christopher Abdo
episodes.abstract: This segment of Dr. Christopher Abdo's lecture on lower extremity weakness uses three cases to teach localization. Case 1: a 34-year-old with slowly progressive unilateral leg weakness turns out to have cervical myelopathy from C5-C6 disc herniation. Case 2: a 67-year-old with acute left leg weakness, distal > proximal, with distal symmetric sensory loss has an ACA stroke; the speaker warns that ordering an MRI of the lumbar spine delayed thrombolysis. Case 3: a 68-year-old on warfarin presents with acute flaccid paraplegia, sensory level at L1-L2, with preserved vibration and proprioception, anterior cord syndrome from spinal cord infarction at the artery of Adamkiewicz territory, missed on initial MRI without diffusion-weighted imaging.
key_points: Localization narrows the differential and avoids unnecessary, expensive, and time-consuming whole-neuraxis imaging.
An MRI of the entire neuraxis can take up to three hours with contrast; patient movement often requires repeat studies.
MRIs cost $1,000, $1,500 each, and overuse contributes to delays in patient discharge.
Acute painless unilateral lower extremity weakness without sensory loss suggests a stroke (e.g., ACA territory), not spinal cord pathology.
ACA strokes typically present with contralateral leg-predominant weakness and often spare sensation because the motor strip is involved but sensory cortex is protected by PCA territory.
A patient with acute flaccid paraplegia, a sensory level, and preserved posterior column function (vibration, proprioception) has anterior cord syndrome.
Spinal cord infarction should be suspected in a patient with acute cord syndrome, especially at the T8, L2 level where the artery of Adamkiewicz is the primary blood supply.
Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) on spine MRI must be specifically ordered to detect acute spinal cord ischemia; it is not performed routinely.
Acute spinal cord injury presents with flaccidity (spinal shock), not hypertonia; hypertonia develops days to weeks later.
Cauda equina syndrome causes severe radicular pain; a painless flaccid paraplegia with a sensory level is more consistent with cord pathology.
Spinal cord infarctions typically occur in the anterior spinal artery territory; cervical cord is rarely affected due to rich collateral blood supply.
Localization of weakness along the neuraxis (brain, brainstem, cord, nerve, NMJ, muscle) is critical for correct diagnosis and treatment.

episodes.title: Dr. Comninellis on Tropical Fever 6/4/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Comninellis
episodes.abstract: Dr. Comninellis presents a lecture on tropical fever, focusing on febrile illnesses in low-resource settings rather than returning travelers. He emphasizes that geographic location is the most critical clue for diagnosis and demonstrates how to use a simple evaluation grid based on fever duration, malaria test, and CBC. Key teaching points include the tourniquet test for dengue, Koplik spots as an early measles sign, rose spots in typhoid, and the importance of rapid diagnostic tests. The lecture also covers the differential diagnosis of prolonged fever, including parasitic diseases with eosinophilia and tuberculosis with neutropenia.
key_points: The number one takeaway for tropical fever is knowing where in the world you are, as disease epidemiology varies by region.
Measles vaccine coverage is a reliable indirect indicator of measles risk; one dose provides ~95% protection, two doses ~98%.
The tourniquet test for dengue is performed by inflating a BP cuff above diastolic but below systolic pressure; petechiae indicate a positive test.
Koplik spots (punctate erythematous lesions on the soft palate) appear before the measles rash and are a key early diagnostic clue.
Rose spots on the chest are erythematous, slightly tender lesions representing septic emboli in typhoid fever, which is a systemic disease.
Scrofula (posterior cervical adenitis) is the most common extrapulmonary presentation of tuberculosis, especially in children.
In acute fever (<2 weeks) with negative malaria test and high WBC, suspect bacterial causes like abscess or sepsis.
Fever >2 weeks with eosinophilia points to parasitic diseases such as schistosomiasis, leishmaniasis, or lymphatic filariasis.
Fever >2 weeks with neutropenia suggests HIV, advanced TB, dengue, or viral hemorrhagic fevers.
Rapid diagnostic tests (e.g., for malaria, typhoid, HIV) have become affordable (malaria test <$1) and provide objective data in low-resource settings.

episodes.title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
episodes.abstract: Dr. Mark Crouch discusses HIV care in Papua New Guinea, drawing on his experience at a referral clinic serving 500,000 people. He covers epidemiology, transmission risks, social determinants, and practical pearls for health workers. The talk emphasizes person-first language, the importance of immediate ART after needle sticks, and the reality that most occupational HIV acquisition is sexual rather than from sharps injuries. He also highlights the need for hepatitis B vaccination in high-prevalence settings.
key_points: HIV prevalence in the province is 1, 2%, estimated from antenatal screening.
The clinic is an ART center offering free testing, counseling, and same-day treatment.
In the US, HIV disproportionately affects MSM and African Americans; globally it is predominantly heterosexual with slightly more females.
Social determinants such as poverty, poor access to care, and gender-based violence increase both acquisition risk and disease burden.
Needle stick transmission risk from a hollow hypodermic needle is about 0.2% without ART and drops to 0.01% with immediate post-exposure ART.
The most common way health workers acquire HIV is through sexual contact, not occupational exposure.
Use person-first language ('person living with HIV') to reduce stigma.
Women have a higher physiologic risk of acquiring HIV during heterosexual sex than men.
Avoid labeling patients as 'noncompliant'; consider the social context that makes adherence difficult.
Health workers traveling to PNG should get a hepatitis B booster due to the world's highest prevalence.
In HIV patients with cough/dyspnea, the differential includes typical and atypical bacterial pneumonias, viral illnesses, COPD, CHF, TB, fungal infections, and PCP.
For PCP pneumonia with hypoxia (O2 sat <92%), treat with Bactrim and add steroids.

episodes.title: Dr. Cunningham on Osteoarthritis of the Knee 5/21/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Cunningham
episodes.abstract: Dr. Cunningham presents a practical, evidence-informed approach to managing osteoarthritis of the knee, emphasizing that running does not worsen arthritis for average runners and that exercise and weight management are foundational. He reviews injection therapies including corticosteroids, viscosupplementation, PRP, and adipose-derived orthobiologics, noting their indications, limitations, and costs. He also discusses genicular nerve cryoneurolysis as a pain-control option for patients who are poor surgical candidates. Throughout, he stresses that no current treatment reverses arthritis and that maximizing motion and strength improves outcomes even if other therapies fail.
key_points: Running does not worsen knee arthritis for average runners; inactivity is more harmful than activity.
Weight loss reduces knee pain: for every pound lost, the knee experiences about four pounds less force.
First-line treatments are exercise, weight management, and acetaminophen or NSAIDs as needed.
Corticosteroid injections are a reasonable first injection option; limit to three per calendar year due to chondrotoxicity.
Viscosupplementation is superior to placebo and may be superior to steroids; it is not chondrotoxic and typically lasts six months.
PRP is the most promising orthobiologic but is expensive ($1,200) and not covered by insurance; leukocyte-poor PRP is preferred.
Adipose tissue injections (often called stem cells) cost about $5,200 and have a 60-70% success rate; they do not regrow cartilage.
Genicular nerve cryoneurolysis provides pain relief lasting about 90 days and is an option for patients who cannot undergo surgery.
No current treatment reverses arthritis; all interventions aim to reduce symptoms and improve function.
Exercise and rehabilitation should accompany any injection therapy to maximize joint strength and mobility.
Cryoneurolysis (iBear) freezes nerves providing sensation to the knee, lasting about 90 days per literature, but some patients experience relief for 5-6 months to a year.
Shockwave therapy, similar to that used for kidney stones, shows promise for tendinopathies, plantar fasciitis, and arthritis, with studies showing reduced fluid on imaging in end-stage arthritis.

episodes.title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma
episodes.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
episodes.abstract: Dr. Dolin presents a practical lecture on COPD and asthma for family medicine residents, emphasizing spirometry-based diagnosis and treatment staging. She reviews the GOLD criteria (FEV1 >80% mild, 50-80% moderate, 30-50% severe, <30% very severe) and the mMRC dyspnea scale, though notes she rarely uses the latter in clinical practice. Key management points include starting with rescue inhalers for mild disease, LAMA/LABA combinations for moderate disease, and adding inhaled corticosteroids (triple therapy) for severe disease or recurrent exacerbations. She highlights the importance of matching inhaler device to patient ability, watching patients use inhalers, and stopping inhaled steroids during pneumonia episodes due to increased infection risk.
key_points: Spirometry is required for a formal COPD diagnosis; without it, you may have emphysema, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, bronchiectasis, or long-standing asthma instead.
Chronic cough workup should focus on four causes: postnasal drip, acid reflux, cough variant asthma, and post-infectious cough (airway inflammation takes 6-8 weeks to resolve).
GOLD stages for COPD: mild (FEV1 >80% predicted), moderate (50-80%), severe (30-50%), very severe (<30%).
For mild COPD (FEV1 >80%, no exacerbations, symptoms ~once/month), a rescue inhaler alone is sufficient.
For moderate COPD (FEV1 50-80%), start a LAMA/LABA combination inhaler; Dr. Dolin typically starts both agents together.
For severe COPD (FEV1 30-50%) or recurrent exacerbations, add an inhaled corticosteroid (triple therapy) to reduce hospitalizations.
Inhaled corticosteroids increase pneumonia risk; stop them during pneumonia episodes even if treating a COPD exacerbation.
Always watch patients use their inhaler; poor technique (e.g., inability to coordinate actuation) is a common reason for treatment failure.
For patients with dexterity issues (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, trach), consider nebulized treatments instead of inhalers.
Lung volume reduction surgery may improve FEV1 by a few hundred cc's but is not a cure; consider for upper lobe predominant emphysema.
Annual low-dose CT for lung cancer screening starts at a 30 pack-year smoking history.
CT protocols vary by indication: low-dose for nodules, interstitial lung disease protocol (thinner cuts) for fibrotic patterns, PE protocol for low DLCO.

episodes.title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea
episodes.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
episodes.abstract: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin, a pulmonary critical care and sleep medicine physician, presents a practical guide to diagnosing and managing obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) for family medicine residents. She emphasizes the STOP-Bang questionnaire and Epworth Sleepiness Scale as screening tools, explains the differences between home sleep tests and in-lab polysomnography, and discusses treatment thresholds including the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI). She also covers documentation requirements for insurance approval, the role of split-night studies, and practical tips for mask fitting and managing comorbidities like hypertension and periodic limb movements.
key_points: The STOP-Bang questionnaire screens for OSA risk using snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, blood pressure, BMI >35, age >50, neck circumference, and male sex.
An Epworth Sleepiness Scale score ≥10 indicates excessive daytime sleepiness and helps decide treatment for mild OSA (AHI 5-15).
Home sleep tests use a thoracic belt, nasal thermistor, and finger oximeter; in-lab polysomnography adds EEG, EKG, EMG, and more detailed airflow monitoring.
Medicare requires a 4% oxygen desaturation rule for scoring hypopneas; using a 3% rule may necessitate repeat testing.
A split-night study can be done if AHI ≥20 in the first 2 hours, with at least 4 hours of PAP therapy needed for a prescription.
Treatment is typically offered for AHI >5, especially if symptomatic; asymptomatic patients with AHI <15 may not need treatment.
Mallampati score and upper airway exam (micrognathia, retrognathia, uvula) are required for Medicare/Medicaid documentation.
Periodic limb movements are treated only if associated with arousals and daytime sleepiness, and OSA should be treated first.
Zolpidem 5 mg is commonly used as a sleep aid for in-lab studies to help patients fall asleep.
Direct referral to the sleep lab should include documentation of snoring, comorbidities (hypertension, depression, stroke, MI), and OSA risk factors.
For direct referral to a sleep lab, document snoring and medical comorbidities like depression, insomnia, hypertension, MI, or stroke to help qualify for insurance authorization.
On CPAP prescriptions, leave the mask type blank because fit is individualized; heated tubing is recommended to prevent condensation and dry mouth.

episodes.title: Dr. Duininck on Controversies in Medicine 8/27/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Duininck
episodes.abstract: Dr. Duininck opens a family medicine residency lecture on controversies by urging residents to think critically rather than rely on protocols, checklists, and defensive medicine. He emphasizes the importance of asking hard questions and challenging conventional wisdom, even when it feels risky. Using his own experience during the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent vaccine mandate debate, he illustrates how fear, institutional pressure, and a desire not to ‘get in trouble’ can override careful reasoning. The core message is that being a good doctor requires listening, empathy, and the courage to wrestle with difficult issues.
key_points: Residents should cultivate independent thinking, not just memorization and protocol-following.
Defensive medicine, doing tests to avoid lawsuits, undermines thoughtful, patient-centered care.
True physician-patient trust is built through listening, empathy, and affirming patient concerns.
Men often avoid medical care due to fear; physicians should encourage preventive care analogies (e.g. checking truck oil vs. routine health checks).
The COVID-19 pandemic challenged physicians to care for patients despite uncertainty and fear.
Emergency use authorization and rapid mRNA development created legitimate concerns about vaccine safety and necessity among some healthcare workers.
Institutional mandates (e.g. COVID-19 vaccine) can force clinicians to choose between their convictions and their jobs.
The goal of medicine is to serve and care for people, not to protect the physician’s ego or practice defensive medicine.
Patients have the right to decline recommended treatments; physicians should not be offended by non-compliance.
Cannabis is described by the presenter as harmful (psychotic effects, addiction, worse than regular smoking), despite being marketed as safe.
Physicians must be willing to ask hard questions and challenge conventional thought, even at personal risk.
Physicians should distinguish themselves from 'providers' by focusing on connection and relationship rather than simply fulfilling patient requests.

episodes.title: Dr. Duininck on Leadership
episodes.speaker: Dr. Duininck
episodes.abstract: Dr. Duininck discusses the importance of knowing one's true identity, grounded in faith, as a foundation for effective leadership. He contrasts self-protection and self-promotion, which stem from fear and a lack of identity, with the confidence of Jesus, who knew who He was and lived for the Father's approval. The talk applies these principles to residency leadership, parenting, and the unique role of family medicine training as a three-year leadership development course.
key_points: Personality traits like enthusiasm, sensitivity, or steadiness can be strengths but also need to be surrendered to God and refined.
Less than 5% of people, including believers, ever discover their true identity, which is not defined by parents, job title, academics, or personality tests.
True identity is revealed by God personally, and it is out of this identity that purpose and meaning flow.
Jesus knew His identity (e.g., 'I am the light of the world') and therefore was not afraid of people's opinions or threats, even death.
Not knowing one's identity leads to fear, which manifests as self-protection (keeping people at a distance) and self-promotion (proving one's worth).
Leaders are under authority (God and organizational boards), which provides protection and support, not weakness.
Being in charge of others (e.g., residents, children) does not mean being better or smarter, but it carries responsibility for their well-being.
Leadership sometimes requires saying 'no' lovingly, even at the cost of being liked, because the leader answers to God.
Residency at IHI is described as a three-year leadership development intensive course that happens to be in family medicine.
Helping others does not mean doing their work for them; the right action may be to guide rather than take over.
Residency should be viewed as a three-year leadership development intensive, not just clinical training.
Leadership often means saying hard things or biting your tongue, not always taking the easy way out.

episodes.title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn, board-certified in psychiatry and addiction medicine, presents on medication for opioid use disorder (OUD). She defines addiction as a primary chronic brain disease involving reward, motivation, memory, and related circuitry, emphasizing that it is a chronic condition like hypertension or diabetes. She reviews the four waves of the opioid epidemic, from prescription opioids to heroin to fentanyl and now psychostimulant-opioid mixtures. The lecture covers the goals of medication-assisted treatment and the FDA-approved medication options for OUD, with a focus on conceptualizing addiction as a treatable chronic disease rather than a moral failing.
key_points: Addiction is a primary chronic disease of brain reward, motivation, memory, and related circuitry, not a behavioral choice.
The opioid epidemic has four waves: prescription opioids, heroin, fentanyl, and now psychostimulant-opioid mixtures (especially methamphetamine in Oklahoma).
Three out of four heroin users started on prescription pills.
Fentanyl has driven up overdose and poisoning deaths dramatically despite efforts to control the epidemic.
Addiction involves cycles of relapse and remission, like other chronic diseases, and is progressive without treatment.
DSM-5 criteria for opioid use disorder include impaired control, craving, lack of insight, and dysfunctional emotional responses.
Behavioral symptoms of addiction often lead to stigma and isolation, unlike other chronic diseases like cancer.
Medication-assisted treatment (MAT) is a key approach for managing OUD, with FDA-approved options available.
The presenter serves as addiction medicine chief at OSU and runs a multidisciplinary addiction clinic at Legacy Plaza.
Without medication, only 20, 30% of individuals with opioid use disorder remain abstinent at 12 months.
Opioid use disorder carries a sixfold mortality risk; MAT reduces it to less than twofold.
Buprenorphine is a partial agonist that caps receptor activation at 40%, making overdose difficult alone.

episodes.title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Medicine - Antidepressants 9/10/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn introduces an antidepressant lecture for primary care, starting with a case of a 45-year-old woman presenting with fatigue and depressive symptoms. She emphasizes the importance of a broad differential diagnosis including medical causes, bipolar disorder, and suicide risk assessment. The lecture covers validated screening tools, safety planning, and the need to screen for mania before treating depression, as misdiagnosis can lead to harmful treatment. Key mnemonics (SIG E CAPS, DIG FAST) and recommended labs are provided to guide the workup.
key_points: Differential for fatigue and depression includes medical causes such as menopause, hypothyroidism, endocrine disorders, oncologic conditions, neurological diseases, infections, adrenal dysfunction, and iatrogenic effects from medications.
Always perform a suicide risk assessment in depressed patients; use the PHQ-9 question and validated instruments like SAFE-T.
Asking about suicide does not increase risk; studies show it is safe.
Past suicide attempts are strong predictors of future risk.
Bipolar depression is often missed because patients present in the depressed phase; treatment differs from unipolar depression.
Screen for mania using the DIG FAST mnemonic or specific questions about decreased need for sleep, increased energy, risky behaviors, and pressured speech.
Hypomania must last at least 4 days to meet criteria.
Family history of bipolar disorder raises suspicion for bipolar depression.
Obtain labs: vitamin D, thyroid panel, CBC, CMP, and urine drug screen.
Use SIG E CAPS to systematically assess DSM-5 criteria for major depressive episode.
Use SIG E CAPS (Sleep, Interest, Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicidality) to systematically assess depression symptoms.
For MDD, at least one core symptom must be depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure.

episodes.title: Dr. Dunn speaks on Depression
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn presents a case of a 45-year-old woman with fatigue, tearfulness, sleep and appetite changes, and a PHQ-9 score of 17. She reviews the differential diagnosis for depression, emphasizing the importance of screening for mania (using the DIG FAST mnemonic) and conducting a thorough suicide risk assessment. Dr. Dunn explains that all antidepressant classes are equally effective, so selection should be based on tolerability and symptom profiles (atypical vs. melancholic features). She provides practical guidance on starting antidepressants low and slow, obtaining baseline labs without delaying treatment, and avoiding bupropion in patients with co-occurring anxiety.
key_points: PHQ-9 score of 17 indicates moderate to severe depression.
Differential for fatigue includes depression, perimenopause, sleep apnea, endocrine disorders, and substance use.
Always screen for mania before treating depression; use the DIG FAST mnemonic (Distractibility, Indiscretions, Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep deficit, Talkativeness).
Suicide assessment should include thoughts (active vs. passive), plan, past attempts, and preparatory behaviors; asking about suicide does not increase risk.
Antidepressant classes (SSRIs, SNRIs, bupropion, etc.) are equally effective; choose based on tolerability and symptom profile.
SSRIs are the best-tolerated first-line agents; venlafaxine and mirtazapine may work slightly faster.
Bupropion is not a good choice for patients with co-occurring anxiety.
Atypical depression features: mood reactivity, overeating, oversleeping, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity.
Melancholic depression features: extreme anhedonia, no reactivity, diurnal variation (worse in morning), anorexia, weight loss, excessive guilt.
Start antidepressants at a low dose and titrate slowly; obtain baseline labs (CBC, CMP, thyroid) but do not delay treatment.
SSRIs primarily target serotonin; SNRIs target serotonin and norepinephrine; bupropion targets norepinephrine and dopamine.
Bupropion is not ideal for patients with co-occurring anxiety because it can be anxiety-inducing.

episodes.title: Dr. Engstrom on ACS
episodes.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
episodes.abstract: This part of the lecture emphasizes that clinical context and patient appearance often matter more than the EKG alone. Dr. Engstrom discusses subtle EKG findings such as hyperacute T waves and posterior MI indicated by anterior ST depression. He reviews ACS management including the importance of nonenteric aspirin, antiplatelet loading with Brilinta or Plavix, and anticoagulation choices (heparin vs enoxaparin). For STEMI, the 90-minute window for PCI is critical; if not feasible, thrombolytics should be given. He also stresses the need for residents to stay updated and to call cardiology when in doubt.
key_points: Patient's clinical appearance is more important than EKG; call cardiology if patient looks bad.
Hyperacute T waves are tall, symmetrical T waves disproportionate to QRS.
Anterior ST depression in V1-V4 is a posterior MI until proven otherwise; obtain posterior leads (V7-V9).
Aspirin for ACS must be nonenteric coated for rapid absorption.
162 mg of aspirin is sufficient to block all platelets; 325 mg is overdoing it.
Brilinta reduces reocclusion by 6-10% compared to Plavix; preferred for patients getting stents.
For unstable angina/NSTEMI, use heparin if there is a chance of going to cath; use enoxaparin if medical management only.
STEMI: if PCI cannot be done within 90 minutes from identification, give thrombolytics (TPA or TNK).
After thrombolytics, rescue PCI if no resolution of symptoms or EKG normalization.
Time is muscle; act quickly when STEMI is suspected.
For STEMI, if PCI cannot be achieved within 90 minutes of identification, administer fibrinolytics because 'time is muscle'.
In cardiogenic shock from ACS, consider heart block and initiate external pacing if bradycardic; otherwise, use epinephrine or dobutamine for pump failure.

episodes.title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock
episodes.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
episodes.abstract: Dr. Engstrom presents a rapid-fire approach to undifferentiated shock for family medicine residents, covering the four major shock types (cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive, hypovolemic) with clinical cases and bedside pearls. The talk emphasizes recognizing shock as a perfusion problem rather than just low blood pressure, and highlights key management steps including IV access, IO placement, and timely antibiotics in septic shock. The session also reviews vasopressors and specific scenarios like massive PE, tension pneumothorax, and cardiorenal syndrome.
key_points: Shock is defined as lack of perfusion to critical organs, not necessarily low blood pressure; cardiogenic shock can occur with hypertension.
Obstructive shock causes include cardiac tamponade, massive PE, tension pneumothorax, and aortic stenosis; treat the underlying obstruction.
Hypovolemic shock from hemorrhage requires blood products, not just crystalloid, because saline does not carry oxygen.
Distributive shock includes sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock, adrenal crisis, and toxicologic causes; sepsis is the most common.
In septic shock, each hour of delayed antibiotics increases mortality by a relative 35%.
For massive PE with hemodynamic instability, give systemic thrombolytics (TNK/TPA); if stable with right heart strain, consider catheter-directed therapy.
Tension pneumothorax requires immediate needle decompression or chest tube; do not hesitate to call for help.
In cardiogenic shock with cardiorenal syndrome, consider inotropes to improve forward flow.
For shock, establish two large-bore IVs (16 or 18 gauge); if unable, place an intraosseous (IO) line, preferably humeral.
Humeral IO placement: fingertips at armpit, thumbs meet, drill 90 degrees straight in; tibial IO is an alternative about an inch below the knee joint.
Vasopressors are the next step after fluids; specific agents are discussed in the full talk.
Anaphylaxis is diagnosed almost exclusively by history; look for rash or swelling in obtunded patients.

episodes.title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
episodes.abstract: Dr. Engstrom encourages residents to ask questions freely, especially early in training, and to use open evidence to understand clinical reasoning. He discusses discharge planning (dispo) for common ER presentations like seizure, stroke, and chest pain, emphasizing the importance of assessing the patient's expected trajectory. He introduces the Carnett test for abdominal wall pain and highlights the value of giving patients a clear plan even when the diagnosis is uncertain.
key_points: Residents should ask nuanced questions about clinical reasoning, not just lookup-able facts.
Discharge planning hinges on whether the patient's trajectory is improving or declining and whether an intervention will intercept a decline.
For seizures, most patients who seize due to medication non-adherence can be restarted on Keppra and discharged.
A new pattern of multiple seizures (2-4 in days) warrants admission or neurology consultation.
For TIA/stroke rule-out, use the ABCD2 score to guide admission; high-risk TIAs should be admitted or started on aspirin and a statin.
A new type of neurologic deficit (e.g., new visual field cut) requires stroke workup, even if the patient has known hemiplegic migraines.
Stable angina can be discharged; unstable angina (new, severe, or with EKG changes) requires admission.
The HEART score helps stratify chest pain risk; a score >2% 30-day MACE risk warrants admission for rule-out.
When no clear diagnosis is found after workup, give the patient a plan (e.g., next steps like endoscopy) to improve satisfaction.
Carnett's test (pain worse with abdominal flexion) suggests abdominal wall pathology, often from nerve entrapment or strain.
IT band syndrome is a common cause of lateral hip/leg pain; palpation along the IT band reproduces pain.
Carnett's sign (pain worse with abdominal flexion) suggests pain originates from the abdominal wall rather than internal organs, common in mystery abdominal pain workups.

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer on Antibiotics
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ganzer
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ganzer provides a practical, clinically oriented review of antibiotic selection for family medicine residents. He emphasizes a three-question framework: microbiology (does the antibiotic cover the likely organism?), pharmacology (does it reach the infection site?), and patient factors (renal function, drug interactions). He teaches how to read susceptibility reports by antibiotic class rather than individual drugs, enabling lateral switches (e.g., IV cefazolin to oral cephalexin) and appropriate de-escalation. He also highlights organisms with predictable resistance patterns (e.g., Enterobacter cloacae is not covered by ceftriaxone) and stresses memorizing the short list of antibiotics effective against Pseudomonas and MRSA.
key_points: When selecting an antibiotic, ask three questions: Does it cover the organism? Does it reach the infection site? Are there patient factors (CKD, drug interactions) to consider?
Susceptibility reports test antibiotic classes, not individual drugs; susceptibility to cefazolin means susceptibility to all first-generation cephalosporins (e.g., cephalexin).
The lab arranges antibiotics alphabetically, not by spectrum; clinicians must reorder them mentally by class and generation.

Oral vancomycin has no GI absorption and cannot treat skin infections; it is only for C. diff. Nitrofurantoin (Macrobid) works for cystitis but not pyelonephritis due to inadequate renal tissue concentration.
Enterobacter cloacae is inherently resistant to penicillins and second/third-generation cephalosporins; ceftriaxone is the wrong drug even before susceptibilities return.

Pseudomonas and MRSA have a limited number of effective antibiotics; clinicians should memorize the list (e.g., ceftazidime, cefepime, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem for Pseudomonas).
The lab only tests antibiotics known to have efficacy against the identified organism; you will never see amoxicillin or ceftriaxone tested against Pseudomonas.
If a susceptibility panel does not include a desired antibiotic (e.g., cefepime), call the lab; they may have already tested it and can provide the result.
When a penicillin is susceptible, it may be more effective than a cephalosporin against certain resistant patterns; do not automatically escalate to broader agents.
Fluoroquinolones are often avoided due to safety warnings; reserve carbapenems (e.g., meropenem) for highly resistant organisms.
Enterococcus is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins; never use a cephalosporin for Enterococcus.
Effective antibiotics for Pseudomonas include ceftazidime, cefepime, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and meropenem.

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer on Induction of Labor 4/9/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ganzer
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ganzer discusses practical strategies for cervical ripening and induction of labor, focusing on the use of Foley balloons, timing of artificial rupture of membranes (AROM), and high-dose oxytocin. She emphasizes that the balloon's most effective work occurs in the first six hours and can be removed then to shorten induction time. For primiparous patients, she advises delaying AROM until active labor to avoid prolonged rupture of membranes, while for multiparous patients early AROM is safe and effective. She also reviews the use of oral versus vaginal misoprostol in cases of fetal growth restriction or suspected placental insufficiency.
key_points: Foley balloon cervical ripening is most effective in the first six hours; removing it at six hours can shorten overall induction time regardless of cervical dilation.
Balloon can be left in up to 12 hours, but removing earlier (6-8 hours) is reasonable as it provides little additional benefit after that.
Before placing a balloon, perform a cervical exam and assess patient tolerance; if a cervical check causes severe discomfort, the patient is unlikely to tolerate balloon placement.
After balloon placement, wait 45-60 minutes for the patient to settle before starting low-dose oxytocin to allow both methods to work together.
For primiparous patients in latent labor, early AROM (at 3-4 cm) risks prolonged rupture of membranes and infection because latent phase can last many hours.
For multiparous patients, early AROM is safe and highly effective; the cervix has dilated before and often responds dramatically to rupture.
High-dose oxytocin (starting at 2 mU/min and increasing by 2 mU/min every 15-30 minutes) is the standard approach, allowing faster titration to effective contraction patterns.
Failed induction is defined as failure to generate regular contractions and cervical change after 24 hours of oxytocin with AROM if feasible; this is rarely reached.
Oral misoprostol may be preferred over vaginal when there is concern for fetal sensitivity (e.g., fetal growth restriction, poor placenta) because it is less intense and can be stopped if needed.
A Foley balloon will not spontaneously expel until the cervix is 4-5 cm dilated; to check cervical dilation with a balloon in place, deflate the vaginal balloon first.

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer on Knee Injuries
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ganzer
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ganzer presents a lecture on knee injuries for family medicine residents, emphasizing the importance of understanding knee anatomy and biomechanics to guide diagnosis. He reviews the four major ligaments (ACL, PCL, MCL, LCL), the menisci, and the joint capsule, explaining how their structure and function relate to injury mechanisms. The lecture covers key history questions, physical exam techniques including the Lachman test, and the timing of effusion to differentiate between ACL tears and meniscal injuries. Dr. Ganzer highlights that a thorough history and physical exam can be up to 93% as accurate as MRI for diagnosing knee injuries.
key_points: The knee joint consists of the femur, tibia, and patella; the fibula is not part of the knee joint.
The four main ligaments are the ACL, PCL, MCL, and LCL; the cruciate ligaments cross each other and control anterior/posterior translation and rotation.
The menisci are C-shaped cartilages that sit between the femoral condyles and tibial plateau, providing stability.
The knee has the largest joint capsule in the body, extending 3-4 finger breadths above the patella, which allows for large effusions and a safe injection site.
A thorough history and physical exam can be 93% as accurate as MRI for diagnosing knee injuries.
Rapid onset of effusion (within 2 hours) suggests ACL tear or intra-articular fracture; gradual onset (over a day) suggests meniscal tear.
ACL injuries are the most common ligamentous injury, with about 70% occurring in noncontact situations.
ACL injuries are more common in females, possibly due to a larger Q angle increasing valgus stress.
The Lachman test is performed with the knee flexed at 20 degrees, stabilizing the femur and pulling the tibia anteriorly to assess for an endpoint.
In the acute setting, patients may guard with their quadriceps, making the Lachman test difficult to interpret.
Always examine the unaffected knee first to establish a baseline before examining the injured knee.
In acute knee injury, patient guarding can make the Lachman test falsely negative; the pivot shift test may catch the patient off guard and yield a positive result.

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer on Outpatient Management of Kidney Disease
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ganzer
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ganzer presents an outpatient-focused approach to kidney disease, distinguishing acute, subacute, and chronic presentations. The lecture emphasizes a practical algorithm for evaluating a subacute creatinine rise, starting with volume assessment and medication review, then proceeding to urinalysis and renal ultrasound. Key teaching points include the definition of CKD (abnormal kidney function for >3 months), screening recommendations for at-risk populations, and the importance of urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio over 24-hour urine protein. The talk uses case-based learning to illustrate workup for intrinsic renal disease, including glomerulonephritis and interstitial nephritis, and highlights when to involve nephrology.
key_points: Subacute kidney injury is defined as renal dysfunction presumed less than 3 months but not meeting AKI criteria; it is the typical outpatient presentation.
AKI is defined by a rise in creatinine of 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, or a 1.5-fold increase over 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours.
CKD is defined by abnormal kidney structure or function lasting more than 3 months, with health implications including cardiovascular events and progression to ESRD.

For a subacute creatinine rise, first assess volume status and review medications (NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, diuretics); if mild (<0.5 mg/dL rise), advise holding NSAIDs, increasing fluids, and rechecking in 2 weeks.
For moderate-to-severe subacute injury (creatinine rise >0.5 mg/dL), obtain UA, renal ultrasound, and repeat chemistry; if ultrasound shows hydronephrosis, refer to urology.

If ultrasound shows no obstruction, urinalysis guides further workup: RBC casts/dysmorphic RBCs/proteinuria suggest glomerulonephritis; pyuria suggests interstitial nephritis; normal UA suggests prerenal or ATN causes.

Screening for CKD is recommended annually for patients with diabetes or hypertension; consider screening for those with CVD, older age, obesity, history of preeclampsia, low birth weight, or family history of CKD.

Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) has replaced 24-hour urine protein due to better convenience and accuracy; urine dipstick alone may miss clinically significant proteinuria in the 30-300 mg/g range.
CKD is more common in women, but men are more likely to progress to ESRD.
In patients with known CKD and new symptoms (joint pain, rash), consider serologic workup (e.g., ANA for lupus) along with other tests like SPEP, hepatitis C, and HIV.
Screen for CKD with serum creatinine, eGFR, and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR); 24-hour urine protein is no longer recommended.
UACR should be obtained on a morning or early afternoon sample; dipstick urinalysis alone misses clinically significant proteinuria (30, 300 mg/g).

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer on Prenatal Screening for Chromosomal Abnormalities of the Fetus 9/4/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ganzer
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ganzer presents a lecture on prenatal screening for fetal chromosomal abnormalities, covering the etiology of aneuploidy and copy number variants, common screening tests (quad screen, first-trimester screening, cell-free DNA), and their performance characteristics. She emphasizes that cell-free DNA (NIPS) is now preferred due to higher sensitivity and specificity, though it does not screen for neural tube defects. The talk also reviews ultrasound markers of aneuploidy, the importance of operator skill in ultrasound interpretation, and the need for sensitive counseling to avoid provoking patient anxiety.
key_points: Aneuploidy is defined as an extra or missing chromosome; copy number variants (microdeletions/duplications) are smaller losses or gains.
Chromosomal abnormalities occur in about 1 in 155 births; Down syndrome is the most common aneuploidy.
Risk of aneuploidy increases with maternal age due to nondisjunction in meiosis I, but most children with trisomy 21 are born to younger parents because more births occur in that group.
Copy number variants (microarray abnormalities) occur in ~0.4% of pregnancies and are independent of maternal age; at age 36, risk of these abnormalities exceeds risk of aneuploidy.
Cell-free DNA (NIPS) is much more sensitive and specific than the quad screen and is now the preferred screening test when prenatal screening is performed.
The quad screen (AFP tetra) also screens for neural tube defects, which cell-free DNA does not; anatomy scan at 20 weeks catches most but not all neural tube defects.
First-trimester screening combines nuchal translucency ultrasound (>3.5 mm abnormal) with PAPP-A and beta-hCG; sensitivity is only ~70%.
Quad screen sensitivity is ~75% for women under 35 and ~80% for women over 35.
Ultrasound markers of aneuploidy include thickened nuchal fold, echogenic bowel, echogenic intracardiac foci, and pyelectasis; many resolve or are operator-dependent.
Resolved ultrasound findings should not be carried forward in the medical record to avoid unnecessary patient anxiety.
Screening tests are only as accurate as the skill of the person acquiring the data.
Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening is the most sensitive and specific screening test for common fetal aneuploidies but is not diagnostic; positive predictive value can be as low as 50%.

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer Overviews Gestational Diabetes
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ganzer
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ganzer provides an overview of gestational diabetes management, emphasizing the importance of tight glycemic control to improve maternal and fetal outcomes. The lecture covers terminology (GDM A1 vs A2), screening timing (24-28 weeks routinely, earlier for high-risk patients), and the rationale for using insulin over newer agents in pregestational diabetes. Key resources include the California Sweet Success program and perinatology.com. The speaker stresses that hyperglycemia is teratogenic in early pregnancy and that GDM represents a spectrum of risk, not an on-off switch.
key_points: GDM A1 is diet-controlled; GDM A2 requires medication (insulin or oral agents).
Hyperglycemia in the first 8 weeks is teratogenic, causing cardiac anomalies and spontaneous abortion.
Preconception counseling is critical for pregestational diabetics to achieve A1c <6% before pregnancy.
Metformin is safe in pregnancy and can be continued; GLP-1s and SGLT2s lack safety data and should be avoided.
Routine GDM screening occurs at 24-28 weeks; early screening (16-20 weeks) is indicated for high-risk patients (BMI >25, first-degree relative with diabetes, history of GDM).
A1c is unreliable in pregnancy due to anemia and increased RBC turnover; glucose challenge testing is preferred.
The HAPO study demonstrated a continuous linear relationship between maternal hyperglycemia and adverse outcomes (LGA, neonatal hypoglycemia, cesarean delivery).
After delivery, insulin requirements drop dramatically as the placenta is removed; true GDM resolves postpartum.
