Postpartum glucose testing is done to rule out overt diabetes, not to manage GDM.
Pregestational diabetes patients are often referred to MFM due to logistical challenges and high complication risk.
General screening for GDM occurs at 24-28 weeks; early screening for high-risk patients is ideal at 16-20 weeks.
Patients with a history of GDM can be managed before 20 weeks if glucose intolerance is already evident.

episodes.title: Dr. Gerald C. Miller on Syphilis Testing Tools and Interpretation of Results
episodes.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller

also_uploaded.title: Dr. Gerald C Miller on Syphilis Testing Tools and Interpretation of Results

episodes.abstract: Dr. Gerald C. Miller emphasizes that the physician's clinical history is the gold standard for syphilis diagnosis, not laboratory tests. He explains the natural history of syphilis, including incubation periods, the progression from primary chancre to secondary rash, and the fact that only one-third of untreated patients progress to late-stage disease. He details the interpretation of nontreponemal (RPR) and treponemal tests, highlighting false positives (11% overall, common in pregnancy and autoimmune disease), false negatives (especially in late-stage disease where 25% lose RPR reactivity), and the serofast phenomenon. The lecture stresses the importance of correlating all lab results with clinical history and challenging discordant results.
key_points: The physician's clinical history is the gold standard for syphilis diagnosis, not laboratory tests.
Only 10 organisms are needed to establish infection, with an incubation period of 10 to 90 days depending on inoculum size.
The chancre of primary syphilis is painless and heals in 2-6 weeks; it may be absent in some patients.
Two-thirds of untreated patients will spontaneously resolve or control their infection; only one-third progress to late-stage disease over 5-30 years.
RPR has an 11% false positive rate overall; titers of 1:4 or greater have 98% specificity.
Pregnancy, autoimmune diseases (especially lupus), IV drug use, and various infections can cause false positive RPRs.
In late-stage syphilis (late latent and tertiary), 25% of patients lose RPR reactivity, making it impossible to monitor treatment response.
The serofast phenomenon occurs when treated patients' titers drop to 1:1, 1:2, or 1:4 and do not decline further despite adequate treatment.
Treatment response is monitored by a fourfold drop in RPR titer over 3-6 months.
Reinfection causes a rapid rise in titer within 3-4 days due to memory cell response.
Immunocompromised patients (HIV, steroids) may have low or negative RPR titers despite active infection.
The reverse algorithm uses treponemal antibody screening first; a reactive treponemal test with a positive RPR indicates active syphilis.

episodes.title: Dr. Glaser on Medical Advocacy 6/11/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Glaser
episodes.abstract: Dr. Glaser, a family physician with almost 30 years of experience, presents a lecture on medical advocacy from a Christian perspective. She defines advocacy as promoting the interests of individuals or groups through recommendations and support, emphasizing the inherent dignity of every person. Dr. Glaser shares her personal journey, including her shock at the AAFP's 2018 shift from opposing assisted suicide to neutrality, which motivated her advocacy work. She outlines barriers to advocacy, such as time constraints and fear of negative consequences, and encourages residents to identify their unique qualifications and passions for advocacy within their professional organizations.
key_points: Physician advocacy involves promoting social, economic, educational, and political changes that reduce suffering and threats to health, as identified through professional work and expertise.
The goal of medicine is to restore people to wholeness while respecting their inviolable inherent dignity, viewing them as more than biological specimens.
Christian reasons for advocacy include affirming the inherent dignity of every person, advocating for the marginalized, and upholding Christ-centered values of justice and mercy.
In 2018, the AAFP Congress of Delegates changed its position from opposing medical aid in dying to neutral, using the euphemism 'medical aid in dying' for assisted suicide.
Advocacy requires working upstream to address social determinants of health and root causes of suffering, such as hunger, homelessness, and illness.
Barriers to advocacy include time constraints, fear of damaging trust with patients, negative publicity, cancel culture, and lack of Christian role models.
Professional medical organizations like the AMA, AAFP, and ACGME include advocacy in their residency curriculum and professional expectations.
Effective advocacy can occur at the state and national level through developing resolutions to change policy within medical organizations like the AAFP.
Dr. Glaser serves as co-chair of the Physicians for Life Interest Group within the AAFP, which has nearly 700 members.
The CMDA offers a mentoring academy and an advocacy academy to help model faith and medicine integration for advocacy work.
Common barriers to advocacy include fear of cancel culture, belief that advocacy doesn't make a difference, and lack of time or training.
Advocacy begins with prayer, seeking counsel, identifying unique gifts, and taking risks.

episodes.title: Dr. Greer on Anxiety & Depression 5/7/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Greer
episodes.abstract: Dr. Greer discusses first-line and second-line medications for anxiety and depression, focusing on SSRIs and SNRIs. She notes the high overlap of anxiety and depression (~95%) and emphasizes SSRIs as first-line. She provides specific dosing guidance for elderly patients, pregnancy, and PMDD, and highlights side effect profiles, including QT prolongation with citalopram and sexual dysfunction with SSRIs. She also covers cross-titration strategies for switching medications and the role of bupropion for atypical depression.
key_points: Anxiety and depression now overlap in about 95% of cases, unlike the past when only ~30% overlapped.
SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, citalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine) are first-line for both anxiety and depression.
Escitalopram and citalopram are isomer molecules; failure on one usually means failure on the other.
Citalopram prolongs the QT interval, especially at 40 mg, so the dose is capped there.
In elderly patients, use escitalopram, citalopram, or sertraline; max doses: escitalopram 10 mg, citalopram 20 mg.
Sertraline is first-line in pregnancy and is more stimulating, so take it in the morning.
Fluoxetine is useful for PMDD and can be taken only perimenstrually (2 days before period until period ends).
Paroxetine has the worst side effect profile (sexual dysfunction, weight gain, interactions) but may work for refractory anxiety.
SNRIs (venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine) are second-line after failure of two SSRIs.
Duloxetine requires higher doses (60 mg, possibly 60 mg BID) for benefit; may help chronic pain modestly.
Do not combine an SSRI and an SNRI because both act on serotonin receptors.
Bupropion is used for atypical depression (lack of motivation, not sadness) and smoking cessation, not as first-line monotherapy.

episodes.title: Dr. Greta Warta on Valve Diseases 11/6/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Greta Warta
episodes.abstract: Dr. Greta Warta, an Ascension cardiologist, presents a lecture on aortic valve stenosis for family medicine residents, focusing on outpatient evaluation and management. She covers causes including degenerative calcific stenosis in older adults and bicuspid aortic valve in younger patients, pathophysiology, symptoms of severe disease, physical exam findings, and interpretation of echocardiographic parameters. Key teaching points include surveillance intervals based on severity, cautious blood pressure management to avoid decompensation, referral triggers, and the importance of detecting murmurs on every patient every visit.
key_points: Aortic stenosis is the most common valvular disorder seen in clinic and hospital.
Bicuspid aortic valve leads to valve replacement in the 5th-6th decade, while degenerative stenosis typically presents after age 80.
Symptoms of severe AS (syncope, dizziness, angina, dyspnea) only appear with severe stenosis; mild-moderate AS is asymptomatic.
Physical exam findings: harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, soft/absent S2, parvus et tardus pulses, possible S4 gallop.
Echo surveillance: mild AS every 3-5 years, moderate asymptomatic every 1-2 years, severe asymptomatic every 6-12 months.
In bicuspid aortic valve, also monitor the thoracic aorta; surgical threshold for aortic dilation is 4.5 cm (vs 5.0 cm for others).
Any diastolic murmur is pathologic and warrants cardiology referral.
Control hypertension cautiously in AS; aggressive BP lowering or diuresis can cause decompensation.
Refer for valve replacement when symptomatic, even if echo measurements seem discordant.
TAVR is now available for intermediate and low-risk patients with excellent outcomes.
Endocarditis prophylaxis: current guidelines only for prosthetic valve or prior endocarditis; speaker uses old guidelines for severe AS with major dental work.
Listen to heart, lungs, and carotids every single visit to avoid missing murmurs or bruits.

episodes.title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
episodes.abstract: Dr. Greuel presents a practical approach to first-trimester pregnancy loss, emphasizing two core principles: determining whether a live pregnancy exists and ensuring reliable follow-up. He reviews definitions of miscarriage types (anembryonic gestation, embryonic demise, incomplete abortion) and discusses expectant, medical, and surgical management options. The talk covers ultrasound technique, the use of misopoprostol with or without mifepristone, Rhogam administration, and patient counseling including bleeding precautions. He highlights the importance of serial HCG monitoring and systematic ultrasound scanning to avoid missed ectopic pregnancy.
key_points: The two essential questions in miscarriage management are: is there a live pregnancy, and is follow-up reliably arranged?
Anembryonic gestation (blighted ovum) is diagnosed when mean sac diameter >25 mm with no fetal pole on transvaginal ultrasound.
Embryonic demise is defined by crown-rump length >7 mm with no fetal heartbeat on transvaginal ultrasound.
Expectant management success rates: ~25% pass within 1 week of diagnosis, another 27% in the second week, then smaller gains thereafter.
Medical management with misoprostol alone is 84% effective by day 8; adding mifepristone increases efficacy to 88%.
Misoprostol dosing: 800 mcg (four 200 mcg tablets) placed vaginally, repeat in 24-48 hours if needed.
Rhogam should be given to Rh-negative patients with miscarriage (weak evidence, low risk).
Baseline CBC is recommended before medical or surgical management.
ER precautions for patients: bleeding >2 pads/hour for 2 hours, fever >101°F, uncontrolled pain, signs of anemia.
Systematic ultrasound scanning: use at least two orthogonal views (sagittal and transverse) to fully evaluate the uterus.
Discriminatory zone for HCG is 1500-3000 IU/L; below this, an intrauterine pregnancy may not be visible.
Pseudogestational sac can mimic early pregnancy; careful measurement and correlation with HCG are needed to avoid missing ectopic pregnancy.

episodes.title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
episodes.abstract: Dr. Greuel discusses management of fetal malpresentation in the third trimester, focusing on face presentations and manual rotation of occiput posterior (OP) position. He explains that mentum anterior face presentations can deliver vaginally because the chin flexes the head naturally, but mentum posterior leads to obstruction and requires cesarean. For OP rotation, he emphasizes that success is limited, often only 20-30 degrees, and requires a complete cervix and adequate anesthesia to avoid cervical laceration. He frames manual rotation as a last-ditch effort before cesarean, noting that success is more likely when the fetal body is not directly OP.
key_points: Face presentation with mentum anterior can deliver vaginally because the chin causes natural head flexion through the pelvis.
Mentum posterior face presentation will not resolve and requires cesarean delivery.
Manual rotation of occiput posterior position is often difficult, usually achieving only 20-30 degrees of rotation.
Successful manual rotation requires a completely dilated cervix to avoid cervical laceration.
Manual rotation is best attempted as a last-ditch effort before proceeding to cesarean section.
The procedure is more likely to succeed if the fetal body is lying on its side rather than directly OP.
Adequate anesthesia, such as an epidural, is necessary for manual rotation due to the pressure required.
If labor is not progressing or there is fetal distress, a low threshold for cesarean section is appropriate.
All non-vertex, non-face presentations (e.g., brow, ear) are not amenable to vaginal delivery.
Manual rotation success rates are lower than those for vacuum-assisted delivery.

episodes.title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jacob Greuel presents a comprehensive overview of early pregnancy loss (miscarriage) for family medicine residents. He emphasizes the importance of sensitive communication, appropriate timing of discussions, and respecting patient autonomy. The talk covers definitions (4, 13 weeks), common myths (e.g., exams do not cause miscarriage), initial assessment including CBC, quantitative hCG, Rh type, and ultrasound criteria for anembryonic gestation and embryonic demise. Management options are expectant, medical (misoprostol), and surgical (uterine aspiration). Key priorities include ruling out ectopic pregnancy urgently and providing follow-up until resolution.
key_points: Nearly 1 in 4 women experience early pregnancy loss (4, 13 weeks).
About 50% of miscarriages are caused by chromosomal anomalies.
Routine pelvic exams, Pap smears, and transvaginal ultrasounds do not statistically increase miscarriage risk.
Initial labs should include CBC, quantitative hCG, and Rh type; baseline hCG helps trend.
Transvaginal ultrasound is the most reliable method; gestational sac should be visible at hCG ~2,000.
hCG rise of 1.5, 2× in 48, 72 hours is suggestive but not definitive; hCG plateaus after 9 weeks.
Ectopic pregnancy must be evaluated urgently if not ruled out; pain is a key symptom.
Management options: expectant (up to 90% effective for incomplete abortion), misoprostol, or uterine aspiration.
Patient preference strongly influences mental health outcomes; allow time to decide unless safety requires action.
Follow-up weekly until resolution; completed miscarriage shows echogenic endometrial stripe or homogeneous uterus with closed cavity.
Color flow Doppler can help distinguish retained placental tissue from blood clot in nonviable pregnancy.
Patients can switch between expectant, medical, and surgical management at any time.

episodes.title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
episodes.abstract: Dr. Greuel presents a practical guide to performing and interpreting transvaginal ultrasounds in a family medicine setting. He covers patient preparation, probe orientation, and scanning technique, emphasizing the importance of a systematic approach to identify the uterus and adnexa. Key diagnostic criteria for early pregnancy, including the double decidual sign and mean sac diameter, are reviewed. The lecture also addresses the evaluation of ectopic pregnancy, anembryonic gestation, and the clinical significance of free fluid in the posterior cul-de-sac.
key_points: Transvaginal ultrasound is preferred for early pregnancy evaluation, especially when spontaneous abortion is suspected, as it may avoid a hospital visit.
Always start a new patient on the machine to clear prior measurements and ensure the correct probe is selected.
Use a condom over the probe with ultrasound gel inside and lubricating gel on the outside; check for latex allergies.
Advance the probe slowly along the posterior vaginal wall, looking for the homogeneous myometrium and the bright endometrial stripe.
Stabilize the probe with your pinky on the patient's thigh and use your dominant hand for scanning.
Keep the uterus centered on the screen and scan systematically from one adnexa to the other to avoid missing twins, heterotopic pregnancy, or ovarian cysts.
A true gestational sac is rounded or elliptical in two planes, eccentric to the endometrial stripe, and shows a double decidual sign; it grows about 1 mm per day.
If no intrauterine pregnancy is seen, scan the adnexa for masses and the posterior cul-de-sac for fluid, as free fluid may indicate ruptured ectopic or infection.
Crown-rump length is the average of three measurements from the top of the head to the bottom of the buttocks; switch to Hadlock biometry at 14 weeks.
By 6 weeks, a fetal pole with cardiac activity should be visible on transvaginal ultrasound; if absent, consider anembryonic gestation and repeat in one week.
A pregnancy of undetermined location should be treated as ectopic until an intrauterine gestational sac is confirmed.
Document the study as a 'limited' ultrasound, not a complete pelvic ultrasound, for coding purposes.

episodes.title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro Exam
episodes.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hadwen reviews the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) as a standardized screening exam for acute neurological changes. He emphasizes using MDCalc, asking month and age for level of consciousness, testing commands without demonstration, and performing horizontal gaze and binocular visual fields. He highlights that a change of 3+ points or an initial score of 4+ indicates a disabling stroke and potential tPA candidacy. Practical tips include speaking loudly for hearing-impaired patients and scoring baseline deficits conservatively.
key_points: NIHSS is a standardized exam with high inter-rater reliability; use MDCalc to guide scoring.
For level of consciousness, ask the month and the patient's age, not orientation to place.
For commands, tell the patient to make a fist without demonstrating and without placing your fingers in their hand to avoid reflexive grasp.
Test extraocular movements horizontally only, holding your finger 2, 2.5 feet away.
Test visual fields binocularly by flashing fingers in the four quadrants while the patient looks at your nose.
Arms are held up for 10 seconds, legs for 5 seconds during motor testing.
A change of 3 or more on NIHSS suggests a significant neurological change; an initial score of 4 or more is considered disabling and in tPA range.
Perform NIHSS for any change in mental status, not just focal deficits.
After the mental status portion, you may demonstrate motor tasks (pantomime) to the patient.
For patients with baseline visual deficits, score conservatively; do not subtract points for chronic findings.

episodes.title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hadwen leads a family-medicine residency prep session focused on neurology topics for the ITE. She covers peripheral nerve injuries (radial, median, ulnar, lateral femoral cutaneous, peroneal), including exam techniques, etiology, and management. The session also reviews cluster headache diagnosis and treatment, and introduces the SNOOP mnemonic for identifying secondary headache red flags. Practical, exam-oriented pearls are emphasized throughout.
key_points: Use the opponens pollicis ‘circle test’ (resisting pull-apart) to assess median nerve function.
Ulnar nerve function can be quickly checked by asking the patient to splay their fingers while you try to squeeze them together.
Radial nerve injury presents with wrist drop and inability to extend fingers at the MCP or DIP joints.
Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression) is benign, typically seen in larger men, and managed with weight loss and avoiding tight belts.
Common peroneal nerve injury (foot drop) is often caused by rapid weight loss (e.g., GLP-1 agonists) or prolonged kneeling.
Differentiate peroneal nerve palsy from L5 radiculopathy by testing ankle eversion; if both dorsiflexion and eversion are weak, the lesion is higher.
Foot drop from peroneal nerve injury should be treated with a stiff ankle-foot orthosis to prevent tripping.
Acute cluster headache responds to high-flow oxygen; prophylaxis includes topiramate and verapamil, while lithium is reserved due to its side effects.
Use the SNOOP mnemonic to screen for secondary headache red flags that warrant imaging or emergent evaluation.
Primary headaches (migraine, tension, cluster) do not show significant findings on brain imaging and are managed with specific therapies.

Distinguish primary headaches (migraine, tension, cluster, trigeminal neuralgia) from secondary headaches by history; primary headaches show no imaging findings except microvascular changes if over 50.
Thunderclap headache (peak within 1 minute) requires urgent ER evaluation for subarachnoid hemorrhage.

episodes.title: Dr. Haney- CHF
episodes.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
episodes.abstract: Dr. Haney presents an outpatient-focused review of congestive heart failure (CHF), emphasizing that it is a clinical syndrome defined by structural/functional heart impairment and symptoms. He distinguishes between NYHA functional classification (which can change) and ACC/AHA staging (which does not), reviews common causes (ischemic disease, hypertension, valvular disease) and less common ones, and discusses the role of BNP as one piece of the diagnostic picture. The core of the talk is guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), starting with sacubitril/valsartan.
key_points: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome characterized by structural or functional impairment of the heart causing symptoms; it is not diagnosed by a single test.
BNP >400 is consistent with CHF, BNP <100 makes CHF unlikely, but BNP is only one piece of the picture and should not be used alone to diagnose.
NYHA functional classification (class I-IV) describes symptom burden and can improve with treatment; ACC/AHA staging (A-D) describes disease progression and does not reverse.
Common causes of heart failure include ischemic heart disease, hypertension, and valvular disease; also consider diabetes, atrial fibrillation, rheumatologic disorders, and peripartum cardiomyopathy.
On exam, JVD is highly specific for CHF but not sensitive; IVC >2.1 cm with <50% collapse on ultrasound is also specific.
Initial workup for suspected CHF includes echocardiogram, labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, iron panel, urinalysis), EKG, and chest X-ray.
HFrEF is defined by ejection fraction ≤40%; HFmrEF is 41-49%; HFpEF is ≥50%; each is treated somewhat differently.
Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for HFrEF begins with sacubitril/valsartan (an ARNI), which can elevate BNP due to neprilysin inhibition.
A predischarge BNP that has not decreased significantly may predict readmission, but should not alone delay discharge.
Outpatient CHF management is more challenging than inpatient because it relies on gradual medication titration and patient education rather than IV diuresis.
GDMT for HFrEF includes four pillars: ARNI (or ACE/ARB), beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate), spironolactone, and SGLT2 inhibitor.
All four GDMT drugs reduce hospitalizations and mortality; diuretics improve symptoms but do not reduce mortality.

episodes.title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology
episodes.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
episodes.abstract: Dr. Haney reviews the epidemiology, classification, diagnosis, and initial management of heart failure in the outpatient setting. He emphasizes the importance of distinguishing between NYHA functional class and ACC/AHA staging, using BNP judiciously, recognizing sensitive and specific exam findings, and initiating guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) with four pillars. A case example illustrates classification and workup.
key_points: Common causes of CHF are hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and valvular disease.
NYHA functional classification describes symptom severity and can change over time; ACC/AHA staging is fixed (A: at risk, B: pre-heart failure, C: symptomatic, D: advanced).
BNP >400 is specific for CHF, <100 rules out CHF; values 100, 400 are equivocal.
Sensitive symptoms (dyspnea on exertion, peripheral edema, weight gain) if absent make CHF unlikely.
Specific symptoms (orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea) and signs (JVD, laterally displaced PMI, IVC dilation with poor collapse) strongly suggest CHF.
Initial workup for new CHF includes CBC, chem14, lipid panel, iron panel, PSA, UA, EKG, chest X-ray, and echocardiogram.
HF classification by ejection fraction: HFrEF (≤40%), HFmrEF (41, 49%), HFpEF (≥50%), and HFimpEF (improved from ≤40%).
GDMT for HFrEF consists of four pillars (four guideline-directed medications).
Pre-discharge BNP is a strong predictor of readmission in hospitalized CHF patients.

GDMT for HFrEF consists of four pillars: ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan), beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, or metoprolol succinate), MRA (spironolactone or eplerenone), and SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin).
ARNI reduces hospitalization and mortality by about 20% compared to ACE inhibitors; a 36-hour washout is required when switching from an ACE inhibitor due to angioedema risk.
Beta-blockers should be started before discharge, but not during an acute exacerbation when cardiac output is low.

episodes.title: Dr. Haney on I-Pass and Senior Addendum
episodes.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
episodes.abstract: Dr. Haney leads a discussion on improving handoffs using the I-PASS framework, emphasizing that handoffs should be tailored to the recipient (e.g., night vs. day team) and focus on active problems rather than chronic details. He highlights that too much information can be harmful, citing a 2014 NEJM study showing a 23% reduction in medical errors and 30% reduction in adverse events with standardized handoffs. The I-PASS components, Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situational awareness, and Synthesis, are reviewed, with emphasis on the action list and if-then contingency planning.
key_points: Handoffs should be tailored to the recipient: overnight coverage needs different information than the day team.
More handoffs lead to more errors; minimizing unnecessary transitions improves safety.
Handoffs should focus on active problems and what the covering person needs to know, not chronic issues or the writer's own to-do list.
A 2014 NEJM study found standardized handoff programs reduced medical errors by 23% and adverse events by 30%.
I-PASS stands for Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situational awareness, and Synthesis.
Illness severity categories: stable, watcher (potential to decompensate), unstable.
The action list is the to-do list for the covering person; it should be where they take notes.
Situational awareness includes if-then contingency plans (e.g., 'If potassium is 2.5, replace and adjust diuretic').
Handoffs should not be written as a reminder for the writer; they are for the covering clinician.
Too much information in a handoff is a negative; brevity and pertinence are key.

episodes.title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy
episodes.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
episodes.abstract: Dr. Haney introduces vaccine hesitancy as a state of indecision before action, not outright refusal. He presents data showing increasing hesitancy, with measles vaccination rates declining in Oklahoma and across the US due to factors like the pandemic, decreased trust, and social media misinformation. He emphasizes that measles is not a benign disease and that understanding the safety process and evidence-based communication is key. This first part sets the stage for discussing the case for immunizations and how to counsel hesitant patients.
key_points: Vaccine hesitancy is defined as indecision or uncertainty before a decision to act, not outright refusal.
87.5% of respondents in the clinic poll encounter vaccine hesitancy, but only 2 feel confident in discussing immunizations.
Measles vaccination rates in Oklahoma dropped from 92.2% in 2018-19 to lower levels by 2022-23, partly due to access issues during the pandemic and exemptions.
Vaccine hesitancy is increasing due to decreased trust, political polarization, and social media misinformation.
The 1998 Wakefield paper linking MMR to autism and the rise of Google contributed to persistent vaccine concerns.
Thimerosal does not cause harm; the AAP removed it preemptively from most vaccines.
In 2024, there were 121 measles cases in the US, mostly in under-5s; many hospitalizations are for infection control, not severe illness.
Globally, Kazakhstan had over 27,000 measles cases due to low vaccination rates.
Measles is not a benign disease and can cause serious complications beyond mortality.
Personal stories about why vaccination matters can be more persuasive than clinical data alone.
Vaccine hesitancy concerns include autism, thimerosal, aluminum, fetal cell lines, autonomy, and distrust of authorities.
Babies are exposed to more aluminum from breastfeeding than from vaccines.

episodes.title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies
episodes.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hannah Howard presents a practical guide to skin biopsies and common dermatologic diagnoses for family medicine residents. She contrasts shave and punch biopsies, emphasizing that shave biopsies are preferred for suspected melanoma to provide the pathologist with the full lesion. She reviews benign skin findings such as cherry angiomas, seborrheic keratoses, and dermatofibromas, and discusses management of warts, molluscum, and infantile hemangiomas. Key clinical pearls include marking biopsy sites before numbing, always sending a differential diagnosis with pathology, and using the Mohs AUC app to guide referrals.
key_points: Shave biopsies are preferred for suspected melanoma because they provide the pathologist with the full lesion for accurate diagnosis.
Punch biopsies are preferred for rashes because they capture deeper skin layers needed for histologic evaluation.
Always mark the biopsy site before injecting lidocaine with epinephrine to avoid blanching that obscures the lesion.
Send all excised tissue to pathology; the only common exception is an obvious skin tag.
Provide the pathologist with a differential diagnosis and as much clinical information as possible on the requisition form.
Take photos of the biopsy site, at least on the patient's phone, and upload to the medical record if possible.
If a pathology report seems inconsistent, check whether a dermatopathologist read the specimen.
Squamous cell carcinoma causes more deaths annually in the U.S. than melanoma due to its higher prevalence.
Mohs surgery offers the smallest scar by allowing real-time margin assessment; the Mohs AUC app helps determine if a lesion meets criteria for Mohs referral.

Infantile hemangiomas may require systemic treatment (e.g., oral propranolol) if they are large, ulcerated, or in cosmetically sensitive areas; referral is needed for >5 lesions or midline lumbosacral location.
Infantile hemangiomas on central face, ears, breast, midline lumbosacral, >4 cm, or ≥5 lesions warrant specialist referral.
Superficial hemangiomas can be treated with topical timolol one drop twice daily; oral propranolol is for complicated cases.

episodes.title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy
episodes.speaker: Dr. Hannah Youmans
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Hannah Youmans covers hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, including definitions of gestational hypertension, preeclampsia with and without severe features, eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, and chronic hypertension. She discusses diagnostic criteria, such as blood pressure thresholds and laboratory findings, and emphasizes that proteinuria is no longer required for diagnosing preeclampsia with severe features if end-organ damage is present. Prevention strategies include low-dose aspirin (81 mg) starting at 12, 18 weeks for high-risk women and calcium only for those with hypocalcemia. Outpatient management is appropriate for non-severe gestational hypertension, while severe-range blood pressures or preeclampsia with severe features warrant immediate referral to labor and delivery.
key_points: Gestational hypertension requires SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90 after 20 weeks, corrected from the initial 120/90 error.
Preeclampsia without severe features = gestational hypertension + proteinuria (≥300 mg/24h or P:C ratio ≥0.3).
Preeclampsia with severe features: SBP ≥160 or DBP ≥110, plus end-organ damage; proteinuria not required.
Eclampsia is new-onset seizures (usually tonic-clonic) in the setting of preeclampsia; can present with seizures alone.
HELLP syndrome: hemolysis (LDH >600), elevated liver enzymes (>2× ULN), low platelets (<100,000).
Prophylactic aspirin 81 mg starting 12, 18 weeks reduces preeclampsia risk but does not prevent it completely.
Calcium supplementation only lowers risk in women with documented hypocalcemia; no benefit in non-deficient women.
For suspected preeclampsia, obtain CBC (platelets), CMP (creatinine, LFTs), and urine P:C ratio; 2+ dipstick protein is acceptable in resource-poor settings.
Non-severe gestational hypertension (BP 140, 150s) can be managed outpatient with weekly NST, BP check, glucose check, and growth ultrasound every 3 weeks.
Delivery at 38 weeks is recommended for gestational hypertension; severe-range BP or preeclampsia with severe features requires immediate delivery.
Lifelong cardiovascular risk is increased after hypertensive disorders of pregnancy; follow-up is important.
Gestational hypertension without severe features can be managed outpatient with weekly MFM visits including NST, blood pressure check, glucose check, and growth ultrasounds every three weeks.

episodes.title: Dr. Harris on Polycythemia Vera
episodes.speaker: Dr. Harris
episodes.abstract: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by overproduction of myeloid cells, especially red blood cells, and carries a median survival of 18 months untreated (13 years treated). It is often found incidentally via elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit; common symptoms include fatigue, insomnia, and difficulty concentrating. Diagnosis requires ruling out secondary causes, then checking JAK2 mutation and erythropoietin level, with bone marrow biopsy as the gold standard. Treatment focuses on therapeutic phlebotomy to keep hematocrit <45%, low-dose aspirin for thrombosis prophylaxis, and cytoreductive therapy (hydroxyurea, interferon, or busulfan) for high-risk patients.
key_points: PV is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm with elevated red blood cell mass, differentiating it from other MPNs.
Untreated median survival is 18 months; treated median survival is 13 years.
Most often found incidentally; three most common symptoms are fatigue, insomnia, and difficulty concentrating.
Aquagenic pruritus (itching worse with warm water, typically within 10 minutes) is a distinctive symptom, worst on chest, back, medial arms, and ventral legs.
Erythromelalgia, burning pain with erythema in hands/feet, is considered pathognomonic for PV.
PV is a hypercoagulable state with increased risk of thrombosis and hemorrhage; acquired von Willebrand disease can occur, especially with platelets over 1 million.
Key labs: elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit, leukocytes >10,000, elevated LDH, decreased erythropoietin, and JAK2 mutation (98% of patients).
Diagnostic cutoffs: hemoglobin >16.5 or hematocrit ≥49% in males; hemoglobin >16 or hematocrit ≥48% in females.
Rule out secondary causes (cardiopulmonary disease, high altitude, testosterone, sleep apnea, smoking, etc.) before diagnosing PV.
Therapeutic phlebotomy goal: hematocrit <45% for both genders; one unit (500 mL) reduces hematocrit by 3 percentage points.
Do not give iron to PV patients undergoing phlebotomy, as phlebotomy works by creating iron deficiency.
High-risk patients (age >60 or prior thrombosis) may need cytoreductive therapy, hydroxyurea is most recommended due to cost and side-effect profile.

episodes.title: Dr. Hermann on Adult Wellness
episodes.speaker: Dr. Herrmann
episodes.abstract: Dr. Herrmann presents a practical guide to adult wellness visits, covering billing nuances, screening questions, physical exam components, and efficiency tips. He emphasizes that wellness visits are primarily for building relationships and delivering preventive care, even though evidence for mortality reduction is weak. Key billing points include when to add modifier 25 for a new problem and how to add a wellness code to a Medicare sick visit. Screening should follow USPSTF grade A/B recommendations: anxiety, depression, fall prevention, partner violence, tobacco, alcohol, and drug use. The physical exam should be tailored to age, with extra attention to skin and gait in older patients, and diabetics should be referred for formal eye exams. Efficiency tips include charting in two to three minutes, reviewing history quickly, and double-checking medications.
key_points: Wellness visits are not proven to decrease mortality but build relationships and allow preventive care.
If a patient has a minor illness during a wellness visit, you can bill both with modifier 25 (if you order labs/meds) or just the wellness visit to avoid patient charges.
For Medicare patients, you can add the wellness code to a sick visit because it is just a questionnaire.
USPSTF grade A/B screenings for adults include anxiety (18, 64), depression, fall prevention (65+), partner violence (women of childbearing age), tobacco, alcohol, and drug use.
Depression screening should start with PHQ-2; if positive, follow with PHQ-9.
In older patients, pay extra attention to the skin for growths and assess gait by having them walk.
Instead of a full gown skin exam, ask patients if they have any abnormal skin lesions; they will usually show you.
Diabetic patients should be referred for a formal eye exam rather than relying on ophthalmoscopy.
Always double-check the medication list yourself even if the MA reviewed it, because they may not know dosing details.
Chart an adult wellness visit code in two to three minutes; it should not take long.
For older patients, pay extra attention to skin exam for growths; ask patients about abnormal skin lesions rather than doing a full gown exam.
USPSTF recommends diabetes screening with A1C or CMP for anyone age 35-70 with BMI >25 (overweight or obese).

episodes.title: Dr. Herrmann on Liver Disease for Primary Care 4/23/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Herrmann
episodes.abstract: Dr. Herrmann presents an outpatient approach to elevated liver enzymes, using a case of a 41-year-old man with mildly elevated AST and ALT. The lecture covers the differential diagnosis for transaminitis, emphasizing fatty liver disease as the most common cause. It provides a stepwise workup: initial lifestyle counseling and repeat labs, followed by ultrasound and hepatitis panel if persistent. The FIB-4 score is introduced to assess fibrosis risk, with thresholds for referral. Management focuses on weight loss (5% reduces steatosis by 30%) and eliminating sugary drinks. The talk also highlights pitfalls such as misinterpreting ferritin for hemochromatosis and the role of muscle injury in ALT elevation.
key_points: Fatty liver disease (MASLD) affects 20-30% of the population and 70% of patients with obesity, making it the most common cause of elevated transaminases.
For mildly elevated LFTs in an asymptomatic patient, initial management is lifestyle counseling and repeat labs in 3-6 months before further workup.
If LFTs remain elevated, obtain an ultrasound (liver lighter than kidney suggests steatosis) and a hepatitis panel to rule out chronic hepatitis C.
Use the FIB-4 score (based on age, AST, ALT, platelets) to stratify fibrosis risk: <1.3 is low risk; for patients over 65, <2 is probably safe.
A FIB-4 score >1.3 warrants referral to GI for elastography (FibroScan) or an ELF test (enhanced liver fibrosis) to assess fibrosis severity.
5% body weight loss leads to a 30% reduction in hepatic steatosis, making modest weight loss an effective treatment.
Eliminating sugary drinks (including diet sodas) is the easiest dietary change; diet drinks may still promote weight gain by triggering sugar cravings.
When evaluating for hemochromatosis, order a full iron panel with percent saturation, not just ferritin, because ferritin is often elevated due to inflammation from fatty liver.
Muscle injury (e.g., recent exercise) can cause isolated ALT elevation and should be considered in the differential.
Severe transaminitis (>1,000) is most commonly due to ischemic liver injury, acute viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury (e.g., Tylenol overdose), or autoimmune hepatitis.
FIB-4 is a simple, noninvasive tool using CBC (platelet count) and routine labs to rule out advanced fibrosis in NAFLD.
5% body weight loss reduces steatosis by 30%; 10% loss achieves 76% reduction, effectively curing NAFLD in most patients.

episodes.title: Dr. Herrmann on Outpatient Management
episodes.speaker: Dr. Herrmann
episodes.abstract: Dr. Herrmann presents an outpatient-focused lecture on hypertension management for family medicine residents. He reviews the importance of blood pressure control, risk factors for primary and secondary hypertension, and the 2017 ACC/AHA diagnostic criteria. The talk emphasizes the need for ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring to confirm diagnosis, lifestyle modifications including the DASH diet, and practical tips for initiating pharmacotherapy. Dr. Herrmann also discusses common pitfalls such as white-coat hypertension and medication-induced hypertension.
key_points: Every 20 mmHg systolic BP above 115 doubles the risk of heart attack or stroke; use this to motivate patients.
Diagnosis of hypertension requires at least three office measurements or ambulatory/home monitoring averaging >130/80.
White-coat hypertension is common; always confirm with home or ambulatory readings before diagnosing.
Lifestyle modifications can lower BP significantly: DASH diet (11 points), weight loss (5 points), aerobic exercise (8 points), sodium <1500 mg/day.
Potassium intake of 3500-5000 mg/day from fruits and vegetables lowers BP.
Common medications that raise BP include NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, steroids, decongestants, stimulants, and antidepressants.
Secondary hypertension causes include renal artery stenosis, hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, obstructive sleep apnea, and CKD.
For stage 2 hypertension (≥140/90), initiate pharmacotherapy and order basic labs (CMP, lipid panel).
The Ascension protocol requires follow-up within one month if BP >140/90, with a second BP check before the visit.
Most hypertension medications are inexpensive compared to diabetes drugs.
Lifestyle modifications for hypertension include increased fruits/vegetables, physical activity (aerobic best), and alcohol limits (men <2 drinks/day, women <1 drink/day).
First-line antihypertensive classes are ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazide diuretics, and long-acting calcium channel blockers.

episodes.title: Dr. Hershberger on Antepartum Fetal Surveillance 6/4/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Hershberger
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers antepartum fetal surveillance for high-risk pregnancies, focusing on indications, timing, and modalities. Dr. Hershberger reviews conditions that warrant surveillance, such as chronic hypertension on medication, obesity with BMI over 40, and advanced maternal age, with a general rule to start at 32 weeks. He emphasizes the importance of consulting maternal-fetal medicine (MFM), not assuming surveillance is being performed, and describing tests like NST and BPP to patients. Pitfalls include forgetting to start on time, misinterpreting nonreassuring results, and overlooking fetal growth restriction as a separate indication.
key_points: Antepartum fetal surveillance is indicated when the risk of stillbirth is increased, not for all pregnancies.
General rule: start surveillance at 32 weeks, but timing is individualized based on the condition.
Common modalities: nonstress test (NST), biophysical profile (BPP), and modified BPP (NST + amniotic fluid index).
For uncomplicated diet-controlled gestational diabetes, weekly NST is not clearly recommended.
Chronic hypertension on medication (e.g., labetalol) warrants starting surveillance at 32 weeks.
Patients who need surveillance should also be seen by MFM for co-management.
Do not assume MFM is performing the surveillance; ask the patient and verify.
Describe NST and BPP to patients because they often do not know what these tests are.
Conditions that should be referred to MFM and not managed by family medicine include twins/triplets, >3 C-sections, placenta previa, and type 1 diabetes.
A pitfall is forgetting that fetal growth restriction requires a different surveillance modality (e.g., Doppler) beyond NST.

episodes.title: Dr. Hershberger on Post Partum Care
episodes.speaker: Dr. Hershberger
episodes.abstract: This segment of a postpartum care lecture emphasizes the importance of ongoing, tailored follow-up rather than a fixed two- and six-week schedule. Speakers discuss managing PTSD after traumatic delivery, ensuring breastfeeding support, and recognizing that gestational hypertension and preeclampsia significantly increase long-term cardiovascular risk (including HFpEF, MI, and stroke) even though these factors are not included in standard ASCVD risk calculators. Practical tips include adding gestational hypertension to the problem list as a chronic condition and asking about pregnancy complications at well woman visits.
key_points: Postpartum care is ongoing care; follow-up should be tailored to the patient's needs (e.g., breastfeeding difficulties).
Women with a history of gestational hypertension or preeclampsia have significantly increased risk of ASCVD and should have yearly blood pressure checks.

Pregnancy complications (hypertension, preeclampsia) are not included in ASCVD risk calculators but increase risk for HFpEF, MI, and stroke, and may change management decisions like statin initiation.
Add gestational hypertension to the problem list as a chronic condition to ensure it remains in the chart.
Always ask about pregnancy complications during well woman visits to capture this elevated cardiovascular risk.
Patients with emergent Cesarean section or other traumatic deliveries should be screened for PTSD and offered support.
Breastfeeding difficulties may require more frequent visits (e.g., every two weeks) and connection to lactation resources.
Patients with gestational diabetes need close postpartum follow-up with a two-hour OGTT to detect persistent diabetes.
Patients are often lost to follow-up; proactive scheduling and resource linkage are essential.

episodes.title: Dr. Hildebrand on Arthritis
episodes.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hildebrand presents a practical, systems-based approach to diagnosing and managing rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in the outpatient family medicine setting. She emphasizes that residents can confidently start disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) like methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine without a rheumatologist, using the ACR 2010 criteria to systematically evaluate joint involvement, serology, acute phase reactants, and symptom duration. Through a case example of a 49-year-old woman with worsening polyarticular pain and morning stiffness, she illustrates key history and exam findings, appropriate lab ordering, and the importance of avoiding unnecessary tests like ANA unless lupus is suspected. The lecture also covers pre-treatment screening (TB, hepatitis, HIV, CBC, CMP) and the role of steroids as a bridge while starting methotrexate.
key_points: RA diagnosis requires symptoms for at least 6 weeks; shorter duration suggests other causes.
Small joint involvement (PIPs, MCPs, wrists) is a key trigger to suspect autoimmune arthritis.
Morning stiffness lasting >1 hour is a classic RA symptom; this patient had 2 hours.
Use the ACR 2010 criteria (joint involvement, serology, acute phase reactants, duration) to classify RA; score ≥6 indicates definite RA.
High positive anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor (e.g., anti-CCP 1400, RF 103) strongly support RA diagnosis.
Avoid ordering ANA unless lupus is on the differential; a positive ANA in low-risk patients creates unnecessary workup and anxiety.
Pre-treatment labs for methotrexate include TB, hepatitis B/C, HIV, CBC, and comprehensive metabolic panel.
Start methotrexate at a low dose and counsel patients that it is a DMARD, not primarily a cancer drug.
Steroids (e.g., prednisone) can be used as a short-term bridge while DMARDs take effect.
Family physicians can confidently initiate methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine for RA when rheumatology is not available.
Use ACR criteria as a checklist with the patient to systematically diagnose rheumatoid arthritis and lupus.
Before starting methotrexate, check TB, HIV, hepatitis panel, and CBC/chemistries.

episodes.title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hildebrand presents two cases of diabetic emergencies: an elderly man with hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) and a young woman with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). She reviews updated diagnostic criteria, including the 2024 change lowering the glucose threshold for DKA from 250 to 200 mg/dL, and emphasizes the importance of identifying the underlying trigger (infection, medication nonadherence, or new agents like checkpoint inhibitors). She explains why urine ketone testing is unreliable for monitoring DKA resolution due to differential clearance of ketone bodies, and highlights that the key to management is understanding the cause of the episode.
key_points: HHS presents with extreme hyperglycemia (glucose ≥600 mg/dL), hyperosmolality (osmolality ≥300 mOsm/kg), mild or no ketosis, and often altered mental status; it develops over days to weeks.
DKA requires all three criteria: hyperglycemia (now ≥200 mg/dL), ketosis (beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥3 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥2+), and metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3, bicarb <15).
Euglycemic DKA can occur with glucose <200 mg/dL in patients with known diabetes; a prior history of diabetes helps meet criteria.

Urine dipstick detects acetoacetate, not beta-hydroxybutyrate; early DKA may show negative urine ketones, and during treatment urine ketones can remain positive after resolution, making them unreliable for monitoring.
The most common triggers for both DKA and HHS are infection (especially GI, cellulitis, pneumonia) and medication issues (nonadherence to insulin, steroids, checkpoint inhibitors).
DKA typically presents with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, and GI symptoms (nausea/vomiting); HHS presents with more profound dehydration and confusion.
Kussmaul respirations are rare but can be mistaken for respiratory distress; they feature increased work of breathing with a slow respiratory rate.
Always investigate the underlying cause of the episode, infection and medication nonadherence are the top considerations.
Urine dipstick can be negative early in DKA; serum ketones are preferred for diagnosis and monitoring.
Using urine ketones to track treatment response can lead to overtreatment because they clear more slowly than serum ketones.
The most common causes of DKA/HHS are infection and medication non-adherence or adverse effects.
Steroids, SGLT2 inhibitors, and checkpoint inhibitors are important medication triggers.

episodes.title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis
episodes.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hildebrand uses the case of a 74-year-old woman with osteoporosis and a foot fracture to guide residents through diagnosis and management. She emphasizes nonpharmacologic measures like weighted vests for spinal loading and tai chi for balance. Bisphosphonates are first-line; she reviews risks (osteonecrosis of the jaw after >4 years), proper administration (upright posture, plain water), and timing with levothyroxine. Alternative therapies include raloxifene, calcitonin, teriparatide, and denosumab, with practical steps for prescribing denosumab.
key_points: DEXA T-score ≤ -2.5 defines osteoporosis; FRAX is unnecessary when osteoporosis is already diagnosed.
Nonpharmacologic treatment should include weighted vests to load the spine and tai chi for balance and fall prevention.
Bisphosphonates are first-line for primary osteoporosis; avoid daily dosing due to GI side effects.
Risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw increases after >4 years of bisphosphonate use; consider drug holiday for dental procedures.
Oral bisphosphonates must be taken with plain water, sitting upright for at least 30, 60 minutes.
Levothyroxine must be taken on an empty stomach; wait ≥1 hour before other medications or food.
In patients with severe GERD or esophageal disorders, IV bisphosphonate may be preferred over oral.
Calcitonin can be used for pain relief in acute or chronic compression fractures.
Teriparatide (anabolic) is indicated for severe osteoporosis or after bisphosphonate failure.
Denosumab reduces hip, vertebral, and nonvertebral fractures; check calcium level before administration.
Denosumab is a subcutaneous injection given every six months that reduces hip, vertebral, and nonvertebral fractures.
Before starting denosumab, check a chem 8 for calcium to avoid hypocalcemia.

episodes.title: Dr. Hoslinger on Spiritual Resiliency
episodes.speaker: Dr. Hoslinger
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hoslinger discusses spiritual resiliency for Christian medical residents, emphasizing that true significance comes from being with God rather than from works or service. He contrasts a 'cycle of grace' rooted in God's love and acceptance with a 'cycle of works' that leads to burnout. Practical recommendations include engaging in Christian community, small groups, accountability relationships, and caring for the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit.
key_points: Spiritual resiliency requires shifting from a works-based identity to a grace-based identity, finding significance in God's love rather than in accomplishments.
Jesus' ministry flowed from His acceptance by the Father (Mark 1:9-11), not from striving; residents should model this pattern.
Being part of a local church and small group is vital, even when residency makes it difficult.
Healthy accountability involves praying together, being real, and sharing Scripture; unhealthy accountability includes gossip under the guise of prayer requests.
Residents should have a mentor ahead of them and a learner behind them (2 Timothy 2:2 principle).
Physical self-care, exercise, nutrition, sleep, rest, and renewal, is an act of honoring God as the temple of the Holy Spirit.
The spiritual disciplines are not empty rituals but practices that shape us to be with Jesus, become like Jesus, and do what Jesus does.
Confession and forgiveness within a confessional community bring healing and blessing.
Secular research (Human Flourishing Project) confirms the importance of close social relationships for well-being.
Ministry should flow from relationship with God, not from a need for approval or significance from others.
The body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, so spiritual resiliency includes caring for the body through exercise, nutrition, sleep, rest, and renewal.
Prayer should be made a habit even when residency leaves little time and the mind is racing.

episodes.title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jeff Perry presents a comprehensive overview of hip maladies excluding fractures and osteoarthritis. He covers bony injuries (osteitis pubis, avascular necrosis/Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, avulsion fractures, stress fractures), muscle/nerve issues (hip adductor strain, psoas syndrome, piriformis syndrome), and bursitis/tendonitis (trochanteric bursitis, iliopsoas bursitis, snapping hip syndrome). The talk emphasizes clinical presentation, exam findings, imaging strategies, and conservative management, with referral thresholds for refractory cases. A biblical reflection on Jacob's hip injury frames the discussion.
key_points: Osteitis pubis presents with progressive groin pain, popping at the symphysis, and is common in athletes and third-trimester pregnancy due to overuse of adductors and relaxin effects.

Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of femoral head) classically presents as insidious limp in males aged 5-8, with loss of hip rotation and external rotation on flexion; early MRI is key as X-rays are initially normal.

Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) occurs in obese adolescents aged 11-16 with delayed puberty; X-ray shows the classic 'ice cream slipping off the cone' appearance, requiring urgent orthopedic referral.
Avulsion fractures of the hip involve the sartorius at the ASIS or rectus femoris at the AIIS from forceful contraction; management is conservative with rest, ice, and progressive weight bearing.
Stress fractures of the femoral neck should be suspected in female athletes with the triad of amenorrhea, overtraining, and endurance activity; bone scan is more sensitive than X-ray early on.
Hip adductor strain typically results from forced abduction (e.g., slipping on ice); exam reveals pain with resisted adduction, and treatment includes rest, ice, NSAIDs, and eccentric strengthening.
Groin pain without clear injury requires a broad differential including testicular torsion, epididymitis, inguinal hernia, lymphadenopathy, and malignancy.
Conservative management for most hip maladies includes relative rest (avoid increasing exercise volume >10% per week), ice, NSAIDs, and physical therapy with eccentric strengthening.
Referral to orthopedics is indicated after 6 weeks of failed conservative therapy for osteitis pubis, or for suspected LCP, SCFE, or stress fractures.
Trochanteric bursitis is now considered a misnomer; iliopsoas bursitis/tendonitis and snapping hip syndrome are related entities that blend with muscle and nerve issues.
Hip adductor strain typically results from forced abduction (e.g., slipping on ice) and presents with pain on resisted adduction.
Without clear trauma, consider groin pain differential including testicular torsion, epididymitis, inguinal hernia, lymphadenopathy, or malignancy.

episodes.title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
episodes.abstract: Dr. John Ashley presents a fast-paced lecture on common vesiculobullous rashes, covering contact dermatitis, herpes simplex, varicella, zoster, eczema herpeticum, and blistering dactylitis. He emphasizes clinical recognition, practical treatment strategies (especially for poison ivy and herpes), and the importance of examining the whole patient when the rash is confusing. He also discusses vaccination for zoster and pearls on antiviral dosing and safety.
key_points: Allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., poison ivy) lasts about a month untreated; systemic or topical steroids speed resolution.
Medrol dose packs are less preferred for poison ivy due to nighttime dosing; a longer prednisone taper given all in the morning is better.
For severe poison ivy, start with 20 mg prednisone in the afternoon then 60 mg the next morning; adjust dose by patient size and sensitivity.
Clobetasol (class 1 topical steroid) works faster than triamcinolone for localized poison ivy.
Herpetic whitlow presents with grouped vesicles on a finger; it is pathognomonic.
For varicella, acyclovir five times daily is impractical; four times daily is acceptable.
Suppressive valacyclovir 500 mg once daily is appropriate for patients with more than 3-4 herpes outbreaks per year.
Eczema herpeticum should be suspected when atopic dermatitis patients develop widespread vesicles; treat with acyclovir and topical steroids.
Antivirals are renally excreted; ensure adequate hydration to prevent crystalluria.
Early gabapentin for zoster pain may reduce postherpetic neuralgia, especially in older patients.
Blistering dactylitis in children is often due to cellulitis; treat with a cephalosporin and follow closely; refer if high fever or inability to move finger.
Bullous impetigo may be missed if seen before honey-colored crust develops; recheck in a few days.

episodes.title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Adnexal Masses 12/4/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert presents a two-session lecture on adnexal masses for family medicine residents. He categorizes masses as neoplastic or nonneoplastic, emphasizing the importance of distinguishing benign from malignant findings. The talk covers functional cysts (follicular and corpus luteum), pathologic masses (endometrioma, tubo-ovarian abscess), and neoplastic growths. Key clinical skills include bimanual examination technique, interpreting ultrasound reports of simple versus complex cysts, and understanding the role of menstrual cycle timing in diagnosis. Management strategies for common conditions like PCOS and hemorrhagic ovarian cysts are discussed, with emphasis on observation and follow-up protocols.
key_points: Adnexal masses are divided into neoplastic (malignant or benign) and nonneoplastic (functional cysts like follicular and corpus luteum cysts).
A normal ovary is about the size of a thumb's distal phalanx; in obese patients, it may not be palpable, and in postmenopausal women, it should not be felt.
On bimanual exam, if the uterus is not felt when pushing the cervix upward, suspect a retroverted uterus; a rectal-vaginal exam can help.
Simple cysts on ultrasound have a 90% chance of being benign; complex cysts (loculated or with solid growth) are more concerning.
In PCOS, ultrasound shows 10-15 follicles of similar size; management depends on pregnancy desire, if not desiring pregnancy, ensure endometrial shedding at least yearly and screen for diabetes.
Functional simple cysts <10 cm can be observed with repeat ultrasound in 3 months; most resolve spontaneously.
Hemorrhagic ovarian cysts present with gradually increasing pain, often after ovulation, and show internal solid structure (clot) on ultrasound; management is observation.
Timing of pain relative to the menstrual cycle is critical, Mittelschmerz occurs at ovulation (day 14).
Uterine displacement on exam suggests a mass pushing or pulling it; ultrasound is indicated.
In a 60-year-old woman, a palpable adnexal mass is highly suspicious for malignancy and warrants ultrasound evaluation.
Increased intravascular pressure causes pain in adnexal masses.
Absence of guarding and tenderness suggests no peritoneal irritation; rebound tenderness indicates peritoneal irritation and surgical abdomen.

episodes.title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Adnexal Masses 1/22/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert reviews the evaluation of adnexal masses, distinguishing non-neoplastic (functional vs. organic) from neoplastic (benign vs. malignant) types. He emphasizes that simple cysts on ultrasound are likely benign, while complex cysts are suspicious for cancer until proven otherwise. Key clinical pearls include the normal ovarian size, the expected palpability of ovaries in reproductive-age women, and the characteristic ultrasound appearances of hemorrhagic cysts, endometriomas, hydrosalpinx, and tubo-ovarian abscesses. The talk uses case-based examples to illustrate how history, physical exam, and ultrasound findings guide management and referral.
key_points: Adnexal masses are categorized as non-neoplastic (functional or organic) or neoplastic (benign or malignant).
Functional masses are associated with the menstrual cycle; organic masses are pathologic.
Normal ovary size is 3.5 x 2 x 1.5 cm; in menopause the ovary is less than half the size of a finger.
In reproductive-age women, ovaries should be palpable 80% of the time, but with obesity this drops to 50-60%.
On ultrasound, a simple cyst is anechoic (black) with a thin wall; any variation is complex and suspicious for malignancy.
Hemorrhagic cysts often have a characteristic irregular appearance; repeat ultrasound in 2 weeks can show resolution as the clot resorbs.
Endometriomas have a classic 'frosted glass' appearance on ultrasound.
Hydrosalpinx appears as an elongated, fluid-filled structure (not ovary-shaped) and is usually an incidental, painless finding.
Tubo-ovarian abscess appears as a complex mass with hyperechoic and hypoechoic areas and irregular margins.
Fibroids can be submucosal (associated with menorrhagia), intramural (associated with bleeding), or subserosal (palpable as lumps).

episodes.title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Infections Genitalia
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert presents a case-based review of genital infections in both males and females, covering bacterial vaginosis, herpes simplex virus, gonorrhea, chlamydia, trichomoniasis, and syphilis. He emphasizes the importance of history, physical exam, and wet prep findings for diagnosis, including the Amsel criteria for bacterial vaginosis and the characteristic discharge patterns of different infections. The lecture also addresses management strategies such as suppressive therapy for recurrent HSV, presumptive treatment for gonorrhea and chlamydia, and the use of metronidazole for recurrent BV associated with menstruation or sex. Key clinical pearls include recognizing that bacterial vaginosis lacks inflammatory cells, that primary HSV infections require more aggressive treatment, and that asymptomatic HSV transmission can occur with lesions that are painless but still visible.
key_points: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is diagnosed using Amsel criteria: thin milky discharge, pH >4.5, positive whiff test, and clue cells on wet prep; three of four are needed.
BV has no inflammatory cells on wet prep, distinguishing it from other infections.
Normal vaginal pH is ≤4.5, maintained by lactobacillus; elevated pH (from semen, menstruation, or trichomonas) promotes BV overgrowth.
Recurrent BV associated with menstruation or sex can be managed with metronidazole for 1-2 days after menses stop.
Primary HSV infection is more severe and treated more aggressively than recurrent episodes; it may require hospitalization.
HSV lesions progress from tingling to clear vesicles to pustules to crusting over 24 hours; lesions can be at different stages simultaneously.
Asymptomatic HSV transmission occurs when a person has a painless lesion they are unaware of; it does not mean no lesion is present.
Gonorrhea and chlamydia are intracellular organisms in columnar cells of the endocervical canal, producing purulent discharge from the cervical os.
When the diagnosis is uncertain between gonorrhea and chlamydia, treat presumptively for both; if one is confirmed, treat only that one.
Trichomonas presents with frothy white discharge, pH >4.5, postcoital spotting, and a strawberry cervix with punctate erosions on the vaginal wall.
Syphilis presents with a chancre (entry point) and a characteristic rash on palms and soles; Oklahoma has high rates, nearly 100 cases per 100,000.
In pregnancy with HSV history, perform a thorough exam of cervix and vaginal walls for active lesions; if any doubt, err on the side of C-section.

episodes.title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Pelvic Pain Cases
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert discusses a case of chronic pelvic pain with bilateral lower abdominal pain that is cyclic and associated with ovulation. He emphasizes the importance of the bimanual exam, noting that a displaced cervix suggests either scar tissue pulling or a mass pushing the uterus. The case reveals chronic endometritis following laparoscopic salpingectomy for ectopic pregnancy, treated with ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and doxycycline. Key teaching points include differentiating physiologic from pathologic pain, interpreting cervical displacement, and recognizing chronic endometritis as a cause of persistent dysmenorrhea.
key_points: Cyclic lower abdominal pain that changes sides is often due to ovulation (mittelschmerz) and can be managed with combination oral contraceptives to suppress ovulation.
A displaced cervix on exam suggests either scar tissue pulling the uterus (ipsilateral) or a mass pushing it (contralateral).
During bimanual exam, attempt to move the uterus side to side; limited movement in one direction indicates scar tissue on that side.
A tender uterus on palpation is abnormal and suggests adenomyosis, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), or endometritis.
PID can involve any single structure (cervix, endometrium, fallopian tube, ovary) or multiple; the term does not specify location.
Chronic endometritis can persist for months to years after pelvic surgery, presenting with dysmenorrhea and heavy bleeding.
Treatment for chronic endometritis includes a single dose of ceftriaxone plus a 14-day course of metronidazole and doxycycline.
Follow-up after antibiotic treatment is necessary to confirm resolution of infection.
Scar tissue from prior surgery can cause pain during bimanual exam due to stretching of adhesions.
A history of ectopic pregnancy treated laparoscopically with tubal removal can lead to chronic endometritis if infection develops postoperatively.

episodes.title: Dr. Jordan Dever on Pregnancy and Respiratory Diseases
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jordan Dever
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jordan Dever reviews normal physiological lung changes in pregnancy, including progesterone- and estrogen-mediated increases in minute ventilation and a compensated respiratory alkalosis. He discusses asthma management during pregnancy, emphasizing that treatment for acute exacerbations should be the same as in non-pregnant patients, and that uncontrolled asthma increases risks of preterm birth and other complications. The lecture also covers flash pulmonary edema in pregnancy, its obstetrical and cardiovascular causes, and the importance of avoiding labetalol and magnesium first in a patient with suspected peripartum cardiomyopathy and fluid overload.
key_points: Pregnancy causes a compensated respiratory alkalosis with increased minute ventilation, increased PaO2, decreased PaCO2, and decreased serum bicarbonate.
Diaphragm is displaced 4-5 cm cephalad and thoracic circumference increases 5-7 cm, decreasing expiratory reserve volume, residual volume, and functional residual capacity.
FEV1 and FVC do not change significantly during pregnancy, so spirometry remains reliable for diagnosing asthma.
Asthma exacerbations in pregnancy most commonly occur between 24 and 36 weeks gestation.
Treatment of acute asthma exacerbation in pregnancy is the same as in non-pregnant patients: oxygen, albuterol, ipratropium, systemic steroids, and magnesium if needed.
Pregnant women are less likely to receive appropriate asthma care, including corticosteroids in the emergency department and at discharge.
Uncontrolled asthma in pregnancy is associated with increased risks of preterm birth, low birth weight, small for gestational age, NICU admissions, and perinatal mortality.
Flash pulmonary edema in pregnancy can be caused by hypertensive disorders, fluid overload from tocolytics or magnesium, peripartum cardiomyopathy, and infections.
In a patient with pulmonary edema and hypertension, avoid labetalol if peripartum cardiomyopathy is possible because it is a negative inotrope.
In fluid-overloaded patients with pulmonary edema, avoid giving magnesium first; instead, give furosemide to reduce fluid volume.
Step-up asthma therapy based on symptom control; consider referral to pulmonology for step 4-6 therapies.
Asthma classification (intermittent, mild, moderate, severe persistent) guides step therapy from step 1 (as-needed SABA) to step 5/6 (medium-high dose ICS + LABA + LAMA).

episodes.title: Dr. Kaleigh Winters on PNG & Tuberculosis 2/29/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kaleigh Winters
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kaleigh Winters shares her experience from a three-month global health fellowship in Papua New Guinea, describing the clinical challenges and emotional weight of working in a resource-limited setting. She then presents a detailed review of tuberculosis, covering transmission, latent versus active disease, diagnostic testing, and bacteriologic examination. The lecture emphasizes practical clinical insights, including the disconnect between lung exam findings and chest X-ray severity in TB patients, and the nuances of interpreting PPD and IGRA tests.
key_points: In PNG, during election season, machete (chop-chop) injuries are common; gun violence is rare.
Post-call days can involve multiple deaths and births, requiring emotional resilience and reliance on team support.
TB is transmitted via droplet nuclei 1 to 5 microns in diameter; smaller particles reach alveoli.
Latent TB infection: immune system controls replication 2-8 weeks after exposure; patient is asymptomatic and non-infectious.
Risk of latent TB reactivation: 5% in first 2 years, another 5% over remaining lifetime (10% overall).
In HIV, latent TB reactivation risk is 7-10% per year.
Diabetes increases lifetime risk of reactivation by 30%.
Chest X-ray may look severe in TB while lung auscultation sounds normal; physical exam is often not helpful.
IGRA (QuantiFERON) is more sensitive and specific than PPD skin test and is increasingly preferred; PPD interpretation varies (5, 10, 15 mm thresholds).
Sputum for AFB smear, NAAT (GeneXpert), culture, and drug susceptibility testing are key for diagnosis; negative AFB does not rule out TB.
Extrapulmonary TB is more common in HIV/immunosuppressed patients; specimens should be taken from the affected site.
All positive TB cases must be reported in the US; high-risk groups include travelers from high-incidence countries, congregate settings, and immunocompromised individuals.

episodes.title: Dr. Keller -GERD
episodes.speaker: Dr. Keller
episodes.abstract: This lecture defines GERD as pathologic reflux causing troublesome symptoms or complications such as erosion, strictures, and Barrett's esophagus. It covers typical symptoms (heartburn and acid regurgitation), dysphagia types (solid vs. liquid), and extraesophageal manifestations including chest pain, water brash, globus, and nausea. Diagnostic approaches include empiric PPI trials, endoscopy for alarm symptoms, and pH/impedance monitoring for refractory cases. Management emphasizes lifestyle modifications (elevate head of bed, avoid eating within 3 hours of bedtime, dietary triggers), step-down PPI therapy, and avoiding unnecessary long-term PPI use.
key_points: Physiologic reflux is short-lived, buffered by saliva, and cleared by peristalsis; pathologic reflux causes symptoms and mucosal injury.
Typical GERD symptoms are heartburn (retrosternal burning) and acid regurgitation.
Solid dysphagia suggests mechanical obstruction and requires urgent workup; liquid dysphagia suggests dysmotility (achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm).
Pill dysphagia is common (up to 40%) and not worrisome if not associated with food dysphagia.
Extraesophageal symptoms include chest pain (postprandial, nocturnal, stress-exacerbated), water brash, globus, nausea, cough, and hoarseness.
Erosive esophagitis is always at the GE junction; LA classification: A (<5mm, no bridging), B (>5mm, no bridging), C (bridging <75%), D (>75%).
NERD (nonerosive reflux disease) is GERD symptoms without endoscopic esophagitis; includes esophageal hypersensitivity and functional heartburn.
ACG guidelines: empiric PPI trial for 2 months; if symptoms improve, confirm diagnosis; if recurrent within 3 months, scope; alarm symptoms warrant immediate endoscopy.
Alarm symptoms: unexplained weight loss, dysphagia, odynophagia, iron deficiency anemia, persistent vomiting, family history of GI cancer, new onset dyspepsia in patients >60.
Management: lifestyle (elevate head of bed, avoid eating 3h before bedtime, dietary triggers), step-down PPI therapy, and avoid stopping PPIs in patients with history of peptic strictures.
Transition patients from PPI to famotidine after 2-3 months of good symptom control to minimize long-term medication use.
PPIs must be taken 30-60 minutes before the first meal of the day; 40% of patients do not time it correctly.

episodes.title: Dr. Keller on GERD, Gastritis, and PUD
episodes.speaker: Dr. Keller
episodes.abstract: Dr. Keller discusses the management of GERD, gastritis, and peptic ulcer disease, focusing on proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use, H. pylori diagnosis and treatment, and histologic patterns of gastritis. He emphasizes proper PPI dosing (before breakfast, 30-60 minutes), the importance of tapering to avoid rebound hypersecretion, and the need to rule out cardiac causes before attributing chest pain to GERD. For H. pylori, he recommends breath or stool testing over serology, outlines first-line optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days, and highlights the carcinogenic risk and associations with ITP and iron deficiency.
key_points: Start omeprazole 40 mg daily, taken 30-60 minutes before breakfast for optimal effect; missing this timing reduces effectiveness by about 50%.
PPI effectiveness plateaus over 3-5 days as all proton pumps are inhibited; BID dosing should be before breakfast and before supper.

Long-term PPI use increases risk of C. diff colitis (mainly in hospital), hypomagnesemia (check magnesium periodically), and fractures after 2 years (especially in petite women; recommend calcium citrate over carbonate).
PPIs are metabolized via CYP2C19; genetic testing is available and can identify rapid or slow metabolizers.
Do not start a PPI trial for extraesophageal symptoms (chronic cough, chest pain) without classic heartburn or regurgitation; work up chest pain first.

For H. pylori, use breath test or stool antigen; avoid serology in the US due to low prevalence causing false positives. Patients must be off antibiotics/bismuth for 4 weeks and PPIs for 2 weeks before testing.

First-line H. pylori treatment is optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days (metronidazole, tetracycline, bismuth); avoid clarithromycin due to resistance and do not substitute doxycycline for tetracycline.
After H. pylori treatment, test for cure at least one month later; if still positive, retreat with different antibiotics; after two failures, refer for EGD with culture and sensitivity.
H. pylori infection carries a 15-20% lifetime risk of peptic ulcer, 1% risk of gastric adenocarcinoma, and is associated with ITP and iron deficiency anemia.
LA grade C or D GERD requires lifelong PPI therapy per ACG guidelines; severe esophagitis should not be treated with H2 blockers alone.
When retreating H. pylori, do not reuse the same antibiotics from the first course.
After two treatment failures, refer for endoscopy with culture and sensitivity to guide therapy.

episodes.title: Dr. Keller on Infant Gastroesophageal 4/16/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Keller
episodes.abstract: Dr. Keller presents a family-medicine oriented review of infant gastroesophageal reflux (GER) versus GERD. She emphasizes that most infants are 'happy spitters' whose regurgitation peaks at 3 months and resolves by 1 year. Red flags include bilious vomiting, forceful vomiting, blood in vomitus or stool, poor weight gain, and signs of aspiration or apnea.
