Management begins with conservative measures: smaller more frequent feedings, upright positioning after feeds, burping, and appropriate nipple flow. When these fail, she discusses thickening feeds with oat cereal (not rice), switching to hypoallergenic formulas for suspected cow's milk protein allergy, and recognizing Sandifer syndrome. She cautions against propping the crib or using wedges due to SIDS risk, and notes that nicotine exposure worsens reflux by decreasing lower esophageal sphincter tone.
key_points: 80% of infants are 'happy spitters'; physiologic reflux peaks at 3 months and resolves by 1 year.
Bilious vomiting suggests small bowel obstruction (intussusception, volvulus) and requires urgent evaluation.
Forceful vomiting, blood in vomitus, poor weight gain, and history of pneumonia/aspiration are red flags for GERD.
BRUE (brief resolved unexplained event) is the preferred term over ALTE; if milk is seen coming from the mouth, the event is explained, not a BRUE.
First-line management: smaller, more frequent feedings; burp during and after feeds; hold upright 20-30 minutes post-feed.
Thicken feeds with 1 tablespoon of dry infant oat cereal per ounce of formula (not rice cereal due to arsenic concerns); do not thicken breast milk because amylase breaks down the thickener.
Do not prop the crib or use wedges for reflux; supine on a flat, firm surface is safest to prevent SIDS.
40% of infants with GERD have cow's milk protein intolerance; consider a trial of hypoallergenic formula (e.g., Similac Alimentum) if reflux is excessive.
Sandifer syndrome (arching back, neck extension, chin lifting) indicates esophageal pain from reflux.
Brick-red gritty substance in the diaper is urate crystals, not blood; it is normal in newborns and resolves in a few days.
Blood in vomitus can indicate esophagitis, pyloric stenosis, or cow's milk protein allergy.
Bright red blood in stool may be proctocolitis; check for anal fissures with a spread sheet exam.

episodes.title: Dr. Kelly Dunn on IHI FM Board Review (9/11/25)
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn presents a psychiatry-focused board review for family medicine residents, covering bipolar disorder diagnosis and treatment pitfalls, PTSD nightmare management with prazosin, methadone-related QTc prolongation, adolescent anorexia nervosa treatment, speech delay risk factors, smoking cessation pharmacotherapy, and insomnia medication principles. She emphasizes screening for mania before treating depression, avoiding SSRIs/SNRIs in hypomanic patients, and using family-based therapy for teens with anorexia. Practical pearls include dosing strategies for prazosin, baseline EKG for methadone, and the superiority of varenicline for smoking cessation.
key_points: Bipolar I requires a single manic episode lasting 7 days or hospitalization; no depressive episode needed.
Bipolar II requires both hypomanic and major depressive episodes.
SSRIs and SNRIs are contraindicated in hypomanic/bipolar depression unless the patient is on a mood stabilizer.
Always screen for mania before starting antidepressants to avoid inducing mania in undiagnosed bipolar patients.
Prazosin is effective for PTSD-related nightmares and sleep maintenance insomnia; doses can be titrated up to 15 mg or more.
Methadone treatment requires a baseline EKG due to risk of QTc prolongation; keep QTc under 500 ms.
Family-based therapy is first-line for adolescent anorexia nervosa, with parents leading meal support.
Male sex is the most important risk factor for speech and language impairment; bilingual households do not cause delay.
Varenicline (Chantix) is the most effective smoking cessation medication; adding nicotine replacement therapy improves rates.
For insomnia, avoid benzodiazepines and antipsychotics as first-line; consider low-dose doxepin or trazodone.
Doxepin (Silenor) is FDA-approved for insomnia and is preferred over trazodone, which lacks FDA indication and is not in AASM algorithms.
Benzodiazepines are not first-line for panic disorder; SSRIs like escitalopram are first-line, with hydroxyzine as a PRN adjunct.

episodes.title: Dr. Kelly Dunn on IHI FM Board Review 6/11/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn leads an IHI Family Medicine Board Review lecture focusing on bipolar disorder diagnosis and management. She clarifies that bipolar I requires only one manic episode, while bipolar II requires depressive episodes plus hypomania. She emphasizes screening all depressed patients for mania, highlights the risk of SSRIs precipitating mania in bipolar patients, and discusses preferred medications for bipolar depression (lamotrigine, lurasidone) versus acute mania (lithium plus antipsychotics). She also introduces the Ohio Spark hotline for real-time psychiatric consultation. The session includes specific diagnostic thresholds, treatment strategies, and practical pearls for primary care.
key_points: Bipolar I disorder requires one manic episode lasting at least 1 week; depressive episodes are not necessary.
Bipolar II requires depressive episodes plus hypomanic episodes lasting at least 4 days.
Rapid cycling bipolar disorder is defined as four or more mood episodes per year; daily mood swings are not bipolar.
SSRIs are contraindicated in bipolar disorder because they can induce mania or worsen cycling.
A history of manic-like symptoms when taking an SSRI raises suspicion for an underlying bipolar spectrum.
For bipolar depression, lamotrigine is a well-tolerated first-line mood stabilizer (goal 200 mg/day, slow titration).
Lurasidone, quetiapine, Symbyax (olanzapine/fluoxetine), and cariprazine are FDA-approved for bipolar depression.
Acute mania often requires dual therapy: a mood stabilizer (lithium or valproate) plus an antipsychotic.
Long-acting injectable antipsychotics (e.g., paliperidone, aripiprazole) are options for maintenance in unstable patients.
Ohio's Spark hotline (spark.org) provides free, real-time peer-to-peer psychiatric consultation for primary care.

Lamotrigine is the preferred mood stabilizer for bipolar depression without psychosis due to tolerability; inform patients about Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk and need to retitrate if stopped for 5 days.
For acute mania, use a mood stabilizer (lithium preferred over Depakote, especially in women of childbearing age) plus a second-generation antipsychotic.

episodes.title: Dr. Kelly Dunn on Sleep Disorders
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn, a psychiatrist, teaches residents about the diagnosis and management of insomnia in a family medicine residency lecture. She reviews the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria, emphasizing the lack of a specific hour threshold, and strongly promotes cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) as the gold-standard first-line treatment. She then systematically reviews pharmacological options, including doxepin, benzodiazepines, z-hypnotics, melatonin receptor agonists, DORAs, and off-label agents like trazodone and antipsychotics, while sharing her personal prescribing preferences, safety concerns (e.g., sleepwalking with zolpidem), and dosing pearls for specific clinical scenarios.
key_points: DSM-5 insomnia criteria include difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or early morning awakening, occurring at least 3 nights/week for at least 3 months, despite adequate opportunity, and causing daytime distress or impairment.
CBT-I is the gold standard and first-line treatment for insomnia; it includes sleep restriction, stimulus control, relaxation training, and sleep hygiene education.
The ideal sleep temperature according to research is 65 degrees Fahrenheit.
Doxepin for insomnia is short-term (4-5 weeks); its impact on sleep wanes after this, and long-term benefit is not recommended.
For benzodiazepines, use a short half-life agent for trouble falling asleep and a longer half-life agent for trouble staying asleep.

Z-hypnotics: zolpidem is associated with more sleepwalking stories; zaleplon (Sonata) is short-acting and can be redosed if at least 4 hours of sleep remain; eszopiclone (Lunesta) is longer-acting for sleep maintenance.
Regular melatonin lacks evidence of efficacy; there is no support for doses above 10 mg, making 10 mg the cap.
Dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs) like suvorexant and lemborexant block orexin, improve sleep onset, and are well tolerated; the presenter would try these before benzodiazepines.
Antihistamines and trazodone are off-label for insomnia; trazodone is the presenter's first-line, though ASSM guidelines do not recommend it due to side-effect concerns.

Antipsychotics such as quetiapine lack evidence for insomnia and carry serious side effects; if used, typical dose is 25-50 mg, and it should be reserved for those with another antipsychotic indication.
In elderly patients, the presenter prefers sedating antidepressants (trazodone, amitriptyline, doxepin) as first-line before DORAs or z-hypnotics.
Z-hypnotics like zolpidem are best used short-term; long-term use leads to tolerance and eventual loss of efficacy.

episodes.title: Dr. Kim on Urban Missions
episodes.speaker: Dr. Janet Kim
episodes.abstract: Dr. Janet Kim, a medicine-pediatrics trained physician, shares the story of founding and growing a Christian health center on Staten Island, New York, starting from a former beer warehouse in 2006. She describes the center's evolution into a federally qualified health center (FQHC) serving a diverse, multi-ethnic community, including migrants from Venezuela and other countries. Dr. Kim emphasizes whole-person care that addresses physical, mental, and spiritual health, and highlights the challenges and rewards of serving a 'forgotten borough' with limited resources. She encourages residents to consider their own life vision and calling, noting that impactful mission work can be found locally in diverse urban settings like New York.
key_points: The health center started from an empty beer warehouse in 2006 and became a federally qualified health center (FQHC) in 2009.
The center serves 5,000 to 6,000 patients annually on Staten Island, which is known as the 'forgotten borough' with fewer city resources.
Whole-person care includes addressing physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual health, with questions about spiritual support normalized in visits.
The staff speaks eight languages, reflecting the community's diversity, including large populations from Nigeria, Yemen, Sri Lanka, and Liberia.
During the migrant crisis starting in 2022, the center began providing care at two hotels housing about 400 migrants, mostly from Venezuela.
Initial care for migrants involved triaging fevers and respiratory symptoms during viral season, using a $99 massage table as an exam table.
The center has expanded behavioral health from one counselor to four, plus a psychiatrist and a psychiatric nurse practitioner.
Dental services are about to launch after 20 years of planning, and the center is seeking to expand due to space constraints.
Patients include a mix of insured (Medicaid, Medicare) and uninsured, as well as union workers (FDNY, NYPD) and homeless individuals.
The presenter encourages residents to pause and reflect on their 10-year vision for life, professionally and personally, and to consider local mission opportunities.
The clinic started with a request to triage sick hotel residents and evolved into a twice-weekly clinic using a $99 massage table as an exam table.
Each family visit takes about an hour because families have 3, 6 members and multiple issues are addressed.

episodes.title: Dr. Kirkpatrick on Bariatric Seminar Presentation 6/18/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kirkpatrick
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ty Kirkpatrick, medical director of the bariatric program at St. John, reviews surgical and endoscopic options for weight loss, including vertical sleeve gastrectomy, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, and the SADI (modified duodenal switch). He discusses patient selection criteria (BMI thresholds, diabetes), the metabolic and hormonal mechanisms of each procedure, and key postoperative considerations such as vitamin supplementation, reflux risk, and smoking/NSAID avoidance. The talk emphasizes the importance of primary care providers initiating conversations about aggressive weight-loss options for patients with obesity.
key_points: BMI ≥35 with a medical comorbidity or BMI ≥40 alone are standard surgical candidacy criteria.
Patients with BMI ≥30 and severe uncontrolled diabetes are now considered acceptable candidates for bariatric surgery.
Endoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (incisionless) is available for BMI 30, 40.
Vertical sleeve gastrectomy removes ~80% of the stomach, reducing ghrelin and providing a modest GLP-1 effect.
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass creates a small gastric pouch and bypasses a portion of the small intestine, producing a profound GLP-1 effect and malabsorption.
Gastric bypass patients must not smoke and should avoid prolonged NSAID use due to risk of marginal ulcers.
The SADI (single anastomosis duodenal ileal bypass) combines sleeve gastrectomy with greater malabsorption; it is reserved for higher-BMI patients (e.g., >50) with diabetes.
Expected weight loss is gradual across procedures: sleeve ~100 lbs, bypass ~115 lbs, SADI ~130, 140 lbs.
All bariatric surgeries are performed robotically with low complication rates (<2% for bleeding, infection, clots).
Postoperative patients need bariatric-specific multivitamins; Centrum Silver is an acceptable over-the-counter option.
Medications can be used as neoadjuvant therapy to make surgery safer and as adjuvant therapy after surgery to maintain weight loss.
Sleeve gastrectomy keeps doors open for revisional surgeries such as conversion to gastric bypass or SADI (modified duodenal switch).

episodes.title: Dr. Landreth on Bites and Stings in the Pediatric ER 11/20/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Landreth
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the management of venomous bites and stings encountered in the pediatric emergency department, including pit vipers (copperheads, rattlesnakes, cottonmouths), brown recluse spiders, black widow spiders, and hymenoptera stings. The speaker reviews initial assessment, laboratory evaluation, indications for antivenom, wound care, and supportive treatment. Emphasis is placed on recognizing systemic complications such as coagulopathy from snake envenomation, systemic loxoscelism from brown recluse bites, and anaphylaxis from hymenoptera stings. Practical pearls include a mnemonic to differentiate spider bites from staphylococcal abscesses and guidelines for observation and referral.
key_points: Snake bite coagulopathy presents with low platelets, prolonged PT/PTT, high D-dimer, and low fibrinogen, mimicking DIC.
Initial snake bite management includes removing constricting items; tourniquets, ice, and suction are contraindicated.
Assess induration by palpating the lateral borders of the bitten extremity, mark the leading edge with a time, and remeasure hourly.
Indications for pit viper antivenom are progressive local injury, systemic toxicity, or significant coagulopathy; minor envenomations may be observed.
CroFab dosing: initial bolus, then maintenance every 6 hours for 3 doses; patients must stay at least 18 hours and are at risk for rebound coagulopathy up to 2 weeks later.
Brown recluse bites cause a classic red-white-and-blue wound: pale center with surrounding erythema, progressing to eschar over 72 hours.
Systemic loxoscelism (intravascular hemolysis) is rare but severe; labs show anemia, thrombocytopenia, high LDH, low haptoglobin; can occur within 2 days or up to 7 days.
Black widow envenomation causes severe cramping pain within 30 minutes to 2 hours, treated effectively with IV benzodiazepines and analgesics; antivenom is rarely needed.
Hymenoptera venom anaphylaxis is the second leading cause of pediatric anaphylaxis (7% of cases, 20% of anaphylaxis deaths); highest risk with yellow jackets and honeybees.

Differentiate spider bite from staph abscess using the NOT RECLUSE mnemonic: multiple lesions, purulence, red center, elevated or chronic wounds suggest staph; solitary, pale-centered, non-purulent wounds suggest spider bite.
Hymenoptera venom anaphylaxis is the second most common cause of anaphylaxis in children, causing 7% of pediatric anaphylaxis and 20% of anaphylaxis deaths.
Yellow jackets and honeybees have the highest incidence of anaphylaxis; fire ants are more prevalent in the Southeast but less dangerous.

episodes.title: Dr. Lawrence Lee on Morning Reports
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee

also_uploaded.title: Dr. Lawrence Lee on Morning Reports

episodes.abstract: Dr. Lawrence Lee presents a case of a 34-year-old woman with dermatomyositis and calcinosis cutis admitted for recurrent cellulitis. The discussion covers the diagnosis and management of dermatomyositis, the types of calcinosis cutis, and a debate on whether to restart steroids in a patient recently weaned off them. Key teaching points include the risk of adrenal suppression persisting up to a year after steroid cessation and the importance of supporting physiology while treating infection.
key_points: Dermatomyositis is a rare autoimmune disease that attacks skin and muscles via inflammation and muscle ischemia.
Diagnosis of dermatomyositis involves muscle biopsy, skin biopsy, specific autoantibodies, and possibly EMG or MRI.
First-line treatment for dermatomyositis includes systemic steroids plus methotrexate or azathioprine; resistant cases may require other agents.
Calcinosis cutis has five main types: dystrophic (tissue damage, normal calcium/phosphate), metastatic (abnormal calcium/phosphate, e.g., hyperparathyroidism, renal disease), and others.
Dystrophic calcinosis cutis is associated with autoimmune diseases like dermatomyositis and can occur after trauma or infection.
Patients on chronic steroids may have iatrogenic adrenal suppression that can persist up to a year after weaning.
In an immunosuppressed patient with infection, withholding steroids may impair the ability to fight infection due to adrenal insufficiency.
A normal white count and absence of fever despite purulent drainage can be signs of adrenal suppression in a patient recently on steroids.
Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., vancomycin and Zosyn) are appropriate for recurrent cellulitis in an immunocompromised host.
Cultures should be obtained before antibiotics when possible, and documentation should avoid blaming other providers.
Pain management in chronic opioid users should follow a scheduled oral regimen with as-needed IV options.
The decision to restart steroids in a patient with recent wean requires balancing the risk of worsening immunosuppression against the need for physiologic support.

episodes.title: Dr. Lawrence Lee on Morning Reports 2/9/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lawrence Lee presents a case of an 86-year-old nursing home patient with a right foot infection, diabetes, peripheral neuropathy, and known osteomyelitis. The discussion covers classification of osteomyelitis (hematogenous vs. nonhematogenous), common pathogens, diagnostic approach emphasizing bone biopsy as the gold standard, and empiric antibiotic management. Key teaching points include the importance of inspecting all wounds, the role of ESR >100 in osteomyelitis, and the need for an antibiotic-free period before biopsy when possible.
key_points: Osteomyelitis is classified as hematogenous (bloodborne seeding) or nonhematogenous (direct inoculation from trauma, puncture wounds, ulcers, or surgery).
Nonhematogenous osteomyelitis is typically polymicrobial, including Staph aureus, anaerobes, and gram-negative rods; hematogenous is usually monomicrobial with Staph aureus.
In IV drug users, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Serratia marcescens are common; in immunosuppressed patients, Bacteroides fragilis must be covered.
Bone biopsy is the gold standard for definitive diagnosis of osteomyelitis; MRI can infer but not confirm.
ESR >100 is suggestive of osteomyelitis or malignancy.
Empiric antibiotics for osteomyelitis should include vancomycin (for MRSA) plus a third-generation cephalosporin.
For MSSA, IV cefazolin is extremely effective and commonly stocked.
For gram-negative rods, levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin are first choices; IV beta-lactams or carbapenems are alternatives.
Antibiotics should ideally be held for an optimal antibiotic-free period before bone biopsy, but this is often compromised by ED quality metrics requiring early antibiotics.
Every wound must be inspected at least once; never assume nursing has checked it, as missed wounds can lead to tunneling and mortality.
A sequestrum is an island of infected bone that blood cannot reach, making it untreatable with IV antibiotics alone.
Acute osteomyelitis presents over several days with pain, possible fever, nonhealing ulcer, and elevated WBC, CRP, and ESR.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Benzo Tapering
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter presents a practical approach to tapering patients off benzodiazepines, based on the Ashton Manual. He emphasizes converting short-acting benzos (e.g., alprazolam, clonazepam) to diazepam for a smoother taper, using gradual cross-tapering over weeks. The talk covers conversion equivalencies, individualized tapering schedules, frequent follow-up, and strategies for managing patients who are reluctant to discontinue benzodiazepines.
key_points: Benzodiazepines with short half-lives (e.g., Xanax) should not be used routinely long-term.
The Ashton Manual provides a structured protocol for converting benzodiazepines to diazepam and tapering.
Diazepam is preferred for tapering due to its longer half-life and less potent dosing, allowing smaller incremental cuts.
Cross-tapering involves gradually replacing one dose of the original benzo with an equivalent dose of diazepam over 1-2 weeks.
Conversion example: 0.5 mg alprazolam ≈ 10 mg diazepam.
Taper cuts are typically made every 1-2 weeks, but can be extended to 4 weeks if needed for psychological readiness.
As total daily diazepam dose decreases, the same milligram cut represents a larger percentage reduction, requiring caution.
Microtapering using compounded liquid benzodiazepines (e.g., 0.1 mg daily cuts) may be better tolerated but is not yet widely used.
Patients should be followed closely (every 1-2 weeks initially) with portal communication for dose adjustments.
Not all patients on benzodiazepines need to be tapered; the decision should weigh benefit vs. risk (e.g., falls in elderly).
If a patient refuses to discontinue benzodiazepines against medical advice, provide a one-month supply to find a new provider.
Patients on the same benzodiazepine dose may have very different experiences during tapering, some struggle physically/psychologically while others progress quickly.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac POCUS 10/9/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter presents a case-based review of cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for assessing left ventricular function, pulmonary edema, volume status, and right heart strain. Key measurements include E-point septal separation (EPSS) greater than 8 mm to predict ejection fraction ≤40%, and the presence of three or more B-lines bilaterally in a single lung zone as highly diagnostic for pulmonary edema. The lecture emphasizes integrating visual estimation with quantitative signs, recognizing hyperdynamic states as markers of hypovolemia, and identifying the D-sign of the interventricular septum as a sign of right ventricular pressure overload. Clinical context is stressed throughout.
key_points: EPSS >8 mm predicts an EF of 40% or less.
Three or more B-lines in a single zone on both sides is highly diagnostic for pulmonary edema in the right clinical setting.
Pleural effusion appears as an anechoic triangle on ultrasound and is more sensitive than chest X-ray.
A hyperdynamic left ventricle suggests hypovolemia and is often accompanied by tachycardia.
The D-sign (flattened septum, D-shaped LV) indicates right ventricular pressure overload.
Visual estimation of ejection fraction is reliable, especially when combined with other signs.
The short-axis view at the papillary muscle level is the best window for assessing LV contractility.
In sepsis, myocardial dysfunction can cause cardiogenic shock.
Tachycardia can occur without a hyperdynamic state; the two are not synonymous.
A mitral valve that does not come within 1 cm of the septum on M-mode suggests reduced EF.
In cardiac POCUS, a dilated right ventricle that is at least as large as the left ventricle suggests right heart strain.
The D-sign (left ventricle appearing D-shaped) indicates elevated right ventricular pressure pushing the septum into the left ventricle.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter teaches family medicine residents how to perform and interpret point-of-care cardiac ultrasound, focusing on the parasternal long-axis and short-axis views. He emphasizes that the goal is not a precise ejection fraction but a rapid bedside assessment of whether it is normal, reduced, or severely reduced. Key visual estimates include E-point septal separation (mitral leaflet should approach the septum within 1 cm), left ventricular cavity shrinkage of at least 30% in systole, and myocardial wall thickening of at least 50%. Practical tips for probe positioning, patient positioning, and transitioning between views are provided during hands-on practice.
key_points: Cardiac POCUS answers specific clinical questions (e.g., reduced EF, PE, hypotension) and does not replace a full echocardiogram.
The parasternal long-axis view is obtained with the probe marker toward the patient's right shoulder, starting parasternal and sliding to find the window.
E-point septal separation: the anterior mitral leaflet should come within 1 cm of the septum in diastole; if not, EF is likely reduced.
Visual estimate of LV cavity size: a normal LV shrinks at least 30% from diastole to systole.
Wall thickening: the myocardium should thicken by at least 50% (nearly doubling) during systole.
To obtain the parasternal short-axis view, rotate the probe 90° clockwise so the marker points toward the left shoulder.
In the short-axis view, identify the papillary muscle level (target), mitral valve level (fish lips), and base (Mercedes-Benz sign of aortic valve).
Change levels in short axis by fanning the probe: toward the base to see great vessels, toward the apex to see papillary muscles.
Patient positioning: rotating the patient slightly to the left (shoulder out) brings the heart closer to the chest wall.
Stabilize the probe by anchoring with a pinky on the patient's chest or using the scanning hand against the body.
During systole, the myocardium should thicken by at least 30%, and visually it may appear to nearly double in size.
Cavity area reduction in the left ventricle should be visually assessed, expect a 30% reduction if ejection fraction is normal.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Hypertension
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter discusses the management of hypertension, focusing on differentiating hypertensive urgency from emergency based on the presence of end-organ damage symptoms. He emphasizes that for non-emergency hypertension, blood pressure should be lowered over days, not hours, especially in older adults to avoid strokes from rapid reduction. The talk covers appropriate management strategies in both inpatient and outpatient settings, including addressing underlying causes such as pain or anxiety, restarting home medications, and avoiding PRN blood pressure medications except for specific conditions like stroke, aortic dissection, or preeclampsia. Key takeaway: a calm, symptom-focused approach often replaces aggressive pharmacologic intervention.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency is defined by symptoms of end-organ damage (brain, heart, kidneys, eyes) and requires lowering BP within hours; urgency lacks such symptoms and can be managed over days.
In elderly patients, rapid BP lowering can cause strokes; therefore, a slower approach is recommended.
For asymptomatic inpatients with elevated BP, first consider non-hypertensive causes (pain, anxiety, missed home meds) before adding new antihypertensives.
Initial rapid BP reduction goal is under 160/100, but no more than 25% reduction over the first 2, 4 hours.
Oral clonidine or captopril can be used in clinic for patients with known aortic dissection (not actively dissecting) to prevent progression to emergency.
For never-treated patients with persistent BP 140s, start one medication; for 160s, 170s or higher, consider two medications initially.
In hospital, avoid adjusting home BP meds except for acute coronary syndrome or heart failure where guideline-directed therapy is changing.
PRN blood pressure medications should not be ordered routinely; they are only appropriate for stroke protocols, aortic dissection, or preeclampsia.
White coat hypertension in hospital is often anxiety-driven; treating the underlying anxiety is preferred over giving IV antihypertensives.
PRN blood pressure medications should not be routinely ordered for hospitalized patients.
Exceptions for PRN antihypertensives include stroke protocol, aortic dissection, and preeclampsia.
Parameters alone are insufficient; decisions should incorporate symptoms and clinical context.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter teaches a hands-on musculoskeletal ultrasound session focused on the knee, covering tissue appearance, anisotropy, probe selection, and a systematic scanning approach. The talk emphasizes identifying effusions, performing joint injections, and recognizing Baker's cysts, with practical tips for probe orientation and patient positioning. The session includes live scanning demonstrations and guidance on using ultrasound to improve injection accuracy and patient satisfaction.
key_points: Muscle in long axis has a feathery appearance; in short axis it looks like a Starry Night with hyperechoic dots.
Tendon in long axis shows parallel hyperechoic lines; in short axis these appear as tiny dots.
Anisotropy means tissue appearance changes with the angle of the sound waves; always try to be perpendicular to tendon and nerve to avoid false tears.
Bone appears hyperechoic at the anterior surface with posterior shadowing.
Use a linear, high-frequency, superficial-depth probe with a musculoskeletal preset for knee ultrasound.
Position the knee in slight flexion (like for Lachman's test) using a pillow or sheets under the knee.
Start scanning suprapatellar in long axis to identify the quadriceps tendon, patella, fat pads, and femur; then rotate to short axis.
A joint effusion appears as an anechoic space above the fat pad; if no fluid, the space is nearly nonexistent.
Follow the patellar tendon from patella to tibia in long and short axes; a bursa may be visible only if fluid is present.
Ultrasound can rule in a medial meniscus tear if seen, but cannot rule one out because much of the meniscus is internal.
Dynamic ultrasound can assess MCL gapping with medial and lateral stress compared to both sides.
For lateral structures, the LCL connects femur to fibula, while the IT band crosses the lateral meniscus; find the fibula to see the LCL.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter discusses the diagnosis and management of pneumonia, emphasizing the superiority of lung ultrasound (POCUS) over chest X-ray, especially in children to avoid radiation. He covers antibiotic treatment for adult outpatient lobar pneumonia, including amoxicillin 1000 mg three times daily plus azithromycin for atypical coverage, with a total treatment duration of 3, 5 days. The lecture provides detailed POCUS technique: probe selection (phased array or curvilinear), patient positioning based on pathology, an eight-zone scanning protocol, and identification of normal findings (A-lines, lung sliding) versus pneumonia (thick pleural line, B-lines, consolidation).
key_points: Lung ultrasound is better than chest X-ray for diagnosing pneumonia in both children and adults, even when performed by novice ultrasonographers.
For adult outpatient lobar pneumonia without allergies, treat with amoxicillin 1000 mg three times daily (two 500 mg tablets) plus azithromycin for atypical coverage.
Azithromycin total dose should be 1500 mg, given as 500 mg daily for 3 days or 500 mg on day 1 then 250 mg on days 2, 4.
Outpatient antibiotic duration for pneumonia should be 3, 5 days, no longer than 7 days; if not improving, consider other diagnoses or hospitalization.
Baseline labs are not needed for outpatient pneumonia unless there is a reason to suspect increased risk.
For lung ultrasound, use a phased array or curvilinear probe; with the Butterfly, use the lung preset for most areas but switch to the abdominal preset for the bases (above the diaphragm).
Patient positioning: lay flat and scan anteriorly for pneumothorax; elevate the patient for pleural effusion; pneumonia position does not matter, but elevate if parapneumonic effusion is suspected.
Use an eight-zone lung ultrasound technique: four anterior zones per side divided by the nipple line and anterior axillary line; if no pneumonia is found anteriorly, scan posteriorly (zones 5, 6).
Keep the probe marker toward the patient's head and maintain the probe perpendicular to the lung to visualize A-lines; angle medially as the lung curves.
In pneumonia, the pleural line may be thick or muddled, and B-lines indicate a mixture of fluid and air (mild pneumonia or pulmonary edema).
Normal lung ultrasound shows lung sliding at the parietal pleural line and A-lines, which indicate air; absence of A-lines or presence of B-lines suggests pathology.
In pneumonia, the pleural line is often thickened or 'muddled' rather than thin and crisp.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter discusses the use of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for diagnosing and managing skin and soft tissue infections, particularly abscesses. The lecture covers probe selection, scanning technique, and key sonographic findings such as cobblestoning in cellulitis versus anechoic or heterogeneous collections in abscesses. It emphasizes the importance of clinical context to differentiate infection from edema, and highlights the role of Doppler to avoid vessels and identify lymph nodes. Additional applications include detecting foreign bodies and guiding procedures like incision and drainage.
key_points: POCUS reduces the failure rate of abscess identification from 17% (physical exam alone) to 3.7%.
Use a linear probe (or Butterfly preset mimicking linear) for superficial abscess evaluation.
Scan the entire area of concern in two orthogonal planes to fully characterize the collection.
Cobblestoning (anechoic lines splitting fat globules) indicates fluid in subcutaneous tissue, seen in both cellulitis and edema; clinical context is essential to differentiate.
Abscesses may appear anechoic, hypoechoic, or heterogeneous; septations suggest need for open drainage rather than needle aspiration.
Doppler is used to confirm the collection is not a vessel and to identify nearby vessels before incision.
Lymph nodes can mimic abscesses; look for a well-defined border and a hilar Doppler pattern to avoid unnecessary incision.
Ultrasound is excellent for detecting foreign bodies (splinters, glass, metal, plastic), often with posterior shadowing.
The water bath technique improves imaging of small structures like fingers and toes by using water as a coupling medium.
Always integrate ultrasound findings with the full clinical picture, POCUS cannot distinguish infected from noninfected fluid.
Foreign bodies like glass appear hyperechoic on ultrasound and cast acoustic shadowing underneath.
The water bath technique improves visualization of superficial foreign bodies by reducing near-field artifact.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter presents a focused POCUS approach to the gallbladder, emphasizing preparation (fasting, positioning, breathing maneuvers) and three scanning windows: subcostal sweep, X7 (subxiphoid to lateral), and right lateral intercostal. Key sonographic findings include gallstones (gravity-dependent, hyperechoic, posterior shadowing), sonographic Murphy's sign (focal tenderness over the fundus), gallbladder wall thickening (normal <3 mm), pericholecystic fluid, and common bile duct dilation (normal 2-6 mm, plus 1 mm per decade after age 40). The talk includes practical tips for distinguishing stones from polyps and sludge, using color Doppler to differentiate the common bile duct from the hepatic artery, and pitfalls such as edge artifact and contracted gallbladder mimicking wall thickening.
key_points: Fasting reduces bowel gas and improves gallbladder visualization; left lateral decubitus position brings the gallbladder more anterior.
Three scanning approaches: subcostal sweep (avoids ribs but may encounter intestinal air), X7 (start subxiphoid, go 7 cm laterally), and right lateral intercostal (look through the liver).
Gallstones are gravity-dependent, mobile, hyperechoic, and produce posterior acoustic shadowing; polyps are non-mobile and usually lack shadowing unless calcified.
Sludge is hypoechoic, mobile, and does not shadow; a hyperechoic top with shadowing may represent clumped stones.
Sonographic Murphy's sign: probe pressure over the gallbladder fundus causes pain that is not reproduced when pressing elsewhere.
Gallbladder wall thickness is measured at the most anterior wall; normal is <3 mm; a contracted gallbladder can falsely appear thickened.
Pericholecystic fluid appears as an anechoic wedge or loculated collection around the gallbladder wall.
Common bile duct diameter is measured inner-to-inner wall; normal is 2-6 mm, increasing by 1 mm per decade after age 40.
Use color Doppler to differentiate the common bile duct (no flow) from the hepatic artery (color flow).
The portal vein has a hyperechoic border; in long axis the gallbladder and portal vein form an 'exclamation point' landmark.
The ultrasound beam must go through the ribs to obtain an adequate view.
When an image is frozen, the trackball can be rolled to scroll through the captured clip.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter presents a practical introduction to point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) of the knee for family medicine residents. The lecture covers essential concepts such as anisotropy and the sonographic appearance of tendons, ligaments, nerves, muscle, and bone. Key scanning views are demonstrated: the suprapatellar recess (long and short axis) for detecting effusion and guiding injections, the patellar tendon, and the infrapatellar space for static guidance of anterior knee injections. The session emphasizes hands-on scanning and includes tips for patient positioning, probe selection, and technique to improve accuracy and patient comfort.
key_points: Anisotropy causes tendons and ligaments to appear hypoechoic when the ultrasound beam is not perpendicular; always fan through to avoid mistaking artifact for pathology.
Use a linear probe with a musculoskeletal preset; adjust depth and gain to visualize superficial knee structures.

The suprapatellar recess is the preferred site for dynamic ultrasound-guided knee injection or arthrocentesis; it lies between the prefemoral and suprapatellar fat pads, deep to the quadriceps tendon.
In a knee without effusion, the suprapatellar recess may not be visible; inject a small amount of fluid to separate the fat pads and confirm needle placement.
For suprapatellar injection, start with a long-axis view to identify landmarks, then center the probe and rotate 90 degrees to a short-axis view; insert the needle from the lateral side.
The patellar tendon is a hyperechoic linear structure connecting the patella to the tibial tuberosity; scan with the knee bent or straight at a depth of about 1 cm.
For static guidance of an anterior knee injection, find the infrapatellar view, then slide the probe medially or laterally until the tendon disappears, that is a safe needle entry site.
The medial and lateral menisci appear as triangular hyperechoic structures between the femur and tibia on ultrasound.
Ultrasound guidance for knee injections improves patient satisfaction and may reduce pain; the presenter uses it routinely.
Patient and operator comfort is important: have the patient sit with leg straight and supported, and position yourself to avoid leaning over.
The patellar tendon appears as a hyperechoic linear structure connecting the patella to the tibial tuberosity.
For static ultrasound-guided anterior knee injection, find the infrapatellar view and slide the probe laterally until the tendon disappears; that is a safe needle insertion site.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for diagnosing pneumonia. Dr. Ledbetter explains probe selection, the four-zone scanning protocol, and normal lung ultrasound findings including lung sliding and A-lines. Key pathological findings specific to pneumonia are reviewed in order of specificity: dynamic air bronchograms (most specific), focal B-lines (≥3 in a single zone), lung consolidation/hepatization, and the shred sign. The presenter notes that ultrasound is more sensitive than chest X-ray for detecting pneumonia and pleural effusions, and can reduce radiation exposure.
key_points: Use a linear probe with the marker toward the head; lung preset on Butterfly for artifact interpretation.
Scan four anterior zones on each side (split by nipple/inframammary line and anterior axillary line); add posterior zones 5 and 6 if needed.
In zones 4 and 6, switch to abdominal preset for better visualization of the diaphragm, liver, and spleen.
Normal lung shows lung sliding, A-lines (artifact lines parallel to pleura at multiples of pleural depth), and the curtain sign (no spine seen above diaphragm).
Dynamic air bronchograms (hyperechoic dots moving with respiration) are the most specific sign for pneumonia on lung ultrasound.
Focal B-lines: three or more in a single zone are 96% specific for pneumonia.
Lung consolidation (hepatization) appears as tissue-like echotexture where normally only artifact is seen.
Shred sign: irregular hyperechoic interface between consolidated and aerated lung is highly specific for pneumonia.
Thickening of the pleural line can indicate infection; thin/crisp pleural line favors pulmonary edema over pneumonia.
Ultrasound is more sensitive than chest X-ray for pneumonia and pleural effusion, with similar specificity.
Symmetrical bilateral B-lines suggest pulmonary edema, while asymmetrical focal B-lines suggest pneumonia.
Set depth deep initially to distinguish true B-lines from short comet tails; adjust dynamically to look for small subpleural consolidations.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter presents a practical guide to point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) of the thyroid for family medicine residents. The lecture covers normal thyroid anatomy, scanning technique in transverse and sagittal views, and measurement of lobes and isthmus. It then focuses on evaluating thyroid nodules, including key sonographic features such as shape, margins, echogenicity, calcifications, and vascularity. Finally, it introduces the TIRADS scoring system to guide decisions on which nodules require biopsy versus follow-up.
key_points: Scan the thyroid in transverse view first, as it looks most like the thyroid and is easier to orient.
Normal thyroid tissue is homogeneous and hyperechoic relative to the surrounding strap muscles.
Thyroiditis appears heterogeneous with black and white specks due to lymphocytic infiltration.
For nodules, assess location, size, shape (taller-than-wide is concerning), margins (halo sign is benign; irregular/infiltrative is malignant), echogenicity, calcifications, and vascularity.
Microcalcifications (<1 mm) are associated with papillary carcinoma; macrocalcifications and eggshell calcifications can be benign or malignant.
Internodular or central vascularity is more concerning than absent or peripheral vascularity.
Nodules ≥1 cm with concerning features or ≥1.5 cm with low suspicion should be considered for biopsy per TIRADS.
TIRADS scoring combines sonographic features to determine malignancy risk and biopsy thresholds.
For TIRADS 3 (mildly suspicious), biopsy if >2.5 cm; for TIRADS 4 (moderately suspicious), biopsy if >1.5 cm; for TIRADS 5 (highly suspicious), biopsy if >1 cm.
Consistency in measurement technique is crucial for reproducible follow-up of nodules over time.

episodes.title: Dr. Lee Morning Report 9/10/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: A 65-year-old man with no known medical history presents with progressive shortness of breath, weakness, bilateral leg edema, and palpitations. EKG shows atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (RVR) and an IVCD. The case emphasizes a systematic EKG interpretation approach and the management of hemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation with RVR, including the importance of assessing blood pressure before rate control therapy. The patient responded to IV furosemide and a Cardizem drip, and the presentation is framed as new-onset decompensated heart failure.
key_points: Systematic EKG interpretation should follow a stepwise approach: standard, rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, QRS complex, ST segment, T waves, and final read.
In atrial fibrillation with RVR, the first step is to assess hemodynamic stability; unstable patients require immediate cardioversion.
For hemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation with RVR, the next step is to check blood pressure before choosing a rate control agent.
A blood pressure of 100 mmHg systolic or higher provides a safety cushion before giving rate-slowing medications like metoprolol or diltiazem.
Giving rate control agents to patients with borderline low blood pressure (e.g., 90/60) can precipitate hypotension, which is preventable.
T wave inversions should be evaluated in leads I, II, V5, and V6, not in V2-V3 where they can be normal.
A wide QRS that does not meet criteria for left or right bundle branch block is called an IVCD (intraventricular conduction delay).
New-onset heart failure in a patient with no prior medical history should raise suspicion for underlying causes such as arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy.
The patient's history of mononucleosis 4 months prior may be relevant to the development of atrial fibrillation or myocarditis.
Documentation should be precise; 'RRR' (regular rate and rhythm) is inaccurate for an irregular rhythm like atrial fibrillation.
Distinguish CAP from HAP by whether the pneumonia was incubating prior to admission.
Hold antibiotics until a specific target is identified; obtain cultures first.

episodes.title: Dr. Lee on Morning Report
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: A 55-year-old woman presents to urgent care with six days of severe bilateral arm pain, found to have platelets of 25 (later confirmed at 5). The case illustrates the importance of maintaining a broad differential for bilateral arm pain, including vascular, neurologic, and hematologic causes, and of explicitly reopening the differential when findings are unexpected. The presenter reviews the differential diagnosis of thrombocytopenia (HIT, ITP, DIC, TTP, splenic sequestration, bone marrow infiltration, cirrhosis, medication-induced, viral illness) and emphasizes that in real clinical practice, clinicians must consciously pause to generate a differential rather than relying on pattern recognition alone.
key_points: Bilateral arm pain has a broad differential including muscular strain, polymyalgia rheumatica, cervical stenosis, bilateral DVTs, fracture, polymyositis, syringomyelia, and cardiac ischemia.
Key history questions for arm pain include numbness, tingling, weakness, skin changes, recent illness, trauma, other joint involvement, and chest pain.
Severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 5) in a patient with severe bilateral arm pain should prompt immediate transfer to the ER, not dismissal as lab error.
When a case feels 'fishy' or unexpected, explicitly pause to write out or verbalize a differential diagnosis, this is often forgotten in real clinical settings.

The differential for thrombocytopenia includes: HIT (check HIT antibody), ITP (peripheral smear, diagnosis of exclusion), DIC (DIC panel), TTP (ADAMTS13 deficiency), splenic sequestration (ultrasound), bone marrow infiltration (biopsy), cirrhosis (liver ultrasound, INR, CP), medication-induced (check outside records), and viral illness (viral panel).
TTP often first presents with a clot, not bleeding.
A normal white count (13.2) makes hematologic malignancy less likely as a cause of thrombocytopenia.
Always check if the patient has had low platelets before, review outside records for prior labs.
Medication-induced thrombocytopenia is easily overlooked; check outside medication records.
The admitting physician's plan for this case included MRI C-spine for suspected spinal stenosis, pain control, and workup for thrombocytopenia of unknown etiology.
Every problem on the problem list should have a corresponding plan, and every plan should address a specific problem (non sequitur plans are a documentation pitfall).
When a patient's presentation is atypical and evolving, inflammatory arthropathy should remain in the differential diagnosis.

episodes.title: Dr. Lee on Morning Reports
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lawrence Lee presents a complex case of a 63-year-old male with alcohol misuse, thrombocytopenia, and multi-system symptoms including confusion, bleeding, and metabolic derangements. The session focuses on building a differential diagnosis for thrombocytopenia, distinguishing thrombotic from bleeding disorders, and systematically interpreting an arterial blood gas. Key teaching points include the importance of thought process over correct answers, the differential for thrombocytopenia, and stepwise acid-base analysis using Winter's formula and anion gap.
key_points: The primary goal of morning report is to learn and think, not just to get the right answer.
When encountering thrombocytopenia, always generate a differential diagnosis before acting.

Differential for thrombocytopenia includes cirrhosis, medication-induced, ITP, DIC, HIT, TTP, HUS, infection, malignancy, vitamin B12/folate deficiency, myelofibrosis, autoimmune/vasculitides, HIV, and splenic sequestration.
Thrombotic thrombocytopenias include TTP, HIT, antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), and vasculitides; DIC is a mixed bleeding and thrombotic disorder.
Wet purpura refers to mucosal bleeding; dry purpura is petechiae on skin.
Acid-base analysis begins with pH, then bicarbonate, then expected pCO2 using Winter's formula (1.5 x bicarbonate + 8 ± 2), then anion gap, then delta-delta to assess compensation.
A normal anion gap does not rule out metabolic acidosis; delta-delta calculation is needed to detect mixed disorders.
A patient with normal oxygen saturation can still have respiratory acidosis due to hypoventilation.
Clinical signs of bleeding in thrombocytopenia include gingival bleeding, epistaxis, ecchymoses, petechiae, and dark stools.
History of alcohol misuse with recent binge drinking and thrombocytopenia should raise suspicion for liver disease and bone marrow suppression.
Anion gap is calculated as sodium minus chloride minus bicarbonate.
Winter's formula helps identify a superimposed respiratory acidosis even when pCO2 appears normal.

episodes.title: Dr. Lee's Morning Report
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lawrence Lee presents a case of a 68-year-old woman with 'worst headache of my life' to teach clinical reasoning in headache evaluation. The case highlights the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis for thunderclap headache, including subarachnoid hemorrhage, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, even when initial CT is negative. The discussion critiques an admitting plan that lacked a differential and failed to rule out serious causes, emphasizing that symptoms like headache waking from sleep and age >50 are red flags. The lecture also reviews migraine pathophysiology as neurogenic inflammation rather than vascular, and stresses the need for a documented differential when a definitive diagnosis is not established.
key_points: Worst headache of life is a buzzword that mandates evaluation for subarachnoid hemorrhage with CT head and consideration of LP for xanthochromia.
A negative non-contrast CT head does not rule out all dangerous causes of thunderclap headache; CTA or MRI may be needed for CVST, RCVS, or dissection.
Headache that wakes a patient from sleep and onset after age 50 are red flags (SNOOP criteria) for secondary headache.
Every symptom without a definitive diagnosis requires a documented differential diagnosis with a plan to rule in or rule out each possibility.
Migraine pathophysiology is now understood as neurogenic inflammation and trigeminal activation, not primarily vascular.
Status migrainosus requires aggressive treatment beyond simple analgesics, including triptans, antiemetics, and sometimes steroids.
Uncontrolled diabetes in a hospitalized patient should be addressed with a basal-bolus insulin regimen, not just sliding scale.
Admission status (inpatient vs observation) should be clearly documented based on clinical stability and need for ongoing workup.
Copy-pasting from prior notes can perpetuate errors; always verify and update the history and physical exam.
Fentanyl provided partial relief in this case, but the headache recurred, indicating incomplete treatment of status migrainosus.
Migraine pathophysiology involves neurogenic inflammation leading to neurochemical changes and trigeminal activation, not primarily vascular mechanisms.
Migraine prevalence is up to 17% in women and 6% in men.

episodes.title: Dr. Leo on Advance Care Planning
episodes.speaker: Dr. Leo
episodes.abstract: Dr. Leo presents a family-medicine residency lecture on advance care planning, clarifying key terminology and legal distinctions. The talk covers advanced directives, living wills, POLST forms, comfort measures only, hospice care, and power of attorney, using a case example to highlight common misconceptions. Dr. Leo emphasizes that hospice and DNR status are not mutually exclusive and provides practical guidance on documentation and palliative care consultation.
key_points: Advance care planning is an ongoing process, not a one-time event, allowing patients to communicate wishes for life-limiting or life-altering events.
An advanced directive is a legal document outlining future medical care decisions in case of incapacity; it is recognized but not legally binding in emergency situations.
A POLST (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) is a portable medical order completed by the patient and provider, serving as a standing order for life-sustaining treatments.
Comfort measures only (CMO) focuses on relieving pain and symptoms at end of life; at St. John, ordering CMO requires also ordering DNR and DNI forms.
Hospice care is for terminally ill patients with a prognosis of six months or less, focusing on comfort and palliative care.
A living will is a written document listing general treatment wishes but may not include specific orders like DNR or intubation.
Power of attorney appoints a named person as health care proxy for medical decisions during temporary or permanent incapacity.
Palliative care can be combined with curative treatments and is not mutually exclusive with aggressive therapy.
In Oklahoma, the health care agent pecking order is spouse, children, parents, siblings, then others; this varies by state.
If no family is available, the closest person to the patient can act as health care agent under Oklahoma law.
Living wills should address four components: pacemaker/ICD, IV hydration, and other life-sustaining treatments; missing components should prompt a follow-up conversation.
POLST is for patients with a life-altering diagnosis who are not imminently dying but are at risk; it includes medical orders and is used in the 'gray zone'.

episodes.title: Dr. Leo on Epidemiology
episodes.speaker: Dr. Leo
episodes.abstract: Dr. Leo reviews foundational epidemiology concepts including relative risk, absolute risk reduction, confidence intervals, and p-values, emphasizing their clinical application. He explains how to interpret sensitivity and specificity using the mnemonic 'SNOUT' and 'SPIN'. The lecture then transitions to the 'Things We Do for No Reason' series from the ABIM's Choosing Wisely campaign, starting with the practice of administering oxygen to patients without hypoxemia, citing a NEJM study on acute cardiac chest pain.
key_points: Relative risk is a ratio comparing incidence between exposed and unexposed groups; a value of 1 means no association, above 1 indicates increased risk, below 1 indicates decreased risk.
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) is the event rate in the control group minus the event rate in the experimental group, and is more clinically useful than relative risk.
Number Needed to Treat (NNT) is 1/ARR and tells how many patients need treatment to prevent one adverse outcome.
Number Needed to Harm (NNH) is the number of patients treated before one is harmed by the intervention.
Number Needed to Screen (NNS) is the number of people needed to screen to prevent one adverse outcome from a screenable disease.
A highly sensitive test rules out disease (SNOUT); a highly specific test rules in disease (SPIN).
P-value is the inverse of the confidence interval; a p-value <0.05 means less than 5% chance the result occurred by chance alone.
P-values do not prove the null hypothesis true or false, only that the result is unlikely due to chance.
Level C evidence includes case series, cross-sectional studies, and expert opinion; UpToDate is a collection of expert opinions.
Administering oxygen to patients without hypoxemia (SpO2 >90%) is a practice done for no reason, based on a NEJM study of 6,629 adults with acute cardiac chest pain.
Oxygen therapy in MI patients with SpO2 >90% does not reduce mortality or improve outcomes.
Oxygen supplementation does not relieve breathlessness in palliative patients with air hunger.

episodes.title: Dr. Liening on Pediatric GI 1/8/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Liening
episodes.abstract: Dr. Liening delivers a high-yield pediatric GI lecture for family medicine residents, covering jaundice, reflux, and pyloric stenosis by age group. She emphasizes that conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in infants is always pathologic and requires immediate ultrasound. For neonatal jaundice, she highlights that a rate of rise greater than 0.2 mg/dL per hour is dangerous and that kernicterus risk is highest in the first 24 hours. She also reviews management of infant reflux (supportive care, positioning, avoiding medications unless the infant is ill) and the classic presentation of pyloric stenosis (projectile non-bilious vomiting, weight loss, eager feeding after vomiting).
key_points: Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia in infants is never normal and always indicates a post-liver obstruction such as biliary atresia.
First step for conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in an infant is an abdominal ultrasound.
Kernicterus risk is highest when bilirubin exceeds 20 mg/dL and in the first 24 hours of life.
Current jaundice guidelines focus on rate of rise (>0.2 mg/dL per hour is dangerous) rather than old low/intermediate risk categories.
Always check the newborn screen in a sick infant with feeding issues in the first month of life.
Infant reflux is normal in about 50% of 2-month-olds and resolves by 9-12 months; treatment is supportive unless the infant is ill.
Poor feeding habits (e.g., overfeeding) are the number one modifiable factor worsening reflux.
Pyloric stenosis presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting, weight loss, and the infant is eager to feed again after vomiting.
Abdominal ultrasound is the next best step for suspected pyloric stenosis in a 4-week to 1-year-old with progressive vomiting and weight loss.
Do not dismiss a mother who reports worsening vomiting; pyloric stenosis can be missed if symptoms are attributed to normal reflux.
Pyloric stenosis presents with progressive, nonbilious, nonbloody projectile vomiting starting around 3-5 weeks, with the infant eager to feed again after vomiting and showing weight loss.
Abdominal ultrasound is the next best step for suspected pyloric stenosis when there is increasing vomiting with weight loss in a 5-week-old.

episodes.title: Dr. Liening on Shoulder Exam 9/18/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Liening
episodes.abstract: Dr. Liening presents a shoulder exam review for family medicine residents, emphasizing the importance of understanding anatomy and pathophysiology to answer board questions and perform efficient clinical exams. The session includes practice test questions covering rotator cuff tears, adhesive capsulitis, cervical radiculopathy, AC joint injury, and biceps tendinopathy, followed by a video demonstration of special tests. Key teaching points include using range of motion to guide exam selection, documenting with test names for efficiency, and adapting the exam for time-limited visits with older patients.
key_points: Understanding shoulder anatomy and movements can get 50-75% of test questions right; knowing test names helps with the rest and speeds documentation.
Acute rotator cuff tear in a young active patient (e.g., 36-year-old) often warrants MRI and possible surgical repair, while chronic tears in older patients are managed conservatively.
The empty can test is specific for supraspinatus weakness and is a key test for rotator cuff pathology.

Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) presents with gradual, constant dull pain, marked stiffness in all planes (especially external rotation), no point tenderness, and no weakness on resisted testing.
Always examine the cervical spine in shoulder pain presentations; Spurling's test (extension, lateral flexion, rotation with axial compression) reproduces radicular symptoms.
Cross-body adduction test reproduces pain in AC joint injury, often with a step-off deformity after trauma.
Speed's and Yergason's tests are specific for biceps tendinopathy; a positive result with negative rotator cuff tests points to that diagnosis.
A quick range-of-motion exam (forward flexion, abduction, internal rotation, external rotation, cross-body adduction) helps select which special tests to perform.
Observe the shoulder from behind during range-of-motion to detect scapular hiking or compensatory movements that indicate pathology.
In time-limited visits, prioritize the symptomatic shoulder exam and gather history first to choose the most relevant tests.
Observe shoulder range of motion from behind to detect scapular hiking that indicates compensation or pathology.
Perform rotator cuff strength testing at 30 degrees of abduction in the scapular plane to minimize deltoid involvement.

episodes.title: Dr. Lucashu on Coronary Artery Disease
episodes.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lucashu presents a case-based lecture on coronary artery disease, focusing on the evaluation and management of chest pain in a patient with nonspecific ST changes on EKG. She reviews the HEART score for risk stratification, discusses the MONA mnemonic and its limitations, and outlines the transition from inpatient to outpatient care including medication management and hospital follow-up. The lecture emphasizes practical tools like MedCalc, the importance of dual antiplatelet therapy, and common pitfalls such as forgetting anticoagulation.
key_points: Nonspecific ST changes on EKG include inverted T waves, biphasic T waves, and flattened T waves, which can be subtle and require careful interpretation.
The HEART score (without troponin) provides a minimum risk threshold; a score of 4-6 indicates moderate risk, warranting admission or observation with troponins and likely inpatient stress testing.
Life-threatening differentials for chest pain include ACS, aortic dissection, tamponade, PE, pneumothorax, and esophageal rupture.
In the HEART score, 'suspicion' refers to typicality of symptoms (substernal, exertional, relieved by rest), not believability of the patient's story.

MONA (morphine, oxygen, nitroglycerin, aspirin) is a helpful mnemonic but has limitations: morphine is not for right-sided MI, oxygen only for hypoxia, and aspirin is the only component with a mortality benefit.

Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus P2Y12 inhibitor like clopidogrel or ticagrelor) is standard after ACS, but avoid loading if multi-vessel disease may require CABG, as antiplatelets delay surgery by 5-7 days.
High-intensity statin should be started immediately after ACS due to anti-inflammatory properties, even though it is primarily preventive.
Anticoagulation (heparin or enoxaparin) is often forgotten; it should be given for in-hospital prophylaxis even if not going to the cath lab.
At hospital follow-up, check the cath entry site, ensure medications were filled and are affordable, refer to cardiac rehab, and confirm follow-up appointments are scheduled.

For outpatient management after ACS, continue antiplatelet therapy as per cardiology, use beta blockers (avoid labetalol), consider calcium channel blockers if beta blockers contraindicated (avoid in WPW), and nitrates for symptom relief (do not decrease mortality).
Post-hospital follow-up should ensure prescriptions are filled and follow-up appointments are scheduled.
Antiplatelet therapy decisions (mono vs. dual) are made by cardiology; primary care continues what cardiology started.

episodes.title: Dr. Lucashu on Outpatient Management
episodes.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
episodes.abstract: Dr. Amanda Lucashu delivers a practical, outpatient-focused lecture on diabetes management for family medicine residents. She emphasizes a stepwise approach starting with metformin and comprehensive lifestyle modifications, then tailoring therapy based on comorbidities like ASCVD, heart failure, or CKD. The talk covers initial diagnostic workup, a 12-point management checklist for new diagnoses, and a shame-free approach to lifestyle counseling. Dr. Lucashu also provides guidance on navigating insurance formularies, particularly for Medicaid patients, and stresses the importance of maximizing metformin dosing before advancing therapy.
key_points: For a new diabetes diagnosis, order hemoglobin A1c and lipid panel per USPSTF guidelines; baseline chem 7 and CBC are not required but often done.

Initial visit management includes 12 items: ACE inhibitor, statin, foot exam, eye exam, urine microalbumin, nutrition referral, lifestyle modification counseling, home blood pressure log, recheck BP, one-month follow-up, provide diabetic education folder, and start metformin.
Start a moderate-intensity statin for all patients with diabetes regardless of cholesterol level; consider upgrading to high-intensity based on ASCVD risk calculator.
Metformin is first-line therapy for all patients; most insurances require failure at maximum dosing (1000 mg PO BID or XR 2000 mg daily) before covering second-line agents.
Metformin XR is better tolerated but often requires prior authorization for Medicaid; regular or SR formulations are tier 1 for SoonerCare.
Home glucose monitoring is indicated for A1c >9%; for lower A1c, a monitor may still be provided but with less frequent checking.

Lifestyle modification should be shame-free; focus on eliminating sugary drinks, reducing carbs (breads, pasta, rice, potatoes), and achieving 150 minutes of aerobic exercise weekly in sessions of at least 10 minutes.
Exercise intensity should be sufficient to elevate heart rate and make completing a full sentence difficult; walking may not always meet this threshold.
Referral to a dietitian should be offered to all patients with diabetes.
Endocrinology referral is appropriate when patients fail to meet glycemic targets despite maximal medical therapy or have complex comorbidities.
Aerobic exercise should be 150 minutes/week, in sessions of at least 10 minutes, with heart rate elevated enough that the patient cannot finish a sentence.
Weight loss goal is 0.5, 1 pound per week; bariatric surgery referral is indicated for BMI ≥40, or ≥35 with a comorbidity like diabetes.

episodes.title: Dr. Lucashu speaks on Thyroid disease
episodes.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lucashu discusses management of hypothyroidism in pregnancy, including the need to increase levothyroxine by 30-50% upon confirmation of pregnancy and to treat subclinical hypothyroidism. She covers screening recommendations for thyroid disease, evaluation and management of subclinical hypothyroidism in non-pregnant adults, and diagnosis and initial treatment of Graves' disease. Practical tips include ordering the correct antibody tests and avoiding unnecessary repeat antibody testing.
key_points: In pregnancy, increase levothyroxine dose by 30-50% automatically when pregnancy is confirmed, without waiting for lab results.
Treat subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH, normal T4) in pregnancy, even though it is not treated outside of pregnancy.
Check TSH monthly during pregnancy; do not rely on Cerner reference ranges for pregnancy, use perinatology resources.
Do not check free T4 in pregnancy; management is based solely on TSH.

For subclinical hypothyroidism in non-pregnant adults (TSH 5.9, normal T4), offer reassurance but do not treat unless exceptions apply (symptomatic, TSH >10, goiter, family history, positive antibodies, pregnancy or planning pregnancy).
Screening for thyroid disease: American Thyroid Association recommends every 5 years starting at age 35; USPSTF does not recommend due to insufficient evidence.
For suspected hyperthyroidism, order TSH first; if low, consider Graves' disease, thyroiditis, adenoma, struma ovarii, or medication effects (dopamine, steroids).
Confirm Graves' disease with anti-TSH receptor antibody (most specific); order as 'TSH receptor antibody' in the lab system.
Do not repeat thyroid antibodies (TPO, thyroglobulin, anti-TSH receptor) after diagnosis; they do not change management.
Initial treatment for Graves' disease: start propranolol for symptom management and methimazole to block thyroid hormone synthesis.
In a patient on methimazole presenting with fever and sore throat, check CBC to rule out agranulocytosis.
TSH receptor antibody is 98% sensitive for Graves' disease but can be positive in 6% of acute thyroiditis cases.

episodes.title: Dr. Mark Crouch on Ingestions 6/11/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
episodes.abstract: Dr. Mark Crouch leads an interactive session on ingestions using case-based learning. He emphasizes the importance of obtaining the bottle, calling poison control, and checking symptoms, timing, and quantity. Key global health pearls include using package inserts for unfamiliar medications, establishing IV access early, and recognizing region-specific toxins like paraquat and improperly prepared cassava or fava beans. The talk underscores that asymptomatic patients can deteriorate quickly and that local knowledge is invaluable for managing unfamiliar poisons.
key_points: Always ask about symptoms, timing, and quantity of ingestion; asymptomatic patients can still deteriorate rapidly.
Obtain the original container or bottle; in the US, it often lists poison control number and first aid instructions.
Call poison control even from overseas; they can provide guidance on unfamiliar toxins.
For unfamiliar medications abroad, open the package insert, global manufacturers include dosing and toxicity information.
Establish IV access early in any potential poisoning or resuscitation scenario, before circulatory collapse.
Check blood glucose in any altered or ingestion patient, as hypoglycemia may be a cofactor.
Activated charcoal is time-sensitive and most effective if given within one hour of ingestion.
Paraquat (Gramoxone) is a highly toxic weed killer banned in many countries; ingestion of >30 mL is universally fatal due to oxygen radical damage to lungs.
Improperly prepared cassava or fava beans can cause cyanide poisoning or hemolytic crisis in G6PD deficiency.
In resource-limited settings, ask local staff about common toxidromes and region-specific poisons.
Paraquat (Gramoxone) is a herbicide banned in over 130 countries; ingestion of >30 mL is universally fatal due to pulmonary fibrosis from oxygen superradicals.

Cyanide poisoning can result from improperly prepared fava beans, cassava, or purple lima beans; it presents with combativeness and can be reversed with Nithiodote (amyl nitrite or sodium thiosulfate).

episodes.title: Dr. Mark Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.1 8/28/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
episodes.abstract: Dr. Mark Crouch shares his experience as a family medicine missionary in Papua New Guinea, describing the rugged terrain, rural population, and high burden of disease. He discusses the unique challenges of practicing medicine in a resource-limited setting with limited diagnostic and treatment options, and emphasizes the importance of being a 'doorkeeper', providing physical care, prayer, and spiritual support to patients. The talk highlights the high volume of deliveries, the prevalence of domestic violence, and the need for discipleship alongside evangelism in a syncretistic culture.
key_points: Papua New Guinea is the most rural country in the world, with 87% of its 8-9 million people living in rural areas and no road connecting the capital to the rest of the country.
There are about 600 distinct languages in PNG, not dialects, making it one of the most linguistically diverse places on earth.
Syncretism is common: many people profess Christianity (75-80%) but also hold animist beliefs, with only about 25% having an authentic biblical faith.
Domestic abuse affects 80-90% of women, and sexual abuse about 50-60%, making women and children the focus of about 80% of Dr. Crouch's work.
The hospital is a 150-bed referral facility that performs more deliveries than the entire St. John health system (over 2,100 per year).

In PNG, there are only about 5-6 treatment options for most conditions, and physicians frequently have to tell patients 'there is nothing more I can do', a contrast to practice in high-resource settings.
The hospital was strategically placed on the boundary between warring tribes, with the threat of closure if fighting occurred, which dramatically reduced conflict.
Dr. Crouch obtained a Master's in Public Health and emphasizes public health approaches alongside clinical care.
Teaching and training of local residents and nursing students has become a major part of the work, with a recent transition from paper charts to an EMR.
The role of a missionary doctor is to be a 'doorkeeper', sharing the gospel, praying with patients, or simply being the first person to touch a neglected patient with dignity.
In resource-limited settings like PNG, there are only about five to six interventions available for many patients, after which you must tell them there is nothing more you can do.
The emotional toll of repeatedly telling patients 'there is nothing more I can do' can be significant for clinicians, especially early in a mission assignment.

episodes.title: Dr. McIntosh on Peds Respiratory Care 3/26/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. McIntosh
episodes.abstract: Dr. McIntosh presents a practical, evidence-informed overview of pediatric upper respiratory infections (URIs), emphasizing clinical diagnosis over testing, supportive care as the mainstay of management, and judicious use of antibiotics. He reviews common viral etiologies (flu, RSV, COVID), bacterial complications (strep pharyngitis, sinusitis, otitis media), and red-flag signs requiring urgent attention. The talk includes specific recommendations for honey for cough, saline irrigation, fever management, and when to consider antivirals or antibiotics, along with strategies for patient education on antibiotic stewardship.
key_points: Diagnosis of pediatric URI is primarily clinical; avoid over-reliance on imaging or lab tests.
Supportive care (hydration, rest, saline irrigation, humidity) is the foundation of management for viral URIs.
Honey (1 tsp at bedtime) is effective for cough in children over 1 year; avoid in infants under 1 year due to botulism risk.
Antibiotics are indicated for bacterial sinusitis only if symptoms persist >10 days or worsen after 5-7 days.
First-line antibiotic for strep pharyngitis or bacterial sinusitis is high-dose amoxicillin; amoxicillin-clavulanate is second-line.
Antivirals (e.g., oseltamivir) are reserved for children with severe influenza or comorbidities; most children with flu do well with supportive care.

Red flags include respiratory distress/tripoding, stridor at rest, fever >5 days, dehydration, lethargy, symptoms >14 days without improvement, and unilateral pharyngitis (suggests peritonsillar abscess).
OTC cough/cold medications (dextromethorphan, phenylephrine) are not recommended in children under 4 years due to overdose risk; use with caution ages 4-6.
Hand hygiene and avoidance of secondhand smoke are key prevention strategies.
Reye syndrome is a rare but serious risk with aspirin use in children; use acetaminophen or ibuprofen instead.
Red flags in pediatric respiratory illness include stridor at rest, tripoding, drooling, fever >5 days, dehydration signs, symptoms >14 days without improvement, and unilateral symptoms.
Croup presents with barking cough and inspiratory stridor, often at night; treat with dexamethasone.

episodes.title: Dr. Megaly on Intro to Peripheral Arterial & Venous Disease
episodes.speaker: Dr. Megaly
episodes.abstract: Dr. Megaly presents an overview of peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and venous disease, emphasizing that PAD is a marker of systemic atherosclerosis and carries high mortality from cardiac events. He reviews screening recommendations, diagnostic approaches including pulse exam and ABI, and the importance of aggressive risk factor modification. The talk also covers DVT and post-thrombotic syndrome, highlighting the need for early treatment to prevent chronic complications.
key_points: PAD prevalence increases exponentially after age 60, especially in African American and Hispanic populations.
Five-year survival is nearly halved in symptomatic PAD compared to no PAD, primarily due to cardiac deaths.
PAD is asymptomatic in 20-50% of patients; atypical leg pain is a common presentation.
Rutherford classification is commonly used: categories 1-3 for claudication, 4-6 for critical limb ischemia.
Claudication location correlates with arterial segment: buttocks/hips for aortoiliac, upper calf for SFA, foot for tibial/peroneal disease.
Screen all patients ≥65, or 50-64 with risk factors (diabetes, smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia), or any age with diabetes plus another risk factor.
Pedal pulse exam is a practical first screening tool; absent or weak pulses warrant imaging.
