ABI <0.9 is abnormal; ABI >1.4 suggests non-compressible vessels requiring toe-brachial index (TBI).
Arterial duplex with triphasic/biphasic/monophasic waveforms assesses stenosis severity.
Medical therapy (aspirin, statin, smoking cessation) is the cornerstone to reduce cardiac mortality in PAD patients.
Acute DVT can progress to post-thrombotic syndrome with venous hypertension, skin changes, and ulceration.
Iliac vein stenting is an option for post-thrombotic syndrome, but femoral vein stenting is avoided due to valves.

episodes.title: Dr. Miller on Pediatric Urology
episodes.speaker: Dr. Miller
episodes.abstract: Dr. Miller introduces pediatric urology as a subspecialty focused on congenital issues and reconstruction, contrasting it with adult urology's emphasis on removal. He highlights two true emergencies in pediatric urology, testicular torsion and posterior urethral valves, both occurring only in boys. He emphasizes the importance of ultrasound for torsion and the deceptive presentation of posterior urethral valves, where children may urinate normally despite high pressure damaging the kidneys. The talk also covers undescended testicles, noting that if they do not descend by one year, they will not do so spontaneously.
key_points: Pediatric urology deals primarily with congenital anomalies and reconstruction, while adult urology is more about removing organs.
Only two true emergencies exist in pediatric urology: testicular torsion and posterior urethral valves, both in boys.
For testicular torsion, ultrasound with Doppler is the key diagnostic tool; presence of flow likely rules out torsion.
Posterior urethral valves cause high-pressure urinary obstruction that can damage kidneys, but affected boys often urinate normally.
Pressure, not voiding stream, is the critical factor in urologic obstruction; men are at higher risk for kidney damage from pressure because they do not leak urine like women.
Antenatal hydronephrosis, especially in a boy, should raise suspicion for posterior urethral valves.
Undescended testicles occur in about 3% of full-term newborns, dropping to 0.9% by one year; after that, spontaneous descent is unlikely.
Surgery for undescended testicles before age one may improve fertility outcomes.
Testicular cancer surgery requires inguinal (not scrotal) approach due to lymphatic drainage along the kidney area.
Hernias in children are due to patency of the processus vaginalis, different from adult hernias.
Undescended testicles are present in about 3% of full-term newborns; this drops to about 0.9% by one year of age, and after one year spontaneous descent is unlikely.
If a testicle is retractile rather than truly undescended, observation is acceptable but referral is always appropriate; the testicle may become more undescended with growth.

episodes.title: Dr. Morgan on Covid Pediatric Vaccines
episodes.speaker: Dr. Morgan
episodes.abstract: Dr. Morgan reviews the epidemiology of COVID-19 in children aged 6 months to 5 years, emphasizing that this age group had the highest hospitalization and death rates among pediatric populations. He explains that 46-68% of hospitalized children had underlying health conditions and that COVID-19 was as severe as or more severe than other vaccine-preventable diseases. The lecture covers the FDA emergency use authorization process and the design of the pediatric vaccine studies, which were observer-blind, placebo-controlled, and randomized but small. The vaccine was found to be safer than contracting COVID-19, with mild side effects.
key_points: Children 6 months to 4 years had the highest hospitalization rate for COVID among all pediatric age groups.
46-68% of hospitalized children in this age group had underlying health conditions.
Hospitalized children were more likely to require ICU care, high-flow nasal cannula, BiPAP, CPAP, or ventilator.
COVID hospitalization rates during Delta/Omicron waves were as high as or higher than prepandemic flu rates.
COVID was the fifth leading cause of death in children 6 months to 4 years, with a higher death rate than flu, hepatitis A, meningitis, varicella, and rubella before their vaccines.
Initial COVID infection in this age range is much worse than MIS-C.
The FDA advisory committee gave 45 minutes each to Moderna, FDA reviewers, Pfizer, and FDA reviewers before public hearing and voting.
The pediatric vaccine studies were observer-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized, and well-designed but small in size.
The vaccine was safer than getting COVID in this age group given high hospitalization and ventilator rates.
Extreme and mild side effects from the vaccine were very low.
Pediatric COVID vaccine studies were small (hundreds to low thousands) but observer-blind, placebo-controlled, and randomized.
No cases of myocarditis were seen in any of the pediatric studies for children under 5.

episodes.title: Dr. Morgan on Failure to Thrive
episodes.speaker: Dr. Morgan
episodes.abstract: Dr. Morgan presents a practical, clinic-focused lecture on failure to thrive (FTT) in children, emphasizing that most cases are straightforward and treatable if diagnosed early. She stresses the importance of correctly using growth curves (CDC WHO for 0, 24 months, CDC beyond) and understanding that FTT is defined by a change of two standard deviations below the patient's own norm, not just a low percentile. The talk covers organic vs. nonorganic causes, the natural progression of weight loss before length before head circumference, and the critical need to diagnose FTT promptly to enable intervention. Dr. Morgan reassures residents that diagnosing FTT is not catastrophic and that close monitoring and social history often resolve the issue.
key_points: The two most important things for managing FTT are being comfortable with growth curves and knowing the definition of FTT.
FTT is defined as a change of two standard deviations below the patient's own norm, usually based on birth percentile.
A baby born SGA or at a low percentile is not automatically FTT; FTT requires a change from a prior thriving state.
Weight loss precedes length loss, which precedes head circumference loss; the body preserves brain growth as long as possible.
Organic FTT involves genetic, GI, or absorption problems; nonorganic FTT is environmental, social, or modifiable.
Weight-for-height or height-for-age below the 10th percentile is a strong indicator of FTT.
Use CDC WHO growth curves for ages 0, 24 months and CDC curves beyond 24 months; these are built into Cerner.
If measurements seem inconsistent, ask for remeasurement; if still off, measure the child yourself.
Diagnosing FTT early allows intervention; delaying diagnosis can lead to missed opportunities and worse outcomes.
Most FTT cases are nonorganic and resolve with social history, feeding education, and close follow-up.
Don't be afraid to diagnose failure to thrive; it's better to diagnose and have it resolve in 3 months than to miss serious pathology.
Symmetric growth failure (weight, length, head all dropping together) suggests an intrinsic problem like growth hormone deficiency or genetic disorder.

episodes.title: Dr. Nakashima on Eczema and Acne
episodes.speaker: Dr. Nakashima
episodes.abstract: Dr. Nakashima reviews oral and topical treatments for acne and eczema, emphasizing stepwise management. For acne, she discusses doxycycline, spironolactone, birth control, and isotretinoin referral. For eczema, she covers first-line emollients (creams over lotions), topical steroids with a two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off schedule, calcineurin inhibitors for sensitive areas, and practical tips like wet wraps and petroleum jelly. She also highlights triggers, types of eczema, and the importance of avoiding scented products.
key_points: For acne in males, doxycycline 100 mg daily is used for up to 4 months with monthly follow-up.
For females, treatment options include doxycycline, spironolactone (especially effective in PCOS), or birth control; spironolactone is preferred first.
Isotretinoin is reserved for severe, resistant acne and requires significant paperwork, two forms of birth control, and regular follow-up; referral to dermatology is recommended.
Early referral to dermatology is important for acne patients with scarring; treatments include laser, dermaplaning, and silicone gel sheets.
70% of people with eczema have a family history; the atopic triad (asthma, allergies, eczema) is not always present.
Risk factors for eczema include low microbial exposure in childhood, high sugar diet, and high unsaturated fatty acid diet; triggers include dry/humid climate, pollen, stress, and certain irritants.
First-line treatment for eczema is topical emollients (creams over lotions, unscented); Vanicream is recommended.
Topical steroids are second-line; choose one from each potency category (e.g., hydrocortisone 1% low, triamcinolone medium, clobetasol high).
Topical steroids should be used twice daily for two weeks, then two weeks off to avoid steroid dependency; petrolatum (Vaseline) is used during breaks.
Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.1%) are third-line, safe for face, eyelids, neck, and folds in patients over 16; not a steroid, good for steroid breaks.
Wet wraps with Vaseline and ACE wraps or gloves can be used at home, especially in children, to enhance treatment.
Lifestyle modifications: use fragrance-free products, All Free and Clear detergent, gentle soaps, avoid bubble baths; keep a food diary if food allergies suspected.

episodes.title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Nakashima
episodes.abstract: Dr. Nakashima presents updates from the AAFP Family Centered Pregnancy Conference, emphasizing care equity, family-centered care, and continuity in obstetrics. She discusses the decline of family physicians providing obstetric care, the impact of obstetric deserts and racism on maternal mortality, and the importance of screening for substance use disorder in pregnancy using tools like the NIDA-4 and 5 Ps. The talk also covers refugee care considerations, including PTSD screening, and introduces the Hadlock formula for detecting fetal growth restriction.
key_points: Only 7% of family physicians now do obstetrics, down from 45% thirty years ago.
Family physicians account for 1 in 4 obstetric clinicians in rural counties.
Black women are 2-3 times more likely to die from pregnancy and have the highest cesarean rates.
Continuity of care reduces mortality in 81% of studies and lowers hospitalization rates.
UDS is not recommended as a primary screening tool for substance use in pregnancy; use the NIDA-4 or 5 Ps instead.
The NIDA-4 asks about tobacco/vaping, alcohol (>4 drinks/day or >10/week), prescription misuse, and illicit drugs (including marijuana).
The 5 Ps screening tool (Parents, Partner, Past, Prescriptions, Personal) is an indirect approach to substance use history.
For refugee patients, educate on the value of prenatal labs and monitoring, and consider PTSD screening.
Fetal growth restriction is defined as estimated fetal weight <10th percentile for gestational age or abnormal abdominal circumference.
The Hadlock formula is superior to NICHD and WHO formulas for detecting fetal growth restriction or small-for-gestational-age.
If a UDS is positive, obtain confirmatory testing and counsel on risks, including DHS referral if positive at birth.
Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is defined as estimated fetal weight <10% for gestational age or based on abdominal circumference using the Hadlock formula.

episodes.title: Dr. Newborn on OMT
episodes.speaker: Dr. Newborn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Newborn and Dr. Hershberger review three osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) techniques: myofascial release, soft tissue, and counterstrain. They discuss appropriate referrals for OMT, emphasizing musculoskeletal causes, acute versus chronic somatic dysfunction, and setting patient expectations. Practical tips include using whole-body mechanics, targeting muscle rather than skin, and incorporating home exercises for chronic issues.
key_points: OMT techniques covered: myofascial release, soft tissue (kneading), and counterstrain.
Soft tissue technique: knead muscle perpendicular to spine or along origin/insertion until relaxation.
Counterstrain: identify point of maximum tenderness, shorten muscle, hold 90 seconds, return to neutral.
Appropriate OMT referrals: musculoskeletal pain, tension headaches, overuse injuries; not non-MSK or chronic without somatic dysfunction.
Acute somatic dysfunction: boggy, edematous, sharp tenderness; chronic: ropey, fibrotic.
Home exercises and stretches are the most effective component for chronic conditions.
Use whole upper body as a lever, not just fingers, for soft tissue to avoid fatigue.
Avoid moving fingers on skin; apply traction directly to the muscle.
For prone soft tissue, use thumbs with direct pressure anterior caudally until T7-T8, then switch sides.
Thenar eminences in the paraspinal groove with perpendicular force is an effective soft tissue method.

episodes.title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain
episodes.speaker: Dr. Newborn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Newborn discusses pain in pregnancy, covering first, second, and third trimester causes, warning signs for non-obstetric emergencies, and imaging considerations. He emphasizes that nausea/vomiting persisting beyond 16-20 weeks with abdominal pain is abnormal, and that CT scans should not be withheld if clinically indicated. Key third-trimester dangers include placental abruption, which can present with or without vaginal bleeding. The talk also reviews labor pain types and ACOG's stance that maternal request alone is sufficient indication for pain relief during labor.
key_points: Nausea and vomiting in the first trimester are common (80% of women), but persistence after 16-20 weeks with abdominal pain is abnormal.
Warning signs that pain is not pregnancy-related include localized or abrupt onset, constant or severe pain, pain with nausea/vomiting, fever, or vaginal bleeding.
Ectopic pregnancy and spontaneous abortion are the most concerning causes of early pregnancy pain.
Appendicitis (1 in 1500 pregnancies) is the most common non-obstetric cause of acute abdominal pain in pregnancy; cholecystitis and nephrolithiasis occur in about 1 in 3000.
Ultrasound and MRI are preferred imaging in pregnancy; CT should not be withheld if clinically indicated, as a single CT abdomen/pelvis delivers radiation below the threshold for fetal harm.
Appendicitis symptoms in early pregnancy are identical to the non-pregnant state; right lower quadrant pain remains consistent throughout pregnancy regardless of gestational age.
Placental abruption is the most dangerous cause of abdominal pain in the third trimester; it can be concealed (no vaginal bleeding) and may present with intense, unrelenting pain.
Round ligament pain typically occurs at the end of the second trimester/beginning of the third, presenting as dull ache or sharp pulling in the lower abdomen and groin.
Lightning crotch is a sudden, sharp, nerve-type pain in the groin radiating down the inner thigh or vagina, typically in the third trimester; its physiology is unknown.
ACOG states that in the absence of medical contraindication, maternal request alone is sufficient indication for pain relief during labor.
Placental abruption can present with or without vaginal bleeding (concealed abruption) and should be on the differential for any labor-like pain.
ACOG states that in the absence of medical contraindication, maternal request is sufficient indication for pain relief during labor.

episodes.title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)
episodes.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
episodes.abstract: Dr. Nichols presents a practical approach to acute kidney injury (AKI) from an outpatient perspective, using a case of a 66-year-old woman with hypertension, diabetes, and new lab findings of creatinine 2.1 and BUN 46. She emphasizes risk factor assessment, distinguishing prerenal from intrinsic causes via BUN/creatinine ratio, and using tools like the RIFLE criteria and KDIGO classification. The talk covers false-positive lab elevations, diagnostic workup including urine studies and renal ultrasound, and management steps, with a focus on medication adjustments and follow-up planning.
key_points: AKI is often asymptomatic; it is frequently discovered incidentally on lab work.
The RIFLE criteria (Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, ESRD) help gauge severity and guide urgency of follow-up.
If baseline GFR is unknown, assume a baseline GFR of 75 to assess AKI severity.

False-positive creatinine elevations can occur with medications like Bactrim, protein supplements, and ketoacidosis; BUN can be falsely elevated by steroids, high protein intake, rhabdo, and upper GI bleed.
Risk factors for AKI include advanced age, female sex, Black race, diabetes, hypertension, ACE inhibitors, PPIs, and low-income country origin.
Prerenal AKI is the most common type; a BUN/creatinine ratio >20:1 suggests prerenal etiology.
Intrinsic AKI typically has a BUN/creatinine ratio between 10:1 and 20:1.
NSAIDs reduce prostaglandins that dilate the afferent arteriole; ACE inhibitors and ARBs block angiotensin II, reducing efferent arteriole constriction.
Renal ultrasound is usually normal in prerenal AKI; it is mainly useful to differentiate CKD or postrenal obstruction.
Urine studies: low urine sodium suggests hypovolemia or diuretics; positive hemoglobin without red blood cells on UA suggests rhabdomyolysis.
Metformin is more a risk for lactic acidosis than for AKI itself, but should be held in AKI.
For outpatient AKI, bring the patient back to the office rather than managing over the phone, as the call becomes a full visit.

episodes.title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
episodes.abstract: Dr. Nicole Tipton presents a lecture on environmental exposures from an emergency medicine perspective, focusing on cold-related injuries. She covers hypothermia stages, EKG findings including Osborn waves, and frostbite classification by degree. The talk includes a case-based discussion of management, emphasizing rewarming techniques from passive external methods to invasive procedures. Practical considerations such as undressing patients, preserving dignity, and addressing the needs of vulnerable populations are highlighted.
key_points: Hypothermia stages are defined by core temperature: mild (35-32°C), moderate (32-28°C), severe (28-24°C), and cardiac arrest (below 24°C).
Loss of shivering is the hallmark of severe (stage 3) hypothermia.
Osborn waves (J waves) on EKG are characteristic of hypothermia, seen in stages 2 and 3, and their height correlates with the degree of hypothermia.

Frostbite is classified similarly to burns: first degree (frostnip) with redness and numbness, second degree with clear blisters, third degree with hemorrhagic blisters and deeper involvement, fourth degree with necrosis of tendons, bones, and muscles.
Do not routinely open frostbite blisters; this is controversial and generally avoided unless infection is present.
Trauma patients are at high risk for hypothermia due to undressing and exposure during resuscitation; remember to cover them back up.
At-risk populations for cold injuries include the elderly, very young, military personnel, those with Raynaud's, and homeless individuals.
Initial management of hypothermia includes removing wet clothing and passive external rewarming (bear hugger, warm blankets).
For moderate to severe hypothermia, active rewarming techniques include warmed IV fluids (0.5°C/hour), gastric lavage (3°C/hour), and bladder irrigation (controversial efficacy).
When undressing patients, communicate with them, preserve modesty with gowns, and consider providing replacement clothing, especially for homeless patients.

Hypothermia rewarming strategies progress from passive external (blanket warmer) to active internal (IV fluids, gastric lavage, bladder irrigation, intraperitoneal/thoracic lavage, ECMO/cardiopulmonary bypass).
Warmed IV fluids increase core temperature about 0.5°C per hour; gastric lavage approximately 3°C per hour.

episodes.title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist
episodes.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe

also_uploaded.title: Dr. Yasmin Keefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

episodes.abstract: Dr. O'Keefe presents a practical approach to coma and disordered consciousness for non-neurologists. She emphasizes the importance of precise terminology to describe a patient's level of consciousness, as this guides urgency and management. The talk covers the spectrum from awake to comatose, the pathophysiology of consciousness (cortex, thalamus, reticular activating system), and common causes of coma including metabolic disturbances, intoxications, and seizures. Key takeaways include recognizing the danger zone when protective reflexes are lost, identifying patients at risk for delirium, and implementing simple environmental measures to prevent delirium in hospitalized patients.
key_points: Use precise terminology for levels of consciousness; 'unresponsive' is too vague and means different things to different people.
The transition from lethargic to stuporous (and to obtunded) is dangerous because protective reflexes and the ability to follow commands are lost.
Patients with preexisting structural brain injury (dementia, stroke, TBI, etc.) are highly susceptible to delirium when medically ill.
Consciousness requires intact bilateral cortices, thalami, and the reticular activating system; damage to any one can cause coma.
Common causes of coma are often non-anatomical: metabolic disturbances (hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia), intoxications, generalized seizures, and toxic-metabolic syndromes.
Delirium prevention in the hospital includes keeping lights on during the day, getting patients out of bed, ensuring glasses/hearing aids are used, and maintaining a day/night cycle.
Correcting the underlying metabolic or toxic disturbance can improve consciousness, but recovery may be slow, especially in delirium-prone brains.
The Monro-Kellie doctrine explains that the skull is a fixed-volume space; cellular damage leads to edema, further damage, and potential herniation.
Differentiate coma from sleep by the inability to arouse the patient with any stimulus.
Cellular damage begets cellular damage in the brain, creating a cascade that worsens injury.
Delirium is exacerbated by environmental factors like dark rooms, immobility, and lack of sensory aids (glasses/hearing aids); advocate for day/night cycling and mobilization.
Bilateral thalamic strokes can occur from artery of Percheron occlusion, causing devastating coma due to medial thalamic involvement in consciousness.

episodes.title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions
episodes.speaker: Dr. Papp
episodes.abstract: Dr. Esther Papp, a family medicine graduate working with Samaritan's Purse in Togo, West Africa, presents a case-based lecture on common pathologies encountered in a resource-limited setting. She covers cerebral malaria, typhoid, severe acute malnutrition, and prematurity/neonatal sepsis, emphasizing practical, hands-on management. The talk highlights the need for rapid action (e.g., physically carrying seizing children to the ER), empirical treatment before test results, and high vigilance for complications like typhoid perforation and refeeding syndrome. She also shares emotional challenges and the importance of support systems.
key_points: In Togo, standard practice for a lethargic, seizing child is to grab and sprint to the ER; this is accepted and expected.
Cerebral malaria is common; treat empirically with IV artesunate before test results (which take 3 hours).

Seizure protocol for cerebral malaria: start with phenobarbital 20 mg/kg (skip diazepam to avoid oversedation), then escalate through Keppra, phenytoin, and repeat phenobarbital, waiting 5, 10 minutes between doses.
Typhoid is the top differential for fever and abdominal pain; treat empirically with IV ceftriaxone (inpatient) or ciprofloxacin/azithromycin (outpatient).
Severe abdominal tenderness in suspected typhoid requires admission for serial exams due to high risk of perforation.
Severe acute malnutrition is diagnosed using WHO criteria (weight-for-length, MUAC, edema) and managed with careful refeeding, electrolyte monitoring, prophylactic antibiotics, and vitamins.
Premature neonates: NG tube feeding if <32 weeks gestational age; trial of PO at 32, 34 weeks; PO usually safe >34 weeks. Increase total fluids by 20 mL/kg/day.
Lumbar puncture is performed routinely as part of neonatal sepsis workup.
Emotional trauma from caring for critically ill children is normal; having a prayer team or support system is essential.
The Ukraine-Russia war has worsened food insecurity in Africa, increasing malnutrition cases.
In resource-limited settings, point-of-care ultrasound is essential for diagnosis and management, such as distinguishing gastric masses or evaluating bladder distension.
For acute stroke, always check blood sugar first, as hypoglycemia can mimic or exacerbate stroke symptoms and is reversible with dextrose.

episodes.title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals
episodes.speaker: Dr. Patrick
episodes.abstract: Dr. Patrick reflects on the dramatic shift in medicine from the 1960s to today, emphasizing the rise of lifestyle-related chronic diseases and the erosion of trust. He traces the ethical foundations of Western medicine back to the Hippocratic Oath, which prioritized trust and moral commitment over technical skill. He argues that the core skill for modern physicians is learning to ask sophisticated, sensitive questions that allow patients to open up, especially about spiritual and end-of-life concerns. He warns against bureaucratic pressures that treat patients as widgets and urges residents to preserve the nobility of caring for the chronically ill.
key_points: The biggest change in medicine is that most patients are now partly responsible for their own disease through lifestyle choices.
Before 1860, seeing a doctor when seriously ill was more likely to hasten death than prevent it; trust, not efficacy, was the foundation of the doctor-patient relationship.
The Hippocratic Oath was originally taken at the start of medical training, not at graduation, to ensure ethical commitment before learning.
The first commitment of Hippocratic physicians was to set rules that would give patients greater trust in their doctors.
In the developing world, auscultation for a hepatic rub can diagnose hepatocellular carcinoma that has breached the liver capsule, a sign of terminal disease.
Patients often thank you for a terminal diagnosis because it allows them to plan and seek reconciliation with estranged loved ones.
The most important skill to learn is how to ask sophisticated, sensitive, and kind questions that allow patients to open up.
Bureaucrats view patients as widgets that can be moved between clinics, but physicians relate better to some patients than others, and that continuity matters in chronic disease.
Physician suicide rates are comparable to those in aboriginal populations, yet the profession often responds with denial rather than open discussion.
Paternalism, when done with genuine care and honesty, can be beneficial; the speaker's own career was shaped by a paternalistic mentor who took a real interest in his life.
Physicians must learn to become sophisticated, sensitive, and kind questioners to help patients open up.
Biblical literacy is declining, which flattens culture and removes metaphysical foundations for meaning.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
episodes.speaker: Dr. Place
episodes.abstract: This lecture reviews the basics of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), including its definition, characterization of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) as obstructive or irritative, appropriate workup, medical treatments (alpha-blockers, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, and a newer third option), and surgical options. The presenter emphasizes using validated instruments like the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) to objectively quantify symptoms and using correct terminology ('LUTS' rather than 'BPH symptoms'). Key clinical pearls include the epidemiology ('50 by fifty and 80 by 80'), the importance of distinguishing obstructive from irritative symptoms, and practical approaches to common complaints like nocturia and urgency.
key_points: BPH is a true hyperplasia (increase in cell number), not hypertrophy (increase in cell size).
The epidemiology is captured by '50 by fifty and 80 by 80': 50% of men in their 50s and 80% of men in their 80s have symptoms.
Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) should be divided into obstructive (hesitancy, weak stream, straining, incomplete emptying, intermittency) and irritative (frequency, urgency, nocturia).
Use the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) as a validated, objective tool to quantify and characterize symptoms.
Nocturia is the most common reason patients present with BPH symptoms.
Always use the term 'lower urinary tract symptoms' (LUTS) rather than 'BPH symptoms' because other conditions (UTI, cancer, STD) can cause similar symptoms, and women also have LUTS.
Medical treatments include alpha-blockers, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, and a newer third medication class.
Surgical options for BPH are constantly evolving and are typically managed by urology.
The presenter intentionally avoids discussing prostate cancer overlap, noting it is a separate lecture topic.
A DRE (digital rectal exam) is part of the workup, though not detailed in this transcript.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
episodes.speaker: Dr. Place
episodes.abstract: Dr. Place reviews the basics of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), emphasizing that it is a symptom-based diagnosis requiring lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). He distinguishes obstructive from irritative symptoms, explains the role of the IPSS questionnaire, and stresses the importance of a digital rectal exam (DRE) in symptomatic patients. Medical management with alpha blockers and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors is covered, along with when to refer for surgical options like TURP.
key_points: BPH is a true hyperplasia (increased cell number), not hypertrophy (increased cell size).
Diagnosis requires symptoms; it is not a radiologic or physical exam diagnosis alone.
Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) are classified as obstructive (weak stream, hesitancy, straining, incomplete emptying) or irritative (frequency, urgency, nocturia, dysuria).
The IPSS (International Prostate Symptom Score) quantifies symptoms and includes a quality-of-life question.
Nocturia is often the earliest and most bothersome symptom; it is a good screening question.
DRE is mandatory in any patient presenting with LUTS; assess whether the prostate is 'big or not' and whether it is smooth or nodular.
PSA is supportive but not diagnostic for BPH; an extremely low PSA may suggest hypogonadism.
Urinalysis is low-hanging fruit to rule out hematuria or infection.
Post-void residual can be assessed by bladder scan after voiding.
Alpha blockers and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors are the main medical classes; TURP remains the standard surgical option.
PSA is supportive, not diagnostic, in BPH evaluation; it is an exam and symptom diagnosis.
Very low PSA (e.g., 0.01) may indicate hypogonadism and warrants checking testosterone.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension
episodes.speaker: Dr. Place
episodes.abstract: Dr. Place argues that blood pressure control is one of the two most important interventions in all of medicine, alongside smoking cessation. He reviews the pathophysiology of hypertension, emphasizing the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) as the dominant mechanism. He then demonstrates proper blood pressure measurement technique, highlighting common errors such as measuring over clothing, insufficient rest time, and caffeine use. The lecture aims to make residents passionate about evidence-based blood pressure management.
key_points: Hypertension is the number one risk factor for ischemic heart disease and cerebrovascular disease, killing about 18 million people annually.
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) accounts for over 90% of the pathophysiology of hypertension.
Angiotensin II is the central molecule in blood pressure management, causing vasoconstriction, increased sympathetic activity, sodium reabsorption, and aldosterone release.

Proper blood pressure measurement requires: patient seated with feet on floor, back supported, arm at heart level, no caffeine or exercise within 30 minutes, bare skin, and a 5-minute rest before measurement.
At the first visit, check blood pressure in both arms and use the higher reading.
Home blood pressure monitors (e.g., Omron) cost about $35 and should be validated; devices may need recalibration every 2 years.
Patients should record home blood pressure readings, either written or in their phone.
Major blood pressure studies (e.g., SPRINT) use an average of three readings taken 5 minutes apart.
Cardiovascular disease kills more people than all top six cancers combined (18 million vs. 10 million annually).
Resistant hypertension and chronic kidney disease are subgroups where renal artery stenosis becomes more relevant.
Clinic blood pressures are often inaccurate; home monitoring with a validated device and proper technique is essential.
For initial visits, check both arms and use the higher reading; for diagnosis, use an average of three readings taken five minutes apart.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Place
episodes.abstract: Dr. Place argues that hypertension management is the single most important clinical intervention in family medicine, surpassing even diabetes and smoking cessation in population impact. He reviews seven pathophysiologic mechanisms of hypertension, emphasizing the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and angiotensin II as the central driver. The lecture covers proper blood pressure measurement technique, evidence-based treatment targets, and the importance of knowing patients' blood pressure numbers. Dr. Place stresses that elevated blood pressure is the #1 modifiable risk factor for ischemic heart disease and stroke, and that controlling it should be a top priority in every patient encounter.
key_points: Hypertension is the most important modifiable risk factor for ischemic heart disease and stroke, the leading causes of death worldwide.
Blood pressure control and smoking cessation are the two most impactful clinical interventions in family medicine.
Most patients cannot accurately sense when their blood pressure is elevated; symptoms only occur at very high levels (e.g., 180/110 or higher).
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is the central pathophysiologic mechanism in hypertension, with angiotensin II as the master molecule.
Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction, increases aldosterone secretion (sodium retention, potassium loss), stimulates ADH release, and increases sympathetic activity.
Hypertension is fundamentally a kidney disease; decreased renal perfusion triggers the RAAS cascade.
Proper blood pressure measurement technique is essential for accurate diagnosis and management.
Cardiovascular disease kills approximately 20 million people annually, more than all cancers combined (about 10 million).
Vascular remodeling, sympathetic nervous system activation, and endothelial dysfunction are key contributors to hypertension pathophysiology.
Patients should know their blood pressure numbers; checking it regularly is a simple but powerful health behavior.
Angiotensin II is the central molecule driving hypertension via vasoconstriction, sodium retention, aldosterone secretion, and ADH release.
Proper BP measurement requires: patient seated >5 minutes, feet flat, back supported, bare arm at heart level, no talking, no caffeine/exercise/smoking within 30 minutes.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Place
episodes.abstract: Dr. Place reviews the history, symptoms, physiology, and laboratory evaluation of male hypogonadism for primary care clinicians. He emphasizes that reduced libido is the most specific symptom, not erectile dysfunction, which is often vascular. He distinguishes primary, secondary, and functional (obesity-driven) hypogonadism, explaining the role of leptin resistance and aromatization. Lab guidance includes using LCMS total testosterone drawn fasting in the morning, repeating borderline results with SHBG and FSH/LH, and relying on the lab's calculated free testosterone.
key_points: Reduced libido is the number one symptom of male hypogonadism, more specific than erectile dysfunction.
Erectile dysfunction is mostly vascular (diabetes, hypertension) and often does not improve with testosterone therapy.
Primary hypogonadism means testicular failure (e.g., Klinefelter syndrome, mumps orchitis, trauma); LH/FSH are high.
Secondary hypogonadism is due to pituitary/hypothalamic suppression (e.g., prolactinoma); LH/FSH are low or inappropriately normal.
Functional hypogonadism (most common) is a secondary type driven by obesity, type 2 diabetes, and hypothyroidism via leptin resistance and aromatization of testosterone to estrogen.
Total testosterone should be drawn fasting between 7, 10 AM; non-fasting can lower the value by 30, 50 points.
Use LCMS (liquid chromatography, mass spectrometry) total testosterone for accuracy at low levels; standard immunoassay is less reliable.
If total testosterone is borderline or low, repeat in 2, 3 weeks and add SHBG, FSH, LH, and calculated free testosterone.
SHBG is decreased by obesity, diabetes, opioids, steroids, and hypothyroidism; increased by aging and liver disease.
Klinefelter syndrome (XXY) is missed in about 50% of cases; consider karyotype in primary hypogonadism.
Physical symptoms include decreased muscle mass, increased body fat, reduced bone density, and anemia.
Psychological symptoms include brain fog, fatigue, depressed mood, poor concentration, and sleep disturbance.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Obesity
episodes.speaker: Dr. Place
episodes.abstract: Dr. Place presents a family-medicine approach to obesity, emphasizing its high prevalence (42% pre-COVID, likely 50% now) and its role as a primary driver of ASCVD, diabetes, and other comorbidities. He introduces the concept of obesity phenotypes and a basic management framework, using patient stories to illustrate the spectrum of outcomes. He cautions against stigmatizing terms like 'morbid obesity,' advocates for using BMI with awareness of its limitations (ethnicity, athletes, short stature), and highlights the importance of addressing obesity as a genetic propensity accelerated by environment and lifestyle.
key_points: Obesity prevalence is ~42% (pre-COVID) and likely 50% now; class III (BMI >40) is ~10%.
Adipose tissue is a hormonally active organ that creates a chronic inflammatory state, worsening COVID and other conditions.
Obesity confers a 7x risk of diabetes in men and 12x in women; check A1c in obese patients.
ASCVD kills 20 million/year globally, double all cancers combined, and obesity is a primary driver.
Avoid the term 'morbid obesity'; use 'class III obesity' instead to reduce stigma.
BMI is a useful but imperfect surrogate; it is inaccurate in athletes, very short/tall people, and varies by ethnicity (Asians get sick at lower BMIs, Black patients at higher BMIs).
Waist circumference has better outcome data than BMI but is rarely measured in clinic.
Obesity is a genetic propensity (over 70 genes involved) accelerated by environment and lifestyle; avoid blaming patients.
Medications like mirtazapine can cause significant weight gain; consider stopping or switching them.
Bariatric surgery can be life-changing even in complex patients (e.g., on dialysis), but carries risks like phrenic nerve injury.
Check BMI before blood pressure; it is the number one thing that can change a patient's life.
Mirtazapine stimulates appetite and should be avoided in patients with obesity or eating disorders.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment
episodes.speaker: Dr. Place
episodes.abstract: Dr. Place presents a practical approach to pre-operative assessment, emphasizing that it is a high-value clinical skill. He defines surgical risk by anesthesia type, duration, and urgency, and introduces the NSQIP online calculator as the gold standard risk tool. He argues for seeing these patients in person and producing a formal report, which improves both patient outcomes and surgeon relationships. The talk also covers patient-centered risk factors beyond cardiac and pulmonary issues, including spiritual, mental health, nutritional, and social support domains.
key_points: Pre-operative assessment is a common, high-impact task that should be done in person, not by chart review alone.
Surgical risk is defined by anesthesia type (local < neuraxial < general), duration (under vs over one hour), and urgency (elective, urgent, emergent).
The NSQIP online risk calculator is the gold standard tool for establishing surgical risk.
Producing a formal written report for the surgeon, in addition to the requested form, distinguishes a thorough evaluation and builds professional reputation.
Patient risk includes spiritual concerns (hope, fear, meaning of illness), which are often overlooked but critical to the patient's experience.
Mental health risk is substantial; about 30% of patients develop major depressive disorder within a year after CABG.
Nutritional optimization before surgery is important because many patients, whether large or frail, go into surgery in a suboptimal nutritional state.
Social support and socioeconomic status strongly influence post-surgical outcomes and must be assessed.
ASA class is a standard component of surgical risk; classes range from 1 (normal healthy) to 5 (not expected to survive without the operation).
Pre-operative evaluation should be structured head-to-toe: spiritual, mental health, cardiac, pulmonary, nutritional, medical comorbidities, and social support.
The ACS risk calculator provides patient-specific risks for serious complications, pneumonia, cardiac events, surgical site infection, VTE, and discharge to nursing/rehab facility.
A serious complication risk of 10% or higher is a reasonable rule of thumb to consider postponing surgery for optimization (e.g., poorly controlled diabetes).

episodes.title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture
episodes.speaker: Dr. Place
episodes.abstract: Dr. Place presents a family-medicine-focused lecture on hepatitis C, emphasizing the role of primary care in diagnosing and managing the infection. He highlights that hepatitis C is curable with modern direct-acting antivirals, which achieve over 90% sustained virologic response. The talk covers screening recommendations, including universal screening for adults 18 and older, and the importance of overcoming stigma to ensure more patients receive care. Dr. Place also discusses the historical context of hepatitis C treatment and the need for family physicians to manage these patients in their clinics.
key_points: Hepatitis C is curable with direct-acting antivirals, achieving over 90% sustained virologic response.
Universal screening for hepatitis C is recommended for all adults aged 18 and older, per USPSTF guidelines.
A positive anti-HCV antibody with a positive HCV RNA test indicates current infection; a negative RNA with positive antibody suggests past infection.
Baby boomers (born 1945-1965) account for about 75% of hepatitis C cases in the US.
Patients with hepatitis C should be screened for alcohol and drug use, offered hepatitis A and B vaccination, and tested for HIV and STIs.
Repeat testing for hepatitis C is recommended every 3-12 months for individuals with ongoing risk factors, not every 5 years.
Deaths from hepatitis C now exceed deaths from HIV, primarily due to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Hepatitis C is rarely transmitted sexually unless blood is involved; injection drug use is a major risk factor.
The biggest barrier to treatment is not the medicine but pharmacy and medical finance issues, as medications are hard to obtain.
Family medicine has a key role in diagnosing and managing hepatitis C, as many patients are not receiving care.
Baby boomers account for about 75% of hepatitis C cases in the US, but CDC now recommends screening everyone over 18.
The best initial test is hepatitis C antibody reflex to genotype, which automatically adds viral load and genotype if antibody positive.

episodes.title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction
episodes.speaker: Dr. Price
episodes.abstract: Dr. Price discusses pelvic floor disorders, which affect one in three women. She covers risk factors, including modifiable lifestyle factors like smoking, obesity, and extreme sports, and reviews anatomy, types of urinary incontinence, and diagnostic approaches. The lecture emphasizes asking about symptoms proactively and provides actionable advice on conservative management with the 'four C's' avoidance for bladder irritation and Kegel exercises for pelvic floor health.
key_points: One in three women will experience a pelvic floor disorder in their lifetime.
Modifiable risk factors include smoking, obesity, extreme sports like CrossFit, caffeine, constipation, and poor blood sugar control.
A 10% reduction in BMI can improve urinary symptoms by 50%.
Pelvic floor disorders include bladder control problems (16% of women), pelvic organ prolapse (3%), and bowel control problems (9%).
Urinary incontinence types: stress (leakage with activity), urge/overactive bladder (sudden urge), mixed (30% of women have both), and continuous leakage.
Avoid the 'four C's' (carbonated drinks, citrus, caffeine, chocolate) to reduce bladder irritation and urgency frequency.
Kegel exercises: imagine clenching buttocks to avoid passing gas; test strength by stopping urine midstream once monthly.
Patients often wait years to seek help; CMS recommends screening for urinary symptoms in primary care.
Incomplete bladder emptying, nocturia (waking >2 times/night), and leakage with sexual activity are common symptoms.
Pelvic floor dysfunction can be managed with lifestyle changes, bladder diaries, and referral to urogynecology if needed.
Differentiate stress (cough/laugh/sneeze) vs urge (sudden intense need) incontinence; 30% have mixed.
Avoid the four C's, carbonated drinks, citrus, caffeine, chocolate, because they are acidic and irritate the bladder.

episodes.title: Dr. Price on Vector Transmitted Disease 6/18/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Price
episodes.abstract: Dr. Price discusses vector-transmitted diseases encountered in Houston, focusing on murine typhus, Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF), Lyme disease, and STARI syndrome. He reviews typical presentations (fever, headache, low platelets, elevated LFTs), the importance of early treatment with doxycycline, and diagnostic nuances such as the rash distribution for RMSF and the two-tiered testing for Lyme. He also covers tick paralysis versus botulism, and notes that Lyme disease is not endemic in Texas, with many cases likely being STARI syndrome.
key_points: Murine typhus (Rickettsia typhi) is transmitted by fleas and presents with fever, headache, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes; doxycycline is treatment of choice.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) often presents with a petechial rash that starts at the ankles and spreads centrally; doxycycline is the only safe and effective treatment for all ages including pregnancy and children as young as 1 year.
In RMSF, the older tetracyclines have more side effects in pregnancy and young children, but doxycycline has very little risk of these problems.
Lyme disease is endemic only in the Northeast, Upper Midwest, and West Coast (deer tick); in Texas, a similar rash is usually STARI (southern tick-associated rash illness) from the Lone Star tick.
For Lyme disease, classic erythema chronicum migrans is diagnostic without blood work; otherwise, ELISA is the first test, if negative, Lyme is unlikely.
Early Lyme disease treatment is doxycycline for 5, 7 days; for cardiac or neurologic involvement, ceftriaxone (Rocephin) is preferred.
STARI syndrome has the same rash as Lyme but rarely causes heart block or arthritis; treatment is still doxycycline (often for a month).
Tick paralysis (ascending paralysis) in a child resembles botulism (descending paralysis from cranial nerves); examine for an attached tick.
No alternative exists for RMSF, doxycycline is mandatory; prophylaxis for high tick exposure can be doxycycline 100 mg daily (once a week is not standard, speaker's phrasing is ambiguous).
In severe malaria without artesunate, total exchange transfusion (removing all blood and replacing it) can be a life-saving measure.
Hookworm larvae can travel up to 20 meters from an open defecation site and enter through bare feet.
Compost heaps, when properly managed, become sterile throughout and can be safely used as fertilizer.

episodes.title: Dr. Purser on Allergic Rhinitis 4/16/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Purser
episodes.abstract: Dr. Purser continues a lecture on allergic rhinitis, covering the practical use of pollen and mold counts sourced from local monitoring stations to anticipate seasonal allergies. She emphasizes starting topical nasal corticosteroids a full month before a patient's known allergy season, and compares different intranasal steroid formulations by their systemic absorption profiles. The talk also provides detailed environmental control advice for cat, dog, dust mite, and cockroach allergens, including breed-specific challenges in dog allergies and humidity management for dust mites.
key_points: Local pollen and mold counts from a rooftop monitor can identify seasonal patterns and guide preventive treatment timing.
The first step for any allergic patient is avoidance, but for airborne allergens, a preventative plan is key.
Pharmacologic first-line therapy for allergic rhinitis is a topical nasal corticosteroid, started four weeks before the anticipated season.
Fluticasone propionate (Flonase) is potent, cheap, but carries a higher risk of epistaxis due to alcohol content.
Fluticasone furoate and mometasone furoate have lower systemic absorption (<1%) and are preferred in pregnancy, osteoporosis, glaucoma, cataracts, and children with growth concerns.
Triamcinolone is also approved down to age 2, with a long safety profile and reasonable generic cost.
Dog allergy testing is complicated because different breeds produce different allergens; male dogs are more allergenic due to a prostate protein in urine.
Cat allergen protein (Fel d 1) is ubiquitous, sticks to walls, and can persist in newly built apartments via fomites.
Dust mites require humidity above 50% to thrive; keeping indoor humidity between 30-50% helps control them.
Hot washing sheets, encasing pillows and mattresses in breathable, allergen-proof covers from specialty vendors (e.g., missionallergy.com) is recommended for dust mite control.
Optimal indoor humidity for allergic rhinitis is 30-50%; use both humidifier and dehumidifier as needed.
Dust mites feed on skin scales; highest concentration is in beds. Hot wash sheets, cover pillows and mattresses with breathable, truly occlusive covers.

episodes.title: Dr. Purser on Anaphylaxis 2/26/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Purser
episodes.abstract: Dr. Purser presents a practical approach to urticaria (hives), emphasizing the initial triage of blanching versus non-blanching lesions to distinguish vasculitis from histaminergic hives, and the six-week cutoff for acute versus chronic urticaria. She reviews common acute triggers (drugs, viruses, insects, food, animals) and highlights NSAIDs as a frequent cause. For chronic spontaneous urticaria, she discusses the autoimmune basis, the role of viral triggers like Epstein-Barr virus, and the importance of checking ESR, CRP, and thyroid studies. She also covers inducible (physical) urticarias including cholinergic, cold, delayed pressure, and dermatographism, and stresses the need to rule out anaphylaxis.
key_points: First step in evaluating hives: determine if lesions blanch; non-blanching suggests vasculitis, not simple urticaria.
Acute urticaria is defined as lasting less than six weeks; chronic urticaria lasts six weeks or longer.
Common acute triggers include drugs (especially NSAIDs), viruses (especially Epstein-Barr virus), insect stings/bites, food, and animal dander.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria is often autoimmune, with autoantibodies against the high-affinity IgE receptor (FcεRI) or IgE itself.
Epstein-Barr virus is a common trigger for chronic spontaneous urticaria, likely through lymphatic changes.
For chronic urticaria, initial lab workup includes ESR, CRP, and thyroid studies (TSH and antibodies).
Histaminergic hives are pink, blanch, itch (not burn or hurt), come and go within 24 hours, and do not scar.
Angioedema often accompanies hives; it typically tingles first, lasts 1-2 days, and may require steroids to resolve.
Inducible (physical) urticarias include cholinergic (exercise/heat), cold, delayed pressure, solar, and dermatographism.
Chronic urticaria is self-limited but can last 5 to 15 years.
Always ask patients with hives about lip or eyelid swelling to identify angioedema and assess for anaphylaxis risk.
Chronic urticaria is now understood as an autoimmune disease mediated by autoantibodies (IgE, IgG, IgA) that stimulate the IgE receptor on mast cells, causing degranulation.

episodes.title: Dr. Richard on Outpatient Peds - Common Respiratory Disorders 3/19/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Richard
episodes.abstract: Dr. Richard leads an interactive session on common outpatient pediatric respiratory disorders, using case-based questions to engage residents. The talk covers the Centor criteria for strep pharyngitis, pitfalls of indiscriminate strep testing in young children, and RSV prevention strategies including maternal vaccination and infant monoclonal antibody timing. Practical advice on nasal suctioning for viral illnesses is also provided.
key_points: Centor criteria help decide when to swab for strep pharyngitis; a score of 2 or more increases likelihood.
In children under 3 years, strep testing is often unnecessary because most pharyngitis is viral and treatment would be the same.
Indiscriminate strep swabbing in infants can lead to false positives due to colonization, resulting in unnecessary antibiotics.
Influenza typically presents with high-grade fever and ill appearance, while COVID-19 now mirrors common cold symptoms.
Maternal RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) given at 32, 36.6 weeks protects the infant for the first 6 months of life.
If the infant is born less than 14 days after maternal RSV vaccination, they may still need monoclonal antibody (nirsevimab) because immunity transfer is insufficient.
For the second RSV season, only high-risk infants (e.g., premature) qualify for monoclonal antibody, unless born late in the season.
Nasal suctioning before every feed is the mainstay of symptomatic treatment for viral upper respiratory infections in infants.
Nasal saline drops or spray should be used prior to suctioning to loosen secretions.
Drive-through nasal suctioning clinics exist in some countries to help infants with RSV-related congestion.
Paxlovid for children requires age >12 years, weight >40 kg, symptom onset within 5 days, and comorbidities or immunocompromised status.
MIS-C should be considered in children presenting with generalized illness 2-3 weeks after COVID-19 infection; treatment includes IVIG and steroids.

episodes.title: Dr. Richard on UTIs 10/2/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Richard
episodes.abstract: Dr. Richard's lecture on urinary tract infections covers the definition of uncomplicated UTI, diagnostic approach, urine sample collection, interpretation of dipstick results, and management considerations including virtual visits. Key teaching points include differentiating uncomplicated from complicated UTI, the importance of asking about systemic symptoms and comorbidities, proper clean-catch midstream collection, causes of false-negative nitrite tests, and when a virtual visit is appropriate. The lecture emphasizes clinical reasoning and common pitfalls in UTI diagnosis and treatment.
key_points: Uncomplicated UTI is limited to the lower urinary tract (bladder/urethra) with no systemic illness, pregnancy, or other complications.
When evaluating UTI symptoms, always ask about chills, flank pain, CVA tenderness, nausea/vomiting, diabetes, and recent procedures to rule out complicated infection.
Differential diagnosis for UTI includes STI, interstitial cystitis, pyelonephritis, and atrophic vaginitis.
The ideal urine sample is a clean-catch midstream specimen: wipe the anatomy, start urinating, then collect midstream.
Urine samples should be processed within 1, 2 hours; delay allows E. coli multiplication and can alter culture results.
Bacteria that do not produce nitrites (e.g., Enterococcus, Staph saprophyticus, Group B Strep, Proteus) can cause UTI with a negative dipstick nitrite.
False-negative nitrite can also occur with frequent urination (short bladder incubation), acidic urine (cranberry), or incontinence in older women.
Sterile pyuria may result from partially treated UTI (patient taking leftover antibiotics) or STI.
Hematuria combined with positive nitrites has the highest predictive value for UTI diagnosis.
Virtual visits for UTI are acceptable for women with uncomplicated symptoms but not for men; recurrent UTI (≥3 in one year) requires in-person evaluation.
Self-diagnosis of UTI by a female patient is a stronger predictor of UTI than clinician diagnosis or lab tests.
For E. coli and Staph, a colony count of 1,000 CFU can be diagnostic if the patient is symptomatic, not the traditional 100,000 CFU.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Acute and Chronic Low Back Pain
episodes.speaker: Dr. Rylander
episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander teaches how to distinguish common causes of low back pain, disc pain, facet joint pain, spinal stenosis, and radicular pain, using history and physical exam alone, before imaging. Disc pain presents as acute localized back pain with paraspinal spasms after bending or lifting, without radicular symptoms. Facet joint pain is more chronic, lateralized, and worsened by extension but relieved by lying down. Spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication: symmetrical leg pain with walking that is immediately relieved by bending forward or sitting, differentiating it from vascular claudication. Radicular pain is unilateral, from nerve root compression at the neuroforamen, often due to disc herniation or facet hypertrophy.
key_points: Disc pain is acute, localized to the back, with paraspinal spasms at the level of the disc, and no radicular symptoms unless there is extrusion.
Facet joint pain is chronic, lateralized, worse with extension, better with lying down, and may radiate to the buttock but not down the leg.
Spinal stenosis presents as neurogenic claudication: symmetrical pain in the upper legs that worsens with walking and is relieved by bending forward or sitting.
Neurogenic claudication is reliably relieved by bending forward, while vascular claudication is not; vascular claudication requires rest and fades slowly.
Vascular claudication is more distal, often asymmetrical, and comes on and goes off slowly over minutes.
Radicular pain is unilateral, follows a dermatomal pattern, and results from nerve compression at the neuroforamen.
The most common cause of radicular pain is a herniated disc fragment protruding into the neuroforamen, but facet hypertrophy can also narrow the foramen.
Muscle strains are common in young active people; disc and facet problems are more common in middle-aged and older adults.
Initial evaluation should include plain X-rays; MRI is reserved for those who fail conservative therapy or have persistent specific patterns.
A careful history, onset, aggravating/relieving factors, location, symmetry, can differentiate these conditions without advanced imaging.
Acute radicular pain from disc herniation is almost always unilateral; bilateral symptoms suggest a different etiology.
Do not prescribe bed rest for acute back pain; it increases DVT risk. Advise decreased activity but staying upright and walking.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Chronic Abdominal Pain
episodes.speaker: Dr. Rylander
episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander presents a conceptual framework for understanding irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) as an autoimmune disorder triggered by infections. He explains how the GI mucosa, with its unique microbiome interaction and enteric nervous system ('second brain'), differs from other body-environment interfaces. The lecture details how viral, bacterial, and food antigens can induce autoantibodies against gut nerve and muscle plexuses, leading to IBS symptoms like constipation, diarrhea, and cramping. He reviews evidence for post-infectious IBS and draws parallels to other autoimmune conditions like type 1 diabetes and asthma.
key_points: The GI mucosa is uniquely engineered for absorption and microbiome interaction, unlike the skin (shield) or respiratory mucosa (transpiration).
The enteric nervous system has two main plexuses: one controls peristalsis (myenteric), the other controls absorption at the mucosal surface.
Autoantibodies against these nerve plexuses can impair function, causing constipation, diarrhea, and cramping in IBS.
Viral infections can trigger autoantibodies when virus particles bud from host cells, carrying both self and viral antigens on their surface.
Post-infectious IBS is a clinically proven entity with augmented cellular immune response and correlating immune cell counts.
Food-induced autoantibodies (e.g., to eggs, wheat, beef, pork, lamb) can also contribute to IBS, and dietary modification removing trigger foods may help.
A gluten-free diet is not more efficient than a low-fermentable diet for IBS; different diets each have their contribution.
Asthma is inversely proportional to microbial exposure, more chronic exposure to diverse bacteria reduces immune system reactivity.
Inflammatory bowel disease is associated with a 20-fold increased risk of psoriasis and other immune-mediated skin disorders.
The concept of shared antigenicity explains how a combined self/non-self protein can trigger autoimmunity in genetically predisposed individuals.
Asthma is inversely proportional to microbial exposure; chronic exposure to diverse bacteria can downregulate immune responses.
IBD is associated with a 20-fold increased risk of psoriasis, linked to shared autoantibodies causing skin lesions.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on COPD and Asthma
episodes.speaker: Dr. Rylander
episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander contrasts COPD and asthma by emphasizing that COPD is driven by chronic inflammation of the alveoli and basement membrane from environmental irritants (usually smoke), leading to alveolar destruction, air trapping, and dead space. Asthma involves both chronic inflammation (hypertrophy/hyperplasia, eosinophils) and bronchial hyperreactivity, making the airways narrower at baseline so that a spasm causes severe obstruction. He then describes the typical COPD exacerbation as a slow, weeks-long buildup of increased cough, sputum production, and dyspnea, distinguishing it from the more rapid onset of heart failure exacerbations. He also reviews systolic versus diastolic heart failure, noting that both can reduce cardiac output and renal perfusion similarly.
key_points: COPD is fundamentally an inflammatory disease of the alveoli and basement membrane, usually caused by smoke exposure.
In COPD, chronic inflammation leads to alveolar destruction, increased compliance, atelectasis, dead space, and air trapping.
Asthma involves both chronic airway inflammation (hypertrophied mucosa, eosinophils, mucus gland hyperplasia) and bronchial hyperreactivity.
In asthma, baseline airway narrowing from inflammation makes a superimposed spasm much more dangerous than in a normal airway.
COPD and asthma can coexist; reversibility on spirometry with bronchodilator challenge indicates a reactive component.
A COPD exacerbation is defined by a change in cough, change in sputum production, and often change in sputum character (e.g., yellow, green, brown).
The typical COPD exacerbation story evolves over weeks, not hours or overnight.
If a patient cannot produce sputum but has two of the three cardinal features, it can still be a COPD exacerbation.
Heart failure exacerbations (systolic or diastolic) present more rapidly (hours to days) with fluid overload, often triggered by dietary salt or medication changes.
Both systolic and diastolic heart failure reduce cardiac output and renal perfusion, leading to fluid retention and similar downstream effects.
Reduced ejection fraction directly reduces glomerular filtration rate by a similar percentage.
Diastolic heart failure preserves ejection fraction but impairs relaxation, requiring higher filling pressures and still reducing cardiac output.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia
episodes.speaker: Dr. Rylander
episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander introduces the four main types of dementia, Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia, and vascular dementia, and explains their underlying pathophysiology centered on tau protein dysfunction. He emphasizes that vascular dementia is the only treatable form through lifestyle changes, high-dose statins, and antiplatelet therapy. The lecture also covers distinguishing dementia from delirium using the FAST scale and obtaining collateral history. Key clinical pearls include the MIND diet for prevention, the stepwise decline pattern of vascular dementia, and the importance of not assuming an acute change is just baseline dementia.
key_points: Tau protein dysfunction is central to most neurodegenerative dementias, including Alzheimer's, frontotemporal, and Lewy body dementia.
Alzheimer's disease involves tau aggregation outside cells with amyloid plaque formation; frontotemporal dementia has tau tangles inside cells.
Lewy body dementia is characterized by hallucinations and Parkinsonism, with a shorter disease course of about 7 years after diagnosis.
Vascular dementia is the only treatable form; management includes high-dose statins, antiplatelet therapy (e.g., clopidogrel), and lifestyle changes.
The MIND diet (Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay) combines elements of Mediterranean and DASH diets, emphasizing berries and vegetables.
The FAST scale (Functional Assessment Staging) helps grade dementia severity and is useful for detecting acute mental status changes suggestive of delirium.
Distinguishing delirium from dementia requires collateral history from family or nursing staff; baseline function must be known.
Alcohol in excess causes its own dementia and increases cancer risk; the MIND diet's wine component is controversial.
Vascular dementia has a stepwise decline corresponding to recurrent infarctions, unlike the more predictable temporal decline of Alzheimer's.
High-dose statins (e.g., rosuvastatin 40 mg) can be better tolerated by starting low and titrating up with vitamin D supplementation.
Delirium involves disorganized thought, inattention, and neural overstimulation, while dementia-related agitation is stimulus-driven and patients quiet down when left alone.
The FAST scale (Functional Assessment Staging) grades dementia severity and helps identify acute mental status changes when a patient's current level differs from their baseline.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Rylander

also_uploaded.title: Dr. Rylander on Gout - Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 1/15/26

episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander presents a comprehensive lecture on gout diagnosis and management, emphasizing that the primary defect in gout is underexcretion of uric acid (90% of cases) rather than overproduction. He stresses the importance of treating to a target uric acid level below 6 mg/dL, where crystals dissolve, and identifies common clinical errors such as focusing on dietary purines instead of addressing alcohol and high-fructose intake. The lecture covers acute flare management with colchicine, NSAIDs, and corticosteroids, highlighting comorbidities that guide drug choice, and introduces advanced diagnostics like dual-energy CT and point-of-care ultrasound for assessing disease burden.
key_points: The most important dietary interventions for gout in order are: 1) stop beer, 2) avoid other alcohols, 3) avoid high-fructose corn syrup, and 4) limit high-purine animal foods (organ meats, shellfish); plant purines are not concentrated enough to matter.
The fundamental defect in gout is underexcretion of uric acid (90% of cases), not overproduction; treatment must focus on enhancing excretion rather than just reducing intake.
Uric acid treatment goal is <6 mg/dL; above 6 crystals form, below 6 crystals dissolve.
The most common chart review error in gout management is giving wrong dietary advice (focusing on animal protein) and failing to follow up to ensure the uric acid goal is met.
Acute gout flare treatment should be started within 24 hours for best outcomes; three pillars are colchicine, NSAIDs, and corticosteroids.
Colchicine should be used at low dose (not high dose), hold statins during flare, and avoid in significant kidney disease.

NSAIDs are now considered a secondary choice due to risks of GI ulceration, kidney dysfunction, heart failure, and cardiovascular disease; indomethacin is traditional but naproxen and COX-2 inhibitors are replacing it.
Corticosteroids (e.g., Medrol dose pack) are an emerging first-line option; a 6-day taper is typical but some patients may need extended therapy due to rebound.
Gold standard for diagnosis is joint aspiration with crystal identification under polarized light microscopy to distinguish gout (negatively birefringent) from pseudogout.
Point-of-care ultrasound can show the 'double contour sign' (crystal deposition on cartilage) and 'snowstorm' crystals in joint fluid; dual-energy CT quantifies total body urate burden.
First MTP joint is most commonly affected due to its distance from the heart (cooler temperature) promoting crystallization; in peripheral vascular disease, gout can affect knees, ankles, or hands.
IL-1 inhibition (e.g., anakinra) is a next-line therapy for refractory cases, blocking the inflammasome pathway that drives gout inflammation.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Knee Pain and Problems
episodes.speaker: Dr. Rylander
episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander discusses knee problems including patellar dislocation, patellofemoral pain syndrome, bursitis, patellar tendonitis, and Osgood-Schlatter disease. He emphasizes the importance of comparing the injured knee to the contralateral side when assessing ligamentous laxity, especially in older patients. For lateral patellar dislocation, he describes a reduction technique involving hyperextension to recreate the window for the patella to return, followed by bracing to prevent hyperextension. He advises against routine aspiration of bursitis due to infection risk and recommends conservative management with activity modification and anti-inflammatories.
key_points: Always compare ligamentous laxity to the contralateral knee; normal aging increases laxity, so comparing to the uninjured side prevents overdiagnosis of injury.
A partial ligament tear has a stretchy but present endpoint; a complete tear has no endpoint and feels like soft tissue distension.
Lateral patellar dislocation is reduced by hyperextending the knee to recreate the window for the patella, then gently guiding it back; do not force it back while the knee is bent.
After reduction, brace the knee in slight flexion to prevent hyperextension and refer to orthopedics; most patients see an orthopedist within six weeks.

Patellofemoral pain syndrome presents with anterior knee pain worse with stairs and sitting; management includes activity modification, topical treatments, and physical therapy focusing on quadriceps and VMO strengthening.

Bursitis (prepatellar or infrapatellar) is best managed conservatively with activity modification and anti-inflammatories; aspiration increases infection risk and steroids can cause joint degeneration.
Osgood-Schlatter disease is an apophysitis of the tibial tubercle common in adolescents, especially those in jumping or kicking sports; it typically resolves by the twenties.
Patellar tendonitis presents with localized tenderness and pain with activity; treatment mirrors that of other overuse injuries with activity modification and topical/oral anti-inflammatories.
Medial or superior patellar dislocations are rare and require urgent orthopedic referral due to possible joint capsule or tendon damage.
The patellar apprehension test reproduces lateral displacement and patient tightening; the grind test causes a grinding sensation in the posterior quadrant.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks
episodes.speaker: Dr. Rylander
episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander teaches residents how to perform common nerve blocks in the clinic, including occipital, dorsal scapular, and suprascapular blocks. He details the preparation of a standard injectate solution using 2 mL of Kenalog 40 mg/mL and 2 mL of 1-2% lidocaine, drawn with an 18-gauge needle and injected with a 27-gauge needle. Landmark-based techniques are emphasized, with specific instructions for needle angles, depth, and aspiration to avoid vascular or pulmonary complications. The lecture also covers CPT coding, indications based on neuropathic pain patterns, and the expected onset of relief within five minutes.
key_points: Use a standard injectate: 2 mL of Kenalog 40 mg/mL plus 2 mL of 1-2% lidocaine (total 4 mL, 80 mg Kenalog).
Draw up the solution with an 18-gauge needle on a 3-5 cc syringe; inject with a 27-gauge ½-inch needle.
For joint injections requiring aspiration, use a larger needle; the 27-gauge is for injection only.
Occipital nerve block: palpate one-third and two-thirds of the distance from midline to mastoid process; inject just lateral to your finger at the hairline with the patient sitting and head forward.
Advance the needle until it hits bone (occiput) for occipital blocks; aspirate before injecting to avoid intravascular injection.
Dorsal scapular block: three injection sites (superior, medial, inferior) based on scapular landmarks; needle depth ~1 cm; aspirate for air (pneumothorax risk) and blood.
Suprascapular block: landmark is the midpoint of the scapular spine; insert needle at a 45-degree angle upward and medially until bone is contacted, then aspirate and inject.
Indications for nerve blocks include neuropathic pain (electric, tingling, shocking) in the distribution of the nerve, not well explained by other causes.
Onset of relief after a block is typically within five minutes.
CPT codes: occipital block 0.9 RVU, dorsal scapular block 64450 (three units), suprascapular block 64445.
If a suprascapular block fails, consider a dorsal scapular median nerve block due to overlapping innervation.
Sterilize the injection site with alcohol; for hairy areas, wet the hair thoroughly with alcohol pads.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26
episodes.speaker: Dr. Rylander
episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander reviews peripheral vascular disease (PVD) and peripheral arterial disease (PAD), emphasizing that arterial and venous disease often coexist and must be assessed together. He highlights the importance of recognizing critical limb ischemia, using toe-brachial index when ankle-brachial index is unreliable due to calcification, and understanding that microvascular disease is as important as proximal blockages. He stresses aggressive cardiovascular risk reduction (smoking cessation, statins, diabetes control) because PAD signals systemic risk. Exercise therapy to stimulate neovascularization is a cornerstone of treatment, but patients must be educated to avoid skin breakdown and recognize acute limb ischemia.
key_points: Arterial and venous disease are not mutually exclusive; assess the degree of each and treat both.
Compression for venous disease is contraindicated if it exceeds arterial perfusion pressure, risking critical limb ischemia.
Microvascular disease often limits perfusion even after successful proximal revascularization.
Toe-brachial index is more accurate than ankle-brachial index when calcified vessels cause falsely elevated pressures.
PAD is a marker for systemic cardiovascular disease; aggressive risk reduction (LDL <50, smoking cessation, diabetes control) is mandatory.
Exercise therapy (walking to claudication, rest, repeat) stimulates neovascularization and improves perfusion.
Patients must be educated to avoid foot injuries during exercise and to seek urgent care for new foot sores to prevent gangrene.
Arterial ulcers have sharp, punched-out borders, clean pink base, and lack hemosiderin staining seen in venous ulcers.
Buerger's test (pallor on elevation, rubor on dependency) is a key bedside exam for severe ischemia.
Reserve CTA/MRA and vascular referral for patients being considered for revascularization; stop workup with duplex if not intervening.
Buerger's test: pallor on elevation, rubor on dependency indicates severe ischemia.
If ABI is noncompressible (too high), measure toe pressures.

episodes.title: Dr. Sakirgil on Abdominal Pain
episodes.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
episodes.abstract: Dr. Sakirgil presents a lecture on evaluating abdominal pain in the outpatient setting, emphasizing that while most cases are benign (gastroenteritis, gastritis), about 5% of outpatient and 10% of ER visits involve severe pathology. He stresses the importance of history (onset, quality, location, associated symptoms) and physical exam (rebound, Rovsing, obturator signs) to identify surgical conditions like appendicitis, cholecystitis, and AAA. Special attention is given to elderly patients (AAA, ischemic colitis) and women of childbearing age (pregnancy test required). The lecture provides practical guidance on when to send patients to the ER, imaging choices (ultrasound for RUQ, CT for RLQ/LLQ in adults), and key pitfalls such as normal WBC not ruling out appendicitis.
key_points: About 5% of outpatient abdominal pain and 10% of ER abdominal pain is severe; the rest is benign.
In elderly patients, consider AAA, ischemic colitis, bowel obstruction, perforated diverticulitis, and cholecystitis.
In women of childbearing age with abdominal pain, always perform a pregnancy test.
Pain that is constant, less than 48 hours, and worse than vomiting suggests surgical disease.
A positive rebound sign indicates acute abdomen; the patient should be sent to the ER immediately.
A normal white blood cell count does not rule out appendicitis.
Ultrasound is the imaging study of choice for right upper quadrant pain; CT is preferred for right lower quadrant and left lower quadrant pain in adults.
For children with suspected appendicitis, send to a pediatric hospital; the obturator sign is a useful maneuver.
Always ask if the patient still has their appendix or gallbladder when concerned about those organs.
If sending a patient to the ER for possible emergency surgery, instruct them not to eat or drink.
EKG should be considered in patients with abdominal pain, especially in the elderly.
To overcome guarding during abdominal exam, start away from the tender area, have the patient relax with arms at sides, and explain what you will do.
