After residency, renting a home initially can be wiser than buying an expensive house, allowing more savings for retirement and children's education.

episodes.title: Drs Jones & Shannon on Addiction Med Part 1
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jones & Dr. Shannon
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Drs. Jones and Shannon focuses on the practical assessment and management of substance use disorders in primary care and hospital settings. It covers how to take a substance use history, apply DSM-5 diagnostic criteria, and determine severity. The presenters discuss treatment options including levels of care (inpatient, residential, outpatient), monitoring programs, 12-step programs (AA, NA, Celebrate Recovery), and psychosocial interventions. A significant portion is devoted to describing Celebrate Recovery, a Christian-based 12-step program, including its structure, step studies, and how it differs from traditional AA in emphasizing identity in Christ rather than labeling oneself as an addict.
key_points: When assessing substance use, start with least controversial substances (caffeine, nicotine, alcohol) before moving to controlled substances and illegal drugs.
USPSTF recommends screening everyone 18 or older for unhealthy drug use.
DSM-5 substance use disorder diagnosis requires a problematic pattern causing clinically significant impairment or distress, with 2 or more of 11 criteria in a 12-month period.
Severity is classified as mild (2-3 criteria), moderate (4-5), or severe (6 or more).

Treatment mainstay is referral to a drug and alcohol rehab program, which can be inpatient (psychiatric hospital), residential (non-hospital setting), or outpatient (IOP, typically half-day 3-5 times/week).
Monitoring programs significantly increase the risk of abstinence; examples include physician health programs and drug courts.
Attendance in a 12-step program is recommended for anyone with substance use disorder; '90 in 90' means attending at least one meeting daily for the first 90 days of sobriety.
Celebrate Recovery is a Christian-focused 12-step program where the higher power is Jesus Christ, and identity is framed as 'who you are in Jesus' rather than labeling oneself as an addict.
Step studies in Celebrate Recovery are gender-split group processes lasting 9-18 months, unlike AA's one-on-one sponsor approach.
Anonymity is a core tradition: no last names are used in meetings, and sharing outside the rooms is discouraged.
Celebrate Recovery is a faith-based 12-step program for any hurt, hang-up, or habit.
CR separates identity from the problem, unlike AA where saying 'I am an alcoholic' becomes an identity statement.

episodes.title: Drs Jones & Shannon on Addiction Med Part 2
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jones & Dr. Shannon
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers practical management of alcohol and opioid use disorders in primary care. The presenters review evidence-based pharmacotherapies including naltrexone, acamprosate, gabapentin, topiramate, and buprenorphine formulations, along with non-medication approaches such as 12-step programs and levels of care. Key clinical pearls include screening recommendations, medication selection based on patient status (abstinent vs. still drinking, liver function, renal function), and practical induction guidance for buprenorphine. Emphasis is placed on reducing barriers to treatment, including the elimination of the X-waiver, and using long-acting injections to improve adherence.
key_points: USPSTF level B recommendation to screen all adults for alcohol use disorder; CAGE is outdated, AUDIT or single-question screen (≥5 drinks men/≥4 women in past year, ≥1 positive) is preferred.
Naltrexone (oral or IM) is first-line for alcohol use disorder; it reduces heavy drinking days and cravings, is more effective in patients already abstinent, and is safe in compensated cirrhosis.
Acamprosate (Campral) is best for maintaining abstinence in those who have already stopped drinking; must be renally dosed in CKD and avoided in severe renal dysfunction.
Gabapentin can be used in patients still drinking and reduces heavy drinking days; dosing varies widely and requires renal adjustment.
Topiramate can be started at 25 mg daily and titrated up; reduces heavy drinking days.
Disulfiram (Antabuse) is no longer first-line due to poor real-world adherence, but may still be considered in highly motivated patients with supervised dosing.
For co-users of alcohol and tobacco, varenicline (Chantix) reduces cravings for both substances.
Buprenorphine is the mainstay for opioid use disorder; it has a ceiling effect with very low overdose risk and high receptor affinity.
The X-waiver is eliminated; any DEA-registered prescriber with 8 hours of training can prescribe buprenorphine for OUD.
For buprenorphine, long-acting injections (Sublocade, Brixadi) improve adherence; Sublocade requires refrigeration, forms a palpable depot that may need surgical removal if adverse reaction occurs.
Buprenorphine/naloxone (Suboxone) is a partial agonist; naloxone deters injection but is inactive when taken sublingually.
Sublocade is a depot buprenorphine injection that forms a subcutaneous knot; requires refrigeration and surgical removal if reaction occurs.

episodes.title: Female Sexual (Dys)function
episodes.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Hildebrand
episodes.abstract: This lecture challenges common myths about female sexual function using a quiz and group discussion. It emphasizes that sexual desire is not a survival drive, genital response does not reliably indicate arousal, and there is no effective female equivalent of Viagra due to the complex interplay of psychological, relational, and physiological factors. The presenters advocate moving beyond simplistic linear models and highlight the importance of intimacy, context, and individual variation in clinical care.
key_points: Sexual activity is not a survival drive; abstinence causes no significant physiological consequences.
Placebo effects for drugs targeting female sexual dysfunction exceed 40%.
Genital response (e.g., lubrication, erection) does not equal sexual arousal; arousal is primarily a mental process.
Increasing genital function alone is ineffective for improving sexual desire, especially in women.
Women and men respond similarly to sexually relevant stimuli; the myth of lower female responsiveness is false.
Arousal can occur without desire (e.g., unwanted physical response), demonstrating non-concordance.
There is greater variation in sexual response within genders than between genders.
Non-concordance refers to an individual's inability to accurately detect their own arousal, not a mismatch between partners.
Primary care clinicians should be prepared to discuss water-based vs. silicone lubricant options.
The traditional four-phase model (excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution) omits desire, intimacy, and emotional context.

Ask every woman with chronic disease or on culprit medications (SSRIs, antipsychotics, amphetamines, beta blockers, spironolactone, hormonal contraceptives, lipid agents) how the condition or drug affects her sex life.
Beta blockers are the worst for female orgasm; never make them first-line antihypertensives in women.

episodes.title: FMIS August MM
episodes.speaker: Dr. Youmans & Dr. Wheeler & Dr. Jones
episodes.abstract: This M&M conference reviews two cases from August FMIS. The first case involves a 50-year-old woman with ESRD on hemodialysis who presented with right-sided weakness, was diagnosed with a TIA, but received IVF from an ischemic stroke order set, risking volume overload. The second case involves a man with shortness of breath and atypical anginal symptoms who was sent home from clinic but later admitted with heart failure and an EF of 20%, highlighting delays in care. Key lessons include checking the MAR at every care transition, tailoring order sets to the patient's diagnosis and comorbidities, and recognizing atypical presentations of acute coronary syndrome and heart failure.
key_points: TIA and ischemic stroke are treated differently: TIA does not receive IVF, while ischemic stroke may receive IVF without dextrose if volume depleted.
For TIA, baseline treatment is aspirin 81-325 mg daily; if ABCD2 score >4, add clopidogrel 300-600 mg loading dose then 75 mg daily.
In ESRD patients on HD, cardiac morbidity and mortality risk is 25-40% higher on the first day after HD due to volume overload and hyponatremia.
Volume overload in ESRD is primarily treated by dialysis; longer and more frequent HD sessions (e.g., q4 vs q3) can help prevent it.
Always check the MAR when assuming care of a patient to identify running IV fluids and other medications that may not be documented in notes.
When using admission order sets, verify each order is appropriate for the patient's current diagnosis and comorbidities.
Atypical presentations of ACS (e.g., dyspnea without chest pain) are common and can lead to delays in care; maintain a high index of suspicion.
Diagnosing CHF is a clinical assessment; an echo is confirmatory but should not delay initial treatment.
Document all treatments, especially IVF, in the H&P and progress notes under the specific problem or in the FEN section.
Consult nephrology early for ESRD patients who have missed HD to get them back on schedule and manage volume status.
Diagnosing CHF requires at least two major clinical criteria: pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly, jugular venous distension, PAN D, and third heart sound.
One third of patients with confirmed MI have no chest pain; dyspnea alone can be an anginal equivalent.

episodes.title: Gina Blevins on Healthy Start
episodes.speaker: Gina Blevins
episodes.abstract: Gina Blevins presents the Healthy Start program, a federal initiative aimed at reducing infant mortality in the Tulsa area. She describes her role as a certified lactation counselor and infant massage educator, offering home visits, transportation, WIC assistance, and breastfeeding support to pregnant and postpartum women in specific ZIP codes, regardless of income. Key teaching points include the timeline for milk coming in (3-4 days), the small size of a newborn's stomach, and common misconceptions about hospital formula brands. She also explains how to refer patients and highlights the program's voluntary, confidential nature.
key_points: Healthy Start is a voluntary program for pregnant and postpartum women in certain Tulsa ZIP codes, not income-based.
Infant mortality in Tulsa dropped from 18 to about 9-10 per 1,000, but is trending back up.
Breast milk typically comes in 3-4 days after delivery; colostrum is sufficient for the first days.
A newborn's stomach is the size of a cherry pit at birth, walnut at 3 days, and golf ball at 10 days.
Hospital formula (often Similac) is chosen by cheapest bid, not medical necessity; families can switch brands.
Similac commonly causes constipation in breastfed babies who supplement.
WIC provides Gerber formula, not necessarily the brand used in the hospital.
Healthy Start offers free breastfeeding support (certified lactation counselor) vs. $75 at hospitals.
The program follows mothers for 18 months postpartum, including ASQ developmental screenings and home safety checks.
Domestic violence patients can use a code word to request police intervention via text.
Referrals can be made by email or chart message; enrollment before delivery is ideal.
Infant massage helps with drug-addicted babies, jaundice, postpartum depression, and failure to thrive.

episodes.title: Gyn with Dr. Calvert
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert discusses chronic anovulation, focusing on PCOS and insulin resistance as the two most common causes. He reviews the current diagnostic criteria for PCOS (irregular menstrual periods, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, elevated free testosterone, requiring two of three). He emphasizes that insulin resistance is often the dominant driver and should be treated primarily with metformin, which can also improve fertility. He also addresses the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and the need for at least two menstrual cycles per year to protect the endometrium.
key_points: Chronic anovulation has two most common causes: PCOS and insulin resistance.
Current PCOS diagnosis requires two of three criteria: irregular menstrual periods, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, elevated free testosterone.
Clinical hirsutism alone is not currently a diagnostic criterion for PCOS.
30-80% of women with chronic anovulation or PCOS have insulin resistance.
Insulin resistance testing involves fasting glucose and insulin, then glucose load with repeat glucose and insulin at 2 hours; ratio >4.5 suggests insulin resistance.
When insulin resistance is dominant, treatment should target insulin resistance, not PCOS directly.
Primary treatment for PCOS is weight loss.
Primary risk of PCOS is endometrial hyperplasia from unopposed estrogen; need at least 2 menstrual cycles per year to protect the endometrium.
Metformin is the treatment for insulin resistance; trend is toward treating all with insulin resistance and metformin.
For PCOS patients wanting pregnancy, 4-6 months of continuous birth control pills can suppress testosterone and allow ovulation after stopping.
Metformin alone can lead to pregnancy within 3-4 months in some patients with PCOS and insulin resistance.

episodes.title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor
episodes.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
episodes.abstract: Dr. Heather Bell, a physician advisor (called a PUMA at the VA and a PA at Ascension), explains her role in utilization management and clinical documentation integrity (CDI). She describes why the role exists, pointing to insurance companies' denial tactics (UnitedHealthcare denies roughly 70% of cases, yet 92% are overturned on peer-to-peer review) and the documentation complexity introduced by ICD-10 and CMS. She covers the two-midnight rule for observation versus inpatient status, how DRG codes tie diagnoses to expected length of stay, and the precise documentation language now required for diagnoses like CKD, malnutrition, and alcohol withdrawal. She also gives practical advice on responding to CDI queries and using documentation, such as noting dramatic overnight improvement, to defend admission status when patients recover faster than expected.
key_points: The physician advisor advises clinicians on compliant coding, utilization management, and clinical documentation integrity, and performs peer-to-peer reviews with insurance company medical directors.
UnitedHealthcare notoriously denies about 70% of cases across the board as a strategy, but peer-to-peer review overturns about 92% of those denials, so fighting back works.

ICD-10 and CMS turned physician notes from communication tools into compliance documents, requiring specific language such as 'acute on chronic kidney injury' instead of 'renal insufficiency' and 'CKD 3a' instead of just 'CKD'.
CDI queries are not personal criticism of clinical care; they ask for the documentation language insurance companies and regulatory bodies require for reimbursement and severity metrics.

CMS uses a two-midnight rule: observation is appropriate when the expected stay is less than two midnights; if conversion to inpatient occurs, the inpatient clock restarts and observation hours do not count.

DRG codes tie diagnoses to expected length of stay, cellulitis alone is about 2 days, but cellulitis with bacteremia and an abscess (a complicated skin and skin structure infection) is 5.7 days, so documentation specificity matters.

Documentation requirements change with regulation: dietitian notes no longer count for a malnutrition diagnosis even if the physician signs them, the physician must put the diagnosis in their own note.
When ordering an alcohol withdrawal (SWA) protocol, SWA scores must appear in the chart because that is the first thing insurance peer reviewers ask about.

Intention, not just the actual course, determines admission status: if a patient expected to be very sick improves dramatically, documenting that in the discharge summary supports the inpatient admission.

When a utilization review nurse says a patient does not meet inpatient criteria but the clinician believes they do, the problem is documentation, the note must describe on paper how sick the patient is.
Patient status (inpatient, observation, outpatient-in-a-bed) is determined in the computer and is independent of geographic hospital location.
High-acuity findings like gram-positive bacteremia indicate a sick patient and almost always warrant an infectious disease consult.

episodes.title: Inflammatory Breast Cancer - Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert reviews inflammatory breast cancer (IBC), a rare (1-5% of breast cancers) but rapidly progressive malignancy that typically presents at stage III or IV with unilateral breast swelling, erythema, warmth, and skin changes including peau d'orange and nipple inversion. Key teaching includes that a palpable breast mass is often absent, mammography may be negative, and the hallmark feature is rapid progression of erythema involving at least a third of the breast within weeks, distinguishing it from mastitis and other mimics. Diagnosis requires biopsy of the inflammatory breast tissue, and treatment follows a rapid three-stage sequence of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgical resection, and post-mastectomy radiation. The presenter illustrates practical management with a clinical case, emphasizing short-interval follow-up and antibiotics when mastitis remains in the differential.
key_points: Inflammatory breast cancer is rare (1-5% of breast cancers), rapidly progressive, and typically presents at late stage with poor survival (~18% at 5 years).
The most common symptom is unilateral breast swelling or heaviness (~79%); the primary presenting sign is erythema.
A palpable breast tumor is uncommon even though the source is a tumor; check axillary and infraclavicular nodes.
Pathophysiology: metastatic tumor cells block dermal lymphatics, producing swelling, peau d'orange, and nipple inversion.
Mammography may be negative; diagnosis requires biopsy of the inflammatory breast tissue.
Erythema progresses within weeks to involve at least a third of the breast - the key feature distinguishing IBC from mastitis.
Treatment is three-stage: neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgical resection, and post-mastectomy radiation, done rapidly.
Differential diagnosis includes mastitis, cellulitis, breast abscess, hidradenitis suppurativa, radiation-induced inflammation, folliculitis, and intertrigo.
Mastitis erythema is typically central around the areola extending outward; treat with antibiotics (e.g., dicloxacillin), warm compresses, gentle compression, and continued breastfeeding.
When IBC cannot be ruled out, treat empirically for mastitis and follow up at short intervals - rapid progression of erythema signals cancer rather than infection.

episodes.title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures
episodes.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
episodes.abstract: Dr. Enis Sakirgil presents a lecture on joint and soft-tissue injections for outpatient family medicine. He emphasizes the importance of an adequate NSAID trial (naproxen 500 mg BID or ibuprofen 600 mg TID for 10, 14 days) before considering injection. Key safety points include never using multidose vials for joint injections, knowing the maximum lidocaine dose (300 mg for adults), and avoiding injection into a prosthetic joint. He reviews contraindications, proper sterile technique, and the properties of common injectable corticosteroids, including mixing short- and long-acting agents.
key_points: An adequate NSAID trial is 10, 14 days of naproxen 500 mg BID or ibuprofen 600 mg TID before considering joint injection.
Always ask about GI history (peptic ulcer, PPI use) and instruct patients to take NSAIDs with food.
Limit corticosteroid injections to four per year per joint to avoid articular cartilage damage.
Never use multidose vials of local anesthetic for joint injections due to contamination risk; use single-dose vials instead.
Maximum lidocaine dose for adults is 300 mg (15 mL of 2% or 30 mL of 1%); exceeding this can cause CNS toxicity and cardiovascular collapse.
Absolute contraindications to joint injection include bacteremia, osteomyelitis, hemarthrosis, impending joint replacement surgery, and prosthetic joint.
For patients on warfarin, an INR < 3.6 is considered safe for injection; always check INR before proceeding.
Never inject into the substance of a tendon; if the syringe plunger meets resistance, do not force it.
After cleaning the injection site, do not touch it again; if you do, reclean before proceeding.
Post-injection flare occurs in 2, 5% of cases and is often due to poor technique, excessive dose, or improper mixing.
Common injectable corticosteroids include triamcinolone (Kenalog), methylprednisolone (Depo-Medrol), betamethasone (Celestone), and dexamethasone (Decadron).
Mixing a long-acting steroid (e.g., Kenalog) with a short-acting one (e.g., Decadron) can provide both rapid and sustained effect.

episodes.title: Internet Addiction - Rev. Joel Leitch
episodes.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
episodes.abstract: Rev. Joel Leitch introduces process (behavioral) addictions, using Internet addiction as a model. He explains that while DSM-5 and ICD-10/11 do not list Internet addiction disorder as a formal diagnosis, they do include gaming disorder. The talk covers subtypes (excessive gaming, sexual preoccupations, email/text messaging), core components (withdrawal, tolerance, negative repercussions), and the challenge of distinguishing dependence from addiction. He emphasizes that the key is not how much someone uses but how it affects their life, and notes that South Korea considers Internet addiction a serious public health issue after deaths in Internet cafes.
key_points: Addictions are categorized as substance (e.g., alcohol, drugs) and process/behavioral (e.g., gambling, pornography, Internet, food).
Internet addiction is not a formal diagnosis in DSM-5 or ICD-10/11, but gaming disorder is included.
Internet addiction is conceptualized as a compulsive-impulsive spectrum disorder.
Three subtypes of Internet addiction: excessive gaming, sexual preoccupations, and email/text messaging.

Core features include excessive use with loss of sense of time, withdrawal symptoms upon stopping, tolerance (needing more time or better equipment), and negative repercussions (arguments, lying, poor achievement, social isolation, fatigue).
Denial is a major defense mechanism; patients may genuinely not perceive their addiction.
A key distinction: dependence (e.g., a diabetic needing insulin) is not the same as addiction; addiction is defined by continued use despite harm.
The amount or frequency of use is less important than the impact on the person's life.
Withdrawal from process addictions is primarily emotional and social, not typically physically dangerous like substance withdrawal.
South Korea treats Internet addiction as a serious public health issue after cardiopulmonary deaths in Internet cafes and a game-related murder.
Ask patients to keep an actual log of internet use for a typical week; they are often shocked by the real extent and direction of their time.
Use time management techniques, including setting a predetermined beginning and end time for internet sessions using a real alarm clock.

episodes.title: Jina Hagen, MS on cfDNA & Carrier Screening 8/28/25
episodes.speaker: Jina Hagen
episodes.abstract: Jina Hagen from Labcorp reviews cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening for fetal aneuploidy, including the technology of massively parallel sequencing, the distinction between maternal and fetal DNA fragments by size, and the evolution of NIPT from high-risk to universal screening following ACOG Practice Bulletin 226. She discusses the importance of positive predictive value (PPV) in interpreting results, the option of reflexing to a genome-wide screen (Maternity Genome) from the same blood sample when later concerns arise, and briefly covers carrier screening for autosomal recessive conditions, noting that 1-2% of couples are at risk.
key_points: cfDNA screens for trisomies 21, 18, 13, sex chromosome aneuploidy, and optional microdeletions/rare trisomies.
Fetal DNA fragments are smaller (~130 bp) than maternal fragments (~160 bp), which helps determine fetal fraction.
Massively parallel sequencing assigns DNA fragments to chromosome bins to detect overrepresentation indicating trisomy.
ACOG Practice Bulletin 226 (2020) recommends offering NIPT to all pregnant women, not just those at high risk.
PPV of cfDNA is ~80% overall but varies with disease prevalence; it is higher in older women and lower in low-risk populations.
A positive NIPT result should not be followed by a quad screen; diagnostic testing (amnio/CVS) is the next step.
Labcorp keeps the blood sample until the due date, allowing reflex to Maternity Genome (whole-chromosome and subchromosomal analysis) within 3 days if later concerns arise.
Maternity Genome provides information comparable to a fetal karyotype, including deletions, duplications, and partial trisomies.
Carrier screening identifies autosomal recessive conditions; most carriers have no symptoms or family history.
1-2% of couples are at risk for having a child with an autosomal recessive disorder; early knowledge improves outcomes.
ACOG accepts ethnic-specific, panethnic, or expanded carrier screening as valid strategies.
Everyone carries recessive gene mutations; collectively, recessive conditions cause significant infant mortality and hospitalizations.

episodes.title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil
episodes.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
episodes.abstract: Dr. Enis Sakirgil presents a practical guide to joint and soft-tissue injections for family medicine residents. He covers indications (osteoarthritis, bursitis, tendinitis, trigger points), contraindications (overlying infection, uncontrolled diabetes, joint replacement, bleeding disorders with INR >3), and the importance of informed consent including the unpredictable duration of relief. He emphasizes never using multidose vials, knowing the milligram dose of lidocaine (300 mg max for adults, 5 mg/kg), and using a 2% concentration for longer effect. He demonstrates a trigger-point injection technique with a 25-27 gauge needle and a steroid-lidocaine mix, and advises against injecting into a tendon by feeling for resistance on the plunger.
key_points: Joint injections are indicated for inflammatory conditions like osteoarthritis, bursitis, tendinitis, and trigger points after failed conservative therapy (NSAIDs, ice).
Never use a multidose vial for joint injections due to risk of septic arthritis; prep your own mix from single-use vials.
Maximum lidocaine dose is 300 mg for adults or 5 mg/kg; know the milligram dose, not milliliters, because concentration varies (1% = 10 mg/mL, 2% = 20 mg/mL).
Contraindications include overlying skin infection, uncontrolled diabetes, joint replacement, fracture, and bleeding disorders with INR >3 (warfarin is safe if INR <3).
Limit corticosteroid injections to 4 per year to avoid systemic effects like osteoporosis and articular damage.
For trigger points, use a 25-27 gauge 1-inch needle with a mix of 1 mL triamcinolone and 4 mL 2% lidocaine, injecting 1 mL per point.
If the plunger meets resistance, do not force it; the needle may be in a tendon or other structure, risking damage.
Duration of relief is unpredictable: some patients get 6 months, others 3 weeks; discuss this in consent.
Avoid injecting near major nerves (e.g., ulnar nerve in medial epicondylitis) and never inject into the substance of a tendon.
For patients on DOACs like apixaban, the same safety data as warfarin is not established; use clinical judgment.
Avoid injecting into the substance of a tendon; if the plunger does not move freely, do not push against resistance.
Always aspirate before injecting to ensure the needle is not in a blood vessel.

episodes.title: Karen Alley on the Hope Pregnancy Center
episodes.speaker: Karen Alley
episodes.abstract: Karen Alley describes the services and approach of pregnancy resource centers, focusing on Hope Pregnancy Center in Oklahoma. These faith-based nonprofits offer free pregnancy testing, limited OB ultrasound, and unbiased education on parenting, adoption, and abortion. They provide social services like parenting classes and material assistance, as well as abortion recovery programs. Alley emphasizes compassionate, nonjudgmental listening and avoiding 'why' questions to support women in crisis.
key_points: Pregnancy resource centers are nonprofit, faith-based, and staffed mostly by volunteers with a small paid staff.
Hope Pregnancy Center offers urine pregnancy testing and limited OB ultrasound solely to confirm pregnancy, then refers to prenatal care.
Centers provide unbiased education on all three options: parenting, adoption, and abortion, but never provide or refer for abortion services.
The 'Pregnancy Decision Guide' is a cognitive tool modeled after the Ottawa decision aid to help women think through their options.
Staff assess clients by asking their stated intention before the test: 'If your test is positive today, what are your plans for your pregnancy?'
Fetal development models and ultrasound are used to compassionately inform women about the life within them.
Avoid 'why' questions as they can put patients on the defensive; use open-ended questions like 'What are the reasons...' instead.
Do not make assumptions about a woman's decision based on her circumstances (e.g., married with children may still consider abortion).
Do not overwhelm with facts and reason when the patient is acting out of emotion; validate, listen, and compassionately offer information.
Do not avoid the hard conversation if a woman says she is not having the baby; take every opportunity to talk it through.
Do not assume a woman's circumstances based on appearance; she may be married with children and still seek an abortion.
Lead with emotional validation and listening, not facts and reason, when a woman is acting out of emotion.

episodes.title: Kelly Dunn, MD on Antipsychotics & Mood Stabilizers
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn reviews first- and second-generation antipsychotics and mood stabilizers, focusing on pharmacology, side effects, and clinical pearls for family medicine residents. She explains dopamine pathways and their role in positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia, extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS), tardive dyskinesia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). Key distinctions include high- vs low-potency first-generation agents, second-generation metabolic monitoring, and specific dosing considerations (e.g., lurasidone with food, aripiprazole in the morning). She emphasizes recognizing akathisia as a suicide risk factor and the importance of monitoring for tardive dyskinesia.
key_points: First-generation antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol, chlorpromazine) block dopamine D2 receptors; high-potency agents (e.g., Haldol) have low histamine/muscarinic effects, while low-potency (e.g., Thorazine) have more.
Second-generation antipsychotics also block D2 but have 5-HT2A serotonin binding, reducing EPS risk; aripiprazole and brexpiprazole are partial D2 agonists.
Dopamine pathways: mesolimbic (positive symptoms), mesocortical (negative/cognitive symptoms), nigrostriatal (EPS), tuberoinfundibular (hyperprolactinemia).
Akathisia (restlessness, pacing) is a risk factor for suicide and must be identified; dystonia (e.g., torticollis) and parkinsonism are other EPS.
Tardive dyskinesia (TD) occurs at ~5% per year with first-generation agents; often irreversible, so early detection (e.g., tongue movements) and switching antipsychotics is key.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) presents with fever, rigidity, mental status changes, autonomic instability, and rhabdomyolysis; requires ICU care.
Second-generation antipsychotics carry a risk of metabolic syndrome; monitor BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, A1c, and lipids at baseline and follow-up.
Antipsychotics can cause QT prolongation; obtain ECG and serum potassium before starting pimozide or IV haloperidol.
Lurasidone (Latuda) requires ~300 calories of food for absorption; aripiprazole (Abilify) is activating and should be dosed in the morning.
Clozapine has unique efficacy but requires weekly blood draws for agranulocytosis monitoring; REMS requirements are being simplified.
Hyperprolactinemia can cause sexual dysfunction; adding a low dose of aripiprazole (partial agonist) may counteract this side effect.
Saphris (asenapine) is absorbed sublingually, not through the GI tract, making it an option for patients with gastric bypass or gastroparesis.

episodes.title: Kelly Dunn, MD on Benzodiazepines
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn reviews the origins, pharmacology, and clinical use of benzodiazepines, emphasizing their risks and appropriate prescribing. She explains that benzos enhance GABA-A receptor activity, leading to sedation, anxiolysis, and memory effects, but chronic use causes tolerance and dependence. The talk covers pharmacokinetics, drug testing limitations, and first-line indications such as alcohol withdrawal, seizures, and catatonia. Dr. Dunn highlights that most benzodiazepine use is nonmedical, with diversion common, and that tolerance to anxiolytic effects develops within months, making long-term use often treat withdrawal rather than the original condition.
key_points: Benzodiazepines were introduced as safer alternatives to barbiturates, with chlordiazepoxide (Librium) first synthesized in 1955.
Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A receptor activity by increasing chloride ion conductance, leading to neuronal inhibition.
Different GABA-A receptor subunits are associated with specific effects: alpha-1 with sedation, alpha-2/3 with anxiolysis, alpha-5 with memory impairment.
Chronic benzodiazepine use leads to tolerance, downregulation of GABA-A receptors, and increased excitatory neurotransmission, similar to alcohol dependence.
Tolerance to the sedative-hypnotic effect develops in 1-2 weeks, and to the anxiolytic effect within a couple of months.
Most benzodiazepine drug screens detect oxazepam metabolites; clonazepam and alprazolam often require separate confirmatory testing.
Lorazepam, oxazepam, and temazepam undergo phase 3 conjugation (glucuronidation) and are preferred in patients with liver impairment as they bypass CYP450.
First-line indications for benzodiazepines include alcohol withdrawal, status epilepticus, acute movement disorders, catatonia, and certain pain syndromes.
About 80% of benzodiazepine use is nonmedical, with diversion from friends or relatives being the most common source.
Benzodiazepines are involved in about 30% of prescription drug overdose deaths, often in combination with opioids.
For patients with opioid use disorder, assess risks/benefits of continued benzodiazepine prescribing at least monthly.
For patients with other substance use disorders, monitor more frequently than the general population (every 3 months).

episodes.title: Kelly Dunn, MD on Pharmacotherapy for Depressive Disorders 12/11/25
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn discusses pharmacotherapy for depressive disorders, emphasizing the importance of matching antidepressant mechanism to symptom profile (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopaminergic). She reviews how side effect profiles can be leveraged therapeutically and provides practical guidance on initiating and switching antidepressants, using cases to illustrate decision-making. The lecture covers key considerations for special populations including elderly patients and those with comorbid anxiety or ADHD.
key_points: ECT is first-line for severe psychotic features of depression; if not an option, combination antidepressant is superior to monotherapy.
Serotonin-responsive symptoms include anxiety, irritability, agitation, insomnia, dysphoric mood, obsessions/compulsions; guide serotonergic agent selection.
Norepinephrine-responsive symptoms include fatigue, hypersomnia, apathy, psychomotor retardation, weight gain, lack of initiative.
Dopaminergic-responsive symptoms include decreased cognition, attention, concentration, motivation, anhedonia, working memory deficits; Wellbutrin is a key option.
Always establish a diagnosis before chasing symptoms with medication selection.
Side effect profiles can be used to patients' advantage: sedating agents for insomnia, activating agents for anergia, weight-gain agents for underweight patients.
Avoid anticholinergic agents (Paxil, Remeron, TCAs) in elderly or dementia patients.
Trazodone at antidepressant doses (300-400 mg) causes excessive sedation; used more for sleep augmentation than first-line depression treatment.
Mirtazapine is sedating at lower doses and more activating at higher doses; weight gain occurs at any dose.
Wellbutrin can be first-line for depression, especially in patients with ADHD, weight concerns, or smoking cessation needs; avoid if prominent anxiety/agitation.
SSRI side effects (GI upset, headache, activation) often improve after first week; efficacy takes weeks due to time needed for receptor adaptation and protein synthesis.
For patients with significant anxiety/agitation, start SSRIs at sub-therapeutic doses (e.g., Zoloft 25 mg) to improve tolerability.

episodes.title: L’Dogg’s Morning Report
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: A 31-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with DKA after not taking insulin for a month. The case focuses on the systematic interpretation of her acid-base status using Winter's formula, which reveals a metabolic acidosis with a superimposed respiratory acidosis. The presenter also walks through a stepwise EKG interpretation, identifying sinus tachycardia with a prolonged QT interval. Key teaching points include the importance of calculating the expected pCO2, the anion gap, and the delta-delta to fully characterize mixed acid-base disorders, as well as a structured approach to reading EKGs.
key_points: Winter's formula (expected pCO2 = 1.5 x [HCO3] + 8 ± 2) is used to determine if a compensatory respiratory response is appropriate in metabolic acidosis.
A pCO2 higher than expected by Winter's formula indicates a superimposed respiratory acidosis.
The anion gap is calculated as sodium minus chloride minus bicarbonate; a normal anion gap is 12.
The delta-delta (excess anion gap = measured AG - 12) is added to the measured bicarbonate to check for a concurrent non-anion gap metabolic acidosis.
In DKA, beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) is the predominant ketone body; a high BHB level favors DKA over starvation ketosis.
Hemoconcentration (elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit) is a sign of volume depletion in DKA.
A structured EKG interpretation includes: rate, rhythm, intervals (PR, QRS, QT), axis, P waves, Q waves, ST segments, and T waves.
A prolonged QT interval (QTc > 450 ms in men, > 460 ms in women) increases the risk of torsades de pointes and requires monitoring.
Sinus tachycardia is common in DKA due to volume depletion and acidosis.
When ordering IV fluids, specify the type, dose (e.g., 1 L bolus), and frequency (e.g., once, then maintenance) rather than relying on order sets.
The diagnosis is not the difficult part; management decisions like IV fluids, potassium, and insulin require deliberate thought.
Lactated Ringer's contains potassium and sodium lactate, which is metabolized to bicarbonate; normal saline can cause hyperchloremic acidosis if given in excess.

episodes.title: L'Dogg's Morning Report
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lawrence Lee presents a complex case of an elderly patient with COPD who presents with progressive dyspnea and fatigue. The case evolves from an initial differential of COPD exacerbation, heart failure, and pneumonia to reveal hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia. The session emphasizes systematic diagnostic reasoning, including interpretation of ABGs with metabolic alkalosis and respiratory acidosis, and the workup for microangiopathic hemolytic anemia including TTP, HUS, and DIC.
key_points: Shortness of breath in an elderly patient with COPD requires a broad differential including COPD exacerbation, heart failure, pneumonia, PE, ACS, and anemia.
A normal chest X-ray with no infiltrate or effusion helps rule out pneumonia and pleural effusion but does not exclude other causes of dyspnea.
Hemoccult-negative stool does not rule out GI bleeding; it only suggests no active upper GI bleed at that moment.
In ABG interpretation, a normal pH with elevated bicarb and elevated PCO2 indicates a chronic compensated respiratory acidosis.
When bicarb is >20, Winters' formula is not used; instead, assess the PCO2 to determine if respiratory compensation is appropriate.
Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3); normal is 12. Excess anion gap = measured AG - 12; add to bicarb to check for hidden metabolic acidosis.
Hemolytic anemia with schistocytes on smear suggests microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) and requires workup for TTP, HUS, and DIC.
For TTP, order ADAMTS13 activity; for HUS, check Shiga toxin; for DIC, order fibrinogen, D-dimer, and INR.
Pancytopenia with hemolysis should also raise consideration for bone marrow production problems, though hemolysis is less common with marrow disorders.
Drug-induced hemolytic anemia and cold agglutinin disease are additional considerations in the differential.
TTP is a medical emergency; it is one of the few conditions that warrants waking a hematologist in the middle of the night.
The classic triad for TTP is thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and end-organ damage (especially kidneys, brain, heart).

episodes.title: Lifestyle/Anemia
episodes.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hildebrand leads a learner-driven session on four common but uncommon causes of anemia that prompt hematology referrals. After a brief review of anemia mechanisms, small groups work up cases on anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, and anemia of chronic kidney disease. The session emphasizes that anemia of chronic disease rarely drops hemoglobin below 9 g/dL, that iron should not be given unless concomitant iron deficiency is confirmed, and that a normal B12/folate/TSH workup for macrocytic anemia should prompt a peripheral smear to rule out myelodysplastic syndrome. Key pearls include the classic triad of multiple myeloma (hypercalcemia, anemia, elevated creatinine) and the need to supplement iron when giving erythropoietin in CKD.
key_points: Anemia of chronic disease typically does not lower hemoglobin below 9 g/dL; a hemoglobin <9 should trigger a search for another cause.
Do not give iron for anemia of chronic disease unless concomitant iron deficiency anemia is confirmed.
In thalassemia, iron supplementation is harmful because it can cause iron overload; diagnosis requires hemoglobin electrophoresis.
For thalassemia major, pre-transfusion hemoglobin threshold is approximately 5.5 to 10 g/dL.
When macrocytic anemia workup (B12, folate, TSH) is normal, obtain a peripheral blood smear to evaluate for myelodysplastic syndrome.
Myelodysplastic syndrome can transform into acute myeloid leukemia.
The classic triad of multiple myeloma is hypercalcemia, anemia, and elevated creatinine.
In chronic kidney disease with hemoglobin <10, consider erythropoietin therapy, which should be managed with nephrology.
When giving erythropoietin, also supplement iron because EPO depletes iron stores rapidly.
Elevated BUN in CKD shortens RBC lifespan, which can confound the interpretation of BUN in GI bleeding.
Initial workup of new anemia should include a careful history, repeat CBC, reticulocyte count, and direct Coombs test to guide further evaluation cost-effectively.

episodes.title: Man - Theology Thursday with Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter presents a theology lecture on the doctrine of man, covering three main points: man was created in the image of God, man sinned, and as a result man is lost and powerless to save himself. He discusses the meaning of the image of God (substantive, relational, and functional views), the nature and consequences of sin (inherited guilt and corruption), and the inability of sinners to do spiritual good or please God on their own. The lecture emphasizes that while this doctrine is sobering, it highlights the need for grace and makes the gospel of Jesus Christ even more significant.
key_points: Man was created in the image of God, which sets humanity apart from the rest of creation.
Being in God's image can be understood through substantive views (e.g., reason), relational views (interaction with others), and functional views (duties like taking dominion).
Sin is failure to live up to God's moral standard in action, attitude, and inherent nature.
Original sin involved questioning God's truth, God's standard of right, and man's identity as creature rather than Creator.
The consequence of sin is death, both physical and spiritual, and inherited guilt and corruption from Adam.
All people are born sinful and are slaves to sin, unable to do anything that pleases God or to save themselves.
Even outwardly good works done without faith are not spiritually good before God.
The moral standard of God is so high that one sin makes a person guilty of the whole law.
The doctrine of man's lostness highlights the greatness of God's salvation through Jesus Christ.
Dr. Ledbetter agrees with the analogy offered and says the point feels less harsh when framed as an opportunity.
He acknowledges that most attendings in the program do not agree with his position on this topic.
He says that disagreement is acceptable, just like with other topics he discusses.

episodes.title: Medical Education as Missions, Part 1 - Mark Crouch MD in PNG
episodes.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
episodes.abstract: Dr. Mark Crouch describes his journey from US family practice residency to serving as medical education coordinator at Nazarene Hospital in the Papua New Guinea highlands. He explains the blend of clinical work and teaching, the unique rural health master's program, and the integration of medical ministry with evangelism. Challenges include adapting Western training templates to limited resources, balancing clinical overload with education, and shifting institutional attitudes toward training national doctors. Successes include growing trainee numbers, formalizing the program, and having a graduate join the faculty.
key_points: Dr. Crouch left the US in 2014 after family practice residency to serve at Nazarene Hospital in Papua New Guinea.
The hospital runs a general surgery program and a master's of medicine in rural health, a generalist specialty with surgical and unique skills.
Medical education is intentionally coupled with spiritual ministry, including evangelism and discipleship of trainees.
The hospital serves as a referral center for about half a million people with only a few surgeons and general doctors.
Early challenges included imposing a US/Western training template that was unrealistic for the resource-limited setting.
Teaching about advanced diagnostics like fetal fibronectin was impractical; the focus shifted to leveraging existing structures.
Clinical overload often forced teaching by osmosis rather than structured precepting.
Momentum grew from institutional reluctance to embracing training, now with 4-8 trainees at a time.
The master's program is a recognized specialist qualification tailored to rural PNG practice.
Having the first graduate join the faculty is a major success, helping adapt training for future cohorts.

episodes.title: Medical Education as Missions, part 4, Drs. Sasha and Irina
episodes.speaker: Dr. Sasha & Dr. Irina
episodes.abstract: Dr. Sasha and Dr. Irina discuss how medical education in Kazakhstan serves as a vehicle for discipleship and professional development. They describe a three-year residency program that integrates rigorous clinical training with intentional spiritual formation, helping Christian doctors grow in both competence and faith. The program is financially self-sustaining through a profitable clinic, allowing it to continue even if the founding missionaries leave. Graduates emerge as trusted professionals who can share their faith naturally with patients, and exposure to the global Christian medical community broadens their vision.
key_points: Medical education in Kazakhstan addresses low quality of training by pursuing international standards.
The program recruits Christian doctors and combines medical training with intentional discipleship over three years.
Graduates become more solid in medical skills and in their love for God, integrating faith with profession.
Patients gain trust in well-trained doctors, making them more receptive to spiritual conversations.
The clinic is financially self-sufficient and profitable, able to subsidize resident training even without external support.
Residents shadow attending physicians for the first 2-3 months, which graduates identify as the most helpful experience.
A Christian psychologist wrote a three-year spiritual curriculum covering Bible knowledge, missions, and leading Bible studies.
Exposure to the global Christian medical community (e.g., a trip to Thailand) broadens residents' vision of what Christian doctors do worldwide.
The program aims to produce doctors who are stable in faith and able to withstand persecution, with a clear societal role.
The model is reproducible in other contexts, as it mirrors Jesus' method of teaching and living with disciples.
Family medicine allows continuity of care, building trust over time for spiritual conversations.
The program supplements the local church's discipleship, which is often weak in a young Christian community.

episodes.title: Moral Injury
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jim Ritchie
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jim Ritchie defines moral injury as occurring when one commits, participates in, or fails to prevent an act that violates deeply held moral values, distinguishing it from PTSD by its spiritual rather than emotional nature. He explains that moral injury is closely linked to guilt, shame, and betrayal, and is associated with depression, anxiety, relational issues, and increased suicidality. Dr. Ritchie emphasizes that cross-cultural medicine is a 'moral injury factory' because differing cultural values can force clinicians to violate their own deeply held beliefs. He notes that standard treatments like SSRIs and secular psychotherapy are ineffective for moral injury, unlike for PTSD.
key_points: Moral injury is defined as committing, participating in, or failing to prevent an act that violates one's deeply held moral values.
Moral injury is distinct from PTSD: PTSD is an emotional, fear-based response to a life-threatening event, while moral injury is a spiritual struggle involving guilt, shame, and alienation.
Moral injury is strongly associated with betrayal, both betraying someone and being betrayed by a trusted person.
Moral injury correlates with depression, anxiety, relational issues, religious distance, and increased suicidality.
Cross-cultural medicine is a 'moral injury factory' because different cultures have different deeply held values (e.g., value of human life, meaning of birth/death, use of money, decision-making).
Standard treatments for PTSD, SSRIs and secular psychotherapy, do not work for moral injury.
Moral injury exists on a spectrum from moral distress (uncomfortable but not damaging) to full moral injury.
Examples from military, mission field, and medical practice illustrate how moral injury arises in diverse settings.
Clinicians may experience moral injury when their own moral values conflict with those of patients, colleagues, or institutional practices.
Moral injury can occur even within one's own culture when deeply held values differ between individuals.
Moral injury is inevitable in cross-cultural medicine and tends to accumulate like a toxin unless metabolized.
Prevention involves identifying mistaken deeply held moral values that have been mutated from biblical truths.

episodes.title: Morning report (SBP and HRS management) - Dr. Lee
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lawrence Lee leads a morning report on a 50-year-old woman with alcoholic cirrhosis, ascites, and back pain who presents with abdominal distension after missing therapeutic paracentesis. The session emphasizes systematic history-taking (asking 'Is there anything more to the story?'), generating a broad differential for back pain and abdominal distension, and interpreting key labs and imaging. The case highlights the high mortality risk (MELD 35, ~50% 3-month mortality), the importance of recognizing severe hyponatremia (Na 120), and the utility of urine sodium as a marker of kidney perfusion in cirrhosis.
key_points: Always ask 'Is there anything more to the story?' after the patient finishes their initial history to uncover additional details.
Use OPQRST (Old cards) to frame the history for each chief complaint before generating a differential diagnosis.
For back pain in a cirrhotic patient, consider compression fracture, epidural abscess, discitis, AAA, MI, and cancer.
For abdominal distension in cirrhosis, consider SBP, pancreatitis, bowel obstruction, constipation, and anasarca from missed paracentesis.
A MELD score of 35 corresponds to approximately 50% mortality within 3 months from liver disease alone.
Urine sodium <10 mEq/L in cirrhosis indicates effective arterial blood volume depletion and intact renal sodium retention.
Severe hyponatremia is defined as serum sodium ≤120 mEq/L and should be explicitly labeled as such.
Bilirubin in the urine is expected in jaundiced cirrhotic patients and is not a new concern.
The icto test (ictotest) distinguishes bilirubin from myoglobin or other pigments in urine.
Portal hypertension is a key problem in this patient, contributing to ascites and varices.
Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a diagnosis of exclusion; other causes of AKI must be ruled out first.
In liver disease patients, BUN ratio may be skewed and less reliable for distinguishing prerenal AKI.

episodes.title: Morning Report with Dr. Lee
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lee presents a case of a 42-year-old woman who suffered respiratory arrest and was found to be in shock. The discussion emphasizes the critical importance of stabilizing the patient before forming a differential diagnosis, using the post-ROSC mnemonic OV-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V-V (oxygenation, volume status, vasopressors, sugar, acid-base, nutrition, DVT and stress ulcer prophylaxis). The team works through initial ventilator settings, assessment of volume status with physical exam and the straight leg raise test, and the decision to start pressors when the patient remains hypotensive after adequate fluid resuscitation. Norepinephrine is identified as the first-line vasopressor in this setting.
key_points: In a post-cardiac arrest patient, stabilize first (ABCs and critical care) before forming a differential diagnosis.
Use the post-ROSC mnemonic: O (oxygenation), V (volume status), V (vasopressors), V (sugar), V (acid-base), V (nutrition), D and S (DVT and stress ulcer prophylaxis).
Intubate if GCS is less than 8 and the patient cannot protect their airway.
Initial ventilator settings: rate 16 (midpoint of normal 12-20), tidal volume 500-600 mL based on height, FiO2 100% titrated down, PEEP 5, then check ABG in 30 minutes.

Assess volume status with history, physical exam (skin turgor, capillary refill, mucous membranes, JVD, lung exam), and the straight leg raise test (raise leg 45° for 30 seconds; a 10-20% fluid bolus to the heart that raises MAP suggests hypovolemia).
For adult hypovolemic shock, give 30 mL/kg of lactated Ringer's or normal saline as the initial bolus (not 20 mL/kg, which is pediatric).
If MAP remains below 65 after adequate fluid resuscitation, the patient is fluid-refractory and pressors are indicated; continue fluids while starting pressors.
First-line vasopressor for most shock states is norepinephrine (alpha and mild beta effects).
Second-line vasopressor is vasopressin (splanchnic vasoconstriction).
Third- and fourth-line options are dopamine (strong beta, then alpha) and phenylephrine (pure alpha). Epinephrine (strong alpha and beta) is a last resort.
Always communicate a 'status plan' (e.g., 'patient is hypotensive, refractory to adequate fluid resuscitation, therefore we are starting pressors') rather than just stating the plan.
The straight leg raise test is a simple, cost-free bedside tool to assess fluid responsiveness.

episodes.title: Pediatric Development with Dr. Bennett
episodes.speaker: Dr. Bennett
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bennett emphasizes the importance of developmental surveillance in well-child checks to identify children at risk for delays or medical conditions. She illustrates this with a case of a 9-month-old whose weight was trending down and who had decreased crawling, despite a normal milestone checklist. By asking the mother about concerns and observing the child, she discovered truncal ataxia and a full fontanelle, leading to diagnosis of a cerebellar tumor. The talk highlights the need to go beyond checklists, use open-ended questions, and directly observe children to detect subtle regressions or red flags. Dr. Bennett also recommends free CDC milestone booklets as a learning tool and notes that SMA is now on Oklahoma's newborn screening with effective gene therapy if given early.
key_points: Developmental surveillance at every well-child check aims to identify children at risk for delays or disabilities for early intervention.
Milestone checklists are not standardized or validated; direct observation and parent questioning are essential.
Ask parents open-ended questions about worries, problems, or concerns regarding growth, development, or behavior.
Regression of a previously acquired skill (e.g., slower crawling) is a red flag that warrants investigation.
Truncal ataxia in an infant who could sit independently suggests a cerebellar mass until proven otherwise.
A full or bulging fontanelle in an infant requires evaluation for increased intracranial pressure.
Always consider child abuse in an infant with unexplained pain on movement, even without other signs.
Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is included in Oklahoma newborn screening; gene therapy is highly effective if given before irreversible damage.
Free CDC 'Learn the Signs, Act Early' milestone booklets are useful references for learning milestones and for parent education.
Surveillance and screening together are the most efficacious approach to identify children with developmental concerns.
Observation of the child's motor skills (e.g., crawling, sitting) in the office can reveal subtle abnormalities not captured by parent report.

episodes.title: Pediatrics Spiritual Care - Roundtable
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
episodes.abstract: This roundtable discussion focuses on spiritual care for pediatric patients, using case examples to explore how clinicians can address spiritual needs with respect, sensitivity, and permission. The panel discusses consent for spiritual interventions by age and degree, the importance of creating safe spaces for vulnerable patients, and the role of community connections. Practical guidance is offered on asking both child and parent for permission before prayer, recognizing that spiritual care may also extend to family members, and avoiding the pressure to force a 'come to Jesus moment.'
key_points: Spiritual care should be approached with respect, sensitivity, and permission, with consent varying by the degree of intervention (e.g., spiritual history vs. prayer vs. sharing the gospel).
For minors, obtain consent from both the child and the parent before offering prayer or other spiritual interventions.
In the hospital setting where there is no prior relationship, it is especially important to get parental permission before proceeding with spiritual care.
When a parent defers to the child's decision (e.g., 'it's fine if she's okay with it'), that can be taken as permission to proceed.
If a child or parent declines prayer, do not force it; revisit the topic on future visits as trust builds.
Creating a safe space for vulnerable patients to express pain without immediately trying to fix it is a key chaplaincy skill that clinicians can learn from.
Acknowledge to adolescent patients that the therapeutic relationship is time-limited, to avoid inadvertently causing harm when the patient latches onto a temporary safe person.
Connecting patients to community resources (e.g., churches, grandparent groups) can extend support beyond the clinical encounter.
Spiritual care may be directed at the parent or caregiver, not just the patient, especially when the parent is struggling.
A lack of a verbal 'come to Jesus moment' does not mean spiritual care was ineffective; the patient may be experiencing change in their heart without articulating it.
Taking a spiritual history is appropriate for all patients and does not require the same level of consent as more intensive spiritual interventions.
Spiritual care is essential for all pediatric patients, including those with autism or intellectual disabilities.

episodes.title: Pelvic Pain Cases - Dr. Calvert
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert presents five cases of pelvic pain, emphasizing a systematic approach using history details such as onset, location, quality, frequency (cyclic vs. random), duration, radiation, aggravating/relieving factors, and change over time. He demonstrates how careful history-taking can diagnose conditions like endometriosis and adenomyosis without labs or imaging. Key teaching points include distinguishing primary from secondary dysmenorrhea, recognizing that pregnancy can improve endometriosis due to progesterone dominance, and diagnosing adenomyosis by cyclic midline pain with bladder/bowel symptoms. The lecture also covers Bartholin gland cyst management.
key_points: Chronic pelvic pain workup requires at least 6-7 specific history questions: onset, location (one-finger point), quality, frequency (cyclic vs. random), duration, radiation, aggravating/relieving factors, and change over time.
Cyclic pain is associated with menstruation or ovulation and suggests a gynecologic cause.
Primary dysmenorrhea does not change over time; secondary dysmenorrhea worsens over time and may indicate endometriosis or adenomyosis.
Endometriosis often improves during pregnancy due to progesterone dominance suppressing endometrial proliferation.
Endometriosis can be diagnosed 85% of the time by history alone; physical exam may show tender posterior cul-de-sac, decreased uterine mobility, and scar tissue.
Adenomyosis presents with cyclic midline pain, heavy/longer periods, and pain referred to rectum (with bowel movements) and bladder (urinary frequency before menses).
Adenomyosis diagnosis is made by history; MRI or ultrasound can confirm but are not necessary.
Dyspareunia has two types: entrance and deep; deep dyspareunia suggests endometriosis or adenomyosis.
Bartholin gland cyst management: first-line is Word catheter; marsupialization is for recurrence.
Interstitial cystitis presents with chronic pelvic pain, urinary frequency, urgency, and dysuria for >3 months.

episodes.title: Petrochemical Exposures and Health Impacts - Dr. Ella Kuchmiy
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ella Kuchmiy
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ella Kuchmiy presents her research on petrochemical exposures from the Tulsa West Refinery and their potential health impacts on nearby communities. She explains the types of pollutants emitted, including hazardous air pollutants (HAPs), volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and criteria pollutants, and discusses the lack of community-specific monitoring standards. The presentation covers specific chemicals like acrolein, benzene, and hydrogen sulfide, their known health effects, and the challenges of applying workplace exposure limits to ambient air. She highlights that the refinery has been in high-priority violation of the Clean Air Act for 12 quarters, though the specific violations are not publicly detailed.
key_points: The Tulsa West Refinery processes approximately 125,000 barrels per stream day and is a major source of air pollutants.
Hazardous air pollutants (HAPs) include 187 substances known or suspected to cause cancer, reproductive effects, or birth defects.
A major emitting source releases ≥10 tons/year of a single HAP or ≥25 tons/year of multiple HAPs.
The refinery has been in high-priority violation of the Clean Air Act for 12 consecutive quarters (about 3 years), with $67,500 in penalties.
Workplace exposure limits (e.g., ACGIH TLVs) are more conservative than OSHA PELs and are not directly applicable to ambient community air.
Specific pollutants from the refinery include acrolein, ammonia, benzene, cadmium, carbon disulfide, and xylene, each with distinct health effects.
Simple asphyxiants like propylene and ethylene are primarily hazardous in confined spaces, not ambient air.
The refinery's flare burns off 99% of propylene, but flare efficiency degrades over time.
No government air monitoring stations are located near the refinery; the nearest PM2.5 monitor is on the Oklahoma-Arkansas border.
Over 80% of West Tulsa residents surveyed perceived a problem with the refinery, and over 90% felt affected by it.
Simple asphyxiants like propylene and ethylene are dangerous in confined spaces but less so in ambient air.

Water-soluble irritants (ammonia, sulfur oxide) cause upper respiratory symptoms; water-insoluble irritants (nitrogen dioxide, phosgene, ozone) affect lower respiratory tract and can cause noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.

episodes.title: Physician Assisted Suicide - Ledbetter
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter presents a lecture on physician-assisted suicide from a Christian worldview, distinguishing it from nutrition, withdrawal of care, and refusal of care. He reviews major worldviews (naturalistic, pantheistic, biblical) and ethical systems (relativism vs. absolutism) to frame the moral debate. Using a caricature patient, Carl Fredrickson, he explores how different perspectives would approach a request for assisted death. The lecture emphasizes the biblical commandment against killing, the slippery slope observed in jurisdictions like the Netherlands, and the moral distinction between active euthanasia and passive withdrawal of care. Clinical guidance includes managing pain at end of life without intending to kill, invoking the law of double effect.
key_points: Physician-assisted suicide involves active injection or prescription of lethal medication, not withdrawal or refusal of care.
Worldviews (naturalistic, pantheistic, biblical) fundamentally shape ethical conclusions about euthanasia.
Ethical relativism includes subjectivism, conventionalism, situationalism, emotivism, and utilitarianism; absolutism grounds morality in God's unchanging character.
From a biblical perspective, life is sacred because God gives it; killing is prohibited by the sixth commandment and illustrated by David's judgment of the Amalekite who killed Saul.
The Netherlands example demonstrates a slippery slope from strict criteria to legal euthanasia of children.
Insurance companies in some states may cover assisted death but deny life-saving treatment, highlighting a dangerous incentive.
There is a morally significant difference between actively killing a patient and passively allowing them to die.
Pain management at end of life should focus on relieving suffering without the intent to cause death (double effect).
The law of double effect is a key ethical concept for end-of-life care but is not detailed in this lecture.
Ten states and Washington, DC currently legalize physician-assisted suicide; 40 states prohibit it.
Legalization of euthanasia can lead to insurance companies covering death but not life-saving treatment.
The slippery slope argument: right to die can become obligation to die, then involuntary killing.

episodes.title: POCUS with Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter leads a hands-on POCUS workshop using cases from coreultrasound.com. Residents practice identifying ultrasound views, naming three pieces of anatomy, and deciding if findings are normal or abnormal. Cases include a traumatic bladder rupture with free fluid and a massive PE presenting with hypotension and tachycardia. The session emphasizes that even beginners can recognize critical abnormalities like a dilated right ventricle or a D-sign, and encourages using POCUS early in undifferentiated shock.
key_points: For each ultrasound image, identify the view, three pieces of anatomy, and whether it is normal or abnormal.
In the FAST exam, free fluid in the right upper quadrant after trauma indicates intra-abdominal injury requiring surgical evaluation.
A bladder that appears heterogeneous with internal echoes instead of anechoic urine suggests bladder rupture.
The right ventricle should normally be about two-thirds or less the size of the left ventricle; a larger right ventricle indicates increased right-sided pressure.
A D-sign on parasternal short axis (left ventricle appearing D-shaped) is an acute sign of right ventricular pressure overload, often from PE.
In undifferentiated hypotension and tachycardia, POCUS of the heart, lungs, IVC, and legs can rapidly narrow the differential.
A normal-appearing bladder is anechoic; any internal echoes or heterogeneous material is abnormal.
Bowel loops appear hyperechoic with shadowing due to air; non-shadowing hyperechoic structures are more likely fat.
Saving and reviewing your own POCUS clips after confirmatory imaging reinforces learning and builds diagnostic confidence.
Even with limited experience, residents can recognize major abnormalities like a ruptured bladder or massive PE on ultrasound.
Do not diagnose right heart strain if the right ventricular border is not fully visualized.
A hyperdynamic left ventricle appears to collapse completely on itself during systole.

episodes.title: Pressors - Engstrom
episodes.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
episodes.abstract: Dr. Engstrom discusses vasopressor use in emergencies, focusing on epinephrine for anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest, and norepinephrine (Levophed) as the first-line pressor for shock. He emphasizes the danger of IV epinephrine in anaphylaxis, the use of small boluses of epinephrine for patients 'circling the drain,' and the importance of starting Levophed in septic and cardiogenic shock. He also critiques dopamine as a prodrug and clarifies synchronized vs unsynchronized cardioversion.
key_points: Epinephrine dose for anaphylaxis is 0.3, 0.5 mg IM; IV administration of 0.5 mg can cause V-fib.
In cardiac arrest, give 1 mg epinephrine IV every 3, 4 minutes; a maxed drip (200 mcg/min) delivers only 0.2 mg over 60 seconds.
More than 5 doses of epinephrine in a code is associated with worse neurological outcomes.
For a patient circling the drain (about to code), give 50, 100 mcg epinephrine IV push every minute as a bridge to an epi drip.
To dilute code cart epinephrine for small doses, draw 1 mg (1 cc) into 9 cc saline to get 100 mcg/cc; then give 0.5 cc = 50 mcg.
Norepinephrine (Levophed) is the first-line pressor for septic shock; you are never wrong to start it.
In cardiogenic shock, start Levophed first to improve MAP and coronary perfusion; add a beta agent if EF remains poor.
Dopamine is a prodrug that requires functional adrenal glands for conversion; norepinephrine is preferred.
Synchronized cardioversion is used when the patient is alive; unsynchronized defibrillation when the patient is dead.
If you have 5 minutes to think before a code, consider alternative causes (e.g., SVT with hypotension needs cardioversion, not epinephrine).
Norepinephrine (levophed) is the first-line vasopressor in almost all shock scenarios; starting with it is rarely wrong.
Dopamine is a prodrug that requires functional adrenal glands to convert to norepinephrine/epinephrine; direct beta agonists like epinephrine are preferred.

episodes.title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP
episodes.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
episodes.abstract: This lecture provides a primary care-oriented overview of radiation oncology, covering the types of radiation (photons, electrons, protons), delivery techniques (3D conformal, IMRT, SBRT, brachytherapy), and treatment settings (curative, neoadjuvant, adjuvant, palliative). The presenters emphasize the importance of reproducibility and immobilization for accurate treatment, and describe the workflow from consultation to treatment planning. They also highlight that about 40% of their practice is palliative, focused on symptom control with minimal side effects, and that radiation oncology is a multidisciplinary field working with medical and surgical oncology.
key_points: Radiation oncology treats patients across all ages, in both curative and palliative settings, often in combination with surgery and chemotherapy.
The three main types of radiation are photons (with skin-sparing at higher energies), electrons (superficial deposition), and protons (Bragg peak with no exit dose).
Delivery techniques range from simple 3D conformal (urgent cases) to complex IMRT (intensity-modulated radiation therapy) and stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS/SBRT) for high-dose ablation.
Brachytherapy involves placing a radiation source inside the patient, either temporarily or permanently (e.g., prostate seeds).
Radiation can be used neoadjuvantly (before surgery), definitively (as backbone), adjuvantly (after surgery), or for consolidation (e.g., in lymphoma).
Approximately 40% of radiation oncology practice is palliative, aiming for symptom control with short treatment courses and minimal side effects.
Reproducibility of patient positioning within 2-3 mm is critical; immobilization devices like masks or frames are used to ensure accuracy.
Treatment planning uses CT simulation, and plans are verified by dosimetrists, physicists, and radiation oncologists before delivery.
Modern techniques like multi-leaf collimators (MLCs) allow conformal treatment to spare organs at risk, reducing toxicity compared to older methods.
Proton therapy offers a low entrance dose and no exit dose, but its advantages over photons depend on the clinical scenario.
Urgent palliative cases can be simulated and treated the same day, while complex curative plans may take weeks to prepare.
Dose-volume histograms (DVHs) are used to ensure organs at risk (e.g., bladder, rectum, small bowel) stay within safe dose limits.

episodes.title: Rev Joel S. Leitch on Suicide Prevention 5/14/26
episodes.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
episodes.abstract: Rev. Joel S. Leitch presents a lecture on suicide prevention for family medicine residents, emphasizing the role of the clinician as a suicide interventionist rather than a therapist. He covers early warning signs, risk evaluation, and effective referral, stressing that most suicidal people are ambivalent and want to be rescued. Key concepts include the three 'H's (helpless, hopeless, hapless), the episodic nature of suicidal crises, and the importance of taking a compassionate, authoritative stance to guide the patient toward help.
key_points: 95% of people with active suicidal ideation do not truly want to die; they want relief from unbearable suffering.
Suicidal people are often ambivalent and highly suggestible, looking for a strong, authoritative person to direct them.
Clinicians should directly ask about suicide rather than waiting for the patient to bring it up.
Hopelessness is a stronger predictor of suicide risk than depression alone.
Most suicidal episodes are brief (seconds to minutes) and occur only once in a lifetime.
The three 'H's, helpless, hopeless, hapless, are key warning signs to listen for.
A family history of suicide is one of the strongest predictors of suicide risk.
Only about 5% of suicidal individuals are truly determined to die; institutionalization may increase risk in this group.
Suicide rates in jails and psychiatric facilities are 20, 30 times the national average.
Clinicians should kindly and compassionately tell the patient what they must do, rather than asking what they want.
Building hope and reorienting the patient toward the future is critical in the intervention.
The ACE (Adverse Childhood Experiences) score can help identify susceptibility to suicidal thinking.

episodes.title: Rev. Leitch on How Continue to Burn Without Getting Burnt Out 1/8/26
episodes.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
episodes.abstract: Rev. Joel Leitch discusses compassion fatigue and burnout prevention for healthcare workers, emphasizing the importance of recognizing warning signs such as silencing responses, withdrawal, and diminished capacity to listen. He introduces the concept of a 'nonanxious presence', maintaining genuine calm in anxiety-provoking situations, and explains how high anxiety impairs cognitive and motor skills. Practical strategies include being proactive, identifying automatic negative thoughts (ANTs), and practicing intentional thinking to regain control and foster resilience.
key_points: Compassion fatigue can occur even when providing excellent care; patients may not improve despite best efforts.
Burnout prevention should be addressed at both organizational and individual levels.
Major warning signs include silencing response, withdrawal, diminished listening, loss of confidence, and sense of dread.
High levels of anxiety impede cognitive skills, language, motor coordination, and judgment.
A nonanxious presence means staying genuinely calm in potentially anxiety-provoking situations.
Being proactive, planning responses ahead of time, helps maintain control and reduces reactivity.
Automatic negative thoughts (ANTs) can be identified and replaced with intentional, positive thinking.
Self-soothing skills involve cognitive, affective, and behavioral techniques to lower reactivity.
The principle of isomorphism: positive change in one area of life can have a generative effect across other areas.
Practice makes permanence; developing healthy habits through repetition is key to lasting change.
Automatic negative thoughts and behaviors can be addressed through Bible study or devotional reflection on how God helps with those areas.
The principle of isomorphism: affecting change in one area of life has a generative effect across other areas.

episodes.title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention
episodes.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
episodes.abstract: Rev. Joel Leitch discusses the role of hopelessness, helplessness, and haplessness in suicide risk. He emphasizes that active suicidal thinking is often brief, so building even a small amount of hope can be life-saving. He introduces the concept of 'suicidal erosion', a gradual wearing away of coping abilities over years, and highlights that truly determined ('hardcore') suicidal individuals are rare but very difficult to identify. He stresses the importance of asking about family suicide history, especially in children under 5 who lose a parent to suicide, and uses psychological autopsies to illustrate common themes like rejection and chronic pain.
key_points: Hopelessness is a stronger marker for suicide risk than depression alone.
