Active suicidal thinking typically lasts only seconds to minutes, making brief hope-building interventions critical.
Ask about family suicide history, a surviving child under 5 has a 9-fold increased risk of suicide.
Suicidal erosion is a gradual process that can span 10-20 years, not a spontaneous act.
The 'hardcore' suicidal (about 5% of the suicidal population) are extremely hard to identify and may give no warning signs.
Institutionalizing hardcore suicidal patients does not stop them and may worsen outcomes; jails and psychiatric facilities have 20-30 times the national suicide rate.
Hopelessness talk, statements like 'nothing helps' or 'I can't keep living like this', signals high risk.
Suicidal behavior can be copycat behavior, especially among adolescents.
The precipitating event (straw that breaks the camel's back) is rarely the root cause; look for longer-term erosion.
Suicide notes commonly cite rejection, chronic illness, disability, or desire to join a deceased loved one.
Suicide is a form of communication, often a last resort when other channels have failed.
Psychological autopsies of suicide notes reveal common themes: rejection, chronic disability, feeling unheard, and unmet needs.

episodes.title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu
episodes.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
episodes.abstract: Dr. Amanda Lucashu presents a rheumatology framework for primary care, focusing on four types of musculoskeletal pain: inflammatory, tissue injury, nerve injury, and central pain syndromes. She emphasizes history and physical exam over indiscriminate testing, advising against ordering ANA for pain alone due to high false-positive rates. The lecture covers appropriate lab workup (ESR, CRP, CBC, CK, TSH, uric acid) and when to refer to rheumatology, specifically for widespread chronic pain involving more than one joint, especially with elevated inflammatory markers. Dr. Lucashu also discusses managing symptoms while awaiting specialist referral, including NSAIDs, duloxetine, and lifestyle interventions.
key_points: Classify musculoskeletal pain into four categories: inflammatory, tissue injury, nerve injury, and central pain syndromes (e.g., fibromyalgia).
Central pain syndromes last >3 months and involve neurotransmitter changes; they include fibromyalgia, IBS, tension headaches, TMJ, and interstitial cystitis.
Do not order ANA to evaluate pain alone; 30% of normal individuals have false-positive ANA, and it can complicate referrals to pain management or rheumatology.
If ANA is indicated (e.g., malar rash, photosensitivity), order the ANA analyzer which reflexively tests specific antibodies based on pattern.
ESR can be stratified: 30-50 low-grade inflammation, 50-100 moderate, >100 severe; CRP has no such stratification and is less clinically useful for severity.
Rheumatoid factor is helpful if positive (especially in younger patients) but cannot rule out RA if negative; CCP is more specific.
Uric acid should be trended over multiple tests; a single normal level does not rule out gout, and a single elevated level does not confirm it.
Refer to rheumatology for widespread pain involving more than one joint that is chronic (>3 months), especially with elevated ESR or CRP.
Fibromyalgia and inflammatory conditions can coexist; an elevated ESR points toward inflammation but does not rule out fibromyalgia.
While awaiting rheumatology, manage symptoms with NSAIDs, duloxetine, cognitive behavioral therapy, and lifestyle measures; do not start disease-modifying drugs like methotrexate as primary care.
Imaging is unlikely beneficial for widespread pain; reserve for focal tissue injury or nerve injury presentations.
Chronic pain is defined as lasting three months or more, and fibromyalgia can overlap with inflammatory conditions, requiring rheumatology to differentiate.

episodes.title: Sarah Janssen on Anemia Outpatient 12/4/25
episodes.speaker: Sarah Janssen
episodes.abstract: Sarah Janssen discusses outpatient management of iron deficiency anemia, emphasizing higher ferritin targets (above 30, with symptomatic patients above 50, and restless leg or hair loss above 100). She covers oral iron supplementation strategies, including every-other-day dosing to reduce side effects, taking iron with meat for better absorption, and avoiding tea/coffee within an hour. She reviews monitoring (recheck hemoglobin in 2-4 weeks, expect 1 g/dL rise), indications for IV iron (CHF, CKD, IBD, cancer, intolerance or non-response to oral), and differentiation of microcytic and macrocytic anemias using MCV, Mentzer index, and iron studies.
key_points: Target ferritin above 30 ng/mL; if symptomatic, aim above 50; for restless leg or hair loss, aim above 100.
Oral iron should not be dosed BID or TID; once daily or every other day is sufficient and causes fewer GI side effects.
Take oral iron with a meal containing meat (chicken, fish, or lamb) to maximize absorption.
Avoid tea or coffee within one hour before or after taking iron, as tannins inhibit absorption.
Recheck hemoglobin 2-4 weeks after starting oral iron; expect a rise of at least 1 g/dL.
If hemoglobin does not rise in 2-4 weeks, consider IV iron or alternative diagnosis.
IV iron is indicated for patients with CHF, CKD, IBD, cancer, or those who cannot tolerate or do not respond to oral iron.
The Fishbane reaction (non-allergic infusion reaction) is common with IV iron; stop infusion, symptoms resolve, then restart at slower rate, do not give Benadryl.
For microcytic anemia with MCV <70 and elevated RBC count, consider thalassemia trait; Mentzer index <13 suggests thalassemia.
In macrocytic anemia, MCV 100-105 suggests alcohol; MCV >110-115 suggests B12 or folate deficiency.
Normocytic anemia is the broadest category of anemia.
It requires the most work to diagnose.

episodes.title: Security Training
episodes.speaker: Officer Latif
episodes.abstract: Officer Latif presents security training focused on active shooter survival. He emphasizes that mindset and immediate decision-making are critical, and that proximity determines whether to run, hide, or fight. He contrasts hostage situations (95% resolved by negotiation) with active shooter events (0% negotiation) and notes that law enforcement response averages 3, 5 minutes, so individuals must act before help arrives. Latif stresses that pre-incident indicators, especially depression and behavioral changes, are always present, and that reporting suspicious behavior is the most effective way to foil planned attacks.
key_points: Survival mindset and immediate decision-making are critical; without a decision to act, survival chances drop significantly.
Proximity dictates response: far away = run, closer but barricadable = hide, immediate = fight.
Active shooter events have zero chance of negotiation, unlike hostage situations where 95% are resolved through negotiation.
Law enforcement response averages 3, 5 minutes; individuals must have a plan to act before then.
55% of active shooters have a relationship with the worksite, so the attacker is often known.
Pre-incident indicators (depression, behavioral changes, social media posts) are always present before an attack.
Reporting bizarre behavior or social media posts is the most effective way to foil planned attacks.
Active shooters are intelligent and meticulously plan their attacks, often over months.
Law enforcement contains the scene; the suspect controls it.
Active shooters view victims as body counts, not human beings, making compliance pointless.
Active shooters are often calculated and intelligent, not stupid; they plan extensively.
Pre-attack indicators include depression, obsession with violence, avenger mindset, and social media radicalization.

episodes.title: Spiritual Warfare
episodes.speaker: Dr. Jenkins
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jenkins discusses spiritual warfare through the lens of 2 Corinthians 10, focusing on the danger of measuring self-worth by comparing with others or an idealized self. He argues that such self-assessment, whether leading to pride or depression, is based on a false scale and reflects a lack of understanding of one's identity in God. Using Paul's response to the 'super apostles' and Jesus' temptations, he emphasizes finding identity not in accomplishments but in God's declaration of us as His children.
key_points: Measuring yourself by comparing to others leads either to pride (arrogance) or depression (wounded pride), both of which are forms of the same false scale.
Feeling bad about yourself is not humility; it is wounded pride or a thwarted ego that would choose to be number one if possible.
Paul refused to defend himself by comparing his eloquence or accomplishments to the false apostles; he went to the heart: they measure by a wrong standard and are without understanding.
Those who compare themselves to others do not know who they are in God's eyes, do not know God's values, and cannot properly love others.
We also sin by comparing ourselves to our theoretical ideal self, leading to regret, self-reproach, anger at God, and despondency.
We cannot accurately judge ourselves or others by human comparison; only the Lord can evaluate motives and give true praise.
Satan tempted Jesus by attacking his identity ('If you are the Son of God'), tempting Him to doubt or prove it by misusing power; Jesus relied on God's proclamation at His baptism.
The same identity attack comes to believers: 'Are you really a child of God?' The temptation is to try to prove it through accomplishments or testing God.
True identity comes from faith in Christ and being led by the Spirit, not from accomplishments, effort, or comparisons.
Living by your identity as a child of God is an act of faith, not performance.
Paul instructs to 'examine yourselves to see if you're in the faith,' not to compare with others.
Jesus answered the high priest's question about being the Son of God with a clear 'Yes,' accepting the cross rather than denying His identity.

episodes.title: The Condies on Surgery
episodes.speaker: The Condies
episodes.abstract: Dr. Angela Condie, a pediatrician, and Dr. John Condie, a surgeon, present a lecture on infectious diseases encountered in South Asia, based on their experience working in rural Pakistan. They organize cases by clinical presentation (hematologic, neurologic) and highlight key diseases including dengue, malaria, measles, neonatal tetanus, polio, and rabies. The presentation emphasizes diagnostic pearls, treatment considerations specific to resource-limited settings, and the importance of vaccination and public health surveillance.
key_points: Dengue, Zika, and chikungunya present similarly with fever and rash; Zika has more conjunctivitis and chikungunya more arthralgias.
Dengue fever can progress to severe disease with capillary leak, pleural effusion, ascites, and hypovolemic shock when the fever subsides.
In children with dengue, avoid aspirin and NSAIDs due to risk of Reye syndrome.
Malaria (falciparum) is chloroquine-resistant and should be treated with artemether-lumefantrine; presumptive treatment for fever is standard in endemic areas.
Measles is diagnosed by Koplik spots (white lacy spots on a red base) and the classic triad of cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis.
Measles causes transient T-cell lymphopenia and increased infection-related mortality for up to three years after infection.
Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare fatal complication of measles, occurring 5, 10 years after infection, more often in children under 1 year.
Neonatal tetanus presents with poor feeding, increased tone, and a characteristic smile (risus sardonicus), often due to unclean cord care and incomplete maternal vaccination.
Polio causes acute flaccid paralysis that is asymmetric, proximal more than distal, with normal sensation, unlike Guillain-Barré which is symmetric, distal, and painful.
Oral polio vaccine (OPV) induces mucosal immunity and prevents transmission, but can revert to circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus in under-immunized populations.
Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis requires risk assessment; in high-endemic areas, pre-exposure vaccination is practical for those at risk of delayed access to immune globulin.
Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis requires both vaccine and immune globulin for unvaccinated individuals; pre-exposure vaccination simplifies management to a two-dose series.

episodes.title: The Ethics of Contraception - Dr. Lisa Gilbert
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lisa Gilbert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lisa Gilbert presents a lecture on the ethics of contraception from a Christian perspective, acknowledging personal biases and the potential for strong feelings on the topic. She reviews the historical Christian stance against contraception from early church fathers through the 1930 Lambeth Conference, which first allowed limited exceptions. The talk explores foundational questions about the purpose of medicine, whether fertility and pregnancy are diseases, and how contraception fits into a covenantal, Hippocratic tradition. She sets up premises for discussion, including that human life begins at fertilization and that sexual relations are designed for union and procreation within marriage.
key_points: Medicine is a covenantal moral calling, not a contractual transaction, rooted in the Hippocratic tradition of doing no harm and not giving abortive remedies.
Fertility and pregnancy are not diseases but functions of a healthy reproductive system, which challenges the assumption that contraception is always a medical good.
Human life begins at fertilization or conception and is endowed with the life of God from that point.
Scripture does not directly address contraception but emphasizes marriage as a symbol of Christ and the church, with children as blessings.
The sin of Onan (withdrawal) is the only possible scriptural reference to contraception, interpreted by early and later church leaders as forbidding it.
All major Christian traditions (Catholic, Orthodox, early Protestant) rejected contraception until 1930.
The 1930 Lambeth Conference of the Anglican Church was the first Christian body to allow contraception under certain moral obligations, not for selfishness or convenience.
The early church fathers, such as Saint Augustine and Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, taught that sex is for procreation and that contraception opposes natural and divine law.
The presenter's views do not represent her academic affiliation or the American Association of Pro Life OBGYNs.
The talk will cover the science of contraception, the principle of double effect, and practical considerations for mission hospitals.

The 1930 Lambeth Conference marked the first major Protestant acceptance of contraception, but only when there is a 'clearly felt moral obligation' to limit parenthood and not from selfishness or convenience.

The 1968 Catholic encyclical Humanae Vitae predicted four consequences of widespread contraception: increased infidelity, less respect for women, government coercion over fertility, and viewing bodies as machines.

episodes.title: Thyroid Disorders - Dr. Amanda Lucashu, DO
episodes.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
episodes.abstract: Dr. Amanda Lucashu presents a case-based lecture on hypothyroidism for family medicine residents. She reviews the differential diagnosis for fatigue, highlights key review of systems and physical exam findings, and discusses the diagnostic approach using TSH and free T4. The lecture covers initial levothyroxine dosing, titration, follow-up intervals, and special considerations in pregnancy, including dose adjustments and trimester-specific TSH targets. She also addresses common pitfalls such as medication interactions, overcorrection risks, and when to consider alternative diagnoses.
key_points: Hypothyroidism review of systems includes fatigue, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, weight gain, hair loss, and increased menstrual flow.
Physical exam may show delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes, bradycardia, thyroid enlargement, and myxedema.
Drugs that can elevate TSH include metoclopramide, lithium, amiodarone, and antipsychotics.
Hypothyroidism can cause secondary lab abnormalities like hypercholesterolemia, hyponatremia, and anemia, but these are not routinely checked.
For routine hypothyroidism, treat based on TSH and free T4 without ordering thyroid antibodies.
Start levothyroxine at 25-50 mcg daily; elderly start low, healthy patients can start higher.
Repeat TSH in 4-6 weeks after dose changes; once stable, follow every 6-12 months.
Goal TSH is toward the higher end of the normal range to avoid overcorrection, which can cause angina, atrial fibrillation, and osteoporosis.
T3 is not recommended due to rapid absorption and short half-life; T4 allows physiologic conversion.
In pregnancy, increase levothyroxine by 30-50% and target a lower TSH to prevent congenital hypothyroidism; use trimester-specific reference ranges.
If levothyroxine dose reaches 200 mcg with persistent symptoms, check for medication interactions, adherence, and consider other diagnoses.
In pregnancy, increase levothyroxine dose by 30-50% and target the lower end of the trimester-specific TSH range to prevent congenital hypothyroidism.

episodes.title: Trauma Informed Care
episodes.speaker: Sara Gadd
episodes.abstract: Sara Gadd, the human trafficking program manager, explains why health care settings are uniquely positioned to identify victims of human trafficking, who often present repeatedly with issues like suicide attempts, overdoses, and miscarriages. She describes how trafficking in Oklahoma frequently starts within the family, with biological mothers sometimes involved, and contrasts common media portrayals with the reality of coercion for labor or sex acts. The talk covers red flags such as inconsistent stories, delayed care, branding tattoos, and third-party control of documents, and emphasizes the importance of getting patients out of waiting rooms quickly to reduce risk. An advocate helps identified victims with long-term needs like housing and job placement.
key_points: Health care workers are in a unique position to identify trafficking victims because victims rarely disclose to police or first responders.
Trafficking does not require movement across borders; it can involve coercion for labor or sex acts within a family or relationship.
In Oklahoma, trafficking often starts within the family, including biological mothers exploiting their own children.
Victims frequently present in the ED with repeated suicide attempts, overdoses, substance use, pregnancy, or miscarriage.

Red flags include delay in seeking medical care, inconsistent stories, fear/anxiety in waiting rooms, extensive psych/substance history, branding tattoos the patient won't discuss, and third-party control of documents.
Getting suspected victims out of the waiting room quickly is critical because traffickers may search waiting areas.
An advocate is needed to help with long-term needs like transitional housing, job placement, and relocation.
Survivors report that no one ever asked them about trafficking during health care visits.
Trafficking of minors under 18 involving any commercial sex act is automatically human trafficking.
The program has offered resources to over 300 suspected victims in five years.
Victims of human trafficking often delay seeking medical care because traffickers control their access.
Inconsistent stories, fear, and anxiety in waiting rooms are common red flags.

episodes.title: Tuberculosis - Kyle Jones, DO
episodes.speaker: Dr. Kyle Jones
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kyle Jones presents a case-based review of pulmonary tuberculosis, covering latent vs. active disease, epidemiology, risk factors, diagnostic testing, and treatment. He emphasizes the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion in patients with risk factors such as foreign birth, immunosuppression, and smoking. The talk highlights key differences between TST and IGRA, the role of directly observed therapy, and the management of drug-susceptible TB with a four-drug regimen.
key_points: Latent TB infection affects an estimated 9.5 million people in the US and about one in four people worldwide.
TB is the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, surpassing HIV.
Only 10% of individuals with latent TB will progress to active disease over their lifetime, with highest risk in the first two years after infection.
HIV co-infection dramatically increases risk: annual risk of active TB is 8-10% in HIV-positive individuals.
IGRA (interferon gamma release assay) is preferred over TST in patients with BCG vaccination history.
False negative results occur in 20-25% of patients with active TB; these tests should not be used alone to exclude disease.
TST interpretation: 15 mm is positive for all patients; 5 mm for immunocompromised (e.g., HIV); 10 mm for other high-risk groups.
Standard treatment for active TB: 2 months of four-drug therapy (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) followed by 4-7 months of rifampin and isoniazid.
Directly observed therapy (DOT) is standard for active TB, typically 5 days per week initially.
Ethambutol can cause decreased visual acuity; monitor during therapy.
Patients on TNF-alpha antagonists (e.g., Humira) should be screened for latent TB before starting therapy.
Sputum AFB cultures and GeneXpert are key diagnostic tests; GeneXpert can also provide drug susceptibility information.

episodes.title: Two Cases with Dr. Lawrence Lee
episodes.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lawrence Lee leads a case-based session on abdominal pain, emphasizing systematic history-taking and differential diagnosis. He teaches to let patients speak without interruption for five minutes, use OPQRST, and ask about associated symptoms while considering differentials. The case of a 42-year-old with epigastric pain and vomiting evolves from a brief history to a longer timeline, ultimately diagnosed as acute pancreatitis. The presenter reviews causes of pancreatitis, gallstones, alcohol, medications, hypertriglyceridemia, autoimmune disease, malignancy, infection, and trauma, and stresses not to miss abdominal aortic aneurysm in insidious-onset pain.
key_points: Let the patient talk without interruption for at least 5 minutes before asking direct questions.
After the patient finishes, ask 'Is there anything else?' to ensure you have the full story.
Use OPQRST to systematically gather details of the pain.
While taking OPQRST, think about your differential diagnosis and ask about pertinent associated symptoms.
For insidious onset abdominal pain, consider abdominal aortic aneurysm; ultrasound is the preferred initial imaging.
Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed with lipase >3x upper limit; initial workup includes CMP, lipase, and RUQ ultrasound for gallstones.
Common causes of pancreatitis include gallstones, alcohol, medications, hypertriglyceridemia, autoimmune disease, malignancy, infection, and trauma.
Check a lipid panel to evaluate for hypertriglyceridemia as a cause of pancreatitis.
Consider medication-induced pancreatitis; ask about all current medications.
If malignancy is suspected as cause of pancreatitis, consider endoscopic ultrasound (EUS).
Supportive care (IV fluids, analgesics, antiemetics) is the mainstay of acute pancreatitis management.
Antibiotics are only indicated for necrotizing pancreatitis (>30% necrosis) or pancreatic abscess.

pearls.text: A CAM boot only removes about 25% of the pressure; for complete offloading use a knee walker ($100 on Amazon) or crutches with heel ambulation.
pearls.verbatim: It only removes about 25% of the pressure, but it sometimes is enough.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.applies_to: patients with forefoot or midfoot wounds
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Grafts are often used as a practice management tool because they bring in thousands of dollars per application; only consider a graft if the patient is compliant with offloading, nutrition, and glucose control and still not healing, or if they have a condition like steroid use.
pearls.verbatim: Grafts are often used as a practice management thing for the clinic to the point where millions of dollars come in to practices for grafts.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: Check shoe fit in patients with fungal toenails; shoes that are too small cause nail trauma and worsen the condition.
pearls.verbatim: Check their shoe fits because if they're wearing too small shoes, nothing's gonna help because they're grinding their nails against the inside of the shoe.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls

pearls.text: To expedite a behavioral health referral, walk the demographic sheet, face sheet, and completed referral sheet to the behavioral health team; they will put it at the top of the pile and may start working with the patient 2-3 weeks before receiving their name on the email list.
pearls.verbatim: you can print out the demographic sheet, the face sheet and the referral sheet that you complete, and send it back to us. Walk it back to us. And we will take it and put it on the top of the pile.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: residents referring patients to behavioral health
pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.text: Psychologists are the only ones typically trained to administer and interpret standardized cognitive and personality tests (e.g., MMPI, PAI, Rorschach); mid-level providers may administer but cannot interpret them.
pearls.verbatim: Or they may administer them but can't score and interpret them.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.text: Neuropsychologists are typically called upon when there is a deficit, change, or injury (e.g., TBI, dementia, chronic illness) to measure specific cognitive functions for life adaptation or prognosis.
pearls.verbatim: Neuropsychologists are typically called upon if there's a deficit or a change or an injury, and we wanna measure specific cognitive functions in order to make recommendations for life adaptation or prognosis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with cognitive changes from injury or illness
pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.text: For patients stable on ADHD medication, advise them to plan ahead for possible future school accommodations because the wait for a comprehensive assessment is 9, 12 months.
pearls.verbatim: if they ever need accommodations for school, they might wanna think ahead. In Tulsa right now, to get this or this to the degree required for schools is a nine to twelve month wait.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with ADHD on medication who may need accommodations later
pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.text: In Tulsa, wait times for comprehensive assessments (neuropsych or psychoeducational) required for schools are 9 to 12 months, so refer early.
pearls.verbatim: In Tulsa right now, to get this or this to the degree required for schools is a nine to twelve month wait.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients needing school-related assessments in Tulsa
pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.text: Primary care can perform an abbreviated ADHD assessment but cannot do a full assessment; refer patients who need comprehensive evaluation.
pearls.verbatim: So I'm saying to them, I can diagnose you to the degree that most med folks with our abbreviated assessment. I could do a full ADHD assessment, but we don't do them here.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.text: For deterioration, change, or autism concerns, refer directly to neuropsychology; specific clinics like the Griffin Clinic in Broken Arrow offer ADHD/autism screening services.
pearls.verbatim: you can send them directly to neuropsych if it's deterioration change, autism special... Well, there are some new Griffin here in Broken Arrow, the Griffin Clinic. Also, there's a specific young ADHD or autism screening service available in Tulsa.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.text: Do not send patients to a psychiatrist for cognitive functioning assessment; they do not perform that. Refer to neuropsychology instead.
pearls.verbatim: If you're sending someone for assessment, we don't send them to a psychiatrist if it's for, like, cognitive functioning. Mhmm. They don't do that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.text: Non-fasting lipid panels are acceptable for LDL measurement; only repeat fasting if triglycerides exceed 400.
pearls.verbatim: It shouldn't grossly affect your LDL, which is the main one we're looking at. So AAP recommends as long as adults get their triglycerides over 400, then all of sudden, you gotta make a comeback.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Herrmann
pearls.episode_title: Cardiovascular Risk& Reduction

pearls.text: For LDL over 190 mg/dL, evaluate for familial hypercholesterolemia using Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria; a score >8 is diagnostic even without genetic testing.
pearls.verbatim: What you can do is you can do the Dutch Lipid Clinic Network diagnostic criteria for familial hypercholesterolemia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Herrmann
pearls.episode_title: Cardiovascular Risk& Reduction

pearls.text: Smoking cessation is more effective than any medication for reducing cardiovascular risk; actively prescribe therapy (Wellbutrin, Chantix, patches, gum) rather than just advising to quit.
pearls.verbatim: Don't just say you should quit. You know? Do something about it. Your chances of quitting are much lower if you start on on medication and really motivate them. So do something about it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Herrmann
pearls.episode_title: Cardiovascular Risk& Reduction

pearls.text: For ASCVD risk 10-20%, start moderate-dose statin; for >20%, start high-dose statin; for <10%, lifestyle modification alone.
pearls.verbatim: less than ten percent ASCVD risk score, lifestyle modifications, ten to twenty percent, moderate dose statins. That's like atorvastatin. Twenty percent higher. Additionally, this is... These guidelines here is based on USPSTF.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Herrmann
pearls.episode_title: Cardiovascular Risk& Reduction

pearls.text: When starting a statin, recheck lipids at 6 weeks, then annually; routine monitoring of LFTs and CK is not indicated.
pearls.verbatim: Up to date recommend liver panel and TSH prior to starting. We check lipids at six weeks and then every year thereafter. Key monitoring of LFTs and creatinine kinase are not actually indicated.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Herrmann
pearls.episode_title: Cardiovascular Risk& Reduction

pearls.text: ASCVD risk score does not include obesity, family history, LDL level, or chronic kidney disease; these are additional risk factors to consider.
pearls.verbatim: We didn't put type in their weight when we calculated the risk score. So good. Metabolic syndrome and obesity. Family history. Right? I didn't type in a family history. That puts someone at higher risk.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Herrmann
pearls.applies_to: adults being assessed for cardiovascular risk
pearls.episode_title: Cardiovascular Risk& Reduction

pearls.text: Statins can increase blood sugar and may push prediabetic patients over the threshold for diabetes diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: It can increase your blood sugars. There are... As a... Will increase your risk of being diagnosed by death... Of diabetes. So those people that are on the threshold who are already almost gonna get diagnosed with diabetes, or some could bump you up close enough to hit that 6.5.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Herrmann
pearls.applies_to: patients on statins, especially those near diabetes threshold
pearls.episode_title: Cardiovascular Risk& Reduction

pearls.text: Providers should practice nonjudgmental care and not take it personally when patients do not follow advice; it is okay to feel frustrated but do not take it out on the patient.
pearls.verbatim: I would really take it to heart when when people would come to me and solicit my advice and then not do what I say. It's like, well, why did you why did you waste my time? ... The Lord has really taught me to practice nonjudgment ... Learning how to detach and not take things personally.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Carroll
pearls.episode_title: Care for the un-homed with Dr. Carroll

pearls.text: Basal cell carcinoma can metastasize, contrary to the common teaching that it never does; Dr. Carroll has seen at least four cases, most commonly going through the skull.
pearls.verbatim: You guys ever hear the basal cell carcinoma never metastasizes? Oh, it never, never, never metastasizes. It does. I've seen at least four in my in my time with good Sam. Yep. ... Them going through their skulls is probably the most common.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Carroll
pearls.episode_title: Care for the un-homed with Dr. Carroll

pearls.text: In unhoused patients, you will see advanced stages of diseases that would normally be caught early, including advanced skin cancers, lung cancers, colon cancers, and necrotic breast cancer.
pearls.verbatim: advanced stages of diseases that would normally be caught and taken care of, you will see a of lots of lots of skin, lots of lung cancers, lots of malignancies because people don't get their their colonoscopies or lots of advanced breast, necrotic breast cancer, seeing a lot of that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Carroll
pearls.episode_title: Care for the un-homed with Dr. Carroll

pearls.text: In unhoused patients, you will see advanced stages of skin, lung, and breast cancers because they do not get routine screenings like colonoscopies.
pearls.verbatim: advanced stages of diseases that would normally be caught and taken care of, you will see a of lots of lots of skin, lots of lung cancers, lots of malignancies because people don't get their their colonoscopies or lots of advanced breast, necrotic breast cancer.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Carroll
pearls.episode_title: Care for the un-homed with Dr. Carroll

pearls.text: Do not blame patients for dietary choices when they have limited options; focus on what you can control, such as insulin dosing.
pearls.verbatim: I don't beat them up for things that are outside of their window.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Carroll
pearls.episode_title: Care for the un-homed with Dr. Carroll

pearls.text: For diabetics with A1C over 8, consider referring to programs that provide fresh produce and cooking classes, as many patients lack basic cooking skills.
pearls.verbatim: crossover clinic in North Tulsa has a program where any of my diabetics on the North Side that have an A1C over eight, they'll sign them up for fresh produce and cooking classes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Carroll
pearls.applies_to: diabetics with A1C >8 in North Tulsa
pearls.episode_title: Care for the un-homed with Dr. Carroll

pearls.text: If a patient's request is reasonable (e.g., lotion for feet), even if you suspect secondary gain, consider giving it because you never know.
pearls.verbatim: if it's reasonable, even if I suspect it, a lot of times, I'll give it to because who knows?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Carroll
pearls.episode_title: Care for the un-homed with Dr. Carroll

pearls.text: For patients with controlled symptoms and no exacerbations, short-acting bronchodilators are fine for symptom relief but do not reduce exacerbations or improve FEV1.
pearls.verbatim: people that have controlled symptoms and they really haven't had any exacerbations, it's okay to use short acting medicines. They help. They're not going to help anything long term. They don't necessarily decrease exacerbations
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients with controlled symptoms and no exacerbations
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: For uncontrolled symptoms without exacerbations, start a LAMA; LAMAs work better for exacerbations than LABAs.
pearls.verbatim: you can do a LABA or a LAMA. Just do a LAMA. Just just make it easy. Don't don't don't think about it. Unless there's a reason that people can't afford a LAMA, which would just be ridiculous to me, just do a LAMA because
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients with uncontrolled symptoms but few exacerbations
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: If a patient is already on a LAMA and has controlled symptoms but exacerbations, you can skip the LABA/LAMA step and consider adding ICS, especially if eosinophils are high.
pearls.verbatim: we're better than LABAs, I just said. So you would use a LAMA. But if you're already on a LAMA, you can skip that step.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients on LAMA with exacerbations
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: For uncontrolled symptoms with frequent exacerbations, you can start either LABA/LAMA or LABA/LAMA/ICS; the choice depends on exacerbation severity and eosinophil count.
pearls.verbatim: You can do a LABA and a LAMA combo, or you can just jump to the LABA LAMA ICS.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients with uncontrolled symptoms and frequent exacerbations
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: If a patient has symptoms but no exacerbations, do not advance to triple therapy (e.g., Trelegy) just because of symptoms; reconsider the diagnosis and check inhaler technique.
pearls.verbatim: You're not advancing to Trelegy just because somebody's having exacerbations. This is where you really need to think, like, is this the right diagnosis?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients with symptoms but no exacerbations
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: If a patient on a LAMA has exacerbations and elevated eosinophils on CBC, consider adding ICS (e.g., LABA/ICS) because eosinophilia suggests a reactive process.
pearls.verbatim: If somebody... If you check the the CBC and their eosinophils are pretty high, that fits more with, a reactive picture. And they probably do better on an ICS,
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients with exacerbations and elevated eosinophils
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: If a patient on triple therapy (e.g., Trelegy) still has exacerbations, consider roflumilast (Daliresp) for those with FEV1 <50% and chronic bronchitis.
pearls.verbatim: That is for people with severe COPD where you're... Remember the gold a or gold one, two, three, four? That's for people that are three or more. So if your FEV1 is low and you have chronic bronchitis, valerus would probably be a good addition
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients with severe disease (GOLD 3-4) and chronic bronchitis on triple therapy
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: After inhaling from a dry powder inhaler, hold your breath for ten seconds or as long as you can.
pearls.verbatim: And you hold your breath for ten seconds or as long as you can.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients using dry powder inhalers
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: If a patient struggles with dry powder inhalers due to inability to breathe fast, consider switching to a soft mist inhaler like Respimat.
pearls.verbatim: But this is when I tried to switch that guy to. So
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients unable to use dry powder inhalers effectively
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: Respimat devices may require prior authorization because they are often more expensive than dry powder inhalers; use this option when a patient cannot use a DPI.
pearls.verbatim: The problem is that, you know, it may not necessarily be covered by insurance. So they should be, especially if you can do a prior auth if, like, this patient just can't use your other inhalers.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients who cannot use dry powder inhalers
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: For Respimat inhalers, you do not need to breathe in quickly; use a slow, steady inhalation after pressing the dose button.
pearls.verbatim: Slow breaths. You don't have to, like, breathe in quickly when you're doing this one. Slow breaths. Hold it for ten seconds or as long as you can.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: For Ellipta inhalers, opening the cap loads a dose; do not shake or exhale into the device, as it can blow the powder away.
pearls.verbatim: So the way these work, guys, is when you have the elliptis, you open the cap, the dose is ready. So don't have a patient, like, face it and take a deep breath in and out because they might. There's a little powder in there, and they could blow it everywhere.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: Use a spacer with MDIs: one puff at a time, inhale deeply, hold breath for 10 seconds, then wait 15, 20 seconds before the next puff.
pearls.verbatim: You're supposed to just do one puff at a time. Deep breath in. Hold it for ten seconds or as long as you can. Breathe out away from the device. And then if you need another one, wait fifteen, twenty seconds, and then do it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients using metered-dose inhalers with a spacer
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: One puff at a time with spacer; do not put two puffs in and take six breaths.
pearls.verbatim: You're supposed to just do one puff at a time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: Inhaler technique: deep breath in, hold 10 seconds, exhale away from device; wait 15, 20 seconds before next puff.
pearls.verbatim: Deep breath in. Hold it for ten seconds or as long as you can. Breathe out away from the device. And then if you need another one, wait fifteen, twenty seconds, and then do it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: Use a spacer with MDI to reduce mouth deposition.
pearls.verbatim: Symbicort is kinda nice because it's a metered dose inhaler. If they use a spacer, they're not gonna have as much deposition in their mouth.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: ICS increase pneumonia risk; do not add ICS without a clear indication.
pearls.verbatim: They increase the risk of pneumonia. So that's why we don't just jump to Trelegy every time because people can get pneumonia more frequently.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with COPD being considered for ICS-containing therapy
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: Never use ICS monotherapy (e.g., fluticasone alone) in COPD; always combine with a LABA.
pearls.verbatim: don't ever put somebody on COPD with, like, Flovent or something. It's just ICS... Don't do that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: Refer COPD patients with persistent symptoms or any exacerbations (GOLD B or D) to pulmonary rehabilitation.
pearls.verbatim: Pulmonary rehab. When should I refer my patients if they're in group b, or d? So that's basically everybody that has persistent symptoms or any kind of exacerbations should be in pulmonary rehab.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with COPD GOLD groups B or D
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: Screen all patients with COPD at least once for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (WHO recommendation).
pearls.verbatim: Often want antitrypsin deficiency. So WHO recommends screening all people with COPD at least once.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: Long-term oxygen therapy reduces mortality when resting SpO2 <88% on room air (or PaO2 <55 mmHg); titrate to keep SpO2 ≥90% (88, 92% goal).
pearls.verbatim: Oxygen therapy. So it does prevent mortality in people that are severely hypoxic. So that's people that are less than eighty eight percent on remeron. Right? For those, if you happen to get an ABG, it's less than fifty five. Those are the kind of people that it's gonna prevent mortality. And then you want the oxygen to be greater than or equal to 90. There's always like this 88 to 92 goal to 90.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with COPD and severe resting hypoxemia
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: Add azithromycin for exacerbations in patients who are not currently smoking (does not have to be former smoker).
pearls.verbatim: You can add azithromycin to that in people that are former smokers... it doesn't have to be former smokers necessarily, just people that aren't smoking currently.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with COPD on triple therapy who continue to have exacerbations and are not currently smoking
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: Use the COPD Pocket Consult app for inhaler demonstration videos and treatment algorithms.
pearls.verbatim: The COPD pocket consult guide is an app on your phone. It has cool videos... inhaler education... treatment guidelines.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: Ask about dyspnea on level ground and exacerbation history to guide therapy adjustment.
pearls.verbatim: get short of breath on a level ground. You, your friends, work faster than you. Symptoms. Ask about symptoms. What's the other thing you're gonna ask? Any exacerbations.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with COPD during follow-up visits
pearls.episode_title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney

pearls.text: The three stages of COVID-19 infection: stage 1 is respiratory infection symptoms; stage 2 is pulmonary phase with pneumonia; stage 3 is hyperinflammatory response with cytokine storm, ARDS, sepsis, and organ failure.
pearls.verbatim: in terms of of the stage one, this is nothing more than due to a respiratory infection, and you're seeing the the characteristics there. You're seeing the characteristics of a respiratory infection. You go to the stage two, which you all well know... Which you all are well aware of in terms of now you got the pulmonary phase. You've got the pneumonia. And you go on over to the stage three, you get into... Oh god. You get into, of course, the the... You get into the hyperinflammatory response, acute respiratory disease syndrome. You start getting the sepsis. You get the kidney. You get the organ. You get the organ failure. That's really due to the reaction of the immune system. You're getting the cytokine storm, which are causing a tremendous amount of inflation... Inflammation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller
pearls.episode_title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD

pearls.text: Order the anti-spike antibody test, not the nucleocapsid test, as the primary test to assess a patient's immune response to COVID vaccine or infection.
pearls.verbatim: the test you need to order is order the anti spike.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller
pearls.applies_to: patients being evaluated for immune response to COVID vaccine or infection
pearls.episode_title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD

pearls.text: Fourteen days after vaccination, you can check the antibody response to see what kind of response the patient generated.
pearls.verbatim: Fourteen days after vaccination, you can take a look and see what kind of a response you got.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller
pearls.episode_title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD

pearls.text: When ordering a nucleocapsid antibody, always order a spike antibody along with it, especially for breakthrough infections, because a negative nucleocapsid alone can mislead you.
pearls.verbatim: And so if... So my one point is if you order nucleocapsid antibody protein, you order... Always order a spike along with it. Okay? Because a lot of folks are doing that, and it seems to be working out well with them, particularly on these breakthrough infections.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller
pearls.episode_title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD

pearls.text: Vaccine-induced antibody titers decrease by about 40% per month; use a half-life of 1-2 months (approximately 1.5 months) to estimate a patient's titer decline.
pearls.verbatim: about their half-life on their antibody was somewhere one... It was from one to two months. So I always calculate about a month and a half. A month and a half, you can divide it by two. Another month and a half, you can divide it by two. Another month and a half, you divide it by two
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller
pearls.episode_title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD

pearls.text: Natural infection-induced antibodies decrease by about 4% per month, with a half-life of about 6-7 months.
pearls.verbatim: the SARS-CoV-2 infected patients, and they're diminishing at four percent each passing month.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller
pearls.episode_title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD

pearls.text: When a patient asks what to do about their antibody titer (e.g., 92, 1,000, 2,000), you can calculate the expected decline: for vaccine-induced, halve every 1.5 months; for natural infection, 4% per month.
pearls.verbatim: hey. I've got a value of 1,000, 2,000, or I got a value of 92. What do you think I should do? We're gonna try giving you some numbers here in a minute. But that's the kind of questions you're getting that you need to be able to answer, but yet you can calculate out on these these infections here.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller
pearls.applies_to: any patient with an antibody titer result
pearls.episode_title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD

pearls.text: After a patient with prior natural infection has been vaccinated with one dose, wait six months and then check an antibody titer to guide further management.
pearls.verbatim: what you do on these patients is that you wait about six months. You wait six months, and you go back in, and you do a titer.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller
pearls.applies_to: patients with prior COVID-19 infection who received one vaccine dose
pearls.episode_title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD

pearls.text: Patients with breakthrough infection after vaccination will have very high antibody titers, in the tens of thousands to over 100,000; manage similarly to those with prior infection plus vaccination, and check titer at six months.
pearls.verbatim: These individuals have breakthrough infections. They have horrendous titers again. You're gonna be shocked when you see the titer. In fact, I'm not gonna be surprised you call me and say, hey. You made a mistake here, because that's gonna be in the tens of thousands, not a 100, over a 100,000. Okay? And so here again... The question goes again. .. I'm gonna say come back in six months and take a look and see what your titer is.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller
pearls.applies_to: patients with breakthrough infection after vaccination
pearls.episode_title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD

pearls.text: If a patient's titer is 500, you can back-calculate using the 40% monthly decline: one month ago it was ~1000, two months ago ~2000, etc., indicating good memory cell response.
pearls.verbatim: We can go backwards. So they were at 500. So three three months ago or thirty days ago, they were at a thousand.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller
pearls.applies_to: patients with known spike antibody titer
pearls.episode_title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD

pearls.text: Order SARS-CoV-2 IgG spike antibody test, not the nucleocapsid antibody test, to assess vaccine-induced immunity.
pearls.verbatim: Don't send me a SARS-CoV-2 IgG. I want you to order a spike.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gerald C. Miller

pearls.text: The culture of powering through sleep deprivation is dangerous; reaching out for help should not be seen as a sign of weakness.
pearls.verbatim: I think that there is this culture that's been built up that powering through is somehow like a badge of honor or a sign of courage or bravery or, like, hard work, resilience, really, it's just stupidity. Right? It's being dangerous to ourselves and to our patients.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: Signs of sleep deprivation appear in order: first decreased vigilance, then memory, cognitive function, mood, and last gross motor performance.
pearls.verbatim: But some of those signs and symptoms, decreased vigilance, memory, cognitive function, mood, and gross motor performance is the last. So these are kind of in order from the first affected to the least... To the last affected.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: Avoid food, alcohol, and caffeine before bed; if not asleep within 30 minutes, get out of bed and do something else.
pearls.verbatim: Having minimal to no food before sleep. So Liz is saying, like, have your dinner, but don't be eating right before going to sleep. ... Avoiding alcohol and caffeine before bed. ... And then getting out of bed and doing something else if not asleep within thirty minutes for the specific things.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: View caffeine as a medicine, not a food; use it when most fatigued, and avoid it before sleep and after naps.
pearls.verbatim: But they said view it as a medicine, not as a food. Avoid it before sleep and after naps. And then use it when most fatigued.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: Even 10 minutes of exercise can improve alertness and reduce the need for caffeine.
pearls.verbatim: I did, like, ten minutes of exercise one morning before clinic just at home. Yeah. I hadn't done that in a long time, and I I didn't need coffee all the way through AA, which was a big difference.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: Strategic naps of 10-45 minutes increase alertness and decrease errors; 1-2 hour naps may cause sleep inertia, and 4-5 hour naps are ineffective.
pearls.verbatim: Naps, ten to forty five minutes seems to be kind of a sweet spot for naps, which is great because when you're on call, you probably don't have longer than that anyway. And it can increase alertness and decrease errors. One to two hour naps, they said, may be effective, but could also lead to sleep inertia where you just get so tired that it's kinda hard going again. And then longer naps, four to five hours, tend to be ineffective.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: Set a 45-minute alarm when napping on call to avoid sleep inertia; even if you want to sleep longer, waking after 45 minutes may leave you more alert.
pearls.verbatim: it might be more effective to actually set that forty five minute alarm even if it's not a phase waking us up so that we don't have that sleep inertia where now we are actually a little bit feel tired or more tired.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: Do not compare your sleep deprivation to others; if you are sleep deprived, intervene regardless of how tired others seem.
pearls.verbatim: we can't compare our amount of sleep deprivation to somebody else's. It's not comparable. We just have to be willing to say, hey. I'm sleep deprived, or if you're sleep deprived, we need to do something to intervene.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: Batching pages and respecting sign-out times (e.g., no pages until 5 AM unless emergency) can give residents larger uninterrupted rest gaps.
pearls.verbatim: Some hospitals will bunch pages or have respected sign out times where they only will page if there's an emergency, those types of things that can sometimes give you larger gaps to be able to rest.

pearls.text: In a diabetic patient with unilateral swelling and redness, do not assume cellulitis; get an X-ray to rule out Charcot neuroarthropathy (dislocating foot).

pearls.applies_to: diabetic patients with unilateral foot swelling and redness

pearls.text: ABI is unreliable in diabetics due to arterial hardening (false normal). Use toe-brachial index or TCOM (TcPO2) for vascular assessment.

pearls.text: All foot abscesses, septic joints, gas noticed on X-ray, or crepitus on palpation of the foot are surgical emergencies that require immediate surgical consultation.
pearls.verbatim: all foot abscesses, septic joints, gas noticed on X-ray, or if you push on a foot or try to milk a wound and it's, like, crackly, crepitation on soft tissue, that's a surgical emergency.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Beasley on Diabetic Foot Disease

pearls.text: For a digital block, use a maximum of 5-6 cc of bupivacaine (Marcaine).
pearls.verbatim: Five to six cc's max is all you need. I usually use Marcaine, like, percent Marcaine or bupivacaine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Beasley on Diabetic Foot Disease

pearls.text: For toenail avulsion, use a freer elevator to free the nail and yank it off; no incisions are needed.
pearls.verbatim: just free up the nail with a freer elevator and yank it off.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Beasley on Diabetic Foot Disease

pearls.text: Avoid phenol ablation for ingrown toenails in patients with uncontrolled diabetes; the nail should be removed without chemical matrixectomy until glucose control is achieved.
pearls.verbatim: If there phenol versus I'm a controlled diabetic, I wouldn't. Like, I had that today. I'm like, hey. You gotta get this under control before I'm gonna burn you with the acid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Beasley on Diabetic Foot Disease

pearls.text: Do not use epinephrine in digital blocks for patients with known or suspected peripheral arterial disease or diabetes.
pearls.verbatim: I think if they have known PAD or any suspicion of, you know, arterial disease or diabetes, I wouldn't do it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Beasley on Diabetic Foot Disease

pearls.text: Do not use epinephrine with lidocaine in patients with known PAD, suspicion of arterial disease, or diabetes.
pearls.verbatim: I think if they have known PAD or any suspicion of, you know, arterial disease or diabetes, I wouldn't do it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.applies_to: patients with known PAD, suspicion of arterial disease, or diabetes
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Beasley on Diabetic Foot Disease

pearls.text: To prevent retained tourniquets during toe procedures, avoid roll-on ring tourniquets; instead, use a long elastic strip with a hemostat attached that remains visible.
pearls.verbatim: I I usually use a a long elastic strip, and it's dangling with a hemostat attached. And I'm not gonna forget that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Beasley on Diabetic Foot Disease

pearls.text: When using a digital tourniquet, use a long elastic strip dangling with a hemostat attached so it is not forgotten under dressings.
pearls.verbatim: I usually use a a long elastic strip, and it's dangling with a hemostat attached. And I'm not gonna forget that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Beasley on Diabetic Foot Disease

pearls.text: Do not remove a toenail solely for nail fungus; it should be reserved for ingrown toenails causing pain, drainage, or repeated wounds.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Brad Beasley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Beasley on Diabetic Foot Disease

pearls.text: Always ask patients with suspected hematemesis if they drank red Gatorade; several patients have been admitted to ICU for what was actually red Gatorade emesis.
pearls.verbatim: Do you have any red gatorade? In my career, I've had at least two patients that got admitted almost to the ICU, one did it to the ICU, and drank red Gatorade.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns

pearls.text: For upper GI bleed in cirrhotic patients, always call ICU first even if the patient seems stable.
pearls.verbatim: if I was in your shoes, there was an upper GI bleed patient that he or wants to try to admit, I always ask the ICU first, especially if they have cirrhosis or varices.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: cirrhotic patients with upper GI bleed
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns

pearls.text: In upper GI bleed without cirrhosis or varices, patients often have more time for workup and can stay on the floor.
pearls.verbatim: They're just upper GI bleed and they don't have that history, then it's probably not like a variceal bleed. They probably have a little more time to work them up, keep them on the floor.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: upper GI bleed without cirrhosis or varices
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns

pearls.text: For first-time pancreatitis, check a lipid panel to rule out hypertriglyceridemia; if positive, high-dose insulin drip can help resolve pancreatitis faster.
pearls.verbatim: Check their lipid panel. Make sure they're not hypertriglyceridemia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns

pearls.text: In pancreatitis with very high triglycerides (thousands) and AKI or other end-organ damage, consider dialysis catheter and plasmapheresis.
pearls.verbatim: one thing that we can do in the in the unit is put in a dialysis catheter in them and then do plasmapheresis on those high triglyceride patients. Very, very high, and they also need to have AKI or other sign of end organ damage.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: pancreatitis with severe hypertriglyceridemia and end-organ damage
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns

pearls.text: Early enteral feeding in pancreatitis protects the mucosal barrier and reduces bacterial translocation; do not withhold oral intake.
pearls.verbatim: So early enteral feeding is thought to protect the mucosal barrier and reduce bacterial translocation. So that's why we do the enteral feeding.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns

pearls.text: If pancreatitis is not improving after 48-72 hours and the patient is becoming more bloated, call surgery to evaluate for abdominal compartment syndrome.
pearls.verbatim: If after about forty eight to seventy two hours, they're not getting it better, actually getting more bloated, that's when you usually call surgery team to evaluate for abdominal compartment syndrome.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns

pearls.text: A ureteral stone >1 cm requires urgent urology consultation regardless of obstruction.
pearls.verbatim: Clotids and obstruction matters more than anything else. If it's greater than one centimeter, you need urgent urology consultation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns

pearls.text: When you see a bad CT finding like pneumatosis or tumor, don't leave it for the surgeon to break the news; be honest with the patient and prep them.
pearls.verbatim: Don't make the surgeons the bad guys here. Be honest with your patients even if you know what's going on.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns

pearls.text: When you see a bad CT, start preparing the patient early by saying something like 'I don't think the CT is looking good' rather than waiting for the surgeon to deliver the news.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: residents delivering bad news to patients
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns

pearls.text: When risks of surgery outweigh benefits (e.g., poor wound healing, multiple repeat operations), prioritize quality of time and have honest discussions about comfort care.
pearls.verbatim: we want we want our patients to get better, their loved ones to stay with us. But at some point, the risks don't outweigh the benefits.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: patients with poor prognosis and high surgical risk
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns

pearls.text: Absolute contraindications to BiPAP include GCS less than 7, vomiting, facial trauma, cardiac arrest, and airway obstruction.
pearls.verbatim: Those are absolute ones. Facial trauma, vomiting, cardiac arrest. Obviously, you're not gonna put a vitamin and for airway obstruction. Those are your absolute, absolute contraindications.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: patients being considered for noninvasive ventilation
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Distress in Adults

pearls.text: If a patient on BiPAP does not improve after two adjustments and repeat blood gas, escalate care by calling ICU.
pearls.verbatim: I usually give it two chances. Adjust it. Get a gas, adjust it again. If I fail that, then we need to step up therapy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Distress in Adults

pearls.text: Advance care planning conversations should start in clinic, ideally early in adulthood, to avoid difficult decisions at 2 AM.
pearls.verbatim: as directed, this starts in clinic. It can start 20 years old, 30 years old. It doesn't matter. Have that conversation. It's a difficult hard to have it. Much easier to have it in clinic.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: all adult patients in outpatient setting
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Distress in Adults

pearls.text: Non-rebreather masks can deliver up to 95% oxygen; if a patient is hypoxic, ensure the mask is on the patient, not on the floor.
pearls.verbatim: But even non rebreathers can give you an oxygen level up to 95%.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Rapids, ICU Criteria 8/27/26

pearls.text: Albumin is not more effective than crystalloid if the patient's albumin level is between 3 and 4; only give albumin when the albumin is under 3.
pearls.verbatim: patients who have the albumin between three and four doesn't really help. It's it's no more different than giving some fluids. So if you're under three, that's that's when you usually give albumin.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: hypotensive patients with ESRD or low albumin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Rapids, ICU Criteria 8/27/26

pearls.text: For chronic atrial fibrillation in patients with COPD and heart disease who are on baseline rate control and have heart rates in the 120s, 140s, calling EP will likely yield the same advice: give beta blockers and see them in the morning.
pearls.verbatim: They might still be in the one twenties, one thirties, one forties. If you call EP, they'll say the same thing I will. Are they fine? Give them beta blockers. I'll see them in the morning.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: patients with chronic AFib, COPD, and heart disease who are stable
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Rapids, ICU Criteria 8/27/26

pearls.text: Stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response (rates 120s-140s) is often difficult to treat; beta blockers or amiodarone can be tried, but if the patient is stable, it is acceptable to call EP and continue management in the morning.
pearls.verbatim: If you call EP, they'll say the same thing I will. Are they fine? Give them beta blockers. I'll see them in the morning.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Rapids, ICU Criteria 8/27/26

pearls.text: For refractory atrial fibrillation in complex patients (COPD, heart disease), try to treat it; if you cannot, get AP (advanced practice provider or attending).
pearls.verbatim: And the best best thing to do sometimes is try to treat it. And if you can't treat it, get AP.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: patients with refractory AFib and comorbidities
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Rapids, ICU Criteria 8/27/26

pearls.text: Ensure the designated healthcare proxy is aware of the patient's wishes and is aligned; otherwise, a proxy who has not seen the patient in months may override the patient's wishes and demand full care.
pearls.verbatim: make sure that the family is on the same page too. Because if they elect their son or daughter who they haven't seen in months or years in their their health care proxy to come to the hospital, you've had conversations where they didn't want rest of care, but then they are unable to make those decisions, and it falls onto their health care proxy. And I say, oh, no. They they want everything done.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: patients with advance directives and a designated healthcare proxy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Rapids, ICU Criteria 8/27/26

pearls.text: Re-check code status and advance directives at every hospitalization and daily on rounds to ensure they match the chart and the patient's current wishes.
pearls.verbatim: every time they get hospitalized, just make sure check the code status on... Or the advance directive that they have that. Make sure that's in line with with the... With whatever seen on the chart.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Rapids, ICU Criteria 8/27/26

pearls.text: Reframe success in critical care: your goal is to ensure the patient isn't suffering and that their goals of care are addressed; if they pass comfortably, that is a win.
pearls.verbatim: my goal isn't to keep the map goal over or whatever or heart beating. My goal is to make sure the patient isn't suffering. If I try to keep every patient alive, I'm gonna have a zero percent success rate.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Bhakta
pearls.applies_to: all patients, especially those at end of life
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bhakta on Rapids, ICU Criteria 8/27/26

pearls.text: Preconception counseling should include CBC and ferritin for women with menorrhagia or short interpregnancy intervals to identify and treat anemia before pregnancy.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bothwell on Anemia of Pregnancy

pearls.text: In pregnant patients with sickle cell disease on hydroxyurea, stop the hydroxyurea as soon as possible because it is teratogenic, and manage symptoms.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Bothwell on Anemia of Pregnancy

pearls.text: For pregnant patients with sickle cell disease, increase folate supplementation to 4 mg daily due to high red blood cell turnover.
pearls.verbatim: And the folate requirement is actually four milligrams daily instead of just the one because they have such of a high red blood cell turnover, higher than average.

pearls.applies_to: pregnant women with sickle cell disease

pearls.text: In the second or third trimester, if hemoglobin is less than 10 and ferritin is less than 30, consider IV iron and repeat labs 4 weeks after last dose.

pearls.text: Avoid whole life insurance; the first year's premium (often $30,000 to $50,000) goes entirely to the broker, and the cash value at 20 years is less than what you put in.

pearls.text: A common rule of thumb is to buy life insurance coverage of 25 times your annual household expenses, which is the same multiple used for the 4% safe withdrawal rate in retirement.

pearls.text: Live like a resident for the first few years as an attending; do not buy an expensive house immediately because 50% of physicians change jobs within the first three years.

pearls.text: Estrogen therapy in natal males may paradoxically decrease bone density, increasing osteoporosis risk.
pearls.verbatim: Can increase osteoporosis in both men and women. Weird. Right? Because estrogen hormone replacement therapy that we don't try to do is in 2005. Don't try to do that just for bone mineral. That's... You got women who really are on it. Really have tons of bone. Why that's the case when you give estrogen to men, it makes their bone thinner?

pearls.verbatim: And she said, well, what should I do? Right? And she wanted to be on it a little longer. And so which time she wanted to get pregnant, and then she wanted to come off it. And I said, if you really wanna get pregnant, you may wanna come off it now.

pearls.verbatim: Overall, suicide attempts doubled after vaginoplasty. And phalloplasty did not reduce the risk of suicide.
