pearls.episode_title: Dr. Christine Liu on Gender Affirming Care

pearls.text: A 2011 Swedish study reported a 19-fold increase in completed suicide among post-surgery trans individuals compared to the general population at 10 years.
pearls.verbatim: completed suicide rate, nineteen times of the general population at ten years out.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Christine Liu
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Christine Liu on Gender Affirming Care

pearls.text: A patient with acute painless unilateral lower extremity weakness without sensory loss should be evaluated for stroke, not a spinal cause, because spinal pathology typically produces associated sensory loss.
pearls.verbatim: This is an acute ischemic stroke. This patient is experiencing painless weakness of the lower extremity without sensory loss. That's an important distinction that you're gonna see in these strokes. If you have problem with the lumbar spine or in the spinal cord, you're gonna see sensory loss associated with that area.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Christopher Abdo
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Christopher Abdo on Approach to Lower Extremity Weakness 2.19.26

pearls.text: A disabling stroke (even with a low NIHSS of 2, 3) should be treated with thrombolysis; the minor stroke criteria for dual antiplatelet therapy (NIHSS < 4) only apply if the deficit is not disabling.
pearls.verbatim: Events reflects to get... Events reflects dual antiplatelet therapy is superior for minor stroke. NIH less than four. Right? So minor stroke is different than disabling. This guy can't walk. This is a disabling stroke even though his NIH is gonna be, like, a three... A two or three.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Christopher Abdo
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Christopher Abdo on Approach to Lower Extremity Weakness 2.19.26

pearls.text: Acute spinal cord injury presents with complete flaccidity (spinal shock), not hypertonia; hypertonia and hyperreflexia develop later.
pearls.verbatim: Do you guys remember what we said on that first... Like, that third slide? Right? What can acute CNS injury present with? Complete placidity.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Christopher Abdo
pearls.applies_to: patients with acute spinal cord injury
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Christopher Abdo on Approach to Lower Extremity Weakness 2.19.26

pearls.text: Most spinal cord infarctions occur between T8 and L2, the territory of the artery of Adamkiewicz, because this region has limited collateral blood supply.
pearls.verbatim: The artery of Adamkowitz is the primary supply of thoracic cord between T8 and L2. Most spinal cord infarctions who go... Occur in this area due to lack of blood, which is typically supplied by your anterior ventricular arteries.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Christopher Abdo
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Christopher Abdo on Approach to Lower Extremity Weakness 2.19.26

pearls.text: Performing plasma exchange (or any procedure that causes fluid shifts) in a patient with spinal cord infarction can worsen ischemia.
pearls.verbatim: The overnight resident, when they signed this patient out to me, set up plasma exchange for this patient because he thought she had. Right? What happens if you pull all the fluid out of somebody who's having a stroke? Not good. Not good. You're gonna cause fluid shift, volume shift. You may make your ischemia worse.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Christopher Abdo
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected spinal cord infarction versus inflammatory myelopathy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Christopher Abdo on Approach to Lower Extremity Weakness 2.19.26

pearls.text: In spinal cord infarction, plasma exchange can worsen ischemia by causing fluid shift; correct localization prevents this harm.
pearls.verbatim: What happens if you pull all the fluid out of somebody who's having a stroke? Not not good. Not good. You're gonna cause fluid shift, volume shift. You may make your ischemia worse.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Christopher Abdo
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected spinal cord infarction
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Christopher Abdo on Approach to Lower Extremity Weakness 2.19.26

pearls.text: IVIG and plasma exchange are equivalent long-term for GBS; plasma exchange may give quicker improvement.
pearls.verbatim: A and B are equivalent long term. Right? These patients are gonna do a little bit better. In some clinical trials, they show... It does show kinda give a quicker onset of improvement after plasma exchange versus intravenous immunoglobulin.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Christopher Abdo
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Christopher Abdo on Approach to Lower Extremity Weakness 2.19.26

pearls.text: To assess measles risk, check vaccination coverage: one dose of measles vaccine provides about 95% protection, two doses about 98%.
pearls.verbatim: One of the best ways to assess measles is to look at vaccination rate. You know, if if a child has one vax... One dose of measles vaccine, what's their likelihood of protection? Ninety percent. About ninety five percent. You know, if they've had two doses, it's like ninety eight percent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Comninellis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Comninellis on Tropical Fever 6/4/26

pearls.text: The tourniquet test for dengue: inflate a BP cuff above diastolic but below systolic pressure so blood enters the extremity but cannot leave; petechiae indicate a positive test, which is specific for dengue.
pearls.verbatim: Tourniquet test, you put a blood pressure cuff on the extremity. You pump it up above the diastolic but below the systolic. So blood gets into the extremity but can't get out, increasing capillary pressure. And so if the person has a bleeding tendency then they will break out in petechiae. And the tourniquet test is is clearly specific for dengue fever.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Comninellis
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected dengue in low-resource settings
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Comninellis on Tropical Fever 6/4/26

pearls.text: Scrofula (posterior cervical adenitis) is the most common extrapulmonary presentation of tuberculosis, especially in children; always palpate for cervical nodes in a febrile child.
pearls.verbatim: What is the most common extrapulmonary presentation of tuberculosis? ... Scrofula. Remember that word from pathology class? So it's actually posterior cervical adenitis. Most common presentation of extraculmonary TB, especially kids.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Comninellis
pearls.applies_to: children with fever of unknown origin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Comninellis on Tropical Fever 6/4/26

pearls.text: Rose spots on the chest in typhoid fever are erythematous, slightly tender lesions representing septic emboli; typhoid is a systemic disease that can affect any organ including skin, cerebellum, lungs, or heart.
pearls.verbatim: Erythematous, slightly tender lesions across the chest. Acute febrile illness. This is another classic. ... These are called rose spots. ... these erythematous lesions on the chest actually represent septic emboli within the skin because it's a systemic disease.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Comninellis
pearls.applies_to: patients with acute febrile illness in areas with unsafe water
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Comninellis on Tropical Fever 6/4/26

pearls.text: Leprosy is difficult to acquire; almost all cases occur in family members of a leper after years of exposure, so do not eliminate it from the differential in endemic areas.
pearls.verbatim: Leprosy is... It's actually very difficult to get leprosy. Almost everybody who has leprosy is a family member of a leper, and and they've been exposed to the to the infectious agent for years, and then they acquire the the disease.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Comninellis
pearls.applies_to: patients in leprosy-endemic regions with anesthetic skin patches
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Comninellis on Tropical Fever 6/4/26

pearls.text: In acute fever (<2 weeks) with negative malaria test and high WBC, suspect bacterial causes like abscess, sepsis, or liver abscess.
pearls.verbatim: Now if it's less than two weeks and your malaria smear is negative and they have a high white count, chances are this is something that's plagiogenic. It's bacterial. And so you're gonna be looking at at joints, abscesses, at liver abscess.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Comninellis
pearls.applies_to: patients with acute fever in low-resource settings
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Comninellis on Tropical Fever 6/4/26

pearls.text: Fever >2 weeks with neutropenia suggests HIV, advanced tuberculosis, dengue, or viral hemorrhagic fevers.
pearls.verbatim: Fever for more than two weeks, neutropenia. So we're gonna look for HIV, advanced tuberculosis, as well as dengue and and those viral anhydragic fevers, which usually suppress the white count.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Comninellis
pearls.applies_to: patients with prolonged fever in tropical regions
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Comninellis on Tropical Fever 6/4/26

pearls.text: Use 'person living with HIV' to reduce stigma and humanize the diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: A person living with HIV is very in vogue when I write a grant, and I'm trying to get money for the clinic.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: Avoid labeling patients as 'noncompliant'; consider the social determinants that make adherence difficult, such as poverty, abuse, and lack of support.
pearls.verbatim: This woman got HIV because her husband is a dirtbag and beats her, potentially rapes her, has given her four children, and does nothing to help her. She doesn't have a job. And we're gonna say... We're gonna call her noncompliant. I'm not.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.applies_to: clinicians caring for patients with HIV, especially in resource-limited settings
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: Taking ART immediately after a needle stick reduces the transmission risk to about 0.01%.
pearls.verbatim: And if you take ART immediately following that, which I've done about three times in my life after needle sticks, what does the percentage go down to? K. Zero zero one. Yeah. It's, like, 0.01 or 0.00.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.applies_to: health workers with hollow needle stick exposure to HIV-positive source
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: For PCP pneumonia in an HIV patient with hypoxia (O2 sat below 92%), treat with Bactrim and add steroids.
pearls.verbatim: Bactrim. If they're hypoxic, below 92%. What else do you add to the Bactrim? Steroids.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.applies_to: HIV patients with PCP and hypoxia
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: Sputum positivity for TB determines transmissibility; the GeneXpert PCR test can give results in about 40 minutes.
pearls.verbatim: the sputum positivity is the thing that determines transmissibility for TB.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.applies_to: patients suspected of active pulmonary TB
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: An HIV patient with pleural effusion who is sick enough to be hospitalized should have the effusion tapped to evaluate for TB, unless platelet count is severely low.
pearls.verbatim: Person living with HIV, pleural effusion. They're sick enough to be in the hospital. You should probably tap it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.applies_to: hospitalized HIV patients with pleural effusion
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: In an HIV patient with odynophagia without an obvious alternative cause, treat empirically for candidal esophagitis with fluconazole 100 mg once daily for 14 days.
pearls.verbatim: In my setting, we do fluconazole hundred milligrams once a day for fourteen days.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: In HIV patients with diarrhea, ask about blood in stool (dysentery suggests Shigella or other invasive pathogens), greasy stool (Giardia), and visible worms (treat with albendazole).
pearls.verbatim: if you have a person living with HIV and diarrhea, you should ask the blood in stool. And if they do, something is ulcerating
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: For an HIV patient with headache, fever, and seizures, start empiric ceftriaxone and malaria medicine while awaiting workup.
pearls.verbatim: I say meningitis because I don't know what it is, but you're getting ceftriaxone and malaria medicine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.applies_to: HIV patients with headache, fever, and seizures
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: Live attenuated vaccines (e.g., MMR, varicella, oral polio) are generally contraindicated in people with HIV, especially if severely immunocompromised.
pearls.verbatim: blank vaccines are contraindicated in people living with HIV.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.applies_to: HIV patients, especially with low CD4
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: Screen for anal cancer in people with HIV using an anal pap, a physical and rectal exam, or endoscopy biopsy, the exact method is still under study, but screening should be done in some fashion.
pearls.verbatim: I'll do a anal pap. ... Some people say do an anal pap. Some people say do a physical and a rectal exam.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: In patients on ART, avoid simvastatin and lovastatin; atorvastatin is safe.
pearls.verbatim: simvastatin. Yep. And starts with an l. lovastatin.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.applies_to: people living with HIV on ART
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: People living with HIV taking ART should not use hemoglobin A1c to screen or diagnose diabetes; it is unreliable.
pearls.verbatim: For people living with HIV taking ART, this should not be used to screen or diagnose diabetes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.applies_to: people living with HIV on ART
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: Tenofovir can cause acute kidney injury and irreversible kidney damage; avoid it in chronic kidney disease. If creatinine rises, consult the HIV provider to switch to abacavir.
pearls.verbatim: tenofovir can cause acute kidney injury. It can cause some forms of kidney damage that are irreversible if not detected. And so somebody with chronic kidney disease, you wanna try to avoid it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.applies_to: people living with HIV with chronic kidney disease or dehydration
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: Screening for osteoporosis in men with HIV should start at age 50; in women, at menopause.
pearls.verbatim: So it's fifty for men. So men with HIV routinely screen them for osteoporosis at age 50. And for women, it's at menopause.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Mark Crouch
pearls.applies_to: men with HIV (age 50) and women with HIV (at menopause)
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25

pearls.text: Always couple any knee injection with exercise and rehabilitation to address tight quadriceps, hamstrings, and calves, and to strengthen the joint.
pearls.verbatim: I always couple any injection I'm doing with exercise of some sort to rehab the joint streamed up as much as possible.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cunningham
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cunningham on Osteoarthritis of the Knee 5/21/26

pearls.text: Viscosupplementation must be placed in the joint to be effective; use ultrasound guidance because the thick fluid is painful if injected outside the joint.
pearls.verbatim: Because if I don't get this in the joint, it's gonna be completely worthless. And, actually, it's gonna be painful because it's more thick.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cunningham
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cunningham on Osteoarthritis of the Knee 5/21/26

pearls.text: Adipose tissue injections (often called stem cells) cost about $5,200 and have a 60-70% success rate; they do not regrow cartilage and are not covered by insurance.
pearls.verbatim: And in my clinic, it's $5,200 injection. Okay? So it's not cheap. And, again, the success rate is not as close to a hundred percent as I'd like it for $5,200.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cunningham
pearls.applies_to: patients considering adipose tissue injection for knee osteoarthritis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cunningham on Osteoarthritis of the Knee 5/21/26

pearls.text: When performing a knee injection, if the patient feels pain, you likely missed the joint space and hit the fat pad or femoral condyle; proper placement should not hurt.
pearls.verbatim: And it shouldn't really hurt if you get in that joint capsule. If they're having pain, you probably missed.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cunningham
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cunningham on Osteoarthritis of the Knee 5/21/26

pearls.text: Use a 22-gauge 1.5-inch needle for knee injections; if you go too straight you'll hit the femoral condyle, if too angled you'll hit the fat pad, both causing pain.
pearls.verbatim: Usually use, like, a 22 gauge? I use a 22 gauge one and a half needle.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cunningham
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cunningham on Osteoarthritis of the Knee 5/21/26

pearls.text: For knee injection without effusion, use ultrasound; the joint space will appear large on ultrasound, allowing easy needle placement.
pearls.verbatim: if you have a super small fusion, you don't feel confident doing it, this degrees with ultrasound because that that space right there will be huge, and you'll be able to pop that needle in there.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cunningham
pearls.applies_to: patients with small or no knee effusion
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cunningham on Osteoarthritis of the Knee 5/21/26

pearls.text: After steroid injection, advise patients to take it easy for a day or two but no strict activity restriction; avoid heavy squats.
pearls.verbatim: I usually tell them take it easy for a day or two. Okay. But I don't I don't limit them too much, and I want You don't need me on weight, man. I I just... One of my patients has asked me that the other day. You know? Like, usually, I I just told them that. I said I just don't do any, like, heavy squats or anything.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cunningham
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cunningham on Osteoarthritis of the Knee 5/21/26

pearls.text: After a steroid injection for knee arthritis, tell patients to take it easy for a day or two, but do not heavily restrict activity; avoid heavy squats.
pearls.verbatim: I usually tell them take it easy for a day or two. Okay. But I don't I don't limit them too much, and I want You don't need me on weight, man. I I just... One of my patients has asked me that the other day. You know? Like, usually, I I just told them that. I said I just don't do any, like, heavy squats or anything.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cunningham
pearls.applies_to: patients receiving steroid injection for knee arthritis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cunningham on Osteoarthritis of the Knee 5/21/26

pearls.text: Medial offloading braces have data behind them, but many patients do not tolerate them because they put pressure on the outside of the knee.
pearls.verbatim: That's a good... I thought that's a good point. Yeah. So there's some piece of data behind medial offloaded braces. The problem is...
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cunningham
pearls.applies_to: patients with medial compartment knee arthritis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cunningham on Osteoarthritis of the Knee 5/21/26

pearls.text: Lung volume reduction surgery may improve FEV1 by a few hundred cc's but is not a cure; consider for upper lobe predominant emphysema.
pearls.verbatim: If they had upper lobe predominant emphysema, they would be more of a candidate to do that because those areas of lung tissue, of course, when they get those bulla, they're not participating in gas exchange. Right? So it's just dead space. And the theory is if you take that out, then the good lung tissue is able to expand into that remaining cavity, and you get better ventilation and oxygenation. The benefit clinically in the spirometry after a lung volume reduction surgery, though, is not night and day. So they may pick up a few 100 cc's in their FEV1s or forced vital capacities. It's not the fix.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: patients with upper lobe predominant emphysema being considered for surgery
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For severe COPD (FEV1 30-50%) or recurrent exacerbations, add an inhaled corticosteroid (triple therapy) to keep patients out of the hospital.
pearls.verbatim: When you get into the more severe category, so folks with an FEV one between thirty and fifty percent, then you start talking about adding in your inhaled corticosteroid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: patients with severe COPD (GOLD stage 3) or recurrent exacerbations
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For home use, prescribe albuterol inhaler (2 puffs q4h PRN) when away from home, and albuterol/ipratropium nebulized treatments (q4h PRN) when at home; use one or the other, not both at the same time.
pearls.verbatim: So the way I write the prescription is I'll say, as needed, albuterol inhaler, two puffs every four hours for shortness of breath when they're away from home. And then I'll list out albuterol and ipratropium nebulized treatments every four hours as needed if they're at home. So one or the other, not both at the same time. Right? Up to every four hours.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients with moderate to severe disease
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Inhaled corticosteroids increase pneumonia risk; if a patient on triple therapy develops recurrent lower respiratory tract infections or pneumonia, stop the inhaled steroid.
pearls.verbatim: If they start having recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, I gotta take it off. Right? Because it increases the risk of pneumonia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients on inhaled corticosteroids who develop recurrent LRTIs or pneumonia
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For patients with dexterity issues (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis with ulnar deviation, trach patients), prescribe nebulized treatments instead of inhalers.
pearls.verbatim: We all have patients who have difficulty doing things with their hands. Right? So... And not only that, you may have a patient who has a trach who can't do a inhaler, so they have to do nebulized treatments. And I I do have, you know, folks who have rheumatoid arthritis with the ulnar deviation that just simply cannot turn and push an inhaler.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: patients with dexterity limitations or tracheostomy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Always watch patients use their inhaler; poor technique (e.g., inability to coordinate actuation) is a common reason for treatment failure, and a spacer may help but patients rarely carry one.
pearls.verbatim: So it is worthwhile to actually watch them do it if you have the samples in your office.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Pulmonary rehabilitation improves FEV1 and lung function as much as starting another pharmaceutical, and it addresses the deconditioning spiral.
pearls.verbatim: the pulmonary rehab is actually improving FEV1s and lung function just as much as starting another pharmaceutical.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients, especially those hospitalized with exacerbation
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Roflumilast (Daliresp) is reasonable for patients with frequent exacerbations, but GI side effects (nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea) are common; start at half dose for 1-2 weeks then increase to full dose.
pearls.verbatim: if they end up coming in and out of the hospital for exacerbations, that's a reasonable therapy. But a lot of folks have side effects with the GI part of things, and it makes it more difficult to get them to stay on it. And so that's one of the reasons when it first came out, I think it was out for a couple years before people realized, well, you start fifty percent the dose, and then after a week or two of therapy, you increase it to the full.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Regular treatment with ICS increases the risk of pneumonia (evidence level A); consider discontinuing ICS when a COPD patient is hospitalized with pneumonia.
pearls.verbatim: Regular treatment with the ICS increases the risk of pneumonia. Here it is in the guidelines, evidence level a, just like I mentioned earlier.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients on ICS hospitalized with pneumonia
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Initiate ICS therapy for COPD patients with: >2 moderate exacerbations per year, eosinophilia >300 cells/μL, history of asthma, or FEV1 between 30-50% predicted.
pearls.verbatim: more than two moderate exacerbations of COPD per year. Again, if you're gonna measure the eosinophilia is greater than 300 cells per microliter and then a history of asthma. For me, it's f e v one between thirty and fifty percent predicted I would start it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Refer for lung transplant evaluation when FEV1 is ≤30% or DLCO <30%, before the patient becomes ineligible; the official criteria say 20% but earlier referral is better.
pearls.verbatim: I mentioned the trigger of the FEV one of thirty percent. They they say twenty percent, the DLCO less than twenty percent. But remember what I told you, when you get to a DLCO less than 30, you start to see people become more hypoxemic. And I'd rather get them to a transplant sitter before they become ineligible
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For a COPD action plan, use a prolonged prednisone taper: 40 mg for three days, then 30 for three, 20 for three, and 10 for three days, then stop.
pearls.verbatim: I will usually do 40 of prednisone for three days and then thirty for three days, twenty for three days, and ten for three days, and then stop.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients not on chronic steroid therapy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For stable COPD, obtain a yearly PFT; if the patient has no exacerbations, no increase in rescue inhaler use, and FEV1 matches their bronchodilator therapy, no change is needed.
pearls.verbatim: On the COPD patients, if they've been stable for an extended period of time, when I follow them up in clinic, I get a yearly pulmonary function test. ... if the answer is no to all of that and their bronchodilator therapy matches where their f e v one should be, whether they're 80 and up or the 50 to 80 or the 30 to 50 or less than 30, then I leave them be.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For asthma, follow patients every three months until they have no exacerbations and use rescue inhaler no more than once or twice a month; the goal is to minimize inhaled corticosteroid therapy.
pearls.verbatim: in asthma therapy, I generally follow those folks every three months until I know they're not having exacerbations and they're not having to use their inhaler therapy for rescue more than once a month or twice a month. ... You're trying to get them down on the inhaled corticosteroid therapy to as minimal as possible
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: IV steroid taper can be done by decreasing the dose by 50% per day; 20 mg of Solu-Medrol every 8 hours is roughly equivalent to 60 mg of prednisone, allowing easy transition to an oral taper.
pearls.verbatim: the rate that I usually decrease is about 50% per day. So that going back to that eighty milligrams every eight hours, if I decrease that by fifty percent one day, that's forty q eight. If I decrease it by 50% another day, that's twenty q eight. Well, twenty milligrams of solubadril every eight hours is roughly equivalent to sixty milligrams of prednisone. I can easily step that over and then continue the taper on the oral even after they go home from the hospital.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For COPD patients, follow radiographic infiltrates with a CT scan at 6, 8 weeks to ensure no underlying nodule is present; do not schedule it sooner.
pearls.verbatim: So about six to eight weeks out, I'm looking to get that CT scan. And I try not to give the scheduling people the option of doing it sooner.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients with infiltrate after hospitalization
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Use IV magnesium more often in asthma exacerbations than COPD exacerbations for smooth muscle relaxation; in the ICU, give 4-6 grams to induce muscle relaxation.
pearls.verbatim: Not so much in COPD as in asthma for smooth muscle relaxation. And, you know, if they're in the ICU with an asthma exacerbation, we do things like heliox to increase laminar flow. We use magnesium, and I mean, like, four grams, six grams to try and induce muscle relaxation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: patients with asthma exacerbation in the ICU
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: In severe asthma exacerbations, use higher-dose IV steroids (125 mg every 8 hours) and consider IV magnesium (4, 6 grams) for smooth muscle relaxation.
pearls.verbatim: We use magnesium, and I mean, like, four grams, six grams to try and induce muscle relaxation. And we generally use higher dose steroids in the asthma patients. So one twenty five q eight.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: In asthma exacerbations, use higher dose steroids such as methylprednisolone 125 mg every 8 hours.
pearls.verbatim: And we generally use higher dose steroids in the asthma patients. So one twenty five q eight.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Pregnant patients in the third trimester with an asthma exacerbation are high-risk; use IV magnesium and high-dose steroids.
pearls.verbatim: the worst calls that I can think of in the hospital are the pregnant patients who are in their third trimester who have asthma exacerbations. Those are the calls I never wanna get. ... IV magnesium brought that to memory
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: pregnant patients in third trimester with asthma exacerbation
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Pregnant patients in the third trimester with asthma exacerbations are the most dangerous calls in the hospital; they can deteriorate rapidly.
pearls.verbatim: The worst calls that I can think of in the hospital are the pregnant patients who are in their third trimester who have asthma exacerbations. Those are the calls I never wanna get.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: pregnant patients in third trimester with asthma exacerbation
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: In a super wheezy patient with audible wheezing who has been on high-dose IV steroids for 48 hours and frequent breathing treatments without improvement, consider giving IV magnesium, especially if there is a history of asthma or peripheral eosinophilia.
pearls.verbatim: Now if I have somebody who's super duper wheezy and it's audible even without a stethoscope and they've been on IV steroids for forty eight hours, high dose breathing treatments every four hours, and they're not getting better knowing this is Oklahoma, and especially if they have the history with asthma or the peripheral eosinophilia that that leads me down that pathway of that asthmatic component, I don't have an issue. Do have any magnesium? I don't think it's gonna hurt them.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: patients with severe wheezing not responding to standard therapy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Use peak expiratory flow monitoring with personal best, yellow zone, and red zone to help asthma patients recognize exacerbations early and call for prescriptions.
pearls.verbatim: I'm still okay doing peak expiratory flows and having someone's personal best and then they're kinda zone and then their red zone as far as their airflow limitation. And that's not so much that that number means I need to do something specific. It just lets the patient know more than anything, hey. They need to call and say, this is starting to occur.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: If IgE level is greater than 30, start montelukast (Singulair) for asthma.
pearls.verbatim: In general, if the IgE level is greater than 30, then I'll I'll start them on Singulair.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Obtain RAST allergy testing before starting montelukast (Singulair), because the drug must be held for weeks before allergy testing.
pearls.verbatim: from an allergy immunology standpoint, you you gotta get the RAST testing and the allergy stuff done before you put them on the Singulair. Otherwise, you have to hold it for weeks before you send them for testing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: asthma patients being considered for montelukast
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Use the STOP-Bang questionnaire to screen for OSA; it includes snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, blood pressure, BMI >35, age >50, neck circumference >16 inches (women) or >18 inches (men), and male sex.
pearls.verbatim: And it comes down to does your patient snore as a form of... Or flag for some degree of airflow limitation? The snoring actually doesn't count towards the diagnosis of sleep apnea. It just lets you know somewhere between their nose and their vocal cords, they've got some airflow limitation. And then the fatigue, excessive daytime sleepiness, screening them for that. When we actually do our intake, we're using an Epworth sleepiness scale score, and that is is part of that initial intake assessment that I'll show you here in a second. And then whether or not their bed partner, significant other, or family member is actually seeing them have a witness cause in their breathing to signify that, yeah, you have apnea occurring, but we're gonna do a study to see if you're doing it more than five times an hour and go forward with that. And then high blood pressure, if someone's on multiple antihypertensives and you're going down the list of differential diagnoses for what's driving up that pressure, making it more difficult to control, sleep apnea is on that list. Their BMI, whether or not they're above 35, their age greater than 50. For women in particular, there's a a more of a peak in incidence when they hit the the perimenopausal area, and then it kinda goes back down. And for men, in general, as you get older, the incidence tends to trend up. And that is a reflection of how everything kinda relaxes as we get older. So, you know, your neck muscles relax, your tongue relaxes, everything relaxes, and it's just not as taut as it is when you're in your twenties and thirties. And then neck size for men, really, it's eighteen inches and up. For women, inches or larger increases their predisposition for this.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: For mild OSA (AHI <15), treat if the patient is symptomatic (e.g., Epworth >10); if asymptomatic, reassure that it is not likely to shorten life.
pearls.verbatim: if it's under 15 events per hour, we may not need to treat you, you know, and just reassure them that this is not something that's gonna shorten their life or kill them if they're asymptomatic and their AHI is less than 15.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: adults with AHI <15 and no symptoms
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: In practice, treat most patients with AHI >5 because symptoms fluctuate and in-lab studies may underestimate severity due to poor sleep.
pearls.verbatim: I tend to just treat everybody with an AHI above five because their symptoms wax and wane... Fluctuate over time. And, also, I'm I'm thinking in the back of my mind, people may not have slept as well in the lab or slept as deep in the lab with all that stuff connected to them as they do at home.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: Insurance requires a follow-up visit within 8, 12 weeks of starting CPAP to document usage and symptomatic benefit; device download must show >70% of nights with >4 hours use.
pearls.verbatim: After somebody starts on CPAP therapy, you have to do a follow-up for insurance to cover the equipment, and it's an eight to twelve week window to do that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: Prescribe a pressure range (e.g., 10, 13 cm H₂O) rather than a single pressure to allow adjustment for weight changes, nasal congestion, or mask changes.
pearls.verbatim: So if I titrate somebody in the lab to a pressure of 10 on their CPAP, I don't put them on 10. I put them on, like, 10 to 13.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: ResMed devices have a clinical menu accessible by holding two touch points; settings include pressure range, mask type, ramp time, expiratory pressure release (EPR), and smart start/stop.
pearls.verbatim: you put a finger on the bottom bar and a finger on the knob and hold it down until the screen changes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: For inpatients with known OSA who don't have their own CPAP, order 'chronic' CPAP at a starting pressure of 8 cm H2O and add a comment: 'Known history of obstructive sleep apnea. Please use nocturnal CPAP therapy during hospitalization.'
pearls.verbatim: an average pressure for an adult is around eight, and so that's where I would start.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: inpatients with known OSA without their own device
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: For inpatients with COPD exacerbation or heart failure, use an 'acute' CPAP order to let respiratory therapy titrate, which will typically default to BiPAP or AVAPS.
pearls.verbatim: steer clear of the chronic order and put more acute and let them titrate. That way they're choosing the mode.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: inpatients with COPD exacerbation or heart failure
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: Transition from CPAP to BiPAP when pressure exceeds 16 cm H2O to avoid patient discomfort from exhaling against high pressure.
pearls.verbatim: we start using BiPAPs when we get an excess of 16 centimeters of water pressure because we don't want the patients to have to exhale against all that air.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: Many doctors practice with a 'do not get in trouble' mindset, which leads to unnecessary testing, e.g. CT scans for every abdominal pain, repeat brain imaging for altered mental status that was normal six weeks ago.
pearls.verbatim: Why does every patient with abdominal pain that goes to the ER get a CT scan? So you don't miss something. And if you miss something, something bad could happen. And if that something bad happens, you're gonna get in trouble.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Duininck
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Duininck on Controversies in Medicine 8/27/26

pearls.text: When a patient demands an antibiotic, consider that if you refuse and they end up in the ER getting one anyway, you may have caused more harm. Balance antibiotic stewardship with the reality of patient outcomes.
pearls.verbatim: But if somebody really wants it, and last time they didn't get it and they ended up in the ER and got an antibiotic because we refused to prescribe, that's real.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Duininck
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Duininck on Controversies in Medicine 8/27/26

pearls.text: During the COVID-19 shutdown of cardiac cath labs, there was no change in the incidence of severe cardiac disease or cardiac death, suggesting many interventions may not affect population-level outcomes.
pearls.verbatim: So what happened to the incidence of severe cardiac disease and cardiac death? There was no change when we stopped all the cardiac interventions.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Duininck
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Duininck on Controversies in Medicine 8/27/26

pearls.text: During a three-month COVID-19 shutdown of the cath lab, including no ablations, cardiac caths, balloon angioplasties, or stents, there was no change in the incidence of severe cardiac disease or cardiac death.
pearls.verbatim: There was no change when we stopped all the cardiac interventions.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Duininck
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Duininck on Controversies in Medicine 8/27/26

pearls.text: Selling natural cholesterol or blood pressure lowering agents from the office creates a conflict of interest; the speaker avoids it because they don't trust themselves.
pearls.verbatim: I never would do it because I don't trust myself.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Duininck
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Duininck on Controversies in Medicine 8/27/26

pearls.text: Doctors should not reflexively refuse to prescribe controlled medicines; each case should be considered individually, e.g., Ativan for a patient with bad anxiety three times a month may be appropriate.
pearls.verbatim: I just don't wanna write Ativan for this person because they need it three times a month when they they have bad anxiety. That's probably okay.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Duininck
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Duininck on Controversies in Medicine 8/27/26

pearls.text: Three out of four heroin users started on prescription pills, highlighting the progression from prescribed opioids to illicit use.
pearls.verbatim: I think it's three out of four heroin users started on pills.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Methamphetamine is now involved in more overdose/poisoning deaths than opioids in Oklahoma, reflecting the fourth wave of the epidemic.
pearls.verbatim: methamphetamine now is actually involved in more of a overdose slash poisoning deaths than opioids now in the state of Oklahoma.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: When a patient no longer controls the drug and the drug controls them, they have entered the substance use disorder spectrum.
pearls.verbatim: when you no longer control the drug, the drug controls you, you've now entered the substance use disorder spectrum.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Without medication-assisted treatment, only 20, 30% of people with opioid use disorder are abstinent at 12 months.
pearls.verbatim: by twelve months, you're looking at only twenty, maybe thirty percent are abstinent from the primary substance at twelve months without medication.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Opioid use disorder increases mortality risk sixfold; medication-assisted treatment reduces it to less than twofold.
pearls.verbatim: those who struggle with opioid use disorder had a six time fold risk of mortality. When they have access to medication assisted treatment, their mortality ratio goes down below two.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist that caps receptor activation at 40%, making it very hard to overdose on buprenorphine alone because it does not cause respiratory depression.
pearls.verbatim: Buprenorphine, no matter when you get to a high dose, it caps the the activity of that receptor. This is one reason why it's really hard to overdose on buprenorphine because you're not you're not getting the receptor enough to get that respiratory depression.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Buprenorphine can displace full agonists and cause precipitated withdrawal because it reduces receptor activation from 100% to 40%.
pearls.verbatim: It's gonna displace the oxy and then only do 40%. Guess what that is? That's withdrawal. That's why we talk about precipitated withdrawal of buprenorphine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.applies_to: patients transitioning from full agonists to buprenorphine
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Sublocade can be used as a tapering agent because it self-tapers over months, avoiding the withdrawal and cravings seen with tapering oral films.
pearls.verbatim: it's been good at as a tapering agent as well because with the tabs, you know, you can only get it so small. And so people still have some withdrawal cravings even if I'm using, like, the tabs of the films. With this, it just self self tapered over months.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Recommend at least one year of buprenorphine treatment; tapering increases the risk of return to use.
pearls.verbatim: I recommend at least a year because a lot of psychosocial things are usually going on. They need a while to stabilize their environment. what the research says is that when you start tapering, return to use goes up.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Recommend patients stay on buprenorphine for at least one year; help the patient with their goals, and if they are motivated to get off, taper together, but recognize requests to discontinue are often driven by stigma, not side effects.
pearls.verbatim: Our clinic stance is, like, we will help the patient with their goals. We will recommend at least a year. That's our recommendation,
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Many patient requests to discontinue MAT are driven by stigma, not side effects or tolerability; clinicians should explore the underlying reasons.
pearls.verbatim: other medical decisions are based on side effects, tolerability, long term consequences. And a lot of these decisions and patients' requests are driven by stigma.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.applies_to: patients requesting to stop medication-assisted treatment
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Other medical decisions are based on side effects, tolerability, and long-term consequences, but many patient requests to stop buprenorphine are driven by stigma.
pearls.verbatim: Other medical decisions are based on side effects, tolerability, long term consequences. And a lot of these decisions and patients' requests are driven by stigma.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.applies_to: patients with opioid use disorder requesting to stop buprenorphine
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: If a patient takes buprenorphine too early (without moderate withdrawal), it will cause precipitated withdrawal, which is moderate or severe.
pearls.verbatim: If you take it too soon and you don't have moderate or severe withdrawal, it's gonna give you moderate or severe withdrawals.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: For patients on Suboxone with headaches or nausea, have them rinse their mouth out after the tablet dissolves to reduce naloxone GI absorption; if that fails, switch to buprenorphine-only product (one-to-one conversion).
pearls.verbatim: So, like, pretty bad headaches or sometimes nausea I hear a lot. And so first, I have them rinse their mouth out after the suboxone. So so you're not supposed see, like, ten minutes before and after. Make sure it's completely resolved, dissolved, and then rinse your mouth out because sometimes they're swallowing it and ends up sitting their stomach They're absorbing some of the naloxone through the GI system.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.applies_to: patients on Suboxone with side effects
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Extended-release naltrexone (Vivitrol) requires the patient to be opioid-free for 7, 10 days before starting; outpatient induction is very difficult and nearly all induction failures relapse.
pearls.verbatim: You have to be opioid free for seven to ten days before you can get it. That's the really hard part here is getting opioids for seven to ten days. Nearly all induction failures relapse.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: For chronic opioid therapy, in the first year the patient must be seen every three months, then every six months; document why the patient still needs that amount and an attempt to reduce it.
pearls.verbatim: If you're doing it for chronic pain, for the first year, you need to see them every three months and then every six months after that. You have to kind of document why they still need that amount
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Do not prescribe opioids and benzodiazepines together in the outpatient setting, this should be a never event.
pearls.verbatim: Don't prescribe opioids and benzos together. Obviously, in the hospital is a little bit different, but outpatient should be a never event.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: The COMBINE study (1,400 alcohol-dependent adults, 11 sites) found that naltrexone plus CBT added to medical management improved outcomes over placebo and medical management alone; acamprosate did not add benefit to naltrexone or CBT.
pearls.verbatim: Combined results, Naltrexone and CBT added to medical management improved outcomes over placebo medical management alone. And acamprosate in this study didn't really add benefit to naltrexone or CBT and was not more effective than medical management alone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Taking pills with medical management was more effective than receiving CBT alone for alcohol use disorder.
pearls.verbatim: Taking pills and medical management was more effective than receiving cognitive behavioral therapy alone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Brixadi is a new buprenorphine injection given once a week or once a month; patients can start after tolerating a single 4 mg Suboxone tablet, with a recommended 7-day window before injection.
pearls.verbatim: It happens once a week and once a month. And the once a week, I know that you can just do a four milligram tab of Suboxone. And once they tolerate it, they can get the injection immediately. So they shall just recommend seven day window.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.applies_to: adults with opioid use disorder, for weekly injection
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Quitting cold turkey has about 30% success, that is not a lack of willpower but a biological challenge; treat addiction with the same evidence-based assistance as other medical conditions.
pearls.verbatim: the studies show quitting cold turkey, know, about 30% of them aren't gonna be successful. So that's not a lack of willpower
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.applies_to: any patient with substance use disorder attempting abstinence
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med

pearls.text: Use the SAFE-T instrument for suicide risk assessment after a positive screen.
pearls.verbatim: If a screen is positive, there's other validated instruments, like, that can help you walk through safe... Like, kind of safety planning. So we do the safe dash t.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Medicine - Antidepressants 9/10/26

pearls.text: Asking about suicide does not increase risk; studies show it is safe to ask.
pearls.verbatim: Studies show that asking about it does not increase in sites.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Medicine - Antidepressants 9/10/26

pearls.text: Screen for mania by asking about decreased need for sleep, increased energy, risky behaviors (spending, speeding, increased sex drive, substance use), and pressured speech.
pearls.verbatim: Have you had any periods of time where, you know, you didn't need to sleep as much? Do you feel like your energy was pretty good? ... What about any times you kind of... To things that were maybe a lot of character for you? Like, you spent more money, maybe you were speeding, maybe you increased sex drive, did drugs and alcohol, anything like that? What about time... Periods of time people think you're just really chatty and you don't like stop talking?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Medicine - Antidepressants 9/10/26

pearls.text: Use the SIG E CAPS mnemonic to systematically check DSM-5 criteria for major depressive episode.
pearls.verbatim: To this day, I still write SIG E CAPS when I'm taking industry, and I circle the letters as I go through my history to see if they're meeting criteria.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Medicine - Antidepressants 9/10/26

pearls.text: Use the SIG E CAPS mnemonic and circle each letter as you take the history to verify if the patient meets depression criteria.
pearls.verbatim: To this day, I still write SIG E CAPS when I'm taking industry, and I circle the letters as I go through my history to see if they're meeting criteria.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Medicine - Antidepressants 9/10/26

pearls.text: Rule out depression due to substances or medical conditions and disallow a history of mania or hypomania before diagnosing uncomplicated MDD.
pearls.verbatim: Symptoms should not be attributable to other physiological effect of a substance or medical condition and not better explained by another psychiatric disorder. And there can never be a manic or hypomanic episode to be considered.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Medicine - Antidepressants 9/10/26

pearls.text: For sertraline, start at 25 mg for at least 1, 2 weeks before increasing to 50 mg to reduce side effects.
pearls.verbatim: For most of my patients, I start twenty five for at least a week or two.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Medicine - Antidepressants 9/10/26

pearls.text: If you start at the standard starting dose, wait 4, 6 weeks before titrating upward.
pearls.verbatim: So if I'm already starting at a starting dose, I will wait four to six weeks before titrate up to the next dose.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.applies_to: patients on a starting dose of an SSRI
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Medicine - Antidepressants 9/10/26

pearls.text: In severely suffering patients with no early improvement, titrate more quickly; if there is a response, hold the dose to avoid overmedicating.
pearls.verbatim: If I have someone who's just really suffering and I'm like, we're not seeing any improvement, I'm gonna go a little faster.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Medicine - Antidepressants 9/10/26

pearls.text: Prozac is a strong CYP450 inhibitor; when a patient is on Prozac, definitely check all drugs being prescribed for interactions.
pearls.verbatim: One of the biggest interact... One one direction, Prozac is the strong inhibitor. So they're on Prozac. Definitely be looking at all the drugs we're prescribing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Kelly Dunn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Medicine - Antidepressants 9/10/26

pearls.text: Reproductive status (not just pregnancy but childbearing potential) should change the medication you prescribe, especially for mood stabilizers.
pearls.verbatim: Reproductive status in general, like, not just if they're pregnant, but if they're childbearing, which that might change the medication you prescribe, especially when we talk about mood stabilizers later.

pearls.text: If a patient is circling the drain and IV access is difficult, place an IO immediately; it is totally effective and can deliver two liters rapidly with a pressure bag.
pearls.verbatim: And if you are... If someone's circling the drain and we're like, we can't find IVs, put the IO in. It is totally effective. You can give them two liters rapidly through an IO with with a pressure bag and
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.applies_to: patients in shock with difficult IV access
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: If a patient does not respond to fluids within five minutes, start vasopressors; it is better to get blood pressure normal and then titrate off than to wait 45 minutes without perfusing organs.
pearls.verbatim: assuming they are not responding instantly to fluids, like, give them five minutes. Start vasopressors. You so much rather get their blood pressure normal and then titrate off the vasopressors.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.applies_to: adults with shock not responding to initial fluid bolus
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: A MAP of 60 is the minimum pressure needed to perfuse critical organs (brain, lungs, kidneys, heart); we set a goal MAP of 65 to give a cushion.
pearls.verbatim: Basically, a MAP of 60 in most people is is a pressure that you need to perfuse your criticals, your brain, lungs, kidneys, heart.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: Warm shock indicates peripheral vasodilation (alpha receptors not working); cold shock indicates vasoconstriction, often from poor cardiac function.
pearls.verbatim: So you've heard people say warm shock versus cold shock. Literally, what they're talking about is is it peripheral vasodilation or vasoconstriction.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: In cardiac arrest, standard epinephrine dose is 1 mg (1000 mcg) push, which is about a thousand times the max infusion rate; excessive doses in shockable rhythms may worsen outcomes.
pearls.verbatim: Put in a code, you're pushing you're pushing a thousand micrograms all at once.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: For refractory V-fib after multiple epinephrine doses and failed shocks, consider giving esmolol (a beta blocker) and then shocking.
pearls.verbatim: So literally, the other day, I got someone back by giving esmolol, a beta blocker, when they were in refractory ventricular fibrillation (V-fib).
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.applies_to: adults with refractory V-fib in cardiac arrest
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: In anaphylaxis, IM route is preferred over SQ because SQ is too slow due to poor blood flow to fat.
pearls.verbatim: Subcutaneous, it's too slow. Not enough blood flow to the fat to things very quickly.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: Pediatric anaphylaxis epinephrine dose is 0.15 mg (150 mcg) IM for children roughly under 5 years.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: Start norepinephrine at a dose proportional to the MAP deficit: 20 mcg/min if MAP is 45, 10 mcg/min if MAP is 55.
pearls.verbatim: I start with however many points I need to make up on their map. So if their map is 45, like, we got a lot of distance to cover, then just start them at 20. That make sense? If their map is 55, just start them at ten.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: Vasopressin is dosed at 0.03 to 0.04 units/min and acts on peripheral V1 receptors to increase systemic vascular resistance.
pearls.verbatim: And it's usually dosed zero point three to zero point four units.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: Milrinone (0.25-0.75 mcg/kg/min) is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor and a good inotrope option for cardiogenic shock with atrial fibrillation, but its half-life is very long.
pearls.verbatim: It is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor, and it's just, like, 0.25 to 0.75 per kilo.

pearls.applies_to: patients with cardiogenic shock and atrial fibrillation

pearls.text: When norepinephrine reaches 15-20 mcg/min without adequate response, add a second pressor (vasopressin or epinephrine).
pearls.verbatim: And then when you start to get to about 15 or 20 on Levofed, you gotta add a second pressor at that point.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: Consider IV hydrocortisone 100 mg for patients who have been sick for more than 48 hours and require escalating vasopressors, as they may have adrenal burnout.
pearls.verbatim: If you're needing more than Levophed, then people who have been sick for more than, like, forty eight hours, like... Especially, like, neemaw's been laying on the floor for a long time or she's sick for a long time, they have probably burned out their adrenals. And so, absolutely, whether you put this before Levophed or after, consider polymorphicol. Like, a hundred milligrams of IV hydrocortisone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.applies_to: patients with prolonged illness (>48 hours) requiring escalating vasopressors
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: If a patient on vasopressors is circling the drain (likely to code), titrate aggressively every 5 minutes; if awake and talking, allow 30-45 minutes to assess response.
pearls.verbatim: If this person is, like... And I keep using the phrase circling the drain. But if if they're like, you wouldn't be surprised if they code anytime. Like, they're terribly sick, then you're probably doing all this at bedside. Right? Like, you're probably not leaving and checking back in. And so if you crank their Levophen to twenty right when it started or thirty and it's like their pressure is still 60 over 40, then then start it instantly. You know? It's like... But if they're, like... If they're not that sick, if they're, like, awake and talking to you and lucid and breathing on their own and look okay, then maybe you're giving it thirty or forty five minutes and and just seeing...
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock

pearls.text: If a patient is taking their seizure meds and has one breakthrough seizure, they may still go home, but if they have 2-4 seizures in a few days, they usually need admission.
pearls.verbatim: if we have a pattern now of ongoing seizing, we're usually staying. If if we got two, three, four seizures all of a sudden in the last couple days, we're usually staying.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: For a TIA, use the ABCD2 score to decide admission; if the score is high, encourage admission or start aspirin and a statin if they refuse.
pearls.verbatim: if their ABCD2 score is high and a TIA, like, as soon as it's completely resolved, you're encouraging them to stay. And if they won't stay for whatever reason, you're probably starting them on aspirin and or antilipidemic
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: A new type of neurologic deficit in a patient with known hemiplegic migraines requires a stroke workup; the same deficit as before does not.
pearls.verbatim: a new a new type of deficit is a stroke work. If it's same deficit that they've had before with their migraines, then do stroke workup.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: Use the HEART score to stratify chest pain; if the risk of a cardiac event in 30 days is >2%, admit for rule-out.
pearls.verbatim: your heart score says that is higher than a two percent chance that something bad happens to your heart in the next thirty days, we admit you for a chest pain rule out.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: For hip pain radiating down the leg, palpate the IT band from hip to knee; if it's tender, it's likely IT band syndrome, which is fixable with a foam roller or PT.
pearls.verbatim: If you start in their hip and just smash all the way down, they're like, ow, ow, ow, ow. Like, they have IT band syndrome.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: When a patient says 'dizzy,' don't fixate on their first description of vertigo vs lightheadedness; 50% change their mind when asked an hour later, so assume the worst and work up for central causes.
pearls.verbatim: When the first word is out of someone's mouth when you try to distinguish is, then, like, it doesn't matter what they say next. They're making it up. So you have to assume it's the worst one, the worst option.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: A negative Dix-Hallpike does not rule out BPPV because it only tests one of three semicircular canals; consider referral to a vestibular therapist for complex cases.
pearls.verbatim: That only tests one of the three. Like, just because they have a negative Dix-Hallpike does not rule out BPPV.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: For Meniere's disease, first-line treatment is salt restriction; if symptoms persist, consider starting a diuretic like HCTZ or acetazolamide.
pearls.verbatim: first line is usually salt restriction. If they're still feeling bad, then you can start on HCTZ or another acetazolamide or whatever.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: If a patient has dizziness about 10 days after a viral illness with no ringing or positional triggers, consider vestibular neuritis and give a short course of steroids.
pearls.verbatim: It could just be vestibular neuritis if they're ten days post viral. And so you could give them a little course of steroids for that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: Start pressors (usually Levophed) early when MAP is low, even before knowing the cause, to prevent organ damage; then treat the underlying issue once identified.
pearls.verbatim: absolutely, I start pressors all the time before I know why I'm starting pressors because I don't want their organs to die.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.applies_to: patients with hypotension in the ER
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: For RSI, use ketamine 1 mg/kg and rocuronium 1 mg/kg as a go-to; write the dose on your reference card.
pearls.verbatim: I always use ketamine and rocuronium. That's my go to. Great. Write the dose out. I always use one mg per kg of ketamine and, you know, one mg per kg of rocuronium.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: Do not intubate wheezing asthmatics or COPD patients unless they are failing despite maximal therapy; a ventilator cannot match their native exhalation and will worsen acidosis.
pearls.verbatim: The rule of thumb is not to intubate people who are wheezing. ... A ventilator cannot suck air out. It can only push air in. ... So you cannot move as much air per minute when they're on a ventilator as you can in someone who is breathing on their own.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: Pressors can run through a peripheral IV for 24 hours; central line placement is not urgent for vasopressor administration.
pearls.verbatim: any presser can run through a peripheral line for twenty four hours.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: Starting a nitro drip at less than 80 mcg/min is less effective than giving sublingual nitro for flash pulmonary edema.
pearls.verbatim: if someone has flash pulmonary edema and you start them on nitro less than eighty mics a minute, that's less effective than if you just gave them sublingual nitro.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: For flash pulmonary edema with a blood pressure of 240 and tripoding, start BiPAP and a nitro drip at 200-400 mcg/min; the patient will improve in about 8 minutes.
pearls.verbatim: when someone has flash pulmonary edema, their blood pressure is two forty, they're tripoding. If you start BiPAP and a nitro drip, they'll be better in eight minutes, and you'll look like a genius. But the nitro drip starts at about 200, maybe 300, maybe 400.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.applies_to: patients with flash pulmonary edema and severe hypertension
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26

pearls.text: Susceptibility to cefazolin means susceptibility to all first-generation cephalosporins; you can switch from IV cefazolin to oral cephalexin (Keflex) even though Keflex was not tested.
pearls.verbatim: you then know that every first generation cephalosporin is susceptible. That's why if it's susceptible to cefazolin... Well, cefazolin's an IV drug. If I wanna use a PO first generation cephalosporin, like Keflex? Would I use that? Yeah. Even though they didn't test Keflex, is in the same class. I can use it.

pearls.text: When a penicillin is susceptible, it may be more effective than a cephalosporin against certain resistant patterns; do not automatically escalate to broader agents.

pearls.text: The lab only tests antibiotics known to have efficacy against the identified organism; you will never see amoxicillin or ceftriaxone tested against Pseudomonas.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Ganzer

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ganzer on Antibiotics

pearls.text: Consult infectious disease for endocarditis and osteomyelitis.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ganzer on Antibiotics

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ganzer on Antibiotics

pearls.text: A thorough history and physical exam can be 93% as accurate as MRI for diagnosing knee injuries, so use imaging to confirm what you already suspect.

pearls.text: When evaluating a moderate-to-severe subacute creatinine rise, first assess for prerenal causes: check for volume depletion (diarrhea, vomiting) and review medications including NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and diuretics.

pearls.text: Screen for CKD annually in patients with diabetes or hypertension using serum creatinine, eGFR, and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio.

pearls.text: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) has replaced 24-hour urine protein due to inadequate collections, inconvenience, and lack of diagnostic advantage; obtain it on a morning sample for accuracy.

pearls.text: Prescribe a structured moderate-intensity exercise program of at least 150 minutes per week for patients with CKD.

pearls.text: When using an ACE inhibitor or ARB for renal protection, titrate to the maximally tolerated dose; the goal is renal protection, not just blood pressure control.

pearls.text: Hold ACE inhibitors or ARBs if potassium is over 5.5. If GFR declines by more than 30% after starting, consider stopping or changing therapy.

pearls.text: Finerenone, a selective nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, is a game changer for stage 3, 4 CKD as it reduces the risk of sustained GFR decline, ESRD, and cardiovascular death.

pearls.text: For diabetic CKD, target A1c to 6.5% up to 8% depending on life situation; use SGLT2 inhibitors and metformin.

pearls.text: Cell-free DNA (NIPS) is much more sensitive and specific than the quad screen, so if doing prenatal screening, it makes more sense to use cell-free DNA.

pearls.text: Cell-free DNA can be drawn at any point in pregnancy after 9, 10 weeks, unlike the quad screen which has a limited window.

pearls.text: For pregestational diabetes, use insulin because newer injectables like GLP-1s and SGLT2s lack long-term safety data and show animal developmental issues.

pearls.text: If a patient has a chancre, 95-97% of the time the serology will be reactive; if not, repeat serology in 2-3 weeks.

pearls.text: The serofast phenomenon: after treatment, titers drop to 1:1, 1:2, or 1:4 and will not go lower no matter how many times you treat the patient.
pearls.verbatim: You treat them, and those titers will come down to a one to one, one to two, maybe even a one to four, and they won't go any lower no matter how many times you treat them.

pearls.text: In late-stage syphilis (late latent and tertiary), 25% of patients lose their RPR reactivity, so a negative RPR does not rule out active disease.

pearls.text: Monitor treatment response with RPR; expect a fourfold drop in titer over 3-6 months.

pearls.text: Successful treatment is defined by a fourfold decrease in RPR titer (e.g., 1:64 to 1:16). Follow titers at 3, 6, and 12 months; RPR should be gone by 6 months, definitely by 12 months.
