pearls.text: Bupropion 450 mg is rarely covered by insurance; prescribe 300 mg plus 150 mg instead.
pearls.verbatim: bupropion comes in one fifty, three hundred, and four fifty. But the four fifty, you'll never get covered, so you'd have to prescribe three hundred and one fifty.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Greer
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greer on Anxiety & Depression 5/7/26

pearls.text: Screen for bipolar disorder before starting bupropion, as it can trigger a manic episode in undiagnosed bipolar patients.
pearls.verbatim: if someone has bipolar, and and you're like, oh, okay. Either... And they're in their depressive state. You don't screen for manic episodes, and then you start on bupropion, and then it initiates.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Greer
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greer on Anxiety & Depression 5/7/26

pearls.text: Start buspirone at 7.5 mg twice daily for one week, then increase to 15 mg twice daily; some need up to 30 mg twice daily.
pearls.verbatim: I'll start them on the fifteen and tell them to cut it in half and just do that. And I have one patient where for... I'll start on the 15, cut it in half for one week, and then they bump it up to the 15
pearls.speaker: Dr. Greer
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greer on Anxiety & Depression 5/7/26

pearls.text: Benzodiazepines should be avoided except for short-term use (30-60 days) after a traumatic event.
pearls.verbatim: I try to avoid them if at all possible except for someone who just had a very traumatic event trying to get them on something in that thirty day, like, you know, thirty to thirty to sixty day period
pearls.speaker: Dr. Greer
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greer on Anxiety & Depression 5/7/26

pearls.text: Magnesium and vitamin D are commonly deficient and may help with sleep; consider supplementation.
pearls.verbatim: Magnesium, good. Like, feel like everybody's deficient in... We talked about this a little bit. Magnesium and vitamin D.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Greer
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greer on Anxiety & Depression 5/7/26

pearls.text: If a patient has paradoxical reactions to SSRIs, SNRIs, and mirtazapine, consider trying Trintellix (vortioxetine) because it works differently on serotonin receptors.
pearls.verbatim: if I've done everything possible and I can't figure it out, I'll I'll try Trintellix.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Greer
pearls.applies_to: patients with treatment-resistant depression or anxiety who had paradoxical reactions to other antidepressants
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greer on Anxiety & Depression 5/7/26

pearls.text: For bipolar depression without weight gain, consider Lamictal (lamotrigine), but titrate up very slowly to prevent Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
pearls.verbatim: if someone has bipolar and they don't wanna gain a ton of weight, a lot of times, first of I'll try Lamictal, but you titrate it up really slowly in order to prevent the Stevens-Johnson syndrome potential.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Greer
pearls.applies_to: patients with bipolar depression who want to avoid weight gain
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greer on Anxiety & Depression 5/7/26

pearls.text: Refer any symptomatic patient with aortic stenosis for valve replacement, even if echo measurements seem discordant; put it together clinically.
pearls.verbatim: if there's any question when to refer anybody that's symptomatic, because once they're symptomatic, it's... Even if the echo doesn't show that, and that's why it becomes important to look at your own echo measurements because that's really important too.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Greta Warta
pearls.applies_to: symptomatic patients with suspected aortic stenosis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greta Warta on Valve Diseases 11/6/25

pearls.text: In bicuspid aortic valve, also monitor the thoracic aorta; surgical threshold for aortic dilation is 4.5 cm (vs 5.0 cm for others).
pearls.verbatim: If someone has a bicuspid valve, you wanna look at their... You wanna watch, measure, and look at their aorta, the thoracic aorta, because that's where it could be different too. You know, if you've got a widened aorta, you know, they're gonna wanna... Their surgery's gonna wanna replace that or, you know, repair it when it's 4.5 over five for everybody else.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Greta Warta
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greta Warta on Valve Diseases 11/6/25

pearls.text: Patients with aortic stenosis feel immediately better after valve replacement because blood flow is restored; symptoms like dizziness, shortness of breath, and fatigue resolve quickly.
pearls.verbatim: They immediately feel better because you can imagine, you know, not much is getting through that valve. And so it does cause dizziness, shortness of breath, really a lot of fatigue, you know, walking across the room. If you notice that with your symptoms, they walk to the mailbox anymore, they used to walk around the block or, you know, going across the room. And immediately, that's better because immediately, that valve is opening.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Greta Warta
pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing valve replacement for aortic stenosis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greta Warta on Valve Diseases 11/6/25

pearls.text: Obtain a baseline CBC before medical or surgical management of miscarriage.
pearls.verbatim: make sure you have that and a CBC on all patients because you want a CBC for baseline.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: ER precautions for patients: bleeding >2 pads per hour for 2 hours, fever >101°F, uncontrolled pain, or signs of anemia (shortness of breath, palpitations, feeling faint).
pearls.verbatim: If it's greater than one zero one, if they have anemia signs and symptoms, if their cramps aren't controlled by medication or if they're bleeding two pads or more for an hour, they need to go to the hospital.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing medical or expectant management of miscarriage
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: Systematic ultrasound scanning: use at least two orthogonal views (sagittal and transverse) to fully evaluate the uterus.
pearls.verbatim: You wanna scan systematically. Make sure you look at the uterus. It has abdominal and transvaginal in a a a left to right and then front to back, you know, top to bottom. Like, you wanna use at least two views of of kinda going all the way through the uterus and and around the uterus.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: For transvaginal ultrasound, always have the patient empty her bladder first to avoid discomfort and improve image quality.
pearls.verbatim: Do you want to do a transvaginal ultrasound? And then I would have her pee and empty her bladder, hopefully.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: A pseudogestational sac can mimic early pregnancy; careful measurement and correlation with HCG are needed to avoid missing ectopic pregnancy.
pearls.verbatim: She may have what's called a pseudogestational sac. There may be a little bit of fluid inside the uterus. And this could be a pseudogestational sac because it's very small.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: Measure crown-rump length as the longest view of the fetus without limbs or yolk sac, and average three measurements.
pearls.verbatim: you're gonna rotate your probe usually at least a 180 degrees and find the longest view of the fetus without limbs or yolk sac. And then you're go... And you're gonna measure that three times to get an average.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: Before giving misoprostol or doing D&C for pregnancy failure, confirm with two points of evidence (e.g., no cardiac activity at ≥25 mm sac).
pearls.verbatim: I like to have two points of confirmation before I give misoprostol or do a DNC.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: Don't let the sun set on an ectopic pregnancy: send patients with significant pain for same-day ultrasound or to the ER.
pearls.verbatim: Don't let the sun set on an ectopic pregnancy. Make sure you send them to the ER that day or get an ultrasound that day for having significant pain.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: For manual rotation of occiput posterior, you need a completely dilated cervix to avoid causing a cervical laceration.
pearls.verbatim: Because you gotta have a baby that's... You gotta have a cervix that is complete because otherwise, you're gonna cause a cervical laceration.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26

pearls.text: When discussing a miscarriage diagnosis, recognize the patient is in distress and less able to retain information; avoid medical jargon, use a translator if needed, and confirm understanding.
pearls.verbatim: the person at the scene of the accident is gonna be less able to retain information anyway, and then you're going into medical jargon or sometimes using a translator.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: all patients with new miscarriage diagnosis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Routine Pap smears, transvaginal ultrasounds, and bimanual exams do not cause miscarriage; inform patients of this to allay fear.
pearls.verbatim: routine medical examinations... pap smears, transvaginal ultrasounds, bimanual exams, they are not statistically significantly causes of miscarriages.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: In initial evaluation of early pregnancy loss, obtain CBC, quantitative hCG, and Rh type unless recently checked.
pearls.verbatim: You need to get a baseline. You need to get a baseline blood work if they've... Whether they've been bleeding or not. It's probably a good idea unless they've had a CBC recently to go ahead and get one.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Ectopic pregnancy is unlikely if the patient has no pain, even with bleeding.
pearls.verbatim: if they don't have any pain, the likelihood of that is... Or bleeding, likelihood of that's pretty low.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: patients with vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Use color flow Doppler to assess intrauterine contents in nonviable pregnancy: blood flow suggests retained placental tissue, no flow is reassuring.
pearls.verbatim: One of the things you can do also if you know it's not a viable pregnancy is you can use color flow Doppler to see if there's any... If you see something in there that you're like, what is that?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: On follow-up ultrasound, use color flow Doppler to assess retained tissue: blood flow suggests retained placenta, no flow suggests clot and is reassuring.
pearls.verbatim: use color flow Doppler because if you're like, this is not a viable pregnancy, but there's still something in the uterus. If it's got blood flow, it might be a chunk of placenta or something. If it doesn't have blood flow, that's gonna reassuring.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Misoprostol repeat dose can be given as soon as 24 hours, but 48 hours is typical.
pearls.verbatim: think, forty eight hours, but if you can do it actually sooner, twenty four hours too.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: patients using misoprostol for miscarriage management
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Misoprostol may be more traumatic for patients prone to anxiety, without good support, or nulliparous, due to heavy bleeding and cramping at home.
pearls.verbatim: Remember the PSS conversation, though. So if you have a person that is prone to anxiety or does not have a good support system or has never had a baby before, misoprostol may be more that an expected management, especially misoprostol, may be more traumatic to them because they're gonna have a bunch of bleeding and cramping at home.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: patients considering misoprostol for early pregnancy loss
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Proceed to surgical management when expectant or medical management fails, with signs like heavy bleeding, prolonged bleeding, dropping hematocrit, or concern for infection.
pearls.verbatim: you do need to proceed to a procedure when these have failed. And we'll talk about that, what that means for when there's pressure bleeding, prolonged bleeding, keen ability to drop, concern for infection.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: failed expectant or medical management of early pregnancy loss
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: If expectant management has not succeeded by 2-3 weeks, start preparing the patient for medical or surgical options.
pearls.verbatim: So usually, I say, like, when you get to two, three weeks, if it hasn't happened, you know, you probably need to start preparing the patient that, you know, work, you know, or thinking about surgical options.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: expectant management of early pregnancy loss
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Document the study as a 'limited' ultrasound, not a complete pelvic ultrasound, for coding purposes.
pearls.verbatim: limited ultrasound. Yeah. Because this isn't a complete pelvic ultrasound. So if you're documenting, you know, you can say limited or bad ultrasound or something.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: Scan across the entire pelvis from one adnexa to the other to avoid missing twins, heterotopic pregnancy, or a giant ovarian cyst.
pearls.verbatim: you're gonna scan across because you don't wanna miss twins. You don't wanna miss a heterotopic pregnancy. You don't wanna miss a giant ovarian cyst.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: If you see a yolk sac, that helps confirm it is a true gestational sac.
pearls.verbatim: Obviously, if you have a yolk sac, that helps you know that is a gestational sac.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: If you have a good crown-rump length and cardiac activity, you do not need to obtain a mean sac diameter.
pearls.verbatim: if you get in there and you scan through and you're like, okay. There's one baby. Baby's moving, or I see a heartbeat, or I think I can get a good crown length. Like, you don't really need to get a mean sac diameter.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: early pregnancy with visible fetal pole
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: Switch to Hadlock fetal biometry at 14 weeks (second trimester).
pearls.verbatim: Switch to Hadlock at fourteen weeks.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: By 6 weeks, you should be able to see a fetal pole with a heartbeat on transvaginal ultrasound; if not, consider anembryonic gestation and repeat in one week with a formal ultrasound.
pearls.verbatim: you should be able to see by six weeks a fetal pole with a heartbeat on a transabdominal ultrasound. I wouldn't go rushing to do a DNC on this lady or anything, but I would say there's a chance you could be having a miscarriage because I don't see a fetal pole. This may be an anembryonic gestation or also called a blighted ovum. But I would repeat this in a week, and I'd probably get a formal ultrasound when I repeat it in a week just to make sure.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: patients at 5-6 weeks gestation with no fetal pole
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: If no fetal pole seen at 6 weeks, do not rush to D&C; counsel about possible miscarriage or anembryonic gestation, give ectopic precautions, and repeat ultrasound in one week.
pearls.verbatim: I wouldn't go rushing to do a DNC on this lady or anything, but I would say there's a chance you could be having a miscarriage because I don't see a fetal pole. This may be an anembryonic gestation or also called a blighted ovum. But I would repeat this in a week, and I'd probably get a formal ultrasound when I repeat it in a week just to make sure.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: pregnancy at 6 weeks with no fetal pole
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: To measure crown-rump length, rotate the probe 180 degrees keeping the baby in the middle of the screen to find the longest axis.
pearls.verbatim: I know I've gotta rotate this probe a 180 degrees, keeping this baby in the middle of the screen.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: Obtain three separate crown-rump length measurements, not one continuous frozen image.
pearls.verbatim: your three measurements, you don't wanna just keep it frozen the whole time and measure the same. Sometimes you want it frozen three separate times.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: For a patient with vaginal bleeding at 6 weeks with a gestational sac and yolk sac but no heartbeat, the appropriate ICD-10 diagnosis is threatened abortion, not embryonic demise.
pearls.verbatim: I'd call it a threatened abortion at this point.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: Practice transvaginal ultrasound whenever possible in clinic, even if it makes you run 10 minutes late, because the skill will be needed in urgent settings.
pearls.verbatim: if you can't get a transabdominal and it's gonna make you run ten minutes late in clinic, run ten minutes late in clinic and learn.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: Speak very loudly to stroke patients to overcome common hearing impairment and get the best exam.
pearls.verbatim: So if you really wanna get your best neurological stroke exam very loudly to your patient.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro Exam

pearls.text: For foot drop from peroneal nerve injury, refer to podiatry or orthotics for a stiff ankle-foot orthosis to prevent tripping during walking.
pearls.verbatim: You get them to get... You get... You send them to podiatry or to orthotics, and they make a a stiff brace that prevents their foot from ankle plantar flexing when they're walking.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.applies_to: patients with foot drop who are tripping
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: Use the SNOOP mnemonic to identify secondary headache red flags; absence of these flags suggests a primary headache that does not require imaging.
pearls.verbatim: This SNOOP mnemonic can help you think about what is a red flag or a secondary headache, meaning something that needs imaging and might need to be dealt with emergently.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: In patients over 50 with new headache, consider giant cell arteritis as a potential cause.
pearls.verbatim: So anyone over the age of 50 having new headaches. The reason why that's important is because giant cell arteritis is something you gotta start thinking about if someone's 50 and having new headaches.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: In hypertensive emergency, lower blood pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour, then to below 160/100 over the next 2, 6 hours.
pearls.verbatim: This is lowering her blood pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour. Over the next two to six hours, blood pressure should be lowered below one sixty over 100.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: Hospitalized patients are at higher risk for stroke, especially after cardiac procedures where catheter manipulation can dislodge calcium or clot from the aortic arch.
pearls.verbatim: They might have just had a cardiac procedure, which predisposes them. Any catheter can nick off pieces of calcium and and clot in the arch and can clot and that can shoot up and cause strokes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: Common causes of heart failure to remember: ischemic disease, hypertension, and valvular disease. Also consider diabetes, atrial fibrillation, rheumatologic disorders, and peripartum cardiomyopathy.
pearls.verbatim: Common causes of heart failure, ischemic disease, and then have had heart attacks. High blood pressure and valves.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: all patients with new heart failure
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: BNP >400 is pretty consistent with CHF; BNP <100 makes CHF unlikely, but cannot completely exclude it. Only order BNP when you have a clinical suspicion (dyspnea, fatigue, swelling).
pearls.verbatim: if it's more than 400, it's pretty consistent with CHF. Not a slam dunk, but it definitely fits that picture. There are other things that cause it to go up. And if it's less than a 100, probably not CHF, but you can't completely exclude it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Only three beta-blockers have mortality benefit in HFrEF: bisoprolol, carvedilol, and metoprolol succinate. Switch patients on metoprolol tartrate to one of these.
pearls.verbatim: Second thing, beta blocker. There's only three, and you have to know these because these will come up on boards and things. Lisoprolol, carvedilol, and metoclopramide. These are the ones that you need to know. These are the only ones that have decreased hospitalization mortality benefit. So if somebody has CHF and they're on metoprolol tartrate, are you gonna switch them over? Probably.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: For HFrEF, start an ARNI (or ACE/ARB) and a beta-blocker first in all patients; add spironolactone if still symptomatic, then SGLT2 inhibitor.
pearls.verbatim: Basically, everybody that's got HFrEF is going to get an ARNI, an ACE or an ARB, whichever one of the three they can get, and a beta blocker. So that's gonna be first line. You're gonna put both of those on. And then if they're still symptomatic after that, then you're gonna have spironolactone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: SGLT2 inhibitors (Jardiance, Farxiga) are heart failure medicines; you do not need diabetes to start them.
pearls.verbatim: You don't have to be on... You don't have have diabetes to start these.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Titrate beta-blocker to target dose as tolerated by heart rate and blood pressure; do not be afraid to increase metoprolol succinate from 25 mg to 200 mg daily if tolerated.
pearls.verbatim: But for somebody with a little succinate, you can start at, like, 25 a day because it's just once a day, and you're shooting for 200. That's a big jump. But I don't want you guys to be afraid to do that as long as their heart rate and their blood pressure is tolerating it because that's the goal we're shooting for.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Diuretics improve symptoms but do not reduce mortality in chronic HF.
pearls.verbatim: Diuretics improve symptoms, not mortality.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: For patients with recurrent volume overload, use torsemide instead of furosemide because torsemide is better absorbed.
pearls.verbatim: Torsemide's absorbed So if somebody is constantly volume overloaded, you would use torsemide instead of Lasix. It's going to be absorbent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: HF patients with recurrent volume overload
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Don't forget palliative care for advanced HF (stage D); it improves quality of life and may prolong survival.
pearls.verbatim: Don't forget that these people that are really sick, they're stage d, don't forget about palliative care. People that have palliative care are well taken care of if they're ahead of that one anyways. And they actually live longer and have a life.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Refer to cardiology early for EF <40% or concern for ischemic cardiomyopathy.
pearls.verbatim: If somebody's got an EF less than 40, I generally send them there because... If there's any concern for ischemic cardiomyopathy, like, they'll they'll probably need ischemic evaluation, so I refer them to cardiology then.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with EF <40% or suspected ischemic cardiomyopathy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Repeat echocardiography only with a change in clinical status, not routinely every year.
pearls.verbatim: One of the things I did see, though, is that you don't necessarily need get an echo, like, every year. But if there's a change in clinical status or there's a concern that the EDH correction may change, then yes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Echocardiography is not needed annually in stable heart failure; repeat only if there is a change in clinical status or concern that ejection fraction may change.
pearls.verbatim: you don't necessarily need get an echo, like, every year. But if there's a change in clinical status or there's a concern that the EDH correction may change, then yes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Titrate guideline-directed medical therapy to target doses even if the patient is doing well, but stop if adverse symptoms such as low blood pressure or low heart rate develop.
pearls.verbatim: I think that you wanna titrate them up to the target. But if they start having symptoms, like, especially adverse symptoms. So, like, if blood pressure starts to drop, heart rate starts to get too low, I wouldn't push it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients on GDMT for heart failure
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: When adjusting ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or Entresto, check potassium and renal function.
pearls.verbatim: you're gonna have to check the potassium, some lab work while you're adjusting the artery or even the ACE.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients starting or adjusting ACE/ARB for heart failure
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: During medication titration, follow up every two to four weeks, not every three months, depending on patient compliance and willingness.
pearls.verbatim: I would say every two to four weeks depending on how compliant the patient is and how willing they are.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing medication titration for heart failure
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Do not order a BNP without a clinical picture (symptoms of heart failure).
pearls.verbatim: You wouldn't order a BNP without a clinical picture.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Start beta-blocker therapy before hospital discharge, but not during an acute exacerbation when cardiac output is already low.
pearls.verbatim: We wanna try to start these guys before discharge if we can. ... if somebody's cardiac output is already down because they're in an acute exacerbation, trying to start a beta blocker, it's going to drop that heart rate and decrease the cardiac output.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: MRA (spironolactone/eplerenone) is contraindicated if GFR <30 or potassium >5; if potassium is borderline, try adding empagliflozin first to lower potassium so you can continue the MRA.
pearls.verbatim: contraindications can be renal function, right, if the GFR is less than 30, or if the potassium is more than five. ... If it's close, you might try adding Jardiance to see if the levels amount so that you can continue to use the spironolactone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with HFrEF being considered for MRA
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Repeat an echocardiogram 3, 6 months after starting GDMT to reassess ejection fraction.
pearls.verbatim: after you start GBMT, you're gonna repeat an echo in, like, three to six months.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with HFrEF after initiating GDMT
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Diuretics improve symptoms but do not reduce mortality in heart failure.
pearls.verbatim: Diuretics, it helps symptoms, not mortality.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Metolazone is a powerful thiazide diuretic; use it only when patients are refractory to loop diuretics, and monitor potassium closely as it can drop significantly.
pearls.verbatim: Folazone, it's a thiazide diuretic. It is powerful. So try not to do that unless people are refractory to loop diuretics. ... you really gotta watch the electrolytes. I mean, potassium will drop. Seriously.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with heart failure refractory to loop diuretics
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Start cardiac rehab early for class II, III heart failure patients; it's a good referral for motivated patients who want to improve.
pearls.verbatim: Start it early. You know? I never knew when to do this, but if somebody's class two through three, at least, I mean, all the way through. If somebody's at least class two, which is gonna be pretty much everybody that we find heart failure in, like, they're a candidate for rehabilitation with that pref.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: For stage D heart failure, do not forget to involve palliative care.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with stage D heart failure
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: After starting GDMT, recheck ejection fraction in 3, 6 months; if EF remains ≤40%, the patient still has HFrEF.
pearls.verbatim: You're gonna recheck in three to six months, kinda see where they're at. If they're still 40% or less, they're going to have HFrEF still.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Standardized handoff programs reduce medical errors by 23% and adverse events by 30%, based on a 2014 NEJM study using I-PASS.
pearls.verbatim: In 2014, New England Journal of Medicine, there's an article. It's talking about changes in medication errors after they implemented a standardized handoff program. ...the medical error rate decreased by twenty three percent just using a standardized handoff. And the adverse events decreased thirty percent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on I-Pass and Senior Addendum

pearls.text: VAERS relies on self-reporting; it captures both true adverse events and coincidental events (e.g., a death unrelated to the vaccine).
pearls.verbatim: So there's the VAERS that everybody has heard of, the Vaccine Adverse Event Report System. This relies on people to self report things. So I got a shot. Now my arm hurts. I can bring that embarrassment too. I got a shot, and then my grandma died. You know? Like, stuff like that. That's how... The whole point is you get a lot of submissions
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: For suspected melanoma, use a shave biopsy 100% of the time to give the pathologist the full lesion for accurate diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: I would use a shave a 100% of the time.

pearls.text: For rashes, use a punch biopsy to capture deeper skin layers needed for histologic evaluation.
pearls.verbatim: How about for these types of rashes? Any idea if we would use a shave or a punch? Punch. Perfect.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Mark the biopsy area before numbing with lidocaine and epinephrine to avoid blanching that obscures the lesion.
pearls.verbatim: mark your area before numbing. Sometimes if you numb with lidocaine and epinephrine, it can cause blanching, and then it can be really hard to see exactly where you wanted to biopsy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Use the free Mohs AUC app to determine if a skin cancer meets criteria for Mohs surgery referral; features include high-risk areas (face, ears, hands), cancer type, size, and aggressive pathology features.
pearls.verbatim: It is great if you're gonna be biopsying things in your clinic and you wanna know, should I send it to a general dermatologist or to a Mohs surgeon? You can plug in features of the skin cancer, and it'll tell you if it meets criteria for Mohs or not.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: skin cancers being considered for Mohs referral
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Liquid nitrogen for warts takes at least three in-office treatments on average; do not promise a one-time cure.
pearls.verbatim: Liquid nitrogen on average takes at least three in office treatments to get rid of a wart, so you just never wanna promise it's gonna be a one and done.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For patients with >6 episodes of HSV per year, consider daily suppressive antiviral therapy.
pearls.verbatim: if they're getting over six episodes a year, that's a good idea for a daily suppressive antiviral therapy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For infantile hemangiomas that are superficial and not on a highly cosmetically sensitive area, prescribe topical timolol one drop twice daily; the gel-forming solution is thicker and stays in place better.
pearls.verbatim: if it's the superficial, the strawberry type, and it's not on a super highly cosmetically sensitive area, sometimes I'll prescribe topical timolol one drop twice a day. That can be an option. They have a gel forming solution that's just little bit thicker thicker, stickier, so it doesn't go everywhere as much.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: If a hemangioma might need systemic treatment, refer urgently because they can rapidly grow at 5-7 weeks; medicines are better at preventing growth than shrinking established lesions.
pearls.verbatim: if you think it might need systemic treatment, really, they need to get in as soon as possible because they can rapidly grow at the five to seven week range. And once they've grown, it's a lot harder to shrink them. The medicines are a lot better at keeping them fully growing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: infants with hemangioma needing systemic therapy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For ulcerated hemangiomas, use good wound care with mupirocin ointment or zinc oxide-based ointment; ulceration is also a reason to consider oral propranolol.
pearls.verbatim: So that would be, like, mupirocin ointment or, like, a zinc oxide based ointment just to keep it comfortable. Because when they do ulcerate, it can be really painful for the kid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Start tretinoin at 0.025% cream, instruct patients to use no more than a pea-sized amount for the entire face, apply to dry skin before bed, and moisturize on top; if sensitive, use the sandwich method (moisturizer, tretinoin, moisturizer).
pearls.verbatim: Just tell patients no more than a pea sized amount for their entire face. You wanna put it on dry skin before they go to bed. You gotta put a moisturizer on top, or if they are pretty sensitive, they can do something sandwich method where it's moisturizer, tretinoin, moisturizer.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Start tretinoin two times a week and work up to nightly as skin tolerates; do not use in pregnancy.
pearls.verbatim: Start out maybe two times a week, work up to nightly just once their skin addressed, and then not to be used in pregnancy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: If a patient uses too much tretinoin and develops retinoid dermatitis, tell them to take a break and stop tretinoin until skin returns to normal, then restart more slowly.
pearls.verbatim: too much tretinoin or too many days in a row, they get something called retinoid dermatitis. And then the... What you do for that is just tell them to take a break, go use the tretinoin until their skin goes back to normal, and then just be a little bit slower about using it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: patients with retinoid dermatitis from tretinoin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For benzoyl peroxide, recommend PanOxyl or CeraVe; use 4% for the face and 10% for truncal breakouts.
pearls.verbatim: PanOxyl or CeraVe. This one specifically with benzoyl peroxide a lot. In two strengths of four percent, which is good for the face, and then ten percent if they have more truncal breakouts.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Do not use antibiotics for acne for more than three months; the typical oral antibiotic is doxycycline 100 mg daily or BID, with counseling on photosensitivity, heartburn, nausea, and avoidance in pregnancy.
pearls.verbatim: I don't really use a lot of antibiotics in acne. No. Never more than three months duration, not long term. The one that I typically use is doxycycline. You can do it a hundred daily or bid. Counsel on photosensitivity, heartburn, nausea, and also not in pregnancy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: patients with acne on oral antibiotics
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Spironolactone is a favorite acne medicine for women; start at 100 mg daily, can be divided 50 mg BID, but once daily is easier; take with food, preferably at dinner time.
pearls.verbatim: My typical starting dose is a hundred milligrams daily. You can divide it to fifty BID, but it's always easier for compliance to take it once a day. It is absorbed better if they take it with food. Typically, just say take it at dinner time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For spironolactone, potassium monitoring is not needed in young healthy women; start checking potassium in early to mid-40s or if on other antihypertensives.
pearls.verbatim: early to mid forties is when we start checking potassium. And if there aren't any other antihypertensives would also be a good reason to check that. And then, otherwise, young, healthy women don't need any blood monitoring.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Spironolactone takes at least 2-3 months to kick in, up to 6 months for full benefit; after months to a year of clear skin, consider a trial off or dose reduction to 50 mg daily.
pearls.verbatim: It's at least two to three months to kick in, really even up to six months to show full benefit. Can be considered a long term treatment. We know that hormonal acne is chronic. And then it's a good idea if, like, they've been clear for months to a year every so often maybe to try to take a break from the medicine, see if they still use it, or try to go down to fifty daily and see if things are still controlled.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For perioral dermatitis, never use topical steroids; treat with antibiotics, Protopic (tacrolimus), or Elidel (pimecrolimus).
pearls.verbatim: Steroid. Steroid. Perfect. Yes. No topical steroids. So it's kinda considered a mix between acne or rosacea and eczema. We treat it often with antibiotics, Protopic or Elidel.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Folliculitis is commonly seen in men on testosterone supplements or people taking whey protein; encourage loose-fitting clothing; treat with benzoyl peroxide wash, clindamycin lotion, or oral antibiotics.
pearls.verbatim: I see it commonly in guys on testosterone supplements or people who are taking pens of whey protein. Wanna encourage them to wear loose fitting clothing. This would be a good use of, like, a benzoyl peroxide based wash, can sometimes treat with clindamycin motion, oral antibiotics, and in some cases, even interact.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Pityrosporum folliculitis is monomorphic tiny red bumps and pustules due to yeast Malassezia, more common with humidity, high oil, or prior antibiotic use; it has no comedones.
pearls.verbatim: it's like they kinda describe it as being monomorphic. So it's just all these tiny little red bumps and pus bumps due to a a yeast Malassezia, more common humidity, high oil, or prior antibiotic use.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For an abscess, do a ring block with lidocaine, use an 11 blade to pierce, apply gentle pressure from the sides, and always culture to know what you are dealing with.
pearls.verbatim: What I do when I see these is I do kind of a ring block. I just numb all around it and then use 11 blade, pierce it, gentle pressure from the sides. Always a good idea to culture just to see exactly what you're dealing with.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For hidradenitis suppurativa, never pack abscesses because it can be painful and introduces a foreign body to an inflammatory wound; intralesional Kenalog (triamcinolone) injection can be used for inflammatory lesions.
pearls.verbatim: never pack it, first of all. Don't pack it yet. And then you could probably drain it just to give them some relief. Or sometimes I'll do an intralesional Kenalog injection into them.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For eczema, avoid long hot showers, baths, and hot tubs; use a gentle soap like Dove; pat dry after showering; apply steroid or nonsteroid topical to active areas, then moisturizer all over.
pearls.verbatim: no long hot showers, hot baths, hot tubs, no lupus or washcloths. A gentle soap like Dove is what I recommend. You get out of the shower. No vigorous toweling dry. Just pat dry. Use a steroid or a nonsteroid topical on active areas, and then put your moisturizer all over.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For applying to hands twice a day for one month, prescribe a 30-gram tube (1 gram per day).
pearls.verbatim: if you were gonna apply to, like, your hands, for example, just your hands, twice a day for one month, it would be one gram a day. So a thirty gram tube for a month would be a good amount.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: outpatient topical steroid prescription for hands
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Calm eyelid dermatitis with a short round of topical steroids for a week or two, then switch to a calcineurin inhibitor like Elidel or Protopic.
pearls.verbatim: You can calm down with a short round of topical steroids, like, for a week or two, and then maybe switch to those calcineurin inhibitors like Elidel or Protopic.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Drug rashes can appear months or years after starting a medication and may take up to three months to resolve after discontinuation.
pearls.verbatim: in many cases, the patient could have been on the medicine for months or years before the rash develops. And then even once you stop the medicine, it can take up to three months until the rash gets better.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For hand dermatitis, advise using hand sanitizer instead of water when possible, and if washing hands, use cold water and apply moisturizer after.
pearls.verbatim: Try to use the hand sanitizer instead of water when possible. And if you have to wash your hands, it must be cold water. And then apply a moisturizer after cleaning the hands.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For painful fissures on hands, consider applying super glue to glue them together, or wear Vaseline and gloves at bedtime; topical timolol can also promote wound healing.
pearls.verbatim: Sometimes people have success putting super glue on their fissures and gluing them together. Sometimes too, just wearing Vaseline and gloves for a couple nights at bedtime can help. And then the other thing that can sometimes help is topical timolol can help promote wound healing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For asteototic eczema (dry skin eczema with cracked riverbed appearance), advise avoiding hot water, rubbing, and scratching; treat with moisturizer and triamcinolone for itch.
pearls.verbatim: This is specifically called aseototic eczema, dry skin eczema, and it's really pots of hot water, rubbing, scratching, and then you treat moisturizer and triamcinolone of itchy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: elderly patients with dry, cracked skin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: The 'two foot one hand' pattern (both feet and one hand involved) is a classic sign of tinea; if suspected, obtain fungal culture and avoid topical steroids.
pearls.verbatim: It involves both feet and just one hand, and then the other hand is totally normal. Very weird. But it's... That's a sign of tinea. If you think it might be tinea, get fungal culture and definitely avoid topical steroids.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For tinea capitis, check for occipital lymphadenopathy; culture to identify species: terbinafine is better for Trichophyton; treat for 8 weeks.
pearls.verbatim: Check for occipital lymphadenopathy. That can be a good tip-off that it is tinea. If you get the culture and it comes back as trichophyton, terbinafine is the better option, whereas microsporum is better. And then it really takes eight weeks of therapy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: children with scaling scalp and hair loss
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Avoid systemic steroids in psoriasis; they can cause flare or pustular psoriasis.
pearls.verbatim: You wanna avoid systemic steroids in psoriasis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For intertrigo, look for satellite pustules as a clue that it is yeast; be very careful with topical steroids, prolonged use on the thighs can cause severe steroid atrophy.
pearls.verbatim: If it is yeast, you see these satellite pustules. So these little tiny dots extending from the rash. That's a clue that it actually is yeast. And then be really careful about steroids for this. I've seen the worst cases of steroid atrophy ever on the thighs from being treated for intertrigo with triamcinolone for a long time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: patients with rash in body folds
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For suspected preeclampsia, order CBC (platelets), CMP (creatinine, LFTs), and urine protein:creatinine ratio; in resource-poor settings, 2+ protein on dipstick can be used but P:C ratio is preferred.
pearls.verbatim: So I would be getting a CBC. I'd be getting a chem 14 or a CMP. I'd be getting a urine protein creatinine ratio.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Youmans
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy

pearls.text: Gestational hypertension with BP in the 140s, 150s can be managed outpatient with weekly NST, BP check, glucose check, and growth ultrasound every 3 weeks; antihypertensives are only indicated for severe-range BP (≥160/110).
pearls.verbatim: giving antihypertensive medicines is only effective and is associated with improved outcomes if it's in the severe range.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Youmans
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy

pearls.text: For gestational hypertension without severe features, manage outpatient with weekly MFM visits including NST, blood pressure check, glucose check, and growth ultrasounds every three weeks.
pearls.verbatim: outpatient by MFM weekly for an NST blood pressure check and a glucose check and then growth ultrasounds every three weeks.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Youmans
pearls.applies_to: pregnant women with gestational hypertension without severe features
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy

pearls.text: Ask about pregnancy history (gestational hypertension, preeclampsia) when assessing cardiovascular risk in women, as it is a risk enhancer for heart scoring and pre-test probability.
pearls.verbatim: One question that I will now be asking is, tell me about your pregnancy history. Did you have gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, those types of things? Because that is a risk enhancer for, like, heart scoring, TIMI scoring.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Youmans
pearls.applies_to: women being evaluated for cardiovascular disease
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy

pearls.text: A history of gestational hypertension or preeclampsia confers a fourfold relative risk increase for future cardiovascular disease, which is higher than the threefold risk from diabetes.
pearls.verbatim: ladies that have had these types of conditions are at a fourfold relative risk increase for cardiovascular disease.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Youmans
pearls.applies_to: women with history of pregnancy-induced hypertension
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy

pearls.text: Counsel women with a history of gestational hypertension to maintain a healthy weight, especially avoid central obesity, as it strongly predicts poor cardiovascular outcomes.
pearls.verbatim: But being mindful and reminding her, hey. We have to keep a healthy weight. Hey. We have to watch the salt in our diet. The biggest thing is is watching weight. Because they find ladies who have increased central obesity in addition to having this history of pregnancy induced hypertension, they have poor outcomes compared to ladies who had a healthy weight after they had pregnancy induced hypertension.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Youmans
pearls.applies_to: women with history of pregnancy-induced hypertension
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy

pearls.text: Postpartum, counsel women with pregnancy-induced hypertension on weight management, diet, and exercise, as central obesity combined with this history leads to poor outcomes.
pearls.verbatim: Being mindful and reminding her, hey. We have to keep a healthy weight. Hey. We have to watch the salt in our diet. The biggest thing is is watching weight.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Youmans
pearls.applies_to: postpartum women with history of pregnancy-induced hypertension
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy

pearls.text: For preeclampsia with severe features at 35 weeks, start magnesium, consult MFM, and proceed with induction; expect a prolonged induction (about 1.5 days), and counsel the mother that the baby may be sleepy from magnesium and likely require NICU admission.
pearls.verbatim: Yeah. No. That's what happened with me. I think it was a Monday. I think that night I came in. I was admitted. I started Mag that night. I was on mag overnight. And then the next morning, we talked with MFM, and we started my induction. And it took a day and a half because I was thirty five weeks and five days at that point. Yeah, and then we had a healthy healthy baby boy the following night. It was a Wednesday night. He was a little sleepy because he was on Max, so just counseling your moms on that. Likely, baby will not stay with them and hang out in the in the the delivery room. They will likely go to the NICU unless they're just camps, which doesn't happen very frequently. Just counseling your moms on that so it's not like this horrible distress when they first realize that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Youmans
pearls.applies_to: patients with preeclampsia with severe features at 35 weeks gestation
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy

pearls.text: Inform patients that their relative risk of heart attack or stroke is 4 times higher than women without a history of pregnancy-induced hypertension, even if they are young.
pearls.verbatim: hey. You're at an increased risk for this. The relative risk of cardiovascular disease, it's relative to a lady that has their same background just without pregnancy induced hypertension. A lady that is 29 is not likely going to have a heart attack or a stroke. I am four times more likely to have a heart attack or a stroke, but it's a relative risk.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Youmans
pearls.applies_to: women with history of pregnancy-induced hypertension
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy

pearls.text: Recommend annual blood pressure checks for all women after pregnancy-induced hypertension to monitor long-term cardiovascular risk.
pearls.verbatim: yearly for a blood pressure check and and just their general well-being
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Youmans
pearls.applies_to: women with history of pregnancy-induced hypertension
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy

pearls.text: Consider PV in younger women (<45) who present with Budd-Chiari syndrome or portal/splenic/mesenteric vein thrombosis.
pearls.verbatim: And then another reason to suspect it would be in patients with Budd-Chiari syndrome and portal splenic or mesenteric vein thrombosis, especially if you're seeing that in a woman, a younger woman less than 45.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Harris on Polycythemia Vera

pearls.text: For diagnosis of PV, rule out secondary causes first: cardiopulmonary disease, chronic hypoxia, left-to-right shunts, EPO-producing tumors, high altitude, testosterone, steroids, blood doping, renal disease, sleep apnea, obesity hypoventilation, smoking/chronic CO poisoning.
pearls.verbatim: So here's just some examples of what could cause a secondary erythrocytosis, and they all make pretty decent sense. So cardiopulmonary disease, chronic hypoxia, left to right shunts, any sort of erythropoietin producing tumor, of course, is gonna elevate the red red blood cells. High altitude habitat. Iatrogenic. So if people are taking testosterone, steroids, or blood doping, renal disease

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Harris on Polycythemia Vera

pearls.text: None of the treatments for PV reduce the risk of transformation to leukemia or other malignancies; the goal is symptom control and reducing thrombotic risk.
pearls.verbatim: Unfortunately, none of the treatments reduce their risk of conversion or transformation to leukemia or anything more severe. So, really, what you're trying to do is just keep their symptoms or their risk of thrombosis or things like that at a minimum.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Harris
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Harris on Polycythemia Vera

pearls.text: One unit of therapeutic phlebotomy (500 mL) reduces hematocrit by 3 percentage points, use this to calculate how many units a patient needs.
pearls.verbatim: And one unit of phlebotomy, which is five hundred mils, should reduce your hematocrit by three percentage points.

pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing therapeutic phlebotomy for PV
