pearls.verbatim: So also on the differential for diabetics is starvation ketosis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.applies_to: diabetic patients with ketosis and low oral intake
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25

pearls.text: Do not use urine ketones to monitor DKA resolution; acetoacetate persists longer in the system and will give false positive results.
pearls.verbatim: so you can't use urine ketones to tell when someone is out of DKA, because acetoacetate sticks around longer in the system.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25

pearls.text: Urine dipstick can be negative early in DKA; use serum ketones instead.
pearls.verbatim: you can miss DKA if it's early, then their dipstick could be negative.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.applies_to: clinic setting when evaluating possible DKA
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25

pearls.text: If you use urine ketones to monitor DKA treatment you can overtreat because the urine dipstick stays positive longer than serum ketones.
pearls.verbatim: if you're using that to monitor when they're treated, you could overtreat because their dipstick will be longer... Will be faster longer.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25

pearls.text: When investigating the cause of DKA/HHS, first consider infection; then consider medication issues (nonadherence, steroids, checkpoint inhibitors).
pearls.verbatim: The top three reasons are infection, infection, infection, and then the next three are medication, medication, medication.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25

pearls.text: IV fluids are the mainstay of treatment for DKA; start fluids before insulin.
pearls.verbatim: after initiating IV fluids, because you know the fluids are the mainstay of treatment
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25

pearls.text: Do not use anion gap to determine DKA resolution; normal saline can cause hyperchloremic acidosis that falsely elevates the gap.
pearls.verbatim: Fluids, ones that we give, right, normal saline have a lot of chlorine in them. You can get a hyperchloremic acidosis, and that will elevate your anion gap. And you will think someone's still in DKA, and they're not.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.applies_to: patients with DKA receiving normal saline
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25

pearls.text: Initial potassium cutoff for supplementation in DKA is serum K <5.0; recheck in about 2 hours as insulin drives K intracellularly.
pearls.verbatim: We didn't have to give anything because we looked up that it's, like, five is the cutoff. So we were just like, we'll recheck it in, like, two hours or so.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25

pearls.text: Subcutaneous insulin may be less reliable in vasoconstricted patients; consider IV insulin in that setting.
pearls.verbatim: If someone's vasoconstricted, there's argument that maybe a subcutaneous insulin won't be as effective. You know? It's gonna be absorbed as reliably.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25

pearls.text: Never give potassium in DKA/HHS until the patient has urinated ('no P, no K').
pearls.verbatim: Dr. Mathis, no P, no K. You never give someone, especially DKA/HHS, potassium until they've peed.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25

pearls.text: The risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw from bisphosphonates increases after more than 4 years of use.
pearls.verbatim: It's more than four. If you've been on it more than four years, your risk goes up.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Avoid daily bisphosphonate dosing due to gastrointestinal side effects; prefer weekly or monthly regimens.
pearls.verbatim: try to avoid the daily dosing because of the GI side effects.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Levothyroxine must be taken on an empty stomach, and patients must wait at least one hour before taking bisphosphonate or eating.
pearls.verbatim: Your Synthroid has to be first on the empty stomach. An hour... Always. It doesn't matter. Always Synthroid only, empty stomach. Wait an hour before you eat or take other meds.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.applies_to: patients on levothyroxine and oral bisphosphonate
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: In patients with abnormal TSH while on levothyroxine, ask about biotin supplementation as it can interfere with TSH assays.
pearls.verbatim: Ask them about Biotin. That's a bonus tip.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.applies_to: patients on levothyroxine with abnormal TSH
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Before administering denosumab, check a chem 8 with calcium to avoid giving it to someone who is hypocalcemic.
pearls.verbatim: you do have to have a current CAM-eight with a calcium level on it, so you don't wanna give it to someone who's hyper... Hypocalcemia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Before administering denosumab, check a complete metabolic panel with calcium to avoid giving it to a hypocalcemic patient.
pearls.verbatim: a current CAM-eight with a calcium level on it, so you don't wanna give it to someone who's hypocalcemia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: For severe osteoporosis (e.g., after a fragility fracture), start teriparatide or romosozumab rather than a bisphosphonate.
pearls.verbatim: Severe osteoporosis. You would perhaps go to teriparatide and ranosumab. I don't think you would start with bisphosphonate.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Repeat DEXA two years after starting osteoporosis treatment; for normal bone density, repeat every five years.
pearls.verbatim: Maybe repeat it in two years after you start treatment. If you have someone with normal bone density, five years repeat their DEXA scan.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.applies_to: patients on osteoporosis treatment or with normal bone density
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Before starting osteoporosis therapy, check vitamin D levels and consider TSH if secondary osteoporosis is suspected.
pearls.verbatim: Before you start treatment, make sure to get a vitamin D because, obviously, if you don't have the blocks to build the building, then it's not as helpful. Check your vitamin D. If you're worried that they may have, like, a secondary osteoporosis, then you would also get, like, a TSH.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.applies_to: all patients before starting osteoporosis treatment
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Only order a DEXA scan if the patient is willing to consider pharmacologic treatment; if not, focus on exercise and nutrition.
pearls.verbatim: if they're not gonna consider treatment, this is a nice public health, you know, approach. Like, if they're not gonna be treated, then don't get the test.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.applies_to: patients with risk factors for osteoporosis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Use the FRAX tool to estimate 10-year fracture risk; it works without DEXA data. Consider treatment if hip fracture risk exceeds 3% or total fracture risk exceeds 20%.
pearls.verbatim: Get a frack. And then you would consider treatment if their hip fracture risk over ten years is three percent or their total fracture risk of any osteoporosis related fracture is greater than twenty percent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.applies_to: adults with osteopenia or risk factors
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Consider treatment if 10-year hip fracture risk is 3% or total osteoporosis-related fracture risk is >20%, as calculated by FRAX.
pearls.verbatim: consider treatment if their hip fracture risk over ten years is three percent or their total fracture risk of any osteoporosis related fracture is greater than twenty percent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.applies_to: patients with osteopenia or risk factors asking about fracture risk
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: For patients starting osteoporosis treatment, recommend 1000 mg of calcium and 800 IU of vitamin D daily, and check vitamin D level before starting.
pearls.verbatim: the recommended patient is still a thousand of calcium and eight hundred of vitamin D. But I check their vitamin D before I start treatment, and so then I know if I need to replace it, I have to take more.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Calcium from food is better than calcium supplements because supplements increase the risk of kidney stones.
pearls.verbatim: calcium from food is always gonna be better than supplementing calcium fills because that increases their ASG.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Do not repeat DEXA more often than every 2 years.
pearls.verbatim: don't do yearly DEXA scans or do it more than... More often than two years.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Biotin supplements cause a falsely low TSH on lab tests; patients should stop biotin at least 2 days before checking TSH.
pearls.verbatim: The biotin causes a, on labs, a falsely lower TSH. So they need to stop their biotin at least two days before you check their TSH.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: After 5 years of bisphosphonate therapy, the benefit decreases and the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw increases, so consider a drug holiday.
pearls.verbatim: The risk of osteoporosis if the jaw goes up, and the benefit of taking the bisphosphonate goes way down.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: Universal vitamin D screening is not helpful; check vitamin D only after a diagnosis of osteopenia or osteoporosis is made.
pearls.verbatim: It is for universal screening. So if you were just getting vitamin D on everybody. So now I've changed to... Okay. Am I worried about their bone health legitimately? I've got a diagnosis now. I'm gonna check their way.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hildebrand
pearls.applies_to: general population vs. patients with bone health diagnosis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis

pearls.text: In sports medicine, avoid increasing exercise volume more than 10% per week to prevent overuse injuries.
pearls.verbatim: Try to not increase your volume of exercise more than 10% a week.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: For osteitis pubis, refer to physical therapy after six weeks of failed conservative measures; steroid injection into the pubic symphysis is an option but requires referral.
pearls.verbatim: So if after six weeks, conservative measures are still having problems, I would think about referral.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.applies_to: patients with osteitis pubis unresponsive to conservative care
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: For suspected Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, prescribe non-weight-bearing and refer to pediatric orthopedics; early containment with splinting can lead to full recovery.
pearls.verbatim: Non weight bearing, do you suspect this? And refer to peds orthopedics.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: For slipped capital femoral epiphysis, treatment is usually surgery, though occasionally immobilization is used; refer to orthopedics.
pearls.verbatim: The treatment is gonna be referring to work of usually surgery, but occasionally, they can just immobilize.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: When groin pain has no clear injury, consider testicular torsion, epididymitis, inguinal hernia, lymphadenopathy, or malignancy in the differential.
pearls.verbatim: you gotta think through a little bit through the groin pain differential. Right? And if it's a male testicular torsion, epididymitis, either either sex inguinal hernia or lymphadenopathy, you know, cold malignancy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.applies_to: patients with groin pain without traumatic injury
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: Iliopsoas bursitis can present with hip pain, swelling, and even an inguinal mass; use ultrasound or MRI to rule out hernia, lymphadenopathy, or cancer.
pearls.verbatim: And it'll present with hip pain, swelling, and maybe even an inguinal mass. So imaging, ultrasound may help. MRI may help. And and particularly to rule out other things in this area, like hernia, lymphadenopathy, or cancer.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: For iliopsoas bursitis, treatment includes relative rest, NSAIDs, oral steroids, and physical therapy; refer if not relieved after conservative measures.
pearls.verbatim: And the treatment for this would be relative rest, NSAIDs, oral steroids, physical therapy. And then if it's not relieved, then refer once you've done that conservatively.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: Psoas abscess/vertebral osteomyelitis can present with back pain, muscle spasms, fever, chills, rigors, and a sense of feeling septic; CT or MRI is best for diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: I then felt the symptoms of being septic, which were fever, chills, rigors, general sense of feeling awful.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.applies_to: patients with severe back pain and systemic symptoms
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: For greater trochanteric pain syndrome, palpate tenderness over the superior posterior aspect of the greater trochanter.
pearls.verbatim: you wanna look for tenderness over the superior posterior aspect of the greater trochanter mostly. So kind of the back... The upper back corner of that greater greater trochanter is where it's gonna be most tender.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected greater trochanteric pain syndrome
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: The resisted abduction test for greater trochanteric pain: patient lies on side with affected side up, extends knee and hip, then abducts leg against gentle resistance; reproduction of pain is specific.
pearls.verbatim: So you have them lay kinda on their side with the affected side up and then extend their leg and hip... Their knee and hip. And then you have them try to abduct their their leg, and you kinda give some gentle back pressure. If that reproduces the pain, that's pretty specific for that area and those tendons.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: For greater trochanteric pain syndrome, give conservative treatment (PT, NSAIDs, activity modification) about three months; if not better, consider MRI; if not better after twelve months, consider orthopedic referral.
pearls.verbatim: So I give those conservative things about three months. If they're not better, you might consider an MRI. If after twelve months they're not better, you might think about orthopedic referral
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.applies_to: patients with greater trochanteric pain syndrome
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: Don't spend 35 minutes doing a complex exam to tell if it's a bursa or the tendon; instead, hone the diagnosis to give exercises.
pearls.verbatim: Don't spend thirty five minutes doing a, you know, complex exam to tell if it's a bursa or the tendon or which one.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: You do want to hone down the diagnosis so you know how to best give them exercises.
pearls.verbatim: You do wanna hone down so you know how to best give them exercises.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jeff Perry
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies

pearls.text: For severe poison ivy, use a longer course of oral steroids rather than a Medrol dose pack; give all the dose in the morning to avoid sleep disruption.
pearls.verbatim: I don't really like mineral dose packs because you're supposed to take two in the morning, two at lunchtime, two at night. A nighttime dose usually screws their sleep up pretty bad. So it's better just to give it all in the morning.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: For severe poison ivy, start with 20 mg prednisone in the afternoon, then 60 mg the next morning.
pearls.verbatim: Now they have terrible poison ivy. I see them at 04:00 in the afternoon. We'll go ahead and take twenty milligrams this afternoon, and then tomorrow, you'll start sixty milligrams.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: For herpes simplex suppression, use valacyclovir 500 mg once daily if the patient has more than 3-4 outbreaks per year, typically for one year.
pearls.verbatim: valacyclovir is probably the easiest to give them five hundred milligrams once a day usually. So they're having, like, more than three or four outbreaks a year, then usually, I'll give them suppressive medicine for a year to try and get it calmed down.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.applies_to: patients with frequent herpes simplex outbreaks
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: When a rash is confusing, examine the whole patient; a review of systems, including genital exam, can reveal syphilis or other systemic causes.
pearls.verbatim: So I did the medical student review systems. So I got down to her areas. I said, well, you're having any trouble with your genitals? She turned crimson. So then I got my nurse, and so she had a primary chancre, and so she had secondary syphilis. So it can just look like crazy stuff. But but sometimes when you're kinda stumped with a derm patient, it's a good idea to kinda look them over, especially can.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: For zoster, give a low dose of gabapentin early for pain, especially in older patients, as it may reduce postherpetic neuralgia.
pearls.verbatim: I'm pretty quick to give them a low dose of gabapentin for pain, especially if they're older, because it seems like if you treat them early, they have less postherpetic neuralgia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: For bullous impetigo in children, avoid tetracyclines due to teeth staining; use a cephalosporin instead and follow up in 1, 2 days.
pearls.verbatim: I can give it to them for ten days. It's not gonna stain their teeth, but it's kinda contraindicated to people who have unrupt teeth.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: For blistering dactylitis in a child, use a cephalosporin and follow closely; if high fever or inability to move the finger, refer to a hand surgeon.
pearls.verbatim: So I'd probably give this kid a cephalosporin and keep my fingers crossed, but then I'd probably have him come back in a day or two too. Usually, what's... You know, kids usually get better fast, though. And then now if they ran a high fever and they couldn't move their finger at all, I would probably send this kid to Children's and let them decide if they wanna have a hand surgeon look at this too.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: In a child with bullous impetigo and high fever with inability to move a finger, consider deeper infection and refer to pediatric hand surgery.
pearls.verbatim: if they ran a high fever and they couldn't move their finger at all, I would probably send this kid to Children's and let them decide if they wanna have a hand surgeon look at this too.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.applies_to: children with bullous impetigo and high fever/finger immobility
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: For scabies, permethrin requires full-body application and repeat in 10 days; oral ivermectin is convenient but may have insurance barriers.
pearls.verbatim: With permethrin, you're trying to cover every square just in from the neck gap. So you put it on, and then, ideally, you wait ten days to do it again. ... I think that's why it's nice to use ivermectin that cover it also.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: All patients with dermatitis herpetiformis have gluten sensitivity; confirm with perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence.
pearls.verbatim: supposedly everyone that has dermatitis herpetiformis also has, you know, gluten neuropathy, but probably the ideal way is the biopsy for human direct immunofluorescence.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: For pemphigus vulgaris with severe oral involvement, start prednisone even before biopsy results if the patient has trouble swallowing.
pearls.verbatim: ideally, you would biopsy him, but you could start him with prednisone because he's having trouble swallowing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.applies_to: patients with pemphigus vulgaris and dysphagia
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: Rituximab is effective for pemphigus vulgaris; consider consulting hematology/oncology for administration.
pearls.verbatim: I think I just feel a lot more comfortable asking hem/onc to do this because they do it all the time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.applies_to: patients with pemphigus vulgaris starting rituximab
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: For biopsy of blistering disorders, use a 4 mm punch including half normal skin and half blister; for direct immunofluorescence, send in Michel's media (not formalin).
pearls.verbatim: for biopsy of a blistering disorder, what I like to do is a four millimeter punch. I'll try and get half the punch on normal skin and half of the blister. ... to get a immunofluorescence biopsy, you have to use Michel's media. If you send it in on formalin, they just can't do it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected autoimmune blistering disease
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: Bullous pemphigoid may begin with urticarial plaques; early perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence can confirm diagnosis before blisters appear.
pearls.verbatim: some patients are cruel enough to start with kind of an urticarial form. ... if you biopsy this and do a direct immunofluorescence next to it, you'll get your answer ahead of time instead of waiting for them to get both.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.applies_to: patients with urticarial plaques suspicious for bullous pemphigoid
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome presents as diffuse sunburn-like erythema with skin pain, not discrete lesions; always check drug history, especially for lamotrigine.
pearls.verbatim: Stevens Johnson, usually, it's more like a sunburn. It's usually not discrete lesions. ... pretty much always, it just looks like a solid sunburn. And then usually Stevens-Johnson's patients will tell you their skin hurts. And then there's almost always a good drug history.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: Lamotrigine is a common cause of Stevens-Johnson syndrome; any new drug causing a generalized rash should be stopped immediately.
pearls.verbatim: if somebody started a new medicine, you should probably stop it if they got a generalized rash. ... Lamictal is famous for causing Stevens Johnson syndrome.
pearls.speaker: Dr. John Ashley
pearls.applies_to: patients on lamotrigine or any new drug with generalized rash
pearls.episode_title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25

pearls.text: Sixty percent of women with STDs have no symptoms, but they may still have scarring. On bimanual exam, check mobility of the uterus, a fixed uterus suggests prior infection.
pearls.verbatim: Sixty percent of women with STDs have symptoms. That doesn't mean they don't have scarring. So patients who've never... Who've denied having anything at all. Signs of infection. I examine the pelvis, and the uterus is fixed.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Adnexal Masses 1/22/26

pearls.text: Submucosal fibroids are associated with menorrhagia (heavy bleeding); intramural fibroids are also associated with bleeding; subserosal fibroids are felt as lumps on exam.
pearls.verbatim: Submucosal fibroids are associated with menorrhagia hairy bleeding. Intramural associated with bleeding. So subserosal beneath the uterine surface. As to the lumps you feel.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Adnexal Masses 1/22/26

pearls.text: In a 60-year-old woman, you probably should not feel an ovary at all; if you do, get an ultrasound to rule out cancer.
pearls.verbatim: in a woman who's 60 years old, you probably shouldn't feel an ovary at all.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Adnexal Masses 12/4/25

pearls.text: In PCOS, ultrasound shows 10-15 follicles of similar size; management depends on pregnancy desire, if not, ensure endometrial shedding at least yearly and screen for diabetes.
pearls.verbatim: They have to find 10 to 15 of them that are same size.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Adnexal Masses 12/4/25

pearls.text: If a woman with PCOS does not desire pregnancy, you must ensure she empties her uterus at least once a year to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer.
pearls.verbatim: We have to make sure she empties her uterus at least once a year. A year.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Adnexal Masses 12/4/25

pearls.text: For a functional simple cyst less than 10 cm, observe with repeat ultrasound in 3 months; most will resolve.
pearls.verbatim: Three months. And so if you wanna follow it, then you're gonna get an ultrasound in three months. Almost always, it's gone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
pearls.applies_to: premenopausal women with simple cysts <10 cm
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Adnexal Masses 12/4/25

pearls.text: Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst appears as a complex cyst with internal solid structure suggesting blood clot on ultrasound.
pearls.verbatim: Complex. Complex. Mhmm. Internal solid structure suggesting blood clot. This is a hemorrhagic ovarian cyst.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Adnexal Masses 12/4/25

pearls.text: A hemorrhagic ovarian cyst presents with gradually increasing pain after ovulation and shows internal solid structure (clot) on ultrasound; management is observation, not surgery.
pearls.verbatim: and so that's where the pain gradually increases. And on ultrasound, we see this clot.

pearls.text: Thicken formula with 1 tablespoon of dry infant oat cereal per ounce; do not use rice cereal due to arsenic concerns, and do not thicken breast milk because amylase breaks down the thickener.
pearls.verbatim: thicken feeds. We can't do this with breast milk because, actually, if you put the thickener in breast milk, the amylase in breast milk dissolves it too fast and becomes thin again.

pearls.text: Nicotine exposure decreases lower esophageal sphincter tone and increases reflux; counsel families to avoid smoking around the infant.
pearls.verbatim: for the smokers in your populations, you're supposed to avoid smoking inhalation because of nicotine that decreases LES tone and therefore increase reflux.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Keller on Infant Gastroesophageal 4/16/26

pearls.text: 40% of infants with GERD have cow's milk protein intolerance; if reflux is excessive, consider a trial of hypoallergenic formula.
pearls.verbatim: switch them from the cow's milk or soy based formulas, especially if they have cow's milk protein intolerance like symptoms like blood in their stool or eczema or family history of allergies, atopy, that kind of thing because forty percent of infants with gastroesophageal reflux disease have a food protein intolerance.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Keller on Infant Gastroesophageal 4/16/26

pearls.text: Bright red blood in stool may indicate proctocolitis; check for anal fissures with a spread sheet exam, and if found, use MiraLAX to keep stools consistently soft.
pearls.verbatim: But in your exam room, check for an anal fissure because that can happen. You get big stools in there, and then babies hoard, and then they tear. pearls.text: Nexium (esomeprazole) comes in delayed release granules in 2.5, 5, and 10 mg packets; add a teaspoon of water, wait a couple minutes for it to thicken, then syringe into the side of the mouth.

pearls.text: Most infant reflux resolves by 1 year; reassure parents that it is normal and developmental, and they do not need to try multiple formulas or medications.

pearls.text: SSRIs are contraindicated in bipolar disorder; they can flip someone into mania.

pearls.text: In a patient with chest pain, shortness of breath, hypotension, and low-voltage EKG, perform a subxiphoid cardiac POCUS to evaluate for pericardial effusion.
pearls.verbatim: 47 year old woman with metastatic breast cancer presents to the ED with chest pain and shortness of breath. On arrival, she is hypotensive, and her initial EKG shows sinus tachycardia with low voltage. Point of care cardiac ultrasound is performed.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac POCUS 10/9/25

pearls.text: Assess myocardial thickening by comparing the muscle thickness at end-diastole (completely relaxed) versus end-systole (completely contracted). Expect at least a 30% increase, visually, it should almost double.
pearls.verbatim: increases by at least 50%. Right? And, really, it's almost doubling in size.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: any patient undergoing point-of-care cardiac ultrasound
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound

pearls.text: Ultrasound is never standalone, it answers a specific clinical question (reduced EF? effusion? wall motion abnormality?) and must be interpreted within the whole clinical picture.
pearls.verbatim: Ultrasound is never standalone. It's just answering a question. What is your question in that patient? Does this patient have a reduced EF? Yes or no? Does this patient have a pericardial effusion? Yes or no? Does this patient have a wall motion abnormality? Yes or no?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound

pearls.text: For a patient with known aortic dissection who is not actively dissecting but has severely elevated BP, give clonidine in clinic and observe for a couple of hours.
pearls.verbatim: This might be somebody that you give them clonidine in clinic and make them sit here for a couple hours to make sure their blood pressure goes down.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: patients with known aortic dissection (not actively dissecting) in clinic
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Hypertension

pearls.text: In patients aged 65 and older, start antihypertensive therapy with a low dose of a single medication to avoid relative hypotension.
pearls.verbatim: If they were old, 65 and up, probably be more inclined to just start them on a low dose of one medication.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Hypertension

pearls.text: Adjusting a patient's lisinopril dose in the hospital for elevated BP often leads to hypotension after discharge; avoid changing home medications unless there is an acute indication like NSTEMI or heart failure.
pearls.verbatim: You address their lisinopril while they're in the hospital because blood pressure's high. They go home, and they become hypotensive.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Hypertension

pearls.text: Parameters for PRN blood pressure medications are acceptable in preeclampsia and stroke protocol, but even then, it's not just the numbers, it's the underlying condition.
pearls.verbatim: Parameters is usually not good enough. It's good enough in preeclampsia. It's good enough in a stroke protocol. But even even then, it's not just the numbers. It's the fact that they have preeclampsia. It's the fact that they had a stroke.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Hypertension

pearls.text: If you suspect hypertensive emergency, send the patient to the emergency room.
pearls.verbatim: Alright. So if you think it's hypertensive emergency, just go to ER.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Hypertension

pearls.text: Always try to be perpendicular to the tissue, particularly when dealing with tendon and nerve, to avoid false tendon tears from anisotropy.
pearls.verbatim: So it's important to try to be perpendicular to the tissue, particularly when you're dealing with tendon and nerve.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: Start scanning suprapatellar in long axis with probe marker towards the patient's head to identify the quadriceps tendon, patella, fat pads, and femur.
pearls.verbatim: probe markers towards the patient's head.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: A joint effusion appears as an anechoic space above the fat pad; if no fluid, the space is nearly nonexistent, which explains why blind injections often miss the joint.
pearls.verbatim: If you are going to see fluid, it's gonna be right above this fat pad, kinda where this line is here. This one doesn't have any fluid. So the space is almost nonexistent if there's no fluid in it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: Use dynamic ultrasound to assess MCL gapping by holding the probe on the medial joint line and applying medial and lateral stress, comparing to both sides.
pearls.verbatim: ultrasound's really fun because it's dynamic. So you can actually hold your ultrasound here and do your medial and lateral pressures to see if there's gapping compared to both sides.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: Ultrasound is better than physical exam for identifying joint fluid; it takes seconds to check for an effusion.
pearls.verbatim: as much as we like physical exam, ultrasound is better at identifying fluid. So just put an ultrasound on there. It takes two seconds to see if there's fluid in there or not.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: For ultrasound-guided knee injections, use a lateral approach with the probe positioned to watch the needle enter the joint space, which improves accuracy and patient satisfaction.
pearls.verbatim: I also use this to do ultrasound guided injections, and I do do those above the knee from a lateral position. So I'll go in this way with my probe right here and watch my needle go right under the probe into the joint space.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: Use the opposite end of a Betadine swab to mark a small circle at the injection spot.
pearls.verbatim: I'll take a Betadine swab and use the opposite side to mark a little circle there.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: For the anterior approach, perform the procedure more sterilely: use Betadine and sterile gloves to feel the spot before inserting the needle.
pearls.verbatim: So this one, I'd probably do more sterilely. And... Oh oh oh, sorry. Yes. As far as making the mark, yes. Using the opposite end of the Betadine to mark the spot. But for these, I will Betadine. I will have sterile gloves so that I can feel that spot and then put the needle in.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: Use a 25-gauge, 1.5-inch needle for knee injections; 22 or 23 gauge are also acceptable.
pearls.verbatim: I generally use a 25, one and a half. Some people will use a 22 or 23.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: Consult published guidelines because they show the anatomy and how the ultrasound probe should be positioned for each joint.
pearls.verbatim: Do look at those guidelines, though. They are really nice. They point out all the anatomy. They show you where the ultrasound probe is and how it's situated.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: Use lung ultrasound for pneumonia diagnosis; it is better than chest X-ray in children and adults, even by novice operators.
pearls.verbatim: So ultrasound, you should definitely get an ultrasound. If you think somebody has pneumonia, you should ultrasound them. Don't get one, just do it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: For adult outpatient lobar pneumonia without allergies, treat with amoxicillin 1000 mg three times daily (two 500 mg tablets) to cover Streptococcus pneumoniae.
pearls.verbatim: Five hundred milligrams, maybe three times a day. So it's a thousand three times a day. To get strep pneumonia coverage.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: adults with outpatient lobar pneumonia, no allergies
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Outpatient antibiotic duration for pneumonia should be 3, 5 days, no more than 7 days; if not improving, consider other diagnoses or hospitalization.
pearls.verbatim: outpatient should only need three to five days, no more than seven days.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: For lung ultrasound, use a phased array or curvilinear probe; with the Butterfly, use the lung preset for most areas but switch to the abdominal preset for the bases (above the diaphragm).
pearls.verbatim: you either want a phased array or a curvilinear probe. Obviously, the Butterfly just changes that for you. When you're looking at the lung with the Butterfly, you want to be in the lung preset, unless you're looking at the bases here, which include the area just above the diaphragm. In that case, generally, you wanna use the abdominal preset.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: B-lines always start at the parietal pleural line; if they start below that, they are something else, not B-lines.
pearls.verbatim: All B-lines always start at the parietal pleural line. They start below that. They're not B-lines. They're something else.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: To evaluate for B-lines, set the ultrasound depth to 12-15 centimeters; otherwise, Z-lines (which are normal and only go a few centimeters deep) can be mistaken for B-lines.
pearls.verbatim: So you have to have your set... Your your depth set to twelve, fifteen centimeters to evaluate if it's a b line or not.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: B-lines are not specific; bilateral B-lines in multiple areas could be multifocal pneumonia, pulmonary edema, interstitial lung disease, ARDS, or atelectasis. Focal B-lines could be pneumonia, pulmonary infarction, contusion, or mass.
pearls.verbatim: Bilateral bee... Bee lines, bee lines in multiple areas could be a multifocal pneumonia, but could be pulmonary edema, could be interstitial lung disease. So just thickened interstitium sufficient to cause B1s. Of course, ARDS, atelectasis, all of these things. Focal could be pneumonia, but could be a pulmonary infarction, pulmonary contusion. It could be a mass.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Point-of-care ultrasound is meant to answer a specific clinical question; always take into account the clinical presentation, history, and other findings when interpreting the ultrasound.
pearls.verbatim: point care ultrasound specifically is meant to answer a specific clinical question. Right? And so you always have to take in the clinical presentation history, all the other stuff in consideration when you're interpreting your ultrasound.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: A subpleural consolidation appears as a 'divot' or discontinuity in the normally smooth, straight pleural line; that is not normal and could be pneumonia, pulmonary infarction, or other causes.
pearls.verbatim: And we can see a little bit of it, but then there's, like, a divot in here. Which is basically a tiny area of hepatization of the lung. So this is a subpleural consolidation, which could be pneumonia, could be a pulmonary infarction, could be a PEEP, could be a lot of different things depending on the clinical scenario.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: The shred sign is the hyperechoic area below a consolidation, caused by the interaction of consolidated tissue with aerated tissue.
pearls.verbatim: So shred sign is the hyperechoic area below the consolidation. So this is not shred sign. The hyperechoic area below it is shred sign.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: In a child with focal crackles, lung ultrasound can confirm pneumonia and guide antibiotic initiation without waiting for chest X-ray.
pearls.verbatim: We did this on a 13 year old. We did hear crackles on the left lower base. Stuck the ultrasound there, and this is what we found. Didn't need the chest X-ray. We got it anyway. But that was after we had already sent in antibiotics for the pneumonia that we had confirmed on ultrasound.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: When scanning the lung, use the spine above the diaphragm to determine if a finding is artifact or pathology: if the spine extends beyond the diaphragm, suspect consolidation or effusion; if it stops at the diaphragm, suspect mirror artifact.
pearls.verbatim: K? Because you need that spine to know whether or not what you're seeing above the diaphragm is an artifact or is something wrong with the lung.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Use a linear probe (or Butterfly preset mimicking linear) for superficial abscess evaluation; most abscesses are superficial.
pearls.verbatim: Butterfly, of course. But in all seriousness, when you're using the Butterfly, you're using a preset that mimics a linear probe. So you want a linear probe.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: Always use Doppler on a suspected abscess to confirm it is not a blood vessel and to identify nearby vessels before incision.
pearls.verbatim: Oh, Doppler. Generally, you wanna put Doppler on these because you wanna make sure it's not a blood vessel.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: any patient before incision of a fluid collection
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: Measure the abscess in three dimensions: depth (top to bottom), width (side to side), and length (rotate probe 90 degrees and measure horizontally).
pearls.verbatim: So it's a good idea to measure. And this is showing two of the measurements. We've got deep, so top to bottom, and we've got, you know, either length or width, side to side. So to get the third measurements, what would we do to the probe? Rotate 90 degrees. Rotate 90 degrees. Horizontal. And measure horizontally.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: any patient with an abscess being evaluated for drainage
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: Beware of lymph nodes mimicking abscesses: look for a well-defined border and a hilar Doppler pattern (anechoic passageways through the middle); do not cut into a lymph node.
pearls.verbatim: Beware of the lymph node. Kinda looks like an abscess. So it's got this well defined border. This doppler here, and it's a little bit difficult to see here, but the hilum of the lymph node is what you're looking for.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: any patient with a suspected abscess in an area with lymph nodes
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: Use the water bath technique for small structures like fingers and toes: submerge the body part in water and place the ultrasound probe in the water (not on the skin) to improve imaging.
pearls.verbatim: So the way they are actually doing this and what's a good idea for small structures like the hand is actually to put it in a water bath. And then the ultrasound probe, you you put the... This part of the probe into the water. You don't put it against the skin. You just cover it above whatever part you're looking at.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected foreign body or abscess in fingers, toes, or hands
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: The Butterfly iQ3 probe can be submerged in water up to the gasket (the rubber ring connecting the head to the body), but always ask the attending before doing so because probes cost over $10,000.
pearls.verbatim: definitely, the head of the probe can go in. With the probes that are around the clinic, I would have to look at them. But there's usually a a gasket right here that's like a piece of rubber that connects the head of the probe to the body. And as long as you keep it below that gasket, definitely be okay.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: clinicians using Butterfly iQ3 or similar probes for water bath technique
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: POCUS is FDA-approved for many applications, but endocavitary (transvaginal) use is not one of them.
pearls.verbatim: It's FDA approved for a lot of things. Endocavitary is not one.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: Use left lateral decubitus positioning to bring the gallbladder more anterior, making it easier to scan.
pearls.verbatim: Left lateral decubitus, just like with the heart, bring it more anterior, so it might make it easier to actually scan.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: The subcostal sweep starts subxiphoid and sweeps below the rib cage to avoid ribs, but may be limited by intestinal air below the liver.
pearls.verbatim: subcostal sweep is just starting just subxiphoid and sweeping below the rib cage, trying to avoid all ribs altogether, be able to see it. The issue here is below the liver is intestine, and intestine is frequently filled with air
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: Measure gallbladder wall thickness at the most anterior aspect; normal is less than 3 mm. A contracted gallbladder can falsely appear thickened.
pearls.verbatim: we wanna look at the most anterior aspect of the gap gallbladder wall, and you're just measuring from one side to the other. Normal is gonna be less than three millimeters. This can be predictive, but it's not specific. Right? Because if you have a contracted gallbladder, that wall is gonna be thick.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: Use color Doppler to differentiate the common bile duct (no flow) from the hepatic artery (color flow), as they run in parallel.
pearls.verbatim: What's hard to differentiate is is it the hepatic artery or the common bile duct? Because they run-in parallel. One's gonna have color flow through it. The other one's not. K? So the artery is gonna have color flow, hopefully. Common bile duct should not.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: To avoid anisotropy artifact, keep the ultrasound beam perpendicular to tendons and ligaments; if you see a hypoechoic area, fan through a few degrees, if it becomes hyperechoic, it was artifact, not pathology.
pearls.verbatim: in musculoskeletal ultrasound, you do wanna be perpendicular to whatever tissue you're looking at to avoid anisotropy. And if you see an area specifically in a tendon or a ligament that you're concerned, like, is there a rupture there? Is there hemorrhage there? You need to make sure you're fanning through appropriately because if you move over a couple of degrees and it all looks normal, well, it was just anisotropy. It was not actually a pathology.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: In a knee with no effusion, the suprapatellar recess may not be visible; inject a small amount of fluid to separate the fat pads and confirm the space before administering medication.
pearls.verbatim: You're going in slow, and you're kinda squirting in a little bit of fluid to try to separate those fat pads to find the space. And once you find the space, then you can start administering the the medication.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: The presenter routinely uses ultrasound guidance for knee injections, finding it hurts less, is more effective, and increases patient satisfaction; when not used, the presenter has always regretted it.
pearls.verbatim: I find it hurts less, and I find that it's more effective. And you will find some mixed literature out there, but at a minimum, it increases patient satisfaction. And so I I almost always do ultrasound, and when I don't, I... Pretty sure I've always regretted it for one reason or another.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: For suprapatellar injection, start with a long-axis view to identify the quadriceps tendon and fat pads, then center the probe and rotate 90 degrees to a short-axis view; insert the needle from the lateral side.
pearls.verbatim: I always start long ways just because that will give me my best landmarks to know where that tendon is specifically. And then once I find the spot that I like, I will center my ultrasound over it. So I'll move it over so the center of my ultrasound's right here because I want this space here, and then I'll turn it 90 degrees to be short. And then I'm looking at it from the short axis. And then my needle, which is actually seen right here, will just come in from the side right into that space.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: For suprapatellar arthrocentesis, use depth information from the long-axis view (where patella and quad tendon are clearly seen) to identify structures in the short-axis view.
pearls.verbatim: If I can figure out what the depth of the quad tendon is in long axis, I know what the depth is gonna be in short axis, and it helps me find it better.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: Anticoagulated patients (e.g., on Coumadin) can receive knee injections; be prepared for bleeding and apply pressure.
pearls.verbatim: Would you do any injection on someone who's Yeah. I mean, on Coumadin? Fully anticoagulated. Go for it. Yeah. Yeah. Just just be prepared and, you know, wear a mask.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: patients on anticoagulation (e.g., Coumadin) undergoing knee injection
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: Use a 25-gauge 1.5-inch needle for knee injections; it is less painful than a 22-gauge.
pearls.verbatim: I use a 25 gauge one and a half. So a lot of people will use, like, a 22, sometimes a 20 if they're really knee. If you're doing an arthrocentesis where you're trying to pull fluid out, you gotta use an 18 gauge, 20. But when it's something like an injection, it's gonna take me longer to get the fluid in, but I don't... It's gonna be less painful for them if I use a 25 over 22.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: For arthrocentesis (draining fluid), use an 18- or 20-gauge needle.
pearls.verbatim: If you're doing an arthrocentesis where you're trying to pull fluid out, you gotta use an 18 gauge, 20.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing arthrocentesis of the knee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: To visualize A-lines, ensure the probe is perpendicular to the pleural line by rocking until the pleural line is straight across, then fan medially to account for lung curvature.
pearls.verbatim: The thing you wanna do to be able to see a lines, because that is important, is to make sure that your probe is perpendicular to the pleural line. The way you do that, one, is by rocking to make sure this line is straight across.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Ultrasound is more sensitive than chest X-ray for pneumonia and pleural effusion and avoids radiation; can safely diagnose pneumonia and initiate antibiotics without X-ray confirmation when clinical context supports it.
pearls.verbatim: We see this localized area of tons of felines, and so we can safely diagnose this 13 year old with pneumonia and and antibiotics. We did end up doing a chest X-ray just... Again, because we were doing ultrasound for educational purposes. And the X-ray did confirm what we found. The X-ray took a whole lot longer than it did to say, oh, look. A ton of declines. And we exposed him to radiation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: patients with clinical suspicion of pneumonia
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: When scanning for B-lines, set depth deep initially to avoid being tricked by short comet-tail artifacts; adjust depth dynamically and look closely beneath the pleural line for small consolidations.
pearls.verbatim: You want to have your depth pretty deep at the beginning because you're looking for beelines, and you don't wanna be tricked by the shorter little comet tails that go a couple centimeters. But adjust your depth. It's dynamic. Look closely beneath that pleural line to see if you see any small consolidations.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: all patients undergoing lung ultrasound for B-lines
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: In a patient with new-onset atrial fibrillation and heart failure, consider underlying causes such as prior viral illness (e.g., mononucleosis) that may have triggered myocarditis or cardiomyopathy.
pearls.verbatim: The wife reports that this 65 year old patient had mononucleosis around four months prior to arrival. Got treatment. Has had irregular heart rate for a few weeks, increased shortness of breath since four days prior arrival
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
pearls.applies_to: patients with new-onset atrial fibrillation and heart failure
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Lee Morning Report 9/10/26

pearls.text: In atrial fibrillation with RVR, first assess hemodynamic stability. If unstable, perform direct current cardioversion. If stable, check blood pressure before giving rate control.
pearls.verbatim: what is question number one when you're facing A fib with RVR? What is the first thing you need to look at? You guys all said it, so go ahead and tell me. What number one is Are they hemodynamically stable? K. Good. Excellent. K. If they're hemodynamically unstable, you must do what? In terms of cardiovert. Cardiovert. Direct current cardiovert. Okay? If they're hemodynamically stable, then
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
pearls.applies_to: patients with atrial fibrillation and RVR
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Lee Morning Report 9/10/26

pearls.text: In atrial fibrillation with RVR, if the patient is hemodynamically stable and blood pressure is normal or high, you can give metoprolol 5 mg IV push every 5 minutes or diltiazem.
pearls.verbatim: I think it's five of metoprolol, and you can give it every minutes, and it's an IV push.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
pearls.applies_to: hemodynamically stable patients with atrial fibrillation and RVR and normal/high blood pressure
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Lee Morning Report 9/10/26

pearls.text: Before giving rate control medication for atrial fibrillation with RVR, ensure the systolic blood pressure is at least 100 mmHg to provide a cushion against drug-induced hypotension.
pearls.verbatim: I think your instincts are right. You want it usually at least a 100. K? Probably. You don't want it to be less than a 100. Right? You wanna be a little more cautious than that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
pearls.applies_to: hemodynamically stable patients with atrial fibrillation and RVR
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Lee Morning Report 9/10/26

pearls.text: Do not use 'RRR' (regular rate and rhythm) in documentation for a patient with atrial fibrillation, as the rhythm is irregularly irregular.
pearls.verbatim: R is a regular rate and rhythm. What's the regular rate? It's a regular rhythm, but it's a normal rate or it's a bradycard rate or a epicard rate. K? Oh, these small things.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Lee Morning Report 9/10/26

pearls.text: Consider drug-induced fever from antibiotics such as levofloxacin as a cause of new fever.
pearls.verbatim: he got levofloxacin when he got here, so it could be also, like, a drug reaction.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lawrence Lee
