pearls.verbatim: Supposed to be done weekly for the first two weeks. And if that's normal, then you can increase every two to four weeks.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nakashima
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: In hypothyroidism in pregnancy, recheck TSH every four to six weeks before 20 weeks, then once at 24-28 weeks and again at 32-34 weeks.
pearls.verbatim: You're supposed to check it every four to six weeks because it changes if they're less than twenty weeks.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nakashima
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: For hyperthyroidism in first trimester, start propylthiouracil (PTU) 100-600 mg/day, divided (e.g., 200 mg TID for 600 mg).
pearls.verbatim: first trimester is gonna be propogyl uro cel, and it's a hundred to six hundred milligrams.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nakashima
pearls.applies_to: pregnant patients in first trimester with hyperthyroidism
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: For hyperthyroidism in second trimester and beyond, switch from PTU to methimazole.
pearls.verbatim: During your second trimester and beyond, you're gonna start with methimazole.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nakashima
pearls.applies_to: pregnant patients in second trimester or later with hyperthyroidism
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: For hyperthyroidism in pregnancy, monitor free T4 every two weeks until stable with medication adjustment.
pearls.verbatim: You're gonna be checking every two weeks, and that's just monitoring until it's stable with your medication adjustment
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nakashima
pearls.applies_to: pregnant patients with hyperthyroidism on medication
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: For patients already on levothyroxine before pregnancy, increase dose by 50 micrograms every four weeks, checking levels to stay in range.
pearls.verbatim: I'm pretty sure that it recommends starting... Just keeping them on their dose. And every four weeks, you increase their dose by fifty micrograms
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nakashima
pearls.applies_to: pregnant patients with pre-existing hypothyroidism on levothyroxine
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: Self-titration for hypothyroidism: as soon as a patient suspects pregnancy (missed period or positive test), take two extra doses of Synthroid per week (e.g., two additional doses of their usual daily dose).
pearls.verbatim: if you think you're pregnant, but you haven't come in yet, start taking two extra doses of your Synthroid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nakashima
pearls.applies_to: patients with hypothyroidism of reproductive age who may become pregnant
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: For counterstrain, ask the patient to rate tenderness 1-10, put pressure at the point of maximum tension, shorten the muscle, hold up to 90 seconds, then return to neutral without activating the muscle.
pearls.verbatim: You kinda ask the patient on a scale of one to 10, how much tenderness do you have, And you put pressure there. But what you do is you shorten the muscle. ... You hold your finger at that point of maximum tension, and then typically up to, like, ninety seconds. And then you should feel that tension resolve, and then the patient should also be able to report, oh, that's not as tender anymore. And then you return them to a neutral position.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on OMT

pearls.text: For acute rib pain in pregnancy, a quick rib manipulation can resolve the pain immediately.
pearls.verbatim: And so all I did is I just manipulated the rib, and it just relaxed. And she's like, the pain was gone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.applies_to: pregnant women with acute rib pain
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on OMT

pearls.text: Consider OMT as an alternative to steroid injections for overuse injuries like tennis elbow or golfer's elbow.
pearls.verbatim: But, honestly, anytime you're sticking a needle into somebody and you're putting steroids in, might wanna consider if OMT is also a good option for them.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.applies_to: patients with overuse injuries (tennis elbow, golfer's elbow, shoulder pain not tear)
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on OMT

pearls.text: Use your whole upper body as a lever, not just finger muscles, when applying soft tissue technique.
pearls.verbatim: I'm doing... I'm being a lever, so I'm not just using my finger muscles. I'm using my whole upper body. And then I push up to the ceiling and towards me, and I lean back.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on OMT

pearls.text: Hold soft tissue technique until the muscle relaxes (30-90 seconds); use deep breathing distraction to help release tension.
pearls.verbatim: Until, really, until you feel the muscles relax. That can be up to thirty to, like, ninety seconds, but you will feel a softening sometimes. If patients are super tense, I'll just have them say, go ahead and take a deep breath. In your happy place, imagine you're at the beach, wherever you're at, and then that kinda distracts them and lets their muscles kind of release the tension.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on OMT

pearls.text: For prone soft tissue, use thumbs and direct pressure anterior caudally for each muscle until T7-T8, then switch sides.
pearls.verbatim: use your thumbs instead of your fingers and kind of put direct pressure anterior caudally for each of those individual muscles that... Of the back until you get to the point of, like, t seven, t eight, then you go towards the other side of the patient and then go back or... Towards petal ad laterally.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on OMT

pearls.text: Warning signs that pain is not pregnancy-related include localized or abrupt onset, constant or severe pain, pain with nausea/vomiting, fever, or vaginal bleeding.
pearls.verbatim: The pain's localized or abrupt in the first or second trimester. It's constant or severe. Pain is associated with nausea and vomiting, fever, or vaginal bleeding. Those are all concerning signs.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.applies_to: pregnant women in first or second trimester
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: Ultrasound is the best test for appendicitis in pregnancy; MRI is second best. If ultrasound is nondiagnostic and MRI unavailable, get the CT scan.
pearls.verbatim: Ultrasound is actually the best test for appendicitis. It's recommended to obtain that in pregnancy. MRI is the second best. But if ultrasound's nondiagnostic, you can't get an MRI, get the CT scan.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: Placental abruption is the most dangerous cause of abdominal pain in pregnancy; it can be concealed (no vaginal bleeding) and typically presents with intense, unrelenting pain.
pearls.verbatim: The biggest thing you don't wanna miss is placental abruption. So that's the most dangerous cause of abdominal pain in pregnancy. Typically intense, typically unrelenting. ... it can have plus or minus vaginal bleeding because you can have a concealed placental abruption
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: Use IV opioids with caution at the time of delivery because they can lead to a baby with increased opioid concentration and depressed respiratory drive.
pearls.verbatim: use with caution at the time of delivery because it can lead to a baby coming out with increased concentration of opioids in their system.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: Start with a multimodal pain plan using NSAIDs and acetaminophen; only use low-dose opioids if needed due to addiction risk.
pearls.verbatim: the idea is we should all start with multimodal pain plan being NSAIDs and Tylenol and only use opioids low dose if they need to
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: Postpartum pain should be managed with a multimodal approach starting with NSAIDs and acetaminophen, reserving opioids for low-dose use only when needed.
pearls.verbatim: we should all start with multimodal pain plan being NSAIDs and Tylenol and only use opioids low dose if they need to
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: Sterile water injections (intradermal or subcutaneous) can be used for natural birth pain relief, targeting somatic distribution of sacral nerves; give 0.1 mL per spot.
pearls.verbatim: about one ml. So if you draw it up, you're actually gonna draw up point five ml. You wanna give point one ml in each of these spots.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: For sterile water injections, draw up 0.5 mL but give 0.1 mL intradermally at each site, using a fine needle like a TB test.
pearls.verbatim: you're actually gonna draw up point five ml. You wanna give point one ml in each of these spots
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.applies_to: patients with back labor wanting natural birth
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: Hydrotherapy during the first stage of labor may be associated with shorter labor and decreased use of spinal/epidural anesthesia in healthy women, with no adverse maternal, fetal, or neonatal outcomes.
pearls.verbatim: during the first stage of labor, might be associated with shorter labor and decreased use of spinal epidural anesthesia in healthy women
pearls.speaker: Dr. Newborn
pearls.applies_to: healthy women in first stage of labor
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: If you don't know the patient's baseline GFR, assume a baseline GFR of 75 to assess AKI severity using RIFLE criteria.
pearls.verbatim: So they suggest that you assume a baseline GFR of 75
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.applies_to: patients with AKI and unknown baseline renal function
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Upper GI bleed is the biggest cause of increased BUN separate from creatinine.
pearls.verbatim: upper GI bleed. This is probably the biggest one to be aware of.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: If UA shows positive for hemoglobin but negative for red blood cells, consider rhabdomyolysis.
pearls.verbatim: if you see the positive for the hemoglobin but not the positive for the red blood cells itself, that can be rhabdo.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Use RIFLE criteria to decide admission: class 3 (failure) or below definitely needs admission; class 2 (injury) can be managed with next-day follow-up.
pearls.verbatim: If they are class three, so the failure. So it was risk, injury failure, loss, and EN 30. So if we get to that failure or below, we definitely need to be admitted for it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: If doing a fluid challenge in a patient with suspected obstruction, do not push fluids because it will make the obstruction worse.
pearls.verbatim: But you wanna do this if you're not obstructed. If you're having an obstruction, we don't wanna just push more fluids into the obstruction because that's just gonna make it worse.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.applies_to: patients with AKI and possible obstruction
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: For hospitalized patients with AKI, do not use prophylactic anticoagulation because uremia causes platelet dysfunction; use sequential compression devices instead.
pearls.verbatim: we don't wanna use prophylactic anticoagulation because uremia can cause platelet dysfunction, and our patient is already at a higher risk for bleeding because of that. So use our SCDs.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: After AKI resolution, trend creatinine for at least three months to ensure they do not develop CKD.
pearls.verbatim: continue to trend the creatinine for up to three months. So we want people with AKI are at an increased risk for developing CKD is one of the complications. And so even if we get the current AKI back down to normal, we wanna trend it out for at least three months to make sure that they're not developing ongoing CKD or other issues.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: For postrenal AKI, consult urology, not nephrology, especially if obstruction is bilateral or a kidney stone needs removal or lithotripsy.
pearls.verbatim: if it's the postrenal, we're probably consulting urology, not nephrology. And especially if it's an obstruction on both sides, as well as any kidney stone that's gonna need removal or lithotripsy, those types of things.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Patients with chronic risk factors or who cannot stop nephrotoxic medications need more frequent creatinine trending, but once stable for two measurements, you can transition to monthly checks.
pearls.verbatim: they're on meds that you can't get off of, right, or some of your risk factors, are there chronic medical conditions that aren't going away? Then I'm gonna be trending that a little bit more frequently.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.applies_to: patients with persistent risk factors for CKD after AKI
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: When trending creatinine after AKI, if the patient has two stable creatinines and is otherwise stable, check monthly for three months.
pearls.verbatim: if they're pretty stable, they've had, like, at least two stable creatinines, I'm probably saying, like, let's do it at... Even with those severe things, let's check it, like, at once a month for three months.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: For stable post-AKI patients with at least two stable creatinines, schedule follow-up and recheck once a month for three months.
pearls.verbatim: They've had, like, at least two stable creatinines. I'm probably saying, like, let's do it at... Even with those severe things, let's check it, like, at once a month for three months.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: After AKI, recheck creatinine at least once or twice a couple months out to ensure the patient has not developed chronic kidney disease.
pearls.verbatim: try to do it a couple months out kind of regardless of what you do in that interim to make sure that this hasn't developed into a CKD.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: When deciding whether to send a patient home or hospitalize after a fluid challenge, consider health literacy, English proficiency, access to transportation, and ability to follow instructions.
pearls.verbatim: you have to think about how reliable the patient is. What's their understanding of English? What's their help... Understanding of health literacy, what's their access to transportation, their availability to follow directions.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.applies_to: patients with AKI being considered for outpatient management
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: If you see Osborn waves on EKG, check the patient's temperature.
pearls.verbatim: if you do see it, you should probably check your patient's temperature.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.applies_to: any patient with EKG showing Osborn waves
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: Do not routinely open frostbite blisters; this is controversial and generally avoided unless there is infection.
pearls.verbatim: as a general rule, I don't open blisters.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: Treat the patient in front of you, not just the temperature; a patient with moderate hypothermia by temperature may have severe symptoms and need airway support.
pearls.verbatim: you always gotta watch out for that too. Right? So we gotta treat the patient in front of us, not just the temperature. This person is someone who might need an airway
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: Warmed IV fluids increase core temperature by about 0.5°C per hour; they are a less invasive active rewarming option.
pearls.verbatim: So warmed IV fluid is point five degrees Celsius.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.applies_to: hypothermia patients receiving active external and internal rewarming
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: In hypothermic cardiac arrest, call the ECMO team very early rather than spending 30 minutes on other rewarming steps first.
pearls.verbatim: Don't do... If you have a patient come in in cardiac arrest and it's because of hypothermia, don't do all these other steps for thirty minutes and then try to call the ECMO.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: For frostbite, if there is a chance of refreezing again before definitive care, do NOT start rewarming, refreezing causes significantly more injury from crystal formation.
pearls.verbatim: They they cannot get refrozen. That is if you take away one thing from this, you have a frostbite patient and... Or, like, you're outside and you're trying to help somebody with frostbite, if there is a chance that they will have true refreezing again, they can actually have significantly more injuries from crystal formation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.applies_to: frostbite patients with potential for re-exposure to freezing before reaching definitive care
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: Frostbite pain is similar to a burn; use NSAIDs on a scheduled basis for the prostglandin response plus morphine or fentanyl as needed.
pearls.verbatim: NSAIDs in particular are very helpful because they have some control, like, the prostaglandin response as well. And so they can actually be administered, take... On a scheduled basis to help with that and then additionally give, like, morphine or fentanyl, whatever you need to to get pain under control.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: Second- through fourth-degree frostbite should prompt consultation with the burn center for blister management and amputation decisions.
pearls.verbatim: And anything second through fourth degree, just like a burn, the burn center is actually going to specialize in these. So because they have the literature on the, like, opening the blisters and amputation and things like that. So they're who you wanna talk to.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.applies_to: patients with second- through fourth-degree frostbite
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: In heat stroke, cool the patient first before giving fluids; antipyretics and dantrolene are not useful.
pearls.verbatim: We're gonna cool them off first. I also like a a good fluid bolus in this patient, but probably not before cooling.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: After heat injury, monitor for rhabdomyolysis: CK rises first, then creatinine, and hyperkalemia can occur up to five days later.
pearls.verbatim: Creatine's up a little bit. I think CK was in the 8 thousands. So this is something that you, as I admit these patients to you, will need to watch out for. K. Because I I might forget to order a CK, so please don't.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: Heat cramps can be managed with oral fluids and low‑sugar electrolyte replacement drinks; avoid Gatorade because of high sugar content.
pearls.verbatim: Heat cramps. So this can just be managed with oral fluids. This is not something that needs IV fluids. They can use things like electrolyte replacement drinks. Gatorade is not great because it has a ton of sugar in it. It's just preferably something less sugar.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: For prickly heat (miliaria), remove tight clothing and use diphenhydramine (Benadryl) or a topical antihistamine cream.
pearls.verbatim: So with that prickly rash, so like we said, take the layers off. And an adult who you might see this on, if they have, like, super tight fitting clothing because they're running and they just start a new running program and now they're covered in this red itchy rash, tell them to not wear tight clothes. And you can use diphenhydramine (Benadryl) or, like, a topical antihistamine cream for this.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: Cold water immersion is the most effective cooling method for heat stroke; a body bag filled with ice water can be used in the ED or field.
pearls.verbatim: Get their clothing off. And then cold water immersion is the most effective form and what I most typically see in the emergency department because it is rapid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: In the field, a body bag can be used as a portable ice bath for rapid cooling of heat stroke patients.
pearls.verbatim: They actually... I should have put one of these articles on here. I've incorporated using this in the field as well because body bags are small relatively. And so we can transport them. If they can get ice, they can just put the person in it, especially, like, during heat waves when people are, like, dying of heat exposure frequently.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Nicole Tipton
pearls.applies_to: field settings (e.g., remote camps, heat waves)
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: Patients with preexisting structural brain issues (cortical atrophy, dementia, stroke, TBI, etc.) are more susceptible to delirium and mental status decline when ill.
pearls.verbatim: And I'll tell you that those with preexisting structural brain issues will be more susceptible to delirium and mental status decline when ill.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.applies_to: hospitalized patients with prior brain injury
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: The Monro-Kellie doctrine states that the skull is a fixed-volume space containing brain, blood, and CSF; any increase in one component requires compensation or leads to herniation.
pearls.verbatim: If you take into consideration the Monro-Kellie doctrine, there are three intracranial contents, brain, blood, and CSF, brain being the biggest volume.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.applies_to: patients with intracranial mass effect or edema
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Common causes of coma are often non-anatomical: metabolic disturbances, intoxications, generalized seizures, toxic metabolic syndromes, and delirium.
pearls.verbatim: Generalized seizures, toxic metabolic syndromes, and delirium.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: To prevent delirium, keep lights on during the day, get patients out of bed, ensure they use glasses and hearing aids, and maintain a day/night cycle.
pearls.verbatim: When I leave, I need you guys to actually be advocates for delirium medication. You gotta be getting your patients up. It's gotta flip on during the day. Gotta keep them day and night set.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.applies_to: hospitalized patients at risk for delirium
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Advocate for delirium prevention: keep lights on during the day, get patients up in a chair, ensure they have glasses and hearing aids to avoid sensory deprivation.
pearls.verbatim: When I leave, I need you guys to actually be advocates for delirium medication. You gotta be getting your patients up. It's gotta flip on during the day. Gotta keep them day and night set.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: If you correct the underlying metabolic or toxic disturbance, you can often improve consciousness, but recovery is slow and requires consistent effort, especially in delirium-prone brains.
pearls.verbatim: If you correct the disturbance, you can often correct the problem, but it's very hard, especially with the delirium prone brain, just fix it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.applies_to: patients with delirium or coma from reversible causes
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Artery of Percheron stroke causes bilateral medial thalamic infarction; strokes are tiny and can be missed on MRI but cause devastating coma with poor recovery.
pearls.verbatim: The medial thalami is specifically mostly responsible for consciousness. So this dude is in a coma for probably the next few years.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.applies_to: patients with sudden coma and no obvious cause
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: A blown pupil in a comatose patient is a sign of increased ICP and possible uncal herniation; in an awake patient, consider topical medications (albuterol, scopolamine) or prior cataract surgery.
pearls.verbatim: Remember that this is a sign of increased ICP. Thus, if that patient is awake talking to you, they're not herniating. Right? That's a different that's a different issue.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Forced eye deviation: if eyes look away from the flaccid side, it's a stroke; if looking toward the flaccid side, it's a seizure.
pearls.verbatim: If they are looking away from the plegic side, so flaccid right looking away, the stroke. If it's looking towards the flaccid side, they're having a seizure.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: In the comatose patient, always start with ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation) and correct hypotension, hypercapnia, and non-perfusing rhythms before any neurological intervention.
pearls.verbatim: Always, a's, b's, and c's. There's no life without those. Right? So make sure that they have an airway and they have circulation. Check and correct the vitals. Hypotension, hypercapnia, and non-profusing rhythms. No neurologist can help you if that's not going.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: EEG is marginally helpful because if the seizure is not happening at the moment you record, it doesn't mean it didn't happen, just like an EKG.
pearls.verbatim: I will say, like I said, EEG is marginally helpful. If it's not happening in the moment you do it, doesn't mean it didn't happen. It just means it didn't happen at that moment, just like an EKG.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Always talk to comatose patients because they may be awake but locked in, as in severe Guillain-Barré syndrome.
pearls.verbatim: This is why I actually make a point to talk to all of my patients now, whether I think you can hear me or not. That case was really, really, really formative.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: In a stroke or structural lesion, the eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion (frontal eye field injury); in a focal seizure, the eyes deviate away from the side of the seizure (hyperactive side).
pearls.verbatim: if a frontal eye field goes out, the eyes will point towards the side of the lesion. How does it go out? Stroke, injury, tumor, whatever. So frontal eye field goes out, eyes point towards injury.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Post-seizure focal weakness is called Todd's paralysis.
pearls.verbatim: After a seizure, what can you have? Like, a focal deficit. It's called a something paralysis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: In a seizure, eye deviation is contralateral to the side of the seizure focus; the eyes point toward the side of the seizure.
pearls.verbatim: Contralateral. Right? So it'll be on the opposite side of the hyperactivity. Right side. Except your eyes are still pointing the direction opposite.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: For a patient with flushing, weight loss, and palpitations, consider carcinoid syndrome, thyroid storm, heart failure, and leukemia in the differential.
pearls.verbatim: Thyroid storm. Sure. Great. Arsinoids syndrome. Okay. Rule number one, can't cheat on the title slide. Okay. Good. Failure. Okay. Great. Remind me your name. Jenny. Jenny. Go ahead. Leukemia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.applies_to: adults with flushing, weight loss, and palpitations
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: In a patient with anemia and palpitations, check an iron panel to evaluate for iron deficiency; low iron, high TIBC, and low ferritin confirm iron deficiency anemia.
pearls.verbatim: Why'd you order an iron panel? Anemia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Order tests that will change management; do not chase incidental findings without clinical suspicion, for example, small liver nodules on CT warrant MRI only if you suspect malignancy that would alter management.
pearls.verbatim: Do things that you think will change your management. Don't just do it because the radiologist said it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: A patient with NET who develops new heart failure symptoms with a normal echo may have infiltrative cardiomyopathy from mets; consider PET scan for diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: Stone Cold normal. And now he has severe diastolic dysfunction. Of the aggressiveness of a tumor. He probably had a malignant NETs on the heart that we just cannot see on an echo
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.applies_to: patients with NET and new CHF
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Most neuroendocrine tumors are diagnosed incidentally when an appendix is sent to pathology after appendectomy; always send the appendix for pathology.
pearls.verbatim: most neuroendocrine tumors are diagnosed when someone gets an appendectomy incidentally, and the appendix goes out to pathology.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Carcinoid syndrome can mimic serotonin syndrome (flushing, palpitations, high fevers) but is due to secreting hormones, not SSRIs; check 5-HIAA in urine.
pearls.verbatim: This is why a lot of these guys with carcinoid syndrome look like they have serotonin syndrome. The flushing, the palpitations, right, And the high fevers. It it certainly looks like it, but they're not on any kind of serotonin receptor uptake inhibitors.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Ethanol can precipitate carcinoid syndrome symptoms, including flushing, in patients with neuroendocrine tumors.
pearls.verbatim: So ethanol can precipitate your carcinoid syndrome type of symptoms.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Carcinoid syndrome symptoms (flushing, diarrhea, palpitations) can be precipitated by ethanol; alcohol intake may cause acute flushing in these patients.
pearls.verbatim: ethanol can precipitate your carcinoid syndrome type of symptoms.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: In outpatient evaluation of flushing and chronic diarrhea, consider non-carcinoid causes like menopause, thyroid disease, asthma; ask when flushing occurs especially after eating or drinking alcohol.
pearls.verbatim: always starts with the basics. Right? Rule out things like menopause. Things like thyroid disease. Everything that you guys talked about earlier. Do they have asthma?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: In outpatient evaluation of flushing and diarrhea, first rule out common causes like menopause, thyroid disease, asthma, IBS, serotonin syndrome, endocarditis, and bloodstream infections before considering carcinoid syndrome.
pearls.verbatim: always starts with the basics. Right? Rule out things like menopause. I mean, this guy's a male, so that's ruled out. Things like thyroid disease. Everything that you guys talked about earlier. Do they have asthma? Right? Yeah. Do they have gastroenteritis? Like, are they eating bad food every single day from the same food truck? I don't know. Do they have IBS? Right? You wanna be... And then do they have serotonin syndrome? Are they on SSRIs? Are they on SNRIs? Do they have a history of structural heart disease or rheum... Rheumatic heart disease, for example? Do they... Is there a possibility of endocarditis? Are they IV drug abusers? Right? Is there a possibility of a bloodstream infection?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Yasmin O'Keefe
pearls.applies_to: outpatient setting, patients with flushing and diarrhea
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: For cerebral malaria with seizures, start with phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV (skip diazepam to avoid oversedation).
pearls.verbatim: Our protocol starts with Valium I skip Valium because it makes it too sedated. I start with phenobarb twenty mg per kg.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: Give IV artesunate empirically for suspected cerebral malaria after drawing blood but before the test result returns (result takes 3 hours).
pearls.verbatim: After I draw it and before I get the result. The result takes three hours, so we just give it ASAP.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: For suspected typhoid with severe abdominal tenderness, admit for serial abdominal exams; do not discharge.
pearls.verbatim: Serial abdominal exams. Admit her.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.applies_to: suspected typhoid with severe abdominal tenderness
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: Maintain a very high suspicion for typhoid perforation; patients can perforate and die quickly.
pearls.verbatim: We have to be really, really high in the suspicion.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: Treat typhoid empirically: IV ceftriaxone for inpatients; ciprofloxacin or azithromycin for outpatients.
pearls.verbatim: Our inpatient treatment, IV ceftriaxone. Outpatient, we're doing Cipro or azithromycin.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: Use WHO diagnostic criteria (weight-for-length z-score, mid-upper arm circumference, edema) to diagnose severe acute malnutrition.
pearls.verbatim: You'll be doing weight for length disease score, the arm circumference, looking for edema.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: In severe acute malnutrition, watch vigilantly for refeeding syndrome: monitor electrolytes and follow a feeding protocol.
pearls.verbatim: I'm looking really closely for refeeding syndrome. So I'm really good at that in The US. So now I'm just doing it for kids. So really high vigilance. We have a feeding protocol. We're watching their electrolytes carefully.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: Give prophylactic antibiotics and multivitamins to all children with severe acute malnutrition due to high infection risk from cracked skin.
pearls.verbatim: They also get tons of vitamins. They also get prophylactic antibiotics.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: For premature neonates <32 weeks gestational age, use NG tube feeding because the suck-swallow-breathe reflex is not developed.
pearls.verbatim: You're gonna do NG tube if it's less than 32 because neurologically, they're not developed enough to know that suck, suck, swallow, breathe, neurologic rhythm, and reflex.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: Increase total fluids by 20 mL/kg/day in premature neonates on a feeding protocol, monitoring weights and growth charts.
pearls.verbatim: You're increasing your your total fluids by twenty mg per kg per day.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: Perform lumbar puncture routinely as part of the neonatal sepsis workup.
pearls.verbatim: Do you do lumbar puncture part of your sepsis? All the time. Yeah.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: In Togo, lumbar puncture is routinely performed as part of sepsis workup, and you become very proficient at it.
pearls.verbatim: Do you do lumbar puncture part of your sepsis? All the time. Yeah. You get really good at lumbar puncture as a thing of all the time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: For herbicide ingestion (suicide attempt), immediately place an NG tube and suction out the stomach contents; atropine may be used depending on the type ingested.
pearls.verbatim: I'm good at pushing atropine if it's... Depending on which type they ingested. I'm good at NG tube suctioning
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: For suspected MALT lymphoma of the stomach when biopsy is unavailable, compare ultrasound images to known MALT pictures and consider empiric treatment.
pearls.verbatim: I pulled up pictures and compared my picture to MALT pictures, and I was like, well, actually, it does look similar. So we're just gonna go ahead and treat them empirically
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: Without CT, ischemic stroke is 90% of cases and hemorrhagic 10%; if blood pressure is very high (e.g., SBP 240), withhold aspirin because hemorrhagic stroke is more likely.
pearls.verbatim: ischemic is ninety percent of the k... Time. Hemorrhagic is ten percent, so you can roll the dice that way. But his BP was super high, so I was like, you know what? We're just gonna we're just gonna not give aspirin because there's a high chance that this could be hemorrhagic.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: When making a labetalol drip without Cardene, titrate slowly because labetalol is longer acting; watch for cumulative hypotension from too much dosing.
pearls.verbatim: Watch out with your Lavella. It's a little longer acting, so you wanna make slower titrations. Really watch out. You don't wanna get accumulative hypotension from too much doses.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Papp
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: When the dying period is shortened by bureaucratic pressures, it robs patients of the time needed for reconciliation with estranged loved ones, which is a deep spiritual need.
pearls.verbatim: So when we shorten the dying period, which, of course, the bureaucrats want because spend most of our money in the last bit of our lives, that doesn't has... That doesn't have to be the case.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Physician suicide rates are roughly the same as those in aboriginal populations. The profession often responds with denial, but you need to learn how to talk about death and handle these issues.
pearls.verbatim: We have... You're in a you're in a profession which has those figures roughly the same as aboriginal people. Nobody ever spoke to me about the fact that the guy before me had committed suicide, because even back then, the capacity to handle those things was diminishing. Now denial appears to be the only way forward, doesn't it?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.applies_to: physicians at risk of burnout or suicide
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Do not give smartphones to your children; if you can wait until university, it will protect their minds.
pearls.verbatim: no phones for your children. If you can make it till university, they will destroy their minds.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Read Jonathan Haidt's 'The Anxious Generation' to understand how smartphone use since 2011 correlates with rising anxiety in young people.
pearls.verbatim: The book that you need to get at some point is called The Anxious Generation
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.applies_to: anyone interested in behavioral pediatrics or mental health
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: The first country to stop slavery was England in the 12th century, led by Archbishop Anselm who persuaded bishops that slavery was wrong based on the image of God.
pearls.verbatim: It's the twelfth century. Oh, that's cool. And it's in England. We had to do it again. And it was Anselm, the great saint, who did it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Ideas and actions have consequences; complicity in administrative death will haunt you and you will feel guilty.
pearls.verbatim: If you are, what shall I say, complicit in administrative death, what's that gonna do to your psyche? You cannot avoid feeling guilty about that over time, can you? It's gonna haunt you.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: In the speaker's malnutrition unit in Jamaica, the death rate came down from just over 50% to about 30% in the first 12-15 years, then in the next 25 years they had 110 two-year-olds in a row without losing one.
pearls.verbatim: we'd taken the death rate and severe malnutrition from... Well, the unit ran for twenty five years. And in the first twelve twelve, fifteen years, the the death rate came down from just over fifty to about thirty. And then in the next twenty five years, when I left Jamaica, we went to a £110 two year olds in a row without losing one.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Reductionism began when William of Ockham pulled apart things we could measure from things we couldn't, leaving love, joy, peace, and justice in God's province while science got reduced to what could be measured.
pearls.verbatim: And what he did was pull apart the idea of things that we could measure and things that we couldn't. So love, joy, peace, justice, they were left in God's province because we we can't measure them, but we can weigh, and we can measure that area. So that's when science got reduced to what could be measured, basically.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: In pagan worldviews, illness may be attributed to evil spirits, making biomedical treatment seem irrelevant; a nurse trained in nutrition let his own child die because he believed an evil spirit took the child's appetite and spent money on a witch doctor.
pearls.verbatim: He said he believed that an evil spirit took the child's appetite away, so he had spent his money on the witch doctor. The child had died.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: In settings where men traditionally eat first, encourage fathers to eat with their children and give slow eaters their own plate to prevent malnutrition.
pearls.verbatim: I watched my children eat. I didn't actually eat with them, he said, but I didn't eat first, which is what the men normally do. And he said, I noticed one of my children was a slow eater, so I gave him his own plate to eat from a common pot. That's malnutrition gone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.applies_to: families where men eat first, in traditional societies
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Pride is the most dangerous sin; it destroys you and others, especially in medicine.
pearls.verbatim: pride is the biggest one by far. It destroys you, destroys lots of people.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Treat every patient with respect as bearing the image of God; treating someone as a fool or unworthy is worse than murder.
pearls.verbatim: if you're angry with your brother, you've committed murder in your heart, and you're liable to judgment. And if you treat your brother as a fool and not worthy of your your attention, you're on your way to hell fire.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Ask male patients over 50 about urinary complaints; they often do not volunteer them.
pearls.verbatim: If you just began querying your male patients over age 50, are you having any urinary complaints at all? You will start it seeing it come out of the woodwork, really. So be sure you're asking that question. It is not usually volunteered by men.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Nocturia is often the first symptom of BPH and the one that bothers patients most; use it as a screening question in men over 50.
pearls.verbatim: Nocturia is usually thought of as kind of a cardinal symptom, probably the one that happens first before some of these physical symptoms occur. And so often, that's kind of my screening question and usually the one that bothers folks the most.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: A DRE is mandatory in any patient presenting with lower urinary tract symptoms; do not skip it even if you order a PSA.
pearls.verbatim: do you have to check the prostate if a patient comes in with lower urinary tract symptoms? Yes. A hundred percent of the time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Advise patients to stop drinking fluids after 6 PM to reduce nocturia.
pearls.verbatim: Don't drink anything after 6PM.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Double voiding means emptying the bladder, then going again after 5-10 minutes (e.g., after brushing teeth) to ensure an empty bladder before bed.
pearls.verbatim: Double voiding is literally what it is. It's empty your bladder. Go brush your teeth. Empty your bladder again.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Nonselective alpha-1 antagonists (e.g., Cardura, Hytrin) cause vasodilation, hypotension, and reflex tachycardia; avoid them for BPH unless no alternative.
pearls.verbatim: vasodilation. That's how they work as a blood pressure medication, but they also cause hypotension and reflex tachycardia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Always use the term 'lower urinary tract symptoms' (LUTS) rather than 'BPH symptoms' because other conditions (UTI, cancer, STD) cause similar symptoms, and women also have LUTS.
pearls.verbatim: Call them lower urinary symptoms. Are other things that cause lower urinary tract symptoms.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Use the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) as a validated instrument to quantify and characterize LUTS; it is not available in Cerner, so print it off or have it up while talking to the patient.
pearls.verbatim: honest, this is not available, I don't think, in Cerner. Print this off or have it up, you know, while you're talking to the patient.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Home blood pressure monitors should be replaced or recalibrated every two years; patients can bring them to clinic to check against the office machine.
pearls.verbatim: I tell people two years. I don't know what the official, you know, word is. I think sooner than later.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: patients using home blood pressure monitors
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: At the first visit, check blood pressure in both arms and use the higher reading.
pearls.verbatim: the technical recommendation is that the first visit for anyone... First visit for anyone is you check both arms, and you take the higher of the two.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Major blood pressure studies (e.g., SPRINT) use an average of three readings taken 5 minutes apart.
pearls.verbatim: all of the studies that are done, Sprint, all these major blood pressure studies, they use three blood pressures five minutes apart, and the and the machine gives an average.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Cardiovascular disease is already developing in the pre-hypertensive range; do not dismiss borderline elevations as normal.
pearls.verbatim: look at how much disease is actually already spread before you get to that point. And so you you need to dial this back in your mind
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Clinic blood pressures are unreliable; do not base clinical decisions on them. Use home monitoring and patient logs instead.
pearls.verbatim: I personally think that the blood pressures we get in the clinic are kind of a work of fiction. I think you could pick a number out of the air and be about as accurate we are.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: For stage 1 hypertension (130-139/80-89), start monotherapy with an ARB.
pearls.verbatim: stage one... So, again, that that chart that we saw at stage one, I will start monotherapy with an ARB.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: For stage 2 hypertension (≥140/≥90), start an ARB plus amlodipine as initial therapy.
pearls.verbatim: For most in stage two, I will start an ARB with amlodipine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Add a diuretic only after maximizing doses of ARB and amlodipine, because diuretics cause urinary frequency that bothers older men and women with incontinence.
pearls.verbatim: I escalate the doses of those, both of those up. And if I get to the maximum dose of those two things, then I add my diuretic.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: older men and women with incontinence
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Consider secondary causes of hypertension, especially obstructive sleep apnea, primary aldosteronism, and renal artery stenosis, in patients with resistant hypertension.
pearls.verbatim: And then these secondaries. And these are the big ones. Right? So secondary hypertension is a lecture all its own. Obstructive sleep apnea is a big one. Primary algo is an interesting one and probably important. Remodular sphincter is, again, interesting, not as common
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: For resistant hypertension after three drugs including a diuretic, consider adding spironolactone before referring to cardiology.
pearls.verbatim: I might start spironolactone and see where we go. If they're like, I don't wanna go see another doctor. You know? I might do that and watch them.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Use longer-acting ARBs like olmesartan for smooth 24-hour control; they are now affordable and preferable to ACE inhibitors due to the risk of cough and angioedema.
pearls.verbatim: olmesartan is used a lot. I use it a lot. Again, these are... At at 06:00 at night or 07:00 at night, they've still got half that drug in their system for the night.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Use longer-acting ARBs like olmesartan instead of lisinopril to avoid cough/angioedema and prevent burning the entire RAS class.
pearls.verbatim: olmesartan is used a lot. I use it a lot. Again, these are... At at 06:00 at night or 07:00 at night, they've still got half that drug in their system for the night.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Avoid ACE inhibitors as first-line therapy; if a patient develops cough or angioedema on an ACE inhibitor, the entire RAS blocker class may be inappropriately avoided by future providers.
pearls.verbatim: Why do I use an ARB a night with lisinopril? And you just Cough. What happens when you get a cough with an ACE or angioedema with an ACE to this class that, as you know, was the center of the slide? RAS. Right? Now you've burned the ACE and probably the ARB
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Potassium chloride salt substitute can lower blood pressure by about 10 mmHg (5 from potassium, 5 from sodium reduction), but avoid in CKD4 patients.
pearls.verbatim: Just use a salt substitute. These are not CKD4 people. I'm not worried. I don't want potassium in those. But this will actually lower it five, and this will lower it another five.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: During medication titration, check BP twice in the morning (after voiding, before breakfast/coffee, sit 5 minutes) and twice at bedtime, recording all numbers.
pearls.verbatim: get up into your bladder before you have breakfast and before you have your coffee. Sit for five minutes. Check your blood pressure twice. I wanna know both those numbers. And then I want you to do that same thing at bedtime.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing medication titration for hypertension
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: A creatinine increase of up to 30% after starting an ARB is expected and indicates the medication is working by reducing glomerular hyperfiltration.
pearls.verbatim: And so when that GFR goes down, the creatinine is gonna go up. It's just going... And that actually is a sign that your medication is working the way it's supposed to work.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: If creatinine jumps more than 30% after starting an ARB, suspect renal artery stenosis (possibly bilateral).
pearls.verbatim: Now if it jumps more than 30%, it could be they are one of these renal artery stenosis people, maybe even bilateral.

pearls.text: Use the 'wagon wheel in a rut' analogy to explain the body's set point and protected fat mass.
pearls.verbatim: I talk with them about this protected fat mass, and I use a little thing about wagon wheels and a set point. What do I mean by that? I say, you know how a wagon is going down the muddy road and the wheels get down in the rut.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Aim for slow weight loss of about 10% per year to avoid triggering the thrifty gene and yo-yo rebound.
pearls.verbatim: Mrs. Jones, I know it doesn't feel like, you know, 18 pounds over over a year. But if you can get 18 pounds every year, that is a win. You win the lottery if you do that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Weight Watchers is the best studied commercial diet, though its recent move to prescribe medications is controversial.
pearls.verbatim: Weight Watchers is the best commercial best commercial diet. It's been studied multiple years. Now they're a little bit in trouble because now they they just bought a huge health care thing that's gonna start prescribing meds.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: patients considering commercial weight loss programs
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Clinicians should personally try weight loss apps (e.g., Noom, Weight Watchers) to give informed recommendations.
pearls.verbatim: You should sign up for these apps. You. You. All of you in the room. Pay for the first month. Do the trial. Whatever. Because you need to tell them, this is easy to use. It's great. Noom is great.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: clinicians counseling patients on weight loss
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Obesity is a chronic illness designated since 2012, not a moral failure; patients may hide medication use due to stigma.
pearls.verbatim: Chronic illness, it's been designated since 2012. It is not a a a failure to be a good human being. Okay? It's been an illness since 2012.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: When starting a GLP-1, tell patients to eat half their normal portion to avoid nausea.
pearls.verbatim: When I start somebody on or or Ozempic, I tell them, take... Eat half of what you normally eat. When you start a GLP-1, cut your portion size down in half, and you'll feel pretty good. If you're still hungry, then you can eat a little bit more. But do not try to eat what you normally eat and start a GLP-1. You will be sick.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: To prevent constipation on GLP-1s, start one tablespoon Metamucil and two tablespoons Citrucel once a day.
pearls.verbatim: I tell them one tablespoon Metamucil, two tablespoons of Citrucel once a day.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Don't use food trackers in patients with eating disorders; it makes them sicker.
pearls.verbatim: Don't use trackers in eating disorders. Kinda goes without saying. These are patients who are tracking everything. And if you say, hey. Use a tracker. You make them sicker.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Do not use activity trackers in patients with eating disorders; it will make them sicker.
pearls.verbatim: Don't use trackers in eating disorders. Kinda goes without saying. These are patients who are tracking everything. And if you say, hey. Use a tracker. You make them sicker.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Ozempic is only FDA-approved for diabetes; do not prescribe it for obesity as it will be denied every time.
pearls.verbatim: it is only FDA approved for diabetes. Don't try to send it in for obesity. It will be denied every time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Titrate GLP-1 agonists to the highest dose for maximal weight loss; do not stop at a low dose, go up monthly until the patient cannot tolerate higher.
pearls.verbatim: All of the all of the studies seem to show much higher weight loss at the higher dosages. So I tell them that. We're not stopping at this dose. We're gonna go to the next dose in a month and after that another dose, and then you tell me when you can't go any higher.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: patients on GLP-1 agonists for weight loss
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Topamax (topiramate) increases risk of kidney stones; Wellbutrin (bupropion) lowers seizure threshold.
pearls.verbatim: So Topamax can increase your risk of kidney stones. We know that Wellbutrin lowers the seizure threshold just a bit.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Orlistat (Alli) can cause anal leakage; counsel patients about this side effect.
pearls.verbatim: And then he said, and orlistat, don't forget anal leakage. My favorite one to counsel.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: For fiber supplementation, recommend two parts Citrucel to one part Metamucil to reduce gas while getting cholesterol benefit.
pearls.verbatim: So what I tell people is do two parts Citrucel to one part Metamucil. Because the Metamucil, you get a little bit of the benefit of the cholesterol, and it works a little bit better than just Citrucel by itself.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: About 30% of patients develop clinical major depressive disorder within one year after CABG, so consider starting an SSRI or SNRI before surgery.
pearls.verbatim: About thirty percent of patients within a year after CABG will have clinical major depressive disorder. So it's to the point where now often discussed, why don't we start your SSRI or SNRI now before you have your CABG?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Use the ACS risk calculator to generate patient-specific risks for serious complications, pneumonia, cardiac events, surgical site infection, UTI, VTE, and discharge to nursing/rehab facility; print and sign the single-page output for the chart.
pearls.verbatim: You can press this. It's a single page. Print that off at your clinic, at your suite printer. You make a... You sign it. Put your name on the bottom of it. Sign it. Put it in the chart, and you and you know where this patient's risk is falling in all of these categories.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: A serious complication risk of 10% or above is a reasonable rule of thumb to consider postponing surgery for optimization, e.g., if A1c is 12.
pearls.verbatim: If they're getting up in the ten percent or above serious complication, that's just kind of a rule of thumb that I that I kinda say, man, your A1c is 12, and you're... You know? Let's let's talk about how we can how we can postpone this.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: If a patient has chest pain or dyspnea on climbing a flight of stairs, they need a workup for that problem (angina or dyspnea), not just cardiac clearance for surgery; pause the surgical process to evaluate.
pearls.verbatim: If any of this kind of stuff comes back positive in the sense that you're picking up something... Like somebody who's got chest pain or is short of breath when they go up a flight of stairs or whatever, Now they need a workup not for the surgery. They need an evaluation for their dyspnea or for their angina. And, yes, you pause and stop process of surgery to evaluate that problem.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: patients with positive cardiac symptom screen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Patients using more than about three servings of alcohol per week should have a conversation about it; the pre-op visit is a great time to address alcohol, opioid use, and other health risks.
pearls.verbatim: Anybody who's using more than about three servings of alcohol a week, I have a conversation with them. If you think about it, this is a great time to talk about all of the health risks that patients have when they come in. Right? It's a great time to talk about, like, are you on an opiate? Should you be on an opiate? How is that making a difference in your life? Like, is this a good idea?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: patients with alcohol or opioid use
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Screen functional status by asking: can you climb two flights of stairs without stopping, without chest pain? That is equivalent to 4 METs, the threshold needed to avoid major adverse cardiac events during surgery.
pearls.verbatim: I screen with, can you climb up a flight of stairs? One flight of stairs is two minutes of work. Two flights of stairs is four minutes of work without stopping. Can you go up two flights of stairs without stopping without any chest pain, without falling down, without, right, filling the blank?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Avoid routine EKG in a 30-something patient because you may find an incidental abnormality that leads to unnecessary echo and anxiety.
pearls.verbatim: But why would you not want to do an EKG on the 30 something that's going in to do a surgery? You're gonna find something that they're gonna freak out about, and now you've gotta do an echo, and now you've gotta do... You know? Like, these things are... They have cost associated, and I don't just mean financial cost.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Smoking cessation is the number one thing you can do to change a patient's life; set a quit date for the day of surgery and use nicotine replacement or Chantix.
pearls.verbatim: The number one thing that you could do to change a patient's life today is to get them to the smoking. Six weeks out from your knee, you're smoking a pack a day. Hey. How do we set your quit date the day you go have your surgery? Let's get all your nicotine and everything in place. Let's get you on your Chantix or whatever.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: patients who smoke and are planning surgery
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Protein is the biggest nutritional predictor of surgical recovery; encourage elderly patients to use Boost, Ensure, or protein shakes to combat sarcopenia.
pearls.verbatim: Protein is the big one that we always talk about because that's the biggest predictor. So especially little old people, man, they have sarcopenia of the elder... Of of the elderly is real, so they lose muscle mass as they get older, and they quit eating protein.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Use the RCRI (Revised Cardiac Risk Index) to communicate cardiovascular risk to the surgeon; include it in your note or quick text.
pearls.verbatim: This is the RCRI. So this is what the surgeon wants to know in terms of just cardiovascular clearance. And so I'll often put this in the chart because he's gonna get my note, right, from my visit with them.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: The biggest barrier to treating hepatitis C is not the medicine but pharmacy and medical finance issues, as medications are hard to obtain.
pearls.verbatim: the biggest part of this you're gonna see is not medicine. It's pharmacy and medical finance because these meds are very hard to come by.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture

pearls.text: Patients with hepatitis C should be offered hepatitis A and B vaccination if not current, and screened for alcohol/drug use, HIV, and STIs.
pearls.verbatim: So you definitely wanna offer them hep A and hep B vaccination.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture

pearls.text: For patients with ongoing hepatitis C risk factors who test negative, repeat testing should be done every 3 to 12 months, not every 5 years.
pearls.verbatim: I often ask people. Right? I mean, you'll see data every three to four months up to every year depending on what the risk factors are. So it's not every five years.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: adults with ongoing HCV risk factors
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture

pearls.text: Hepatitis C is rarely transmitted sexually unless blood is involved; injection drug use is a major risk factor.
pearls.verbatim: it's very difficult to pass HCV sexually unless there's blood involved.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture

pearls.text: Order hepatitis C antibody reflex to genotype as the initial test; if antibody is negative the patient is charged only for the antibody, but if positive it automatically adds viral load (HCV RNA) and genotype.
pearls.verbatim: hepatitis C analyzer reflex to genotype. So what does that do at LabCorp? Well, they run on hepatitis C antibody. If it's negative, they stop. Patient is charged for the antibody, and that's all they get. If it's positive, you get a viral load, HCV RNA, and you get a genotype.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: adults being screened for hepatitis C
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture

pearls.text: Do not manage HCV in patients on warfarin in primary care; consider referral.
pearls.verbatim: They're on warfarin. You probably shouldn't be taking care of them in your clinic for hep C if they're on warfarin.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture

pearls.text: No lab monitoring is required during hepatitis C treatment; just bring the patient in once a month to check on side effects and adherence.
pearls.verbatim: No lab monitoring is required. They do this by telehealth. Most of the time, we could do it by bringing them in once a month.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture

pearls.text: Check HCV RNA 12 weeks after completing treatment to confirm cure; a viral load that was 4.5 million at start should be zero at 12 weeks post-treatment.
pearls.verbatim: Post treatment, you wanna do a viral RNA at twelve weeks. This is the most fun that you'll ever have. When you do when you do a a viral load and it's four and a half million when they start, Twelve weeks later, it is zero
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: patients after completing hepatitis C treatment
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture

pearls.text: For HCV on Medicaid SoonerCare, prescribe Mavyret as three tabs daily for eight weeks; no prior authorization is required with your signature.
pearls.verbatim: You can write this prescription from Cerner for three tabs a day for eight weeks on Medicaid SoonerCare, and it will be filled by PA.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.applies_to: patients with HCV on Medicaid SoonerCare
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture

pearls.text: At monthly visits during HCV treatment, do not order labs routinely; only if clinically indicated, such as suspicion of AKI.
pearls.verbatim: If I feel like they're having an AKI or, you know, they're at risk for whatever, then I might order that lab. Okay. But I don't do that routinely.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture

pearls.text: MiraLAX at night is recommended to prevent constipation and reduce straining that can worsen pelvic floor disorders.
pearls.verbatim: So MiraLAX at night is everyone's best friend.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

pearls.text: Advise patients to avoid carbonated drinks, citrus, caffeine, and chocolate because these acidic items irritate the bladder and worsen urgency/frequency.
pearls.verbatim: I always tell patients to avoid the four c's. Carbonated drinks, citrusy things, caffeinated drinks, and chocolate.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

pearls.text: Limit fluid intake 2, 3 hours before bedtime to reduce nocturia.
pearls.verbatim: so two to three hours before you're going to sleep, limit your fluid intake.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

pearls.text: For overactive bladder, gradually increase time between voids by 10 minutes each week.
pearls.verbatim: you would tell them, okay. I know you go to the bathroom every hour, but for next week, go every hour and ten minutes. Then the next week after that, every hour and twenty minutes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.applies_to: patients with overactive bladder or frequent voiding
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

pearls.text: Avoid oxybutynin due to severe dry mouth; it also takes 4, 6 weeks to see effect.
pearls.verbatim: I'm trying not to prescribe oxybutynin because that has the most severe dry mouth for patients.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.applies_to: patients needing an anticholinergic for overactive bladder
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

pearls.text: Prefer solifenacin (Vesicare) for overactive bladder; start at 5 mg, can increase to 10 mg, once daily, fewer side effects.
pearls.verbatim: I really like Vesicare. The generic name is solifenacin because it does have the less side effects. It's five milligrams or ten milligrams, so you can start low with five milligrams, and then it can go up if they're like, I really like it, but I want more. And it's only a pill that you take once a day.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.applies_to: patients needing an anticholinergic for overactive bladder
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

pearls.text: Avoid mirabegron in patients with hypertension because it elevates blood pressure.
pearls.verbatim: If you have a patient who has blood pressure issues, and I try to stay away from mirabegron because that's one of the things that mirabegron can do is elevate blood pressure.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

pearls.text: If using desmopressin for nocturia, monitor electrolytes monthly to prevent sodium/potassium derangements.
pearls.verbatim: Sometimes we'll do desmopressin for nocturia. But, honestly, that's definitely a medication that they have to come to your office every month to make sure that their electrolytes within normal limits because you don't want them to be out of whack with their sodium and their potassium.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

pearls.text: Autologous fascial sling avoids mesh but may increase risk of overactive bladder symptoms.
pearls.verbatim: as far as the autologous sling, it's risk. Sometimes it increases the risk for what we call overactive bladder.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.applies_to: women with stress urinary incontinence who choose autologous sling
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

pearls.text: After fitting a pessary, have the patient void into a hat to confirm it stays in place.
pearls.verbatim: They usually go to the restroom. Make sure to put a nursing hat in the toilet so if it falls out, it doesn't fall in the toilet.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

pearls.text: Vaginal estrogen does not increase endometrial cancer risk, but coordinate with oncology for patients with gynecologic cancer history.
pearls.verbatim: There's been studies that show that using vaginal estrogen cream does not increase the risk endometrial cancer.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.applies_to: patients with history of gynecologic cancer
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction

pearls.text: For Rocky Mountain spotted fever, there is no alternative to doxycycline; if not used, the patient may die.
pearls.verbatim: There's no alternative unless you go if you wanna live.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price

pearls.text: For Lyme disease with a classic erythema chronicum migrans rash, you do not need a blood test; the rash alone is diagnostic.
pearls.verbatim: If you have everything erythema chronicum migrans, you got the diagnosis, and you don't need doing blood test.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.applies_to: patients with classic expanding rash in endemic area

pearls.text: When testing for Lyme disease, start with an ELISA; if negative, Lyme is unlikely.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected early disseminated or late Lyme disease
