pearls.text: Tick paralysis causes ascending paralysis in young children, whereas botulism causes descending paralysis starting from cranial nerves.
pearls.verbatim: Either child two or three years old is all of sudden not walking anymore. And they become a neurological disease, and it kinda ascends. ... That's botulism starts from the cranial nerves down.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Vector Transmitted Disease 6/18/26

pearls.text: In onchocerciasis (river blindness) endemic areas, annual ivermectin distribution is done by health workers who visit huts, watch the patient take the pill, and record it in a log.
pearls.verbatim: everyone there gets ivermectin once a year. So the health care workers also come to their huts. It has a little book, and it gives you the pill, watch you take the pill.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Vector Transmitted Disease 6/18/26

pearls.text: In areas where Loa loa is also endemic, mass ivermectin administration cannot be done because it can increase the filariae burden and cause major complications.
pearls.verbatim: in areas where there's lower lower also, that can't be done because that could cause the... Kinda increase in the filariae and the Loa loa can cause major problems.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Vector Transmitted Disease 6/18/26

pearls.text: Jigger flea infestation is very painful and can lead to major infections, sepsis, and death; it is debilitating and requires regular removal (e.g., every Friday) in affected individuals.
pearls.verbatim: You can even get major infections and sepsis, and you can die from it. But it's very debilitating.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Price
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Price on Vector Transmitted Disease 6/18/26

pearls.text: Ciclesonide (Omnaris, Zetonna) is a pro-drug that activates inside the cell, reducing local side effects, but it is very hard to obtain.
pearls.verbatim: It's actually a pro steroid. It's a pro drug. It's called ciclesonide, and it it is an inhaler as well as a nasal spray. It's a pro drug. It doesn't become a steroid it is inside the cell, then it becomes a steroid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Purser
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Purser on Allergic Rhinitis 4/16/26

pearls.text: Dog allergy testing is unreliable because commercial 'mixed dog' extracts don't specify which breeds are included; male dogs are more allergenic due to a protein in their prostate that appears in urine.
pearls.verbatim: Every single breed has a different allergen. And so when we have a dog skin test, it's from a bottle that says mixed dog. Mhmm. You can turn that bottle around, and they do not tell you what's in there.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Purser
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Purser on Allergic Rhinitis 4/16/26

pearls.text: Nasal irrigation cleans sinuses better than sprays, but avoid in immunocompromised patients unless they reliably use sterile distilled water.
pearls.verbatim: Immunocompromised is a fair statement if you're not sure... If they're not reliably going to be sterilizing and using distilled... Clean distilled water.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Purser
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Purser on Allergic Rhinitis 4/16/26

pearls.text: If a patient is too congested to use a nasal rinse, first use a topical decongestant (e.g., Afrin) or a few days of low-dose oral prednisone to reduce swelling before rinsing.
pearls.verbatim: If they're overly stuffed up, that's not the time to use the full lot. You have to get them unstuffed with something like topical decongestant. Right? Topical decongestant. Afrin is the same name or with some oral prednisone, a few days of that. Low dose, but decrease that in... That swelling of those turbinates going back there, and then let them wash it out.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Purser
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Purser on Allergic Rhinitis 4/16/26

pearls.text: Proper nasal spray technique: use opposite hand for same-side nostril, pull nostril open, aim away from septum to avoid epistaxis.
pearls.verbatim: I ask them to pull out their nose like this. Right? God bless you. Because we have a... We have oftentimes nasal vault collapse or septal deviation, and so pull out that side of the nose, put the nose spray in their other hand with the thumb on the bottom like this, and then they're gonna come up.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Purser
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Purser on Allergic Rhinitis 4/16/26

pearls.text: If a patient has nasal vault collapse or septal deviation, pull that side of the nose outward before inserting the spray to ensure the medication reaches the nasal cavity.
pearls.verbatim: We have oftentimes nasal vault collapse or septal deviation, and so pull out that side of the nose,
pearls.speaker: Dr. Purser
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Purser on Allergic Rhinitis 4/16/26

pearls.text: For skin prick testing, use the back rather than the arm because the back skin is more sensitive and yields better reactions.
pearls.verbatim: I use the back more than the arms because the back is a more sensitive skin.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Purser
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Purser on Allergic Rhinitis 4/16/26

pearls.text: A common acute trigger for hives is NSAIDs, especially when taken intermittently (start and stop), which 'baits' the immune system.
pearls.verbatim: NSAIDs is one of the most common. And why why it is is because people take it and stop it. Take it and stop it. Take it and stop it. It's just baiting, baiting, baiting on the system.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Purser
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Purser on Anaphylaxis 2/26/26

pearls.text: Histaminergic hives are pink, blanch, itch (not burn or hurt), come and go within 24 hours, and do not scar; these features distinguish them from vasculitic lesions.
pearls.verbatim: They're gone within a day. They're gone within twenty four hours. And this is what are on boards. It's what... It's the definition of a histaminergic hive. These are all the questions. They are pink. They blanch. Go away. They itch. They don't hurt.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Purser
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Purser on Anaphylaxis 2/26/26

pearls.text: Always ask patients with hives if they have ever had lip or eyelid swelling; angioedema often accompanies hives and may require steroids to resolve.
pearls.verbatim: When you see that hive patient in the ER or the urgent care, you should ask them, does your lips sometimes swell or an eyelid swell? And, usually, they'll say, yeah. It did happen one time. They usually require steroids to get it to go down.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Purser
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Purser on Anaphylaxis 2/26/26

pearls.text: Cholinergic urticaria (tiny bumps from exercise or heat) is common in 10- to 30-year-olds; cold urticaria can cause anaphylaxis, as seen in a child who went into anaphylaxis after entering a cold swimming pool.
pearls.verbatim: Cholinergic, Absolutely common in ten to thirty year olds, which is why I asked you guys how many of you had had it. For whatever reason, people who are out running or walking in the freezing cold or they've skied, and they come in, and they're covered with these tiny little bumps.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Purser

pearls.text: For chronic urticaria, use a longer course of steroids like prednisone IV with a two-week taper, not a Medrol Dose Pack, to get antibody levels down.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with mild to moderate dementia
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Cholinesterase inhibitors were FDA-approved only for mild to moderate dementia to delay institutionalization, not for long-term use in nursing homes; if a patient has been in a nursing home for years, consider stopping these medications.
pearls.verbatim: Were approved for mild to moderate dementia to delay the requirement for institutionalization. That was the only way it got through the FDA was the drug company said, no. No. We don't wanna treat people with this. We wanna slow them down so they can stay home longer, and the benefit to society is great enough that they should be able to be used for that purpose to to delay the requirement for nursing home placement based on their progression.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with dementia in nursing homes
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Beer is the number one dietary intervention to stop for gout; it is worse than other alcohols and high-purine foods.
pearls.verbatim: beer. Number one thing to stop.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: The three most important dietary interventions in order are: stop beer, avoid other alcohols, and avoid high-fructose corn syrup; high-purine animal foods are fourth.
pearls.verbatim: beer is worse, rest the alcohols, the wine, and the hard liquors and things, and then the high fructose corn syrup.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: The most common chart review error is giving wrong dietary advice (focusing on animal protein) and not following up to ensure the uric acid goal is met.
pearls.verbatim: They give them the wrong dietary advice. They focus on animal protein, and they don't ever follow-up that they treated them to get their goal met.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: Colchicine should be used at low dose; hold statins during a flare when giving colchicine.
pearls.verbatim: I always tell people to hold their statins when they're in a flare, and you're giving them colchicine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with acute gout flare on colchicine
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: Corticosteroids (e.g., Medrol dose pack) are an emerging first-line option for acute gout; a 6-day taper is typical but some patients may need extended therapy due to rebound.
pearls.verbatim: That's kind of a mid range taper is six days of therapy, and some people will need an extended therapy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: When assessing ligamentous laxity in an older patient, always compare to the contralateral knee because normal aging increases laxity; failing to do so may lead to overdiagnosis of injury.
pearls.verbatim: And if you just do one side where the injury is, you'll say, well, this is... You know, I'm used to examining a 20 year old. This is a 45, 50 year old, and this is too far. There's a a a damage here. But it's really not that there's damage. It's that you didn't compare it to the other side. So you always wanna compare the other leg
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: adults being evaluated for knee ligament injury
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Knee Pain and Problems

pearls.text: To reduce a lateral patellar dislocation, hyperextend the knee to recreate the window for the patella, then gently guide it back; do not force it back while the knee is bent.
pearls.verbatim: Hyperextend the knee, recreate the window, and allow it to move in easily. You don't wanna fight this back into place because you'll do damage, and you'll cause more trauma.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with acute lateral patellar dislocation
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Knee Pain and Problems

pearls.text: After reducing a patellar dislocation, brace the knee in slight flexion to prevent hyperextension and refer to orthopedics; most patients see an orthopedist within six weeks.
pearls.verbatim: You prevent hyperextension again. So you get a a brace. It doesn't have to be a tight brace, but it needs to be a brace that's going to hold the knee in some degree of flexion at that hyperextension.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Knee Pain and Problems

pearls.text: Medial or superior patellar dislocations are rare and require urgent orthopedic referral due to possible joint capsule or tendon damage.
pearls.verbatim: When it's not lateral, needs to go fairly urgently to the orthopedist. That's a rarer than mandate surgery, but there can be other displacement. There can be other lacerations going on in the joint capsule or tendon damage.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Knee Pain and Problems

pearls.text: For bursitis, avoid aspiration because it increases infection risk; steroids further increase infection risk and can cause joint degeneration. Manage conservatively with activity modification and anti-inflammatories.
pearls.verbatim: The risk benefit ratio is is really skewed. If you leave it natural, you leave it alone, you know, work with anti inflammatories and stress reduction and just make them... Let it kind of gradually reabsorb, your outcome long term statistically is a lot better.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Knee Pain and Problems

pearls.text: Use a standard injectate for all blocks and joint injections: 2 mL of Kenalog 40 mg/mL plus 2 mL of 1-2% lidocaine, giving 4 mL total with 80 mg of Kenalog.
pearls.verbatim: So you get two mls from that, and you get two mls out of the ampule. So you've got four mls, one or two percent Xylocaine, and eighty milligrams of Kenalog that you've got in your syringe now.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: adults receiving nerve blocks or joint injections in clinic
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: Use a 27-gauge ½-inch needle for injection; if aspiration is needed (e.g., joint effusion), switch to a larger needle.
pearls.verbatim: You put a 27 and a half needle on it, and that's how you're gonna inject people. And you can use that for joint injections as long as you don't need to aspirate.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: clinic nerve blocks and joint injections
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: For occipital nerve block, palpate one-third and two-thirds of the distance from midline to mastoid process at the hairline; inject just lateral to your finger with the patient sitting and head forward.
pearls.verbatim: What you're focusing on is a third of the way down this line from here to here, third of the way, and two thirds of the way.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with occipital neuralgia or occipital headache
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: Always aspirate before injecting a nerve block; if blood returns, do not inject. If air returns, obtain a post-procedure chest X-ray to rule out pneumothorax.
pearls.verbatim: do not inject with it. Do not inject with blood comes back. You aspirate and you don't get air and you don't get blood, You go ahead here, and you can put a CC of your solution around that nerve.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: any patient receiving a nerve block near the thorax or scapula
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: If a suprascapular block does not provide relief within five minutes, consider performing a dorsal scapular median nerve block due to overlapping innervation.
pearls.verbatim: Within about five minutes if you do your block.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with shoulder pain not relieved by suprascapular block
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: Do not apply compression for venous disease above the arterial perfusion pressure, or you risk creating critical limb ischemia.
pearls.verbatim: You gotta make sure you don't compress venous disease above the arterial perfusion pressure, or you create what? Critical lymph ischemia.

pearls.applies_to: patients with mixed arterial and venous disease

pearls.text: Use toe-brachial index when ankle-brachial index is falsely elevated due to calcified vessels.

pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected PAD and calcified arteries (e.g., diabetes, CKD)

pearls.text: Reserve CTA, MRA, and vascular referral for patients being considered for revascularization; stop workup with duplex if not intervening.
pearls.verbatim: If you've got this workout and you say, you know, we're not really gonna talk reperfusing this person, then you stop. You you go stop with the duplex where you've got your anatomy. You don't have to go into that full workout.

pearls.applies_to: patients with PAD not being considered for intervention

pearls.text: PAD in the leg is a marker for systemic cardiovascular disease; aggressively reduce risk with LDL target <50, smoking cessation, and full-court press risk reduction.
pearls.verbatim: These are the people that you really do full court press risk reduction. You want the LDL what? What are you shooting for in LDL in these people? ... Even 50 for some of the people that really do work like this.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Exercise therapy for claudication: walk to the point of ischemic discomfort, rest, then repeat; this stimulates neovascularization and bypasses blockages.
pearls.verbatim: You get them to do that level of work to where they're limited by that muscle group feeling that ischemic change? And then by resting and doing it again and resting and doing it again, what is it that you're you're causing their body to do? ... Neovascularization. They'll automatically bypass themselves.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: When prescribing exercise, warn patients not to exercise to the point of skin breakdown; ensure good shoes and educate about foot injury prevention.
pearls.verbatim: The the big caveat is you don't want them to exercise to the point of skin breakdown on their feet or legs. So you gotta make sure they've got good shoes, just diabetic shoes if they qualify.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with PAD starting exercise therapy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: For noncritical lesions, do physiologic studies yourself and start an exercise program before referring to vascular.
pearls.verbatim: But most of the time on the early part of the workup for the noncritical lesions, you do these studies yourself and get them ready to go and start them on the exercise program
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Patients with active critical ischemia (cool, infected, need reperfusion) require urgent vascular referral.
pearls.verbatim: people with active critical ischemia. So when they're, you know, cool, they're infected, they've they've gotta be reperfused. Those people need to go urgently.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: For chronic ischemia without exacerbation, refer to vascular within a few days to a week; for acute exacerbation, send to the ER for vascular consult.
pearls.verbatim: So if it's if it's chronic and if they don't have an exacerbation, those people can go to vascular. And I usually will call them and make sure they get them in within a couple of days or a week. pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: When you suspect critical limb ischemia, start anticoagulation while the patient is waiting for the vascular consultation; do not leave it for the vascular surgeon to order.

pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected critical limb ischemia

pearls.text: High-intensity statin should be your default; plan to add additional therapy at 3-month intervals until LDL goal is reached, not a 'maybe later' approach.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: For borderline PAD patients not ready for vascular referral, reassess every 2-3 months with exercise log, smoking status, diabetes control, and blood pressure log.

You know, your exercise log, your diabetes control log, your blood pressure log. How are we doing with controlling things? And and then every three months until they're ready to go

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: In women of childbearing age with abdominal pain, always perform a pregnancy test.

And what's your action in seeing this patient and walk in? They're going to ER. Positive rebound sound. I am done. You're on ER. I don't even have to know why is it there.

pearls.verbatim: So Cipro five hundred TID or Flagyl five hundred TID. The only time we do Flagyl five hundred TID is this. Usually, it's BID. Remember? BID is t... TID. Right? That's how I memorize it. Cipro five hundred tid, Flagyl, or by itself.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on Decreased Fetal Movement

pearls.text: For lactation suppression after fetal loss, recommend ibuprofen, cold cabbage leaves, tight bra, and no stimulation; avoid pumping.
pearls.verbatim: I actually recommend ibuprofen in everybody, because it's gonna help with the engorgement. It's gonna help with all the delivery stuff. ... Whole cabbage leaves so they can put the cabbage leaves in the refrigerator and then put them directly on their breast. That can help with discomfort. ... Tight fitting bra. No stimulation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.applies_to: patients after fetal loss who wish to suppress lactation
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on Decreased Fetal Movement

pearls.text: Cabergoline and pseudoephedrine can be used for lactation suppression but are contraindicated in patients with hypertension.
pearls.verbatim: Sudafed has side effect profile too. Both of them are not recommended in people with hypertension. The cabergoline. Cabergoline. Yep. And the Sudafed.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.applies_to: patients without hypertension seeking lactation suppression
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on Decreased Fetal Movement

pearls.text: Cabergoline 1 mg single dose within 48 hours postpartum can be used to suppress lactation after intrauterine fetal death.
pearls.verbatim: UpToDate, it says, like, you can do a onetime dose cabergoline, one milligram. And I, personally, I wish I would have known that for, like, this mom with IUFD. It's like a onetime single dose within forty eight hours postpartum.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on Decreased Fetal Movement

pearls.text: For elevated blood pressure at ≥37 weeks, consider delivery; by 39 weeks, delivery is indicated.
pearls.verbatim: Same thing if you have elevated blood pressure and you're nine weeks or more. I'm just gonna deliver you thirty seven weeks. I'm probably also gonna deliver you, but thirty nine weeks, absolutely gonna deliver.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.applies_to: patients ≥37 weeks with elevated blood pressure
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on Decreased Fetal Movement

pearls.text: When sending a patient to the hospital for decreased fetal movement, send them directly to labor and delivery for admission, not the emergency room.
pearls.verbatim: if you're sending somebody to the hospital, very important to clarify where you want them. So if you are not going to want this person to go home for any reason, that means you should go to labor and delivery. You don't need to send them to the OR. Just an extra charge, an extra work for everybody.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.applies_to: patients with decreased fetal movement at term
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on Decreased Fetal Movement

pearls.text: When starting a patient on meloxicam, explicitly list which NSAIDs to avoid (e.g., Advil, Motrin) because saying 'no NSAIDs' means nothing to patients.
pearls.verbatim: If I'm starting somebody on meloxicam, I'm gonna say, I don't want you taking any NSAIDs, and then I'll make a list of them to the patient because I think patients don't... I mean, you say no NSAIDs, and that means nothing to them.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: In pregnancy, antihistamines and Tylenol are safe, but avoid decongestants (phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine) and anything with '-D' in the name.
pearls.verbatim: But tell them anything that says dash d is not gonna be safe. And anything that's got decongestant, so the phenylephrine and the pseudoephedrine, you don't want them taking.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: Infant ibuprofen is 100 mg/5 mL, while children's ibuprofen (Motrin for infants) is 50 mg/1.25 mL; always include the concentration when prescribing weight-based doses.
pearls.verbatim: Infant ibuprofen is a hundred milligrams in five ml, and ibuprofen or Motrin for infants is fifty milligrams in one point two five ml.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: For patients with outdoor allergies, recommend using a nasal saline rinse immediately after coming inside to reset the sinuses, then use nasal spray afterward.
pearls.verbatim: If you have somebody who has really bad outdoor allergies and they're like, have them, I do recommend as soon as they come inside using it to kind of reset. And then maybe if they're using nose spray, they use the nose spray after they've nailed their sinuses.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: For patients with frequent UTIs, cranberry supplements can be tried as a preventive measure.
pearls.verbatim: So if you have somebody who has frequent UTIs, one of the things they can try is cranberry supplements, and there's lots of cranberry supplements.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: Salonpas patches come in two formulations: one with lidocaine 4% (similar to prescription 5% patches) and one with menthol; avoid aspirin-containing creams (e.g., Aspercreme) in children.
pearls.verbatim: One of the things I do recommend is the Salonpas. So there's two different formulations of the Salonpas, and one of them has lidocaine. So, basically, a lot of interns won't cover lidocaine patches because Salonpas makes 4% versus the 5% patches that we have prescription.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: OTC diclofenac gel is very effective; patients who say it doesn't work likely didn't use it correctly.
pearls.verbatim: Because that has, like, cured so many things in my life. And patients... I... My my belief with that is patients who tell me that they use it and it doesn't work didn't actually use it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: For diaper rash, start OTC clotrimazole early to prevent progression to pain and crying; most diaper rashes become fungal.
pearls.verbatim: if you have a kid who's prone to diaper infections, that probably as soon as they start having anything to do start putting on because it's really bad, and you don't want it to get to the pain and crying and all this other stuff. Early.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: Colace (docusate) is a cheap laxative option at $4 for 120 pills; it works well for patients starting pain medicine or iron.
pearls.verbatim: Colace, you can see that you can get, like, a 120 of a weight Colace for, I think, $4.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.applies_to: patients with constipation, especially starting opioids or iron
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: Ask patients with insomnia what they are currently taking and ensure they know the maximum recommended dose of OTC sleep aids.
pearls.verbatim: So whenever somebody's having insomnia, I ask them, what are you on now? And then make sure they know the max recommended dose.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: Long-term use of Benadryl (diphenhydramine) for sleep may be associated with a higher incidence of Alzheimer's; avoid it if possible.
pearls.verbatim: I don't know long term if you take Benadryl overdose if there's any, like, long term ramifications. I know that they've populated that maybe there's a higher incidence of Alzheimer's, which I think is enough.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: For applying sunscreen to a child's face, use a stick formulation (like a deodorant stick) and make it fun by asking what animal they want to be.
pearls.verbatim: But they also make basically a deodorant or a paste stick. Mhmm. And so that's what I think is the best for cases. And when I was a kid, my parents would tell me that they're making whatever animal, so that's what I do now. I'm like, what animal you wanna be today? And then I put the stick on his face.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: Cimetidine, due to its antiviral properties, may help treat warts when used at high doses.
pearls.verbatim: But that's why because of its antiviral properties is why high dose metadine usually works.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: Taking multiple products containing the same active ingredient can be fatal and cause liver failure; always check for duplicate ingredients.
pearls.verbatim: taking an active ingredient or the same active ingredient, those can damage people, can be fatal, can cause liver failure.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.applies_to: patients taking multiple OTC or prescription medications
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: Screen for anxiety and depression every year in all adults and in children age 8 and older.
pearls.verbatim: we say that anxiety and depression should be screened every year now for adults and for ages eight and up for anxiety.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Use adjustment disorder with anxiety when a clear stressor is present and the patient had no prior anxiety disorder meeting clinical criteria; if symptoms persist more than 6 months after the stressor ends, reconsider the diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: If they didn't have anxiety before that that met clinical criteria, I'm gonna go with the adjustment disorder. Now if it ends and then six months later, they still have this, then I'm gonna start thinking about, oh, maybe now it's moved into something else.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with anxiety following a specific stressor
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: When differentiating ADHD from anxiety in primary care, consider that an SSRI takes 5, 6 weeks to work while a stimulant works in 30 minutes, allowing a faster trial.
pearls.verbatim: If you wanna treat someone with anxiety or an anxiety disorder, bad or some kind of anxiety state that's causing trouble, how long does it take for that medication to work? Five to six weeks. How long does it take a dose of Adderall work? Thirty minutes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: primary care, patients with possible ADHD and anxiety
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Acute stress disorder lasts up to one month, begins within 3 days of a life-threatening event, and must persist at least 3 days; symptoms beyond one month indicate PTSD.
pearls.verbatim: One month. Up to one month. Could begin within three days. Has to last and persist at least three days. ... Acute stress disorder at one month would roll over if they're still having symptoms into PTSD.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: The key marker distinguishing OCD from anxiety disorders is the presence of compulsions (repetitive, narrow behaviors to reduce anxiety) rather than generalized worry.
pearls.verbatim: coming back to the same rather narrow thing versus worry as a way to be safe.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: In the first appointment for anxiety, essential steps are: assess safety (suicide, environmental threats), rule out medical causes (e.g., cardiac), and gather duration, onset, frequency, and intensity.
pearls.verbatim: What's essential? Are they gonna hurt themselves? Are they safe? Are they gonna hurt themselves?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Use the PC-PTSD-5 screener (five items) early in differential, especially if an SSRI is not working; a score of 3 is positive for women, 4 for men in VA primary care samples.
pearls.verbatim: I would really look at a PTSD screener, which is a five item. It's called the PC PTSD five screener. A three is considered positive, especially for women. In VA samples, when primary care, four, they found for men had a better balance between sensitivity and specificity.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with anxiety not responding to SSRI
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Cerner's behavioral health screeners are split between the ambulatory and behavioral medicine folders; clinicians should check both to find all available tools.
pearls.verbatim: The behavioral med screeners in Cerner are split really oddly. Actually, you just wanna open the ambulatory folder for most of them. If you open the behavioral med folder, your same list, you end up with a different set of screeners.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: The main physical risk of a panic attack is head injury from fainting, not cardiac arrest (if cardiac causes are ruled out).
pearls.verbatim: Head injury is actually kind of an... Actually, the main physical risk.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with panic attacks after cardiac workup is negative
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Deliver the 'lean in' message with genuine sympathy and empathy; never treat the patient's panic lightly.
pearls.verbatim: you cannot say that without sympathy and empathy. And you cannot treat it lightly.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Give the body an explanation for panic symptoms by doing burpees, ball push-ups, or jumping jacks for two minutes (like HIIT training) so the mind attributes the fast heart rate to exercise rather than panic.
pearls.verbatim: Another option is if they start feeling panic is to give their body an explanation for those symptoms. So start doing burpees. Start doing ball push ups. Start doing jumping jacks. Do that for two minutes like a HIIT training. Because if you do that, at the end of it, your body, your mind is like, oh, I know why my beating fast. Got it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients who cannot use the 'lean in' approach
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Grounding techniques are helpful in early stages of panic but less effective once the patient is in the throes of a full attack; at that point, it is something to move through, like a seizure.
pearls.verbatim: a lot of grounding techniques are helpful to people. That's something they can learn to do. Or in the early stages of panic, you can look those up. That's fine. But really, if they're already in the throes of panic, it is something like a seizure. Something to may move through.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: During panic, ensure the exhale is longer than the inhale to prevent hyperventilation and the sensation of not catching one's breath.
pearls.verbatim: the biggest deal is, like, that the exhale is longer than the inhale because that's why people hyperventilate. They don't make enough room to then inhale what they need. That's why they say I can't catch my breath.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: MRI for suspected arachnoiditis must be done with contrast; without contrast, the diagnosis can be missed.
pearls.verbatim: when you talk about an MRI in setting, it's important what what specific type of an MRI do you need to have when you're talking about arachnoiditis, spinal stenosis, and post traumatic. With contrast. Yeah. You have to have with contrast to see the arachnoiditis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: In post-traumatic spinal stenosis, flexion-extension X-rays are essential to evaluate spinal instability (laxity), which may not be seen on a supine MRI.
pearls.verbatim: X rays with flexion and extension views. Right? Because you're looking for of the spine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Explaining pain purely through anatomy and biomedical model can be counterproductive because it removes the patient's sense of agency; use a biopsychosocial or pain neuroscience education approach instead.
pearls.verbatim: if we just explain it from a biomedical model, if we just explain it through anatomy, just explain it in that way, it can actually, like, be counterproductive
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: clinicians educating patients with chronic pain
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Use the 'rules about pain' exercise: ask patients to complete statements like 'If my pain is this, that means what?' to connect pain levels to functional meaning.
pearls.verbatim: There's a kind of, like, little exercise called the rules about pain. So if if my pain is this, that means what? If my pain is this, that means what? And it gives you some starters to those statements.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Once a functional neurological symptom disorder diagnosis is on a patient's chart, it can follow them across healthcare systems and delay proper diagnosis of other conditions, so use the diagnosis thoughtfully.
pearls.verbatim: once that's on her chart as, you know, she goes to the hospital for what feels like seems like stroke symptoms, she has a history of stroke. They can't find a list of evidence that she's had a stroke, so now she has this functional neurological symptom disorder on her chart.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with functional neurological symptom disorder
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Be cautious about using the somatic symptom disorder label; consider treating underlying anxiety or adjustment disorder first, as generalized anxiety can focus on health concerns and may respond better to that approach.
pearls.verbatim: I'm cautious about using the somatic symptom disorder unless I really have to. Because if we can kind of address the anxiety and address the health concern... Because you can have generalized anxiety that focuses on health concerns.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with somatic complaints and anxiety
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Somatic symptom disorder must cause significant impairment in daily life, such as excessive healthcare use, inability to work, or avoiding driving, not just distress.
pearls.verbatim: We have to see this distress turn into dysfunction in life. It has to impact the way I do life. Maybe it's that I spend so much money seeking diagnoses or further testing. Maybe it's that I spend tons of time in health care. Maybe it's that I don't go to work.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: If a patient's chart shows they have been to multiple hospital systems, that raises questions about possible somatic symptom disorder, though it doesn't confirm it.
pearls.verbatim: inconsistent story, history of extensive diagnostic testing. So if you open a chart and it's like, you're the third hospital system they've been to, there's a reason it raises questions.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with extensive diagnostic workup across multiple systems
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: When discussing functional neurological symptom disorder with a patient, do not say symptoms are caused by stress or that the patient is faking; instead, say 'our bodies and minds are connected at levels we don't fully understand' and take the symptoms seriously.
pearls.verbatim: the standard of care is to have a conversation and to not attribute... To not say, like, these are caused by sight concerns, but to say our bodies and our minds are connected at levels we don't fully understand.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Confirm a dipstick-positive urine with microscopic analysis; only >3 RBC/HPF on microscopy defines hematuria.
pearls.verbatim: you need to confirm that with a microscopic analysis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Do not exclude a hematuria workup just because the patient is on an anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug.
pearls.verbatim: Antiplatelet, anticoagulant drugs do not exclude you from working up somebody who has hematuria.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: all patients on anticoagulants/antiplatelets with hematuria
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: If a patient has gross hematuria with a UTI, treat the infection and then retest for persistent microscopic hematuria.
pearls.verbatim: If somebody has gross hematuria, their hematuria goes away after treatment, it should be retested to see if they have persistent microscopic hematuria.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: patients with gross hematuria and UTI
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Recurrent urinary tract infections may be a sign of underlying bladder cancer; consider urology referral, especially if hematuria persists after treatment.
pearls.verbatim: It is extremely common for us to get a patient who's been treated for urinary tract infections for years. They now have muscle invasive bladder cancer because it was their bladder cancer.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: patients with recurrent UTIs, especially older adults
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: For low-risk microscopy hematuria (3-10 RBC, women <60/men <40, <10 pack-years, no additional risk factors), repeat urinalysis in 6 months; if still positive, reclassify as intermediate risk.
pearls.verbatim: We generally recommend a repeat urinalysis within six months rather than performing immediate imaging or scoping.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: low-risk patients with first episode of microscopic hematuria
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Gross hematuria always requires urology evaluation with CT urogram and cystoscopy; refer these patients regardless of other factors.
pearls.verbatim: If a patient is peeing blood, they need to come and see us no matter what.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: If a patient has gross hematuria, refer to urology regardless of whether it has resolved or a cause is apparent.
pearls.verbatim: if somebody comes into you with gross hematuria and you can't figure out a cost, even if it's... Yes. Even if it's gone
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: In a male patient complaining of urinary symptoms, a digital rectal exam is a diagnostic test for the cause of his symptoms, not a screening test for prostate cancer.
pearls.verbatim: digital rectal exam is no longer a screening test for prostate cancer. It is a diagnostic test to examine what the patient is telling you they are experiencing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: In obese men with nocturia, obstructive sleep apnea is a common cause; they wake up because they stop breathing, not because the bladder is full.
pearls.verbatim: obstructive sleep apnea. A lot of these guys have OSA, and they're waking up because they're not breathing at night.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Advise patients with LUTS to reduce caffeine and alcohol intake, as these are common bladder irritants.
pearls.verbatim: coffee and alcohol. Okay? Also spicy, salty foods and everything like that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: In a man with LUTS, it is very reasonable to start tamsulosin (Flomax) in primary care; it is cheap, fast-acting, and has a low risk of postural hypotension.
pearls.verbatim: it's very rare that there's not a good reason just to put him on Flomax ... It's the first thing that I will do.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: men with LUTS in primary care
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Warn every man starting an alpha blocker about retrograde ejaculation: semen goes backward into the bladder, orgasm feels the same but nothing comes out. Otherwise patients will be alarmed.
pearls.verbatim: If you're on Flomax, that squeeze doesn't happen, and semen will go backwards into your bladder. Nothing comes out when they have an organism. That freaks guys out.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: PSA can be used as a diagnostic test for evaluating prostate health in men with urinary symptoms, not just as a screening test for prostate cancer.
pearls.verbatim: that PSA is being ordered because of the diagnosis of BPH with obstruction. It is not being ordered as a screening test. It's being ordered so that I have more information about the disease that I am evaluating and treating.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Double voiding, void, stand, then sit back down and void again, can help women with pelvic prolapse empty their bladder completely and reduce UTIs.
pearls.verbatim: I want you to void, and I want you to stand, sit there for a second. I want you to sit back down and void again. There are a lot of women who have pelvic prolapse and that sort of thing, and the anatomy of their bladder will shift as they stand and move and stuff like that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: women with pelvic prolapse or incomplete bladder emptying
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: In little girls with recurrent UTIs, the cause is almost always constipation and holding urine all day.
pearls.verbatim: little girls who have recurrent urinary tract infection, it's almost always because they're not pooping, and they're not sitting to pee. They're just holding their urine all day long.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Azo (phenazopyridine) should not be taken for more than five days because prolonged use can dye the skin orange.
pearls.verbatim: Azo, generally, you don't wanna take that one for more than five days because if who's in a prolonged period, it can actually dye your skin orange, which is a little weird.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Macrobid (nitrofurantoin) does not penetrate tissue and should not be used to treat pyelonephritis; use Cipro, Bactrim, or Augmentin instead.
pearls.verbatim: Macrobid does not penetrate tissue. It is a urinary antibiotic. It does not treat pyelonephritis. If you have somebody who's getting flank pain or a female that's having a lot of problems and having fevers and stuff like that, put them on something Cipro, Bactrim, any... Augmentin, all of them penetrates tissue. Do not treat pyelo with Macrobid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Do not treat pyelonephritis with Macrobid; use Bactrim or Augmentin as they penetrate tissue.
pearls.verbatim: Bactrim, any... Augmentin, all of them penetrates tissue. Do not treat pyelo with Macrobid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Patients with recurrent UTIs do not need three positive cultures before urology referral; refer if they are miserable and not improving.
pearls.verbatim: You do not have to have three positive cultures. If you have a patient who is saying, I am completely miserable. I feel like I an ear or chest infection all the time. This is really driving me crazy. I take antibiotics. Nothing happens. Send them over to us.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: C-section scar ectopic pregnancy is dangerous because it can cause rupture of the uterus, not just the tube.

pearls.text: Order all four antibodies (GAD, IA-2, ICA, zinc transporter) when suspecting type 1 diabetes; absence of GAD alone does not rule it out.
pearls.verbatim: I would encourage you when you're thinking about type one diabetes to obtain all of the antibodies and not just the GAD because it could be any one of them. It could be multiple of them. The more antibodies you have, the more likely you are to see type one diabetes.

pearls.text: Patients with type 1 diabetes have a 30% higher likelihood of having thyroid disease and increased risk of celiac; screen for other autoimmune conditions.

pearls.text: Do not use C-peptide to classify diabetes type during DKA or severe hyperglycemia because glucotoxicity suppresses insulin secretion, giving a falsely low result.

pearls.text: Withholding basal insulin in a type 1 diabetes patient can rapidly lead to DKA; always ensure long-acting insulin is continued during hospitalization.
pearls.verbatim: if they're deficient and you come in and you say, oh, no. They're on lantus. I'm not gonna put it on. You withhold it. That person will end up in DKA.

pearls.text: When in doubt about diabetes type, start basal insulin to control glucose and figure out the classification later; you will not be faulted for using insulin.

pearls.text: Teplizumab can delay onset of type 1 diabetes by 2-3 years in at-risk individuals; screen children over age 2 with family history or personal autoimmune disease.

pearls.applies_to: children over age 2 with family history of type 1 diabetes or personal autoimmune disease
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Screen for type 1 diabetes antibodies in anyone with a family history of type 1 diabetes, any thyroid disorder (hypo or hyperthyroidism), or celiac disease.

pearls.text: If a patient tests positive for only one antibody, they are not a candidate for teplizumab, but guidelines exist for repeat antibody testing based on age.

pearls.text: Prescribe modern glucagon preparations (Gvoke injectable or Baqsimi intranasal spray) for patients on insulin MDI, as the old red-box kit is too difficult for families to use in emergencies.

pearls.text: Advise patients using CGM to wait 20 minutes after treating hypoglycemia before rechecking sensor glucose, or use a fingerstick for immediate confirmation.

pearls.text: Overnight low alarms on CGM are often false positives due to compression of interstitial fluid when lying on the sensor; always verify with a fingerstick before treating.

pearls.text: The ADA 2025 guidelines recommend offering a CGM to all patients with diabetes to identify glycemic patterns and reduce glucose variability.

pearls.text: Automated insulin delivery pumps (since 2018) communicate with CGM to suspend insulin for predicted lows and increase delivery for highs, improving glycemic control with less patient effort.

pearls.text: When interpreting a CGM report, first check how long the sensor was active; you need at least 70% of the 14 days for the data to be reliable.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: The AGP requires 15 minutes in a glucose zone to register; if a patient has a brief hypoglycemic dip that pops back up, it may show as zero on the AGP, so always scroll through daily graphs.
pearls.verbatim: So to to make it onto the AGP here, you have to have fifteen minutes in that time zone. So if someone has hypoglycemia where it drops and pops right back up, but they're not there for fifteen minutes, it's gonna show zero.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Always correct hypoglycemia first before targeting hyperglycemia; one hypo can lead to another within 24 hours.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: Consider historical marginalization and potential distrust of medical institutions as psychosocial factors when evaluating patients from marginalized groups.
pearls.verbatim: Historical marginalization, possibly underserved by medical institutions, something to think about.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: When a patient's trauma is racially charged, be aware that they will naturally take note of who is evaluating them, which can affect trust and the clinical interaction.
pearls.verbatim: He's gonna be taking note of who... Who's evaluating him. Right? Naturally, I would. Right? I think we all would.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: Adjustment disorder is diagnosed when there is out-of-proportion distress and functional impairment after a stressor, but the symptoms do not meet full criteria for another disorder like PTSD.
pearls.verbatim: So adjustment disorder with anxiety. What does that mean? Right? It means he has out of proportion distress and functional impairment after a stressor.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: patients with distress after a stressor
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: Trauma-focused CBT is the best evidence-based therapy for trauma-related symptoms; refer to a therapist trained in trauma work.
pearls.verbatim: Chiral therapy is a really good one for... Is is probably the best one.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: When evaluating mood instability in an adolescent, order labs including thyroid panel, pregnancy test, STI screening, and toxicology screen.
pearls.verbatim: Get labs. Thyroid. Yep. Thyroid. K. CVS. Okay. Pregnancy test. Good stuff. Gonna get a Lifestyle. ST... STI.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: Mood stabilization should be prioritized over ADHD treatment when hypomanic symptoms are present; consider stopping the stimulant to assess the underlying mood disorder.
pearls.verbatim: Mood stabilization, a priority over ADHD, which is we're thinking, what's going on with this? Could this ADHD medication be a problem for her?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: adolescents with ADHD who develop hypomanic symptoms
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: In an adolescent with new-onset depression and mood lability, ask about timing and potential trauma, as a change in behavior beginning about a year ago could signal a traumatic event.
pearls.verbatim: Notice the timing of when these things happened. A year ago, dot dot dot. What happened a year ago?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: In a patient with cyclothymic disorder or any mood cycling, be cautious with SSRIs as they can worsen manic/hypomanic symptoms; consider consulting a psychiatrist.
pearls.verbatim: when you have, like, manic, hypomanic concerns, you wanna be careful with those. Be careful.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: patients with cyclothymic disorder or bipolar spectrum concerns
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: Rule out somatic symptom disorder and illness anxiety disorder when the patient is not primarily distressed by physical symptoms, but by the psychological/behavioral cycle they produce.
pearls.verbatim: You have to rule out the somatic symptom disorders. Illness anxiety disorder, you have to rule these these things out because Sophia is not concerned about physical symptoms that distress her. Rather, it is her cycle psychological and behavioral responses that are causing the problem.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: patients with medical conditions and prominent anxiety/behavioral responses
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: If the patient has a genuine medical condition and is not consciously deceiving, you can rule out factitious disorder and malingering.
pearls.verbatim: We can rule out factitious disorders. She's not trying to deceive. She actually does have a medical diagnosis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: patients with known organic disease who show psychological/behavioral exacerbations
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: When psychological/behavioral factors are exacerbating a medical condition, consider the DSM-5 diagnosis 'Psychological Factors Affecting Other Medical Conditions'.
pearls.verbatim: Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: patients whose psychological/behavioral responses worsen a medical condition
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: Consider a home visit to evaluate the patient's environment, family dynamics, and adherence to treatment.
pearls.verbatim: Consider a home visit. ... We used to do them. ... We need to do them.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: patients with complex psychosocial factors affecting medical care
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: For a patient with hypercapnia or other metabolic abnormalities, order a neuropsych assessment to evaluate if the condition is impairing cognition and decision-making.
pearls.verbatim: Neuropsych assessment. Why? Hypocapnia. ... What's going on? It's how is that impairing her decision making?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: patients with hypercapnia or suspected metabolic encephalopathy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: Open-ended questions yield more information and often reduce the need for additional questioning; patients may give you everything you need without a long list of follow-ups.
pearls.verbatim: asking open questions. Yeah. And not being afraid of us. Explain that to me.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Reflection of meaning goes beyond reflecting content to capture what something means to the patient; use it as you get to know patients better.
pearls.verbatim: What a reflection of meaning is they'll say something, a whole bunch of stuff, and you reflect what it actually means to them or to you.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Use the BATHE technique (Background, Affect, Trouble, Handling, Empathy) to assess psychological distress in 1, 5 minutes; it does not add time to the visit.
pearls.verbatim: research says that using BATHE does not add time to your visit.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: When a patient discloses a maladaptive coping skill like drinking, do not support it; instead say, 'That sounds like it caused some other challenges' and lean in with empathy.
pearls.verbatim: You're not gonna support that one. Right? You can say, wow. That sounds like it caused some other challenges.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: For a patient who is receptive to prayer, you can stop, pray about the issue, and then move on with the clinical visit.
pearls.verbatim: For someone who's receptive to prayer, let's definitely pray about that. You can even stop right then, pray about it, and say... And then move on with the clinic with your visit.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Simplify complex medication schedules for elderly caregivers; ask if you can reduce dosing frequency (e.g., avoid three-times-daily meds).
pearls.verbatim: you present some complex medication schedule to them. Is there any way that you can simplify that?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: clinicians caring for older adults with cognitive impairment
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Remember the caregiver is your patient too, do not forget them during visits focused on the dementia patient.
pearls.verbatim: don't forget caregiver. Don't forget the caregiver.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Ask about tasks the caregiver is not capable of; shame may prevent them from disclosing these gaps.
pearls.verbatim: That's a great question. A really good question. And they may not have shared that with anybody. They may be hiding it too. Right? Shame.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Common symptoms of caregiver stress include denial, anger, social withdrawal, anxiety, depression, exhaustion, sleeplessness, irritability, lack of concentration, and neglect of their own health.
pearls.verbatim: Common symptoms of caregiver stress for you to be aware of and to educate your patient about.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Use geriatric care managers or case managers to help caregivers organize and implement a plan; they are exceptional and should be employed.
pearls.verbatim: In some systems, they have geriatric care managers. So, specifically, that's what they do.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: If alkaline phosphatase is elevated in isolation and the source is unclear, check GGT or 5'-nucleosidase to differentiate liver from bone origin.
pearls.verbatim: if you have the elevated alk phos and you're not sure where it's coming from, right, because it can also be bone or Then you can get the GGT or the five, you know, nucleosidase, and that can help differentiate.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.applies_to: patients with isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: For intermediate-risk choledocholithiasis (abnormal LFTs, dilated CBD but not markedly elevated bilirubin), obtain MRCP before ERCP.
pearls.verbatim: Now if it's intermediate, alright, you've got some abnormal LFTs and definitely CBD, but no... But at least like that, markedly elevated like that, you know, then then you would go to MRCP.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.applies_to: patients with intermediate risk of choledocholithiasis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: CA 19-9 is not useful for ruling in or out pancreatic cancer; it is most useful as a baseline to monitor response to treatment.
pearls.verbatim: So where it's actually most useful is if you found that they've got pancreatic cancer, get your level so you can see what it is. Because then when you're treating it, if it actually is protectable or you are able to really diminish its size, then you can kind of use it later on to get the levels down and see if they're starting to bump up.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: For intermediate pancreatic cancers with some invasion, use neoadjuvant chemotherapy first to shrink the tumor and treat micrometastases before surgery.
pearls.verbatim: But for those that are more intermediate that have a little bit of invasion or some part of those, you'll actually do neoadjuvant chemo first. Right? So you'll do some chemo beforehand.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.applies_to: patients with borderline resectable pancreatic cancer
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: For painless jaundice in an outpatient setting, order a CT scan with contrast ASAP and refer to oncology if anything is found.
pearls.verbatim: Definitely get the CT Okay. With contrast ASAP. And if you find anything on there, you know, get them in with the nonbiliary oncology.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: IBS involves augmented cellular immune response with elevated production of proinflammatory cytokines like tumor necrosis factor, similar to asthma.
pearls.verbatim: Augmented cellular immune response with elevated production of proinflammatory cytokines, tumor necrosis factor.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: If diarrhea persists beyond 7 days, suspect a bacterial cause and consider stool culture.
pearls.verbatim: symptoms or lasting longer than seven days. Right? Now that we're going more towards... So seven days, it makes something bacterial more likely.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.text: Check for C. difficile if the patient has had antibiotics or hospitalization in the last three months.
pearls.verbatim: C. Diff testing. Right. Antibiotics or hospitalization last three months.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.applies_to: patients with acute diarrhea and recent antibiotic use or hospitalization
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.text: Test for C. diff if the patient has had antibiotics or hospitalization within the last three months.
pearls.verbatim: C. Diff testing. Right. Antibiotics or hospitalization last three months.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.text: Loperamide (Imodium) is safe for symptomatic relief if there is no fever, no bloody stool, and the illness is not severe; do not use in dysentery as it may prolong the disease.
pearls.verbatim: no fever or it's very low grade. You know, it's not severe. It's not bloody. Then you can do Imodium.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.text: During acute diarrhea, the BRAT diet is helpful; avoid fat and dairy except yogurt.
pearls.verbatim: the BRAT diet can help ... Fat is gonna make it worse, and then dairy can also make it worse other than yogurt.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.text: In children with acute diarrhea from overseas areas where zinc deficiency is prevalent, or who are malnourished, give zinc supplementation.
pearls.verbatim: if they're coming from, you know, overseas where zinc deficiency is prevalent or they are malnourished, you may need to give them some zinc.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.applies_to: children with acute diarrhea in resource-limited settings
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.text: For outpatient ova and parasite testing, give the patient a collection kit and have them drop off a sample each day for three consecutive days.
pearls.verbatim: all stool testing has to be done at home so we can give them the kit every day for three days to drop off the sample.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.applies_to: outpatient stool collection for ova and parasites
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.text: You do not need great faith; you need faith in a great God. The trustworthiness of the object is what matters.
pearls.verbatim: whether we have a lot of faith or a little faith.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: You do not need great faith, but faith in a great God.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.verbatim: the question at the end of this weekend will not be depth of your trust. It will be, is Christ worthy of your trust?

pearls.text: When a patient presents with fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity, perform a full neurological exam including fundoscopy to check for papilledema, which indicates increased intracranial pressure.
pearls.verbatim: I knew, oh my goodness. Something really neurological is going on. I need to do a full blown neurological exam, so I did. And sure enough, she was weak on the left side of her body. And I looked in her eye, did the eye exam, a fundoscopic exam, and I saw, which a clear sign that I'd almost never seen in residency or medical school in real life, which was florid papilledema, bilateral florid papilledema.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: In a child with progressive hemiparesis, papilledema, and vision loss, consider post-viral leukomyeloencephalitis and start steroids early to prevent permanent brain damage, even if infection is a possible cause.
pearls.verbatim: she was having such symptoms of intracranial pressure that I thought, you know, maybe we should put her on steroids. That's a risky thing. We didn't know it was an infection or not. And so I consulted the neurosurgeon back in The USA, and we decided, okay. Let's just go ahead and take the risk and put her on steroids.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.applies_to: children with suspected inflammatory brain disease
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: When performing an appendectomy in a resource-limited setting, consider a midline incision if the appendix may be malpositioned, as a retrocecal appendix may not be accessible through a right lower quadrant incision.
pearls.verbatim: In the book, it had a little PS. Sometimes the appendix is flipped over and you'll need a midline incision. At the last moment, I thought, I think I need to cut midline. So I cut the midline and out the appendix way over by the umbilicus.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: When performing an appendectomy, if the appendix is not found in the right lower quadrant, consider a midline incision because the appendix may be flipped over near the umbilicus.
pearls.verbatim: Sometimes the appendix is flipped over and you'll need a midline incision.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.applies_to: during appendectomy when appendix not in typical location
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.verbatim: And so wonderfully, that means we don't have to be paralyzed by uncertainty. Sometimes we get paralyzed by an overchoice. There's just too many choices. Don't have to be paralyzed. We can move forward. We can take a risk. Maybe this will work out. Maybe the Lord will help us.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26

Even if you can't say that, I hope you will be able to say, always, whoops, always be able to say, Christ is worthy of our absolute trust.

pearls.text: Refer infants with dacryostenosis by six months (Dr. Swan's preference) or by one year per UpToDate if not resolving.
pearls.verbatim: According to UpToDate, you refer them... They need to be referred by one year, but Doctor. Likes to refer them by six months.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: If a dacryocystocele (swelling over the lacrimal sac) is present, refer to ophthalmology urgently because it can impair breathing in young infants.
pearls.verbatim: the times to be concerned is whenever they have a dacrocystocele, and that's basically where there is swelling. They're basically where the duct is. It can also especially... They need to go to ophthalmology right away.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.applies_to: infants with swelling over the lacrimal sac
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: Refer constant strabismus at any age or intermittent strabismus persisting after four to six months.
pearls.verbatim: constant strabismus at any age or intermittent strabismus after four to six months.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: For preseptal cellulitis, start oral antibiotics, arrange close follow-up within 24, 48 hours, and if not improving by then, manage inpatient with IV antibiotics.
pearls.verbatim: if you think that it's preseptal cellulitis, then you start oral antibiotics and you need close follow-up as well as appropriate return precautions. You should have them coming back within twenty four to forty eight hours. And if they're not improving by that time, they need inpatient management with IV antibiotics.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: Contact lens use changes management for almost any eye problem; always ask about contacts.
pearls.verbatim: Whether or not a patient uses contacts changes the management for almost any eye problem.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: Contact lens use changes management for almost any eye problem; contact lens users with bacterial conjunctivitis need pseudomonas coverage with their eye drops.
pearls.verbatim: Whether or not a patient uses contacts changes the management for almost any eye problem. So that's a key thing to know for a lot of different eye problems.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: For viral conjunctivitis, if patients use over-the-counter decongestant drops, warn them they could have rebound worsening congestion or worsening goop in their eyes if used prolonged.
pearls.verbatim: If they decide to use something that has decongestant in it, you have to warn them that they could have rebound worsening congestion or worsening goop in their eyes if they use it prolonged.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.applies_to: patients with viral conjunctivitis using decongestant drops
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: Avoid topical steroids and topical NSAIDs in allergic conjunctivitis.
pearls.verbatim: we also avoid topical steroids or topical NSAIDs.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: For a stye, if it doesn't resolve within two weeks, refer to a specialist. For a chalazion, if it doesn't resolve within one to two months, refer to a specialist.
pearls.verbatim: for a sty, what I read is if it doesn't resolve within two weeks, then you can send them to... Refer them to specialist. Whereas for the chalazion, if it doesn't resolve within one to two months, then he sends them to a specialist.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: For corneal abrasion, avoid topical anesthesia and topical NSAIDs; use oral meds like ibuprofen instead. Topical NSAIDs can melt the cornea.
pearls.verbatim: you should avoid analgesia if possible. With pediatric population, you often do need to use it just to be able to do the eye exam, but both topical anesthesia as well as NSAIDs are not good.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: For corneal abrasion involving over 50% of the cornea, you can give cycloplegic drops; homatropine is preferred in pediatrics.
pearls.verbatim: if the cornea involvement is severe, it's over 50% of the cornea, you can, you know, give cycloplegic drops. Homatropine is what they prefer in pediatrics.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.applies_to: pediatric patients with corneal abrasion involving >50% of cornea
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: For corneal abrasion, refer promptly to ophthalmology if there is any corneal infiltrate, foreign body, purulent discharge, vision problems, or if the child is unwilling to keep the eye open for exam.
pearls.verbatim: you should refer them promptly to ophthalmology if there's any corneal infiltrate, foreign body, purulent discharge, vision problems. And then also if the infant or child is just unwilling to keep the eye open for an exam, then they should go.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: For corneal abrasion, do not use a pirate patch because kids can open their eye and it can cause more damage; use something that keeps the eye closed.
pearls.verbatim: Not the pirate patch. I heard that that actually can cause more problems and more damage to their eye because the kids are able to open their eye. You want something that'll kind of keep their eye closed
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25
