pearls.text: Pre-COPD (PRISm) describes symptomatic patients with normal spirometry who are at risk for progression; consider bronchodilators and risk factor modification.
pearls.verbatim: There's a new thing that Gold kinda came out with that's called pre COPD or prisms. They call them too. It's kinda like prediabetes. So they're trying to make that enroll. And so you have all the symptoms, but you do the COPD. You do the spirometry, and it doesn't meet quite meet criteria. So those people they found are at risk for progressing.

pearls.text: During the swallow screen, have the patient take a small sip, hold it, swallow, then repeat 'a b c one two three' to check for voice quality changes; coughing or voice changes indicate failure.

pearls.text: For thrombectomy candidacy, the time window is 4.5 to 24 hours; order CTA stat to evaluate for large artery occlusion, especially anterior circulation (ICA, ACA, MCA).

pearls.text: After tPA, keep blood pressure below 180/105; before tPA, must be below 185/110 to administer.

pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: If a very sick patient improves much faster than expected, document 'dramatic improvement overnight with fluids, got better much quicker than expected' in the discharge summary, this supports arguing that the inpatient admission was justified by intent.
pearls.verbatim: dramatic improvement overnight with fluids, got better much quicker than expected,
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.applies_to: patients admitted as inpatient who recover much faster than expected
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: When a patient in observation is converted to inpatient, the inpatient clock restarts, the observation hours do not count toward the inpatient two-midnight rule.
pearls.verbatim: And when we admit them, the clock restarts for inpatient.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.applies_to: patients transitioning from observation to inpatient status
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: If you change a Medicare patient's status from inpatient to observation, a MOON letter must be issued before discharge informing them their copay will increase.
pearls.verbatim: If you admit them and then change their status to something lower, My case managers have to go to that patient. Tell them we are decreasing your status to observation. That's going to increase your co pay and your responsibility. Here's your letter. Best of luck with that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.applies_to: Medicare patients whose status is changed from inpatient to observation
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: For Medicare patients to qualify for SNF, they need three inpatient midnights. If you know a patient will need SNF placement, admit them as inpatient with proper documentation.
pearls.verbatim: if you know that your patient is gonna need placement, give them an inpatient, but document why. If they need sniff, they're sick, and they should qualify for inpatient with the proper documentation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: Use InterQual criteria for most insurances; MCG (Milliman) is used for private insurers like Blue Cross Blue Shield, Aetna Better Health, Humana, and is harder to meet.
pearls.verbatim: MCG, it used to be called the Milliman criteria. Blue Cross Blue Shield owns that. That is not embedded in Cerner. My nurses don't have access to it. So if they are a private insurance like Blue Cross Blue Shield, Aetna Better Health, Humana, that kind of stuff, they go through MCG.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: Utilization nurses reassess acute status every 3 days; if a patient remains in the hospital, continued stay criteria must still be met.
pearls.verbatim: utilization nurse is your friend. They will tell you. They'll do this. They'll do this every three days. If your patient's still there, they'll see if the acute is still met.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: The utilization nurse can pull up the InterQual criteria screen and show you exactly which items are not met, so ask them to help find what is missing.
pearls.verbatim: And they can pull these up and show them to you and say, hey. Here's here's where I can't get it to meet.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.applies_to: physicians with patients not meeting criteria
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: Do not use creatinine elevation above baseline in a dialysis patient to meet acute kidney criteria, chronic CKD does not count.
pearls.verbatim: creatinine being greater than two times their baseline, but it was chronic kidney disease. They were dialysis patients, so it didn't count.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: If you admit a patient for a procedure, ensure the prior authorization and admission status (inpatient vs. outpatient) match; a mismatch can result in full denial even if the procedure was authorized.
pearls.verbatim: So if you're admitting somebody to have a procedure done, make sure your prior auth and your admission status match.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: Ensure prior authorization matches admission status; if a surgeon gets an outpatient prior auth for a knee replacement but admits the patient as inpatient, the entire stay will be denied.
pearls.verbatim: make sure your prior auth and your admission status match. So we have orthopedic surgeons that do this all the time. They get a prior auth for outpatient knee replacement... and they'll admit the patient. And the insurance company goes, got the wrong one. Sorry. Whole thing. Denied.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.applies_to: patients admitted for elective procedures (e.g., joint replacements)
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: You can be wrong about the initial diagnosis as long as you document intent and illness severity; the diagnosis can change and be updated on the discharge summary.
pearls.verbatim: You just have to show intent Okay. And and illness. So if they have altered mental status that's worse from baseline and you think it's from a UTI, then that's what you go with.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: CDI nurses cannot tell you that a query will result in a denial or affect patient safety; they are not part of the care team and must give multiple-choice answers to avoid leading you.
pearls.verbatim: They can't tell you that this is going to result in a denial if you don't answer it. They can't tell you any of that. Why? Because that is practicing medicine. They are not a part of the patient care team.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: Document present on admission (POA) for conditions like malnutrition or hypertensive urgency; otherwise, complications may be counted as unexpected and worsen your expected vs. observed mortality metrics.
pearls.verbatim: not documenting enough on things present on admission is super, super important.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: Document 'present on admission' explicitly for chronic conditions like cachexia or malnutrition; do not use 'likely' or 'presumed', state it directly.
pearls.verbatim: And I would just say present on admission. You don't have to say likely. You don't have to say presumed. You can say this this is present on admission. It's chronic.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: For sepsis, insurance companies like UnitedHealthcare require Sepsis-3 criteria (SOFA score, end-organ damage), even though Medicare still uses Sepsis-2.
pearls.verbatim: Insurance companies are requiring us to meet sepsis three. None of that criteria is embedded in our EMR.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.applies_to: inpatients with suspected sepsis, especially those with managed Medicare (e.g., UnitedHealthcare)
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: Document lymphocytopenia because it shows immunologic compromise and can help classify a complication as unavoidable, avoiding a PSI.
pearls.verbatim: If they have low lymphocytes, always behooves you to document that because that will get us out of a lot of trouble because that is... That really shows immunologic potential.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: If a nurse documents a wound, get a wound care consult and copy the findings into your own note, otherwise the pressure ulcer may be coded as hospital-acquired.
pearls.verbatim: So anytime the nurses... So if you look at the nurse's notes and they say something about a wound, get a wound care consult. And whatever the nurse puts in that wound care consult, by god, grab it and put it in your notes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: Bacteremia is not a codable diagnosis, it is a lab value and must be linked to a condition such as 'sepsis due to gram-negative UTI with bacteremia.'
pearls.verbatim: bacteremia is not a codable diagnosis. It's a lab value. You have to... It has to be linked to something.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: If you order tube feeds for a patient but do not document a diagnosis of malnutrition, the therapy lacks justification for coding purposes.
pearls.verbatim: If you've got a core track in a person, giving them tube feeds, and you don't have a diagnosis of malnutrition on there, what exactly are you doing? How are you justifying that therapy for them?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: If a patient has a DVT documented as present on admission, answering the query with the location and POA status can avoid a PSI for a preventable post-op complication.
pearls.verbatim: If he had just answered a query appropriately, would it have not It would have avoided it completely because they had the DVT already when they came in. It was not a post op complication.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.applies_to: post-op patients with DVT present on admission
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: Check your Cerner inbox at least every other day, and definitely before going off shift for a week or on vacation, to ensure all queries are handled.
pearls.verbatim: Check your Cerner inbox, especially if you become attendings here. So check your inbox at least every other day.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: When documenting sepsis, list the specific type (e.g., sepsis, severe sepsis, septic shock) and link it to the cause, such as 'sepsis due to urinary tract infection' or 'bacteremia secondary to UTI.'
pearls.verbatim: Sepsis, severe sepsis, whatever criteria it was, septic shock. And then it should be due to urinary tract infection, bacteremia secondary to the urinary tract infection.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: For diabetes documentation, do not use 'not controlled'; instead, use specific terms like 'with hyperglycemia' or 'with hypoglycemia' to indicate labile disease.
pearls.verbatim: And you can't say not controlled. That's not what they want anymore. It's with hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, that kind of thing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: 'Fever of unknown origin' is a distinct diagnosis requiring persistent fever for at least two weeks with a negative workup; do not use it for a patient with fever for only two days.
pearls.verbatim: You better be prepared to talk about the last two weeks of workup is negative and persistent fever.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Heather Bell
pearls.episode_title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor

pearls.text: Remember to palpate for enlarged infraclavicular lymph nodes, feeling around the clavicle, in suspected inflammatory breast cancer.
pearls.verbatim: Remember to feel around the clavicle infraclavicular nodes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected inflammatory breast cancer
pearls.episode_title: Inflammatory Breast Cancer - Dr. Jon Calvert

pearls.text: The presenter recommends dicloxacillin as the antibiotic of choice for mastitis ('that's what I would use').
pearls.verbatim: That's... I'm I'm... That's what I would use, but I don't know if you've got something better that you guys use now.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
pearls.episode_title: Inflammatory Breast Cancer - Dr. Jon Calvert

pearls.text: Mammogram can be negative in inflammatory breast cancer, so a negative result does not rule out the diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: Can you send her for a mammogram? Negative. Yes. You could.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected inflammatory breast cancer
pearls.episode_title: Inflammatory Breast Cancer - Dr. Jon Calvert

pearls.text: When inflammatory breast cancer is suspected, obtain a biopsy of the inflammatory breast tissue to confirm the diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: Get a biopsy Light biopsy Of the inflammatory breast tissue. Do that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jon Calvert
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected inflammatory breast cancer
pearls.episode_title: Inflammatory Breast Cancer - Dr. Jon Calvert

pearls.text: Always ask about GI history (peptic ulcer, PPI use) and tell patients to take NSAIDs with food, not on an empty stomach.
pearls.verbatim: And always and always ask if they have a stomach problem. Tractors, peptic ulcer, if they're on PPI, and always tell them to take it with food, not an empty stomach.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: Limit corticosteroid injections to four per year per joint to avoid articular cartilage damage.
pearls.verbatim: How many injections you can do in one year? Four. Four. Alright. Correct? And the reason why?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: Lidocaine toxicity first causes CNS symptoms (sweating, heart racing) then cardiovascular collapse; exceeding 300 mg requires intubation and life support until the drug clears.
pearls.verbatim: And over this, it's a huge problem. It it goes to the central nervous system. It creates a sympathetic discharge first, like sweating, like something in your chest, heart racing, and then cardiovascular collapse follows. I've seen those multiple times. Those go... And you have to intubate that person, you know, support them life support until the medicine goes away.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: Absolute contraindications to joint injection include bacteremia, osteomyelitis, hemarthrosis, impending joint replacement surgery, and prosthetic joint.
pearls.verbatim: Contraindication change. Have osteomyelitis. You have bacteremia. The joint has blood in it. You have impending schedule within days joint replacement surgery.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: For knee injections, use 1 mL Kenalog 40 mg, optionally 1 mL dexamethasone, and 4 mL of 2% lidocaine without epinephrine; total volume 5, 6 mL is fine for a large joint.
pearls.verbatim: So on a knee injection, it's total five to six ml. In the forty milligram kenalog, that's one ml or one ml of dexamethasone or not. Alright? Four ml of two percent lidocaine with no epi. I do not recommend one percent lidocaine in 22 because of the duration.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: For knee injection, use the lateral superior patellar approach with the patient supine and knee slightly bent on a towel; avoid the inferior approach in severe arthritis (bone-on-bone) as it is difficult to find the space.
pearls.verbatim: This is the lateral... Superior lateral side. You have the patella border, and you have the other lateral end of the patella. You go lower, and that's where you go. You take... You basically go just like that. I tend them... I tend to put a little towel underneath. It's a little bent, and they're supine, and I'll just go there.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: For plantar fascia injection, use 1 mL Kenalog 40 mg and 2 mL of 2% lidocaine without epinephrine; approach from the tender spot posterolaterally, avoid injecting into the heel to prevent fat pad atrophy.
pearls.verbatim: The two, three ml total, forty milligram Kenalog, two two ml, two percent lidocaine, no epi. That's what you should do.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: Limit corticosteroid injections to no more than twice a year in the same site to avoid long-term sequelae such as tissue atrophy or tendon rupture.
pearls.verbatim: Over twice a year, wouldn't expect major issues.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: For AC joint injection, use a very fine 27-gauge 1-inch needle; only inject 1.5 mL total (0.5 mL Kenalog + 0.5 mL 2% lidocaine) because the space is very tight.
pearls.verbatim: You wanna use a a one inch. That probably is a 27. It's a very tight space and a small trim. And now all you can do is 1.5. Really? I mean, that's half an ml of Kenalog and half a ml two percent lidocaine. That's all you can do.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: For subacromial shoulder injection, use a 22-gauge 1.5-inch needle inserted posteriorly (patient not watching), advancing the entire needle into the space; volume is 5, 6 mL (1 mL Kenalog + 4 mL 2% lidocaine, ± dexamethasone).
pearls.verbatim: I always go from back. You do to do that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: For greater trochanteric bursitis injection, use a 22-gauge spinal needle; advance to touch the bone then retract slightly; ensure the pelvis is at 90 degrees to the exam table (not tilted) to avoid missing the target.
pearls.verbatim: use a 22 gauge spinal needle, advance to touch the bone, then retract, inject over the lateral or fix.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: Use a 22-gauge spinal needle for trochanteric bursa injection, not a smaller needle.
pearls.verbatim: You wanna grab a spinal needle at the 22 gauge.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: SI joint injections should be performed under fluoroscopic guidance; blind injection is difficult and often inaccurate.
pearls.verbatim: Blind injection of this thing is not easy, and it's pretty tricky... Usually, these kind of injections are always done under fluoroscopic guidance.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures

pearls.text: Addiction is defined not by how much or how often you use something, but by the effect it has on your life, specifically, continuing to use despite it causing trouble.
pearls.verbatim: A basic definition of alcoholism, for example, is if you continue to use alcohol when using alcohol causes you trouble.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Internet Addiction - Rev. Joel Leitch

pearls.text: Withdrawal from process addictions is primarily emotional and social, not physically dangerous or deadly like substance withdrawal.
pearls.verbatim: With processed addictions, you don't usually think of it in terms of being deadly, the withdrawal. I mean, you don't have to have a certain amount of medication in order to this person still stays alive. But definitely, there's a lot of emotional stuff and even sociological stuff that happens pretty frequently with withdrawal from process addictions.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Internet Addiction - Rev. Joel Leitch

pearls.text: Tolerance in Internet addiction manifests as needing a more powerful computer, more memory, faster speed, more software, or more hours of use to achieve the same enjoyment.
pearls.verbatim: Tolerance. You know, with addiction, you all... You know, very often a tolerance you build up to, including the need for... You you want the... You need a greater, more powerful computer, more memory, faster, and all this kind of stuff, more software. You want more hours of use. You you develop a tolerance in what you used to enjoy in a little while. Now need a lot longer in order to have the same amount of enjoyment.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Internet Addiction - Rev. Joel Leitch

pearls.text: For children, set a predetermined homework time from a fixed start to end time every single day; this is not punitive but teaches discipline and prioritization.
pearls.verbatim: When you come home from school at 03:30. Give yourself a half hour, whatever, predetermined amount of time, though, to shift gears, get a snack, you know, maybe go out and play a little bit or something. But from this time to this time, every single day is homework.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Internet Addiction - Rev. Joel Leitch

pearls.text: Don't require patients to go cold turkey from the internet; set a reasonable goal, such as reducing from 40 hours per week to 20 hours.
pearls.verbatim: Internet addiction doesn't require them to go cold turkey. I never suggest we'll just get off the computer for a month. That doesn't work. You get to go through all the withdrawals and the anger and all that kind of stuff.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Internet Addiction - Rev. Joel Leitch

pearls.text: Use reminder cards that list problems from the addiction and benefits of cutting down; this is good cognitive behavioral therapy.
pearls.verbatim: List some of the problems that are coming from your addiction, some of the benefits from cutting down. That's good cognitive behavioral stuff there, by the way.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Internet Addiction - Rev. Joel Leitch

pearls.text: In a 10-15 minute encounter, you cannot do everything; start with simple screening: ask how much time they spend on the internet, about their friends, activities at school, and grades.
pearls.verbatim: How are you doing with this? How much time do you spend on the Internet? Tell me about your friends. Are you involved in any activities at school? How are your grades?
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.applies_to: clinicians in brief primary care encounters
pearls.episode_title: Internet Addiction - Rev. Joel Leitch

pearls.text: Fetal DNA fragments are smaller (~130 bp) than maternal fragments (~160 bp); this size difference is used to calculate fetal fraction.
pearls.verbatim: fetal DNA fragments tend to be smaller in size, only about a 130 base pairs, and maternal DNA fragments tend to be larger in size, so maybe a 160 base pairs.
pearls.speaker: Jina Hagen
pearls.episode_title: Jina Hagen, MS on cfDNA & Carrier Screening 8/28/25

pearls.text: If a patient has NIPT, do not then do a quad screen or other serum screening; it would not make sense.
pearls.verbatim: if someone does do NIPT, for example, then it wouldn't make sense to then do a quad screen or some other type of serum screening.
pearls.speaker: Jina Hagen
pearls.applies_to: pregnant women who have had NIPT
pearls.episode_title: Jina Hagen, MS on cfDNA & Carrier Screening 8/28/25

pearls.text: Offer expanded carrier screening preconceptually to avoid the stress of finding a carrier couple during pregnancy.
pearls.verbatim: preconceptually, if you get patients that are looking to become pregnant, it's a great time to introduce the idea of carrier screening. There's no ongoing pregnancy, and so you can find out if you have a carrier carrier couple without that stress of being pregnant.
pearls.speaker: Jina Hagen
pearls.episode_title: Jina Hagen, MS on cfDNA & Carrier Screening 8/28/25

pearls.text: To cover ACOG recommendations, order CF and SMA carrier screening plus hemoglobin fractionation for hemoglobinopathies.
pearls.verbatim: if you were able to draw someone for CF and SMA and then can always do, like, a hemoglobin fractionation for hemoglobinopathies, then you've covered all your bases as far as ACOG is considered.
pearls.speaker: Jina Hagen
pearls.episode_title: Jina Hagen, MS on cfDNA & Carrier Screening 8/28/25

pearls.text: Cell-free DNA screening has a screen positive rate of about 1% or less, compared to serum screening which puts a larger group in the high-risk category to find the few true positives.
pearls.verbatim: with cell free DNA, you know, our our overall screen positive rate is about one percent. So... Or less. So most patients will get a normal result.
pearls.speaker: Jina Hagen
pearls.episode_title: Jina Hagen, MS on cfDNA & Carrier Screening 8/28/25

pearls.text: Use 2% lidocaine for joint injections because it is more concentrated, lasts longer, and allows smaller volume.
pearls.verbatim: For my joint injections, I like two percent. Concentrated, it's gonna last longer. And I can use a lesser volume to do that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil

pearls.text: For trigger points, use a 25-27 gauge 1-inch needle with a mix of 1 mL triamcinolone and 4 mL 2% lidocaine, injecting 1 mL per point.
pearls.verbatim: One ml of triamcinolone and four ml of two percent lidocaine mix is five ml. And I use a very fine needle, something like a 25 gauge, 27 gauge.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.applies_to: patients with trigger points in the shoulder/back
pearls.episode_title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil

pearls.text: For medial epicondylitis, be aware of the ulnar nerve; avoid injecting near major nerves or arterial landmarks.
pearls.verbatim: Left lateral epicondylitis is okay. But the medial, if you wanna do that, be aware of the ulnar nerve there.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil

pearls.text: For knee injection, use a superolateral approach: patient supine with a towel under the knee, find the top and lateral aspect of the patella, and enter at a 45-degree angle under the patella.
pearls.verbatim: patient will be supine. I'll put a towel underneath. It's raised a little bit, and I found the top of the patella and the lateral aspect of the patella. So I join them. There's a triangle there. That's my point of entrance. And I'm going in 45 degree right under the patella.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil

pearls.text: If you hit bone during knee injection, do not scrape the needle against it because you can scrape cartilage.
pearls.verbatim: if you're hitting bone, don't don't scrape because you can scrape cartilage.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil

pearls.text: For plantar fasciitis injection, approach from the medial side, not through the heel, to avoid fat pad atrophy and fascia rupture.
pearls.verbatim: You never wanna go through the heel this way. That's a very bad idea. You're coming from the side and into this area.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil

pearls.text: Use no more than 3 mL of injectate for plantar fasciitis to avoid complications.
pearls.verbatim: all of this three ml. That's all it's going to be. Not more than that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil

pearls.text: Do not inject medial epicondylitis because it is too close to the nerve.
pearls.verbatim: I don't inject medial. As I said, it's too close nerve.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil

pearls.text: For lateral epicondylitis injection, use 40 mg Kenalog and the rest 2% lidocaine, total 3-4 mL; go in, hit the bone, come back, and infiltrate the area, sometimes fanning 1 mL in different spots.
pearls.verbatim: Usually, it's a forty milligram canal and rest of it 2%. Just go in, and you can hit the bone and come back and just infiltrate that area. And sometimes I fan it, you know, one ml there, one ml there, one ml there, one ml there. Works good.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.episode_title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil

pearls.text: Greater trochanteric bursitis pain will never pass the knee; same with SI joint pain.
pearls.verbatim: It can hurt, but it will never pass the knee. Same with SI joint pain. It won't... It should never pass the knee.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.applies_to: patients with hip or SI joint pain
pearls.episode_title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil

pearls.text: Use a 22-gauge spinal needle for trochanteric bursitis injection; advance to bone, then hold the needle hub with your non-dominant hand to stabilize it so pressure from the syringe does not push the needle deeper.

pearls.verbatim: It's a prodrug that counts on having working adrenal glands to convert it into norepinephrine and epinephrine. So why would I not just give you what I want you to have rather than depending on your already sick body to be physiologically intact and convert it into reppi or epi.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Pressors - Engstrom

pearls.text: Choose epinephrine over dopamine because dopamine is a prodrug that requires working adrenal glands to convert it into norepinephrine and epinephrine; give the active drug directly.
pearls.verbatim: It's a prodrug that counts on having working adrenal glands to convert it into norepinephrine and epinephrine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Pressors - Engstrom

pearls.text: Choose the starting dose of norepinephrine based on how many MAP points need to be gained to reach 65; if MAP is 45, start at 20 mcg/min to rapidly perfuse organs.
pearls.verbatim: I literally choose my dose of levophen based on how many points on their MAP I have to make up to get to 65.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.applies_to: patients in shock with low MAP
pearls.episode_title: Pressors - Engstrom

pearls.text: In septic shock, favor early vasopressors over aggressive fluid resuscitation if the patient is not clearly hypovolemic; a single liter challenge can guide decision-making.
pearls.verbatim: I tend more toward... I see what they do with a single liter.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Pressors - Engstrom

pearls.text: To become proficient at ultrasound-guided IV placement, practice on patients who do not need it; the rule is you have to miss 10 times, then you will rarely miss again.
pearls.verbatim: here's the rule of thumb on ultrasound IV. You have to miss 10, and then you'll never miss again.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Pressors - Engstrom

pearls.text: When starting norepinephrine, a reasonable starting dose for a MAP of 64 is 1 mcg/min; a more typical starting dose is 5 mcg/min.
pearls.verbatim: Start them on one. I get them to sixty five. A five is a much more normal, reasonable where you would often start.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.applies_to: adults with septic shock requiring vasopressors
pearls.episode_title: Pressors - Engstrom

pearls.text: Dobutamine is indicated for cardiogenic shock or as a stress test agent, not for septic shock.
pearls.verbatim: that's when they're in cardiogenic shock. That's not a septic shock. Or you're giving them a stress test.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Pressors - Engstrom

pearls.text: In hypotensive septic children, epinephrine is the first-line vasopressor.
pearls.verbatim: Epinephrine is our first line in kids.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Pressors - Engstrom

pearls.text: For children on vasopressors, it is common to give an IV bolus of calcium for additional inotropic support.
pearls.verbatim: Kids who are on vasopressors, is not at all uncommon to give them a bolus of calcium.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.episode_title: Pressors - Engstrom

pearls.text: Diagnose anaphylaxis when there is an allergic exposure plus a rash and any two systemic symptoms (e.g., GI symptoms, respiratory difficulty, hypotension, tachycardia).
pearls.verbatim: allergic exposure and a rash. And any other two systemic symptoms?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected acute allergic reaction
pearls.episode_title: Pressors - Engstrom

pearls.text: For ESRD patients with refractory bradycardia and a wide QRS, give calcium empirically for hyperkalemia, it can narrow the QRS and increase heart rate within 60 seconds.
pearls.verbatim: I don't wait to see what the potassium is. I give them calcium. And within, like, sixty seconds, their their QRS is narrowed. Their heart rate's picked up.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Engstrom
pearls.applies_to: ESRD patients with refractory bradycardia and wide QRS
pearls.episode_title: Pressors - Engstrom

pearls.text: For skin cancers like basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma, use electron beam radiation because it deposits energy very superficially and stops quickly, sparing deeper tissues.
pearls.verbatim: So this would be the patient's skin, and this would be deeper into the patient. They deposit almost all of their energy and stop very superficially. So we use that when we're treating the cancer. So basal cells, squamous cells, we treat a lot of that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: For urgent palliative cases requiring same-day or next-day treatment, use a simple 3D conformal plan with 2-4 beam angles, as it is quick to set up and QA.
pearls.verbatim: So three d Conformal is kind of the simplest that you can get. So an urgent case that comes to us, and we wanna get started that day or the next day. It's a plan that has, you know, two, three, or four of the beam angles, but relatively simple to set up in QA and get treated.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.applies_to: inpatients or outpatients needing urgent palliative radiation
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: Reproducibility of patient positioning is critical in radiation therapy; the tolerance is 2-3 millimeters maximum to ensure the radiation hits the target accurately every day.
pearls.verbatim: So reproducibility is very important. We're looking at two to three millimeters max.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.applies_to: all patients undergoing fractionated radiation therapy
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: When planning pelvic radiation (e.g., for endometrial cancer), critical organs at risk include the bladder, rectum, and small bowel; dose-volume histograms (DVHs) are used to ensure these organs stay within safe dose limits.
pearls.verbatim: And so as we're doing the planning, we're looking for, you know, the areas that we wanna treat as well as the areas that we wanna protect. So the bladder is important, the rectum right here, and then the small bowel. And then we're looking at the dose volume histogram.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.applies_to: patients receiving pelvic radiation for gynecologic or other pelvic malignancies
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: Always obtain tissue diagnosis before treating an oncologic emergency; 'no meat, no treat' applies.
pearls.verbatim: So tissue is always important. Tissue is the issue. I've heard some people say no meat, no treat.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected cancer in emergency settings
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: Use the NOMS framework (Neurologic, Oncologic, Mechanical, Systemic) to evaluate the need for radiation versus surgery in spinal metastases.
pearls.verbatim: It's called the NOMS framework. It's developed by Memorial Sloan Kettering. And so, basically, when you have a patient like this come in, you can think NOMS. I use this. I don't really like NOMS as a as a mnemonic, but neurologic, oncologic, mechanical, and systemic.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: For spinal cord compression, start high-dose dexamethasone early in the ED or on the floor; it can provide symptom resolution or improvement by reducing spinal cord edema.
pearls.verbatim: starting dexamethasone, it's pretty high dose. Usually, we're the ones that will taper it because they'll come to us. We'll start treating them, and then we'll taper off. But that helps with the edema in the spinal cord. A lot of times, you can have symptom resolution or some symptom improvement just by initiating the dexamethasone early in the ED or hit to the floor.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.applies_to: patients with spinal cord compression from metastatic cancer
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: Lymphomas, small cell lung cancer, and germ cell tumors in SVC syndrome respond better and faster to chemotherapy; start chemotherapy first, then add radiation.
pearls.verbatim: So lymphomas, small cell lung cancer, germ cell tumors will respond better and faster to chemotherapy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.applies_to: patients with SVC syndrome and these tumor types
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: In SVC syndrome from non-small cell lung cancer, start with about three to four sessions of radiation before moving to concurrent chemoradiation.
pearls.verbatim: If it's a non small cell lung cancer, then we usually start with radiation about three to four sessions,
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.applies_to: patients with SVC syndrome from non-small cell lung cancer
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: For grade 1-2 radiation dermatitis, use Aquaphor or similar emollient applied at least three times daily: when you get up, when you go to bed, and at least one other time in between.
pearls.verbatim: Anything like Aquaphor, I don't get paid by them, but it's great. You put a layer. I always say, when you get up, when you go to bed, and at least one other time in between,
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: For grade 2-3 radiation dermatitis with moist desquamation, use dressings like Mepilex or Medihoney to keep the area dry and prevent infection.
pearls.verbatim: If it's a grade two or grade three or you see a lot of the moist desquamation, that's when you're thinking about some dressings. There are, again, a plethora to choose from, Mepilex or Metahoney. Like, there's just a ton. But that can help keep that area dry.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: Radiation side effects are location-specific: pelvis causes bladder and rectal toxicity; breast causes skin toxicity and fatigue; head/neck causes mucositis, dysphagia, and weight loss.
pearls.verbatim: So any... Anywhere in the pelvis, our target for gynecologic cancers and our target for, you know, prostate cancers, that target basically lies between or below the bladder and the rectum. So bladder and rectal toxicities are always possible when we're treating in the pelvis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: After radiation, wait two to three months for a PET scan because early inflammation causes false-positive uptake from recovering tissues.
pearls.verbatim: We wanna wait two to three months, for example, to get a PET scan because you're gonna have a lot of inflammation in the tissues from the radiation. So if you were to get one right after radiation, everything's gonna light up because you've got a lot of metabolic activity as the tissues are recovering.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Gabriel S. Vidal
pearls.applies_to: patients after radiation for solid tumors
pearls.episode_title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP

pearls.text: When intervening with a suicidal patient, kindly and compassionately tell them what they must do; do not ask them what they want, as they don't know.
pearls.verbatim: They don't know what they wanna do. They've tried everything that they know how. They've listened to all the people, give all kinds of suggestions and stuff, and nothing has effectively worked up to that point. So they don't know what they wanna do, so don't ask them what you wanna do.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Rev Joel S. Leitch on Suicide Prevention 5/14/26

pearls.text: Hopelessness talk is a stronger predictor of suicide than depression; listen for it and always try to build hope for the future.
pearls.verbatim: hopelessness, very strong predictor, even stronger than depression. Hope... You know, hope's our anchor in life. We don't have hope. There's not much motivating us anymore.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Rev Joel S. Leitch on Suicide Prevention 5/14/26

pearls.text: A family history of suicide is one of the biggest predictors; use the ACE test to assess cumulative risk.
pearls.verbatim: a family of history of negatives, it's a good idea a lot of times to do the ACE. You know the ACE test. So you you you look for, you know, suicides in the family because one of the biggest predictors of a family member having committed suicide is somebody in their family has tried it or had it.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.applies_to: patients with family history of suicide or ACEs
pearls.episode_title: Rev Joel S. Leitch on Suicide Prevention 5/14/26

pearls.text: Major warning signs of compassion fatigue include silencing response, withdrawal from engaging life, diminished capacity to listen and communicate, loss of confidence, and sense of dread for no obvious reason.
pearls.verbatim: Major warning signs, silencing response, withdrawal from engaging life, diminished capacity to listen and communicate.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on How Continue to Burn Without Getting Burnt Out 1/8/26

pearls.text: Identify automatic negative thoughts (ANTs) such as 'I'm worthless' or 'I'll never amount to anything,' and replace them with intentional, positive thinking.
pearls.verbatim: I call them ants, automatic negative thoughts, and we all have them at some level.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on How Continue to Burn Without Getting Burnt Out 1/8/26

pearls.text: Hopelessness talk such as 'nothing helps,' 'nothing will work,' 'will never change,' or 'I can't keep living like this' signals high suicide risk.
pearls.verbatim: Hopelessness talk equals high risk. Nothing helps. Nothing will work. Mhmm. Tried everything. Will never change. I can't keep living like this.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention

pearls.text: Institutionalizing the hardcore suicidal patient will not stop them and can make things worse, jails and psychiatric facilities have 20-30 times the national suicide rate.
pearls.verbatim: Placing them in an institution setting, which is usually what people end up doing, will not stop them, and it may even make things worse. ... jails, prisons, psychiatric facilities have 20 to 30 times the national suicide rate.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention

pearls.text: The truly determined ('hardcore') suicidal individuals, about 5% of the suicidal population, are unlikely to give warning signs because they are invested in not being rescued; they use very lethal means like guns.
pearls.verbatim: Hardcores are virtually impossible to stop because they're really, really hard to identify. They are hardcore. If they are totally intent on killing themselves, they probably aren't gonna give you any clues. They have no motivation whatsoever to test the waters to see if somebody will help them at that point.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.applies_to: patients who are truly determined to die
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention

pearls.text: When assessing suicide, the immediate precipitating event (the 'straw that broke the camel's back') is usually not the root cause, look for the longer-term erosion.
pearls.verbatim: The sudden ending of a romance or marriage may be the precipitating event. Think about the straw that broke the camel's back. If you have that suicidal erosion and things are gradually becoming less and less resilient, at one point, one more thing can be the straw breaks the camel's back. But it's not likely the ultimate cause.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.applies_to: patients with suicidal ideation or attempts
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention

pearls.text: Ask about family or extended family suicide history, it is a strong sign of risk for the patient and other relatives.
pearls.verbatim: Has anybody in your family or your extended family ever committed suicide. That's a such a strong sign that you better be careful with kids and with other relatives.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention

pearls.text: Treating a suicidal patient poorly, for example, a nurse roughly shoving a suction tube down a repeat overdose patient's throat, may make the person feel worse, and next time they won't come in; they'll just die.
pearls.verbatim: The nurse was angry. I'll show him. And she very roughly, you know, grabbed a a suction tube and shoved it down the guy's throat with the kind of thinking, by the time I'm done with him, he'll never do this again. The absolute opposite may be true. ... That just may make the person feel a lot worse. And next time, they won't come in. They'll just die.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention

pearls.text: Ambivalence, holding opposite feelings about living and dying at the same time, is the emotional state most associated with suicidal behavior; small positive actions can tip the scale toward life.
pearls.verbatim: Ambivalence is the emotional state most closely associated with suicidal behavior.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.applies_to: anyone intervening with a suicidal person
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention

pearls.text: Avoid using the term 'hostage' with patients or even in professional discussions about suicidal patients, as it has negative connotations and perpetuates stigma; instead frame the pattern as codependency or dependency.
pearls.verbatim: the dyadic quality of suicide, there... People are... They are taking hostages, but they're not in... That's not their intent.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention

pearls.text: Avoid using labels like 'hostage' about a patient; instead describe that the patient feels that way, because the clinician's language shapes their own thinking and can perpetuate negative feelings toward patients with suicidal ideation.
pearls.verbatim: But it was always really important in that case to remember that it was Mhmm. Even though it felt like it was intentional and it was a cry for help and they didn't... They couldn't do anything after, like... And it was really frustrating. It's just always important to remember when you use the language in your own head, when you're speaking to other professionals, we just are very mindful of that. Because I think even using terminology that we think is is adequate, but it maybe has negative connotations, I think it helps perpetuate this kind of negative feeling that can come up when we have these people who flood our ERs, who flood our our clinics, who who who put up... Take up space in our hospital with... You know, when there are really... You know, when there are physically ill people.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.applies_to: healthcare professionals interacting with suicidal patients
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention

pearls.text: Suicide is not always due to mental illness; other drivers include loss, frustration, grief, physical pain, loneliness, and alienation.
pearls.verbatim: But the idea is to look for a cluster of warning signals that start piling up together, especially if it's a... There's a context of something dramatic having happened in the person's life. Maybe it'll be some loss, frustration, grief, depression, physical pain, mental illness, sadness, disappointment, alienation, loneliness, mental anguish. It's not always mental illness.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention

pearls.text: Use the SLAP assessment: Specificity, Lethality, Availability, Proximity.
pearls.verbatim: Always begin your assessment by asking, how would you harm yourself? You can find the details of the plan by using the SLAP assessment. ... SLAP is quick but not foolproof, not good with extremely impulsive people.
pearls.speaker: Rev. Joel S. Leitch
pearls.episode_title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention

pearls.text: Do not order an ANA to evaluate for pain alone; 30% of normal individuals can have a false positive. Only order it if there are other symptoms like malar rash or photosensitivity.
pearls.verbatim: Dr. Howard suggests not to order an ANA to evaluate for Thirty percent of normal individuals can have a false positive. And to only order it if there's other symptoms, like a malar rash, photosensitivity, something else that's kind of pointing you in that lupus direction, but not to do it for pain itself.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.applies_to: patients with pain without other lupus symptoms
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: Rheumatoid factor is helpful if positive, especially in younger patients, but not helpful if negative, you cannot rule out RA with a negative RF.
pearls.verbatim: rheumatoid factor is really helpful if it's positive, especially in younger patients, but it's not helpful if it's negative. You're not... You can't rule out RA, just tell you negative RF.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: Fibromyalgia and inflammatory conditions can coexist; an elevated ESR points toward inflammation but does not rule out fibromyalgia.
pearls.verbatim: fibromyalgia... So having an inflammatory condition does not necessarily rule out fibromyalgia. You can have both. But the ESR specifically is going to point us more towards an inflammatory condition.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.applies_to: patients with widespread pain and elevated ESR
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: Consider a rheumatology referral for any patient with widespread pain involving more than one joint and chronic pain lasting three months or more, especially with elevated ESR or CRP.
pearls.verbatim: we're going to consider a rheumatology referral anytime that there's widespread pain, which is involving more than one joint and pain that's chronic.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: Do not start methotrexate as primary care for suspected rheumatoid arthritis; Dr. Howard was negative against PCPs initiating disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs.
pearls.verbatim: Dr. Howard was pretty negative against PCPs
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: Primary care providers should not typically start DMARDs or biologics for inflammatory arthritis; referral to rheumatology is recommended.
pearls.verbatim: Dr. Howard was pretty negative against PCPs starting DMARDs, whether that's methotrexate or or biologics.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: The newer fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria use a widespread pain index of at least 7 out of 19 pain areas and a symptom severity score greater than 9.
pearls.verbatim: you have to have at least seven of those. And then the second is really three symptoms here, fatigue, waking unrefreshed, and cognitive symptoms. And then these ones actually get a numerical score of how bad they are. And then you go back up to the physical symptoms of, like, all of the pain of those 19 places, and you add a severity score to those as well. And so then you're looking for a symptom severity score that's gonna be greater than nine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: If a patient meets the diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia, go ahead and make the diagnosis rather than treating it as a diagnosis of exclusion, so you can start education and set expectations.
pearls.verbatim: I think part of that is that in my mind, it's still a diagnosis of an exclusion. And so I'm like, well, I don't know. It still could be something out. Like, we have diagnostic criteria. And so if they meet the criteria, go ahead and put that label on, and then be able to start having some of the education, setting some good expectations.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.applies_to: patients with chronic widespread pain meeting fibromyalgia criteria
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: Treat fibromyalgia with a multimodal approach similar to IBS: use medications, dietary changes, and referrals for symptom management.
pearls.verbatim: I'm still gonna be prescribing, like, Amitiza and things like that, you know, if that's appropriate anxiety. I stop. But you know what I mean? Like, I'm still gonna be like, okay. Let's try a low FODMAP diet. Let's try this. Let's do a GI referral. Like, we're gonna be working with the patient for a symptom management, and I think that that needs to be the same thing with fibromyalgia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: Use the five pillars of mental health: biological (neurotransmitters and chronic diseases), situational, personal (self-care), relational (counseling), and spiritual.
pearls.verbatim: I talk about my five pillars as being the biological. So looking at neurotransmitters, but also looking at chronic diseases that contribute to anxiety or depression, looking at the situational, looking at personal, which is where I talk about self care, looking at relational, which is also where I talk about counseling, and then looking at the spiritual.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: Refer to rheumatology for any widespread chronic pain, whether suspected inflammatory or fibromyalgia, but know that the diagnosis may not be as accepted with that referral.
pearls.verbatim: And then you can refer to rheumatology for any widespread chronic pain, whether it's suspected to be inflammatory or possibly fibromyalgia, just knowing that the diagnosis may not be as accepted with that referral.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: Do not prescribe any controlled medications to a patient who is using marijuana.
pearls.verbatim: And so I will not prescribe any controlled medications to a patient who's using marijuana.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Lucashu
pearls.applies_to: patients using marijuana who need controlled medications
pearls.episode_title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu

pearls.text: Recheck hemoglobin 2-4 weeks after starting oral iron; expect a rise of at least 1 g/dL.
pearls.verbatim: you can recheck in as little as two weeks. So somewhere in the two to four week range, and you should already see your hemoglobin go up by one.
pearls.speaker: Sarah Janssen
pearls.episode_title: Sarah Janssen on Anemia Outpatient 12/4/25

pearls.text: A two-week trial of oral iron can serve as a therapeutic trial to confirm iron deficiency when diagnosis is unclear.
pearls.verbatim: Even in your diagnostic process. If it's not totally clear that they have iron deficiency because they have you can do a two week trial of supplementation,
pearls.speaker: Sarah Janssen
pearls.episode_title: Sarah Janssen on Anemia Outpatient 12/4/25

pearls.text: IV iron is indicated for patients with CHF, CKD, IBD, cancer, or those who cannot tolerate or do not respond to oral iron.
pearls.verbatim: certain page populations are not gonna do well with oral supplementation, which is our CHF patients and CKD, if they have ongoing inflammation, such as cancer patients or IBD.
pearls.speaker: Sarah Janssen
pearls.episode_title: Sarah Janssen on Anemia Outpatient 12/4/25

pearls.text: For microcytic anemia with MCV <70 and elevated RBC count, consider thalassemia trait; Mentzer index <13 suggests thalassemia.
pearls.verbatim: when the MCV starts getting really low, so under 70. And then your elevated RBCs can help you there.
pearls.speaker: Sarah Janssen
pearls.episode_title: Sarah Janssen on Anemia Outpatient 12/4/25

pearls.text: If you don't make a decision to do something in an active shooter, whether to run, barricade, or fight, your chances of survival drop significantly.
pearls.verbatim: if you don't make a decision to do something in an active shooter, whether that's run, whether that's barricade, whether that's even fighting, then the chances of your survival go way down.
pearls.speaker: Officer Latif
pearls.applies_to: anyone in an active shooter event
pearls.episode_title: Security Training

pearls.text: Active shooters are extremely intelligent and always leave some indication of their plans.
pearls.verbatim: these active shooters are extremely intelligent, and there's always some kind of indication.
pearls.speaker: Officer Latif
pearls.episode_title: Security Training

pearls.text: Pre-attack indicators often start with depression; look for someone who is unhappy, emotionless, distraught, or a victim of bullying, and who detaches human beings into objects.
pearls.verbatim: More over than none, it usually starts with some type of depression. Right? There's something going wrong in their life, and they feel like the only out is to hurt other people.

pearls.applies_to: all healthcare interactions with potential trafficking victims

pearls.text: If a patient leaves before help arrives (e.g., runs from a Lyft to a shelter), do not be discouraged; they may return later because they now know you are a safe place.

pearls.text: In diabetics with a swollen, red, painless foot, suspect Charcot arthropathy rather than infection or DVT; get an X-ray to look for bone fragmentation.

pearls.text: If a diabetic patient presents with a change in foot shape and no wound, it is likely Charcot, not infection; get them off the foot and refer.

pearls.text: SoonerCare offers some of the best mental health benefits for children and those under 21, but finding adult providers who accept it is more difficult.
pearls.verbatim: To be honest, if they have SoonerCare, they have some of the best insurance benefits for mental health care, especially if they're kiddos or 21. But if they're adults, finding the providers take SoonerCare and are approved for SoonerCare or Medicaid can be more difficult.

pearls.text: For patients with insurance, start with their insurance list to find in-network mental health providers, then cross-reference with other sources.
pearls.verbatim: If your patients have insurance, really, the number one way to start for a mental health referral, unless you have someone specific and even then you need to check with insurance, but is really to start with their insurance list and then cross reference that other sources.

pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.verbatim: you guys don't take SoonerCare for patients over 21. Correct. You do not.

pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.text: Psychoeducational evaluation is a less extensive and less expensive subset of neuropsych, used specifically for educational accommodations (IEP, 504 plans).
pearls.verbatim: These are for accommodations, educational accommodations. If someone needs to have an IEP or needs to be able to get accommodations for testing, That's a psychoeducational test. It's a subset of the neuropsych. It's less extensive. It's also less expensive.

pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.episode_title: Behavioral Med

pearls.text: For a patient with memory deficits and focus problems after a traumatic event, start with a regular psych referral rather than neuropsych, because neuropsych is the most expensive and extensive option.

pearls.text: Exacerbations are defined as acute worsening requiring systemic steroids, not just chronic dyspnea; two or more exacerbations or one hospitalization count.

pearls.text: Natural immunity generates antibodies to many epitopes across the whole virus, whereas vaccines produce antibodies only to spike protein epitopes, a much more limited but still effective response.

pearls.text: At about 6 months after vaccination, memory B cell levels in recovered-vaccinated patients are about the same as in naive patients who received the vaccine.

pearls.text: Memory T cells are long-lived, still detectable in SARS-1 patients from 2003, while memory B cells were gone by about six years, so T-cell memory is the more durable protection.
pearls.verbatim: But if we look back at SARS one in two thousand three, there's... There's some of these patients that had... They can still find memory T cells today, but the memory B cells were were gone by six years.

pearls.episode_title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD

pearls.text: Virus-induced antibodies decline about 4% per month, whereas vaccine-induced antibodies decline about 40% per month, a dramatic difference in antibody half-life.

pearls.text: Leukemia, lymphoma, organ transplant, advanced HIV, and diabetes are comorbidities that lead to poor or absent vaccine antibody response; these patients need closer attention and monitoring.

pearls.text: Ask patients if they could eat their favorite food during the headache; a migraine patient typically cannot, while a tension headache patient can.
pearls.verbatim: If I gave you some really good ramen cheese ramen, would you be able to eat that right now? A kid who has, like, a tension headache can probably eat that. A migraine, mm-mm.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Ask patients if they could run around the clinic during the headache; migraine is aggravated by routine physical activity, so they would feel worse.
pearls.verbatim: If I told you to go run around this clinic, would you feel the same, better, or worse? And it's like, when I have a migraine, you... Like, mm-mm.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Common migraine triggers include stress, lack of sleep, interrupted sleep, skipped meals, weather changes, humidity above 80%, neck pain, alcohol, bright sun, dehydration, caffeine (too little or too much), processed foods, aged cheese, chocolate, and menstruation.
pearls.verbatim: Stress, lack of sleep. I woke up two hours late. Is that changing how I'm living my life? Yes. Interrupted sleep. Depressed mood. Anxiety. Skip a meal. Very variable weather. Storm. Humidity above 80% also. Neck pain, alcohol, bright, sun, or dehydration. Caffeine, so, like, too little or too much. Processed foods. Aged cheese, chocolate.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Prodromal symptoms of migraine can include yawning, mood changes, and neck pain; recognizing these can help patients take rescue medication earlier.
pearls.verbatim: Honestly, for me, maybe I'm just gonna be yawning a lot before I get a migraine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: In the Migraine Buddy app, patients can log medications taken during an attack, including time taken and whether it helped, to track efficacy.

pearls.text: Non-pharmacologic relief for migraine includes dark room rest, ice packs, heat packs, hot shower, hydration, and caffeine.
pearls.verbatim: A dark room rest, go down to meditation, staying indoors, ice packs. Also, heat packs is there. Heating pad. Food, caffeine, hot shower, full shower, drink water.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: For acute migraine, take naproxen and drink a Coke at headache onset, rest in a dark room, and if still having headache after one hour, take the triptan.
pearls.verbatim: Take the naproxen and drink a Coke beginning of your headache and, like, get in a dark room and rest. If in an hour you're still having that headache, take the triptan.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: If sumatriptan 50 mg is not working, try a different triptan rather than increasing to 100 mg.
pearls.verbatim: If fifty is not working on one triptan, try a different triptan. Don't go to a 100.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Limit analgesics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs) to 3 days per week or 10 days per month; limit triptans to 2 days per week or 8 days per month to prevent medication overuse headache.
pearls.verbatim: For analgesics, so acetaminophen and NSAIDs, three days per week, days per month. For triptans combined with triptans, other medicine, two days per week or eight days per month.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: CGRP inhibitors are a great option for migraine patients who have significant nausea and vomiting because CGRP receptors are abundant in the gut.
pearls.verbatim: My neurologist told me that a CGRP would be good for me because I have significant nausea with my headaches and occasionally vomiting. And so she's like, here are all the receptors of that in your body. And your gut is a major one of them. So people who have bad nausea with their migraines, this is a great option for them.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Give a triptan at least six tries before writing it off as ineffective.
pearls.verbatim: I wouldn't write off a triptan on, like, one dose. I would give it, I don't know, six tries.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Sumatriptan has the highest side effect profile of all triptans; rizatriptan works faster and has a lower side effect profile.
pearls.verbatim: The sumatriptan that we have, my neurologist told me it has the highest side effect profile of all the other triptans. So we had rizatriptan, and she said that's very good. It has a very low side effect profile, and it, like, works faster and better.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.applies_to: patients with migraine choosing a triptan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Frovatriptan is good for menstrual migraines because it is very long acting, but may cause a reliable rebound headache the day after.
pearls.verbatim: frovatriptan, good for menstrual migraines. Very long acting. Every day of your period. And then for me, I had a reliable rebound headache the day after.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: For frequent triptan users, set a goal of 12 triptan days per month, then eventually 6 per month.
pearls.verbatim: They they need to cut, like, cut back. So, like, maybe if your goal is 12 and eventually your goal is, like, six a month.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: Tell patients that overusing abortive migraine medication can make their headaches worse.

pearls.applies_to: patients who use frequent abortive migraine medications

pearls.text: Take naproxen with a bottle of Coke, a cup of coffee, or a shot of espresso; caffeine causes vasoconstriction that helps the headache.
pearls.verbatim: Take that with a bottle of Coke. She said it can be a cup of coffee. It can be a shot of espresso, but, like, that caffeine is gonna cause the vasoconstriction that's gonna help.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.speaker: Dr. Cyr
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26

pearls.text: As a physician, it's appropriate to use scientific/biological frameworks, but also deliberately draw on spiritual frameworks when caring for patients.
pearls.verbatim: You are trained as a physician to look at their life through the lens of science and more specifically through biological frameworks. And this is appropriate for a physician, but we can also thoughtfully draw on frameworks foreign to science, and in fact, we do as Christians.

pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: View each patient as a whole, inseparable biopsychosocial spiritual being.

pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: Do not compartmentalize patients into physical vs. spiritual; in biblical thinking, there is no separation between the supernatural and natural.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: The ancient world had no conceptual distinction between physical, spiritual, and emotional illness, this integrated view is more faithful to lived reality than modern dissection.

pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: The biblical concept of shalom means completeness, wholeness, rest, peace, and harmony with self, God, and the created world, this is the goal of whole-person healing.
pearls.verbatim: Biblical shalom. And we're not... I'm not gonna go deep dive into this theologically, but it needs an inward sense of completeness or wholeness, a a rest, a peace, harmony with self, God, and the created world.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: Peacemakers in the Beatitudes are not just mediators; they are people so embodied with shalom that they share peace by their very existence.
pearls.verbatim: What he's saying is they they will be so embodied with shalom that they will they will walk around, and they will they will be sharing shalom. They will be shalom.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: For a patient with persistent worry impacting function, do not default to Xanax; explore whether the anxiety has spiritual, situational, mindset, or physical roots.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: Discernment begins in the physician's own spiritual life, rooted in time spent with God and Scripture, not just in the clinical encounter.

pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: Spiritual consolation includes feeling alive, connected to others and God, interior joy, being of service, experiencing shalom, and gratefulness to God.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: The PERMA model of well-being (positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, accomplishment) lacks explicit reference to God and can become a trap of self-reliance without a Christian framework.
pearls.verbatim: Without this frame, this stuff actually could be a trap. Right? Because what is it gonna do? It's gonna help me serve me.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: Spiritual poverty means complete reliance on God, modeled by Jesus, in contrast to the world's teaching of self-reliance.
pearls.verbatim: That's so so spiritual poverty is complete reliance on an other. Father. Right. That's spiritual poverty.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: Spiritual poverty is complete reliance on an other, on God, not on yourself.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Discernment & Perspective

pearls.text: If a patient is lying in bed shaking their head and symptoms are not getting worse, it is not vertigo.

pearls.text: At end gaze, two to three beats of nystagmus that goes away with refocusing is physiologic, not pathologic.

pearls.text: Primary gaze nystagmus (present when looking straight ahead) indicates something is wrong with the vestibular system.

pearls.text: Direction-changing nystagmus is a central finding, but can also be caused by intoxication, medications (especially AEDs), or seizures.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: Duration of vertigo: less than 1 minute suggests BPPV; 2-15 minutes suggests TIA; hours suggests vestibular migraine or Meniere's.
pearls.verbatim: Less than one minute, probably BPPV. Several minutes, like two to fifteen... Two to three to fifteen minutes is suggestive of TIA. Six hours, vestibular migraine or Meniere's.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: Failure to extend the patient's head back during the Dix-Hallpike test will result in a falsely negative test because the otoliths will not fall.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: A positive Dix-Hallpike test requires a slight delay followed by upward torsional nystagmus that abates after 15-30 seconds; reproducing dizziness alone is not a positive test.
pearls.verbatim: A positive test consists of a slight delay followed by upward torsional nystagmus, beating kinda like this, which abate after several seconds. A positive test does not mean you reproduce dizziness.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: Isolated horizontal nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike may indicate horizontal canal BPPV, which requires a different treatment than posterior canal BPPV.
pearls.verbatim: Isolated horizontal nystagmus may indicate... When you do this, if they have a horizontal nystagmus, that may indicate a horizontal canal nystagmus, which requires a different treatment.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Christopher Abdo
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: Large cerebellar strokes can present with minimal symptoms like mild dizziness and headache, and may later require craniotomy.
pearls.verbatim: Occasionally, you can have a large cerebellar strokes which present with minimal clinical symptoms. pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: A normal head impulse test (no catch-up saccade) in acute vertigo suggests a central lesion until proven otherwise.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: A positive Dix-Hallpike with typical nystagmus is diagnostic for BPPV.
pearls.verbatim: If you have if you have a positive Dix Hallpike, like the Dix Hallpike... An actual positive Dix Hallpike. Right? It's... It it... That's that's the only thing that this could be.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Christopher Abdo
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: When performing the Dix-Hallpike, extend the neck at least 20 degrees and drop the patient quickly to achieve high sensitivity (high 90s).
pearls.verbatim: it's sensitivity when you do the exam correctly is in the high, high nineties. If you do the exam incorrectly, you don't extend the neck back, drop the patient quickly enough, the sensitivity increases.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: If a patient does not improve after an Epley maneuver, either the maneuver was performed incorrectly or the patient does not have posterior canal BPPV.
pearls.verbatim: If the patient does not get better when you do the Epley maneuver, you're either doing the Epley maneuver wrong or they don't have BPP.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: The head must be extended at least 20 degrees back off the edge of the bed for the Dix-Hallpike test to be effective.
pearls.verbatim: At least 20 degrees.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: Teach patients with BPPV to watch YouTube videos on how to perform the Epley maneuver themselves if symptoms recur.
pearls.verbatim: The other the other thing I would tell you for some of these BPP patients is tell them to go watch YouTube on how to do the Epley maneuver themselves if they get the symptoms again.

pearls.applies_to: patients with BPPV in outpatient setting
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes

pearls.text: Extrinsic causes of shoulder pain commonly include cervical spondylitis and cervical nerve compression, most often at C5-C6.
pearls.verbatim: Cervical arthritis or cervical spondylitis, cervical nerve compression, C5, C6 most commonly.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Acker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Acker on Shoulder Disorders & Examination

pearls.text: A brachial plexus stinger presents as 1-3 minutes of stinging pain from the acromion down to the fingers after a compression injury to the head or shoulder during sports.
pearls.verbatim: one to three minutes of stinging pain from the acromion down to the fingers. And it usually happens in a... in a sports injury. Right? So if you get hit, compression injury of the head or of the shoulder, that's when you get the brachial plexus stinger.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Acker on Shoulder Disorders & Examination

pearls.text: Types I and II AC injuries should be treated conservatively with ice, sling, rest, and gradual activity; they almost always heal given enough time.
