pearls.text: For type I AC injury, palpate over the coracoid (bony prominence under the clavicle); it should not be tender. Tenderness there suggests type II or higher injury.
pearls.verbatim: If you palpate the cracoclavicular ligament, you're you're... What you're gonna do is you're gonna palpate over your coracoid, which is right under your clavicle, and it's a bony prominence that sticks out right right about there. That should not be tender with this type of injury.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Acker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Acker on Shoulder Disorders & Examination

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Acker on Shoulder Disorders & Examination

pearls.text: Biceps tendon tear presents with a visible bulge, ecchymosis, weakness, and a history of a pop with severe pain; MRI is needed to determine if surgery is required.
pearls.verbatim: They'll say, I heard a pop. I felt a terrible pain in my shoulder, my upper arm, and this is how my arm's been since, and it's been weak. And, oh, yeah. By the way, there's this huge ecchymosis or bruise. Right? That's almost always gonna be there.

pearls.verbatim: You can inject directly into the AC joint right there. You only have to go half a centimeter or maybe a centimeter at most to get right into the joint if you wanna if you wanna treat with steroids for that.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Acker on Shoulder Disorders & Examination

pearls.text: Normal shoulder flexion should reach at least 180 degrees; inability to do so is abnormal.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Acker on Shoulder Disorders & Examination

pearls.text: Scapular winging from serratus anterior palsy (long thoracic nerve injury) typically heals with conservative treatment alone.

pearls.text: The triad of positive open can test, Hawkins test, and external rotation weakness is 98% sensitive for rotator cuff tear.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Acker on Shoulder Disorders & Examination

pearls.verbatim: External rotation's positive, meaning you have pain, you have pain weakness, and you have night pain, and you're greater than 65 years old, 91 of those are gonna have a tear of the rotator cuff.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Acker on Shoulder Disorders & Examination

pearls.verbatim: 90 degrees abducted. You flex the elbow and externally rotate. As you you push the external rotation, they're not... They're gonna pull against it. They're not gonna want it. And that's if you have joint laxity or instability.

pearls.text: Complete rotator cuff tears need to be fixed sooner rather than later; partial tears allow more time.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Acker on Shoulder Disorders & Examination

pearls.text: Patients over 40 are much more likely to have glenohumeral osteoarthritis, adhesive capsulitis, or rotator cuff tear; those under 40 are more likely to have tendinopathy.
pearls.verbatim: 40. Yeah. So just be on your guard for anybody forty years older. They could they could have these things. They're much more likely is what I'm trying to say. If they're younger than 40, they're much more likely to have a tendinopathy, rotator cuff tear, and these other things.

pearls.text: Sleep deprivation causes a decline in clinical performance by 1.5 standard deviations among physicians.

pearls.text: Fifty percent of residents experience burnout during training, and sleep deprivation is a component of that.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols

pearls.text: Sleep deprivation leads to low-grade systemic inflammation and impairs the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis, causing graded impulsivity or disinhibition.
pearls.verbatim: And then studies have shown that there's actually low grade systemic inflammation, and it impairs our hypothalamus, pituitary, adrenal access, leading to graded impulsivity or disinhibition.

pearls.text: Good sleep hygiene includes using the bedroom for sleep only, not for studying or other activities.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: Moonlighting and charting time must be included in total work-hour restrictions; moonlighting shifts should be the first to be cut if needed.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: The phone call person is intended as a backup on call; use it when you are not safe to drive home or make medical decisions.
pearls.verbatim: the phone call person is intended to be a backup on call person.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: Use bright lights in report rooms instead of dimming them to help mitigate fatigue.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: If you don't feel safe to drive home, you are probably not safe to be practicing medicine; use backup or transportation.
pearls.verbatim: I started to realize, I am not in a spot where I feel safe to drive home. And I was like, if I don't feel safe to drive home, I'm probably not safe to be practicing medicine right now.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: More frequent handoffs are better than sleep-deprived residents continuing to care for patients; avoid unnecessary handoffs, but never let a tired resident power through.

pearls.speaker: Dr. Amanda Nichols
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation

pearls.text: Sleep deprivation on shift is akin to having a fever: just as you would call backup for acute illness, you should call backup when acutely fatigued to protect patients from medical errors.

pearls.text: Buprenorphine is the treatment for complex prescription opioid dependence (CPOD) even if you are not sure whether the patient has true addiction or is diverting meds.

pearls.applies_to: patients with CPOD or complex pain syndrome

pearls.text: Full agonist opioids (oxycodone, dilaudid, morphine) are supported for acute nociceptive pain and chronic progressive nociceptive pain (e.g., cancer pain), but not for chronic nonprogressive pain, nociplastic pain, or neuropathic pain.
pearls.verbatim: It's really just acute nociceptive and chronic progressive nociceptive where there is good support for using full agonist opioids in general.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amell
pearls.applies_to: patients with pain being considered for full agonist opioids
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amell on Opioid Stewardship 5/14/26

pearls.text: IV opioid administration is associated with 4.2 times more nausea and vomiting compared to PO, based on a large observational study of 30,000 patients in a tertiary ED.
pearls.verbatim: Nausea, vomiting is much higher with IV. You can see four point two times more likely to have nausea or vomiting with IV compared to PO.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amell
pearls.applies_to: patients receiving IV vs PO opioids in the ED
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amell on Opioid Stewardship 5/14/26

pearls.text: An 81% reduction in IV opioid usage by MME was achieved over 8,000 patient days with no change in pain scores, by making providers more aware of their prescribing (Hawthorne effect).
pearls.verbatim: We had about an eighty one percent reduction in IV opioid usage by MME, and this is over 8,000 patient days pre post. There was no change in pain scores.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amell
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amell on Opioid Stewardship 5/14/26

pearls.text: When risks of an intervention greatly outweigh benefits, physicians should guide the decision and not offer it as a shared decision; controlled substances should be controlled when not going well.
pearls.verbatim: If something has much, much greater risks than benefits, it's stupid to be like, oh, do you wanna go left or right as if both sides are good.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amell
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amell on Opioid Stewardship 5/14/26

pearls.text: Buprenorphine has a ceiling effect due to being a partial agonist, so taking higher doses produces diminishing returns and does not reinforce bad behavior.
pearls.verbatim: And so you could take all of your two weeks of bup at once, but you'll get diminishing effects. It's not gonna reinforce bad behavior
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amell
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amell on Opioid Stewardship 5/14/26

pearls.text: One milligram of buprenorphine is approximately equivalent to 30 milligrams of morphine in potency.
pearls.verbatim: So one milligram of buprenorphine is, like, thirty of morphine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amell
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amell on Opioid Stewardship 5/14/26

pearls.text: Buprenorphine is not renally cleared, so it does not accumulate in dehydration or renal impairment, unlike Dilaudid.
pearls.verbatim: Because it's not renally cleared. So if you're in a stupor and dehydrated, you're not gonna build and build and build the dose because it's like Dilaudid, and then it's not renally cleared.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amell
pearls.applies_to: patients with renal impairment or dehydration
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amell on Opioid Stewardship 5/14/26

pearls.text: Sublingual buprenorphine can be taken even if the patient is vomiting or NPO, making it safer than oral full agonists.
pearls.verbatim: But buprenorphine is sublingual, which makes it safer. You have no excuse. Even if you're vomiting or NPO, you could take it sublingual.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Amell
pearls.applies_to: patients who are vomiting or NPO
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Amell on Opioid Stewardship 5/14/26

pearls.text: Buprenorphine causes less hyperalgesia and hyperkatifia (emotional hyperactivity) than full agonists because it antagonizes kappa-opioid receptors.

pearls.text: Low-dose buprenorphine formulations like Belbuca (buccal) or Butrans (patch) can be started in opioid-naive patients without trialing other opioids first.
pearls.verbatim: But, yeah, sometimes, you know, low dose Belbuca can start. You don't have to go do oxycodone first.

pearls.text: Most patients on long-term full agonist opioids never adapt to chronic pain and continue to perseverate on it.

pearls.text: Having a peer champion familiar with buprenorphine can help solve logistic barriers and disseminate best practices.

pearls.text: Risk factors for malignancy in hematuria include age >35 (men >40, women >60), smoking (more pack-years = higher risk), male sex, history of gross hematuria, persistent microscopic hematuria, irritative voiding symptoms, prior pelvic radiation, certain chemotherapies, occupational exposure to rubber/petrochemicals/dyes, and chronic indwelling foreign bodies.

pearls.text: Irritative voiding symptoms (e.g., frequency, urgency) in a patient with hematuria are actually a higher risk for malignancy than painless hematuria, contrary to the classic teaching.

pearls.text: For diabetic patients, daily self-foot inspection is critical since neuropathy eliminates protective sensation; ulcers or foreign bodies (e.g., a nail) may go unnoticed.

pearls.text: You need at least 4-5 dedicated nurses for a neonatal unit to cover shifts, leave, and sickness.
pearls.verbatim: you need at least four or five nurses that are now additional staff that your hospital's, like, committing to pay long term. So that's the biggest cost.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.applies_to: hospital administration planning a neonatal unit
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: Adapt protocols to locally available medications and equipment; do not simply copy from textbooks.
pearls.verbatim: all of these protocols couldn't just be cut and paste from a textbook. Like, they had to be adapted to what medicine available you had
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.applies_to: any clinician writing protocols for a resource-limited setting
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: Expect referrals to increase dramatically once the unit is known to provide care; initial needs assessments may underestimate demand.
pearls.verbatim: Well, it's because the health centers had not been sending us their babies because they knew that we weren't doing anything for them. So once there was hope that there was treatment, everybody wanted to come with their sick or premature babies.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.applies_to: any new neonatal unit in a resource-limited area
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: Kangaroo Mother Care (skin-to-skin with only a cap) provides near-perfect thermoregulation for almost 100% of preterm babies, regardless of how premature they are, eliminating the need for electrical warmers.
pearls.verbatim: Almost hundred percent of babies will have perfect thermoregulation if you do skin to skin this way no matter how premature they are.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: Homemade CPAP bottles deliver 100% oxygen, which is known to be very harmful; avoid this if possible.
pearls.verbatim: we're unfortunately giving them a 100% oxygen, which is... We know is, like, really, really, really bad.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: The five or six essential interventions for preterm survival in low-resource settings are: warmth, basic antibiotics, vital sign monitoring, blood sugar checks, and dextrose administration.
pearls.verbatim: with someone checking their vital signs, with someone checking their sugar and giving them dextrose. There's, like, five or six things you need to do to keep the vast majority of babies do well.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: Do not judge local nurses' motivation; they may lack context for neonatal care. Once they see survival is possible with simple interventions, they often become passionate advocates.
pearls.verbatim: That was a huge humbling lesson for me, not judge people's motivations, but to give them a chance. And really, I should go into it assuming they have a good reason why.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.applies_to: foreign staff working with local nurses
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: The Mira Cradle hypothermia protocol failed because nurses were trained to keep babies warm and feared license revocation; it requires IRB approval and bedside monitoring every 30 minutes.
pearls.verbatim: And our nurses just, like, nodded and smiled. And at the end of the day, they were like, mm-mm. We're not doing this. And it wasn't because they don't want great outcomes. They just, like, touched me a little bit. But it was because all of their training has been keep that baby warm or the baby will die. And there's always a concern for their license getting revoked if they kind of become cowboys and do whatever they think they should do.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: Rolling up sleeves to help with tasks like suctioning and changing nappies builds trust and shows teamwork, even if it feels beneath a physician's role.
pearls.verbatim: I'll suction them. I'll change the nappy. I'll do whatever because we're doing we're doing all of it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.applies_to: foreign physicians in low-resource neonatal units
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: The Biu CPAP includes a humidifier, preventing the mucus plugging seen with the Pumani CPAP after 12 hours.
pearls.verbatim: What I hate about the Poumani CPAP we've been having is there's no humidifier, so you get big mucus plugging after even just twelve hours.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.applies_to: neonates on CPAP in resource-limited settings
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: Surfactant can be administered via LMA using the salsa technique: insert a tiny LMA, thread an OG tube, and push aliquots of surfactant. Cost is $400 per dose; many babies need one dose, some need two.
pearls.verbatim: salsa technique, which is surfactant administration through laryngeal or supraglutide airway. So, basically, it's the cutest, tiniest little LMA. The baby's still wearing their pee pad usually, and so you don't even take that off. You just pop their mouth open, slide this teeny tiny little LMA into their mouth, and you thread your OG tube through that, and you push your aliquots of surfactant in it. So we've never had surfactant. It's $400 for one dose. And many babies will be okay with just one, but many will need two.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.applies_to: neonates with respiratory distress syndrome in resource-limited settings
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: Scaling and root planing lowers A1c by approximately 0.4 percentage points, similar to a DPP-4 inhibitor like Januvia; diabetic patients should be encouraged to have dental cleanings every three months if insurance allows.

pearls.text: If a toothache 'gets better' after being severe, the pulp has likely necrosed; the patient will develop an abscess later and needs dental evaluation.
pearls.verbatim: You'll hear patients say, and I would assume that you all run run across this, that my tooth was killing me for a few weeks, and then suddenly it got better. Once a tooth is killing you, it never gets better.

pearls.applies_to: patients reporting tooth pain that resolved spontaneously

pearls.text: Swelling below the mandible or into the periorbital space from a dental infection requires immediate antibiotics covering anaerobes (e.g., penicillin VK with metronidazole) and referral to an oral surgeon, not a general dentist.
pearls.verbatim: if you see someone who has swelling that is below the mandible or into the periorbital space, it's really important to start them on antibiotics right away and antibiotics that also cover anaerobes. So that can either be like a pen VK with Flagyl or something like that.

pearls.applies_to: patients with dental infection spreading below mandible or to periorbital space
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: Fluctuance on exam in a dental infection indicates an abscess that needs drainage; antibiotics alone are unlikely to resolve it.
pearls.verbatim: Also, cellulitis is one thing. But if a patient would come into an ER and you feel fluctuance, that is something that would need to be drained. So... And something that probably antibiotics alone isn't isn't going to take care of.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.applies_to: patients with dental infection and fluctuance on exam
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: Spontaneous tooth pain (e.g., waking at night) indicates irreversible pulpitis requiring definitive treatment, root canal or extraction; antibiotics alone will not resolve it.
pearls.verbatim: if someone has a toothache with spontaneous pain, it's something that is going to require definitive treatment. And by that, I mean, if someone has spontaneous pain, they're either going to need a root canal or an extraction.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: Sudden development of spaces between teeth is a strong indicator of periodontal disease and warrants prompt dental referral.
pearls.verbatim: If someone comes to your office and they say, you know, suddenly, I have all these spaces in between my teeth, that's a huge indicator that they have periodontal disease, and you see the dentist right away.

pearls.applies_to: patients reporting new spacing between teeth
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: For infants, lift the lip to examine the front teeth; decayed front teeth indicate the child is sleeping with a bottle.
pearls.verbatim: Lift a kid's lip to see how their front teeth look. And that's a great indicator. I mean, if if a child has decayed front teeth as an infant, you know they're going to sleep with a bottle.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: To wean a baby from a nighttime bottle, gradually dilute the formula with water so the bottle becomes less appealing; sucking is 75% of the need, so start with formula, then water it down.
pearls.verbatim: sucking is 75% of that. So, sure, you can start with formula in the beginning, but then water it down so that their nighttime bottle doesn't taste good. So, you know, maybe 75% then 50% milk, then 25% milk. And soon, they don't want that bottle to sleep.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Catherine Hodge
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup

pearls.text: For an abscessed tooth that is draining pus, antibiotics are not needed if the tooth can be extracted, unless the patient is immunocompromised.
pearls.verbatim: even for someone who may have an abscess tooth that is draining pus, As long as you can take the tooth out most of the time, unless the patient is immunocompromised, you don't need to give them an antibiotic for that either.

pearls.text: Antibiotic prophylaxis for joint replacements is no longer routinely recommended beyond six months post-surgery; clindamycin is avoided due to C. diff risk.

I have to say my mom had about of nine months of in and out of the hospital, the C. diff. And so I personally... And I know other antibiotics can can lead to C. diff too, but I don't prescribe.

pearls.text: When a patient is gearing up for head and neck radiation, clarify whether the entire mouth will receive radiation or be shielded to guide whether all teeth need extraction.

And because there are times that, you know, you... The entire mouth is going to receive radiation, and you know that everything needs to come out. pearls.text: In shared decision-making for gender-affirming care, explain risks and benefits enough for the patient to make an informed decision, and guide them; there is a balance between paternalism and patient autonomy.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For mild COPD (FEV1 >80% predicted, no exacerbations, symptoms about once a month, no hospitalizations), a rescue inhaler alone is sufficient.
pearls.verbatim: So in general, if you have somebody with mild COPD, you're gonna put them on a rescue inhaler. So we're talking about an f e v one of greater than eighty percent, and they're not having exacerbations. They might have symptoms maybe once a month. They've not been hospitalized. Rescue inhaler's fine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For moderate COPD (FEV1 50-80%), start a LAMA/LABA combination; Dr. Dolin usually starts both agents at the same time.
pearls.verbatim: Moderate COPD, like you're seeing here in group b, that's the LAMALABA therapy where you have a longer acting beta agonist and a longer acting muscarinic agent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Nebulized albuterol and ipratropium every 4 hours is safe even in patients on long-acting beta agonists, unless they have tachycardia or difficult-to-control atrial fibrillation.
pearls.verbatim: We don't have any issues with side effects for the most part unless they have tachycardia or difficult to control A-fib.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients on LABA therapy, excluding those with tachycardia or difficult-to-control atrial fibrillation
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Peripheral eosinophilia is not routinely used to guide inhaled steroid therapy in COPD; Dr. Dolin bases it on airflow limitation (FEV1 30-50%) and exacerbation history.
pearls.verbatim: The bloody eosinophilia, I don't really practice based off of that. I notice it, especially with the asthma patients. I'll get an IgE level in a heartbeat. But the actual peripheral eosinophilia, unless I'm looking for something like chronic eosinophilic pneumonia or acute eosinophilic pneumonia or Schurz Strauss or something off the beaten path, I'm not particularly measuring it specifically to determine whether or not I'm gonna put them on an inhaled steroid. I'm going more off of their airflow limitation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For patients with rheumatoid arthritis and ulnar deviation who cannot turn and push an inhaler, a spacer may help, but most patients will not carry a spacer; observe their technique with samples if available.
pearls.verbatim: you have to remember who you're prescribing for when you pick your inhaler.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: patients with dexterity limitations (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, trach)
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Oxygen therapy criteria: ambulatory pulse ox showing desaturation below 88% on room air with ambulation, and recovery above 88%.
pearls.verbatim: you're looking for desaturation below 88%.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: COPD patients being evaluated for oxygen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: All new COPD patients should be tested for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency because treatment differs (enzyme replacement therapy like Zemaira or Prolastin).
pearls.verbatim: when new patients come into the pulmonary clinic, I always test them for alpha one antitrypsin deficiency. And because the reason is the treatment's different.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: new COPD patients in pulmonary clinic
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: During hospitalization for COPD exacerbation, arrange for CT scan and spirometry if not already done, to identify structural lung disease and guide future options.
pearls.verbatim: Do they need oxygen when they leave? Do they need noninvasive support? Have they had a CT scan or a pulmonary function test? If they haven't, can they do them while they're there so that I have them already done before they come to the pulmonary clinic.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Adequate spirometry requires a sustained exhalation of at least 6-8 seconds; otherwise the data is invalid.
pearls.verbatim: to get an adequate spirometry test, they have to be able to sustain a prolonged exhalation for at least six to eight seconds. Otherwise, the data is invalid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For a valid spirometry test, the patient must sustain a prolonged exhalation for at least six to eight seconds; otherwise the data is invalid.
pearls.verbatim: they have to be able to sustain a prolonged exhalation for at least six to eight seconds. Otherwise, the data is invalid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: If a COPD exacerbation shows peripheral eosinophilia >2% (e.g., 4% or 6%), IV steroids are particularly helpful.
pearls.verbatim: especially if you see a little bit of peripheral eosinophilia, you know, see something more than two percent, you see a four or a six percent on that peripheral eosinophilia, the IV steroids would be helpful.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Lung cancer screening with low-dose CT is indicated for smokers with >30 pack-years, age >55, presence of emphysema/COPD, low BMI, or family history of lung cancer.
pearls.verbatim: when you go to get that low dose CT scan once a year for your smokers who've been smoking more than thirty pack years, the other things are age greater than 55, presence of emphysema, COPD or fixed airflow obstruction, BMI, family history of lung cancer to consider
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: For COPD exacerbation failing outpatient therapy, if purulent phlegm is present, get a sputum culture; if an infiltrate is seen, broaden antibiotics with vancomycin and Zosyn or cefepime.
pearls.verbatim: So if they failed outpatient therapy, then I would consider broadening their antibiotic therapy if they have purulent phlegm production, get a sputum culture. ... they come into the hospital and they've got an infiltrate, they're gonna get put on broader spectrum antibiotics, usually vancomycin and Zosyn or cefepime
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: COPD exacerbation in hospital with infiltrate
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Asthma exacerbations can blow up quickly even in patients who are stable at baseline, so you must be careful.
pearls.verbatim: the asthma patients, because it's not that they are so bad functionally when things are okay and they're stable on therapy. It's when they have an exacerbation. It just can blow up so quick, and they go down so fast. You have to be careful.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: Refer patients with multiple positive allergy panel results to allergy/immunology for further management and biologics like Xolair.
pearls.verbatim: if I would see people who would come in that had multiple things light up on those panels, I was like, okay. You you go to Suzanne's, you know, or you go to allergy clinic at Tulsa. And so for me, that's where all those biologics came in. You know, Xolair injections, I... I'm comfortable with.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: patients with multiple positive allergy tests
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma

pearls.text: An Epworth Sleepiness Scale score ≥10 indicates excessive daytime sleepiness and helps decide treatment for mild OSA (AHI 5-15).
pearls.verbatim: And if they're scoring greater than 10 that, it's an indicator that they've got excessive daytime sleepiness.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: Medicare requires a 4% oxygen desaturation rule for scoring hypopneas; using a 3% rule may necessitate repeating the sleep study even if AHI is very high.
pearls.verbatim: The 4% rule is based on Medicare guidelines. So when I run into Medicare sometimes based on a patient coming in and saying, I need a new piece of equipment. And I have to look at that study. And if the tech wasn't certified in a certain way or we used a 3% rule instead of a 4% rule, they're actually making me go back and repeat the study even if their AHI was a 120.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: Periodic limb movements are treated only if associated with arousals and daytime sleepiness; treat OSA first, as it often resolves the leg movements.
pearls.verbatim: with the periodic limb movements, if they're not symptomatic with breathless legs when they're awake, I don't get excited about it at all because I'm not gonna put them on medication to treat something that's occurring while they're asleep that's not bothering them while they're awake unless there's zero findings of anything else that's disrupting their sleep, and they're excessively tired. And we do have an associated arousal index assessment with our legs. So for example, if they they can kick all night long, if it causes no arousals, I wouldn't treat that. But if they're waking up 30 times an hour associated with leg movements, I... And they're tired with an Epworth of 15, I'd say, okay. You know, that's probably worth addressing. The the other thing to remember, though, is if they have something else also occurring at the same time with the leg movements, particularly apnea. A lot of times, if we treat the apnea, everything else just kinda falls into place and smooths out.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: adults with periodic limb movements on sleep study
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: For in-lab sleep studies, offer zolpidem 5 mg thirty minutes before sleep to help patients fall asleep in the unfamiliar environment.
pearls.verbatim: The most common one we prescribe is Zolpidem, a five milligram pill, to take thirty minutes before sleep just to kind of take the edge off and help them fall asleep. Because we realize they're not in their own bed. They got all the stuff stuck to them, and they may not sleep as easily.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing in-lab polysomnography who have difficulty sleeping
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: For in-lab polysomnography, a split-night study can be done if AHI ≥20 in the first 2 hours, with at least 4 hours of PAP therapy needed for a prescription.
pearls.verbatim: If they have 20 events per hour in the first two hours of monitoring, we're able to do what's called a split night and switch to treatment the second part of the night. Medicare guidelines tell us we have to have at least four hours of treatment to get a prescription their PAP therapy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: On CPAP prescriptions, leave the mask type blank because fit is individualized; heated tubing is recommended to prevent condensation and dry mouth.
pearls.verbatim: And down here, the the main types of mask, I leave those blank because, again, it's like trying on shoes, and I don't wanna box them in to getting something that ultimately they don't want. And these things are good for a year.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: For dry mouth on CPAP, increase humidification and decrease the temperature of the climate control tubing.
pearls.verbatim: So if you have somebody come in and say, you know, my mouth is extremely dry. What can I do to fix this? Usually, the first thing I do is increase the humidification and decrease the temperature.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: patients on CPAP with dry mouth
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: Weight gain of about 20 pounds on average may require an upward pressure adjustment.
pearls.verbatim: if they gain weight in an... On average, about 20 pounds before we start noticing that you're gonna need to adjust the pressure, just an average.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: patients on CPAP who gain weight
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: On the download report, the goal apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) is under 3 events per hour; if AHI is 4 but the patient feels well and is at high pressures, that may be acceptable.
pearls.verbatim: When I look at a report, I wanna see this under three.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: Expiratory pressure release (EPR) reduces pressure by 1, 3 cm H₂O during exhalation as a comfort feature.
pearls.verbatim: when I exhale, it backs off by three. And your expiratory pressure release can be a difference of one, two, or three centimeters of water pressure, and it's it's a comfort feature.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: Remote pressure adjustments can be made via the ResMed system using the device serial number, without requiring the patient to bring the machine in.
pearls.verbatim: we're actually able to log in to ResMed There's there's a serial number on those devices, and they're registered in the ResMed system. And we can log in and make those adjustments without them having to haul in the machine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: Auto-adjusting CPAP is the default mode; even if the range is narrowed (e.g., 10, 13), keep it on auto rather than switching to fixed pressure.
pearls.verbatim: we just do the auto. Even if we put it down to a range of 10 to 13, we keep it on auto.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: Home-based sleep tests are not good at detecting central or complex apnea; patients who are pregnant, on narcotics, or have heart failure/Cheyne-Stokes should be studied in the lab.
pearls.verbatim: the home based tests are not super good at central apnea or complex apnea.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected central or complex apnea (pregnancy, narcotics, heart failure, Cheyne-Stokes)
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea

pearls.text: On BiPAP, keep pressure support (IPAP minus EPAP) at 4 cm H2O or less; otherwise it affects ventilation.
pearls.verbatim: we don't want a pressure support of more than four on a BiPAP. Otherwise, it affects their ventilation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Elizabeth Dolin
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea
