pearls.verbatim: Twenty five percent of the time, you would have passed this on your own. If you... Let's... You know, if if you look expected management, well, hey. You're gonna gain another 27% in the next week.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: patients with first-trimester miscarriage choosing expectant management
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: Rhogam should be given to Rh-negative patients with miscarriage; evidence is weak but risk is low and alloimmunization can prevent future pregnancies.
pearls.verbatim: If the patient is Rh negative, I would give them Rhogam. It's questionable. It's like class C evidence or whatever, it's kinda weak evidence, but rhogam is not very harmful, if it is at all. And if you have a person that becomes alloimmunized than a mother, then you probably not going to ever be able to have a child again.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: Rh-negative patients with first-trimester pregnancy loss
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: When prescribing misoprostol in Oklahoma, specify 'medical management of miscarriage' on the prescription.
pearls.verbatim: Remember how you specify, like, for acute pain for your pain pills? You have to specify for miscarriage, medical management of miscarriage, or something like that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: Misoprostol alone is 84% effective by day 8; adding mifepristone increases efficacy to 88%.
pearls.verbatim: Mifeprostone and misoprostol together, remember, eighty eight percent effective by day eight. So it's eighty four percent effective. So you only lose four percent effectiveness without the mifeprostone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: medical management of early pregnancy loss
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: The discriminatory zone for HCG is 1500-3000 IU/L; below this, an intrauterine pregnancy may not be visible on ultrasound.
pearls.verbatim: Scrimmatory level, you need to know that. Okay? Question about that? Yes. 1,500 to 3,000. Yeah. 3,000.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected early pregnancy loss
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: By the end of 6 weeks on transvaginal ultrasound, you should see a yolk sac; describe it to patients as 'maybe first Cheerio'.
pearls.verbatim: I usually say by the end of the six week, transvaginal ultrasound, exact. ... Maybe first Cheerio.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: At 7 weeks transvaginal, you should see a fetus with a heartbeat.
pearls.verbatim: by seven weeks, transvaginal should have a fetus with a heartbeat.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: For serial HCG, expect 1.5× rise at 48 hours and doubling at 72 hours, but only reliable up to about 9 weeks gestation.
pearls.verbatim: If I check it in forty eight hours, I'm expecting 1.5 x. If I check it in seventy two hours, I'm expecting double. ... you can only really use that probably up to about nine weeks.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: Positive pregnancy test with no intrauterine pregnancy and free fluid in posterior cul-de-sac is a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
pearls.verbatim: free fluid in the posterior cul de sac. ... So that goes with the ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy

pearls.text: Non-vertex and non-face presentations (e.g., ear, brow) are not amenable to vaginal delivery.
pearls.verbatim: it's either the vertex or the face. Obviously, like, if you've got an ear, you know, baby's head is like this, like, it is not gonna work.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26

pearls.text: Mentum anterior face presentation can deliver vaginally because the chin causes the head to flex naturally as it comes through the birth canal.
pearls.verbatim: As baby comes through the birth canal, its chin's gonna be up. It's gonna cause the head to flex naturally.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26

pearls.text: Mentum posterior face presentation will not resolve and the baby will get stuck, requiring cesarean delivery.
pearls.verbatim: But mentum posterior, baby's just gonna get stuck. It's not gonna it's not gonna resolve.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26

pearls.text: If labor is not progressing or there is fetal distress, have a low threshold to proceed to cesarean section for malpresentation.
pearls.verbatim: If you're not progressing for those fetal distress, like, you're gonna be much more quick to do those... To take those to a C section.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26

pearls.text: Manual rotation of OP is often only partially successful, achieving 20-30 degrees of rotation, and is hard to truly rotate the baby's body.
pearls.verbatim: I can get them usually, you know, twenty, thirty degrees, but, you know, most of the time, it's it's hard to get them to really truly, like, rotate their body.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26

pearls.text: Manual rotation of OP is worth trying as a last-ditch effort before proceeding to cesarean section.
pearls.verbatim: I think it's worth trying. To me, it's kinda like a last ditch. You know? We'll see if we can do it before the C section.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26

pearls.text: Manual rotation of OP requires significant pressure with three fingers and is best done in a patient with an epidural for adequate anesthesia.
pearls.verbatim: for me, like, I mean, I've gotta put a lot of pressure. I've gotta have, like, three fingers in there. I mean, it's, you know, definitely something for a lady that's got an epidural.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26

pearls.text: Manual rotation of OP is more likely to be successful if the fetal body is lying on its side rather than directly OP.
pearls.verbatim: If if the baby's, you know, laying on its back, you know, what if what if baby's, like, laying on its side where some umbilicus is is over here? You know? But its head is opaque. You know? It's gonna be pretty easy to, like, go with that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26

pearls.text: If the fetal body is straight OP, manual rotation is very hard to turn, though sometimes the baby seems to want to turn.
pearls.verbatim: if if baby's body is straight OP, yeah, I mean, it's gonna be pretty hard to turn it. But, you know, sometimes they seem to wanna turn, but, yeah, it's not it's not the most successful thing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26

pearls.text: Before performing a pelvic or speculum exam on a patient with threatened or incomplete miscarriage, explain the reason and reassure them it is safe.
pearls.verbatim: if you have an incomplete or a threatened abortion, you need to talk with the patient before you do that that exam that...
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: patients with threatened or incomplete abortion
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: For anembryonic gestation, transvaginal ultrasound criteria: gestational sac ≥13 mm with yolk sac but no embryonic pole, or sac ≥18 mm without a yolk sac.
pearls.verbatim: gestational sac, 13 millimeters with ayogue sac, 18 without an embryonic pole.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: By the end of the sixth week, transvaginal ultrasound should show an embryonic pole (MRV).
pearls.verbatim: if you're past the end of the sixth week, you should be able to see MRV.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Patients can switch between expectant, medical, and surgical management at any point; they are not locked into their initial choice.
pearls.verbatim: And then remember that you can switch to medical or surgical management at any point in time. So you can... That... That's just an ongoing discussion. Just because they've decided on one doesn't mean they need to stick with that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Standard of care in Tulsa for surgical management is suction dilation and curettage (D&C), not manual vacuum aspiration.
pearls.verbatim: But the standard of care in Tulsa, Oklahoma is a suction dilation curettage. That's what all the OB/GYNs do.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: surgical management of early pregnancy loss in Tulsa, Oklahoma
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Do not project your own expectations onto patients; expectant, medical, and surgical management are all equally safe.
pearls.verbatim: But we don't need to put our expectations on the patient when these are all essentially equally safe.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: counseling patients with early pregnancy loss
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not needed for miscarriage management.
pearls.verbatim: People do not need antibiotic prophylaxis, by the way.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Subsequent fertility is not statistically significantly adversely affected by the choice of management.
pearls.verbatim: Subsequent fertility is not statistically significantly adversely affected depending on, you know, which one they do.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: For anembryonic gestation with expectant management, only 25% pass within 1 week, 52% by 2 weeks, and 66% by day 46.
pearls.verbatim: So only twenty five percent of it are gonna pass within one week. If you go up to two weeks, fifty two percent, that's a pretty good right... Rise. Right? But if you go all the way out to to day 46, so that's why wild, it only goes up to sixty six percent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Misoprostol alone is 67% successful within 2 days and 84% within a week.
pearls.verbatim: Misoprostol works sixty seven percent within two days, eighty four percent within a week if used alone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: medical management of early pregnancy loss with misoprostol alone
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: For pain with miscarriage, advise patients to take NSAIDs beforehand as part of the protocol.
pearls.verbatim: you said you will expect a little bit of pain with me. So do you, like, usually advise patients to, like, some pain medication in a sense? It's in the protocol. Just take the NSAIDs
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Pain not controlled by Tylenol or ibuprofen is an ER precaution that suggests something else may be going on.
pearls.verbatim: Like, usually, pain not controlled by Tylenol or ibuprofen because that that makes me worry that something else is going on.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: Take a spiritual history because it can impact management decisions.
pearls.verbatim: Don't forget spiritual history because people can do your illnesses. That can impact your management.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26

pearls.text: For transvaginal ultrasound, advance the probe very slowly along the posterior aspect of the vagina and look for the uterus as a homogeneous appearing structure with a bright endometrial stripe.
pearls.verbatim: one tip is as you're advancing it, you want to advance it very slowly and look for the uterus. Okay? So the uterus is going to be... this kind of homogeneous appearing structure.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: Free fluid in the posterior cul-de-sac may indicate a ruptured ectopic or infection; trace fluid can be seen with dysmenorrhea.
pearls.verbatim: So there's fluid in the posterior cul-de-sac. So what does that make you think of potentially? Ruptured ectopic. Could be ruptured ectopic. Could be infectious. This is not trace fluid. Sometimes you can see trace fluid with dysmenorrhea.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: patients with pelvic pain and positive hCG
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: A pregnancy of undetermined location should be treated as an ectopic pregnancy until one is found in the uterus.
pearls.verbatim: Don't sleep on them. They're they're ectopic pregnancy unless find one in the uterus.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: patients with positive hCG and no intrauterine pregnancy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: A true gestational sac is rounded or elliptical in two planes, eccentric to the endometrial stripe, shows a double decidual sign, and is greater than 4 mm, growing by 1 mm per day.
pearls.verbatim: Normal is rounded or elliptical in two planes, eccentric to endometrial stripe, double decidual sign, and then size greater than four millimeter grows by one millimeter a day.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: Crown-rump length is the average of three measurements from the top of the head to the bottom of the buttocks; the knees are usually flexed.
pearls.verbatim: a CRL is gonna be your average of three measurements. It's gonna be from the top of the head to the bottom of the butt. Okay? Most of the time, the knees are gonna be up like this.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: By 6 weeks on transabdominal ultrasound you should be able to see a fetal pole with a heartbeat.
pearls.verbatim: by six weeks a fetal pole with a heartbeat on a transabdominal ultrasound.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: No yolk sac by the end of 6 weeks is abnormal.
pearls.verbatim: if you don't have a yolk sac by the end of six weeks, that's abnormal.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: No embryonic pole by 49 days is abnormal.
pearls.verbatim: No embryonic pole by forty nine days.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: Mean sac diameter greater than 25 mm with no fetal pole is a criterion for pregnancy failure.
pearls.verbatim: greater... Mean sac size, than 25 millimeters with no fetal pole.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: If the same findings are present at 8 weeks, it is an embryonic demise.
pearls.verbatim: now if this was eight weeks, now it's an embryonic demise.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.applies_to: pregnancy at 8 weeks with no heartbeat
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: At 6 weeks, beta-hCG should double in 72 hours (1.15x in 48 hours); after 9 weeks it plateaus and trending is not useful.
pearls.verbatim: around the sixth week, it should be doubling in seventy two hours, one one five x in forty eight hours.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: IUDs appear as very echogenic bright white lines on transvaginal ultrasound, much brighter than the endometrium.
pearls.verbatim: here is your IUD. They're very echogenic. Okay? And you can kind of move it around, and you will see a bright white line that is much brighter than the endometrium.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Jacob Greuel
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25

pearls.text: Use MDCalc to guide NIHSS; it is a screening exam and you cannot get it wrong with the tool.
pearls.verbatim: If you have MD calc with you, you can't really get wrong.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro Exam

pearls.text: For NIHSS level of consciousness, ask the month and the patient's age, not orientation to place.
pearls.verbatim: So I would say, what is the month, and how old are you, or what is your age?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro Exam

pearls.text: When testing commands, do not put your fingers in the patient's hand because they will reflexively grasp; that does not count as following the command.
pearls.verbatim: And you don't put your hands in their... Your fingers in their hand because they're gonna just reflectively grasp onto your hand, and that doesn't count.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro Exam

pearls.text: Hold your finger about two to two and a half feet away when testing extraocular movements.
pearls.verbatim: holding your finger out about two, two and a half feet when you're doing extraocular movements.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro Exam

pearls.text: Test visual fields binocularly by holding your fists about two feet away and flashing fingers in the lower and upper quadrants while the patient looks at your nose.
pearls.verbatim: hold your hands about two feet away, two and a half feet away, and then just... You just put your fists in the lower quadrants, fists in the upper quadrants.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro Exam

pearls.text: If the patient is not moving, use your face as the strongest stimulus to get them to look.
pearls.verbatim: The strongest stimulus is the human face. So if you really can't get them to move, you just move your fist.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.applies_to: patients who are not responding to visual field testing
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro Exam

pearls.text: For visual fields, if the patient looks at the stimulus, that counts as seeing it.
pearls.verbatim: If you look over, you know that they've seen it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing NIHSS visual field testing
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro Exam

pearls.text: For patients with baseline visual deficits, score conservatively; do not subtract points for chronic findings.
pearls.verbatim: I'll do it on the conservative side.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.applies_to: patients with chronic visual loss undergoing NIHSS
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro Exam

pearls.text: Test the median nerve by having the patient make a circle with thumb and finger and resist your attempt to pull them apart, that tests opponens pollicis.
pearls.verbatim: opponens pollicis is an easy one to do. You just get someone to do a circle like that, and you say, don't let me, like, hold your finger to your thumb, and it can be any finger. Okay?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected median nerve or carpal tunnel syndrome
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: Radial nerve injury presents with wrist drop and inability to extend the fingers at the MCP or DIP joints.
pearls.verbatim: if you've got, like, a wrist drop or your your fingers can't extend at the MCP or the DIP, like, that's that's all radial nerve.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected radial nerve palsy (e.g., Saturday night palsy)
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression) is benign; manage with weight loss and avoiding tight belts.
pearls.verbatim: You just lose weight. Or do you... Or you stop using really tight belts? That's the main thing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.applies_to: larger men with burning/numbness on anterolateral thigh
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: Rapid weight loss, particularly with GLP-1 receptor agonists, is a common cause of peroneal nerve injury (foot drop) due to loss of protective fat pad.
pearls.verbatim: So when you wanna ask them if they've had any traumatic weight loss recently, which is one of the things that lots of people are doing now with GLP-1 receptor agonists.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: Acute cluster headache can be aborted with high-flow oxygen; it is a first-line acute therapy.
pearls.verbatim: I was like, well, let's just give her some oxygen. And we were happy. It worked? And she was like, my headache's gone. Amazing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.applies_to: patients with cluster headache during an attack
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: Cluster headache prophylaxis includes topiramate and verapamil; lithium is considered a third-line agent due to its side-effect profile.
pearls.verbatim: So topiramate, there's a couple other treatments that can be used prophylaxis. Lithium is just a nasty drug.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.applies_to: patients with cluster headache requiring prevention
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: Primary headaches (migraine, tension, cluster) typically show no significant findings on brain imaging; in patients over 50, minor microvascular changes may be seen but are not diagnostic.
pearls.verbatim: Person with primary headache, you're gonna see some microvascular changes if they're over 50, and that's about it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: In a pregnant patient with headache and elevated blood pressure, suspect preeclampsia.
pearls.verbatim: Pregnant, obviously, we know why we need to worry about headaches in pregnancy, especially if you have elevated hypertension... Elevated blood pressure, you got preeclampsia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: A pseudo-flare (recrudescence of old MS symptoms due to infection like pneumonia or sinusitis) does not require high-dose IV steroids. Differentiate from true flare by assessing whether symptoms are truly new.
pearls.verbatim: But there are these pseudo flares where a person... Basically, they have an inflammatory state in their body, like they have a pneumonia or they have bronchitis or even like a sinusitis, and they can have kind of like a recrudescence of their... Of the symptoms they had previously. So that's not that's not necessarily a flare. And so you wouldn't, like, you know, dose them up on, like, a gram of Solu-Medrol for that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: COVID-19 vaccination was associated with cases of central spinal cord inflammation (transverse myelitis) during the initial vaccination period.
pearls.verbatim: I actually diagnosed two cases of this when I was still in my neurology residence in Canada. So it's actually fairly common overall. I mean, you're probably not gonna see it if you're not on a neurology service. But if you're on a neurology service, it it was... Especially when everyone was getting vaccinated initially, it was it was certainly a risk factor that was that was being seen.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.applies_to: patients presenting with myelopathy after COVID-19 vaccination
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: Brisk deep tendon reflexes with clonus indicate a CNS lesion; in Guillain-Barré syndrome, reflexes go down, not up.
pearls.verbatim: remember, when you get deep tendon reflexes, it's a CNS issue. It's not a peripheral nerve. And with Guillain Barre syndrome, it's peripheral nerves. So you Yeah. Mhmm. Reflexes go down, not up.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.applies_to: patients with neurological symptoms and reflex examination
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: Multiple sclerosis is a central nervous system disorder, so patients will have brisk reflexes.
pearls.verbatim: MS is a central Central. You're gonna get... You're gonna get reflexes that are gonna be brisk.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hadwen
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25

pearls.text: NYHA functional classification can change (e.g., a stage C patient can become class I with treatment), but ACC/AHA stage does not change once assigned.
pearls.verbatim: MyHA classifications can change. You can have somebody that's stage C had symptomatic heart failure, and they can become asymptomatic later. So I can go to stage one or not stage class one.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: A predischarge BNP that has not decreased significantly can be a strong predictor of readmission, but should not alone delay discharge; it should prompt reassessment of congestion.
pearls.verbatim: there is some evidence that if you get a predischarged BMT, patient's ready to go. They're ready to go. But it could be a strong predictor of readmission. And so I don't think that I would hold up a discharge based on a BNP, but it would make me think twice if... To see if they're really not congested anymore.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: hospitalized patients with CHF being considered for discharge
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: High-sensitivity symptoms of CHF: dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, and weight gain. Specific signs: PND, orthopnea, and JVD.
pearls.verbatim: high sensitivity stuff, so things that you're gonna see in people with CHF are gonna be dyspnea on exertion and fatigue and weight gain.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: On ultrasound, IVC >2.1 cm with <50% collapse is pretty specific for CHF.
pearls.verbatim: the IVC is more than 2.1 centimeters and it doesn't collapse at least 50%, that's pretty specific for CHF.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Initial workup for suspected CHF includes echo, labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, iron panel, urinalysis), EKG, and chest X-ray. Echo is essential to assess structure and function.
pearls.verbatim: once you have a suspicion for it and once you get the... You're gonna order an ultrasound. And after you get the ultrasound, it's the picture. So you see problems with the structure or the function or the bowels and you have the clinical syndrome, then you have CHF.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: HFrEF is EF ≤40%; HFmrEF is 41-49%; HFpEF is ≥50%. These are treated somewhat differently.
pearls.verbatim: It's HFrEF if he's 40 year old. Yeah. This splitting hairs. Yeah. If he was 41%, he'd have HFrEF Mr. F, which I'm gonna start calling that. That's good. And then if 50% and above, and that's treated a little different.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: GDMT for HFrEF starts with sacubitril/valsartan (an ARNI). This can elevate BNP due to neprilysin inhibition, so BNP is not a reliable marker of worsening in patients on this drug.
pearls.verbatim: sacubitril, valsartan, whatever floats your mouth. I don't care. Anyways, it's an angiotensin receptor blocker and neprilysin. So these people are going to have an elevated BNP because neprilysin.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Sodium restriction to <3 g/day is reasonable; fluid restriction is not helpful except in advanced (stage D) HF.
pearls.verbatim: I tell people all the time, do less than two grams a day. But, really, this morning, recent studies have shown that if you do just shoot for less than three grams, you're not really aiming for a really goal. It might actually be harmful.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: In HF with improved ejection fraction (HFimpEF), continue GDMT indefinitely even if the patient becomes asymptomatic.
pearls.verbatim: You wouldn't change it. Mhmm. Great. So just keep doing. If it's not broke, we want you to fix it. Right? So just keep doing what you're doing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Entresto is preferred for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, but if cost is prohibitive, lisinopril or losartan are acceptable alternatives.
pearls.verbatim: Usually trying to get people on Entresto if they can. I don't wanna break the bank. You know? All you can do is lisinopril or losartan do it. That's great.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: Cardiologists may increase beta blocker dose even if heart rate is as low as 50 beats per minute.
pearls.verbatim: And sometimes they go, like, really low. Like, the heart rate is 50, and they're, like, increase the beta blocker.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients on beta blockers for heart failure
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney- CHF

pearls.text: The top causes to investigate in CHF are hypertension, ischemia, and valvular disease.
pearls.verbatim: I want you to remember hypertension, ischemia, and valvular diseases are the top things that you should remember when investigating why somebody has CHF.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Stage A is not heart failure; it is just risk factors for heart failure.
pearls.verbatim: Stage a isn't even heart failure. It's just you're at risk for heart failure.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: If BNP is >400, it is pretty specific for CHF; if <100, it rules out CHF.
pearls.verbatim: if your BNP is more than 400, that's pretty consistent for CHF. That's pretty specific. If it's less than a 100, that's pretty pretty much rules out CHF.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: A pre-discharge BNP that remains elevated is a strong predictor of readmission.
pearls.verbatim: getting a pre discharged BNP. It's still elevated, and it's a pretty strong predictor of readmission.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Dyspnea on exertion, peripheral edema, and weight gain are sensitive for CHF; if one of these is missing, it is probably not CHF.
pearls.verbatim: things that are gonna be there in people with CHF that aren't really specific to CHF are gonna be dyspnea on exertion, the PE, weight gain, all this stuff. ... If one of those guys is missing, it's probably not CHF.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (waking up gasping for air) is pretty specific to CHF.
pearls.verbatim: if somebody's got orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, meaning they wake up in middle of night gasping for air, that's pretty specific to CHF.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: An IVC diameter of 1, 2.1 cm that does not collapse at least 50% with sniff test is pretty specific for CHF.
pearls.verbatim: if your inferior vena cava is one to 2.1 centimeters, doesn't collapse at least 50% with the sniff test. Pretty specific for CHF.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Initial workup for new CHF includes CBC, chem14, lipid panel, iron panel, PSA, urinalysis, EKG, and chest X-ray.
pearls.verbatim: you get a CBC, a chem fourteen. You're gonna get a lipid panel, an iron panel, mostly for hemochromatosis, a PSA channelizer, and a urinalysis. And on top of that, you're gonna get an EKG and a chest X-ray.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Ejection fraction of 40% or less defines HFrEF.
pearls.verbatim: that is when your ejection fraction is 40 or less.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: HFmrEF (ejection fraction 41, 49%) is a midrange category; these patients are teetering and could get better or worse.
pearls.verbatim: if you get the ejection fraction, it's 41 to 49%. ... Then they have F with mildly reduced or midrange ejection fraction. ... The big thing about HFrEF midrange is just gonna be... These people are kind of teetering. They could get better. They could get worse.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: GDMT stands for guideline-directed medical therapy and consists of four pillars (four medicines) for HFrEF.
pearls.verbatim: There's four pillars of GDMT. It's just like there's four letters in GDMT. It's not goal directed medical therapy. It's guideline directed medical therapy. There are four medicines that we really need. Four pillars, four letters.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: When switching from an ACE inhibitor to an ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan), a 36-hour washout is required because of the high risk of angioedema.
pearls.verbatim: if somebody comes to you, they're on lisinopril, and you wanna start them on an ARNI, you have to have a washout for thirty six hours. That's because of the high risk for angioedema.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with HFrEF on ACE inhibitor being switched to ARNI
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Only three beta-blockers are proven for HFrEF: bisoprolol, carvedilol, and metoprolol succinate (long-acting).
pearls.verbatim: Beta blockers, a decreased hospitalizations mortality, but only these three, bisoprolol, carvedilol, foprolol succinate, the last... The long lasting one.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Empagliflozin (Jardiance) for HFrEF is dosed at 10 mg once daily; no titration is needed. If the patient also has diabetes, the dose can be increased to 25 mg.
pearls.verbatim: Jardiance ten milligrams. That's what it is. You don't adjust it. It's just Cardium's ten.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with HFrEF (with or without diabetes)
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Titrate GDMT medications to target doses even if the patient's symptoms improve, because higher doses provide additional mortality and hospitalization benefit.
pearls.verbatim: you're supposed to titrate people up even if their symptoms get better. Like, you're trying to reach these doses. ... you're still trying to be intentional about getting to these target doses.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Cardiac rehabilitation is indicated for patients with NYHA class II, III HFrEF.
pearls.verbatim: if somebody's class two through three, at least, I mean, all the way through. If somebody's at least class two, which is gonna be pretty much everybody that we find heart failure in, like, they're a candidate for rehabilitation with that pref.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with HFrEF, NYHA class II–III
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Recommend sodium restriction to less than 3 grams per day; more restrictive goals are not helpful and may discourage patients.
pearls.verbatim: Try to keep their sodium less than three grams a day. If you try to get more restrictive than that, it's probably not gonna be helpful.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Fluid restriction is only recommended for stage D heart failure (symptoms at rest); it is not beneficial for stage C patients and they are unlikely to adhere.
pearls.verbatim: If they're in stage D, we do a fluid restriction. There's not a whole lot of benefits to doing a fluid restriction, you're normal stage C person is probably not going to be helpful, and they're probably not going to do it anyways.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: patients with heart failure; stage D vs stage C
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Offer palliative care to stage D heart failure patients; it provides symptom management and end-of-life preparation, not just terminal care.
pearls.verbatim: So if somebody's stage D, though, that meaning that they have symptoms even at rest, you have fluid restriction. They're gonna do that. And then palliative care. Right? Somebody that's stage D, don't forget. That's a diagnosis. People that go through palliative care, I mean, they get a lot of benefits. It's not just symptom management, but it's also, like, end of life care things they should... They get prepared for.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Nonpharmacologic measures (diet, rehab, smoking cessation) help patients feel in control of their condition, which improves adherence.
pearls.verbatim: But I do think it's really helpful when you can tell the patient, alright. I want you to take these pills, but here's some other things I want you to do. I think it helps them feel in control. Whenever they can say, I'm a watch myself. I quit smoking. I'm doing cardiac rehab. I'm doing all the things I'm supposed to do, and I'm taking my pills. You just give them pills. Sometimes people... They still don't feel like they're in control. So give them something they can control.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: Consider ICD placement when EF is 35% or less, especially if the patient is symptomatic (NYHA class II, III).
pearls.verbatim: Yeah, what I want you to remember, if the EF is, like, 35% or less, there's a good chance they might need an ICD.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology

pearls.text: I-PASS stands for Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situational awareness, and Synthesis.
pearls.verbatim: IPass. So let's just get into the the nuts and bolts of this. Alright? Eye is the illness severity. So are they stable? Are they unstable? Are they a watcher? Kind of the in between, the potential to crump. Right?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on I-Pass and Senior Addendum

pearls.text: The action list is the to-do list for the covering person; it should be where they take notes.
pearls.verbatim: And then you got the action list. I need you to do a post op on him after his cath tonight, or I need you to follow up on his lab that he's going to get at 5PM today. It's your to do list. This is where people should be taking notes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on I-Pass and Senior Addendum

pearls.text: Situational awareness includes if-then contingency plans (e.g., 'If potassium is 2.5, replace and adjust diuretic').
pearls.verbatim: Situational awareness that you're talking about, Jeremiah, this is the if then stuff. If you get his potassium back and it's 2.5, please replace and adjust his diuretic dose or something to that effect.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on I-Pass and Senior Addendum

pearls.text: Approach vaccine-hesitant parents by acknowledging their vulnerability and desire to do what's best for their child; this builds trust and opens dialogue.
pearls.verbatim: people want what's best for their kids. Right? And so they're trusting you to tell them what's best for their children.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: Thimerosal in vaccines is not a safety concern; the AAP removed it preemptively to address public concern.
pearls.verbatim: Thymarisol doesn't really matter with vaccines, but the AAP took it out.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: When evaluating measles hospitalization data, know that many admissions are for isolation purposes to prevent spread, not because all patients are severely ill.
pearls.verbatim: I think in a good faith discussion, we should know that a lot of that is from isolation. These aren't all people that are getting super sick.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: When discussing vaccines with patients, share a personal illustration of why vaccination matters to you, this is more important than any strategy.
pearls.verbatim: I would encourage you guys, as you're talking about patients with this kind of stuff, have an illustration, not a manipulative illustration, but a why does this matter to me? Why am I having this discussion with you? That matters more than any kind of strategy that we're gonna go into later.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: Smallpox was eradicated globally due to vaccination; we no longer vaccinate for it because it is completely gone from the world.
pearls.verbatim: smallpox was eradicated, meaning it's not in the world anywhere right now. It's probably in a lab somewhere, I'm sure. But we don't even vaccinate for it anymore because it's completely eradicated.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: Babies are exposed to more aluminum from breastfeeding than they get from vaccines.
pearls.verbatim: babies are exposed to more aluminum from breastfeeding Mhmm. They get in a vaccine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: Phase I clinical trials for vaccines check safety in 20, 100 people over a few months; side effects and immune response appear during this phase, not years later.
pearls.verbatim: First phase is they're just checking for safety. So they're just small amount of people, 20 to a 100 people. Just wanna make sure that it's safe for people so that they can move on to bigger trials. Usually lasts a few months. That's typically when you're gonna get your immune response and your side effects. It's not gonna be years down the road.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: Phase II trials check for effectiveness in several hundred people and take months to years in a normal timeline.
pearls.verbatim: Phase two, once they see that's okay, they check-in for effectiveness. So no longer just... Is it safe? Then now is it effective? What kind of immune response do we get? This is gonna be several 100 people, so starting to move up. This takes months to years in a normal world.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: Phase III trials involve thousands of volunteers and evaluate both safety and effectiveness; they typically take several years.
pearls.verbatim: And then phase three, you're looking for both safety and effectiveness. This is the ones that you hear about where there's thousands people that can volunteer. Sometimes you might even be able to get involved with those trials. I thought about it with COVID stuff. But, anyways, it was a time thing for me. Typically takes several years.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: The FDA reviews both the vaccine product and the manufacturing process, and inspects the production plant before licensing a vaccine for general use.
pearls.verbatim: FDA has to review, like, the clinical trial data and the manufacturing protocols. And then the plan has to be inspected before they can license the vaccine for general use. So it's not just like they say, vaccine works. People make it. Right? So they're involved in every step of the way to make sure that there's processes that are followed.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: VAERS relies on self-reporting to detect safety signals, not to prove causality; it is designed to see a signal, like a pattern of people getting really sick from a vaccine.
pearls.verbatim: This relies on people to self report things. So I got a shot. Now my arm hurts. I can bring that embarrassment too. I got a shot, and then my grandma died. You know? Like, stuff like that. That's how... The whole point is you get a lot of submissions to improve causality because that's not what it's set up for. It's to see a signal.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: The Vaccine Safety Datalink (VSD) uses EHR from nine healthcare organizations to study rare adverse events, specifically looking for questions or concerns that have come up from VAERS.
pearls.verbatim: It's created to study rare adverse events. So it uses EHR from nine health care organizations, specifically looking for questions or concerns that have come up from VAERS.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: CISA (Clinical Immunization Safety Assessment) is a collaboration between the CDC and seven academic medical centers that focuses on conducting studies involving targeted or specific populations sometimes left out from prelicensure clinical trials.
pearls.verbatim: the Clinical Immunization Safety Assessment, that's a collaboration between the CDC and seven academic medical centers. It complements the other systems, just focuses on conducting studies that involve targeted or specific populations that are sometimes left out from the prelicensure clinical trials.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: subpopulations often excluded from vaccine trials
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: The Johnson & Johnson COVID vaccine was paused after VAERS detected a signal of people getting clots in their brain; they investigated and decided it was okay to go forward.
pearls.verbatim: You remember whenever we... Oh gosh. What was that shot? Johnson & Johnson maybe? We started to see that people were getting clots in their brain. There was... There's something there. And then they stopped, and they they investigated it. They decided it was okay to go forward.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.applies_to: recipients of Johnson & Johnson COVID vaccine
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: Vaccine development phases: preclinical studies in animals, phase I (small group checking safety), phase II (few hundred checking effectiveness), phase III (thousands checking safety and effectiveness), then FDA review, ACIP recommendations, and phase IV ongoing monitoring.
pearls.verbatim: Starts with research, preclinical studies. Right? Because they identified it. They said, alright. Let's study it. They see that it's safe, that it works in animals, that it creates an immune response. Submit for an IND, which is the the drug license, and then they can start testing it in humans. Phase one, small amount of people checking for safety. Phase two, a larger amount of people, a few 100 to see if it's effective. And then finally, in phase three, which is hundreds to thousands of people, a few thousand maybe, check and see if it's safe and effective. And then FDA meets to see if they can approve for their biologic license. And then once that's approved, the ACIP committee gets together and says what our recommendations can be about it. And then phase four is ongoing, and it's just monitoring afterwards.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Matt Haney
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy

pearls.text: Provide the pathologist with a differential diagnosis and as much clinical information as possible on the requisition form.
pearls.verbatim: It's really, really, really helpful for the pathologist if you give them a differential diagnosis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Take photos of the biopsy site, at least on the patient's phone, and upload to the medical record if possible.
pearls.verbatim: Always take photos of the biopsy side, at least on the patient's phone, but if possible, to be uploaded to their medical record.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: If a pathology report seems inconsistent, check whether a dermatopathologist read the specimen.
pearls.verbatim: if you ever get a weird report that doesn't really fit, you can always see if the person who read your biopsy result was a dermatopathologist.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: any skin biopsy with unexpected pathology
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Keratoacanthoma is a form of squamous cell carcinoma; it is firm, rapidly growing, does not respond to antibiotics, and should be treated as SCC.
pearls.verbatim: Sometimes I get sent these after they've been in urgent care and were given antibiotics thinking it was a bite or something. So just really important, not a bite. They're normally firm to the touch and obviously don't respond to antibiotics. They rapidly grow, and they typically don't go away. And you wanna treat them as if they were a squamous cell.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: patients with firm, rapidly growing skin lesion
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Squamous cell carcinoma causes more deaths annually in the U.S. than melanoma due to its higher prevalence.
pearls.verbatim: there's more deaths from squamous cell carcinoma on the skin than from melanoma every year in America because it's so much more common than melanoma.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis (IGH) presents as small white spots on arms and legs, is not flaky or scaly (unlike tinea versicolor, which is scaly and more common on the torso).
pearls.verbatim: These are actually called idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis, and they are just really normal. They're not flaky or scaly, whereas tinea versicolor is normally flaky and scaly, and it's way more common on the torso. These are typically on arms and legs.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: patients with small white spots on arms/legs
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Insurance typically does not cover skin tag removal; do not promise patients that a dermatologist will remove them for free.
pearls.verbatim: normally, insurance really does not cover skin tag removal. So if you send someone to a dermatologist, don't promise them that the dermatologist is gonna remove their skin tags for them. It be a cosmetic charge for the patient.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Molluscum contagiosum typically resolves on its own within one to two years; encourage patients not to share towels or bathe with others.
pearls.verbatim: pretty much ninety percent of the time, I try to encourage people just to let them go away on their own. This is a type of kind of viral wart that always goes away on its own, normally between one to two years. You wanna encourage them not to share towels or bathe with others.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Recurrent shingles in the lower back/buttock region is almost always HSV, not recurrent VZV.
pearls.verbatim: pretty much any recurrent area of shingles on the lower back, buttock region is pretty much always HSV, not recurrent VZV.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.applies_to: patients with recurrent vesicular rash in lower back/buttock
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Infantile hemangiomas that are >4 cm, on midline lumbosacral area, or if there are ≥5 hemangiomas, warrant referral for possible systemic treatment or liver ultrasound.
pearls.verbatim: Midline lumbosacral, if it's more than four centimeters or if they have greater than equal to five hemangiomas. If so, send to someone who treats who treats these.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For superficial infantile hemangiomas not in cosmetically sensitive areas, topical timolol one drop twice a day can be used; oral propranolol is reserved for larger or complicated cases.
pearls.verbatim: if it's the superficial, the strawberry type, and it's not on a super highly cosmetically sensitive area, sometimes I'll prescribe topical timolol one drop twice a day.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Isotretinoin (Accutane) is for moderate to severe, scarring, or recalcitrant acne; requires monthly visits and monthly pregnancy tests for females; main side effects are dry lips, dry skin, nosebleeds, and joint pain.
pearls.verbatim: It is for moderate severe acne, scarring acne, or recalcitrant acne. It requires monthly visits and monthly pregnancy tests for females. And the main side effects are dry lips, dry skin, nosebleeds, and some joint pain.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: Triggers for perioral dermatitis include removing wipes, whitening toothpaste, oils on the skin, inhaled steroids, other steroids, and hormonal factors.
pearls.verbatim: Triggers for perioral dermatitis can be things like removing wipes, whitening toothpaste, oils on the skin, inhaled steroids, other steroids, hormonal factors.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies

pearls.text: For rosacea, topicals include metronidazole, ivermectin, and azelaic acid; oral antibiotics and sometimes isotretinoin are options; lasers are especially good for the broken blood vessel type.
pearls.verbatim: Options for this would be things topicals like metronidazole, ivermectin, azelaic acid. And then these latter two can kinda temporarily help with the redness, like, in this type of rosacea, but they're really hard to get covered with insurance, and they're kinda so so. Oral antibiotics, sometimes isotretinoin, lasers, especially for this time, the broken blood vessel type, and then sun protection and avoiding triggers.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Hannah Howard

pearls.verbatim: And sometimes you can see that fluid moving back and forth, which is called a dynamic air bronchogram, which is essentially pathognomonic for pneumonia on ultrasound.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: To be considered pathologic, you need three or more B-lines in a single zone; one or two B-lines, especially in the bases, are not uncommon and not pathological.
pearls.verbatim: To be considered pathologic, you need three or more B-lines in a single zone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: If you see the spine (vertebrae) continuing beyond the diaphragm, that indicates something is in the pleural space, such as fluid or consolidation; normally the spine should stop at the diaphragm.
pearls.verbatim: Normally, the vertebrae, we should stop seeing it at the diaphragm. As the vertebrae is behind all the lung tissue, which is supposed to be full of air, we shouldn't see anything behind the parietal pleural line except for aline artifact. Right? If we are seeing vertebrae back here, we know there's something going on in this space.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Ultrasound is better than chest X-ray for assessing complications of a pleural effusion.
pearls.verbatim: Ultrasound is better than chest X-ray for assessing complications of an effusion.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: The curtain sign, seeing the lung slide down over the diaphragm during inspiration, is a good indication that the lung is full of air.
pearls.verbatim: That's called the curtain sign. That's a good indication that the lung is in fact full of air.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: If the spine stops at the diaphragm when an echogenic area is seen above it, suspect a mirror artifact of the liver or spleen rather than consolidation.
pearls.verbatim: Spine stops at the diaphragm.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Mirror artifact can mimic consolidation; if the spine stops at the diaphragm, it's likely mirror artifact, not lung pathology.
pearls.verbatim: This is mirror artifact. What you're seeing is a mirror image of the liver on the cephalad side of the diaphragm. Right? If it was actual lung tissue, the spine would go beyond the diaphragm.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Scan the entire area of concern in two orthogonal planes to fully characterize the collection and avoid missing deeper extension.
pearls.verbatim: You generally wanna do it in two directions.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: Cobblestoning (anechoic lines splitting fat globules) indicates fluid in subcutaneous tissue; it is seen in both cellulitis and edema, so clinical context is essential to differentiate.
pearls.verbatim: This is another one of those times... Like every time with ultrasound, you have to have a clinical picture. So don't just go scanning everybody with CHF and, you know, swelling in their legs. Both sides are red. See cobblestoning and say, oh, look. Cellulitis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: Doppler can help differentiate cellulitis from edema: cellulitis shows hyperemia (increased blood flow), while volume overload edema does not.
pearls.verbatim: cellulitis is inflammatory, so you would expect more or less blood flow. More. More. Right? Whereas in just volume overload causing lower extremity edema, not necessarily gonna have hyperemic tissue.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected cellulitis vs edema
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: If an abscess has septations (hyperechoic lines inside), it likely requires open drainage with hemostats rather than simple needle aspiration.
pearls.verbatim: Do you see septations? So hyperechoate lines sort of going through the abscess. If you do, you probably don't wanna just stick a needle in it. You probably have to open that one up and drain it, and you're gonna have to use the hemostats to open things up.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: A hyperechoic foreign body like glass will produce acoustic shadowing underneath it, similar to bone, because it reflects sound waves away from deeper tissues.
pearls.verbatim: if it's reflecting all the sound waves away and back to the probe, then it's gonna produce shadowing underneath it just like bone does.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: any patient with suspected foreign body on POCUS
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: Fasting before gallbladder ultrasound reduces the likelihood of seeing the gallbladder; advise patients to fast beforehand.
pearls.verbatim: If you eat pie beforehand, it will reduce the likelihood that you will actually see a gallbladder
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: Having the patient take a deep breath and hold it, or Valsalva, can help push the gallbladder out for better visualization.
pearls.verbatim: You can also play with their breathing. So having them take in a deep breath and hold it can be helpful. Having them Valsalva to, again, like, push out the gallbladder can also be helpful.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: The X7 technique: start subxiphoid and go directly laterally about 7 centimeters to find the gallbladder; you may need to work around the ribs.
pearls.verbatim: X7 means start subxiphoid and go directly laterally about seven centimeters, and then you're likely to see the gallbladder there. The issue here is you're looking through the rib cage, so you're gonna have to work around the ribs.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: The right lateral intercostal approach looks through the liver to the gallbladder, which appears deep on the screen.
pearls.verbatim: is actually coming right lateral and looking through the liver all the way to the gallbladder. So the gallbladder is gonna be deep on your screen.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: Use big movements to window shop; once you have a clear window, make fine adjustments and fan through the entire gallbladder.
pearls.verbatim: big movements to window shop, once you actually find the gallbladder, have a clear window to it, then you can make your adjustments to make sure your access is right, fan through the whole thing
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: In long axis view of the gallbladder, the portal vein appears as a dot, forming an 'exclamation point' landmark.
pearls.verbatim: when you have the gallbladder in a long axis view, you get this classic exclamation point where the gallbladder is the tall part and your portal vein is the dot.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: Gallstones are gravity-dependent, mobile, hyperechoic, and produce posterior shadowing; polyps are non-mobile and usually lack shadowing unless calcified.
pearls.verbatim: They're gravity dependent. They're mobile. So if you move the patient around, they may shift around in the gallbladder. This can be helpful to distinguish from polyps. They they don't move. They're stuck in one spot. K? Other part of it is they're hyperechoic, and there's usually gonna be posterior shadowing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: Sonographic Murphy's sign: press the probe over the gallbladder fundus; pain only at that spot (not elsewhere) is positive.
pearls.verbatim: you wanna get your probe over the fundus over here. Push. Other gallbladder, and you wanna push. If it hurts right there and not really anywhere else, that's a positive sonographic Murphy's sign.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: Pericholecystic fluid appears as an anechoic wedge or loculated collection around the gallbladder wall.
pearls.verbatim: look in both planes. This is a pretty brief view, but you see the, again, hyperechoic gallbladder wall, and then you can see anechoic fluid right above it right here. It's gonna be a wedge, generally. Sometimes it can be sort of loculated, but a wedge around the wall.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: Common bile duct diameter is measured inner-to-inner wall; normal is 2-6 mm, increasing by 1 mm per decade after age 40.
pearls.verbatim: You're gonna measure inner to inner wall on the common bile duct. So that's here. Two to six millimeters is normal, but as you get older, it's normal to be more dilated. So each decade adds a millimeter.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI

pearls.text: Use a linear probe with a musculoskeletal preset on the Butterfly; adjust depth and gain to adequately visualize the target structures.
pearls.verbatim: Linear probe or musculoskeletal preset on the Butterfly. Adjust your depth and gain so you can adequately see whatever it is you're trying to look at.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: The suprapatellar recess is the preferred site for dynamic ultrasound-guided knee injection or arthrocentesis; it lies between the prefemoral and suprapatellar fat pads, deep to the quadriceps tendon.
pearls.verbatim: between the fat pads and underneath the tendon is the actual recess that you're looking for where fluid will collect. So if you are doing a suprapatellar joint injection under... Whether you're doing it under ultrasound guidance or not, this is the space you're shooting for.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing knee injection or arthrocentesis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: When scanning the patellar tendon, set the depth to about 1 cm unless there is a large bursitis; the tendon appears as a linear hyperechoic structure crossing the patella.
pearls.verbatim: So notice my depth is one centimeter. K? So unless they've got a big bursitis on their patella, one centimeter depth is probably gonna be good for you. And you're just looking for that tendon going across the top here
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: Position the patient sitting against a wall with the leg straight out and a pillow propping the knee; ensure the operator is seated comfortably to avoid leaning over.
pearls.verbatim: what I would recommend for whoever's having their knee scans, I would have you sit, like, against the wall with your leg straight out with a pillow propping your knee.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: For static guidance of an anterior knee injection, find the infrapatellar view of the patellar tendon, then slide the probe medially or laterally until the tendon disappears, that is a safe needle entry site.
pearls.verbatim: While you're looking at your screen, come off to the side a little bit. And when you lose the tendon, that's a safe place for you to stick your needle.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: anterior knee injection in patients with difficult anatomy (e.g., obesity)
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: The medial and lateral menisci appear as triangular hyperechoic structures between the femur and tibia on ultrasound; identify them by finding the femur and tibia and looking for the triangular structure in between.
pearls.verbatim: Find the femur, find the tibia, and then find that triangular structure going in between. Try to identify the medial and the lateral meniscus.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: The MCL is visualized in the same view as the meniscus, attaching femur to tibia; the LCL requires a more lateral and inferior view as it attaches femur to fibula.
pearls.verbatim: MCL is gonna be in the same view as the meniscus. Right? MCL attaches femur to tibia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: Sterility for joint injection requires only a sterile site, sterile needle, and sterile medication; full draping and sterile gloves are not mandatory.
pearls.verbatim: as long as the site is sterile and the needle and the syringe and the medication is sterile and it stays that way throughout the entire procedure, you have a sterile joint injection.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: A typical knee injection mixture is 40 mg Kenalog (1 mL) plus 4-5 mL of 1% lidocaine without epinephrine.
pearls.verbatim: Generally, what I do is forty milligrams of Kenalog, which is one mil, and then four to five mils of one percent lidocaine, no epi.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: Use surface tension to fill a syringe by inverting the vial and keeping the needle tip visible in the fluid to avoid drawing air.
pearls.verbatim: just flip this upside down and stick your needle in. Alright. And then you can start withdrawing, and I can see my needle tip the entire time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: Use a filter needle when drawing from glass vials to avoid glass shards.
pearls.verbatim: The purple part of my syringe is a filter, which you're gonna wanna use whenever you're using a glass vial.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: When using iodine for skin prep, start in the middle and go out, do not touch the same place twice with the same swab, and repeat three times, waiting for it to dry.
pearls.verbatim: with iodine, you start in the middle and you go out. Right? Throw that away, and you do that three times. Wait for it to dry.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: sterile skin preparation for joint injection
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: For billing ultrasound guidance, save an image of the needle at its endpoint in the joint space.
pearls.verbatim: I generally save an image of the needle at its endpoint, so where it's supposed to be.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: Ethyl chloride spray is not sterile but studies show it does not affect infection rates; it improves patient comfort.
pearls.verbatim: This is not sterile. And, yes, you are spraying the spot that's supposed to be sterile. The studies show it doesn't make a difference.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: If you cannot upload images via the Capture app, send them to the cloud and the presenter can add them to the chart.
pearls.verbatim: But if you're doing this with me, it probably still... I'll still have you send it to the cloud because I can put it into the chart. If you really wanna know how I put it in Cerner, I can show you sometime.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: Use a filtered 18-gauge needle (purple) to draw up medication to avoid glass particles or crystals; the red 18-gauge is unfiltered.
pearls.verbatim: That's a 18 gauge filtered one pill needle. And then they have... Where is it? Here it is. Here's another 18 gauge. This one's without the filter. So the purple is filtered. The red one is without a filter.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: For ultrasound-guided knee injection, there is no need to maintain suction because the needle tip is visible; for non-dynamic procedures like parathyroid aspiration, keep suction the whole time.
pearls.verbatim: No. There's no need to because I can see my needle tip. Right? So for a parathyroid, not dynamic. You can't see your needle tip. Yeah. You keep suction the whole time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: ultrasound-guided knee injection vs. parathyroid aspiration
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: When using ultrasound guidance, if the needle tip is out of view, move the probe, not the needle.
pearls.verbatim: If your needle is out of view, you don't move your needle around like this. You move your probe.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: In lung ultrasound, lung sliding (sparkling movement of the pleural line) is normal and must be confirmed; absence suggests pneumothorax or other pathology.
pearls.verbatim: So one thing you're gonna be looking at is for lung sliding. You've got rib here, rib here. This is all soft tissue probes, of course, up here. This bright hyperechoic line is the parietal pleura line.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: The curtain sign (absence of spine above the diaphragm) is normal; if you see spine extending above the diaphragm, it indicates loss of aeration (consolidation or effusion) allowing sound waves to pass.
pearls.verbatim: Also, what you're looking for is this diaphragm, the hyperechoic line going up this way. And notice what you don't see is the spine extending towards the head past the diaphragm. That's because there's air in the lung. So there's... It's... The the sound waves just get scattered
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Dynamic air bronchograms (hyperechoic dots moving with respiration) are super highly specific for pneumonia.
pearls.verbatim: One of the findings you're looking for is called dynamic air bronchograms. So if you see right here, you've got a hyperechoic dot coming down and going back up.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Focal B-lines (three or more in a single zone) are 96% specific for pneumonia.
pearls.verbatim: These are consolidated b lines. There's a lot of b lines here. And, again, 96% specific. Specifically, if there's three or more in a single zone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Lung consolidation (hepatization) appears as tissue-like echotexture where normally only artifact is seen; this is highly specific for pneumonia.
pearls.verbatim: Lung consolidation or hepatization. So this is actually lung tissue. Normal lung ultrasound, you don't actually see lung tissue. It just is artifact. K? So if you actually see organ that looks like lung or liver, something's wrong.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: The shred sign (irregular hyperechoic interface between consolidated and aerated lung) is very highly specific for pneumonia.
pearls.verbatim: This is shred sign. So shred sign is the interaction between the consolidated lung and the aerated lung. It produces this shredded appearance. It's hyperechoic.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Thicker pleural lining can be indicative of infection (pneumonia), whereas a thin/crisp pleural line favors pulmonary edema.
pearls.verbatim: Something else I didn't talk about but want you to notice is look how thick the pleural line is here. See it over here at the beginning. Now look at that. Much thicker. So thicker pleural lining can also be indicative of infection
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected pneumonia vs. pulmonary edema
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Symmetrical bilateral B-lines are more likely pulmonary edema; asymmetrical focal B-lines suggest pneumonia. In multifocal pneumonia, look for tiny subpleural consolidations beneath the pleural line.
pearls.verbatim: If you only see B lines and you see it both sides and it's pathologic on both sides, that's highly suspicious for pulmonary edema. But you could have a multifocal pneumonia as well that would present similarly.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.applies_to: patients with B-lines to differentiate cause
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Measure the isthmus in the transverse plane; it should be less than half a centimeter top to bottom.
pearls.verbatim: You're in the transverse plane top to bottom. It should be less than half a centimeter.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: In thyroiditis, the thyroid appears heterogeneous with black and white specks throughout due to lymphocytic infiltration.
pearls.verbatim: you get a heterogeneous look because the lymphocyte infiltration. You get the black and white specs throughout the entire.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: Be consistent in how you measure nodules (e.g., AP and perpendicular planes or greatest dimensions) to ensure reproducible follow-up.
pearls.verbatim: the most reproducible so that if you're following these up in six months or a year, you know exactly where to measure. So you wanna be consistent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: Simple cysts and colloid cysts are usually benign and not a big deal.
pearls.verbatim: simple cyst, like you were saying, Adam, that's no big deal. Okay. So even though circle, that's fine. These colloid cysts as well, they have this... I forget what they call them, hyperechoic sign side of them. I think it's just because of how the sound waves bounce off the colloid, but these are usually not a big deal.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: Microcalcifications (<1 mm) are associated with psammoma bodies and papillary carcinoma, which is concerning for malignancy.
pearls.verbatim: microcalcifications are associated with psammoma body... Bodies and papillary carcinoma, which is bad.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: For TIRADS 3 (mildly suspicious) nodules, biopsy if >2.5 cm; for TIRADS 4 (moderately suspicious), biopsy if >1.5 cm; for TIRADS 5 (highly suspicious), biopsy if >1 cm.
pearls.verbatim: you got a TI RADS three greater than two and a half centimeters, you're gonna biopsy it. But if it's less than one and a half, you're just gonna watch it. Moderately suspicious, if it's less than a centimeter, you're just gonna biopsy it. Highly suspicious, it's less than half a centimeter, you're just gonna watch it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: When interpreting an EKG, scan up and down the tracing to compare QRS width in different leads; a wide QRS may be more apparent in some leads than others.
pearls.verbatim: So you have to scan up and down. That's the hardest thing. Right? So you can see now that it's actually wide. Do you agree?
