pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on COPD and Asthma

pearls.text: Alzheimer's disease follows a predictable temporal decline: about 14 years from diagnosis, with FAST stages progressing yearly through stages 1-5, then monthly through stage 6.
pearls.verbatim: So when you get diagnosed with one of the topopathies, especially with Alzheimer's disease, you can kinda set your watch and say, okay. I'm on a fast stage one now, but in in a year, I'm gonna be a fast stage two. And in in a year, I'm gonna be a fast stage three. And then another year, gonna be a four and a five. Then I'm gonna go into the six. And in monthly increments, I'm gonna step through the sixes. Now, it's fourteen years, and I'm on hospice. I'm ready to go home.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Lewy body dementia has a shorter course: diagnosis typically occurs about one year into symptoms, with about six to seven more years of survival.
pearls.verbatim: But with with most people, they'll be diagnosed about about a year into the process, and they'll have about six or seven more years. So so this one's relatively fast, seven years.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Vascular dementia has a stepwise decline with plateaus between events; it is the only dementia where you can intervene to prevent further decline.
pearls.verbatim: vascular dementia has a very strong vent kind of a horizon where they'll step, and then they may not have step again for a couple of years until they have another event, and they have another step.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Vascular dementia is the only treatable form of dementia; management includes high-dose statins, antiplatelet therapy, and lifestyle changes to prevent further decline.
pearls.verbatim: It's the only one we can treat. We can't do anything. If we talk till we're blue in the face about these three and until we get some kind of a towel dialysis unit or something, we're not gonna be able to do anything. But with this one, we can fix the... We can't repair the dementia. We can fix the problem and keep it from getting worse.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: The MIND diet combines the DASH diet and Mediterranean diet, emphasizing vegetables, legumes, and berries, with optional small amounts of wine.
pearls.verbatim: So if the DASH diet and the Mediterranean diet went out and got a date and had too much wine, got married, and had a baby It's called the MIND's diet, isn't it? You have a MIND diet. Okay. You stayed in Chicago. DASH diet, Mediterranean diet together, and put a little glass of wine in there. And you've got the mine diet.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients seeking to prevent or slow cognitive decline
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: In delirium, thought is disorganized with inattention and distraction; it is a neural overstimulation, whereas dementia-related agitation is a direct response to a stimulus (e.g., being moved or bumped) and patients quiet down when left alone.
pearls.verbatim: Delirium is disorganized thought, periods of inattention or distraction. They're unable to focus. Generally, with delirium, it's a flight of ideas. It's a lot of stuff going on. It's that they're being distracted from what's going on.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: any patient with altered mental status
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: In Alzheimer's dementia, short-term recall is impaired while long-term recall is relatively preserved; patients cannot lay down new memories but can access old ones, sometimes even singing along to old hymns when otherwise non-communicative.
pearls.verbatim: Short term recall. Long term recall is usually better than short term in Alzheimer's. Transition from short term to long term gets lost, So they don't lay down new memories. They have old memories. They can access those.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Lewy body dementia has a prognosis roughly half that of Alzheimer's; when you correct the diagnosis, you should advise families to expedite hospice, life insurance, and legal paperwork.
pearls.verbatim: He cut the prognosis in half. Right? So those are the people that you say, look. We, you know, we need to get you to hospice. We need to make sure the life insurance stuff's in order. You need to get the paperwork off. Dig it out of the safe and get him to sign what he needs to sign and get things organized and in place because this is not a slow process as they were telling you about.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients newly diagnosed with Lewy body dementia
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Frontotemporal dementia presents with executive dysfunction, emotional flatness, and language difficulty; it has a 10-12 year prognosis and progresses erratically through FAST stages.
pearls.verbatim: Frontotemporal... The big thing, you know, frontal lobe, what does it do? It's executive function. Right? So as you get more of the intracellular damage in the front, you're having problems controlling your behaviors, emotional flatness, planning and organizing parties and things.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Any dementia patient with hallucinations, especially visual hallucinations, should be presumed to have Lewy body dementia until proven otherwise; auditory hallucinations are also mostly Lewy body.
pearls.verbatim: Anybody with dementia that has hallucinations that's not been caused by giving them a medication that caused them to have, that this is really a big part of it. You need to go to Lewy body dementia first and and prove that it's not Lewy body.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with dementia and new hallucinations
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Mixed dementia is common; a patient can have Alzheimer's plus vascular dementia, or Lewy body plus vascular dementia.
pearls.verbatim: You can have Alzheimer's dementia and vascular dementia. It's very common. You can have Lewy body and vascular dementia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: The MIND diet has the best evidence for dementia prevention, supported by randomized controlled trials; it combines elements of the DASH and Mediterranean diets.
pearls.verbatim: how they look at the different diets and why I say the MIND diet is probably gonna be the best lifestyle intervention. And and it's evidence based. Both the DASH and the Mediterranean diets have good evidence base.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Physical activity and an active lifestyle help prevent cognitive deterioration; fight against the idea that being old and retired means it's okay to live on the couch.
pearls.verbatim: So really kinda combating and coming against the effect of, oh, I'm, you know, I'm retired, and now I'm gonna live on the couch kind of the thing. I'm old, and it's okay for me not to exercise. Those are things you wanna fight against in your patient group.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Anticholinergic drugs, especially bladder medications, directly cause dementia with an additive effect: a little bit does a little bit, more does more, and the longer you take it, the worse it is.
pearls.verbatim: No. It's a... It's an additive effect. It's a poison. Little bit does a little bit. More does more. The longer you take it, the worse it is.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: In nursing homes, you will commonly find patients on both anticholinergic drugs (like oxybutynin) and cholinergic dementia drugs simultaneously, which is inexcusable and universal.
pearls.verbatim: If you go down to University Village or any nursing home in town, you will find people that are on both of those drugs at the same time regularly. It is inexcusable, and it is universal.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: The Cochrane review of cholinesterase inhibitors showed a statistically significant but clinically trivial 2.7-point difference on a 70-point scale; you could not tell the difference between a 67 and a 70 in conversation.
pearls.verbatim: Oh. Scale. On a 70 scale? So it's So what's the difference of 2.7 points on a 70 scale?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with dementia on cholinesterase inhibitors
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: When discussing deprescribing cholinesterase inhibitors with families, present the data (one in 42 chance of benefit, one in 12 chance of harm) and let them decide, respecting their relationship with their primary doctor.
pearls.verbatim: I think they're in the hospital and your care and your discharge. You know, I I think that you have to talk to the family and explain the situation to them and find out how they want that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: hospitalized patients with dementia and their families
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: For bladder issues, there are non-pharmacologic alternatives with fewer side effects, including Kegel exercises, pelvic physical therapy, Botox injections, slings, and bladder training; most patients are not evaluated for these and are just put on a medicine that causes dementia.
pearls.verbatim: You can have localized silicone injections that are there. You can have slings done. You can have bladder training, physical therapy. You can have all kinds of things done. And most of the time, people aren't evaluated for any of those things. They're just put on a medicine that's gonna cause dementia.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Kegel exercises, especially with a good pelvic physical therapist, can make a life-changing difference for many patients with bladder issues, though it requires more effort than taking a pill.
pearls.verbatim: But kegel exercises, especially with a good pelvic physical therapist, can can make a life changing difference for a lot of people if they work at it. It's just you... It's it's harder. It's not, oh, here's your prescription. Here's your pill. Go ahead and take this.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia

pearls.text: Uric acid treatment goal is less than 6 mg/dL; above 6 crystals form, below 6 crystals dissolve.
pearls.verbatim: above six, crystals form. Below six, crystals dissolve.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: The fundamental defect in gout is underexcretion of uric acid (90% of cases), not overproduction; treatment must enhance excretion.
pearls.verbatim: most commonly due to underexcretion. So ninety percent of the cases.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: Gold standard for diagnosis is joint aspiration with crystal identification under polarized light microscopy to distinguish gout from pseudogout.
pearls.verbatim: The gold standard for diagnosis is getting fluid from that joint and getting... Be able to look at it under the microscope or have your lab look at it under the microscope and just find the crystal so you can distinguish between gout and pseudogout.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: Point-of-care ultrasound can show the 'double contour sign' (crystal deposition on cartilage) and 'snowstorm' crystals in joint fluid to aid diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: Snowstorm crystals in that fluid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: First MTP joint is most commonly affected due to its distance from the heart (cooler temperature) promoting crystallization; in peripheral vascular disease, gout can affect knees, ankles, or hands.
pearls.verbatim: It's the the distance from the heart. So it's a cooler area.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: Acute gout flare treatment should be started within 24 hours for best outcomes.
pearls.verbatim: Started within twenty four hours of the acute onset and your best outcome.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: NSAIDs are now a secondary choice for acute gout due to risks of GI ulceration, kidney dysfunction, heart failure, and cardiovascular disease.
pearls.verbatim: what we don't think about is the effect on kidney function, heart failure, and cardiovascular disease with nonsteroidals.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: IL-1 inhibition (e.g., anakinra) is a next-line therapy for refractory gout, blocking the inflammasome pathway that drives inflammation.
pearls.verbatim: Implantisome pathway drives the gout. So if you block it, you stop the inflammation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25

pearls.text: The patellar apprehension test reproduces lateral displacement and patient tightening; the grind test causes a grinding sensation in the posterior quadrant.
pearls.verbatim: Posterior quadrant causes the grinding sensation. So that's a grind test. Okay. The apprehension test is when you reproduce that lateral displacement just a little bit, and they tighten up and say, oh, I'm not gonna let you do that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Knee Pain and Problems

pearls.text: Most patients who present with a 'dislocated knee' actually have a patellar dislocation; the tibiofemoral joint is rarely dislocated.
pearls.verbatim: I've seen probably a hundred people for dislocated knees. Do you know how many people actually had a dislocated knee? That would be where the tibia and fibula were in out out of position. Right? That's what they think happened. And so far, none of them have been right. So far, they've all had color dislocation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients presenting with knee dislocation history
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Knee Pain and Problems

pearls.text: For patellofemoral pain syndrome, management includes activity modification, topical treatments, and physical therapy focusing on strengthening the quadriceps and VMO to improve patellar tracking.
pearls.verbatim: Obligation of activities. Stop doing what hurts you. Topical stuff, we already talked about. Physical therapy, physiotherapy, those kinds of things.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Knee Pain and Problems

pearls.text: Osgood-Schlatter disease is an apophysitis of the tibial tubercle common in adolescents, especially those in jumping or kicking sports; it typically resolves by the twenties.
pearls.verbatim: Worse with running and jumping, kneeling, and kicking. Tubercle is tender with resisted knee extension.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Knee Pain and Problems

pearls.text: For occipital block, inject 0.5 mL at each of four spots (greater and lesser occipital nerves, bilaterally if needed), redirecting the needle as needed.
pearls.verbatim: You said point five cc. I usually put point five cc in each of the the areas where I'm blocking. So you go four spots.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: Indications for nerve blocks include neuropathic pain that is electric, tingling, or shocking in the distribution of the nerve, not well explained by other causes.
pearls.verbatim: So based on where the pain is and also the quality of the pain, that kind of neuropathic, electrical, tingling, shocking, irritating.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected nerve entrapment or neuralgia
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: For dorsal scapular block, needle depth should be only about 1 cm; if you aspirate air, you are too deep and risk pneumothorax.
pearls.verbatim: And only about a centimeter deep is as far as you go. If you aspirate and you get blood, what do you do?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients receiving dorsal scapular nerve block
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: For suprascapular block, insert the needle at a 45-degree angle upward and medially from the midpoint of the scapular spine until you contact bone, then aspirate and inject.
pearls.verbatim: we're going end to end halfway point. You've got your finger there, and now you're going 45 degree angle up. And you hit that, and it'll droop down into that area.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: Perform a single nerve block at the dermatome where allodynia is present, rather than routinely blocking above and below the lesion.
pearls.verbatim: So Well, there's there's been some discussion of doing it, you know, kind of blanketing the areas. Yep. One and one above and one below. I don't know that I've ever bought into that. I don't know whether that's just somebody that to run the bill up a little bit.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with shingles or similar lesions needing nerve block
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: A second block is legitimate if after the first block the patient still reports significant pain above or below the lesion; document the pain to justify the second injection.
pearls.verbatim: If you block that lesion and they still say, oh, no. I've got some significant pain up here above it or below it, and then you go ahead and do a second block. I think that's very legitimate. We have to document that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with persistent pain adjacent to a blocked dermatome
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: Lidocaine provides about six hours of anesthesia; adding Marcaine (bupivacaine) prolongs the effect.
pearls.verbatim: the lidocaine will last for... For about six hours, something like that. If you wanna include Marcaine in it, if you want it to last longer, you can do that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients receiving nerve blocks for acute pain
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: The steroid component of the nerve block lasts longer than the local anesthetic, providing prolonged anti-inflammatory benefit.
pearls.verbatim: the steroid component should last
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients receiving a nerve block with corticosteroid
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: During a suprascapular nerve block, a small tendon crosses the area but is not functionally important, so it is safe to perform the block there.
pearls.verbatim: there's a little tendon that goes right across there, but it doesn't serve any purpose. So that's okay.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: For inpatient nerve blocks, verify if the hospital requires specific credentialing; if not required, you may perform the block under your general privileges.
pearls.verbatim: Yes. So it's kind of a a blind area right now. So if there is credentialing for that in the hospital credentials package, then you would need to have that. If it's a procedure that is not elevated to the level where that hospital has demanded that you credential for it, then you can do it under your general
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks

pearls.text: Arterial and venous disease are not mutually exclusive; assess how much of each is present and treat both.
pearls.verbatim: So we're saying when you're looking at something, you're not saying is this arterial or venous. We're saying how much arterial and how much venous, and what's the predominant symptomatology
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Arterial ulcers have sharp, punched-out borders and a clean pink base; venous ulcers have raised edges, shallow base, hemosiderin staining, and are wet.
pearls.verbatim: sharp border. Right? And it's like a cookie cutter lesion if you look at it. It's like there's a hole there that just got cut in, and it's sharp right down into it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Buerger's test: pallor on elevation and rubor on dependency indicate severe ischemia.
pearls.verbatim: Pallor on elevation, rubor on dependency
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: If the ABI is too high (noncompressible), move on to toe pressures.
pearls.verbatim: Remember, if it's too high, you can have noncompressed, and you gotta move on to the the toes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected PAD where ABI is elevated
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Duplex ultrasound is the anatomic test to localize the lesion; everyone should get it along with the physical exam.
pearls.verbatim: duplex ultrasound, whatever you wanna call it, is the anatomic test for the patients to see what's going on and to localize the lesion. So so that's... You start out, and everybody should get that to go along with your physical exam.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Avoid CTA unless necessary because it hurts kidneys and vascular will redo it when they are ready to operate.
pearls.verbatim: CTA is a rapid road map, but it's got contrast and calcification limitations. So you're gonna hurt kidneys. You're not gonna be able to see everything you need to see with the the CTA.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Arterial claudication is not relieved by bending forward; neurogenic claudication is relieved by bending (shopping cart test) because it reduces spinal stenosis.
pearls.verbatim: If you're bent over and you're walking, it really doesn't matter if you've got peripheral vascular disease. You're still exerting energy. You're still requiring oxygen in those muscles, and it's not getting there.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with leg pain on walking
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Neurogenic claudication lacks the pallor, rubor, and hair loss seen in arterial disease.
pearls.verbatim: neurogenic claudication won't have any of the pallor and rubor and all the other kind of things going on, won't have... Generally have any of the hair loss or anything.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Older patients often have neurogenic claudication, arterial claudication, arthritic changes, and neuropathic changes simultaneously; determine which is predominant and causing the acute problem.
pearls.verbatim: older people will have neurogenic claudication, arterial claudication, arthritic changes, neuropathic changes in their leg because they're diabetic and some degree of venous. So it's not which of these four is going on. It's which is predominant and which is causing the acute problem at this time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Venous claudication presents with bursting pain after walking and slow relief with elevation, due to obstruction and reflux.
pearls.verbatim: The venous claudication, the type of bursting pain with walking after, and then the obstruction, slow relief with elevation are things to remember with venous claudication
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Revascularization is not as successful in patients who continue to smoke; be brutally honest with patients about the need to quit.
pearls.verbatim: And some of them have the idea, well, I can keep smoking, and you can just operate and fix it. But revascularization isn't successful in somebody that's ongoing smoker. It just doesn't come out nearly as well.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with PAD who smoke and are candidates for revascularization
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: For secondary prevention in high-risk patients who have had revascularization, the evidence supports driving LDL below 50 mg/dL; the new guidelines are moving toward that target.
pearls.verbatim: somebody that's got revascularization happening that's LDL is below 50, the outcome is better because that's the high risk population. So the higher the risk population going into the intervention, the lower the number needed to treat for the result from that intervention.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BID plus aspirin is FDA-approved and evidence-based for secondary prevention in PAD; insurance covers it.
pearls.verbatim: low dose Xarelto, BID, and aspirin reduces the data for for these kind of things because this is important.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with PAD for secondary prevention
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Cilostazol improves microvascular circulation, helping translate higher perfusion pressure into better tissue perfusion in the small arterial beds.
pearls.verbatim: the microvascular circulation making things slide better through the real small arterial beds. So, you know, we're talking about proximal disease and distal disease, and it doesn't exist in a vacuum and making sure once we get higher perfusion pressure, we actually translate it into better tissue perfusion, and that's what the Plido brings into the equation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with PAD and microvascular disease
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Post-revascularization antiplatelet therapy duration depends on the procedure and patient risk; talk with vascular about how long they need to do antiplatelet.
pearls.verbatim: duration depends on the procedure and patient risk. So you've gotta talk with vascular about how long they need to do antiplatelet.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: After revascularization, schedule follow-up every 3 months with exercise log, blood pressure log, and glucose log; patients often lose motivation after the first month and fall off after discharge from vascular.
pearls.verbatim: making sure they don't start smoking again, making sure they're keeping their sugars down, making sure they're losing weight, that they're continuing to exercise even after you've done the revascularization is important because these are the people that are all excited for the first month, and then they get less excited the second and the third month. They're discharged from vascular, and they just fall off the the map. If you don't say no, we need to see each other every three months. You need to bring in your exercise log and your blood pressure log and sugar log, and we need to know that you're doing this stuff.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Venous ulcers are shallow with rolled edges, fibrin deposits, and hemosiderin deposits around them; arterial ulcers are gangrenous, black, and hard.
pearls.verbatim: the edge is rolled, and it's more shallow. And it's got all the deposits in it. Again, a rolled edge, a shallow ulcer with fibrin deposits in it, rolled edge, and and the deposits in it's wet and red. Remember the one that we had that was arterial? It was gangrenous black, and hard.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Venous claudication is bursting pain in the foot and ankle, while arterial claudication is crampy pain from mid-calf upward.
pearls.verbatim: the claudication, bursting type pain with walking and distinguishing that claudication, which is pale leg, and it's kinda crampy pain. They'll describe it completely different. And the the claudication of ischemia is generally, depending on the lesion, kinda upper legs, at least the upper part from the mid calf up, and the the venous changes are always foot and ankle dependent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with leg pain on walking
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: For proximal DVT, get the cardiologist to suction the clot out early to preserve venous function and prevent post-thrombotic syndrome.
pearls.verbatim: By doing that early on, you can preserve venous function. So when somebody's got a bad DVT in their proximal leg, you wanna get the cardiologist to suction the clot out of there so they don't get this kind of stuff later on.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: Compression is a cornerstone to control venous disease, but arterial perfusion has to be adequate to allow compression; use small compression on arterial patients, not moderate or severe.
pearls.verbatim: The compression is a cornerstone to control this, and arterial perfusion has to be adequate to allow compression. You can use small compression on arterial patients, but you don't want moderate or severe compression on an arterial patient.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with venous disease and possible arterial disease
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26

pearls.text: When concerned about appendicitis or gallbladder disease, ask the patient if they still have that organ; medical records may be outdated.
pearls.verbatim: You're concerned about appendicitis. Ask them. You still have your appendix in there. It may not be in there.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Enis Sakirgil
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected appendicitis or cholecystitis

pearls.text: Pain that is constant and less than 48 hours in duration is more likely to be a surgical condition; intermittent pain is less serious.
