pearls.text: For patients with ear ringing (tinnitus), OTC products found in the discount section of Walmart may be worth trying.
pearls.verbatim: I've had a lot of recently who've had ear ringing, and I'm like, you know, if you're walking around Walmart and you have a problem with ear ringing, you might go and try this.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Santillano
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips

pearls.text: Use F41.9 (anxiety unspecified) instead of GAD if diagnostic criteria are not fully met, because once GAD is in the record it is hard to remove from the patient’s mind.
pearls.verbatim: If you are not sure, I would rather you put F41.9 than put GAD. Because GAD is a very specific diagnosis. And once it's there, it's hard to take out of someone's mind.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Panic disorder is defined not just by panic attacks but by a preoccupation and fear of future attacks that leads to avoidance or changes in life choices.
pearls.verbatim: panic disorder, also have a preoccupation or fear of having them to the point that then I start changing my life choices.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: A precise DSM/ICD diagnosis is not critical in the first visit because treatments for most anxiety disorders overlap; focus on broad symptom categories.
pearls.verbatim: It is not really important that you get an absolute diagnosis as far as DSM or ICD if the symptoms fit certain profiles. Why is that? Because the treatments are very much the same.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: For patients with diffuse, broadly described anxiety, consider exploring childhood adverse experiences (ACEs), as this may indicate a more resistant underlying cause.
pearls.verbatim: The broader they describe it, the more diffuse they describe it, then you probably wanna start getting some information about, like, their childhood exposure.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Clonidine is not first-line for panic; propranolol is safer and addresses physical symptoms without blocking trauma processing.
pearls.verbatim: First of all, clonidine is not first line for panic, by the way.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Benzodiazepines (e.g., Xanax) and clonidine can interfere with trauma processing in the brain, requiring therapy to be redone; propranolol controls physiological symptoms without blocking processing.
pearls.verbatim: Those, for example, who have been prescribed Xanax, all that work that they do in therapy while taking Xanax has to be redone. And same in some ways with clonidine.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with PTSD or trauma history
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Benzodiazepines like Xanax and clonidine interfere with trauma processing in therapy; work done while on them must be redone.
pearls.verbatim: all that work that they do in therapy while taking Xanax has to be redone.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with PTSD or trauma undergoing therapy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Propranolol controls the physiological response to anxiety but does not block cognitive processing of trauma, unlike benzodiazepines and clonidine.
pearls.verbatim: propranolol just controls the response physiologically.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: SSRIs are frontline for panic disorder because they lower baseline arousal, reducing the likelihood of crossing the panic threshold.
pearls.verbatim: for panic, one of the frontline medications is still the SSRI because you're trying to pull that baseline down
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: When a patient has a strong narrative (e.g., attributing symptoms to low testosterone), clinicians can choose to join that story to build trust and maximize treatment engagement.
pearls.verbatim: Are we gonna lean into his story and join him, or are we gonna keep trying to do what seems to just meet the diagnostic criteria?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with anxiety who avoid standard treatments
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Irritability is a symptom of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).
pearls.verbatim: irritability is a symptom of GAD.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Coach patients to lean into panic like riding a tidal wave or not fighting quicksand; paradoxically, this can reduce intensity.
pearls.verbatim: leaning into panic is like riding out a tidal wave. You're actually better off to float, or it's like not fighting quicksand.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Encourage patients to lean into panic rather than fight it; use the metaphor of floating in quicksand or riding out a tidal wave.
pearls.verbatim: leaning into panic is like riding out a tidal wave. You're actually better off to float, or it's like not fighting quicksand.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Do not use relaxation techniques solely to make panic stop, as that creates a monitoring loop ('Is it stopping?') that worsens anxiety.
pearls.verbatim: But that can't be the goal, paradoxically. Because if relaxing is only there to make it stop, now I'm like, is it stopping? Is it stopping? Is it stopping? Is it stopping? Is it stopping?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: At the first sign of palpitations, have the patient set a 15-minute timer and engage in something meaningful, then reassess whether symptoms persist.
pearls.verbatim: when I'm starting just to feel the palpitations, okay, I'm gonna give it fifteen minutes. I'm gonna do something important to me, and I'll check back in in fifteen minutes to see if I'm still having palpitations.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients in early stages of panic
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: The best outcomes come from first understanding what terrifies the patient about their panic, not from immediately prescribing a fix.
pearls.verbatim: We get the best effect if we've done this really well. Mhmm. From their perspective. Not like, oh, okay. Yeah. This is panic. Now let me tell you how to fix it. But, like, really knowing what it's like for them, what terrifies them about it, what their biggest associated fear is with it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: True panic attacks are self-limited; the body will not allow one to last more than 15, 20 minutes.
pearls.verbatim: Your body will not allow it to last more than fifteen, twenty minutes at the most. It just won't. Not if it's true panic.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: A patient who self-modulates their opioid dose (e.g., 'I tried four times a day, it made me sleepy, so I cut it down') is more likely exhibiting pseudoaddiction than true addiction, because addictive behavior lacks self-insight and modulation.
pearls.verbatim: I've never met anybody that was an addict that was sophisticated enough Well, we tried it four times a day. It made me sleepy, and it was too much, so I had to cut it down.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: When evaluating chronic back pain with radiculopathy that worsens with exertion, the differential includes spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication) and post-traumatic arachnoiditis.
pearls.verbatim: it's radiculopathy that gets worse with exertion. So what is that by definition? What do you have to rule out? There's two things. Stenosis is the main one. And then what's the secondary one?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Caregiver stress and mental health issues (depression, anxiety) are common in chronic pain patients and must be addressed as part of the treatment plan.
pearls.verbatim: She's a caregiver for congenital problems with her daughter. Her daughter also has orthopedic problems, worried and having problems that way. So you've got that dynamic going on
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: chronic pain patients who are caregivers
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: When repeating a workup that has already been done, frame it collaboratively: 'I want to make sure I know exactly what's going on so we can develop the best game plan moving forward.'
pearls.verbatim: man, we're gonna be working on this a while, and so I wanna make sure I know exactly what's going on. And so I know this has happened before. I'm gonna ask to go ahead and do some things so that I am very clear about what the picture is so that we can develop the best game plan moving forward.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: The primary goal of opioid therapy is functional improvement, increasing physical activity, quality of life, and family engagement, not simply reducing pain scores.
pearls.verbatim: what your expectation of them is is that narcotics are going to allow them to increase their physical activities, increase their quality of life, increase their ability to interact with their family.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Monitor opioid effectiveness with performance-based logs: time in bed, time sitting in a chair, activities attended, activities skipped, not just pain scores.
pearls.verbatim: The logs that I'm gonna want you to keep are gonna be much more performance based. How much time are you laying in the bed? How much time are you sitting in a chair? How much time are you out doing those things with your families and friends?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Multimodal pain management requires patients to fill and take all prescribed non-opioid medications (e.g., duloxetine, gabapentin, amitriptyline) and engage in physical therapy, aqua therapy, and cognitive therapy.
pearls.verbatim: multimodality pain approach means multiple medications. So we're gonna give you some medications, and each of those medications should do the same thing. And I need you to take all your medication. I don't wanna your pharmacy and find out the only medication you filled was the narcotic, and you left all the other ones go.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: In the opioid contract, include both patient responsibilities (medication safety, single pharmacy, no early refills) and physician commitments (regular follow-up, collaborative care) to increase buy-in.
pearls.verbatim: I think you may actually gain some extra buy in if you are very explicit in the contract about what you're committing to.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: When a patient has a long problem list and you see them monthly, rotate through the list: address the first three problems one month, the next three the next month, etc.
pearls.verbatim: Setting up... You know, you've got a problem list of eight things and you're seeing them every month and you do the first three, the first month, the second three, third three. Root through.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients seen monthly with multiple comorbidities
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Three pain-bearer relationships: resigning (pain wins), automatic counteracting (obsessive quest to eliminate pain), and behavioral adapting (accepting and adapting daily). Behavioral adapting is the goal.
pearls.verbatim: Three ways of relating. One is resigning. The pain wins. The pain has taken over all autonomy in my life. The pain is the active agent in my life.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Use metaphors like 'pain is an alarm system' to frame pain in functional terms, giving the patient a sense of what they can do in response.
pearls.verbatim: What this is is an example of metaphors to target specific aspects of talking with patients about pain and, like, even things like what they should expect after surgery or procedures. Right? But notice the metaphors are functional in terms of, like, what you can do with the information.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Spoon theory: every day the patient wakes up with a limited number of spoons; activities like showering cost spoons. This helps explain energy limitations.
pearls.verbatim: every day I wake up, and I don't know how many spoons are in the drawer. And then if I take a shower, that day, it may cost me three spoons. And then I only have two spoons left through all the things I need to do that day.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: patients with chronic pain (any condition causing fatigue/limited energy)
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: When a patient uses a metaphor that becomes their identity (e.g., 'I'm a spoonie'), do not directly challenge it; instead, ask probing questions to gently pull it apart.
pearls.verbatim: I feel like that's a lot less flexible. It is. It is. As soon as it becomes, like, my identity, it's a little bit less flexible. So I would... I mean, I've clarified it. They're my patient. What do you mean by your spooning? And then I would start to use language to pull that apart. I probably wouldn't directly go after it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.applies_to: clinicians when patients over-identify with a metaphor
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Pivot from a 'fix me' approach to a collaborative pain plan by reframing what you can do together, rather than promising to eliminate pain.
pearls.verbatim: Practicing the pivot. And this is kind of in the crux of a lot of our conversation today. How do we move from the fix me to a collaborative pain plan?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Agree to monitor what matters to the patient specifically, not just pain scores, and keep track of that.
pearls.verbatim: we wanna agree to monitor, but very specifically, for what matters to them. And and that that requires that we that we know and that we keep track of that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee & Dr. Rylander
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Perilymph fistula is a tiny tear in the inner ear that causes patients to hear all their internal body sounds, blood flow, bowel shifts, breath, leading to coordination problems and symptoms that mimic conversion disorder.
pearls.verbatim: something in the ear where you get fistulaization between the inner ear and the tear. And so then you get lip flow that's all funky. Mini tear.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with unexplained neurological symptoms after fever and head injury
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Perilymph fistula is often triggered by a combination of fever and head injury occurring close together, and for a long time the only way to diagnose it was during exploratory surgery, after which 90% of patients wake up completely normal.
pearls.verbatim: the only way to really diagnose it was to go ahead and act like you were gonna do the surgery and the repair and find it. And then patch it. Come out. Patient wakes up, and ninety percent of the time, it's, like, completely back to normal.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: In illness anxiety disorder, the patient has mild or no symptoms but is preoccupied with the fear of having or acquiring a serious illness, like a stomach rumble interpreted as cancer.
pearls.verbatim: I might have mild symptoms, but it's not like actual back pain, or it's not like actual migraines, or it's not like actual GI distress. It's like, oh, my tummy rumbled. Oh, the cancer.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: In somatic symptom disorder, the symptom itself would normally be distressing to anyone, but the patient's reaction to it is disproportionately larger.
pearls.verbatim: The symptom is... Would normally be distressing to anybody? Yes. But my reaction to it is even bigger.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Functional neurological symptom disorder requires that test results are incompatible with the loss of function, for example, normal nerve conduction studies but the patient cannot move their leg.
pearls.verbatim: The standard is that the results are incompatible with the loss of function. So the lab test, the imaging, whatever is conducted is incompatible with that particular loss of function. Nerve conduction tests are fine, but they can't move their leg.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected functional neurological symptom disorder
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Factitious disorder involves clear deceit and intentional production of symptoms, even without any obvious external benefit like money or avoiding work.
pearls.verbatim: The real key here is that there's clear deceit. And it could be with an external benefit, like money or something in mind. But the point is that it's actually, in this case, in the absence of it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: These somatic symptom and related disorders very seldom occur in isolation; the isolated case where this is the only diagnosis would be unusual.
pearls.verbatim: You very seldom see these in isolation. The isolated cases where this is all the... This is the only diagnosis that applies would actually be the unusual case.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with somatic symptom and related disorders
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: In somatic symptom disorder, the key is not that the abdomen doesn't hurt, but what the patient attributes that to and whether it leads to dysfunction like not driving or spending excessive money on healthcare.
pearls.verbatim: So it's it's not that his abdomen does not hurt. It's, like, what he attributes that to. And whether he, for example, doesn't drive his car because if it's that and he gets hit, then what? Right? So we have to see this distress turn into dysfunction in life.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected somatic symptom disorder
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Patients with somatic symptom disorder tend to be inconsistent historians because their perception of illness is based on the experience in the moment, and their story may change over years.
pearls.verbatim: They tend to be inconsistent historians, though, because so much of their perception of their illness is based on the experience in the moment. Right? So I I... Maybe, like, they told me it was this, but as I tell the story over the years, it becomes something else.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Illness anxiety disorder is characterized by fear of getting something or fear of finding out you have something, not by being bothered by symptoms you already have.
pearls.verbatim: remembering the difference with this one is that it's a fear of getting something. The fear I'll find out I have something. Not that I'm ex... So bothered by what I do have, but the fear that I might have something.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Illness anxiety disorder can present as either care-seeking or care-avoiding patterns, because the patient may not want to know they have a disease.
pearls.verbatim: So maladaptive avoidance. And, again, this can be a care seeking or care avoiding pattern because I might not wanna know that I have a brain.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Illness anxiety disorder is the somatic disorder that appears most equally in males and females.
pearls.verbatim: This is the one that's actually most equal in terms of appearing with males and females.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: In functional neurological symptom disorder, there must be evidence that the loss of function is incompatible with every diagnostic assessment used.
pearls.verbatim: But there has to be some kind of loss of that. And then there has to be evidence that it's incompatible with every diagnostic assessment used.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected functional neurological symptom disorder
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Functional neurological symptom disorder can be intermittent, not necessarily constant; there are acute and long-term stipulations for the diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: So we actually have an acute and a and a long term stipulation for this. Not someone who has, like, episodes of weakness. It's someone who has It can be intermittent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with functional neurological symptom disorder
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: The prognosis for functional neurological symptom disorder is better than for other somatic disorders; patients can see significant improvement over time, sometimes waking up with symptoms gone.
pearls.verbatim: the prognosis for this in some ways, even though it may have more impact on daily life when it occurs, the prognosis for improving is a little bit better than some of the others, which tend to just keep coming back.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with functional neurological symptom disorder
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: For functional neurological symptom disorder vs. somatic symptom disorder, the key question is: does the patient have actual loss of function, or is their reaction to the symptoms exaggerated?
pearls.verbatim: Does... Can she not walk, or does she feel so much pain that she needs the wheelchair?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.applies_to: patients with possible functional neurological symptom disorder
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: To distinguish factitious disorder from functional symptoms, look for clear evidence of deceit: if the patient complains of symptoms but gets up and walks when not being observed, that is evidence of factitious disorder.
pearls.verbatim: So if she shows those symptoms or complains of those symptoms and then when you're not looking, she gets up out of bed and walks or whatever the other evidence would be, then you might wonder about the seed.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Intermittent presentation of a symptom, such as new onset stuttering with prolonged intact speech, is a sign that points toward functional neurological symptom disorder rather than a fixed neurological deficit.
pearls.verbatim: Well, it says, like, new onset stuttering, but then other prolonged instances of intact speech.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: If a patient cannot perform a motor task but then does better on a more difficult motor task involving the same muscle group, that inconsistency suggests functional disorder rather than factitious disorder with clear deceit.
pearls.verbatim: She's not able to do well, but then she does better on a more difficult motor task, the same muscle group.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: When collecting urine from a female, if contamination is suspected (e.g., vaginal epithelial cells on microscopy), catheterize to obtain a good specimen.
pearls.verbatim: You may need to catheterize females to get a good specimen and to figure that out.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: females with suspected hematuria or UTI
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: The most common cause of urinary symptoms (frequency, urgency, dysuria) in older women is vaginal atrophy from decreased estrogen, not a UTI.
pearls.verbatim: The most common cause for urinary symptoms in a older female, which is a lot of the women that you're gonna be seeing, is decreased vaginal estrogen.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Vaginal atrophy not only causes urinary symptoms but also predisposes to UTIs by replacing normal flora with pathogenic bacteria.
pearls.verbatim: Vaginal atrophy causes a majority of the symptoms that people feel like when they believe they have urinary tract infection. It also is probably the most common reason why they get urinary tract infections.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: If a patient has microscopic hematuria but a negative culture (no UTI), they need urology referral because it may be carcinoma in situ of the bladder.
pearls.verbatim: if they feel like they have a UTI, but they they do not, but they have microscopic hematuria, those patients need to be referred or referred. Those are the patients we find who have partial in situ of the bladder.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: patients with microscopic hematuria and negative urine culture
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Recurrent UTIs without clear infection or with persistent microscopic hematuria warrant urology referral; the workup may find carcinoma in situ.
pearls.verbatim: if they feel like they have a UTI, but they they do not, but they have microscopic hematuria, those patients need to be referred or referred. Those are the patients we find who have partial in situ of the bladder.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: patients with recurrent UTI symptoms and persistent microscopic hematuria
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Patients with chronic indwelling catheters or suprapubic tubes need urology follow-up at least every two years because of the risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
pearls.verbatim: Those patients get bladder cancer. They should be seen by a urologist every year anyway. But if you get some of those patients in your clinic that have chronic indwelling catheters, get them over to us. We need to be seeing them because they need to get scoped at least once every two years because they... A lot of them develop squamous cell carcinoma.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: patients with long-term indwelling bladder catheters or suprapubic tubes
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: In intermediate-risk hematuria, the preferred imaging is now renal ultrasound instead of CT urography, plus cystoscopy.
pearls.verbatim: Renal ultrasonography has replaced CT urography in intermediate risk patients.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: A CT urogram for high-risk hematuria is a three-phase scan: non-contrast (for stones), IV contrasted (for renal parenchymal tumors), and delayed images at ~10 minutes (for ureteral and bladder masses).
pearls.verbatim: A CT urogram is a three phase CT scan. The first phase is non contrast. That allows kidney stones and bladder stones and those sorts of things. The second is an IV contrasted phase. ... And then we get delayed images. The delayed image is usually about ten minute delayed, and that highlights the contrast moving through the ureters down into the bladder and gives us an idea about whether or not there are ureteral masses or bladder masses or anything like that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: high-risk hematuria patients undergoing CT urography
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: If a patient reports seeing blood in their urine, work them up even if the urinalysis is negative; ignoring it risks missing a large renal mass.
pearls.verbatim: if a patient thinks they saw blood and they tell you they saw blood and then, you know, they they don't do anything about it, and a year later, they come in and they've got a 14 centimeter renal mass, it's gonna suck.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: To differentiate prostatic from non-prostatic nocturia, have patients record nighttime voided volumes. If they void only small amounts (e.g., 40 cc) while feeling a strong urge, the cause is not the prostate.
pearls.verbatim: And then you have them write down the volumes that they pee at night, and they pee up 40 ccs at night, they feel like they really need to pee. Like, something is going on that has nothing to do with their prostate.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Weight loss (including with GLP-1 agonists) can dramatically improve LUTS in obese men by reducing pressure on the bladder.
pearls.verbatim: because these patients lose a lot of weight, and I don't see them in my clinics anymore because they don't have urinary symptoms that they had before.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in non-pregnant women should not be treated; tell the patient to call if symptoms develop.
pearls.verbatim: unless they're pregnant and they're not having symptoms, I would not treat that. Okay? Leave that alone. You can tell them, hey. We grew out some stuff. If you start having symptoms, call me, and I'll get you the prescription.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Catheterized urine specimens are the best way to avoid contamination in women with suspected UTI.
pearls.verbatim: A lot of voided specimens in females are contaminated, so catheterized urine specimens are the very best way.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Vaginal estrogen cream is a first-line treatment for recurrent UTIs in postmenopausal women.
pearls.verbatim: vaginal estrogen cream, very important in the treatment for coronary tract infections. It's one of the first things that we do in a patient who's postmenopausal.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: In children, most UTIs are due to bowel/bladder dysfunction; management includes MiraLAX and potty training.
pearls.verbatim: The vast majority of kid UTIs are because they have weight dysfunction. So they should be... You know, they should have, you know, potty training slash bowel. You know, they should be on some sort of MiraLAX, basically.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Febrile UTI in an uncircumcised male under 6 months warrants urology referral and ultrasound.
pearls.verbatim: If an uncircumcised male has a UTI and he's, you know, a febrile UTI and he's six months old, yeah, that patient could probably come over see us. We can get an ultrasound and and work them up and everything like that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: uncircumcised males under 6 months with febrile UTI
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: UTIs are uncommon in boys after age 1; if they occur, refer to urology.
pearls.verbatim: It's uncommon for boys after one to have UTIs at all. So if that happens, send them to us.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Sean Doyle
pearls.applies_to: boys over 1 year old with UTI
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems

pearls.text: Interstitial (cornual) pregnancy is less common but more likely to rupture because there is less space for the gestational sac to grow.
pearls.verbatim: that's an important one to remember just because it's a little bit more likely to rupture. There's less space for the gestational sac to grow in that area.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: Ruptured abdominal (peritoneal) ectopic pregnancy carries approximately 10% maternal mortality.
pearls.verbatim: about ten percent of the people who have a ruptured abdominal ectopic pregnancy end up dying as a result.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: A history of one prior ectopic pregnancy gives a 10% recurrence risk; two or more prior ectopics gives >25% recurrence risk.
pearls.verbatim: If you've had one ectopic pregnancy, you're one in ten chance that you're gonna have another one if nothing changes. And if you've had two or more, then you have a greater than twenty five percent chance that you'll have another one if nothing changes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: Chlamydia infection can cause tubal scarring and also secretes interleukin-1, which signals the embryo to implant at the site of infection in the tube.
pearls.verbatim: It causes a lot of scarring, and it also causes the secretion of interleukin one, which is an inflammatory response to the infection in the tubes, but is also a signal that the embryo can detect. It's one of the body's signals to say, hey. You're in the uterus. You should implant now.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: Smoking is a risk factor for ectopic pregnancy because it impairs smooth muscle and ciliary function in the fallopian tubes.
pearls.verbatim: Smoking is gonna generally impact your capacity to have smooth muscle and ciliary function.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: If a pregnancy occurs while an IUD is in place, 50% of those pregnancies are ectopic.
pearls.verbatim: But if a pregnancy does happen in the presence of an IUD, half of them are ectopic pregnancies.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.applies_to: women with IUD who become pregnant
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: For low-hCG ectopic pregnancies (88% resolve spontaneously), expectant management is permissible.
pearls.verbatim: And if this is one of those eighty eight percent of people with a low HCG where you can monitor them and they resolve, that's okay to do.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.applies_to: patients with low hCG and stable ectopic pregnancy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: Salpingectomy treats the risk of tubal rupture by removing the tube that would rupture, without directly harming the child.
pearls.verbatim: And then the salpingectomy, it treats the risk of tubal rupture by removing the tube that would rupture without directly harming the child.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.applies_to: patients with ectopic pregnancy requiring surgical management
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: Keep ectopic pregnancy high on your differential.
pearls.verbatim: please do keep ectopic pregnancies high on your differential.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.applies_to: all clinicians evaluating women of reproductive age
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: After ectopic pregnancy, some guidelines recommend waiting one cycle before trying again; others recommend three months for higher-risk situations.
pearls.verbatim: Some guidelines said one month. You just wait one cycle and then you're ready to try again, which would be the same recommendation we often have for spontaneous miscarriages. Other places said, hey. If it's a higher risk situation, you might wanna wait three months.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.applies_to: patients who have had an ectopic pregnancy and wish to conceive again
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: Methotrexate has the lowest recurrence rate because it causes the embryo to detach without changing the tube, but it is not recommended in Catholic hospitals due to ethical concerns.
pearls.verbatim: So methotrexate is the one that has the lowest recurrence rate because it just causes the embryo to detach, and it doesn't cause any change to the tube.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.applies_to: patients considering medical management of ectopic pregnancy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: Salpingostomy carries a risk of scarring in the tube and subsequent recurrence.
pearls.verbatim: The salpingostomy does have a risk of causing scarring in the tube subsequently and having a recurrence because of the salpingectomy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing salpingostomy for ectopic pregnancy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: Salpingectomy has very low risk of recurrence but greater impact on future fertility if the other tube is not healthy.
pearls.verbatim: And then the salpingectomy has very low risk of recurrence because you've taken that tube out, but it does have a greater impact on future fertility if the other side is not healthy to begin with.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing salpingectomy for ectopic pregnancy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26

pearls.text: AmniSure is highly sensitive (>95%) for ruling out rupture of membranes when negative, but has a false positive rate of 17, 30%.
pearls.verbatim: And when they tested it, it was very sensitive. It was, like, high nineties sensitive, but it wasn't very specific. So if the amnosure is negative, and then what does that mean? You don't have the rupture. Yeah. You're you're very sure. You're, like, over 95% sure that you do not have rupture of membranes, which is helpful because if you're designing this test, you wanna be able to confidently say that it hasn't happened because a lot of the time, especially as you approach term, erring on the side of delivery is usually okay. And it was, however, not very specific, so it actually has a high false positive rate. So the false positives were, like, anywhere from seventeen to thirty percent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: ACOG recommends AmniSure as a second-line test after speculum exam with pooling, nitrazine, and ferning; it is also expensive at about $100 per test.
pearls.verbatim: But ACOG recommends that this be a second line test. It's also, like, super expensive. And it's, like, a $100 every time, which I'm an advocate for doing what's best for the patient. Know, it costs a lot of money, but people will keep this in mind when they're trying to, like, decide whether they need it or not.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: The risk crossover for maternal versus fetal complications in PROM occurs around 34 weeks gestation; the goal is to reach 34 weeks to minimize risk for both.
pearls.verbatim: The complications for baby and mom cross over right around thirty four weeks gestation. And so the goal is to get to thirty four weeks gestation because that minimizes the risk for both mom and baby.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: In PPROM, 40, 50% of women deliver within one week, and 70, 80% deliver within 2, 5 weeks; only about 20% deliver after 5 weeks.
pearls.verbatim: Forty or fifty percent of the women will deliver within a week, and seventy to eighty percent of the women will deliver within two to five weeks. So that means that only twenty percent will deliver after five weeks.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: Indications for delivery in PPROM after 23, 24 weeks include infection (maternal fever, fetal tachycardia, rising white count), spontaneous labor, and fetal intolerance (abruption, cord compression).
pearls.verbatim: Infection is a big one. If infection is present, how would you tell if infection's present? Mom's got a fever, and baby's heart rate is fetal tachycardia. Because you're gonna be monitoring fetal status in here. So fetal tachycardia, maternal fever, a little bit of white cells, probably physiologic in pregnancy, but big jump in the white count if you're taking labs, etcetera. What else would be a reason to deliver? Mom's going into labor spontaneously. Yeah. Labor. Labor is a reason to give birth. And let's see. The last one is kind of a big category, but it's gonna be fetal intolerance, which I say because it helps to just remember three things. So, like, infection, labor, fetal intolerance, but fetal intolerance can be caused by a number of things. So in this category, abruption is more common. Abruption and then cord compression.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: Antibiotics for PPROM should be given for exactly 7 days; extending beyond 7 days shows no benefit.
pearls.verbatim: Does not show any benefit if you extend past seven days, so it's just one week of antibiotics.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: In PPROM, steroids (betamethasone) are considered only if delivery is expected within 7 days; they promote fetal lung development.
pearls.verbatim: But, really, steroids aren't only gonna be if you think delivery is gonna happen in less than seven days.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection in PPROM is given from 24 weeks up to about 32-33 weeks; it reduces the relative risk of cerebral palsy.
pearls.verbatim: And, really, the studies only show that this goes up to, like, thirty two or thirty three weeks.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: After PROM, expect pulmonary hypoplasia in 10-20% of cases because amniotic fluid is critical for lung development; also watch for limb contractures from restricted movement.
pearls.verbatim: things to expect when the baby delivers, right, are fully developed lungs in, like, ten to twenty percent of the cases because the amniotic fluid is critical for lung development, the expansion of the lungs. ... limb contractures and skeletal deformities because the baby doesn't have the freedom to move in the uterus that's full of fluid.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: The amnitrip test is convenient but may have false positives; guidelines may be outdated.
pearls.verbatim: Yeah. I mean, it can it can be false positive with a bunch of things.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: At term (≥37 weeks) with PROM, expectant management for 12-24 hours is reasonable; after that, infection risk outweighs induction risk, so recommend induction.
pearls.verbatim: So if the lady comes in at 37 or beyond and she's ruptured, but she's not in labor, it's just prom. It's not PPROM. ... you can give her some time for expected management, usually twelve to twenty four hours. At that point, the risk of infection starts to outweigh the risk of induction.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: Immediate induction for term PROM is not unreasonable and should be discussed with the patient.
pearls.verbatim: But you could even say right off the bat, do you wanna just induce? And that's not unreasonable.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: Microscopy for ferning requires a microscope; if unavailable, the amnitrip test may be used instead.
pearls.verbatim: It seemed to me like we got the amitriptan because the microscope was offline, and you do need the together, or else it's, like, not really the same.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: There is no standard recommendation for how often to perform ultrasound during watchful waiting for PPROM; practices vary.
pearls.verbatim: The guidelines I was reading didn't show any, like, standard recommendation that they found is, like, best.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Seeley-Hacker
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)

pearls.text: Adult-onset type 1 diabetes often presents with a smoldering course over months to years, leading to misdiagnosis as type 2; maintain a high index of suspicion.
pearls.verbatim: As an adult, it's actually a slower smoldering type presentation. So think about it this way. Right? If you have t... Your T cells, you're having an autoimmune attack. T cells are responding. The beta cells are dying. If you are five or six, the death rate is happening very quickly, and you've nuked out all of your beta cells. If you are 30 or 40, that immune attack is slower, and there's usually still beta cell prevalence.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: In a euglycemic state (glucose ~80), the pancreas should not be secreting insulin; a C-peptide should be low (near zero).
pearls.verbatim: If your blood sugar is 80, what should the pancreas be producing from the level of insulin production from? It's all secreting insulin. Say it again. You should not be secreting insulin. You should not be secreting insulin. That is correct because you're at a good blood sugar.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: C-peptide must be interpreted with a simultaneous glucose level; a low C-peptide (e.g., 0.3) when glucose is 80 indicates type 1 diabetes.
pearls.verbatim: it is absolutely important to get a C peptide. I think I've jumped ahead of myself. I think this is multiple slides later. But to get a glucose with that C peptide. You cannot just look into C peptide and send your diagnosis. You need to know where the person is, so it must be in... Or glucose dose... Glucose level with the C peptide.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: patients being evaluated for pancreatic function
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Insulin autoantibodies are only helpful before significant exogenous insulin exposure; after 2-3 years of insulin therapy, they may be positive due to recombinant insulin, not autoimmunity.
pearls.verbatim: You can obtain it initially before they've had significant exposure to insulin. But if you get someone in your clinic who's been on insulin for two or three years, that insulin antibody may be positive, low levels just because they're getting exogenous insulin.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: patients being evaluated for type 1 diabetes
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Cost of teplizumab antibody screening to the patient should be no more than $25.
pearls.verbatim: It should cost no more than $25 to the patient.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: patients undergoing type 1 diabetes antibody screening
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Stage 2 presymptomatic type 1 diabetes carries a 100% risk of progressing to clinical type 1 diabetes within 5 years.
pearls.verbatim: If someone reaches stage two, there is a hundred percent risk at five years they will progress to type one diabetes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: patients with stage 2 presymptomatic type 1 diabetes
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: To qualify for teplizumab, a patient must have two or more positive antibodies and dysglycemia (fasting glucose less than 126 mg/dL) without symptoms, this is stage 2 presymptomatic type 1 diabetes.
pearls.verbatim: my person with two plus antibodies dysglycemia, passing blood glucose less than one twenty six, right, they're in that prediabetes stage without symptoms, that's the category that currently can be treated with TZL.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: presymptomatic individuals with two or more positive type 1 diabetes antibodies
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Teplizumab can delay onset of type 1 diabetes by 2-3 years on average; some patients have no benefit, while others remain diabetes-free 5-6 years later.
pearls.verbatim: TZLs has been shown to delay the onset by two to three years, which means some people that have gotten the infusion had no benefit, and some people that got the infusion still don't have type one diabetes five and six years later.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: patients with presymptomatic type 1 diabetes receiving teplizumab
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Teplizumab is given as a 14-day course of 30-minute infusions; the most common side effects are lymphopenia around day 5 and rash, and lymphopenia may indicate a better response.
pearls.verbatim: the medication is fourteen days, thirty minute infusion. Most common side effects are lymphopenia at about day five, sometimes a rash. And, actually, the more... Like, if patients have lymphopenia, it actually indicates a better response.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: patients receiving teplizumab for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: In type 2 diabetes, lipotoxicity from fat in muscle, liver, and pancreas prevents cells from responding to insulin, causing the pancreas to overproduce insulin (high C-peptide).
pearls.verbatim: when the insulin is coming out because there's fat in the muscle, there's fat in the liver, there's fat in the pancreas, it doesn't work as well. So then the pancreas has to spit out more insulin to overpower the insulin resistance
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: For Asian patients, the BMI threshold for type 2 diabetes screening is 23, not 25, because Asians have higher visceral adiposity at lower BMIs.
pearls.verbatim: if you are Asian, the BMI is twenty three, not twenty five. Because Asians and Indians, we pack our fat all in our belly and right up in our liver.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: Asian patients being screened for type 2 diabetes
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Thin diabetes in nonobese, nonwhite individuals involves a deficiency of insulin secretion rather than classic insulin resistance, but treatment with metformin and pioglitazone is still appropriate.
pearls.verbatim: Is a deficiency of insulin secretion, not necessarily insulin resistance. So we make enough, but it's just not good enough. So it's enough to keep you out of DKA and not to call you type one diabetes
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: nonobese, nonwhite patients with diabetes (especially Asian and African descent)
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: The most critical initial step when seeing a new diabetes patient is to assess for insulin deficiency (via C-peptide) to determine if insulin therapy is needed to prevent DKA.
pearls.verbatim: The most important thing that you guys need to do when you're first seeing someone is try to figure out do they have insulin deficiency? Do I need to put this person on insulin?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: patients with new diagnosis of diabetes
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Serial C-peptide and antibody testing may be needed to distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes in atypical presentations, such as thin African American adults.
pearls.verbatim: So the point is sometimes serial monitoring is needed.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Serial monitoring of C-peptide and antibodies may be needed when diabetes type is unclear, as glucotoxicity can transiently lower C-peptide.
pearls.verbatim: the point is sometimes serial monitoring is needed.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: patients with unclear diabetes type or suspected glucotoxicity
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: A glucose of 1000 with beta-hydroxybutyrate of 0.5 suggests HHS rather than DKA, challenging the assumption of type 1 diabetes based on thin body habitus alone.
pearls.verbatim: That's what I wanna know. It sounds like HHS. Right? And then I... What I left out is that when he had the A1c of 12, his admission beta hydroxybutyrate was, like, point five.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: CGM data interpretation is a billable office procedure; providers should obtain access to patient CGM data and review the AGP report.
pearls.verbatim: This is a billable procedure in the office. You should... If you're putting a person on a CGM, you should have access to their CGM data, and you should look at it because you can bill for your interpretation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: The GMI (glucose management indicator) estimates A1c from 2 weeks of CGM data, whereas a standard A1c reflects 3 months.
pearls.verbatim: This is basically the sensor driven a one c over two weeks, the GMI. Okay? So that's looking at two weeks of data as opposed to an a one c that looks at three months of data.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Target time in range is 70%, time below range less than 4%, and very low glucose (<54 mg/dL) should be 0%.
pearls.verbatim: Most patients will want a time in range of 70%, time below range of less than four. And, really, that very low range, which is less than 54 blood group o c one at zero. Zero. Okay? So the low range is 54 to 69. Less than 54, we want that at zero. This one should be less than 4%, 70%.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: most patients with diabetes on CGM
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: Coefficient of variation (CV) reflects glucose variability; target is in the upper 20s; a CV of 38 indicates significant peaks and troughs.
pearls.verbatim: The coefficient of variation is how squiggly is the line. Are there peaks and troughs and peaks and troughs, are we pretty flat? 38 still says we have some good peaks and troughs. K? We wanna be in the upper twenties.

pearls.text: If a patient cannot afford newer diabetes medications, cash-pay options include approximately $75/month for some agents and around $100 for others like Stello and Lingo.
pearls.verbatim: Some insurances do cover it. Some do not. If your patient can afford it, right, $75 for a month's supply cash pay. Stello and lingo, my understanding is they're closer to 100.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: patients without insurance coverage for diabetes medications
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: When documenting CGM interpretation for billing, describe patterns such as 'mealtime hyperglycemia with overnight limited glucose variability' and note significant variability.
pearls.verbatim: So what I would say, you have to document this in the chart if you're gonna bill for it. I would say, mealtime hyperglycemia. Right? With overnight limited glucose barrier. He has significant variability.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: In a patient with type 2 diabetes diagnosis, if A1c and glucose continue to bounce despite weight-loss agents and oral meds, reconsider the diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: he's got it diagnosed for three years on and off medications, on and off medicines that can help him lose weight. His a one c has bounced around.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: Adults with type 2 diabetes failing therapy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: If a patient's glycemic control remains poor despite escalating therapy, reconsider the diagnosis, adult-onset type 1 diabetes (LADA) is possible even in adults.
pearls.verbatim: So always take a step back and say, did I get the diagnosis right? Just because he is an adult does not mean that he has had.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: adults with diabetes and poor control

pearls.text: Even a modest elevation of islet antibodies confirms autoimmune diabetes, and low but detectable C-peptide prevents DKA but does not negate the need for insulin.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25

pearls.text: For adult-onset type 1 diabetes, the definitive treatment is insulin, both mealtime and long-acting; non-insulin therapies may be ineffective.
pearls.verbatim: So I put him on insulin, mealtime and long acting. We turned everything else off.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shah
pearls.applies_to: Adults with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes
