pearls.text: A 7-year-old with tachypnea and bradycardia is a red flag for inaccurate monitoring; the heart rate should be elevated with respiratory distress.
pearls.verbatim: If you're sick and your heart... And you're breathing a lot, what should the heart rate do? So why is it low? That's kinda funny, isn't it?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: If the heart rate is inappropriately low for the respiratory rate, the pulse oximeter may be faulty; check the vitals yourself.
pearls.verbatim: You should check it yourself.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.applies_to: any patient with discordant vital signs
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: Subcutaneous emphysema feels like 'bubble wrap' under the skin when you put your stethoscope on the chest wall.
pearls.verbatim: like bubble wrap, like, as you're putting it on the chest wall and you're listening
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: Sputum acid-fast bacillus testing is difficult to obtain in children because they cannot produce adequate sputum.
pearls.verbatim: This sputum acid fast is really difficult to obtain on kids because they don't know how to really produce that spectrum.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: A butterfly ultrasound can help assess for pneumothorax or cardiac tamponade even when subcutaneous air is present.
pearls.verbatim: But the Butterfly might be able to help you because you can push and displace a lot of that air.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: In TB-endemic areas, empiric TB treatment may be warranted even with negative sputum if clinical suspicion is high and the patient is from a high-prevalence region.
pearls.verbatim: we decided to treat as TB because endemic area, and this patient demand... Or the family was demanding to go back to India.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.applies_to: patients from TB-endemic areas with high clinical suspicion
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: In TB-endemic areas, if GeneXpert is unavailable and clinical suspicion is high, empiric TB treatment may be appropriate even without microbiologic confirmation.
pearls.verbatim: we decided to treat as TB because endemic area, and this patient demand... Or the family was demanding to go back to India.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.applies_to: patients in TB-endemic areas with high clinical suspicion and unavailable diagnostics
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: If a patient with suspected TB has no known history of asthma, the asthma route should not be pursued.
pearls.verbatim: There was no known history of asthma, so that's why we weren't going the asthma route.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.applies_to: patients with dyspnea in TB-endemic areas
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: On ultrasound, a pericardial effusion with right atrial 'dancing' indicates early tamponade physiology and requires close monitoring.
pearls.verbatim: if you see a person with pericardial effusion, the first thing you're gonna see is the atria start to dance. The the the right atrium is gonna get this little, like, dancing motion. Just because it's dancing doesn't mean they're already in credit tamponade, but you really wanna watch those patients close
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.applies_to: patients with pericardial effusion on ultrasound
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: When ultrasound guidance is not mastered, the subxiphoid approach for pericardiocentesis is safer than parasternal or apical approaches, which risk coronary vessel injury or pneumothorax.
pearls.verbatim: underneath is best when you don't know what you're doing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: In a patient with tamponade, removing at least 100 mL of pericardial fluid can produce immediate clinical improvement.
pearls.verbatim: We got out at least a 100 mls. Mhmm. And he got better right away
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: Cardiac TB requires 9, 12 months of antituberculosis therapy, longer than the 6 months used for pulmonary TB.
pearls.verbatim: usually, we do six months of TB treatment, which is pulmonary TB, but these patients get nine to twelve months if they're a cardiac TB
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: A pericardial window (surgical drainage) should be considered early in pericardial TB to prevent constrictive pericarditis.
pearls.verbatim: we do what's called a pericardial window. That fluid continues to drain out to prevent these types of complications
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.applies_to: patients with pericardial TB and effusion
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: A very high ADA level in pleural, pericardial, or peritoneal fluid strongly indicates TB; borderline high suggests cancer.
pearls.verbatim: if it's high, that is a strong indicator. If it's borderline high, then it could be cancer. But if it's really, really high, it's more... Most likely tuberculosis
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: Anti-TB medications penetrate effusion spaces well, so drainage is not needed for drug delivery (unlike an abscess).
pearls.verbatim: the anti TB medication can get into that space well, so it's not like an abscess where we have to drain it
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: Nepali patients have high adherence to TB treatment because the government pays for medications and they receive monthly supplies at TB clinics.
pearls.verbatim: our Nepali patients, there's an amazing TB program, and the government pays for all their medications. They go to a TB clinic before discharge, and they get, like, a certain month's supply at a time. Then come back to the clinic. Nepalis are very compliant with that
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: BCG vaccine does not prevent pulmonary TB but reduces extrapulmonary TB, especially in children under 5.
pearls.verbatim: No. It doesn't. We give it because it reduces... It reduces extrapulmonary TB, especially in children.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: In TB-endemic areas, latent TB is usually not treated because of risk of resistance and reinfection; exception is children under 5 with known exposure, who get 3 months of treatment.
pearls.verbatim: We don't treat latent TB. I think that's the main thing. Here, if if their skin test is positive, we think they have late TB, we probably treat it for a three month course. Not every person would get that treatment because if you treated their latent TB, you might increase the risk of having any resistant bacteria, or you might... Or they're just gonna give it anyway later on. They'll get they'll get it latency again, so that's why they don't treat it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.applies_to: adults in TB-endemic areas; children under 5 with exposure are exception
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: Standard pulmonary TB treatment is 6 months; extrapulmonary TB may require longer courses per local guidelines.
pearls.verbatim: classic pulmonary TB is almost always six months, and you've got it somewhere else. So, usually, it's like... I'm sure The US has guidelines for tuberculosis treatment. Nepal has guidelines, so you would just kinda follow what the guidelines are.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: If concerned about a newborn, be nosy and call the neonatologist to come check the baby; they will appreciate your interest.
pearls.verbatim: Bother the neonatologist. Right? If you've got a baby you're concerned and you're calling them, then be like, hey. Can I come and and check out the baby? You know? And just be super nosy. They're probably not gonna mind. They're probably gonna like that you're nosy.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Shields
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal

pearls.text: Compassion involves an emotional response to suffering with an authentic desire to help and taking action, distinct from sympathy or empathy.
pearls.verbatim: Scientists define compassion as an emotional response to another pain and suffering involving an authentic desire to help. It's different from sympathy or empathy between the feeling and understanding components and that compassion also involves taking action.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: Nearly 50% of Americans believe healthcare and providers are not compassionate; two-thirds of patients have had a meaningful experience with lack of compassion.
pearls.verbatim: Research from Harvard University found that nearly fifty percent of Americans believe that our health care system and our providers are not compassionate. Two thirds of patients have had a meaningful health care experience with a lack of compassion.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: Burnout involves depersonalization (inability to connect), and physicians spend more time looking at computer screens than into patients' eyes.
pearls.verbatim: Data are compounded by an epidemic of burnout in health care providers. Burnout is characterized by depersonalization, which is an inability to make a personal connection. And in the era of electronic medical records, rigorous research shows that health care providers spend more time looking into computer screens than looking patients in the eyes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: High physician compassion in diabetes is associated with 80% higher odds of optimal blood sugar control and 40% lower odds of acute metabolic complications.
pearls.verbatim: in patients with diabetes, research shows that high physician compassion is associated with an eighty percent higher odds of optimal blood sugar control and forty percent lower odds of acute metabolic complications.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: In patients with a common cold, high physician compassion is associated with enhanced immune response, shorter duration of symptoms, and lower severity of symptoms.
pearls.verbatim: in a University of Wisconsin study in patients with a common cold, high physician compassion as rated by patients was associated with enhanced immune response, shorter duration of symptoms, and lower severity of symptoms.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: When patients with HIV feel their physician knows them as a person, adherence to therapy is 33% higher and odds of undetectable virus are 20% higher.
pearls.verbatim: In a Johns Hopkins study of seventeen hundred patients with HIV, researchers ask patients, does your physician know you as a person? Knowing the patient as a person was associated with thirty three percent higher odds of adherence to therapy and twenty percent higher odds of having no detectable virus in the blood.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: In primary care, compassionate patient-centered care is associated with fewer diagnostic tests, fewer referrals to specialists, fewer unnecessary hospitalizations, and lower total healthcare charges.
pearls.verbatim: research from the University of Rochester and UC Davis have shown that compassionate patient centered care is associated with lower discretionary resource utilization. So fewer diagnostic tests, fewer referrals to specialists, fewer unnecessary hospitalizations, and lower total health care charges.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: Spending more time talking to patients may reduce the need for tests and referrals. 'If health care providers actually spend more time talking to patients, maybe we don't need so many tests and referrals.'
pearls.verbatim: If health care providers actually spend more time talking to patients, maybe we don't need so many tests and referrals.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: primary care and other outpatient settings
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: Compassion for others triggers reward pathways in the brain and positive emotion that can buffer or counteract activation of stress pathways and negative emotion.
pearls.verbatim: Neuroscience studies show that compassion for others can trigger reward pathways in the brain and positive emotion that can buffer or even counteract the activation of stress pathways and negative emotion.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: The speaker argues that the antidote to burnout is personal connection at the point of care, not escapism like vacations or hikes.
pearls.verbatim: I believe that the antidote to burnout had to be at the point of care in personal connection, human connection, not in an escape.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: Compassionate behaviors can be learned; the preponderance of evidence shows people are not simply wired for compassion or not.
pearls.verbatim: I used to think that people were either wired for compassion or they were not. But the preponderance of evidence in the scientific literature, both in health care workers and in the general population, shows quite clearly passionate behaviors can, in fact, be learned.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: When you feel pressure to just get through a patient encounter, you address the problem but not the person; addressing the person will help address the problem as well.
pearls.verbatim: when you do that, you address the problem but not the person. Right? And this is where you address the person, and the problem will be addressed as well.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: Use the 'triple E' technique to interrupt a talkative patient: excuse yourself, empathize, then explain why you need to redirect.
pearls.verbatim: the triple e's. Excuse. Remember what it is now. Excuse, empathize, and explain.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: When taking notes during a patient encounter, turn to the patient and listen; if you need to write something important, say 'Hold on one second, I want to make sure I get that down.'
pearls.verbatim: Turn to the patient. Listen to them. If you have to take a six... Hold hold on one second. I wanna make sure I get that down.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: If you function in medicine without compassion, you will burn out a lot faster and may not come back from it.
pearls.verbatim: if you function in medicine without it, I can promise you you'll burn out a lot faster, and there won't... You may not come back from it.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Connections

pearls.text: Sleep disturbance and nightmares should be a flag for possible trauma-related disorders like PTSD or acute stress disorder.
pearls.verbatim: We have sleep, so he's avoiding all media. Sleep disturbance and nightmares should be a bit of a flagger flag for people. Right?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: patients with stress or trauma history
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: When a patient has a history of substance use starting earlier in life (e.g., age 19) and current use is increased, ask whether this is new or escalated to clarify the diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: He started using substances at age 19. So he started doing this before. Yeah. Right? It's... That might be relevant in history. In his history, he he started this this stuff. He's done that before. That's... Is this new? Is it increased? That's a question we're gonna have. Right?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: patients with substance use and possible trauma
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: When referring to a mental health provider, coordinate care and obtain consent; stay involved to share information the patient may not tell the specialist.
pearls.verbatim: Refer and coordinate with a mental health provider. So... And coordinate. That's the key there. Refer and coordinate care. Stay stay involved in the care.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: Substance use is the 'X factor' for all psychiatric conditions; significant substance use must be addressed first to make progress on other issues.
pearls.verbatim: Substance use is the... It's the x factor for everything. We can't... If we don't... If we're not dealing with that, it's gonna be really hard to make gains in anything.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: In adolescents, a change in ADHD medication effectiveness with new mood symptoms (depression, elevated mood, irritability) should prompt evaluation for bipolar disorder rather than simply increasing stimulant dose.
pearls.verbatim: But at 14, her mood became low. She'd be sad. She'd sleep more. She'd had issues in her friendships and loss of interest in things and then conflict at home. Her ADHD medication was increased.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: adolescents with ADHD and new mood symptoms
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: Family history of psychiatric illness (e.g., father treated with lithium) is a critical clue for bipolar disorder in a young patient.
pearls.verbatim: She never met her dad. Her dad left the family because of psychiatric issues. He was treated with lithium, but we don't know his actual diagnosis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: patients with mood symptoms and family psychiatric history
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: Personality disorders are not diagnosed before age 18 because personality continues to develop and is not solidified until the mid-twenties to thirties.
pearls.verbatim: Usually, it's fairly fairly solidified by mid twenties or so later. By 30, usually.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: For cyclothymic disorder in adolescents, the time criterion is halved from adults: symptoms must be present for at least one year, with no more than two consecutive months without symptoms.
pearls.verbatim: For adolescents, it's... As far as half the time frame to to meet criteria.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: adolescents being evaluated for cyclothymic disorder
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: If an adolescent on stimulant medication develops mood lability and hypomanic symptoms, consider a 'medication holiday' to see if symptoms change, which helps clarify if the medication is contributing to the mood instability.
pearls.verbatim: We essentially just hold the methylphenidate for the period to see if their symptoms change.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: adolescents with ADHD on stimulants who develop mood lability
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: In a young adult with cystic fibrosis and respiratory distress, refusal of treatment and intolerance of the mask in the hospital may reflect separation anxiety disorder or panic disorder rather than simple noncompliance.
pearls.verbatim: Refusing medical treatment. Let's go home. Flames intolerance of mask. Makes her really anxious and feels more short of breath.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: young adults with chronic illness who refuse treatment in hospital
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: When a patient tolerates a medical device at home but not in the hospital, this discrepancy can be a clue that anxiety, particularly separation anxiety, is driving the intolerance.
pearls.verbatim: Just to add at home, she tolerates a mask, and her home is just gonna be that here. Really important detail there, actually.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: patients who refuse medical devices in hospital
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: When the patient is able to tolerate a mask or device at home but not in the hospital, ask about environmental differences to tailor treatment.
pearls.verbatim: At home, she tolerates this device or some other things, some other assistance... The mask and so forth.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: hospitalized patients who refuse respiratory devices
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: Maintain a high index of suspicion for human trafficking in young adults with unclear psychosocial history and concerning patterns of control.
pearls.verbatim: Yes. Can we also consider from the human trafficking? ...Maybe. Maybe it's there. ...You have your radar up.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: young adults with complex social dynamics and limited collateral history
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25

pearls.text: If patients do not leave with expectation of change and hope, they will not come back.
pearls.verbatim: if they don't leave with expectation and hope, expectation of change and hope, they're not gonna come back.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: all patients in counseling or behavior change encounters
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: The therapeutic relationship, listening, reflection, empathy, emotional support, accounts for 45% of treatment outcomes based on meta-analyses.
pearls.verbatim: instilling hope and expectation of change in the process along with having a good relationship, that's 45%
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: counseling and mental health encounters; likely similar in family medicine
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: The clinician's belief in their technique is more impactful than the technique itself; it helps set up expectation and hope.
pearls.verbatim: my belief in the technique is actually what is most impactful.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Do not dive into the clinical agenda until the patient's full list of concerns is complete, keep asking 'is there something else?' until they say no.
pearls.verbatim: Do not dive in until this list is complete, even if they give you a thousand of them.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Ask the patient to prioritize their concerns when multiple issues are raised, because they often do not know what is most important medically.
pearls.verbatim: ask the patient to prioritize the list if if that's necessary. They give you one thing. They give you a few things. The priority is obvious. No worries. But prioritize if you need to. That's very important.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Use the three Es to politely interrupt a runaway patient: Excuse me, Empathize, Explain why you need to redirect.
pearls.verbatim: Excuse, empathize, and explain.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: when a patient goes off-topic during a visit
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Using structured communication skills like agenda setting does not prolong the encounter; skipping them can lead to longer visits later.
pearls.verbatim: doing these things does not actually prolong your encounter. It's built in to the system.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Attending means being fully present, leaning in, making eye contact, minimizing computer use, to connect with the patient.
pearls.verbatim: Being present. Listening, leaning in a little bit, you know, just being actually present, not not on your computer.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Self-disclosure should remain shallow; avoid sharing your deepest, darkest secrets.
pearls.verbatim: self disclosure, you're probably gonna keep them pretty shallow. You're not gonna tell your deepest, darkest stuff.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Confrontation may be needed more often to address dangerous behaviors: 'This is really bad for you. I need to tell you that.'
pearls.verbatim: you might have to do that. Challenge them or confront them about things they're not doing. Well, you know, maybe you you really need to stop this really bad behavior because it's literally killing you.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Practice active listening skills (eye contact, nodding, leaning in) to encourage patients to share; these skills can be practiced with patients, MAs, or attendings.
pearls.verbatim: what are some skills that you could practice in your clinic next week with your patients or your MAs or your attendings or whomever that definitely wanna do some with your patient.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: For the Handling question, support only positive coping skills; if a patient reports maladaptive coping (e.g., drinking every night), respond with empathy and acknowledge the challenge without endorsing the behavior.
pearls.verbatim: I've been going out and getting drunk every night. You're not gonna support that one. Right? You can say, wow. That sounds like it caused some other challenges.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: If a patient presents with a biomedical complaint (e.g., knee pain), you can still use BATHE; if they go emotional, capture that, be present, then return to the presenting problem.
pearls.verbatim: if they go totally emotional on you, you can capture that, work with them, be present with them, and come back to the knee problem.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Practice the technique by the book until you have it down, then you can adapt it to your own style, but don't be so flexible that you never use it.
pearls.verbatim: you practice by the book until you get the book down. Right? And then you learn... Then you say, oh, let me try this other way. It seems to maybe fit me better.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: The final 'E' in BATHE is not just empathy, it is 'empathy and exit', a way to acknowledge the patient's emotion and then pivot to the medical agenda.
pearls.verbatim: Empathy and exit. Right? It helps you to move in the direction that you need to move with your patient to get to the physical thing that's bringing them in.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling

pearls.text: Research shows BATHE improves patient satisfaction across both outpatient and inpatient settings without significantly increasing time per visit.
pearls.verbatim: improve patient satisfaction across outpatient and inpatient settings. This is not just for the outpatient setting.

pearls.text: A UVA family medicine resident RCT found higher patient satisfaction with BATHE, mediated by patients' perception that the physician was genuinely interested in them.

pearls.text: Hypervigilance in caregivers leads to constantly high cortisol levels, increasing risk for anxiety and depression.
pearls.verbatim: Hypervigilance. ... So there's an underlying stress. ... Cortisol levels were, like, constantly high.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: When exploring spiritual distress, use a normalizing statement like 'Sometimes my patients in similar situations feel angry at God or frustrated. Have you ever experienced those kinds of things?' to give permission for these feelings.
pearls.verbatim: you never experienced those kinds of things. Right? So you're kinda... You're laying it out there giving them a little bit of permission to have these thoughts and these feelings.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.applies_to: caregivers of patients with neurocognitive disorders
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Ask about social outlets: 'Are you able to get out and spend time away from your loved one? Have any other social outlets?'
pearls.verbatim: This is also a good time to ask about, are you able to get out and spend time away from your loved one? Have any any other social outlets?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Role captivity, caregiver overload, and adverse life events outside the caregiver role are the strongest predictors of stress; assess these specifically.
pearls.verbatim: world captivity, caregiver overload, adverse life events outside of their caregiver role are the strongest predictors of stress.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Know the dementia stage to help caregivers anticipate and navigate future stressors they may not see coming.
pearls.verbatim: Knowing where the person with dementia is, this is again where it's helpful to know... For you to know kinda where they are because you can help them navigate the stressors that they may not see coming yet.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Many caregivers, especially older adults, may not know how to find online resources; offer to hold their hand or involve a medical assistant or social worker.
pearls.verbatim: There's information out there, they don't have access to easily. They do. They might need you to hold their hand a bit or get your MA or a social worker to hold on.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Sleeplessness in caregivers often occurs because the dementia patient's sense of time is disrupted, leading them to sleep during the day and be up at night.
pearls.verbatim: One of them is the fact that their person is now on a new schedule. Right? What happened to people with dementia? Whole sense of time is all jacked up. They sleep in the day. They're up at night.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Caregivers often forget to take care of their own health because they are hyper-focused on the crisis of caring for the dementia patient.
pearls.verbatim: Can't remember the last time I I took care of my own health, or they forget to take care of their own health. They're so hyper focused on the crisis in front of
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: When counseling a caregiver, remember they are a biopsychosocial-spiritual person; address their biological, spiritual, social, and physical needs, not just the dementia patient's.
pearls.verbatim: Or don't forget. She's a biopsychosocial spiritual person as well. What are her biological needs? What are her spiritual needs? What are her social needs? What are her physical needs?
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Connect caregivers to resources such as counseling, support groups, dementia-specific community resources, and senior resources, since caregivers are often seniors themselves.
pearls.verbatim: Counseling, support groups, which we talked about earlier, Dementia specific community resources, which I'll point you to in this moment. Senior resources, generally, because oftentimes they're seniors as well.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Schedule regular follow-ups (e.g., every 3 months) to track the caregiver's health and progress, and to see if they accessed recommended resources.
pearls.verbatim: Follow-up in a month. Follow-up. Whatever the time frame is. Follow-up. Why? To track to track progress on what they're doing and how they're managing it on their burnout.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Recommended free websites for caregivers include alz.org (Alzheimer's Association) and Community Resource Finder, which help locate community resources.
pearls.verbatim: If you're anywhere on the planet, right, go to alzheimer's.org. Right? And it's not just for Alzheimer's.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Types of resources caregivers might need include adult day care programs, geriatric care managers, transportation, elder law attorneys, and relocation advisers.
pearls.verbatim: Day care programs. Day Adult day care program. Yeah. That's actually one of them. I would suggest you think about adult day care program.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: The Community Resource Finder is an assessment tool that helps caregivers work through what resources they need and where to go.
pearls.verbatim: This is an assessment product. This is like a thing that they kinda work through, and it helps them figure out what resources they use for.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: Medicare/insurance may cover limited home health (e.g., medication management, toileting, showering) for a few hours a couple times a week, but round-the-clock care is expensive and often paid out of pocket.
pearls.verbatim: You can get home health, which is medication management, help with, like, toileting, getting a shower, and that's going for a couple hours a couple times a week. So that's not, like, twenty four hour care you're paying out of pocket.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.verbatim: And that's why I ended up with elder care law attorney saying, hey. Maybe you need to get a divorce so you can I'm not sure. You can afford it. Right. So that you can qualify for the for the aid, basically.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: For end-stage dementia (stage 7), patients may qualify for hospice, which provides a different set of resources.
pearls.verbatim: If they're an end stage dementia, like, stage seven that are not then they could be likely to qualify for hospice.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Simpson
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders

pearls.text: If a patient has chronic hyperbilirubinemia, bilirubin can bind to albumin, so even after fixing the underlying cause, bilirubin may remain elevated until the albumin is recycled.
pearls.verbatim: If somebody has that chronic hyperbilirubinemia, you can get basically to the albumin. And so even if you fixed the underlying cause, you may have a persistently elevated bilirubin until the albumin has been recycled.

pearls.text: In a post-surgical patient with a hematoma, unconjugated bilirubin rises from hemolysis; if the liver's ability to excrete conjugated bilirubin is impaired, both fractions rise, creating a confusing mixed picture.
pearls.verbatim: a hematoma after surgery. Right? ... After surgery, have a bilirubin going up. ... It can be primarily underconjugated, but then it gets complicated because of people with liver disease, basically, their ability to excrete the biliary... Conjugated bilirubin is impaired.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Ultrasound is the first imaging step for jaundice with elevated LFTs, but bowel gas can limit sensitivity.
pearls.verbatim: It's pretty sensitive as long as there's not a lot of bowel gas. Okay? Bowel gas is the old one. So just be aware of that.

pearls.applies_to: patients with jaundice and elevated LFTs
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: For high-risk choledocholithiasis (stone on imaging, acute cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 with dilated CBD), proceed directly to ERCP without MRCP.
pearls.verbatim: High risk. If you have it on any of those imaging modalities, if you see a stone on there, you can proceed directly to ERCP. You don't have to get an MRCP to confirm it.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Normal common bile duct diameter is 6 mm with gallbladder, 8 mm without; post-cholecystectomy CBD >10 mm is common due to loss of reservoir.
pearls.verbatim: the per guidelines, it's six millimeters. If they have gallbladder, eight millimeters. If they don't, but it's, I mean, it's super common to see somebody who's had a cholecystectomy with a CBD greater than one.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: If ERCP fails due to difficult anatomy (e.g., post-bariatric surgery), options include endoscopic ultrasound-guided rendezvous, precut sphincterotomy, or external biliary drainage.
pearls.verbatim: ERCP doesn't always work. Sometimes the anatomy is really complicated. ... Or even think about, like, what if somebody's had bariatric surgery? That's pretty difficult.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: CT with dedicated liver protocol and contrast is best for characterizing masses seen on ultrasound or ERCP.
pearls.verbatim: you do CT scan doing dedicated liver for for all with with contrast. And so that... And that's an important part.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: For suspected pancreatic cancer, get a CT scan of the liver and pancreas with contrast as the preferred imaging modality.
pearls.verbatim: getting a CT scan of the liver and pancreas with contrast.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: The only potential cure for pancreatic adenocarcinoma is surgical resection, which for head tumors requires a Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy).
pearls.verbatim: the only cure... Natural cure is surgical resection.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Most pancreatic cancers causing jaundice are in the head of the pancreas because the head is close to the biliary tree.
pearls.verbatim: The majority of it is gonna be in the pancreatic head, especially if it's causing jaundice. Right? Because the head is what's actually close to biliary tree.

pearls.text: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors are rare (1-2% of pancreatic tumors) and less aggressive; if small and inactive, they can be monitored with surveillance.
pearls.verbatim: So much less common, one to two percent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Almost all patients with MEN type 1 will develop a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor at some point.
pearls.verbatim: MEN type one, almost all of them end up with this at some point.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Ampullary malignancies account for about 20% of neoplastic common bile duct obstructions.
pearls.verbatim: are about twenty percent of the common bile duct obstructions from neoplasms.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Cholangiocarcinoma is often advanced at diagnosis; only about 1.5% of cases are resectable.
pearls.verbatim: One So and a half percent that you're able to resect.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: IBS patients have a higher incidence of systemic inflammatory diseases, similar to IBD patients, suggesting a shared inflammatory mechanism.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: IBS accounts for 12% of primary care visits and 28% of gastroenterology referrals.
pearls.verbatim: twelve percent of primary care visits, twenty eight percent of gastroenterology referrals.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.verbatim: One third of primary care physicians, gastroenterologists concur they agree, which is hard to get a third of them to agree on anything. IBS management is highly frustrating.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Higher peristalsis reduces absorption; lower peristalsis increases water extraction and leads to constipation.
pearls.verbatim: Higher peristalsis, less absorption. ... lower peristalsis, less ability to produce a normal stool, more likely to have a constipated stool
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: The enteric nervous system coordinates peristalsis via the myenteric plexus and controls absorption and vascular tone via the submucosal plexus.
pearls.verbatim: primarily, it's thought of as coordinating peristalsis. ... it's gotta coordinate absorption. ... vasoconstriction and vasodilation so you control how much is coming into the body.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: If circular muscles tighten down, peristalsis is blocked; if longitudinal muscles do not coordinate, peristalsis fails.
pearls.verbatim: If the circular muscles tighten down, you're not gonna get peristalsis through. If the longitudinal muscles don't coordinate one segment to the other, you're not gonna get peristalsis through.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Viruses steal host membrane, so antiviral antibodies are directed against self-antigens, leading to autoimmunity.
pearls.verbatim: virus self antibody is formed from whatever cell that virus happens to infect.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Post-infectious IBS can develop after acute gastroenteritis; a subset of patients develop IBS symptoms as postinfectious irritable bowel syndrome.
pearls.verbatim: following acute gastroenteritis, subset of patients IBS symptoms as postinfectious irritable bowel syndrome
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Gastroenterologists should biopsy the colon even if it looks normal under scope, because not everything is mucosa-based; pathology can reveal immune cell infiltration.
pearls.verbatim: we finally convinced the gastroenterologist that just because it doesn't look different under your scope, maybe you should biopsy this and send it to the pathologist for them to be able to help us see what you're not able to see because not everything is mucosa based.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Autoantibodies as biomarkers for IBS are still controversial because sensitivity and specificity are not as high as for IBD, but combining multiple autoantibodies in a panel improves differentiation from healthy controls.
pearls.verbatim: They're not as specific. That's why it's in controversy. Okay? But when you start to get them together, start to do a little bit better.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Anti-IgE monoclonal antibodies used for asthma can also result in almost complete resolution of IBS symptoms, but this is only indicated if the patient has both asthma and an approved indication for anti-IgE.
pearls.verbatim: administration of anti IgE monoclonal antibodies not only improved asthma, because we said it was the same disease process, just different tissue, but also resulted in almost complete resolution.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.applies_to: patients with both asthma and IBS who qualify for anti-IgE therapy
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Anti-IgE monoclonal antibodies improve both asthma and IBS symptoms, supporting a shared disease process across tissues.
pearls.verbatim: administration of anti IgE monoclonal antibodies not only improved asthma, because we said it was the same disease process, just different tissue, but also resulted in almost complete resolution.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Anti-IgE therapy is not approved for IBS alone; it is only indicated if the patient has asthma or another approved condition.
pearls.verbatim: Now that doesn't mean you can use anti IgE for your IBS patients. It means if somebody has both asthma or one of the approved indications for it, that you can fix their IBS as well.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.applies_to: patients with IBS without concurrent allergic condition
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Traditional IBS therapies include stress reduction, soluble fiber, probiotics, MiraLAX, bromide, and bile acid sequestrants.
pearls.verbatim: So historic therapy. Right? Stress reduction, soluble fiber, probiotics, MiraLAX, bromide, and bile acid sequestrants.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Historic therapies for IBS, stress reduction, soluble fiber, probiotics, MiraLAX, antispasmodics, and bile acid sequestrants, should still be used even with new immune-based approaches.
pearls.verbatim: historic therapy. Right? Stress reduction, soluble fiber, probiotics, MiraLAX, bromide, and bile acid sequestrants. You still have to remember that. You still have to use that.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: An IgG elimination diet involves blood testing to identify positive IgG antibodies to foods, eliminating those foods, then reintroducing them while monitoring symptoms.
pearls.verbatim: Doing an IgG elimination diet. So you do the blood test. You find out what the IgG panel shows is positive. You eliminate that. You do a reintroduction, and you monitor their symptoms, and you can re... Redo their blood testing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Slaughter

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis

pearls.text: Onset of diarrhea between 8 and 16 hours after exposure suggests Clostridium perfringens; onset >16 hours suggests viral or other bacterial causes.
pearls.verbatim: eight to sixteen hours, you're looking at more likely cholesteatreperfringens, and then greater than sixteen hours is gonna be any viral cause or other bacterial.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.verbatim: if there's somebody who's likely to spread it to another person, we might wanna check them. So if they're a food handler, health care worker, day care center.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.verbatim: we don't do as often as we should if we're, like, willing to have much diarrhea, but now they're not, because they're still feeling terrible. We can get a rectal swab, and we can send that. It's gonna be less sensitive, but still gets the ball moving.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26

pearls.text: For ova and parasite testing, collect three stool samples on consecutive days because organisms are not shed every day.

pearls.verbatim: The price that gets billed to insurance is $819 for the patient. If they're gonna self pay, it's, like, $400. ... stool culture, $3.

pearls.verbatim: Azithromycin is preferred agent because there is resistance more likely to the fluoroquinolones. ... you can do a onetime dose, which is kinda nice.

pearls.verbatim: Lomotil, we see that. It works, but it's not recommended as much because of... It's just not as well studied, and there's the chance of it causing, like, central opioid or cholinergic side effects.

pearls.text: God often teaches us about trust when we are stretched beyond our normal comfort zones.

The classic spy movies, the the older spy is saying to the younger spy, you know, trust no one. Trust no one. Now that may work for spies, but that really is not a good policy for life. Going through life suspicious and doubtful of other people all the time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: Trust is key to walking well with Jesus.
pearls.verbatim: Trust is key to walking well with Jesus.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: Jesus calls us to trust in Him, especially in troubling moments, as seen in John 14:1.
pearls.verbatim: Jesus calls us to trust in him. You know, at the end of the last supper, so Jesus had already told them he was leaving them. And Judas had already left the room and had gone off to betray him. And just the immediate context of this was where Jesus had said Peter, you, you know, you will deny me three times. So this is kind of a troubling moment, as it were. This is not we're having a good time partying moment. This is a troubling moment. And then Jesus says, let not your hearts be troubled. Maybe he could see something in the disciples already happening. Let not your hearts be troubled. Trust in god. Trust also in me.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: The Greek word for trust, believe, and faith is essentially the same (pistis).
pearls.verbatim: basically one Greek word or several forms of that word that means that all. And you see in the English language, they're very similar, aren't they? I could say, I trust this help... This talk is gonna be useful to you, or I believe this talk is gonna be useful to you, or I have faith that this talk is gonna be useful. They all kind of overlap even in English. But in Greek, they really... It's just one word.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: The same Greek root (pistis/pisteuo) is used for both the devil's belief in God and Abraham's saving faith; context determines the meaning.
pearls.verbatim: James two nineteen, he says, you believe, there is one god. Even the devils believe his duo and shudder. And then a few... James, same author uses at that... Few verses later, and he says, Abraham believed god to and was credited to him as righteousness. Now, obviously, the believing of the devils and the believing of Abraham are a bit different, aren't they? And yet that same Greek word.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: The Greek word pisteuo in 2 Timothy 1:12 includes the nuance of being persuaded, which goes deeper than mere belief.
pearls.verbatim: Second Timothy one twelve. For I know who I have believed pisteuo and am persuaded, hey, though, that he is able. That persuaded kinda takes it in another level, doesn't it? It takes it down. This is persuaded, kind of like really, really believing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: Jesus calls us to trust Him specifically when our hearts are troubled (John 14:1), addressing the heart, not the head.
pearls.verbatim: And because he's given it in the in the context of a troubled heart. It's about hearts. It's not about hair. Let not your hearts be troubled. Trust in god. Trust also in him.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: Trusting God brings peace and joy; Isaiah 26:3 and Romans 15:13 connect trust with perfect peace and joy.
pearls.verbatim: You will keep him in perfect peace whose mind is steadfast. Why? How? Because he trusts in you. And then may the god of hope, Paul's prayer for the Romans, fill you with all joy and peace as you trust in him.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: God connects our trust with His honor; Moses was punished not just for disobedience but because he did not trust God enough to honor Him (Numbers 20).
pearls.verbatim: the Lord said to Moses and Aaron, because you did not trust in me enough to honor me. So trust was at the heart of it, but also God connected Moses' trust with his honor. Because you didn't trust me, I didn't get the honor.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: Trust is demonstrated by action and reaction under pressure, not just by words; the helicopter pilot showed real belief by turning off the engine.
pearls.verbatim: who believed in autorotation? I said I believed in autorotation. Did I really, really believe in autorotation? No. And you could see through my actions and reactions that I didn't really, really believe in autotation. Did he believe in autotation? Absolutely. Absolutely. You could see by his actions turning off the engine, his reactions. He really, really believed in autorotation.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: Dr. Sutton's simple definition of trust is "really, really believe", not just saying we believe but truly trusting in person and character.
pearls.verbatim: Really, really believe in god and Christ. Of course, they are the same. God is... Christ is god. There's the triune god. But for whatever reason, Jesus, that point, as he often does, he's saying talking about god and himself.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: Trust is not just believing facts about God but trusting in the person of Christ Himself, not in outcomes or doctrine.
pearls.verbatim: We're trusting in a person or a... We're trusting in god. We're trusting in the person of Christ. We're not trusting so much in facts or in outcome or in doctrine or in things that we hope for. It's trusting in a person who is living and moving and sometimes knowable and sometimes unknowable.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: In a moment of trouble, it is not helpful to focus on facts about God (like credentials); what matters is the personal promise 'He is coming to get me and take me to a safe place.'
pearls.verbatim: he's coming to get me, and he's taking me to a bad place.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.applies_to: anyone facing a stressful arrival or transition
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: When you are in a troubled heart moment, don't focus on a full theological treatise; remember simply that God is good and God is able.
pearls.verbatim: God is good, and god is able.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: When you doubt in your faith, the underlying issue is usually either a doubt of God's love or a doubt of God's power.
pearls.verbatim: We usually doubt either his love or his power.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.applies_to: anyone struggling with trust in God
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: The worthiness of our trust depends on the worthiness of the object of our trust, not the strength of our believing.
pearls.verbatim: Worthiness of our trust depends on the worthiness of the object of our trust.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: Autorotation works because the physics principles are true and reliable, not because the pilot has great faith.
pearls.verbatim: No. It was because the object of his faith, autorotation, the principles, the physics principles of autorotation were true and real and reliable, worthy of his trust.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: Christ is worthy of our absolute trust, even when we are not absolutely trusting Him at the moment.
pearls.verbatim: Christ is worthy of our absolute trust.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26

pearls.text: The turning point came when he realized he didn't need more information about Christ, but to trust more deeply the information he already had.
pearls.verbatim: The turning point came for him in his life He realized that he didn't need more information about Christ, but he needed to trust more deeply the information he already had.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: Childlike surrender and trust is the defining spirit of authentic discipleship, and the supreme need most often overlooked is trust.
pearls.verbatim: he said, I can state unequivocally that childlike surrender and trust is the defining spirit of authentic discipleship, The supreme need in most of our lives and often the most overlooked is trust.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: Trust is to really, really believe at such a deep level that it impacts our actions and reactions.
pearls.verbatim: The trust is to really, really believe. Really, really, really believe. Not just to say things in our head, but to really, really believe at such a deep level that it impacts our actions and our reactions.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: Trust ultimately depends not on gritting our teeth to believe, but on the worthiness of the object of that trust.
pearls.verbatim: trust ultimately depends not so much on that really, really believing as if we have to kind of grit our teeth and really, really believe, but on the worthiness of the object of that trust.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: Peaceful trust is described in Isaiah 26:3: in perfect peace because they trusted you; in quietness and trust is your strength.
pearls.verbatim: the first one I have called his peaceful trust, and that is the trust of Isaiah twenty six three. In perfect peace because they trusted you. In quietness, trust is your strength.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: God can supernaturally intervene and help us to trust; it is not just gritting our teeth.
pearls.verbatim: God can supernaturally intervene and help us to trust. It's not just to grit your teeth. We have to do this. This is god sometimes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: When God intervenes to help us trust, it is often in the crisis moments.
pearls.verbatim: I often found in my life that when God intervenes and helps me to trust, it was often in the crisis moments.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: In a remote setting with no CT scanner, medical evacuation is necessary for a patient with signs of increased intracranial pressure such as papilledema and hemiparesis.
pearls.verbatim: The whole country of Chad didn't have. At that point in time, Chad didn't have a single CT scan. We were three days from the nearest international airport, much less back to The USA where we could get medical help. And so we knew, okay, this is medical evacuation time.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.applies_to: patients with suspected intracranial pathology in remote areas
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: In a crisis, supernatural peaceful trust can be granted by God, independent of the outcome, and is sustained by the prayers of others.
pearls.verbatim: We had this incredible sense of trust. We just had this overwhelming sense that god was good and that god was with us and that god... No matter what the outcome, we knew god was good.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: Trust is not the absence of fear; it is a response to fear, and it is acceptable to pray 'Lord, I believe; help my unbelief' when trust is mingled with doubt.
pearls.verbatim: trust doesn't mean the absence of fear. Trust is sometimes the response to fear. And sometimes trust is a little bit of fear and a little bit of trust. Sometimes it's a clinging trust. Sometimes it's a mingled trust.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26

pearls.text: The myth that trust equals no uncertainty is false; trust and uncertainty fit together, as shown by Jonathan's words 'Perhaps the Lord will act on our behalf' alongside 'Nothing can hinder the Lord from saving.'
pearls.verbatim: Perhaps the Lord will act on our behalf. Nothing can hinder the Lord from saving, whether by many or by few.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26

pearls.text: In cross-cultural teams, different tolerances for uncertainty (e.g., Singaporeans wanting exact times vs. Fijians being more relaxed) can create tension that requires understanding.
pearls.verbatim: the Singaporean lady would say to Aliki, so when are we going to conference? You know? I need a ride with you. It's in the next town. He said, well, you know, we might go tomorrow or, you know, tomorrow afternoon. And she was like, I know. I need to know. Is it twelve or 12:05 or, you know, 12:15? I need to plan.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26

pearls.text: When faced with a lose-lose situation between principles and compassion, the best approach is to keep to your principle but trust the Holy Spirit for every patient, every time, to make a good decision.
pearls.verbatim: The best way must be the hardest way. Was to have a principle, obviously keep to my principle, but trust the Holy Spirit, every patient, every person, every time to make a good decision.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.applies_to: missionary or clinical settings with conflicting demands
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26

pearls.text: Formulas give us control and make us feel certain we are doing the right thing, but they can prevent us from relying on the Holy Spirit for moment-by-moment decisions.
pearls.verbatim: I wanted a formula. A formula would have made it easier for me, and it would put me in control. And I could always be certain I was doing the right thing.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.applies_to: anyone in leadership or clinical practice
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26

pearls.text: There is pressure on doctors to be sure, but historical examples (like malaria being thought to come from bad air) show that medical certainty can be overturned.
pearls.verbatim: they were teaching him in medical school that malaria had to do with a mosquito. And he went home to his grandfather and told him that, and his grandfather just said, no. No. No. No. No. You know, that is crazy. A mosquito. You know? And and we all know malaria comes from bad air.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26

pearls.text: Biblical risk is obedience in uncertainty; it is not a risk if you know how it will turn out.
pearls.verbatim: biblical risk, I think this was John Piper who said this, is actually obedience in uncertainty. That's what a risk is. It's not a risk if you know how it's gonna turn out.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26

pearls.text: Abraham obeyed and went, even though he did not know where he was going; he obeyed without knowing the endpoint or outcome.
pearls.verbatim: Abraham. He moved out, he obeyed, and went, even though he did not know where he was going. He didn't have the final instructions. He obeyed without knowing the endpoint, without knowing the outcome.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26

pearls.text: Trust means being so certain of some things (or someone) that we can move forward even if uncertain about other things.
pearls.verbatim: trust means being so certain of some things or someone, maybe better say someone, that we can move forward even if uncertain in other things.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26

pearls.text: We can have peace and trust even amidst uncertainties because God knows the way and is with us, like the shepherd who knew the way to the village.
pearls.verbatim: But he knew the way, and he was with me. And so I could be at peace. And in that wonderful sense, we have a good shepherd who is with us. And even if we don't know the way, he knows the way. And he is guaranteed to never leave us nor forsake us.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26

pearls.text: Even Jesus on earth lived with some uncertainty, as He said about judgment day: 'but about that day or hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven nor the Son.'
pearls.verbatim: And then even Jesus, speaking of judgment day, he he said, but about that day or hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven nor the sun. So even Jesus himself on Earth lived with some uncertainty.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Lewis Sutton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26

pearls.text: For dacryostenosis, apply light downward pressure over the lacrimal sac 3, 5 times, about three times daily, and have parents do this at home.
pearls.verbatim: you kind of put light pressure kind of in this area and do downward pressure. You do that three to five times about three times daily of that type of pressure, and you have the parents do that.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: Leukocoria should be higher on your differential; it can be retinoblastoma even if cataracts look similar.
pearls.verbatim: if you have leukocoria, that should be higher on your differential.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: If you see no red reflex (leukocoria), call ophthalmology right away and get the patient seen urgently.
pearls.verbatim: the basic takeaway is if you see no red reflex, call ophthalmology right away and get them in right away.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.applies_to: any child with absent red reflex
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: Pain with eye movements is a key feature distinguishing orbital cellulitis from preseptal cellulitis.
pearls.verbatim: Pain with eye movements is key.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: For bacterial conjunctivitis, antibiotic eye drops can help symptoms resolve a little sooner, but it usually self-resolves within five to seven days either way.
pearls.verbatim: It sounds like antibiotic eye drops can help the symptoms to resolve a little sooner, but usually, it self resolves after, like, within five to seven days either way.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: If a patient is a contact lens user, antibiotic eye drops must include pseudomonas coverage.
pearls.verbatim: If there... The patient is a contact user, they do need pseudomonas coverage with their eye drops.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.applies_to: contact lens users with bacterial conjunctivitis
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: Red flags requiring ophthalmology referral: loss of vision, photophobia, decreased extraocular motility, pain with eye movement.
pearls.verbatim: if there is loss of vision, photophobia, decreased extraocular motility, pain with eye movement, then they should just go to ophthalmology.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: A stye is acute onset and painful; a chalazion is not as painful. A stye, if inflammation goes down, can become a chalazion.
pearls.verbatim: styes usually are more acute onset and are painful, whereas... they're not chalazion as much with pain.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: In adults with chalazion, doxycycline is often given because it gets penetration.
pearls.verbatim: In adults, especially, they usually give doxycycline because they get penetration.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: For corneal abrasion, topical antibiotics are very important no matter what, and they change depending on whether or not the patient is wearing contacts.
pearls.verbatim: Topical antibiotics are very important no matter what for these patients, and it changes depend on what... Depending on whether or not they're wearing contacts.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: For corneal abrasion, if not healing by three to four days, send to ophthalmology; better to send by one to two days and have follow-up within 24 to 48 hours.
pearls.verbatim: I know it says if the abrasion is not healing by three to four days, probably better to send them by one to two days and have follow-up within twenty four to forty eight hours.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Swan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25

pearls.text: When a patient in the hospital has an unclear problem, examine them thoroughly from top to bottom, flip them over, look everywhere, not just a quick med refill check.
pearls.verbatim: And then you get a patient in the hospital, and it's like, what the heck is going on? And you, like, examine everything. You're, like, flipping them over. You're like, I never flipped over a patient in the ear. You know, we're looking back there, looking for everything.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on Abiding in Christ

pearls.text: Be honest and open about your sins and struggles with God and trusted others; this leads to growth and healing, as seen in the speaker's marriage improvement.
pearls.verbatim: it's where I'm sinful at, and I need help. And same thing as, like, you know, truly today, being willing to be honest and open, it's like, our marriage is the best it has been.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on Abiding in Christ

pearls.text: When God asks you to produce wine in your life, He is really asking you to be faithful and fill the jars with water; He does the miracle.
pearls.verbatim: Jesus is like, hey. Just go go fill it with water. Go do... Go just be faithful and do this.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on Abiding in Christ

pearls.text: When you feel like you are just throwing water on a patient, a small prayer or a brief mention of faith, trust that God can turn that into wine, into life in them.
pearls.verbatim: But that's the trust and hope too. It's like when we are faithful to those things, it is God that does that. We're just throwing this little bit off, and it's like, it's wine inside of them. It's life.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on Abiding in Christ

pearls.text: Even small, seemingly insignificant acts of faithfulness, like pouring water, are used by God in amazing ways.
pearls.verbatim: And even if they're little things like that, like, pouring water in there, like, it's amazingly.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on Abiding in Christ

pearls.text: The most characteristic symptom of COPD is dyspnea, though chronic cough is often the first symptom.
pearls.verbatim: The chronic cough is typically the first symptom. The most characteristic is dyspnea,
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on COPD

pearls.text: Smoking accounts for 70% of COPD in high-income countries.
pearls.verbatim: So here in high income countries, seventy percent of causes is cigarette smoking.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on COPD

pearls.text: You cannot diagnose COPD without spirometry; clinical suspicion is not enough.
pearls.verbatim: you can say you have a suspicion for COPD, but you cannot diagnose them with COPD. So you must have spirometry to establish diagnosis.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on COPD

pearls.text: Diagnostic spirometry requires a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio less than 0.7.
pearls.verbatim: B b one FVC ratio less than point seven. Less than point seven. Excellent.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.applies_to: patients with clinical suspicion of COPD
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on COPD

pearls.text: Use the mMRC scale: grade 2 or higher (breathless when walking at a regular pace on level ground) indicates more severe symptoms.
pearls.verbatim: The marker that we're looking at is really grade two. So that's where we're of looking at more severe symptoms versus less severe symptoms.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on COPD

pearls.text: Use the mMRC question: 'Do you get more breathless than people your age when walking at a regular pace?' A positive answer indicates more severe symptoms.
pearls.verbatim: The question that you probably wanna ask people is this one, where you say, you know, if people the same age, so I get more breathless than I am, and I have to stop when I'm just doing kinda like a regular pace. So the positive for that, they have been more severe based on this scaling criteria.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on COPD

pearls.text: Use the CAT score: 10 points or more indicates more severe symptoms.
pearls.verbatim: 10 points or more is more severe symptoms.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on COPD

pearls.text: A moderate exacerbation is defined as one treated with steroids or antibiotics, not necessarily requiring hospitalization.
pearls.verbatim: Moderate too, just to let you know, is you are treated with steroids or antibiotics for an exacerbation. So I mean, doesn't necessarily mean hospitalization.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on COPD

pearls.text: To classify patients into GOLD groups A, B, or E, ask: 'Have you had exacerbations, been hospitalized, or needed steroids in the last year or two?'
pearls.verbatim: Really, all I gotta ask people is, have you had exacerbations, been hospitalized, or need steroids, general last year or two? And then you can use your symptoms to kind of classify them in a, b, or e.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on COPD

pearls.text: If high blood eosinophils or hospitalization despite LAMA/LABA combination, consider adding ICS.
pearls.verbatim: If high blood eosinophils are hospitalization despite your combo LAMA/LABA, consider Yes.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.applies_to: patients with COPD and high blood eosinophils or prior hospitalization
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on COPD

pearls.text: Pulmonary rehabilitation within 90 days of hospital discharge is associated with statistically significant reduced mortality.
pearls.verbatim: This has a systematic review. Really good. 190,000 patients. If they did it within ninety days of discharge from the hospital, associated with a statistically significant reduced mortality.
pearls.speaker: Dr. Tischler
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Tischler on COPD

pearls.text: Inhaled corticosteroids are indicated for patients with blood eosinophils >300 cells/µL, history of asthma, or recurrent exacerbations despite LAMA/LABA.
